3---tags/behaviorism-psychology.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology
Behaviorism Psychology
Details
In the first half of the 20th century, Behaviorism was the dominant school of thought in American psychology. Championed by figures like John B. Watson and B.F. Skinner, its core doctrine was that psychology should be the science of observable behavior, not of unobservable mental states like consciousness, thoughts, or feelings.
The central idea was that all complex behaviors could be built up from a few simple “atoms” of learning: classical and operant conditioning. This philosophy was rooted in empiricism—the belief that knowledge comes from experience and that an individual is shaped almost entirely by their environment and reinforcement history. It carried a democratic appeal: anyone could become anything, given the right environmental shaping.
However, Behaviorism ultimately proved to be an incomplete psychology. Its strict refusal to study internal mental life meant it could not address fundamental aspects of the human experience like consciousness, emotion, or subjective thought. Furthermore, it struggled to explain phenomena that pointed to innate biological preparedness, such as the rapid, seemingly instinctual acquisition of language in children. While the principles of association learning remain a critical part of psychology, the idea that they alone could explain all of human nature was shown to be too simplistic.

Evolutionary psychology is a relatively new approach that is ‘‘informed by the additional knowledge that evolutionary biology has to offer, in the expectation that understanding the process that designed the human mind will advance the discovery of its architecture’’ (Cosmides, Tooby, & Barkow, 1992, p. 3). Its central assumption is that all present-day humans have inherited from their prehistoric ancestors a standard collection of psychological mechanisms that facilitated survival and reproduction in ancestral times. Consequently, the goal of evolutionary psychology is to discover and understand the universal, or species-typical, architecture of the human mind and brain (Tooby & Cosmides, 1992).

6---full-notes/a-critique-of-charisma.title: A Critique of Charisma
6---full-notes/a-critique-of-charisma.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology sociology philosophy
A Critique of Charisma
Details
“The spectacle is not a collection of images; it is a social relation between people that is mediated by images.” - Guy Debord, The Society of The Spectacle
Imagine this, a teenage girl comes to high school for the first time. It is a novel experience for her, and so, naturally, she is quiet, perhaps a little awkward. Suddenly, a random dude comes up to her and charismatically engages with her, which makes her feel that he is inherently attractive. Subsequently, they become friends. Some time after, the girl feels like the more that she engages with him, the more differently the girl feels from her original conception - when she attempts to be emotionally vulnerable about her upbringing, he makes a completely inappropriate joke about how her parents “just couldn’t keep their hands off her”, even putting his arms around her to close off the moment fully. Eventually, she has enough of it and disconnects herself away from him, wondering about why she had even made the decision to be with him in the first place. Perhaps it is because she was never engaging with the actual person but rather a mere projection of said person in a social setting. This is precisely what Debord’s framework illuminates - the fact that a social image that someone constructs of themselves inherently has nothing underneath when genuine relation is demanded.
And yet, the charismatic individual is rarely the one accountable. Virtually in every social context, charisma is an admirable quality, a sign of social intelligence and something that should be trained. For the quiet individuals, they are instead told to “come out of their shell” or “work on their social skills.” Never once are their needs and personality actually understood and validated.
To fully engage ourselves into the discussion and critique on charisma, we must first understand what charisma actually stands for. From my point of view, charisma is not a trait, but a skill based in behavioral mechanisms that is treated as a simulation of a person rather than expression of it. And so, it is a set of skills rooted in managing expressions and impressions, eliciting certain responses from others. The problem does not come from the existence of the mechanism itself, but rather the gap between the image and substance of the person utilizing it that the problem actually roots.
Perhaps to go about this in a more personal way, the biggest problem I have with charisma is the excessive relational value that it contains. In this sense, I mean the inherent nature of charisma allows its user to get themselves out of heavy, difficult situations when what they should do is sit with it and try to emotionally engage with the very factors that make those situations hard - because through these predicaments they can develop their own identity and internal values. I believe this is so because emotionally difficult situations by nature forces the individual to confront their deeper discomfort, whether it be unresolved trauma or past emotional pressures. And so these individuals never actually face the emotional problems because they can escape so easily with charisma. Furthermore, this prompts them to habitually avoid similar social confrontations that can have the same effect. Conclusively, charisma works against personal development not only by allowing the person to have an out to a challenging situation but also encouraging them to do so in all future instances.
The second point that I want to shortly address is the amount of social power it possesses - which is constitutive of the moral problem that charisma presents. Coming back to the aforementioned example of the couple, or now, ex-couple. In said situation, it is highly unlikely that the charismatic individual would have ever been seen as what caused the relationship to fall out despite the severe lack of objective information that anyone can have. Perhaps the girl might even be shunned and rumored to be what she is not (as I have argued elsewhere). This subsequently comes round to the points about morality made in said essay: that people are morally responsible for wrongly interpreting someone and harming them, even if the ways they do so are invisible. But to extend on that point in this situation, the responsibility now also stands in the other individual - the charismatic dude. Now, why does that person have said accountability ? After all, they are in no way responsible for the observers’ harmful and downright morally wrong views on their ex-partner. I agree with the point made in the previous sentence, but I still believe that the individual now bears moral responsibility due to how their charismatic simulation has conjured a false social image of reality onto the girl that others interpreted as real. Due to the manufactured personality that he has differing so much from who he fundamentally is, he is now morally obliged to disclose said gap because of how people are making real judgements on the basis of it.
For the reasons stated above, it is, from my own belief, enough as a criticism towards charisma and how society interprets it. Of course, the essay is in no way extensive in its philosophizing, defending, or clarifying and connecting the points as the aim is only to bring up certain issues that charisma as a social concept presents and maybe push some to think about it more deeply.

Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience
A More Complex Neuron
Details
The neurons that Dale laws instated were all about how each had one neurotransmitter to put out, in all of its axon terminals. This allowed for easy classifications like “serotonergic,” “dopaminergic,” and so on, suggesting a straightforward signaling system. But of course this was disproved by the works of Jerry Letvin about co-transmission. It is now understood that each neuron can release different transmitters, packaged together in the same vesicle. These may have different characteristics, functions, and so on.
The second principle, Dale’s first law, is concerned with action potential. A basically “all-or-nothing” principle that every axon terminal will fire out neurotransmitter. Again, Jerry Lettvin disproved this, by demonstrating branch point failure. This is a phenomenon where the action potential does not travel down every branch. Combining with the above, this meant they can choose which neurotransmitters to be released.

6---full-notes/a-new-world's-theory.title: A New World's Theory
6---full-notes/a-new-world's-theory.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology philosophy 3 - Tags/environment
A New World’s Theory
Details
As the mid-20th century unfolded, the intricate, shadow-filled cathedrals of Freudian and Kleinian psychoanalysis began to feel alien to the sunnier optimism of post-war America. Theirs was a vision of humanity forged in the anxieties of “Old World” Europe: a self at war with its own drives, haunted by primal aggressions, and forever retracing the tragedies of its earliest relationships. Into this landscape stepped Carl Rogers, a figure who did not simply revise the old theories but offered a profoundly different answer to the question of what it means to be human. Drawing on a uniquely American philosophical heritage and integrating fresh insights from his contemporaries, Rogers proposed a revolutionary idea: that constant, unconditional acceptance was not a form of indulgence, but the very engine of personal growth.
At its core, Rogers’ work was a therapeutic expression of American Transcendentalism. The defiant self-reliance of Ralph Waldo Emerson and the quiet integrity of Henry David Thoreau flowed through his theories. Where Freud saw a caldron of repressed desires, Rogers, like Emerson, saw an innate, organismic wisdom—an “actualizing tendency” pushing every individual toward growth and fulfillment, much like a plant pushes toward the sun. This was a radical reframing of the human spirit. The goal of therapy was no longer to excavate and interpret a damaged past, but to create a nurturing environment where the client’s inherent potential could finally blossom. The problem was not a flawed interior, but a hostile or conditional exterior that had stunted this natural growth.
This “New World” perspective was powerfully bolstered by new knowledge emerging from the fringes of psychoanalysis itself. Harry Stack Sullivan’s interpersonal theory was a crucial bridge. Sullivan had shifted the focus from the “intrapsychic” to the “interactional,” arguing that our personality and its disorders are forged between people, not just within one person. He demonstrated that we are fundamentally social beings, our sense of self constructed through a lifetime of seeking approval and avoiding disapproval from others. Rogers took this revolutionary idea and placed it at the heart of the therapeutic encounter. If relationships could wound, a new kind of relationship could heal.
Rogers’ central concept of Unconditional Positive Regard is the logical conclusion of this interpersonal view. He argued that most human suffering stems from a “condition of worth”—the implicit message we receive from parents, teachers, and society that we are only lovable and acceptable if we think, feel, and act in certain ways. This forces us to build a false self, burying our authentic experiences for fear of rejection. The therapist’s role, then, was to offer the opposite: a constant, unwavering acceptance. This was not a passive stance. It was an active, powerful, and deeply challenging practice of “prizing” the client as a person of worth, regardless of their feelings, choices, or behaviors.
This climate of acceptance was nurtured by a cohort of innovative, and often rebellious, therapists who were breaking free from rigid doctrine. The iconoclastic work of figures like Murray Bowen, who revealed the family as an interlocking emotional system, reinforced the idea that individuals cannot be understood in isolation. The radical creativity of Milton Erickson, who met each client in their unique reality, and the confrontational authenticity of Carl Whitaker, who used his own personality as a therapeutic tool, were part of the same zeitgeist. They all shared a deep trust in the client’s capacity to heal themselves, if only the therapist could create the right conditions.
In synthesizing these streams—transcendentalist faith in the individual, Sullivan’s interpersonal focus, and the field’s growing emphasis on authentic relationship—Rogers created his tripod of therapeutic change: Unconditional Positive Regard, Empathy (a deep, non-judgmental listening), and Congruence (the therapist’s own genuineness). He believed that when a person is truly seen, heard, and accepted without condition, their need for defensiveness falls away. For the first time, they can look at their own incongruities—the gap between their real self and their carefully constructed facade—without fear. In the safety of the therapist’s welcoming gaze, they begin to accept themselves, and in that self-acceptance, the stalled process of growth restarts, powered from within. This was more than a new technique; it was a democratic, hopeful, and quintessentially American vision of the soul’s potential for becoming.

6---full-notes/a-single-cognitive-tool-c.title: A Single Cognitive Tool Can Solve Different Problems
6---full-notes/a-single-cognitive-tool-c.content:
Status: baby
Tags: Cognitive Psychology Fodor’s mind model
The reusage of cognitive solutions
Details
Shapiro and Epstein (1998) argue against the idea that every adaptive problem requires a unique cognitive mechanism. Their position rests on two main points: They claim the error argument mistakenly identifies the cognitive process (the tool) with the task it performs. A single screwdriver can tighten (turn right) and loosen (turn left). The tool is the same, but the use is different. Therefore, a single cognitive process could solve different problems. Natural selection is economical. It is more likely to recruit or co-opt existing cognitive abilities for new purposes than to evolve entirely new ones from scratch for every novel problem. Their conclusion is that there isn’t a one-to-one relationship between adaptive problems and cognitive solutions.

6---full-notes/a-society-beyond-justice.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology morals philosophy
A Society Beyond Justice
Details
Marx famously stated that “all science would be superfluous if the appearance of things and the essence of things were to directly coincide.” In a capitalist system, economic science (like the Labor Theory of Value) is necessary to pierce the ideological illusions of the free market and reveal the hidden essence of exploitation. A “full communist society,” therefore, is structurally defined as a society where appearance and essence finally coincide. It is a society completely devoid of ideological consciousness, false delusions, and hidden surplus value extraction.
In a fully communistic society, the means in production are held in common and social labor is applied consciously according to a visible, democratic plan. The means of production here is merely a metric to balance the needs of the community and determine individual consumption shares. Because the economy is consciously planned and administered by everyone, there are no hidden forces ruling over the populace. Because class domination is abolished, the very need for juridical superstructures—like political “justice” and liberal “rights”—evaporates. Instead of fighting over rights to mitigate exploitation, the society operates organically on principles of the “good,” emphasizing autonomy, self-development, and meaningful work.

6---full-notes/a-teenager's-moral-respon.title: A Teenager's Moral Responsibility
6---full-notes/a-teenager's-moral-respon.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy morals academia
A Teenager’s Moral Responsibility
Details
“I have used the word ‘attention,’ which I borrow from Simone Weil, to express the idea of a just and loving gaze directed upon an individual reality.” — Iris Murdoch
Introduction
A man walks into a room full of people who are strangers to him. He is quiet, perhaps a little bit awkward — the normative discomfort of navigating unfamiliar social terrain. Then, someone in the room decides, based on absolutely no certain information at all, that he is strange. Perhaps even unsettling. This judgement was made in seconds, almost unconsciously, and from that moment onward, a framework is erected around him that he does not know exists, cannot see, and perhaps most damningly, cannot do anything about. When he finally tries to make a joke, it is “trying too hard” or “conforming.” When he is kind, he is “suspicious” and “manipulative.” When he eventually withdraws from the situation due to his conscience having noticed the distinct feeling of being uninvited or unliked from the group, his withdrawal becomes the final confirmation: See? There was always something wrong with that guy. The architecture is now complete, and it is, by design, unfalsifiable — because every piece of evidence, no matter how contradictory, is metabolized into the same conclusion.
This is no rare occurrence. In fact, it is one of the most common and destructive patterns in social life in general. A woman is labeled “difficult” in her workplace on the basis of a single disagreement; and from that point on, her confidence is now “aggression,” her thoroughness is “controlling,” and her eventual frustration at being perpetually misread is taken as a fact that the people viewing her have always been right. A young man is rumored — perhaps by someone with a grudge, perhaps by someone who simply dislikes him — to have done something terrible; the rumor metastasizes, and suddenly his entire history is rewritten through the lens of the accusation. His friendliness becomes “predatory.” His protest becomes “defensiveness.” His silence becomes “guilt.” His life, as he had it, is now socially over — just because someone decided what he was.
This raises a particular question that I believe is too frequently ignored and passed on despite how important it is in our everyday lives: do we bear moral responsibility for how we perceive other people?
My answer is an unequivocal yes. In the following paragraphs, I will substantiate my claim through arguing that the act of perceiving another person — of constructing a narrative about who they are, what they intend, and what they deserve — is not simply an amoral psychological process but holds moral responsibility in and of itself, and that it carries genuine obligations for which we can be held genuinely accountable. The argument will proceed in four stages: first, I will examine the psychological mechanisms underlying the phenomenon and how it is definitively cruel; second, I will argue, through the concept of culpable ignorance and Daniel Kahneman’s framework of dual-process cognition, that these mechanisms, though automatic, are not involuntary, and that their operation does not absolve us of moral responsibility but in fact deepens it; third, drawing on the work of Iris Murdoch, I will argue that moral attention — the effort that one exerts to be able to see and understand the other person — is not merely a peripheral virtue but a foundational ethic; and finally, I will contend that the failure to exercise this attention constitutes a distinct and undertheorized form of moral harm — one that I will describe, following Miranda Fricker, as a kind of epistemic injustice — before addressing the deeper question of why people so reliably abdicate moral responsibility for the perceptions they construct.
The Architecture of Bias
The psychological mechanisms that are involved in this context are particularly well-documented in social psychology but are insufficiently examined in their moral dimensions. But to understand how a single impression can calcify into an unshakeable belief about another person’s character, one must understand the very machinery that produces it — specifically, heuristics.
Heuristics, as known in social psychology, are cognitive shortcuts. They are fast, automatic, and designed by our minds to be useful as they allow us to deal with our daily complicated social positions without being paralyzed by deliberation at every single instance. The thing is, that is exactly why they fail in person perception — they are designed for efficiency, not accuracy.
The most relevant heuristic here is what Kahneman and Tversky term the “representativeness heuristic:” the tendency to judge something by how closely it resembles the example that we conjure in our minds rather than the individual features of it. When using this on an object, like something that looks like a chair, it is fair to assume, perhaps even necessary to do so. But in truly seeing a person, the implication is flipped upon its head due to the fundamental difference in these situations. When we encounter another human being, the representativeness heuristic prompts us to perceive the person through preexisting categories of people in our minds rather than as a living, breathing, unique individual. The man in the opening example is quiet and awkward; the heuristic matches him to the prototype of “strange” or “unsettling,” and from that point forward, the cognitive machinery does the rest.
What the heuristic initiates, confirmation bias completes. Once the initial categorization is done, a second mechanism takes over — one that blocks off all future information from making any meaningful difference to the perception of the person. Confirmation bias makes people search for, interpret, and recall information in ways that confirm their preexisting beliefs. Contradictory evidence may not only be ignored but wrongly interpreted. If the hypothesis is that someone is abusive/cold, then their warmth/care becomes “performative” or “manipulative.” If the hypothesis is that someone is dishonest, then their transparency becomes “calculated.” Every attempt that a person could make to demonstrate any truths is subsequently absorbed back into the framework to prove it is right.
Effectively, the person is trapped in an epistemic prison that they themselves cannot actually do anything about: a constructed reality in which the person being perceived is trapped inside a narrative they did not author, cannot access, and are structurally prevented from escaping. Not only that, the prison itself is fundamentally self-reinforcing, as every future situation only serves to contribute to its walls.
The crucial feature of this prison is its unfalsifiability. In the philosophy of science, Karl Popper argued that a theory which cannot, even in principle, be proven wrong is not a genuine theory at all — it is a dogma. We can apply the same logic here: the framework works upon the subjective interpretation of the person only, and so any evidence that counts against it is merely reinterpreted to support the hypothesis. It is no longer a framework but rather a conscious projection of a stereotype. And yet the observer experiences it as objective reality. As simply seeing what is there.
Culpable Ignorance and the Obligation to Think
It is possible now for one to anticipate a basic response: that because these mechanisms are automatic and uncontrollable in our minds, the person who is performing these perceptions cannot reasonably be held morally responsible for their consequences. You cannot blame someone for a process they did not choose and cannot control. This is, in essence, an appeal to involuntariness: heuristics are reflexes of the mind, and we do not hold people responsible for their reflexes.
The reply, however seductive it is, is inherently wrong. The objection is as follows: as heuristics are automatic, they are therefore beyond our control — that their automaticity places them in the same moral category as a sneeze or a flinch. But this obviously does not follow. The question was never about whether the heuristic was automatic or not, but rather about whether we are beings who are capable of becoming aware, of noticing that a snap categorization has occurred, of interrogating whether it is fair — and we are. That capacity for awareness is not incidental to our cognition. It is one of its defining features.
A heuristic judgement is merely the beginning of the process of understanding a person — yet we treat it as the endpoint and do not recognize the nature of choices that we have when performing it. The judgement lands in consciousness: this person is strange, this person is threatening, something is off. At that moment, two paths are available. One can accept the output uncritically, allow it to settle into conviction, and proceed to interpret all subsequent information through its lens. Or, one can pause, register the judgement as a judgement rather than a fact, and ask what evidence it is actually based on, holding it provisionally while attending to the person in front of them. The first path requires no effort; the second requires considerable effort. But it is precisely that moral effort that makes the paths a moral choice rather than a moral inevitability.
So, the point is, the automaticity of heuristics does not grant them authority. A process that we have the capacity to notice, question, and override is not something that gets to be treated as a fact just because it came easily and quickly. To treat it as though it does — to allow the heuristic output to harden into settled perception without ever subjecting it to scrutiny — is to make a decision, even if it does not feel like one. It is the decision to let a cognitive shortcut, designed for efficiency rather than accuracy, serve as the finality of who another human being is. And that is not a decision one gets to make without morally paying for it.
This is where the concept of culpable ignorance becomes decisive. In discussions of moral responsibility, culpable ignorance refers to the ignorance for which one is morally responsible — not because they chose to be ignorant, but because they could have known better and failed to take the reasonable steps to do so. A drunk driver is not condemned because he intended to kill a person, but because he decided to drink, decided to drive, and failed to account for the worst possible situation happening despite the risks of his prior actions. The incapacity he had at the critical moment does not absolve him from the responsibility because that incapacity was culpable.
The same logic applies to the situation mentioned above. A person who places a human into a category and never revisits their perception of the human being, allowing confirmation bias to harden an initial impression without ever stopping to test it and construct a more accurate interpretation of the person, is not just making a cognitive error but committing culpable ignorance. They could have paused. They could have questioned whether their initial categorization was fair. They could have sought out disconfirming evidence, or taken seriously the other person’s own testimony about who they are. They are capable adults who can use their System 2, as is the case for any neurotypical adult, and yet they did not. Not because they could not, but because it was easier not to. Because the heuristic judgement felt right, and interrogating it would have required a level of effort, humility, and the uncomfortable possibility of discovering that they had been unjust.
And so the argument is formed: heuristics may explain how the failure of perception happens, but they do not absolve anyone from the moral responsibility they bear, according to the principle of culpable ignorance. Because the mechanism, though automatic, is not uncontrollable, and the failure to control it, when another person’s selfhood, mental health, and social relationships are at stake, is a failure for which you can and should be held to account.
Murdoch and the Ethics of Attention
To further the framework, we must now consider Iris Murdoch’s moral philosophy, as Murdoch provides the positive account of what the moral obligation identified above actually looks like in practice.
Murdoch argued that morality is not primarily a matter of action and choice but also one of perception and attention. One’s moral life, as Murdoch would have it, begins not at the moment of decision but long before — in the quality of regard we direct toward the world and, above all, toward other people. After all, “I have used the word ‘attention,’ which I borrow from Simone Weil, to express the idea of a just and loving gaze directed upon an individual reality.”
The defining word in this quote is “just.” Murdoch is not speaking of a sentimental or uncritical gaze but one that is disciplined, honest, and oriented toward seeing what is actually there rather than whatever our ego, preconceptions, and anxieties want us to find. This fair perception is something that she considers to be the foundational moral act — not merely because it leads to good actions, though it does, but because it is itself a form of moral goodness. To make the effort to see a person clearly, to resist every single psychological pull that one feels and to know them for who they actually are — is what love fundamentally means. As she writes elsewhere: “Love is the extremely difficult realization that something other than oneself is real.”
Murdoch’s term here for this practice is unselfing: the deliberate turning of one’s consciousness away from the self’s concerns, projections, and habitual categorizations and toward the reality of the other. It is fundamentally the act of overriding heuristic perception to effortfully understand and attend to the person. She arrives at the same point that Kahneman does, that our default mode of perception is reductive and self-serving, and that genuine moral perception requires the sustained, often uncomfortable effort of moving beyond it.
Murdoch illustrates this principle with a famous example. She imagines a mother-in-law, M, who finds her daughter-in-law, D, pert and juvenile, “lacking in dignity and refinement.” M’s perception of D is colored by prejudice — perhaps class-based, perhaps temperamental. In the terms of this essay, M has applied the representativeness heuristic — she has matched D to a prototype (“vulgar,” “common”) and is now perceiving her through that category rather than as an individual. But M, recognizing that her perception may be unjust, undertakes the difficult inner work of revising it. She engages, in Kahneman’s terms, System 2. She does not simply change her behavior toward D; she changes her way of seeing D. Over time, through sustained moral effort — through unselfing — M comes to see D as “not vulgar but refreshingly simple, not undignified but spontaneous.” No outward action has changed. D has not changed. What has changed is the quality of M’s attention — and this, Murdoch insists, is a genuine and significant moral achievement.
And this therefore exemplifies that the reversal of this act is also a reversal of moral success — a moral failing. M had the capacity to revise her perception, and she did. If she had refused to use her abilities to reinterpret and see D for who they really were, then she would not merely have been mistaken about D, but also culpably mistaken.
The Epistemic Prison and Its Injuries
Finally, Miranda Fricker’s concept of epistemic injustice provides a framework for understanding the specific harm inflicted by the mechanisms described above. There are two key forms that she addresses: testimonial injustice, in which prejudice causes a hearer to give a deflated level of credibility to a speaker’s word; and hermeneutical injustice, in which a gap in collective interpretive resources puts someone at an unfair disadvantage when it comes to making sense of their own social experiences.
Of course, both of these concepts have been demonstrated in the cases I have presented. When a person has been imprisoned within a false narrative, any attempts they may make on their own behalf — to explain, to correct, to say that is not who I am — are systematically discredited. Any defenses they have conjured for themselves have already been accounted for: their protest is “defensiveness,” their explanation is “manipulation,” their frustration is “proof” that the original judgment was correct. Despite having every piece of information one could possibly need to evaluate who they are, the speaker is fundamentally disallowed from doing so because their reasoning and words are now treated as untrustworthy.
But epistemic injustice only actually accounts for constituting the harm. The actual pain comes from consistently being misperceived and denied the ability to defend oneself and to prove oneself. Or, in other words, from being denied the very dignity of being treated as a human being. Not a saint, not a paragon of virtue, just a person whose actions are granted the deserved presumption of good faith that most people receive without ever having to earn it. Most people move through the world with this presumption intact. When they smile at someone, it is taken as friendliness. When they offer help, it is taken as kindness. When they are quiet, it is taken as quietness. They are, in other words, allowed to simply be — to act and to have those actions received at something close to face value, with the charitable interpretation that social life depends upon but rarely acknowledges.
The imprisoned individual has been stripped of this presumption entirely. For them, no matter what they do, they will never be faithfully interpreted. Every single gesture and word passes through the distorting lens of the framework before it reaches the perceiver, and what arrives bears little resemblance to the input. They cannot be kind, because their kindness is “manipulation.” They cannot be honest, because their honesty is “a performance.” They cannot be hurt, because their pain is “guilt” or “self-pity.” They are, in every sense possible, not seen — not because they are physically invisible but metaphysically so; the very person standing in front of the observer and what the observer actually sees are fundamentally different human beings.
There is a particular cruelty that deserves to be named. The cruelty of being punished not for what you have done but for what someone has decided you are. Yet, they are forced to carry the weight and meaning of a version of themselves that they had no say in, that they do not recognize. The weight is not dramatic; the weight is not singular. It is the cumulative weight of a thousand small interactions between others. The psychological toll of this is not incidental. It compounds with the number of interactions; it makes people begin questioning their own actions, their own words, focusing on what went wrong and what made people think differently about them, not realizing that there is nothing happening there. Because the reaction was never to them. It was to the construct. Over time, this can lead the person to doubt themselves, and it would take extraordinary psychological resilience not to begin wondering whether they might be right. Whether perhaps you are the person they seem to see. Whether your own understanding of yourself — your intentions, your character, the reasons behind your actions — might be less reliable than the consensus of those around you. The epistemic prison does not merely trap you and deny you the understanding you deserve; it begins to make the person within it doubt the very truth of who they know themselves to be.
The damage does not stop at the individual, though; it radiates outward, into the social world around them, poisoning relationships that the person inside the prison had no hand in contaminating. Friends begin to hear things. Not accusations, but merely impressions. A raised eyebrow. A careful tone. I don’t know, there’s just something about him. And now the friend is placed in an impossible position. They know this person, deeply, and their own experience contradicts what the world around them is saying, yet they have to weigh that against the social weight of the narrative. They may risk being considered as an extension of the doubted, of the shunned; they also have to fight against the issue of conformity, risk losing other friends, even though they understand and know, from direct personal experience, that it is wrong.
Some friends may resist. They hold to what they know, they defend the person, they refuse to let a framework constructed by others override the reality of their own experience. But it does not come without cost — because to defend someone who has been seen as a risk is, in and of itself, a risk. Why are you defending him? What does that say about you? The social penalty for dissenting from a consensus — even an unjust one — is real and significant, and not everyone is willing to pay it. And so, gradually, the circle contracts. People who once felt warmly toward the person begin to pull away — not because their own experience has changed, but because the social cost is too high. This comes back to bite the subject as well, as they cannot comprehend why their friends would suddenly do so, which adds to all the other mechanisms contributing to their self-doubt.
But just because these injuries are abstract, are unseen, are not physical does not mean they are justifiable in any sense at all. And so, treating them as though they are not harmful only because they are not recognized as such is a foundational error.
Conclusion
None of this is to say that first impressions are always wrong, or that every single negative judgement of another person is a projection. Some people are dishonest. Some are dangerous. Some are evil. The capacity that allows us to make assessments of character has obvious adaptive and social value. Exercising them is not, in itself, morally problematic.
What is problematic, however, is the refusal to hold said assessments accountable — to treat them as settled truths, to close oneself off from disconfirming evidence, to deny every piece of information that goes against their narrative. What is morally problematic, above all, is the abdication of moral responsibility for the act of perception itself — the comfortable fiction that we are merely seeing what is there, when in truth we are, at every moment, choosing what to see.
Murdoch understood that the moral life is a matter of the quality of attention we direct toward the world in the ordinary course of living — the slow, unglamorous, largely invisible work of seeing other people for who they truly are. It is difficult; it requires humility; it demands that we acknowledge our own limitations, which requires, perhaps, courage of the highest level.
But that is not to say that it is supererogatory; it is still what we owe to one another. Not as charity, not as a virtue, but as a basic requirement of moral life. To be a moral agent is to both act rightly and see rightly — or, at the very least, not act upon incomplete and interpretive information. The philosophical frameworks to understand why we must are well-established. What remains is the willingness — the moral willingness — to use them. To reject those premises, to reject those frameworks and settle into distorted perception is not merely a cognitive error. It is a moral failing at the most fundamental level. It is a failure of attention, a failure of justice, and, in Murdoch’s deepest sense, a failure of love.
The people we misperceive do not disappear. They continue to exist and endure every single narrative from every single person around them, something that they cannot escape. And so, the least we owe them, and to our own morals, is the willingness to look again.

6---full-notes/a-note-on-popular-science.title: A note on popular science
6---full-notes/a-note-on-popular-science.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading science
A note on popular science
Details
•	Definition: Popular science works are books or articles meant for a general audience, not specialists . They explain scientific ideas in simpler terms.
•	Simplified Content: Such works intentionally omit dense parts of science. They usually report results of experiments instead of detailing them, and they avoid heavy mathematics . This makes them more accessible if you know some basics.
•	Reporter Filtering: Many articles (e.g. in Scientific American) are written or edited by journalists. If they do a good job, readers benefit. If not, we have “almost no recourse” , so be alert to oversimplifications.
•	Active Reading Needed: Even though pop science skips tough bits, it’s not easy reading. Short pieces on DNA or climate still demand full attention . Identify terms, outline arguments, and understand the content before critiquing – the usual active-reading steps apply with particular force .
•	Examples & Significance: Good pop-science books connect theory to life. For instance, Barry Commoner’s The Closing Circle links environmental science to everyday issues (air, pollution, resources) . Barnett’s The Universe and Dr. Einstein and Whitehead’s Introduction to Mathematics similarly demystify big ideas, showing why they matter today.
Takeaways / Heuristics
•	Treat popular science like a guided tour: it’s simplified, but you still need to think. Read actively – take notes, outline the logic, and keep questioning (you need full attention) .
•	Leverage what you know: basic science background makes popular explanations click more easily.
•	Be skeptical of shortcuts: reporters may gloss over complexity . Check surprising claims or analogies.
•	Focus on ideas, not details. Aim to grasp the core concept and its significance, rather than the technical minutiae left out.

6---full-notes/a-note-on-theology.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading philosophy
A note on theology
Details
There are two kinds of this, natural and dogmatic. Natural theology is a branch of philosophy; it is the last chapter, as if it were, in metaphysics. If you ask, for example, whether causation is an endless process, whether everything is caused, you may find yourself, if you answer in the affirmative, involved in an infinite regress. Therefore you may have to posit some originating cause that is not itself caused. Aristotle called this uncaused cause an unmoved mover. You could give it other names—you could even say that it was merely another name for God—but the point is that you would have arrived at the conception by the unaided effort-the natural working—of your mind.
Dogmatic theology differs from philosophy in that its first principles are articles of faith adhered to by the communicants of some religion. A work of dogmatic theology always depends upon dogmas and the authority of a church that proclaims them.
If you are not of the faith, if you do not belong to the church, you can nevertheless read such a theological book well by treating its dogmas with the same respect you treat the assumptions of a mathematician you treat the assumptions of a mathematician. An article of faith though is not something that the faithful assume. Faith is the most certain form of knowledge, not a tentative opinion for those who have it.

Tags: Zettelkasten workflow writing
A process to make balanced notes
Details
To break out of this, we need a good system, and the mere necessities of the workflow will help us work virtuously without being more virtuous. First, we must turn the whole writing process on its head, and secondly, we find information indiscriminately regardless of what argument it supports.
This is the bottom-up approach of opening ourselves up to insights. We will be able to focus on the most insightful ideas we see and we can welcome the surprises that it may bring without it jeopardizing our progress, and even better, bringing it forward. And to do so we must separate the writing process properly, verify if the contents that we reproduced are true or not and lastly find relevance and connect them all together.
The slip-box allows us to be selective but only in what is relevant to a discussion in it, as it opens up connections within the slip-box. Everything can contribute to its development, contradictions, connections, even the questioning of ideas as well as the differentiation of an argument.
After that we can take a step back to look at what we have developed and only then can we make out what conclusion could be drawn from it. Plus, it is in fact a lot more interesting to write from a lively discussion with many pros and cons than from a collection of one-sided and seemingly fitting notes.

6---full-notes/a-summary-of-effective-le.title: A summary of effective learning
6---full-notes/a-summary-of-effective-le.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning
A summary of effective learning
Details
Practice at retrieving new knowledge or skill from memory is a potent tool for learning and durable retention. This is true for anything the brain is asked to remember and call up again in the future—facts, complex concepts, problem-solving techniques, motor skills.
Effortful retrieval makes for stronger learning and retention. We’re easily seduced into believing that learning is better when it’s easier, but the research shows the opposite: when the mind has to work, learning sticks better. The greater the effort to retrieve learning, provided that you succeed, the more that learning is strengthened by retrieval. After an initial test, delaying subsequent retrieval practice is more potent for reinforcing retention than immediate practice, because delayed retrieval requires more effort.
Repeated retrieval not only makes memories more durable but produces knowledge that can be retrieved more readily, in more varied settings, and applied to a wider variety of problems.
While cramming can produce better scores on an immediate exam, the advantage quickly fades because there is much greater forgetting after rereading than after retrieval practice. The benefits of retrieval practice are long-term.
“Simply including one test (retrieval practice) in a class yields a large improvement in final exam scores, and gains continue to increase as the frequency of classroom testing increases.
Testing doesn’t need to be initiated by the instructor. Students can practice retrieval anywhere; no quizzes in the classroom are necessary. Think flashcards—the way second graders learn the multiplication tables can work just as well for learners at any age to quiz themselves on anatomy, mathematics, or law. Self-testing may be unappealing because it takes more effort than rereading, but as noted already, the greater the effort at retrieval, the more will be retained.
Students who take practice tests have a better grasp of their progress than those who simply reread the material. Similarly, such testing enables an instructor to spot gaps and misconceptions and adapt instruction to correct them.
Giving students corrective feedback after tests keeps them from incorrectly retaining material they have misunderstood and produces better learning of the correct answers.
Students in classes that incorporate low-stakes quizzing come to embrace the practice. Students who are tested frequently rate their classes more favorably.

6---full-notes/a-summary-of-immutable-as.title: A summary of immutable aspects of learning
6---full-notes/a-summary-of-immutable-as.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning
A summary of immutable aspects
Details
These are some aspects that we probably could agree on about learning:
First, to be useful, learning requires memory, so that we can make use of the information later down the line.
Second, we need to keep learning and remembering all our lives. From middle school where we have to gain mastery of something to get a job. Then in jobs where learning better might give us a chance at promotion, and so on and so forth.
Third, learning is an acquired skill, yet the most effective strategies go against the norms (counterintuitive).
Claims that are made
Learning is deeper and more durable when it takes effort.
We are really bad at recognizing whether we’re learning effectively or not. When it becomes harder and it does not feel productive, we may turn to other strategies that do not provide any merits, or temporary ones, that feel more fruitful.
Rereading text and massed practice are the preferred methods of learning by most learners, but they are also among the least productive. This means just repetition or rote memorization as we say it. It may be useful before you are taking a test, but for mastery or durability, its a no.
Retrieval practice is a more effective strategy. Flashcards are an example of this type of learning, it strengthens the memory and interrupts forgetting. A single, simple quiz after we finish a lesson or a lecture is better than merely rereading the lecture notes. This is related to neuroplasticity, when the brain neural pathways strengthen, and the memory is reinforced.
Space out practice may make you a little bit rusty in between sessions, or you interleave the practice of two or more subjects, retrieval may become harder and feel less productive, but this is the opposite, as it actually enables long lasting learning and allows you to be more versatile in future application.
Try to solve a problem before checking the solution, resist the urge, its much better this way even if errors are made.
Do not limit yourself to any form of learning, empirical evidence does not support the existence of learning styles. Go wide, utilize everything you have at your disposal.
When you become adept at analyzing the underlying rules to differentiate between types of problems, you will become more successful at picking the correct solutions for unfamiliar situations. This can be acquired through varied practice and interleaved practice.
As humans, we can make illusions that hijack our judgement of what we know and what we do. Testing helps calibrate this.
All new learning requires us to have a foundation of prior knowledge about the topic.
Elaboration is explained in Elaboration
A method called Zettelkasten can exemplify the key ideas extraction from new material and organizing them and connecting them into a master mental model will show an advantage in learning complex mastery.

6---full-notes/ace-study.title: ACE Study
6---full-notes/ace-study.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology trauma
ACE Study
Details
Felitti-chief of the Kaiser Permanente’s Department of Preventive Medicine in San Diego (1985) conducted a large study with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The result was the monumental investigation of Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE).
More than 50000 Kaiser patients came through for an evaluation, filling out a questionnaire. Felitti and Anda spent more than a year developing 10 new questions to define categories of adverse childhood experiences, including physical, sexual, emotional neglect, and family dysfunction, such as having had parents who were divorced, mentally ill, addicted, or in prison.
Each yes answer was scored as one point, so possible scores ranged from 0 to 10. For example, someone who experienced frequent verbal abuse, alcoholic mother, and whose parents divorced would have an ACE score of three. Of the 2/3 of the respondents, 87% scored 2 or more. 1/6 had 4 or higher. The respondents were mostly white, middle class, middle aged, well educated, and financially secure, yet 1/3 reported having none of the adverse experiences.
And in short, Felitti and his team found that adverse experiences are interrelated, even though they’re usually studied separately. A family whose brother is in prison but everything else is fine doesn’t happen. Incidents of abuse never stand-alone (they have cause and effect).
The important thing out of this study is that when children matured, they didn’t “outgrow” the effects of their childhood trauma, but rather it gets lost in time and concealed by shame, secrecy and social taboo (or their own fear due to fear of people getting mad at them for saying something so supposedly crazy).

ADHD Recognition Period
Details
Although the DSM-5 recognizes that ADHD symptoms develop around 12 years old and symptoms must already exist since then, it is probable that people do not recognize their symptoms from back when they were children as they were occupied with other tasks such as studying and so on.
A person can have ADHD symptoms when they are far older than 12 as ADHD is a mental disorder that persists throughout the course of a person’s life. Symptoms can pop up latter in life when a routinely schedule gets ruined or a person is going through a tough time, which can throw them off-course and allow ADHD to take root, preventing them from focusing effectively again.
In fact, statistics support this fact as Approximately 14.3% of adolescents aged 12–17 in the U.S. have been diagnosed with ADHD, according to data from the CDC. CHADD This rate is higher than the 8.6% prevalence among children aged 5–11. These conditions may be recognized much later in life rather than within the time period of developing the disorder.
Furthermore, the delay of getting a formal diagnosis can also stem from a lack of information on the subject as ADHD is not common knowledge.

6---full-notes/adhd-vs.-add,-genetics,-i.title: ADHD vs. ADD, Genetics, IQ, Rates in Kids & Adults
6---full-notes/adhd-vs.-add,-genetics,-i.content:
Status: adult
Tags: biology ADHD genetics
ADHD vs. ADD, Genetics, IQ, Rates in Kids & Adults
Details
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, or ADHD, is a condition with a longer history than many realize, first appearing in medical literature around 1904 under the name Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD). The name evolved in the mid-to-late 1980s to more accurately include the hyperactivity component that so often accompanies the attentional challenges. This crucial change in terminology also led to a significant improvement in diagnostic accuracy and public understanding. ADHD is not a failure of character but a neurodevelopmental condition with deep biological roots, stemming from a strong genetic component that influences how the brain’s circuits are wired and how they use key neurochemicals. The heritability is remarkably high; an identical twin of someone with ADHD has about a 75% chance of also having it, while a fraternal twin has a 50-60% chance. This genetic link underscores that it is a condition of brain function, not a choice.
A critical and often misunderstood point is that ADHD has absolutely no correlation with a person’s intelligence. It is a disorder of attentional regulation, not a deficit in cognitive capacity. Individuals with high, average, or low IQs are found across the spectrum of those with and without the condition. The struggle lies in directing and sustaining focus, not in the ability to think or learn. Today, it’s estimated that 10-12% of children have ADHD, with about half of those cases potentially resolving with effective treatment. Simultaneously, we are seeing a notable rise in adult ADHD diagnoses. This has sparked a debate as to whether these are cases that went undetected in childhood or if the relentless demands and constant context-switching of modern life, particularly driven by smartphones, are capable of inducing ADHD-like symptoms in the adult brain.

Academia on society
Details
The society that runs on a low tank of intelligence will make those such as artists lose the inspiration to paint, as they have seen every painting ever to find inspiration, but the man who lives will lost nothing at all. As we take a look on humanity itself, we have all become these herds, these masses. Their value has congealed into some monolith in which each is nearly indistinguishable from one another. Perhaps this has some utility in broad public measures or policymaking, but this tendency creates subjugation.
Emerson has an example, the low who exalt the glory of the chef. These are the individuals who are willing to cast aside their individuality, to accept their status as a part of the herd, they sun themselves in the light of someone who they believe to be a great man, thinking that to be their own element. People believes that he lives for us, and that we live in him, but this is a lie. This can be solve by letting the masses run into the wild, to dissociate themselves from the herd, only then can each lamb’s beauty be understood and valued to their utmost potential, only then can the voices of individuals be heard, instead of the voice of institution; and only then, can true nourishment, be achieved.

Status: teen
Tags: academia intelligence
Academic Capability
Details
To be admitted into college, an individual generally must be able to thrive in formal academic settings. This highly focused and specific ability can be called “academic capability.” But institutions like colleges have taken this academic capability to be the same thing as intelligence. Certainly, anyone who has gone into the world would realize how incorrect this is. A person doesn’t need to have academic capability to offer wisdom, but institutions have locked this entire genre of thought out of their halls. So, with their vast expanse of knowledge, academic institutions offer only one segment of the wisdom that the world has on offer. These places are full of the academically capable, not necessarily the intelligent.
So what is this genre of intelligence that institutions find so uninteresting? It is tempting to consider this idea of going out into the world as traveling to faraway places and distant locales. That would be a mistake. Instead, as Emerson notes, we must sit at the feet of the familiar. We must learn the insight of the commonplace—of songs in the streets, of the breeze through the meadows—of things which are not found in the fortress of academic pursuit. Only then can we understand the world in which we live, rather than the picture of it we have chosen to accept. Simple things have meaning. As Emerson says, a drop is an ocean, the pleasing is the sublime, the decent is the beautiful.
Perhaps one may be able to live their whole life studying academia and even making a decent salary for the work. Perhaps they can live happily in the world created by these academic pursuits. But when that individual lies on their deathbed, they must realize the world they have lived in is a fiction. It is missing pieces. It is a cabin that is missing a wall. And then, with death, it is of course far too late to build that wall.

6---full-notes/adler's-individual-psycho.title: Adler's Individual Psychology
6---full-notes/adler's-individual-psycho.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology Freudian
Adler’s Individual Psychology
Details
Alfred Adler, another early colleague of Freud, also broke away due to a fundamental disagreement over the role of sexuality in personality. Adler proposed Individual Psychology, a theory that viewed each person as an indivisible whole, driven by a primary, conscious goal.
The central force in Adler’s theory is the striving for superiority. This is not necessarily a desire to be better than others, but an innate drive to overcome challenges, improve oneself, and reach a state of personal excellence and completeness.
Adler believed this striving is shaped by our early experiences of perceived weakness or inadequacy. As children, we naturally compare ourselves to others and become aware of things we are not good at. This creates what he famously termed an inferiority complex. Our personality, according to Adler, is largely a product of how we choose to compensate for these feelings of inferiority.


Compensation: We tend to focus on and develop the skills we are good at to accentuate our positives.


Justification: We simultaneously de-emphasize or devalue the areas where we feel weak. For example, a person who is not athletic might decide that sports are “stupid anyway.”


This continuous process of assessing our strengths and weaknesses, and striving to overcome our perceived deficits, shapes our values, interests, and behaviors, ultimately forming our unique personality.

6---full-notes/adult-persistence-in-adhd.title: Adult Persistence in ADHD
6---full-notes/adult-persistence-in-adhd.content:
Status: adult
Tags: ADHD developmental psychology
Adult Persistence in ADHD
Details
There is a pervasive myth that ADHD disappears at puberty. While the overt “squirmy” physical hyperactivity often diminishes as the frontal lobes develop, the internal symptoms—inattention, disorganization, and impulsivity—frequently persist. However, diagnosing adults is notoriously difficult because of the “insight gap.”
A famous study by Russ Barkley followed 175 children with ADHD in Milwaukee into young adulthood (mid-20s). The study highlighted a massive discrepancy in prevalence depending on who was asked. When the young adults themselves were interviewed (“Do you have symptoms of ADHD?”), only about 4.5% met the criteria. They tended to report, “I’m fine, my boss is just a jerk,” or “I’m just a creative type.”
However, when researchers interviewed the parents of these young adults, the prevalence rate jumped to 50%. If the researchers adjusted the criteria slightly to account for adult manifestations (e.g., internal restlessness rather than running around), the rate rose to nearly 70%.
This suggests two things. First, ADHD is highly persistent (approx. 2/3rds of cases continue into adulthood). Second, people with ADHD often lack self-awareness regarding their impairments. They tend to “externalize” their problems, blaming teachers, bosses, or partners for their failures rather than recognizing their own cognitive deficits. This lack of insight makes self-reporting a dangerous tool for diagnosis.
Additionally, the gender ratio shifts significantly in adulthood. While childhood ADHD presents as 3:1 (boys to girls), adult ADHD is closer to 1.5:1. This suggests that women may have a more persistent form of the disorder (often the inattentive type), or perhaps that men with the disorder are more likely to drop out of the system entirely or succumb to comorbid risks like the 5x higher rate of automobile fatalities associated with the condition.
Supporting Content
When ADHD appears in children, the ratio is often quite skewed between the boys and girls, (5:1 ratio), and the boys show clear signs of aggression and ADHD. The thing is the boys keep this trait even when they grow into adolescence or further, whilst the girls’ trait instead is multifinal, meaning there are many ways this trait manifests into behaviors including depression, suicidality, somatic complaints, and relationship dysfunction.

6---full-notes/advices-on-reading-philos.title: Advices on reading philosophy
6---full-notes/advices-on-reading-philos.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading philosophy
Advices on reading philosophy
Details
In reading philosophy, the central task is to uncover the core questions a work is trying to answer. These may be explicitly stated or only implied. The way an author answers these questions will be shaped by their foundational principles—assumptions, values, or self-evident truths that underpin their thinking.
Even when authors aim for clarity, they may not always state these principles outright. Nonetheless, these assumptions pervade their work and can be inferred with careful reading. Identifying them is crucial to understanding the structure and purpose of the argument.
Once the principles are found, assess whether the author is consistent in applying them. Philosophers, even the great ones, are not always consistent. If contradictions arise, you must choose: either the principles are faulty, or the conclusions are. Sometimes, neither holds. Inconsistency, while human, weakens philosophical arguments.
Philosophers often develop technical vocabularies. As a reader, you must respect these definitions and use terms in the way the author intends. Philosophy aims to make sense of reality, not merely describe it, and precise use of language is essential to that process.
A recurring challenge for readers is grappling with abstractions. Yet abstraction is not inherently difficult. We deal with abstract ideas daily—any general thought involves them. What the senses perceive is concrete; what the mind understands is abstract. To grasp an abstract term is to understand a general idea beyond any single instance. Confusion arises when people try to visualize abstractions rather than understand them conceptually.
In scientific texts, attention should be paid to experimental reasoning or inductive logic. But in philosophical works, the reader must focus primarily on the author’s first principles—those they assume or consider self-evident. Even if you disagree with them, it’s valuable to adopt these assumptions temporarily to follow the argument. Doing so not only sharpens your analytical skills but also helps you recognize your own presuppositions more clearly.
Problems occur when authors fail to state their assumptions, especially if they take them to be universally obvious. These assumptions, however, are often drawn from shared human experience—not from specialized or personal knowledge—and thus require active interpretation by the reader.
Ultimately, philosophical reading is a solitary endeavor. There are no shortcuts or external aids that replace direct engagement with the text. But precisely because of this, philosophy adheres more strictly to the rules of deep, active reading than most other genres.

Alexithymia
Details
This is the definition of not being able to describe how one feels. It happens when one cannot describe what their physical sensations are telling them, they look furious but deny anger, appear terrified but say they’re fine. Not being able to discern what is going inside their body because they’re out of touch with their needs, and have trouble taking care of themselves. We all have this problem to an extent but these people have it worst. People with this tend to register emotions as physical problems rather than as signals that something deserves their attention. Instead of feeling angry or sad, they experience muscle pain, bowel irregularities, or other symptoms for which no cause can be found. About three quarters of patients with anorexia nervosa, and more than half of all patients with bulimia, are bewildered by their emotional feelings and have great difficulty describing them. Because traumatized people have trouble sensing their own bodily feelings, they react to stress differently, spacing out or excessive anger, but they can’t tell what is upsetting them.

6---full-notes/altruistic-suicide.title: Altruistic Suicide
6---full-notes/altruistic-suicide.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology
The Soldier’s Suicide
Details
Émile Durkheim identifies the soldier’s suicide as a primary example of altruistic suicide. This type is not driven by personal despair but by an excessive degree of social integration. The individual’s identity is so completely absorbed into the group—the army, the nation—that the collective honor and goals are perceived as being of a higher value than their own life.
Consequently, the act of self-sacrifice, such as a soldier taking their own life to avoid capture or to complete a mission, is not experienced as a tragedy. Instead, it is seen as the ultimate fulfillment of one’s duty. In Durkheim’s view, the soldier is not melancholic or fearful but is often calm, resolute, and finds a sense of honor and purpose in dying for the cause. The basis for existence is situated entirely beyond individual life itself, making the act of dying for the collective a logical and even fulfilling choice.

6---full-notes/amygdala-in-ptsd.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
The brain structure
Details
The rational, cognitive part of the brain is the youngest and occupies about 30% of the area inside the skull. It is concerned with the world around us, trying to understand how things and people work and figuring out how to accomplish the goals that we want to.
Beneath it are two evolutionarily older and somewhat separate, brains, which are in charge of everything else, such as registering what is happening to the body and management of our physiology and the identification of comfort, pain, safety,…
The brain is built from the bottom up, just like in the course of evolution. The most primitive part is the reptilian brain, which is in the brain stem, just above the spinal cord entering the skull. It is responsible for all the things that is necessary for an infant to survive: eat, sleep, wake, cry, breathe,… The hypothalamus (sits directly above this) control the energy levels of the body, they coordinate the function of organs like the heart and lungs, endocrine and immune systems, ensuring that we have a stable internal balance known as homeostasis.
Not having one of these functions or one of them being wrong can throw us into disequilibrium, which can psychologically affect a lot of parts of us. Any effective treatment for trauma must deal with these body housekeeping functions.
Above the reptilian brain is the limbic system which is where emotions, danger, and such are managed, it is the arbiter of which things are necessary for our survival. It is also a head to help us cope with the challenges of living in society’s complex social networks. It is shaped in term of experience, with the genetic makeup and inborn temperament. Whatever happens to a baby will contribute to developing this brain, this makes it use-dependent, adapting to whichever the host needs.
These two systems makes up the “emotional brain”, it is the heart of the central nervous system and it is to look out for the host’s welfare. If it detects danger or an opportunity, it will release hormones. This can have a huge influence on the decisions humans make throughout our lives.
The neocortex, on the other hand, is rational and assesses incoming info more globally, unlike the emotional brain, which jumps to conclusions based on similarities and initiates preprogrammed escape plans, such as fight-or-flight. These reactions are automatic, is done immediately without any thought or planning at least until later, when the rational brain has caught up.

An Application Puzzle
Details
Securing a coveted scholarship or admission is less like filling out forms and more like assembling a complex and deeply personal puzzle. Each document required is a distinct piece, and only when they are all thoughtfully crafted and fitted together do they create a complete, compelling picture of who you are and what you hope to achieve. Success lies not just in completing each part, but in understanding how every single piece contributes to the final image.
The process begins with the foundational pieces that form the frame of your puzzle: the Application Form, your Academic Transcripts, your CV, and your Test Scores (like IELTS/TOEFL). These are the unshakeable facts—the “what,” “where,” and “when” of your journey. They provide the structure and hard evidence of your qualifications and experiences. Alongside them are the logistical pieces like Proof of Eligibility and Financial Information, which ensure the puzzle can be accepted for consideration.
But a frame alone is not a picture. The heart of the puzzle lies in the narrative pieces that fill the center with color, depth, and meaning. Your Personal Statement/Statement of Intent (SoP) is the most crucial piece, the one that explains the “why” behind all the others. It’s the narrative thread that connects your past achievements to your future aspirations. The Essay Questions are opportunities to highlight different facets of your character and intellect, while a Research Proposal (for a Master or PhD) becomes a centerpiece demonstrating your scholarly vision.
Supporting these core elements are pieces that add external validation and specialized texture. Letters of Recommendation are unique pieces you entrust to others to place, offering an objective viewpoint that confirms the image you are presenting. For creative or technical fields, a Portfolio/Video can be the most dynamic piece of all, showcasing your talent in action. Finally, components like an Aptitude Test and the Interview are the final quality checks, ensuring that the assembled puzzle is a true and authentic representation of the applicant. Each piece must be handled with care, for when they lock together seamlessly, they reveal a portrait of a candidate who is not just qualified, but undeniable.

6---full-notes/analogies-of-experience.title: Analogies of Experience
6---full-notes/analogies-of-experience.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy physics
Analogies of Experience
Details
To counter David Hume’s skeptical view of causality as a mere psychological habit formed by constant conjunction, Kant proposes the Analogies of Experience. These analogies are not mere observations, but rather the vital a priori rules that act as the “instruction manual” for the mind’s spontaneous synthesis, transforming subjective sensory sequences into an objective, external reality. Without these rules, the mind could not distinguish between its own subjective sequential eye movements across a static house and the actual objective sequential movement of a boat floating down a river. The first analogy establishes the permanence of substance, arguing that we can only perceive localized changes against the permanent backdrop of an enduring reality, effectively providing the philosophical foundation for principles like the conservation of mass. The second analogy dictates that all alterations must follow a necessary, rather than coincidental, law of cause and effect, elevating causality from a mere associative habit to a structural requirement of conscious experience. Finally, the third analogy establishes thoroughgoing interaction, allowing us to perceive distinct objects as coexisting simultaneously in a shared spatial environment rather than merely experiencing them in a disjointed timeline. This mutual interaction forms the philosophical justification for Newtonian physics, asserting that objects sharing a space must inherently influence one another, thereby weaving raw intuition into the coherent, physical world.

6---full-notes/analytical-behaviorism.title: Analytical Behaviorism
6---full-notes/analytical-behaviorism.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy psychology Behaviorism Psychology
Analytical Behaviorism
Details
From Ryle’s argument against Descartes about how the latter mistaken expression and states that we found ourselves in to be different from the mind itself develops Analytical Behaviorism. This view posits that all the psychological terms are not referring to our inner, hidden world but rather logical constructions to classify complex social behaviors.
For example, Wittgenstein’s analysis of “expecting tea at 4 o’clock” involves putting on the kettle, looking at the watch, and glancing out the window. There is no special “expectation pang” inside the soul that constitutes the expecting; the set of behaviors is the expecting. Psychology, therefore, is not the search for the hidden causes of behavior, but the analysis and classification of behavior itself. We are not “ghosts in machines”; we are organisms that behave intelligently.
Supporting Content
To dismantle Logical Behaviorism, Hilary Putnam relies on the linguistic distinction between analytic and synthetic truths. An analytic truth is true by definition; one cannot understand the words without acknowledging the truth (e.g., “Bachelors are unmarried” or “Tuesday comes after Monday”). A synthetic truth on the other hand is well, truths that can still be interpreted wrong with words perhaps ? (This is quite difficult for me to put into words). But basically, for example, the statement “Whales are mammals”. One may be able to understand both whales and mammals but think that whales are fishes rather than mammals.
The core error of Behaviorism, as Putnam argues, was linking the state (pain) to behavior (wincing) whilst pain can lead to other reactions rather than JUST wincing. They thought that this was an analytic truth rather than a synthetic one.

6---full-notes/anchoring-and-adjustment.title: Anchoring and Adjustment
6---full-notes/anchoring-and-adjustment.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Anchoring and Adjustment
Details
When estimating unknown quantities, people seize on whatever number is possible as a mental anchor, and then adjust insufficiently on it. Groups asked “Is the Mississippi River longer or shorter than 750 miles?” then estimate its length cluster around 1,200–1,300 miles. Groups anchored at 3,700 miles estimate around 2,500. Same as for the birthday problem: knowing 366 people guarantee a shared birthday, people anchor on 366 and estimate 182 (half) for 50% probability. The actual answer is 23—but reaching it requires genuine computation, while anchoring requires only lazy arithmetic. This connects directly to Gilbert’s sequential operations model of attribution: the initial dispositional inference serves as an anchor, and situational correction is the (insufficient) adjustment. In both domains, the starting point exerts disproportionate influence because adjusting away from it requires cognitive effort, and effort is the scarce resource that cognition perpetually conserves.

6---full-notes/anhedonia.title: Anhedonia
6---full-notes/anhedonia.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology biology
Anhedonia
Details
Anhedonia, the inability to experience pleasure, is the defining symptom of major depression. It is not merely sadness or grief, but a fundamental loss of the capacity for joy, reward, and contentment. This makes it arguably the most devastating aspect of the illness, as it robs a person of the very thing that makes life feel worth living.
The biological roots of anhedonia lie primarily in the dysregulation of the brain’s dopamine system. While often associated with the feeling of pleasure itself, Sapolsky clarifies that dopamine is even more critical for the anticipation of pleasure. A healthy brain releases dopamine when a reward is expected, creating the motivation and goal-directed behavior required to obtain it. This is the “happiness of pursuit.”
In depression, this system is depleted. The brain loses its ability to generate these anticipatory dopamine spikes. The result is a profound loss of motivation and a feeling of flatness. It’s not just that a favorite meal or hobby no longer brings joy; it’s that the person lacks the drive to even initiate the activity. They cannot anticipate a positive outcome, so the “why bother?” of learned helplessness takes over.
This biochemical failure manifests as a complete detachment from sources of pleasure. A beautiful sunset, a kind word, or a personal achievement registers as emotionally empty. This is not a choice or a mood; it is a neurological inability to process and experience reward, making anhedonia a direct and debilitating symptom of depression’s underlying biology.

And so hyper anxiety may not be a broken biological system but rather a defective or maladaptive one.
Diagnosing anxiety requires a strict developmental lens due to how fears change as cognitive maturity increases. Toddlers fear separation, darkness, animals since their survival. Children fear injuries, the paranormal, death. Teenagers fear social and existentialism. A clinician must determine if the fear is suitable to diagnose the disorder.

6---full-notes/anxiety.title: Anxiety
6---full-notes/anxiety.content:
Status: adult
