Anxiety
Details
This is a commonplace observation when someone considers themselves to be in imminent danger, in which they will be likely to feel anxious. Threats of any kind, be it physical, economically,… can have this effect. Moreover, it can even be a threat (even imaginary) to the safety, health, or psychological state of anyone else in his own domain may do this. A person may also become anxious if he perceives a danger to some institution or principle he values.
This anticipation is what we call fear, and people’s reaction to it is what we call anxiety. But there is a way to alleviate this, it is that the person experiencing is confident they can cope an deal with it. But it will increase when he feels that this damage is unavoidable, extremely destructive and such, and it may also be increased by uncertainty with regard to when the harm may occur.
In identifying a situation as dangerous, a person usually makes two simultaneous judgements. The first is termed “primary appraisal” by Richard Lazarus, who identifies the situation as a threat and assesses all the factors of harm in it, the intensity, the probability, the imminence,… The second is “counter-harm” resources; that is, the ability to cope with the danger. The ratio between the negative in the primary with the positive of the secondary constitutes the perceived risk. The latter then determines the intensity of anxiety.
It is important to recognize that the same situation can have different effects on different people and even some situations perceived generally to be safe and normal can become dangerous for certain individuals.

6---full-notes/approaches-to-research.title: Approaches to Research
6---full-notes/approaches-to-research.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology
Approaches to Research
Details
Firstly is the case study method, which is incredibly good for rare things, something that is hard to find a lot of people to test on. This could then set the stage for future research, it can be used for things like trying a new treatment, finding out a new mental disorder and so on. It usually has a very small samples, down to one person. The drawback is that it is quite prone to generalization, as one person or multiple can expand the symptoms of such patients to everyone. This shows that it cannot prove a hypothesis, but it can prove it. Still, it is used because of the rich information that it can give us.
Another method is correlation, which is incredibly popular in academics. As stated in psychopathology, a truly random experiment is quite difficult, as the methodologies just take a lot of effort and often is not worth it. Correlation coefficient is the value for us to determine if two variables correlate with each other synonymously or autonomously. It is denoted by the symbol r, which range between -1.00 and +1.00, and it measures the magnitude and relationship of the two variables. For example, some dumbass correlation like if you’re dumber, your girlfriend is more pretty (I don’t actually know if this is true). Maybe the correlation will be negative, which mean if you’re smarter then your girl is more pretty. But we do not know that, one causes the other, causation does not mean correlation.
A form of correlation is epidemiological studies, which studies the distribution of disorders in a population. That means data are gathered about the rates of a disorder and correlates in a large sample. This helps us see the following factors of a disorder:

Prevalence: proportion of people that has the disorder during their lifetime.
Incidence: proportion of people who develop new cases of the disorder in some period, usually in a year.
Risk factors: likelihood of developing the disorder (variables).

These studies only represent the sample of the population being studied - meaning if you test the population of Berkeley for a certain mental disorder for example, that would only represent the population in Berkeley, not other states.
Lastly, experiments, these are the the most powerful tools for determining causal relationships. It will include a random assignment of participants to conditions, meaning the participants will be split into different groups randomly, one group will manipulate the independent variable, and the measurement of a dependent variable. The group that does not have the dependent variable changed is called the control group.

Approaching Pediatric Bipolar Disorder

One attempted resolution to the debate has been coined by researcher Ellen Leibenluft, proposing that the disorder should be split into phenotypes according to how close it matches the adult version. The “Narrow” phenotype would be those who fully match the adult criteria, which is extremely rare. The second is the “Intermediate” phenotype which describes children who experience these symptoms temporarily (1-2 days) or characterized by irritability. The “Broad” phenotype or Severe Mood Dysregulation would describe children with chronic, non-episodic explosive behavior and irritability. Longitudinal data suggests that the former two would grow into adult Bipolar disorder and the latter would turn more to depressive or anxiety disorders.

6---full-notes/around-the-book.content:
Status: adult

Around the book
Details
The structure of a book and its story is the skeleton that is hidden between its covers, how it is pieced together to become a well-written book is the flesh, the clothes of it. The reader doesn’t have to tear through all this to get at the firm structure that underlies it, but they must see the book with x-ray eyes.
This leads into the second rule of analytical reading. Rule 2: State the unity of the whole book in a single sentence, or at most a few sentences (a short paragraph). This means that one must summarize what the book is about as short as possible, not what kind of book it is (rule 1). This kind of “about” is colloquial, it is what the author is up to, what he is trying to do with the book.
Continuously, this connects to Rule 3: Set forth the major parts of the book, show how these are organized into a whole, by being ordered to one another and to the unity of the whole. The only way one can grasp the complex unity of a book is if one knows how it is one. Considering many parts of it, how they are organized and so on. And so we come to the point that a book is like a house, and its parts are like rooms, they all have different furniture, purposes, but they are not independent and separate. They are all connected and missing neither of them will make the house unlivable.
This also corresponds to the readability of books, the most readable books are like the most functional houses, they have the most intelligible structure, they are complex but in that is an even greater simplicity because they are organized, unified.

6---full-notes/attachment-theory.content:
Status: teen

Attachment Theory
Details
Children usually take after their caregivers, this is not just a saying, it is scientifically proven. As babies get into this world, they automatically have someone to take care of them, to feed, to sleep with and so. When they grow up, they learn to take care of themselves, and the first lesson that they ever get to know how to do this is of how they are cared for. Children are inherently sensitive to facial expression, postures, tones, everything. This is theorized to be a trait of evolution to help them survive,  and that they also choose a few adults to learn from, attach to and develop healthy ways of living in life. Attachment is a secure base that would allow children to function without being afraid of being left behind, doing something wrong as such. This safe haven also allows them to develop empathy, self-awareness, impulse control and many other functions as they realize that people will have different feelings and thoughts from themselves.
Now the physiological part, to describe the connection between these two, I’d say… “in sync”. And not just emotionally, but physically as well, children don’t just feel sad when they notice that others or sad or something along those lines, their bodies also do that, it tenses, releases hormones, and all that jazz. We can tell equilibrium has been restored when the physiology calms down.
Newborns are soothed, but their toleration are also taught, a role given to their fathers. Learning how to manage this is especially important in life, and parents must do this before babies can do it for themselves. If the baby shits itself, the parents are gonna clean it up, if the baby is hungry, the mother feeds,… Associating these intense feelings with safety, comfort is the foundation of self-regulation, self-soothing, and self-nurture. These securely-attached children knows what makes them feel good, what makes others feel bad and so on. But abused children don’t, their cries, their needs are often responded with negligence from their caregivers. In effect they are being conditioned to give up whenever they face challenges in life.
Supporting Content

6---full-notes/attribute-substitution.title: Attribute Substitution
6---full-notes/attribute-substitution.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Attribute Substitution
Details
After defining heuristics for so long, Kahneman proposed a single mechanism underlying all of them: attribute substitution. This practically allows us to attribute an irrelevant answer to a question that we were asked in the first place. The important thing is we never really realize that we substituted: as seen in heuristics, we replace questions constantly, and its almost automatic.  The availability heuristic substitutes “how frequent is X?” with “how easily can I think of examples of X?” The representativeness heuristic substitutes “what is the probability of X?” with “how much does X resemble my prototype?” Anchoring substitutes “what is the true value?” with “how far from this number should I adjust?” In each case, the substitute attribute is computationally cheaper to evaluate than the target attribute. In conclusion, this framework explains why we aim for the inaccurate explanation, because its easier, and it feels right for us.

6---full-notes/auditory-cortex.title: Auditory Cortex
6---full-notes/auditory-cortex.content:
Status: baby
Tags: neuroscience psychology
Auditory Cortex
Details
The primary auditory cortex (A1) is the region of the cerebral cortex responsible for processing auditory information. It is located in the superior temporal gyrus of the temporal lobe.
Its main function is to perceive and interpret the fundamental aspects of sound, including pitch (frequency), loudness (amplitude), and the location of the sound source. Information from the ears is relayed through the thalamus to the auditory cortex for conscious perception.
The auditory cortex is organized tonotopically. This means that neurons are arranged according to the sound frequency they respond to, creating a “frequency map” across the cortical surface. Lower frequencies are processed at one end, and higher frequencies at the other. This organization is critical for distinguishing between different sounds.

Autism Spectrum Disorder
Details
ASD affects about 1 in 88 children around the world, and although some people with autism have an unnatural ability for certain subjects, others still suffer from its symptoms quite a lot. Starting with the social and emotional disturbances, autism can cause children to have profound problems with the social world, meaning they are gonna act really weirdly whilst socializing, if you can call that socializing at all. They also suffer from joint attention, which is they have a problem with communicating or paying attention to one person in a mutual activity. Weird symptom but they usually focus on the mouth (lower face) rather than something like the eyes (upper face).
These children also suffer from communication deficits. Babbling, for example, which is usually used to describe the nonsensical sounds that infants make before they begin to use words, is less frequent than those with ASD and conveys less information as well (Ricks, 1972). ASD children also lag behind on the language development process. They also suffer from echolalia, which means they are gonna repeat whatever the person is saying to them, indicating that they do not understand what the other is saying. Together with echolalia, they also suffer from pronoun reversals.
A “symptom” that sometimes can turn into a blessing is repetitive and ritualistic acts that these children perform, they can keep their habits of these things up to even when they are adults, and they would become extremely talented in that one specific thing.
Supporting Content
Children with ASD may even have an undeveloped “theory of mind”, they will not be able to recognize that other people have a different understanding/view of the world than them.

6---full-notes/automatic-thoughts.title: Automatic thoughts
6---full-notes/automatic-thoughts.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology CBT
Automatic thoughts
Details
These are certain kinds of ideation where it is usually not omit in free association. This isn’t due to the fact that there was any resistance or defense to not express these thoughts but rather of the patient not knowing the thought persisted in the first place. The thoughts are appeared to be of transference nature, which means they are related to the patient’s evaluation of what he was saying or planning to say and how they expect the other to react. This meant that, unconsciously, the patients were communicating to themselves in every conversation everyday, and so by training them to focus on these thoughts, we can get to the key of the problems.
In order to access this information, one must recall the thoughts that one had prior to feeling some intense or unpleasant feeling or sensation. This will help sharpen patient’s awareness of their thoughts, and eventually they will identify these thoughts.
But why are these thoughts so obscured in their minds ? M.D Aaron Beck says that it is because the patients are presenting material that had to do with current problems, dreams, and memories; or presenting narratives of their own experiences; or jumping from one idea to another in a chain of associations. But they were not concentrating on their thoughts, but rather what they “must be thinking”.
He also theorized that the reason free association failed to recognize these thoughts was because people are accustomed to speaking to others and themselves differently. And even though these internal signals can have a powerful influence over them, they don’t have a history of paying attention to them.
Continuing in depression, or in situations where the patient is disturbed - these thoughts are more prominent. Aaron also said that he become more cognizant of their presence when he tried to elicit the thought content from severely depressed patients. He also recognized the compelling nature of them in the ideation of obsessional patients.

6---full-notes/automaticity-and-donald.title: Automaticity and Donald
6---full-notes/automaticity-and-donald.content:
Status: teen

Automaticity and Donald
Details
In the hallmark experiments on automaticity, most of the human subjects were Donald, not in the sense that the participants had that name but the object of the experiment was Donald. Now actually explaining the experiments, basically people were put through variations of priming, which is basically showing them words in one way or the other, some were negative, others were positive, and they would relate or not relate to the object.
After that, they were then shown a passage of Donald doing neutral things, and then asked to evaluate him. For the words that were related, people were much more likely to say he was reckless or something if that was the word that they were primed with in a “separate” experiment minutes ago. And of course, these people did not realize that they were in the experiment or anything of the sorts.
There were many other experiments that tested if automaticity was real, like the John Bargh experiments to show that flashing hostility-related words influenced participants’ judgments of Donald, leading them to perceive him as more hostile.
There was also the Bob the priest experiment, testing that if people could realize the inconsistency of the priest’s kindness (not assuming that all priests are kind) through his actions. And yes, they could if they weren’t in a cognitive task, but if they are, they would be more likely to just follow the normal understanding.

6---full-notes/bdnf-and-memory.title: BDNF and Memory
6---full-notes/bdnf-and-memory.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience neuroplasticity
BDNF and Memory
Details
BDNF, or Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor, is a neurochemical that the brain releases whenever we are doing a cardio-heavy exercise of some sort. This is the most important chemical to increasing our focus and memory in our neural circuits. Normally, if we move for just 10 minutes (which is already beneficial), the brain releases dopamine, serotonin, and noradrenaline, regulating our moods. BDNF works this by acting as a growth factor for the hippocampus, allowing it to grow new cells (neurogenesis), a process that occurs in humans well into the ninth decade of life.
There are two pathways that BDNF works through our body, the first being the muscles; when striated muscles work, they release proteins called myokines, which cross the blood-brain barrier and stimulate BDNF production. The second pathway is through the liver; exercise is a physical stressor that causes the liver to release a ketone called beta-hydroxybutyrate, which also crosses the blood-brain barrier to trigger BDNF.
Supporting Content
These effects can last for a maximum of 2 hours and is recommended to happen in a 30-45 minute period to truly get the benefits.

6---full-notes/balanced-responses-to-bet.title: Balanced responses to better outcomes
6---full-notes/balanced-responses-to-bet.content:
Status: adult
Tags: therapy
Balanced responses to better outcomes
Details
Building a so called “protocol” to respond to people in their crisis is very important so as not to get drawn into their spiral and be able to help them.
Firstly, pause, take a breath, notice your physical sensations, label them as the emotion you are experiencing. For example, “Uh oh, I’m having a panic attack, I just saw my abuser, my feeling here is RAGE (or ANGER).” Then, pay attention to your body posture, try to relax your muscles, unclench your hands, smile a bit (not because you’re happy but because you’re trying to calm down). Validate and cheerlead yourself. This can be something like “my emotions are understandable given what’s going on.”, “I love this person, so of course I would feel mad.”
In addition to that, you can also try to find triggers that makes you yourself more emotionally vulnerable to their actions:

Recall a few times when the interactions went poorly.
Did it start off emotionally, or was there a build, or an explosion ?
Were there other factors that may have affected you that particular day ? Sickness, tired, work ?
Do a little analysis of the event
A. When did it start ?
B. When did it get to the point of no return and problems would start happening ?
C. What happened after the explosion ? Did you change ? Did they change ?…

And so when you feel something like anger, you DISENGAGE. Give them space, tell them a word that you need to go because its too much and that you love them. Then completely disengage, do not stay connected as anger will stay up or even increase. After that, practice kindness, compassion. Do something kind for them… as anger cannot be maintained in the face of compassion.
Sadness on the other hand makes you wanna give up, because they’re hopeless. Try to do stuff, just activate your support system to do things unrelated to the BPD person, don’t let yourself stay still and upset.

Being Wrong in test comparisons
Details
Reality is one of two things and you make one of two calls, which gives a two-by-two. Either the null or the research hypothesis is true, and either you reject the null or you do not. Rejecting a null that is true is a Type I error, and its probability is alpha (the threshold that you set for yourself). Failing to reject the research hypothesis when it is true is a Type II error, with probability beta, and you do not get to set this one. You would actually want to reject a false null, meaning the probability is power = 1 - beta.

The reason fight and flight happens is adrenaline, which is a chemical that helps us to defend or flee from danger, it can increase our heart rate and blood pressure. This is also present in traumatized patients, its just that these hormones take immensely more time to return to normal and spike quickly and disproportionately while reacting to light stress. The result of the spike in hormones can attribute to memory and attention problems, irritation, and sleeping disorders. It can also effect the body in the long-term, depending on which body part is the most vulnerable. In trauma patients, they cannot get themselves out of this state as their brain/body constantly misinterpret normal things as danger, pumping adrenaline and getting them into this state.
Moreover, the body pumping this much adrenaline can also affect the patient’s physicality: sleep disturbances, headaches, pain, oversensitivity. Being so agitated or shut down keeps them from concentrating and focusing.  And to counter this, they would engage in activities to relieve their tension (Hurting themselves included). 6---full-notes/best-response.title: Best response
6---full-notes/best-response.content:
Status: teen
Tags: economics math
Best response
Details
Only using dominance would get you nowhere most of the time, because in situations nothing is totally dominated by either player.
Left	Right

Up	5, 1	0, 2
Middle	1, 3	4, 1
Down	4, 2	2, 3
For Player I, compare the first numbers within each column. Down loses to Up against Left (4 vs 5) but beats it against Right (2 vs 0). Down loses to Middle against Right (2 vs 4) but beats it against Left (4 vs 1). Up and Middle also each win one column. So no row is better in every column.
For Player II, compare the second numbers within each row. Right is better against Up (2 vs 1) and against Down (3 vs 2). Left is better against Middle (3 vs 1). So neither column dominates either.
So your new best friend here is best response: what is your best choice assuming what the other person will do.
So Down is the best response to that belief.
A student defended Down as safer, and it is: its worst outcome is 2, against 0 for Up and 1 for Middle. But Polak’s point is stronger. Under a 50–50 belief, Down isn’t just safe; it earns the most on average. Those are different reasons that happen to agree here. Lecture 1’s angels faced the same split between a safety rule and a belief, and there too the belief settled it.

6---full-notes/betting-on-the-future,-wo.title: Betting on the Future, Worth?
6---full-notes/betting-on-the-future,-wo.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy death
Betting on the Future, Worth?
Details
The thing about human life is, there will always be some chance of recovery. Be it by medicine advances, or just miracle remissions. Death would close that chance permanently. So the argument can be that the option that preserves the chance to live must win.
Kagan’s first move is to deny that anyone gets to opt out of gambling. Continuing is a bet too, made under the same ignorance. There is no cautious choice available and no non-gamble on the menu, so “don’t gamble” cannot be the advice.
The second move is the two doors. Door one: overwhelmingly likely a week of torture, with a one-in-ten-thousand chance of a superb holiday instead. Door two: certain dreamless sleep for the week, which is neither good nor bad — call it zero. Someone insisting door one is the only rational choice, on the grounds that door two discards the chance of the holiday, is not tracking any decision rule we use anywhere.
A student objects that the analogy cheats, since a week of sleep ends and death does not. Kagan rebuilds it at full scale: fifty or sixty or seventy years of torture at the same odds against a permanent dreamless coma ending in death. He still takes door two to be a permissible choice. Note carefully what he claims and what he does not: not that door two is required, but that door one is not the uniquely rational option. He concedes real room for argument about where the balance tips — how bad the torture, how good the holiday, one percent versus five — and rests only on the denial that no probability, however small, could ever be outweighed.

6---full-notes/budget-constraint.title: Budget Constraint
6---full-notes/budget-constraint.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Budget Constraint
Details
The practical implications of preferences lie in this variable as it is what breads scarcity and in turn makes people try to optimize for the best economical decision. A consumer may prefer many possible bundles of pizza slices and cookies, but only some of those bundles are affordable. The budget constraint is the line separating what the consumer can afford from what lies outside their resources.
The basic budget constraint says that income equals spending, here we are ignoring the possibility of saving and only focusing on the situation where the person spends every single cent of their income. Mathematically, we will mark income by I, cookies by C, pizza by S, and the price of cookies by PC, and the price of pizza slices by PS, then the consumer’s total spending is PC times C plus PS times S. It is also not an absurd approximation for many real households, because people with little savings often do live close to paycheck-to-paycheck, where income effectively bounds immediate consumption.
Graphically, the budget constraint has cookies on one axis and pizza slices on the other. The cookie intercept shows how many cookies the consumer could buy if they spent all income on cookies. The pizza intercept shows how many slices they could buy if they spent all income on pizza. The slope of the budget constraint is the negative price ratio, minus the price of cookies divided by the price of pizza. This slope expresses opportunity cost. If cookies cost two dollars and pizza slices cost four dollars, then each cookie costs half a slice of pizza. Buying one more cookie effectively means giving up half a pizza slice, because the same money cannot be spent twice. This is what Gruber calls the marginal rate of transformation: the rate at which the market allows the consumer to transform one good into another through spending decisions.
And so this is the other factor that relates to the Marginal Rate of Substitution, the amount the market allows the person to trade these goods off each other.

6---full-notes/bystander-effect.title: Bystander Effect
6---full-notes/bystander-effect.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Bystander Effect
Details
The Kitty Genovese catalyzed research on helping behavior, but the phenomenon is not an anomaly; similar cases recur across decades and cultures. Latane and Darley’s experimental replication had subjects hear a confederate (undergraduate Dick Nisbett) suffer an epileptic seizure over headphones. With only one other person present, most subjects helped quickly. With five others present, helping rates dropped dramatically, and even those who helped took significantly longer. There were basically three gates to the bystander effect. The first was noticing: When alone, 70% noticed smoke entering a room within 5 seconds; with others present, detection slowed because social norms make us keep eyes down and earphones in around strangers. The second is interpretation as emergency: Alone, subjects interpreted smoke as potential fire; with passive confederates, subjects generated absurd alternative explanations (“steam from the ventilator”) because others’ calm demeanor defined the situation as safe—pluralistic ignorance in action. Last is the acceptance of personal responsibility: A subway study showed subjects corrected wrong directions only when the question had been directed specifically to them; when asked generally or to the confederate beside them, they stayed silent despite knowing the answer. Each gate requires passing the previous one, and the presence of others creates friction at every stage.

CBT Principles
Details
Conceptualization of clients using their data and cognitive formulation (cognitions, behavioral strategies, and maintaining factors). We can also include data on their strengths and such as well, then throughout the therapy process we will try to continue adding information to the conceptualization to better understand the patient.
For example, Judith Beck’s popular case - Abe - was conceptualized into three time frames. From the beginning, she identified his cognitions that prevented his aspirations, then the behavioral obstacles that server to maintain his depression and then precipitation factors that influenced his original depression. These factors were because he struggled at work -> his wife became increasingly critical and divorced him, leading him to think he was incompetent. Third, she then hypothesized what were the key events in his past that may have created the suitable conditions for him to experience depression.
Additionally, various studies have shown that monitoring the therapy sessions and even in-between sessions improves outcomes. Getting feedback also helps this as they can be sure about the progress they are making and where they need to improve.
Even if you do not think it is in place, emphasize the positives. Recent research demonstrates the importance of this as it can cultivate their moods and subsequently allow them to hope. If we continue letting them ruminate, they would be able to go on to the end of the session, so its not advisable we do that. Redirect them.
An important factor is to LET THEM WORK WITH YOU, please, this will foster the relationship further and also improve and help them improve their skills and abilities. But before this, you need to remember that CBT is educative, teach them about the process, walk them through what you’re going to do and also the skills of course.
CBT is flexible, very very flexible. From its base form back 50+ years ago, so many therapies and such have emerged from it, schema therapy, dialectical behavioral therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy,… and you can use the modules and skills from these therapies to use alongside CBT as well.

6---full-notes/cbt-vs.-psychoanalysis.title: CBT vs. Psychoanalysis
6---full-notes/cbt-vs.-psychoanalysis.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology CBT therapy
CBT vs. Psychoanalysis
Details
While both Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and psychoanalysis aim to alleviate psychological distress, they represent vastly different philosophies and methodologies. In the landscape of modern mental healthcare, CBT stands out as a more pragmatic, efficient, and empowering approach for many individuals. Its superiority lies in its clear, evidence-based principles and its direct focus on providing tangible relief in the present.
CBT is built on the straightforward and powerful principle that our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are fundamentally interconnected. It posits that psychological distress is not caused by events themselves, but by our interpretation of those events. This cognitive model empowers individuals by showing them that by changing their patterns of thinking and behavior, they can directly alter their emotional state. Unlike the lengthy, archaeological dig into the past that characterizes psychoanalysis, CBT is a forward-looking and goal-oriented therapy. It operates like a targeted training program for the mind, equipping clients with practical skills to tackle their current problems head-on. The therapist acts as a collaborative coach, helping the client identify specific, unhelpful thought patterns—such as overgeneralization or catastrophic thinking—and systematically challenge and replace them with more realistic and adaptive ones.
This contrasts sharply with the psychoanalytic method, which involves a long-term, often years-long, exploration of the unconscious mind to uncover conflicts rooted in early childhood. While this deep dive can be insightful, it is often an inefficient and abstract process for those seeking relief from acute symptoms like anxiety or depression. The focus on the past can feel untethered from the immediate challenges a person is facing.
The practical advantages of CBT are significant. Its structured nature and shorter duration, typically between 6 to 20 sessions, make it a more accessible and cost-effective option. More importantly, CBT demystifies therapy by providing a clear framework and teaching concrete, lifelong skills. Clients don’t just talk about their problems; they learn specific techniques like cognitive restructuring and behavioral experiments that they can apply independently. This emphasis on self-efficacy is profoundly empowering, transforming the individual from a passive recipient of treatment into an active agent in their own recovery. For these reasons, CBT is often the superior choice for those seeking a direct, effective, and lasting solution to their psychological struggles.

Capitalism is not Unjust
Details
Marx does not actually critique the system of capitalism in a moral sense. His critiques of the “utopian socialists” reveals that Marx deliberately avoids moralizing. For Marx, “justice” is merely a juridical and political conception that belongs to the ideological superstructure (which exists to regulate and support the Mode of Production), it is entirely relative to its historical epoch.
Therefore, under capitalism, the extraction of surplus value is perfectly “just.” When a capitalist buys a worker’s labor-power at its true market value (the socially necessary labor time required to sustain and reproduce the worker) and then extracts more value from the worker than was paid in wages, an exact exchange of equivalents has formally taken place. Marx is reasonable enough to recognize that there is no inherent value in applying a moral framework to capitalism as every moral framework does not apply universally to every epoch.

6---full-notes/carl-roger's-background.title: Carl Roger's Background
6---full-notes/carl-roger's-background.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology therapy
Carl Roger’s Background
Details
The intellectual trajectory of Carl Rogers, a foundational figure in humanistic psychology, is best understood as a direct outgrowth of his formative experiences, which consistently positioned him as an intellectual outsider. His early life in Oak Park, Illinois, was characterized by a strict, devoutly Christian household that fostered an environment of isolation and intellectual self-reliance. This upbringing, while restrictive, inadvertently cultivated in Rogers a profound trust in his own observations, a skill he honed through the scientific study of agriculture and biology after his family relocated to a farm. This empirical mindset stood in stark contrast to the faith-based dogma of his home, establishing a foundational preference for evidence over doctrine.
This predilection for self-directed inquiry proved to be a pivotal factor during his university years. Initially pursuing a career in the ministry, Rogers’s perspective was irrevocably altered during a trip to China, where he encountered sincere individuals with vastly different belief systems. This experience, coupled with his time at the liberal Union Theological Seminary, led him to question the validity of subscribing to any single, unassailable truth. He subsequently abandoned theology for psychology, entering a field then dominated by the deterministic models of Freudian psychoanalysis and Skinnerian behaviorism. While his peers were trained to accept these prevailing psychological doctrines, Rogers’s personal journey had already instilled in him a deep-seated skepticism toward expert-driven, top-down systems.
This skepticism crystallized into his revolutionary “person-centered” approach. In his early clinical work with troubled children, Rogers found that the established practices of diagnosis, interpretation, and advice-giving were largely ineffective. Instead, he observed that therapeutic progress was contingent upon a specific relational climate. He diverged from his contemporaries by proposing that growth is not facilitated by an expert therapist, but by a relationship characterized by genuineness, unconditional positive regard, and empathic understanding. This model posited that individuals possess an inherent “actualizing tendency,” and the therapist’s role is not to direct, but to create the conditions for this natural development to unfold. Rogers’s great contribution, therefore, was to reframe the therapeutic relationship, shifting power from the practitioner to the client and championing the individual’s own experience as the ultimate authority—a direct reflection of the principles he had gleaned from a lifetime of independent thought.

6---full-notes/case-study-of-development.title: Case Study of Developmental Psychopathology
6---full-notes/case-study-of-development.content:
Status: adult
Tags: developmental psychology sociology environment genetics
Case Study of Developmental Psychopathology
Details
The story of Stephen Hinshaw’s father, Virgil Hinshaw Jr., serves as a poignant case study in developmental psychopathology. Virgil experienced a significant traumatic experience when he lost his mother at the early age of three. Developmental psychopathology posits that the loss of a parent before age five is a risk factor for future mood disorders; however, this is usually modulated by protective factors. Unfortunately, Virgil lacked these protections: his father remarried a missionary woman who subjected him to severe physical abuse. This created a specific “non-shared environment” where he suffered differently than his brothers, allowing the vulnerability for illness to take root.
The culmination of these risk factors occurred in 1936 when he was 16. Amidst a family atmosphere charged with his father’s work in the Prohibition movement, and rising political anxiety regarding fascism in Europe, Virgil experienced his first manic episode. Triggered by sleep deprivation and the late-summer seasonality often associated with the onset of mania, he developed a grandiose delusion that he could stop the fascists by flying. This culminated in a psychotic break where he jumped off a porch roof, resulting in physical injury and immediate institutionalization. Because the distinction between bipolar disorder and schizophrenia was not well recognized at the time, he was misdiagnosed with the latter.
As discussed in Development of Asylums, institutional care during this era was primitive, and this case was no different. Virgil was restrained to his bed nightly and received no medical intervention when he stopped eating due to a delusion that the food was poisoned. His family was only contacted long after his condition had deteriorated. Eventually, Virgil was released due to “improving” spontaneously. However, the family never discussed the event, adhering to a strict code of silence driven by Stigma.
Virgil went on to excel academically, completing his PhD at Princeton. However, the stress of his doctoral dissertation combined with relationship troubles triggered a second severe psychotic episode in 1945. He was admitted to Philadelphia State Hospital (Bybury), infamous for its deplorable conditions and immortalized in The Snake Pit. During a visit, Virgil refused to leave, insisting the road signs were in German and that he was in a concentration camp. At the time, this was viewed as a total break from reality.
Years later, a historical re-examination of the hospital suggests this delusion had a grain of truth. Photographs of the men’s dormitory reveal conditions shockingly similar to the concentration camps of Europe; his psychosis was, in part, a reaction to his dehumanizing environment.
Despite these struggles, Virgil was able to marry and secure tenure as a philosophy professor. He possessed protective factors (intelligence, resilience) that allowed him to function where others might not have. However, the “rule of silence” persisted. His wife was only informed of his history after he became manic during her pregnancy. Furthermore, the genetic risk was evident in the family tree: other brothers struggled with substance abuse, and several nephews succumbed to severe mental illness or suicide.
Despite being a loving father, the cycle of silence affected the next generation. Stephen Hinshaw was kept in the dark about the true nature of his father’s absences because psychiatrists of the era believed discussing mental illness would “ruin” the children. Consequently, the children were left to internalize the confusion, only learning the truth after they had left for college.
Supporting Content
And so what conclusion can we get from this ? Telling your children about your conditions and problems can significantly impact the risks of them developing mental disorders down the line. Proven by a multitude of case studies, the rate at which people suffer from mental illnesses later in their adult lives actually halves if their parents educated them about how they suffered mentally.

References
Bipolar Disorders
Schizophrenia
Developmental Psychopathology
Risk Factors and Protective Factors

6---full-notes/case-studies-of-quaic.title: Case studies of QuAIC
6---full-notes/case-studies-of-quaic.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology university
Case studies of QuAIC
Details
The three case studies presented in the paper provide a vivid, qualitative illustration of this data in action, serving as a proof-of-concept for the entire tiered response system. They demonstrate how the initial risk level, informed by the QuAIC, is not an arbitrary label but a meaningful category that triggers a distinct, defensible, and proportionate level of institutional intervention.  


Case 1 (Low Risk): A staff member reported a welfare concern about a student’s declining hygiene. The triage risk level was assessed as “Low.” The SCU’s response was efficient and minimalist: they provided advice and referral information to the reporting staff member, who then conducted a welfare check. The case was closed after the student was successfully referred to internal support services. This demonstrates a “light touch,” low-intensity response appropriate for low-risk matters.  


Case 2 (Moderate Risk): A student reported stalking by an ex-partner, involving persistent and intrusive communication. The triage risk level was assessed as “Moderate.” This triggered a more intensive and sustained response. The SCU provided ongoing case management, including specialist safety planning and psychoeducation for the target. As the stalking behavior continued despite these initial interventions, the institutional response escalated systematically: from an informal warning, to a formal no-contact direction, to a temporary suspension under misconduct provisions, and ultimately to a referral for the target to report the matter to local police. This case perfectly illustrates a managed, persistent, and escalating response pathway for a moderate-risk situation.  


Case 3 (High Risk): A student with a known history of multiple problem behaviors, including threats and stalking, was referred for assessment. The triage risk level was assessed as “High.” The response was immediate and coercive. The case was escalated directly to the multi-disciplinary SAT team, which issued a temporary suspension from the university. The student’s return was made contingent upon the completion of a mandatory psychological assessment with an external threat assessment specialist and compliance with all recommended safety measures. This demonstrates a rapid, high-level, and authoritative response reserved for the most serious cases.  


Taken together, these cases provide the narrative evidence that the entire system—from QuAIC-informed triage to final case resolution—functions as a coherent and proportionate whole. The principle of proportionality, a cornerstone of fair and effective risk management, requires that the institutional response match the level of risk. The case studies show a near-perfect alignment: a low-risk case received a low-intensity response; a moderate-risk case received a moderate and escalating response; and a high-risk case received a high-intensity response. Because the QuAIC is a key input into determining that initial risk level, these qualitative examples serve as powerful validation of the tool’s foundational role in initiating this proportionate response pathway.

6---full-notes/cash-vs-in-kind-transfers.title: Cash vs In-kind transfers
6---full-notes/cash-vs-in-kind-transfers.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Cash vs In-kind transfers
Details
SNAP, or the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, is something that gives low-income Americans a debit card that only works for food. People below the poverty line, about $14,000 a year for a single person, or a little above it, get a couple of hundred dollars a month. Gruber asks why the government doesn’t just give them cash, and answers with budget constraints rather than intuition.
To exemplify how it affects people with different needs we can take a very poor person with 5,000 who can spend it only on food (x-axis) or shelter (y-axis). Set both prices to 1. Gruber calls this using a numéraire: fixing prices at 1 so dollars and quantities are the same number. Since “food” and “shelter” are vague baskets anyway, choosing units this way costs nothing. The budget line runs from 5,000 on each axis, with a slope of −1. A 500 cash gift shifts it out in parallel to $5,500, since prices haven’t changed. Two people use the gift differently:

























Before: food, shelterWith $500 cashX (mostly wants shelter)200, 4,800300, 5,200Y (mostly wants food)4,900, 1005,100, 400
Both are better off. Gruber’s spoken description of Y doesn’t match the figure. Going by the figure, Y puts more of the new 500 into shelter than food, 300 against 200. Nothing hangs on it, because what matters is that Y spends far more than 500 on food either way.
If we instead make it food only, the graph changes. It would cut off from the top on the Oy axis (shelter) because the budget doesn’t cover that. And well in MRS wise, it is clear that the person preferring shelter is worse off.
For Y, nothing changes. Y was going to spend 5,100 on food anyway, so Y calls 500 of it SNAP and buys exactly what they would have with cash. Money is fungible: a dollar is a dollar, whatever it’s labeled. Economists call people who would spend more than the benefit on food anyway inframarginal. They should treat a food-only benefit exactly like cash.
X can’t do that. With cash, X wanted 300 of food and 5,200 of shelter, but that bundle is in the cut-off corner. The best X can do now is the kink, 500 of food and 5,000 of shelter, on a lower indifference curve. X is worse off than with the same $500 in cash, though still better off than with nothing.
This generalizes. Judged by the person’s own preferences, a restricted transfer can never beat the same amount in cash. It leaves everyone it actually constrains worse off than cash would.
So why do people help this way? Why does the government do so? 
The positive question is whether SNAP raises food spending compared with cash. The graph can’t say, because the answer depends on how many recipients are like X. Experiments say yes, but by much less than a dollar. Gruber puts it at about 15 cents more food per dollar given as SNAP rather than cash. So some recipients are X’s, but most behave like Y’s. He presents this as part of the rise of field experiments in economics, which he credits to MIT’s Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee.
The normative question is whether benefits should be restricted at all. Here Gruber points to J-PAL, the Jameel Poverty Action Lab in MIT’s economics department. He credits it to the three 2019 Nobel winners, Duflo, Banerjee and Michael Kremer (now at Chicago), and calls it the world’s leading center for answering economic questions with randomized experiments. Its dozens of experiments in developing countries compare cash with goods. They find little cash goes to “bad” goods; nearly all goes to children’s education, food or shelter.

6---full-notes/categorical-imperative-pr.title: Categorical Imperative Procedure
6---full-notes/categorical-imperative-pr.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy
The Categorical Imperative Procedure and the Perturbed Social World
Details
The Categorical Imperative Procedure is Immanuel Kant’s practical framework for determining whether our intended actions align with universal moral duty. This procedure is not a simple algorithmic trap for catching liars; it is a profound thought experiment requiring sincere moral sensibility. The process begins with an agent’s subjective, sincere maxim: a rational policy outlining what they intend to do in specific circumstances to achieve and specific personal end. They must then generalize this personal maxim into a universal precept. This is then eventually converted into a hypothetical law of nature which they must adjoin to the existing laws of physics and human psychology to construct a “perturbed social world.”
From then, to determine if this action is morally permissible, the agent must subject it to a two-part test: they must be able to rationally intend to act within this world, and they must be able to consistently will that this world exists. Though it is an impenetrable test, it is also one that is too strict. This would then cause the moral law to inevitably cross some of the random personal desires; and so it would need to be evaluated from The Original Position rather.

6---full-notes/categorical-imperative.title: Categorical Imperative
6---full-notes/categorical-imperative.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy
Categorical Imperative
Details
To properly grasp Immanuel Kant’s moral framework, we must strictly separate the concept of the “rational” from the concept of the “reasonable.” When an individual formulates a maxim—a personal policy for action—we can evaluate its rationality using a hypothetical imperative. A hypothetical imperative simply asks whether the chosen means are effectively calculated to achieve the agent’s subjective desires or aims. However, Kant argues that our empirical desires cannot serve as the foundation of morality. Instead, true morality requires the Categorical Imperative Procedure, which represents the “reasonable.” In Kant’s philosophy, the reasonable has absolute priority over the rational and subordinates it completely. When an agent tests their intended action against the Categorical Imperative, they are never allowed to use the intensity or urgency of their personal desires to counterbalance or override the moral law. If an intended action fails the procedure, the agent must abandon or alter their maxim, even if it means repressing a deeply held desire.

6---full-notes/center-of-high-acuity-vis.title: Center of High-Acuity Vision (Fovea)
6---full-notes/center-of-high-acuity-vis.content:
Status: baby
Tags: psychology neuroscience
Center of High-Acuity Vision (Fovea)
Details
At the very center of the retina lies the fovea, a small pit that represents the pinnacle of visual acuity. When we need to see something with the utmost clarity—to read fine print or examine a detailed photograph—we instinctively move our eyes to focus the image directly onto this specialized region. The fovea’s power comes from its unique structure. It is composed exclusively of cones, the photoreceptors responsible for detail, and these cones have dedicated, almost one-to-one, neural pathways to the brain. This direct line preserves the maximum amount of visual information. Consequently, a disproportionately large area of the brain’s visual cortex is devoted to processing the rich stream of data that originates from the fovea.

Cessation of Tobacco
Details
Quitting usually requires an extensive motivation and commitment to the process, which includes a multi-modal approach combining behavioral changes with pharmacological support. Commitment can come in the sense of leveraging social pressure, ritualizing, setting a quitting date, or even therapy. They also have to deal with cravings, even though short lived, they can mimic the breathing they do when they smoke to alleviate it.
Pharmacologically, Nicotine Replacement Therapies (NRT) mitigate withdrawal symptoms without the toxicity of combustion. These include:


Over-the-counter: Nicotine gum (buccal absorption) and patches (transdermal maintenance).


Prescription: Nasal sprays and inhalers, which mimic the rapid onset of smoking more closely.


Additionally, antidepressants can also help, Bupropion (marketed as Zyban for smoking and Wellbutrin for depression) has proven effective in reducing cravings and relapse rates.

Chaining Habits
Details
To extend one’s list of good habits, we can use a method called Habit Linking (or Stacking). Because our environments are filled with cues, we can use an existing habit as the reliable cue for a new habit, chaining them together for ease of performance. The starting point is keeping track of a current habit and simply adding the new one immediately after. Furthermore, we can turbocharge this through “Pairing” (Temptation Bundling). Dopamine functions not just upon receiving a reward, but during the expectation and anticipation of pleasure. We can abuse this biological fact by pairing a habit we need to do alongside a habit we inherently want to do. The anticipation of the desired activity makes the difficult activity significantly more attractive.

6---full-notes/challenges-and-conclusion.title: Challenges and Conclusions in Nature-Nurture Research
6---full-notes/challenges-and-conclusion.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Cognitive Psychology genetics 3 - Tags/environment
Challenges and Conclusions in Nature-Nurture Research
Details
The elegant models of twin and adoption studies, while powerful, are complicated by the messy reality of human life and the dynamic interplay between genes and environment. For instance, the phenomenon of assortative mating—the tendency for individuals with similar traits to partner up—means that parents may be more genetically similar than assumed. This, in turn, makes their fraternal twin offspring share more than the expected 50% of their genes, shrinking the statistical difference between identical and fraternal twins and potentially skewing research results. Furthermore, adoption studies often can’t account for the potential of selective placement, where adoption agencies may place children with families who are similar to their biological parents.
These complexities lead to profound questions that defy easy answers. Is the prenatal environment of the biological mother, including factors like stress or diet, a genetic or an environmental effect? Is a child’s environment a function of their genotype, or is their genotype only expressed because of their environment? The research makes it clear that we can no longer think in simple, causal terms. The ultimate conclusion is that we are not solely our genes, nor are we solely the product of our life experiences. We are the result of a continuous, reciprocal, and deeply entangled relationship between our nature and our nurture, where each one constantly shapes and influences the other throughout our lives.

Child Monitoring

One of the difficulties in parenting is child monitoring, or more specifically, the degree of it. As the child grow, one cannot treat or monitor them as if they are still a child when they are a teenager and so on, but nonetheless it is difficult to assess how much monitoring one actually needs. Over monitoring stifles the child’s autonomy and results in rebellion or secrecy. Under monitoring results in them maybe getting into groups of delinquents, drug use, or risky behavior.

Children Bipolar Disorder
Details
For most of history, bipolar disorder has been considered a teenage or adult mental disorder. However, roughly 35 years ago, clinicians started diagnosing children who had ADHD or conduct problems with bipolar disorder. This change caused a massive upheaval in the psychiatric space as people argued whether they had bipolar or were just severely dysregulated. The main point was how different bipolar disorder presented itself in adults and children. Though adults may suffer from grandiose, euphoria in manic episodes, children have these things all the time. And so people would have to look for chronic irritability and explosive temper tantrums rather than distinct manic episodes. But because of this diagnosis, children started to be given heavy-duty mood stabilizers and antipsychotics, causing them to overdose.

6---full-notes/chmess.title: Chmess
6---full-notes/chmess.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy intelligence
Chmess
Details
In 2006, Daniel C. Dennett wrote about a fictional game he called “chmess.” This game, Dennett said, existed in the context of philosophy. I would suggest that it exists across all academic pursuits. The game of chmess is played by professional academics. In this game, a series of rules are mutually agreed upon. These rules may be Plato’s theories on this or that, Nietzsche’s ideas about some other thing. One individual enters the game of chmess. This happens in the form of papers, studies, or dissertations which are written about the agreed-upon rules. Another player engages the first individual, publishing some other thing about how the first player’s chmess moves were either triumphant or embarrassing. The two players fancy themselves quite good at chmess, and so they stick to it. The implications and applications of the rules are then debated, articulated, refined, and spun in circles. This goes on and on as more people enter the ongoing game, until we have a whole segment of individuals who have dedicated their lives to playing this game.
Thing is, all these people are just playing a game. They are not engaging with reality, the very reality that created the game, they are merely thinking thoughts upon thoughts of interpretation of that reality. The players are both parasites and producers, they cite each other work and make a result of their own, not knowing if that will even function in practice. We no longer have any experts on how to do a thing, but instead experts on how to do responses to a thing, or how to do a thing about a thing, or what is the nature of how to do a thing. We stop asking how knowledge can be applied to life, but instead how it can be applied to other knowledge. The result is some bizarrely irrelevant, self-sustaining cesspool of highly applauded works
Then the question becomes: “What do we do with all this knowledge when its only context is a self-contained circuit of other knowledge?”
Supporting Content

The Society of the Spectacle

6---full-notes/choice-in-determinism-and.title: Choice In Determinism and Free Will
6---full-notes/choice-in-determinism-and.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Choice In Determinism and Free Will
Details
While thinking about this problem, it may be productive first to try and define the meaning of “choice” as it is one of the main terms involved throughout the discussion. People often semantically hijack this term to use to debate, even though it is quite unproductive to do so. Incompatibilists frequently argue that if a brain state is determined by prior causes, a “choice” is an illusion. This though, ignores the standard acquisition and utility of the world. We learn the concept of choices through daily cases and context, not from the deterministic probability of the world. This is to say that the word “choice” is inherently BUILT on grounds not considering determinism, and so we cannot use determinism to try and redefine the function of the word. The compatibilists, on the other hand, think that our choices are simply a process guided by internal desires and purposes, regardless of if it was predetermined or not. And so, causal determinism does not negate existence of choice, provided we do not require acausal origins.

6---full-notes/choosing-personal-stateme.title: Choosing Personal Statement Topic
6---full-notes/choosing-personal-stateme.content:
Status: adult
Tags: university writing
Choosing Personal Statement Topic
Details
**What are admission committee looking for in a personal statement?
Content-wise, admission officers look for insights into what you would contribute to the college.
Many colleges give points to certain things which may not be obvious. Continuity of activity, showing consistency over years is valued at most colleges. Another factor which is valued is Intellectual Curiosity (IC), showing that you have broad interests and actively pursue them. Outside of that, well known factors like leadership, cooperation, and collaboration are valued. In the last few decades, demonstrations of cultural diversity and awareness have also been gaining prominence in admissions. Resilience, the ability to not only cope but to overcome adversity may not be specific rating but has been associated with higher rated essays. Lastly, self-reflection, metacognition, and the ability to process experiences have also shown relatively high performances on essays.
Very few essays will effectively show all of these things. What a student like yourself should do though, is try and incorporate as much as is possible without sacrificing narrative consistency.
What are the prompts?
There are two main college application platforms: Common Application and Coalition Application. Every year, these two platforms each publish a list of prompts for the personal statement. While the two lists are not entirely identical and vary slightly year to year, the most common prompts include:


Central aspect of your identity (background, activity, interest, talent, pursuit, etc.)


Overcoming a failure


Demonstration of leadership


Experience that challenged or changed your belief or perspective


Problem you would like to solve


Subject or idea that captivates you


The best way to approach these prompts is to sit down in a quiet space and brainstorm personal qualities and important events in your life. 
Begin by writing out 30 to 40 statements like:
I am a _________ person.
We will call these statements “quality statements.” 
From here, it is a good idea to write 5-10 statements like:
I impressed myself when ___________.
Then, see if you can write 5-10 statements like:
My life would have been completely different, if __________ had not happened.
We will call these two types of statements “experience statements.”
Whether you write it down or use post-it notes, or a brainstorming site on the web, use what works. Listen to music if you need to. Speak into a recording device while going for a walk if that is who you are. Whatever method you are using, make sure to carefully document all of your ideas so you can revisit them later. Having an organized process like this will provide you with the important material you need for the next steps. 
Tips for choosing the right topic
Tip 1: Pick something that shows your best qualities
The personal statement is designed for you to show college admissions who you are, in your own word. You should take this unique opportunity to show off some of your best qualities. 
“How do I do that?” You may ask. We recommend a process of quality mapping, where you connect specific experiences and stories with personal qualities that those experiences and stories demonstrate. 
Take a look at the experience statements you have written. Now, match each of these experience statements with 1-2 quality statements. Many quality statements might correspond with more than one experience statement. That is okay. You can put them all in one cluster. 
Our examples:

























ExperiencesQualitiesSpending 30 minutes every day to self-study Spanish and finding an online language speaking partner to practice.I am a disciplined person.I am someone who takes initiatives.Organizing my school’s annual potluck event to encourage my peers to share the cuisines of their countries.I am a responsible person.I am a culturally curious person.Taking care of my bedridden grandma’s the entire summer: feeding, washing, clothing her, etc. when my parents had to work.I am a patient person.I am a family-oriented person.
Once you are done with the quality mapping, you can start ranking your combinations. On a scale of 1 to 10, assign a score for each of the following criteria for each of your combinations (a maximum of 40 points possible for each combination):


These are qualities I am proud of and want to show to admission counselors.


This experience has made me a better person.


I have enough material to write about from this experience.


Writing about this experience/ these values adds something new to my application.


You can now use the total score to help you rank your story/qualities combinations, from which you can then connect to other experiences and expand to a broader topic.
Tip 2: Pick something that demonstrates personal growth
Whatever event or experience you choose to write about, it is critical to highlight how you have changed after the fact. For instance, in a successful essay to Northeastern University, a student reflects on losing her grandmother who suffered from Alzheimer’s and how that loss motivated her to become bolder, more resilient, and committed to bringing more goods to the world. The essay made evident how this mournful experience led to substantial growth in character and enabled the writer to undertake greater challenges.
Perhaps failing to get “first place” in an important competition forced you to re-evaluate your definition of failure and the metrics you use to measure self-worth. Perhaps an uncomfortable conversation with your best friend inspired you to confront your privileges and explore intercultural communication. Perhaps a brief encounter with a staff member at your local bakery completely shifted your understanding of and increased your appreciation for food science.
Your essay does not necessarily have to be about personal growth, but it does need a critical moment of change. Whatever it is you choose to write about, admission officers want to see how you have grown. In demonstrating personal growth, you are showing college admissions your potential to further develop with the help of their resources.
To get started, review at the statements you have written above: My life would have been completely different, if __________ had not happened. These experience statements offer great starting points because they carry moments of change. Go through each statement and ask yourself: What was I like before this event happened? What three words would I use to describe my personalities then? How did I use to handle difficult situations?
Then, what was I like after? What three words would I use to describe my personalities now? Does this change highlight the qualities in my quality mapping?
Tip 3: Tell a specific story
It is good to remember that when writing your personal statement, you are first and foremost a storyteller, sharing a personal narrative. You will want to provide enough details for your audience to be engaged in the story. 
Example 1: Something must have been so funny about me because people were looking at me and laughing all around. I was disoriented by my public humiliation. 
Example 2: Suddenly, I was overwhelmed by the laughter of the crowd. I wanted to understand what was so funny. Yet, wherever I looked, all the faces and fingers were directed at me, as if to accuse me of something. Yet, all the faces were in thralls of laughter, distended into some kind of riotous and terrifying mass.
These two examples discuss the same event: the writer feels overwhelmed while being scrutinized by a laughing crowd. However, the level of specificity differs dramatically. Example 1 is more generic with few descriptions. Example 2, on the other hand, provides evocative sensory inputs (fingers pointing, riotous thralls of laughter) to transport the audience to the scene and experience the event alongside the writer. 
Though the essay prompts are intentionally broad to give you maximum flexibility, don’t be tempted to tell your whole life story and run the risk of being disingenuous or shallow. You only have 650 words. 
Instead, choose a single theme, or even a single moment, to concentrate on. You can even choose to break things down scene-by-scene like one of our students who got into Northwestern University. What happened? Who was involved? Where and when did the relevant events occur? What was the space like? Were there any sounds? Colors? Scents? 
Remember that it is the depth, level of details, and thoughtfulness that make a memorable essay!**

6---full-notes/chronic-accessibility.content:

Chronic Accessibility
Details
What is Chronic Accessibility ? So basically, this concept entails the schemas of ourselves, based off of how influenced we are by our environment, culture, and so on. Its as if you’re chronically primed, like being called your name so many times, you would instinctually respond whenever someone calls it.
But this phenomenon also extends externally to other works like Romeo and Juliet, if you were to hear one, you would immediately jump to the other, or your brain would, unconsciously, it would bypass the cognitive barrier. So John Bargh (surprise surprise) did another hallmark experiment that proved this. By getting people who were chronically accessing the word “talkative” and what else, he would then prime them with a different word. Then after certain amounts of time, he would then test which word would come out if they were told a neutral story that could be interpreted either way ? Short time (15s) resulted in the primes winning, long time (180s) resulted in the chronic winning.
From that, we can conclude that even though primes have a significant effect on us shortly after we interact with them, who we are and what we are internally eventually drives it all back into our system after a certain amount of time.
Supporting Content
Even more interestingly, he then researched the effects the same things would have on behaviors, priming on behaviors. People would act accordingly to the words that they were primed with time ago in situations after. For example, in his RCTs, he let people see two words, rude or kind and then they were to then placed into a situation where they could act either way. If they were primed with rude, they would be ruder, if they were primed with kind, they would be kinder.

6---full-notes/chronic-stress-as-a-pathw.title: Chronic Stress as a Pathway to Depression
6---full-notes/chronic-stress-as-a-pathw.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology neurology biology
Chronic Stress as a Pathway to Depression
Details
Chronic psychological stress is a primary trigger for major depression, acting as the bridge between life experience and biological illness. Psychological stress that is defined by a lack of control, predictability, social support, and outlets for frustration activates the same biological stress response (e.g., glucocorticoid release) as a physical threat.
When faced with uncontrollable stress, an individual first enters an anxious state of frantic, maladaptive coping. Over time, if these efforts consistently fail, the system transitions into helplessness, the kind where one is no longer expecting success so they shut down. This state of learned helplessness is the psychological model for depression.
Repeated exposure to major stressors can lead to a phenomenon called kindling. After the first few depressive episodes are triggered by external events, the brain’s circuitry changes. The depressive state becomes “kindled,” like a fire that has caught, and begins to run on its own internal, endogenous rhythm, no longer requiring a major external stressor to be activated.
This is particularly true for early life stress. Childhood adversity, especially poverty, teaches a lifelong lesson in helplessness. This early training rewires the developing brain, making it more vulnerable to depression for the rest of the person’s life by altering the very structure of its stress and reward circuits.

6---full-notes/chunking-1.title: Chunking 1
6---full-notes/chunking-1.content:
Status: baby
Tags: psychology learning
Chunking
Details
Chunking is a powerful encoding strategy that helps overcome the natural limitations of short-term/working memory. While working memory can typically only hold a small number of items (around 7 +/- 2), chunking allows us to effectively increase this capacity by grouping individual elements into larger, meaningful units known as “chunks.”
This process works by organizing disparate items based on patterns, similarities, or meanings drawn from our long-term memory. For example, the 10-digit sequence 0912199010 is difficult to hold in memory. However, by chunking it into a familiar format like a date and a number, 09-12-1990-10, it becomes four manageable chunks. Similarly, the letter string FBICIAIRS becomes easy to recall when chunked into three familiar acronyms: FBI, CIA, IRS. By reducing the number of discrete items to be stored, chunking makes complex information easier to encode and recall.

6---full-notes/circumscribed-accuracy.title: Circumscribed Accuracy
6---full-notes/circumscribed-accuracy.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Circumscribed Accuracy
Details
Bill Swann (1984) posed quite a question: if FAD is so pervasive, why hasn’t social life collapsed ? Well, he shows that people visit same situations and such repeatedly. A waiter behaves subserviently every visit; even if you wrongly attribute this to his personality rather than his job, your prediction of his future behavior in that restaurant remains correct. You’re wrong about why but right about what he’ll do next time. The error only surfaces when you encounter him outside the restaurant and ask him to fetch you a Diet Coke from 7-Eleven. Second, outside the lab, people choose their situations—a librarian probably does prefer quiet environments, so the dispositional inference that happens to be wrong for the wrong reasons may accidentally be right. Third, prolonged situational exposure may genuinely reshape personality, making initially wrong dispositional attributions retroactively accurate. The implication is unsettling: we navigate social life successfully not because our reasoning is sound, but because ecological regularities compensate for systematic inferential errors.

Clarifying Addiction
Details
Even though people attribute addiction to simply the overall symptoms like having physical or psychological reactions to a drug, it is in fact much more complicated than that. We are actually able to split the generally accepted meaning of addiction into three much more detailed terms.
Firstly, addiction, still, basically means the inability to control drug use (The Drug Abuse Potential), regardless of whether physical dependence withdrawal symptoms are present or not. Secondly is the termed just mentioned, physical dependence, which are symptoms that a person physically present when they are “off” the drug. And lastly psychological dependence which manifests in cravings or need.
But to exemplify this further, we will consider the example of a patient who is on opiates due to chronic pain or medical conditions, this individual may have physical dependence symptoms but is not actually addicted to the medication, simply using it to function. An addict of something like morphine on the other hand will have more signs, like looking different, or psychological dependence.
Supporting Content
The DSM on the other hand… it does have a diagnostic for addiction but is rather named “Substance Dependence”. To be diagnosed, a patient must exhibit three of seven criteria, which include tolerance and withdrawal, but also behavioral markers like time spent obtaining the drug and giving up social activities.

6---full-notes/class-and-the-values-of-c.title: Class and the Values of Child-Rearing
6---full-notes/class-and-the-values-of-c.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology
Class and the Values of Child-Rearing
Details
The pioneering research of sociologist Melvin Kohn showed us a consistent pattern of the alignment of parents’ values and their own children.
Middle-class parents, whose professional careers often demand autonomy, creativity, and self-direction, consistently value independence and self-reliance in their children. They encourage them to question authority, negotiate for themselves, and develop their unique talents. In contrast, working-class parents, whose jobs historically required following orders, adhering to strict procedures, and showing deference to supervisors, tend to value obedience and conformity more highly. This is not because they are inherently more authoritarian, but because they are engaging in a rational adaptation. They are equipping their children with the cultural tools they believe are necessary to survive and thrive in the world they know. Kohn’s research further showed that when working-class parents had jobs with more autonomy and protection—such as those in unionized factories—their values shifted to more closely resemble those of the middle class, reinforcing the direct link between one’s position in the economic structure and the cultural values one transmits.

6---full-notes/cognitive-dissonance.title: Cognitive Dissonance
6---full-notes/cognitive-dissonance.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Cognitive Dissonance
Details
Festinger witnessed this at scale when he embedded himself in Marian Keech’s doomsday cult, The Seekers. Members had abandoned careers and families based on a prophecy that the world would end December 21, 1954. When nothing happened, they faced catastrophic dissonance. Rather than admitting error, the leaders announced God was so impressed by their faith that He spared the entire world. Disconfirmation was reframed as ultimate confirmation. This looks absurd from outside, but the same mechanism operates constantly in ordinary life — the person rejected by a romantic interest who suddenly claims they “were never that interested,” the reality show contestant eliminated early who insists it proves they were “too strong.” The structure is always identical: when reality contradicts belief, belief bends reality rather than breaking itself.
The deepest paradox here is about authenticity. People are powerfully motivated to see themselves as consistent and authentic (Hypothesis 5). Yet dissonance reduction involves changing beliefs after the fact to align with actions already taken — a process that looks transparently inconsistent to anyone watching. But from the inside, rationalization doesn’t feel like changing your story. The attitude shift is experienced as genuine realization, not motivated distortion. This is precisely what makes it so effective and so invisible to the person doing it: the mechanism that produces inauthenticity generates the subjective experience of authenticity. If you could feel yourself rationalizing, it wouldn’t work.
