6---full-notes/cognitive-therapy.title: Cognitive Therapy
6---full-notes/cognitive-therapy.content:
Status: adult
Tags:  psychology CBT
Cognitive Therapy
Details
The cognitive therapist assists the patient to apply the problem-solving techniques he has used throughout his life on himself. Basically they help patients to identify their faulty thinking and learn better ways to formulate these experiences. By viewing it as more of an everyday misunderstanding, it would start to make sense to the patient because it is in line with his previous experiences.
Psychoanalysis was all about digging deep into the unconscious mind, looking for hidden drives and past conflicts. Behaviorism, on the other hand, wanted to be strictly scientific and objective, focusing only on observable behaviors and how they were learned through rewards and punishments. Both were influential, but Beck points out they both kind of ignored the active role of conscious thoughts, interpretations, and beliefs in people’s emotional problems. They hit a wall, realizing there were “legitimate and important problems left unsolved” because they weren’t paying attention to the “cognitive realm.”
Interestingly, both schools started shifting slightly towards this middle ground. Within psychoanalysis, Ego Psychology started getting more attention. Thinkers like Hartmann, Kris, and Rapaport began focusing more on how people adapt to reality and the functions of the conscious mind – essentially, cognitive processes. Meanwhile, behaviorists, who had always studied learning, started looking beyond simple physical actions (like pressing a lever) or memorizing nonsense. They got interested in how people learn concepts, words, and complex thought processes – things that are definitely cognitive. Beck calls this a “growing confluence,” like streams merging together.
This is where cognitive psychology and therapy really stepped in. It directly addressed those thinking processes that the other schools were starting to edge towards. It focused on how our interpretations, assumptions, and core beliefs shape our feelings and actions. Beck makes a key point: even therapists who still identified as psychoanalytic or behaviorist began increasingly using cognitive techniques with their patients. Behavior therapy, for example, started incorporating methods aimed at changing thought patterns, even if the overall therapy was still presented as behavior-based

6---full-notes/cognitive-change-in-the-h.title: Cognitive change in the human behavior
6---full-notes/cognitive-change-in-the-h.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology learning CBT
Cognitive change in the human behavior
Details
The cognitive method can be applied for any patient, but certainly it will work most to the people who have the ability to introspect and reflect about their own thoughts. As this method to therapy is just an extension and refinement of what people have been doing to various degrees since the earliest stages of their intellectual development. They have always been making, building up hypotheses then testing, weeding out, which then will get sorted into the skills that they unconsciously use.
This type of function is actually analogous to the formation of speech in which how the rules of pronunciation and grammatical construction are applied without us consciously thinking about the rules. When learning a new language or having problem speaking a language which one has already supposedly “mastered” they must focus on forming the sentence by seeing the rules and such. Same goes for cognitive therapy, one must focus on the rules which he is applying to make false judgements, and in so he will find that such rule is incorrect to change it.
As this can easily become a habit that is hard to get rid of (as the patient is not aware of it), we must take several steps to correct it. Firstly, we have to make him aware of it, secondly, he needs to recognize which thoughts are awry. Then he has to substitute such thoughts. Finally, he needs feedback to inform him if he was correct in changing it. The same kind of sequence is necessary in correcting faults like playing an instrument, or sports.
Supporting Content
To illustrate the process of cognitive change, let us take as a rather gross example a person who is afraid of all strangers. When we explore his reactions, we may find that he is operating under the rule, “All strangers are unfriendly or hostile.” In this case, the rule is wrong. On the other hand, he may realize that strangers vary, but he may not have learned to discriminate among friendly strangers, neutral strangers, and unfriendly strangers. In such a case, his trouble is in applying the rule, that is, in converting the available information in a given situation into an appropriate judgment.
It is obvious that not all people who think erroneously need or want to get their thinking straightened out. When a person’s erroneous ideation disrupts his life or makes him feel miserable, then he becomes a candidate for some form of help.

Cognitive content of the emotional disorders
Details
The capacity of human beings to adapt and integrate themselves into society (which consists of myriad environmental events) proves the ability and depth of our own psychological system. Despite all of the abilities that we have from this singular system, there are of course some challenges that we do not respond consistently to.
These are “fault lines” which stresses accumulate and may set up for total eruptions that can be labeled as “over-reacting.” Under such conditions unrealistic appraisals will override the realistic ones, and we may realize that our reactions are largely irrational.
Some people can be so engulfed in these fantasies that their behaviors become controlled by it all. And so when these reactions burgeon beyond a certain point or level, then we are likely to label them into the categories of “mental illnesses” which can include “emotional disorder,” “neurosis,” “psychological disturbance” or “psychiatric disease”. These things frequently assume a characteristic that allows them to be fitted into recognized category such as depression, anxiety state, or paranoid state. Although related to the aforementioned, these differ from normal reactions due to the intrusion of unrealistic thinking of the key aspects of the patient’s life.

6---full-notes/college-application-check.title: College Application Checklist
6---full-notes/college-application-check.content:
Status: adult
Tags: university writing
College Application Checklist
Details
Things you need to do:


Make substantial and consistent academic progress at school


Aim to achieve and maintain a GPA of 3.5 or higher.


Make substantial and consistent personal progress outside of class


Cultivate intellectual curiosity and personal qualities such as resilience, leadership, diversity and awareness, collaboration, creativity, curiosity, etc. (Check out our blog for more information.)


Commit to clubs and extra-curricular activities that align with your personal interests.


Prepare for and take standardized tests.


Develop a shortlist of colleges to apply to.


Develop your set of criteria for selecting a college. (Check out our blog for more tips on this topic).


Research.


Record your information in an easily accessible spreadsheet or document.


Register for the Common Application or Coalition Application (and any other school-specific application portal).


Fill out and submit your application. We elaborate on the different components of the application below.


Write your essays.


Compile a list of extra-curricular commitments, work, and family responsibilities.


Compile a list of honors, awards, and achievements.


Prepare your resume.


Fill out and submit your financial aid/ scholarship application. Gather the following materials:


Income and tax information from parents/ legal guardians (such as the completed tax returns, W-2 forms, and other records of current year income).


Records of untaxed income.


Records savings, stocks, bonds, and trusts.


Records of small businesses and other assets.


Bank statements.


Ask for letters of recommendation from 2-3 teachers.


Give them at least 3 weeks to write your letters.


Remind them 3-5 business days before the deadline if they have not submitted your letters.


Send in your standardized test scores.


Make sure you have the right school codes if submitted through an online portal, and the right school address if mailed.


Work closely with your school counselor to make sure they submit your school report to each school on your shortlist.


Things you need to submit:
Submitted by you

The application: Some colleges, notably the UC system, have their own application form. Most colleges use the Common Application or the Coalition Application—unified undergraduate admissions portals—that allow you to apply to multiple college at the same time and through the same portal. Below, we outline the different things that colleges ask for in the application:



Personal information: this includes your name, date of birth, contact information (email address, home address, phone number, high school), standardized test scores, and other demographic information.


Family information: this includes their name, email address, phone number, occupation, highest education level. 


Coursework: a list of current or most recent year courses.


Standardized test scores: you will self-report your scores in the application. This is separate from the official test report, which will be sent from respective testing organizations (such as ETS for the TOELF, College Board for the SAT).


Extra-curriculars: a list of things you have done outside of class and how much time you devoted to it. In addition to tradition extra-curricular activities such as student clubs and organizations, make sure to include any part-time jobs, internships, community service, or other family obligations such as taking care of grandparents/ siblings, mowing your neighbor’s lawn, etc.


Honors & awards: a list of any honors and awards you have received, along with the context. For what did you receive the award? How many people received the award? Why is this award important or relevant?


Resume (optional)


Disciplinary infractions: information of any suspensions or expulsions.


Application fee: you will need to pay an application fee for every college you apply to. The amount varies by school. Fee waivers are available depending on your eligibility, so if the cost is a barrier, make sure to check in with your school counselor and the college’s admissions office.



Standardized test scores: Schools require you to submit official score reports, which must be sent directly from the testing organization’s online portal. Each school has a specific school code for receiving test scores, which you input in the portal. You can select colleges to receive your scores while you are registering for the tests. Alternatively, you can choose to send it later, after you get your scores back.



The two standardized tests are the SAT (through College Board) and the ACT (through the ACT). Many schools have adopted a test-optional policy due to the COVID pandemic. You should check each college’s website carefully to determine whether you need to submit the SAT/ACT.


For international students, you will need to submit one of the following proofs of proficiency: TOELF (through ETS), IELTS (through British Council IDP), or Duolingo English Test (through Duolingo). You might be able to waive this proficiency requirement if you attend a high school in an English-speaking country or if your high school’s language of instruction is English. You should check each college’s website carefully to determine whether you need to submit your proficiency test scores.



Financial aid/ Scholarship applications: If you are applying for federal loans, make sure to fill out the FAFSA. If you are an international student, make sure to fill out your CSS Profile. Some colleges also have specific merit-based scholarships or need-based financial aid packages that you might be interested in applying. 

Submitted by your school counselor


Official high school transcript: The official transcript details each of the classes you have taken in high school, as well as the grades and credits you have earned. This transcript will have the school’s official letterhead and seal and is sent directly to each college by the school counselor. Make sure you keep your school counselor updated of deadlines so they can submit your high school transcript on time.


Mid-year and Final-year grade reports: The initial transcript included in your application only details your classes and grades through the end of the junior year. Colleges typically ask your school counselor to submit an updated transcript half-way through your senior year, and again at the end of the year. Colleges reserve the right to change their admission decision if there is a significant, inexplicable deterioration in your academic performance (meaning: they might reject you even after you have been accepted).


School report/ Counselor recommendation: The report and recommendation allow your school counselor to situate your academic experience in the context of your larger graduating class. They typically provide information about your school and class (how many students, how many AP classes offered, college attendance rate, your academic strength in relation to your class, etc.) If you take a “non-traditional” course at school, this report might also include an information sheet explaining the nature of the course. The counselor will also be able to provide insights into any special circumstances you may have faced in high school, as well as what your contribution to the high school’s academic and social community.


Submitted by your teacher

Letter of recommendation: This letter allows the teacher to speak to your academic performance in class, and secondarily, your extra-curricular presence if they happen to supervise a club or organization you are a part of.

This is the third category of extrinsic aids and a part of books that aren’t necessarily connected to each other but rather guides. These references should be use wisely, and sparingly.
This is because that commentators are not always right, their works can be enormously useful, but this does not mean that it is always. These guides are used to support students and so it will contain the details and definitions necessary to pass a class, not understand a book deeply.
The second reason is that to not be enslaved to them, you should try to discover the important meanings of a book yourself as reading a commentary can limit yourself to that realm of knowledge, even though there is more. And so the advice to read reference books are… to read it after one has read and tried to understand the book (like a conversation or questioning).
The rule of extrinsic reading given here applies also to abstracts and plot digests. They are useful in two connections, but in those two only. First, they can help to jog your memory of a book’s contents, if you have already read it. Ideally, you made such an abstract yourself, in reading the book analytically, but if you have not done so, an abstract or digest can be an important aid. Second, abstracts are useful when you are engaged in syntopical reading, and wish to know whether a certain work is likely to be germane to your project. An abstract can never replace the reading of a book, but it can sometimes tell you whether you want or need to read the book or not.

6---full-notes/comparative-analysis-of-q.content:
Status: adult

Comparative Analysis of QuAIC vs Triage Risk Levels
Details
A primary test for a screening tool like the QuAIC is its ability to produce results consistent with those of a trained expert. The study found a “high degree of overlap between levels of concern determined by triage and levels of concern determined by the QuAIC”. This finding, which speaks to the tool’s concurrent validity, is the study’s most direct piece of evidence supporting its use. The paper concludes that the QuAIC levels “closely matched the overall triage risk level, demonstrating a high degree of consistency with professional judgment”.  
The specific data supporting this conclusion are presented in Table 3 of the source document and summarized below in Table 2 for clarity.  





























Table 2: Comparative Analysis of QuAIC vs. Triage Risk Levels (n=256)Concern LevelHighestHighModerateLowNot Applicable / NoneSource: Data from Darwinkel, Chan & Sheridan (2020), Table 3
The data in Table 2 reveal a remarkable degree of alignment, particularly at the upper end of the risk spectrum where accuracy is most critical. For the “Highest” concern level, there is a perfect match, with both methods identifying exactly 5 cases (2.0%). For the “High” concern level, the numbers are nearly identical (82 cases for QuAIC vs. 84 for Triage Risk). This strong concordance indicates that the QuAIC, when used by non-clinicians, can effectively identify and flag high-priority cases in a manner that aligns with a more holistic professional assessment. The minor discrepancies in the “Moderate” and “Low” categories are also informative, likely reflecting the SPJ process in action, where the practitioner might use information from the warning signs checklist or other contextual factors to slightly adjust a final rating up or down from the QuAIC’s initial output.

Competitive Infanticide as a Reproductive Strategy
Details
The killing of infants by adults of the same species, particularly by males, is not pathological behavior. It is a predictable, adaptive strategy under specific conditions. Competitive infanticide occurs when a new male takes over a breeding group and the average time a female spends nursing (and thus not ovulating) is longer than the average time the new male can expect to remain dominant. This concept would support the individual selection theory. The killings of the infant ensures that other males’ genes will not be passing on and that the female would start ovulating again so that they can mate.

Compliance Techniques
Details
Beyond group conformity, there are techniques to exploit psychological principles to change behavior without changing beliefs. The foot-in-the-door technique leverages our desire for self-consistency: residents who agreed to display a tiny “Drive Carefully” sign were later 76% likely to accept a large, ugly version of the same sign, versus near-zero compliance from those approached only with the large request. Agreeing to the small request caused people to encode themselves and identify themselves as “the kind or person who cares about the neighborhood safety,” and subsequently requests that fit this identity were accepted to maintain consistency. The lowball technique is another: a car salesman offers 25,000, you mentally purchase the BMW during the 10-minute wait, and when he returns saying 35,000, the psychological calculation isn’t “do I want to pay 35K?" but "do I want to pay 10K to avoid losing the car I already own in my mind?”

6---full-notes/comprehension-principle-a.title: Comprehension Principle and Russell's Shadow
6---full-notes/comprehension-principle-a.content:
Status: teen
Tags: logic
Comprehension Principle and Russell’s Shadow
Details
Sets are typically named in two ways, listing elements or by providing a defining property for it. The latter relies on the Naive Comprehension Principle, which suggests that for any property, there exists a set containing exactly those things to satisfy said property, being \{x : x \text{ is } \phi\}.
However, the reason this is naive is because when pushed to the logical extreme, it actually fails. If we attempt to define a set consisting of “all sets that are not elements of themselves,” we encounter Russell’s Paradox. If this set contains itself, it contradicts its own definition; if it does not contain itself, it satisfies the definition and must be included. This paradox revealed that the naive ability to define sets by arbitrary properties is flawed, necessitating a more rigorous, restricted approach to set formation in twentieth-century mathematics to avoid such logical absurdities.

Computational Processes
Details
The mechanical application of logic involves two distinct, inverse processes: Evaluation and Satisfaction. Evaluation is a forward-chaining where, given a truth assignment, one calculates the resulting truth value of a complex sentence. Satisfaction on the other hand is reverse-search. Given a logical sentence, the goal is to discover which possible truth assignments render the sentence true. which is the truth table. While conceptually simple, this method reveals a critical complexity constraint: the size of a truth table grows exponentially (2^n) with the number of constants. Consequently, proving satisfiability for large systems becomes a computationally expensive task, distinguishing it sharply from the linear simplicity of evaluation.

Computer Functionalism
Details
The dominant view in psychology and artificial intelligence (AI) for the last several decades has been the Computer Model of the Mind. For the AI, its rules (algorithms) are the states and its physical symbols (syntaxes) are the inputs and outputs.
The litmus test for this model is the Turing Test, proposed by Alan Turing in 1950. Turing argued that if a computer could converse with a human (e.g., in English) so convincingly that the human could not distinguish it from another person, we must grant that the machine is intelligent. This relies on a behaviorist assumption: if the output is indistinguishable from human intelligence, the internal process must be equivalent. John Searle challenges this by arguing that a machine can pass the Turing Test—simulating intelligence perfectly—without having any genuine understanding or mental life, or the Chinese test.

6---full-notes/concepts-of-humane-and-in.content:
Status: adult
Tags: science
Concepts of humane and inhumane
Details
Russell and Burch sought out to understood and basically defined what it meant for us as people experimenting on animals to be humane or inhumane. And so the concepts of humanity and inhumanity that they came up with is purely descriptive and empirical, meaning they will refer only to the objectively verifiable and measurable aspects of the process, not the ethical or psychological reasons of it all.
Inhumanity can be defined in many ways, and most of the time it is the ethical and philosophical aspects of it that matters in these discussions. But that is subjective, so due to that fact, we will instead define it like a metric, like the amount of distress that an animal can be subjected to, its mental states. The first of these states is the state of conflict, which is characterized to be when an animal is beset by 2 or more external forces, making them feel fear. This derives from the fact that their primary response to danger, flight, is neutralized, which is some of the same of humans and so it becomes a neuros or an acutely unpleasant state, similarly to anxiety. Although we cannot exactly quantify the levels of these states, we know they exist and there is a metric defining which is worse. Prolonged time in these states can make the animal have physiologic stress syndrome, affecting their body and systems.
But further than that, they also define inhumanity into categories as well, direct and contingent. Direct is defined by the fact that certain amounts of distress are completely unavoidable in the process of experimenting, or “the infliction of distress as an unavoidable consequence of the procedure employed, as such, even if it is conducted with perfect efficiency and completely freed of operations irrelevant to the object in view”. In contrast, contingent inhumanity is defined as “the infliction of distress as an incidental and inadvertent by-product of the use of the procedure, which is not necessary for its success.”
Finally, they also define it by the sum of the amount of distress in a group, like how the decreased amount of pain inflicted on one animal will reduce the sum total of pain that animals as a whole would have sustained. And so in certain situations, we would have choices to decide whether or not we want to inflict all the pain onto one or spread the pain out onto multiple (which can be applicable to overall to reduce the sum total distress).

“We may, then define distress of a certain degree (of whatever origin) as a central nervous state of a certain rank on a scale, in the direction of the mass autonomic response which if protracted, would lead to the physiologic stress syndrome. Inhumane procedures are those which drive the animal’s mood down in rank toward this point. Removing inhumanity must ultimately mean driving the animal as near the other end of the scale as we can. “More humane” then simply means “less inhumane” in the above sense. … We need only add that inhumanity can take two forms—acute and chronic—with no doubt every possible gradation between the two (24, italics in original).16”

6---full-notes/conformity-without-author.title: Conformity without Authority
6---full-notes/conformity-without-author.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Conformity without Authority
Details
What drives conformity ? Two distinct mechanisms: informational influence operates when situations are ambiguous, Sherif’s autokinetic effect had groups estimate movement of a stationary light dot in a dark room, and within trials, individuals’ wildly divergent estimates converged to a shared group norm. Due to the ambiguity, people believed others might possess better information, and so they internalized that the group answers were correct, which reduced anxiety. Another follow-up study demonstrated the extent of this effect even further, replacing group members one by one across 20 rounds; by round 20, no original members remained, yet the arbitrary norm established by the first three persisted. Normative influence on the other hand, operates when the correct answer is obvious: Asch showed subjects a line-matching task with an unambiguous correct answer. And you know what happens next. The majority giving the false answer making the minority do the same thing out of fear of social rejection.

6---full-notes/conformity.title: Conformity
6---full-notes/conformity.content:
Status: teen
Tags: 3 - Tags/Social Psychology
Conformity
Details
Conformity is the act of altering one’s behavior or opinions to match those of other people or to align with social expectations. While many people believe they are non-conformists, the pressure to go along with the group is a powerful and often underestimated social force.
Asch’s Classic Experiment Psychologist Solomon Asch conducted a famous experiment to see if people would conform to a majority view, even if it was obviously incorrect.


The Setup: A participant was placed in a group with several other people (who were secretly confederates of the experimenter). The group was shown a standard line and then asked to identify which of three comparison lines was the same length. The task was simple, and the correct answer was clear.


The Deception: On 12 out of 18 trials, the confederates were instructed to unanimously give the same wrong answer. The real participant was positioned to answer only after hearing most of the others give their incorrect responses.


The Surprising Results: Asch found that the pressure to conform was remarkably strong. 74% of participants conformed to the incorrect majority at least once. On average, participants conformed on about one-third (33%) of the trials where the group was wrong. When interviewed later, some participants said they conformed because they thought the group must be right, while others admitted they knew the group was wrong but went along out of fear of ridicule.

6---full-notes/connections-of-the-centra.content:
Status: adult
Tags: biology psychology
Connections of the Central Nervous System to the body
Details
The CNS connects with the body through nerve fibers that conduct excitation towards the brain and spinal cord or away from them. These fibers that transmit info from the sense organs to the brain and spinal cord are called afferent nerves. The fibers that transmit the messages from the CNS to the effectors, the muscles and glands are the organs of actions, or efferent nerves.
The spinal cord is a trunk line of the fibers: some are efferent, some are afferent, with still others just making local internal connections within the cord. These connections can initiate or regulate movements on their own and modulate the sensory info as it gets to the brain.
Not all nerves between the body and brain are through the spinal cord though. Separate nerves, twelve pairs in all, enter and exit from the hindbrain (the parts that connects with the spinal cord) and poke through holes in the skull. These are cranial nerves, and they have both functions of the above. They control the movements of the head and neck, carry sensations and regulate various glandular secretions in the head, control life-sustaining visceral functions, like digestion and excretion.
All this culminate to the peripheral nervous system, with two divisions, called the somatic, which controls the skeleton and transmission from the sense organs, and autonomic, set of spinal and cranial nerves that regulate and inform the brain about the viscera.

Consumer Choice
Details
This is the result that we derive from as we combine Budget Constraint with the Indifference curves and tradeoffs, or in particular the tangency. As the indifference curves represent the customer’s preferences and the budget constraint represents their ability to fulfill these preferences, bundled with the fact that higher indifferences curves are preferred, the best affordable bundle is the point where they touch each other at the highest point.
The tangency represents the equality between these two different slopes, and mathematically, they are perfect when they are equal. In the pizza-cookie example, the MRS is the negative ratio of marginal utilities, while the MRT is the negative ratio of prices. Setting them equal gives the central rule of consumer utility maximization: the ratio of marginal utilities equals the ratio of prices. This means the consumer chooses a bundle where the subjective value of another cookie relative to another pizza slice matches the relative cost of cookies and pizza in the market. If the consumer values cookies more than their market cost, they should buy more cookies and less pizza. If they value pizza more than its market cost, they should buy more pizza and fewer cookies.

6---full-notes/consumer-surplus.title: Consumer Surplus
6---full-notes/consumer-surplus.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Consumer Surplus
Details
Positive economics describes how things are; normative economics asks how they should be. Until now, the course has been entirely positive. Take Lecture 8’s result that long-run competitive profits are zero:

For consumers, that’s great: prices are as low as they can go, because firms produce at minimum average cost.
For producers, it’s bad, and maybe we care about firms too, since they’re the ones who hire us.

To measure if this is good or not, we have to use “welfare economics,” which measures the wellness of society in its entirety.
The obvious move would be to use utility, but it is only ordinal. Only the ranking means anything, so utils can’t be added up or compared. Economists for around this with something called “compensating variation.”Instead of asking how happy something makes you, ask how much you’d pay to get it, or how much you’d need to be paid to give it up. This is revealed preference: people show what they value through what they’d pay.
Consumer surplus is the benefit a customer gains from a good beyond what they paid for it. Gruber’s example is his favorite band’s tours:
If he’d pay only $90, he doesn’t go.

If he’d pay exactly $100, he’s indifferent. He might go, but he gets no surplus.
If he’d pay 300–400, which is more realistic for a first show, going leaves him 200–300 better off than if the concert had never happened.

The willingness to pay can be drawn as the demand curve here, the surplus would be the area below it and above the price.
Willingness to pay is just the demand curve, so consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price (Figure 9-6). Gruber’s demand starts at about 500 for the first concert and falls to 100 by the fifth. Suppose it falls by 100 per concert. Then at a 100 ticket his surplus is 400 + 300 + 200 + 100 + 0 = $1,000, and the fifth concert adds nothing.
A student asked what surplus actually does for you. Nothing is stored up. It’s simply a money measure of how much better off the purchase makes you. Anyone who has thought “what a deal, I’d have paid twice that” has felt it.
Market consumer surplus works the same way for the whole gas market (Figure 9-7). To keep it simple, suppose each person buys one gallon, so the quantity axis counts people, lined up from the most eager buyer to the least. At 3 a gallon, the 1,000th person (A) is indifferent. Everyone to their right doesn't buy, and everyone to their left gains surplus. The total is the triangle under demand and above 3.
Because demand curves can be written down and that area computed, there’s now a measurable stand-in for utility. With it, you can make normative statements.
A price rise from 3 to 3.50 (Figure 9-8) costs consumers in two ways:

The first 900 people still buy, but each pays 50 cents more. That’s a rectangle: 900 × 0.50 = 450.
People 901 to 1,000 stop buying and lose the surplus they had. That’s a small triangle; if demand is a straight line there, it’s ½ × 100 × 0.50 = 25.

The total loss is a trapezoid, $475 here. The lecture only draws the shapes; the dollar figures assume a straight-line demand curve between the two points.

6---full-notes/contestable-markets.title: Contestable markets
6---full-notes/contestable-markets.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Contestable markets
Details
Between monopoly and competition lies the contestable market: one firm may dominate, but entry is cheap enough that if it charged a full monopoly price, rivals would come in. The threat of entry keeps its price down.
Airlines are the famous case. When Gruber was a kid, airlines were a regulated monopoly: the government decided who could fly which routes and at what fares, and, fed inflated cost figures by the airlines, it set fares high. Economists argued that the market was contestable, so regulation was unnecessary. They won, and airlines were deregulated. The results:

Fares fell by about a third. In the 1980s Gruber flew Boston to Newark on People Express for $19.99, with no reservation and payment collected on board.
Routes multiplied, because many routes the government hadn’t allowed turned out to be profitable.
Quality collapsed. Free food and drinks, real silverware, legroom and free bags all disappeared. Under regulated fares, airlines on the same route could compete only on quality; once they could compete on price, well they dropped the ball on everything to keep prices low (but of course quality nowadays can’t be too low).
Safety didn’t fall. It was excellent before and stayed excellent.
Economists missed one barrier: airport slots. Runways and gates are almost impossible to add — Boston’s Logan had one runway at night until about 12 years ago, and adding a second took 25 years. Airlines built hub-and-spoke networks around airports they dominate, like Northwest at Minneapolis, which threatened to leave and take its jobs if the city gave its slots to rivals. So competition rose less than hoped.

Is the fall in quality bad? Gruber uses revealed preference. High quality at high prices is still available: you can fly business class, or start a premium airline (JetBlue tried, then drifted back toward the pack). Low-cost airlines keep entering and high-end ones don’t, so people are choosing low price over high quality. Everyone would prefer high quality at a low price, but that isn’t on offer.
The lesson: industry is endlessly creative at protecting profits, so policy has to anticipate how firms will respond, not assume the industry will stay as it is today.

Context, Hidden Premises, and the Three Levels
Details
In our society, we reason logically a lot, and we do so mostly with suppressing the premises instead of stating them outright and rationalizing them completely so. But this could also prove to be conspicuous, because bad reasoning can hide in those hidden premises. Real-world arguments routinely leave premises unstated. “It’s Friday, so Marianne’s wearing jeans” omits “Marianne always wears jeans on Friday.” We suppress premises when context makes them obvious. But hidden premises are also where bad reasoning hides — a dubious assumption left unexamined because it was never made explicit. Surfacing suppressed premises is a core skill.
There are three levels to talking about arguments and about how the premises are hidden. Firstly, language, the word red has three letters; secondly, the thought red is a concept of it; and lastly, the property of it. They are three factors that we as human can comprehend and understand yet no one else can.

6---full-notes/contractualism-and-utilit.title: Contractualism and Utilitarianism
6---full-notes/contractualism-and-utilit.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy
Contractualism and Utilitarianism
Details
Both are impartial moral theories. But these two differ massively. Utilitarianism is a consequentialist moral model - it is concerned with bringing about the best possible outcomes.
Nonetheless, there are three fundamental contrasts between these philosophies. The first area is one of scope. Utilitarianism applies to every area of morality whilst contractualism only covers the realm of what we owe to one another.
Contractualism also does not aggregate, it focuses on the standpoint of individuals as persons. It also does not regard well-being as the singular moral concept but allows a variety of reasons.
The only reasons for and against a principle that count when we are judging whether or not it can be reasonably rejected are “various individuals’ reasons for objecting to that principle and alternatives to it” (Scanlon 1998, p. 229). The acceptability of a principle depends on a one-by-one assessment of the strength of the reasons that individuals would have for rejecting the principle, compared to the alternatives to it. Since individuals must be objecting on their own behalf and not on behalf of a group, this restriction to single individuals’ reasons bars the interpersonal aggregation of complaints; it does not allow a number of lesser complaints to outweigh one person’s weightier complaint.

6---full-notes/controlled-processes.title: Controlled Processes
6---full-notes/controlled-processes.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Social Psychology
Controlled Processes
Details
Controlled processes are intentional, require awareness, interfere with other controlled processes, demand effort, and tend to be linguistic. You will never accidentally find yourself counting backwards by sevens from 16,358. These properties are the exact inverse of automatic processes.
They are also simultaneously the reason that we have buildings, electricity, architecture, science, these fields all combine the understanding and perception of multiple fields that require well, knowledge on multiple things to build it.
Yet, they are also the reason that people can feel safe in their certain logical system when the logic itself is GARBAGE. Two extended examples:
The elevator. The lecturer has elaborate rules about which floors it’s acceptable to take the elevator between, modulated by time of day and direction. He presents this as a rational system — but then admits the entire logic reduces to “I don’t want you on my elevator when I’m trying to go somewhere.” If he worked on the 8th floor instead of the 4th, every rule would shift accordingly. He catches himself judging a person in a suit taking the elevator one floor (probably a visitor who doesn’t know the building) and even after having gout himself and taking the elevator one floor, he still doesn’t extend that charitable interpretation to others. The logic feels valid because it’s complex and reportable. It isn’t.
The Monty Python witch. Witches burn → wood burns → wood floats → ducks float → if she weighs the same as a duck, she’s a witch. Each step sounds locally reasonable. The woman herself agrees it seems fair. The whole chain is insane. Hyperbolic, but it demonstrates how step-by-step conscious reasoning can feel compelling while being completely detached from reality.
The point is, when the logical chain is linguistical and reproducible, we tend to value it much higher even if it is completely horseshit. What is not on the other hand, like gut feeling, gets dismissed way more.

Core Deficit of Communication Disorders
Details
The core deficit of the majority of reading disorders is auditory and linguistic. It is the failure of phonological awareness, unable to realize that words are made up of different components and the rules governing them and linking them together. While visual reversals are common for younger kids in kindergarten and first grade, persistent reading failure stems from an inability to “crack the code” of sound-symbol correspondence. Research of the brain shows that this is a rather difficult task for those with these disorders.
Identifying these issues early is crucial for intervention, yet the behavioral predictors are often misunderstood. It is not that aggressiveness (traits of ADHD) predict these disorders, though it may be quite understandable due to the symptoms of it, the best predictor is actually inattention. Interestingly, the aforementioned traits tend to emerge after the academic failure has started, due to the sheer frustration of failure and loss of self-esteem from peers.

6---full-notes/cornea,-iris,-and-lens-(f.title: Cornea, Iris, and Lens (Focusing)
6---full-notes/cornea,-iris,-and-lens-(f.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience psychology
Cornea, Iris, and Lens (Focusing)
Details
Before the brain can interpret an image, the eye must first act as a sophisticated optical instrument, capturing and focusing light onto the retina. This journey begins at the cornea, the eye’s transparent and rigid outer layer. It performs the initial and most significant bending of light, starting the process of creating a sharp image. From the cornea, light passes through the pupil, an adjustable opening whose size is meticulously controlled by the iris, the colored muscle that we see. The iris is a dynamic structure, constricting the pupil in bright sunlight to prevent overexposure and dilating it in dim conditions to let in as much light as possible. Finally, the light reaches the lens, a remarkable, flexible structure that fine-tunes the focus. Through a process called accommodation, the ciliary muscle alters the lens’s shape—making it thicker for nearby objects and thinner for those far away. Once perfectly focused, the light travels through the clear, jelly-like vitreous humor to its final destination at the back of the eye: the retina.

6---full-notes/correctness-and-persuasiv.title: Correctness and Persuasiveness
6---full-notes/correctness-and-persuasiv.content:
Status: teen
Tags: logic rhetoric
Correctness and Persuasiveness
Details
Logic is a different discipline from rhetoric, which is the art of being persuasive. Now, logic works on premises, meaning if the premises are correct, then it would sufficiently be able to lead propositionally from said premises to a conclusion. For example, a murder case, if the premises (evidences) are true and hold up, then logic is able to take said premises to the conclusion.
The measure of an argument’s “correctness” is objective and structural: an argument is correct if, and only if, accepting the premises compels one to accept the conclusion. This relationship holds regardless of whether the premises are actually true in the real world or whether the audience is psychologically convinced. Persuasiveness on the other hand is if it relies on emotional appeals or prejudices to convince the jury and judge. Conversely, a logically correct argument might fail to persuade if it is too complex or dry.

6---full-notes/correlation-from-statisti.title: Correlation from statistics to case outcomes
6---full-notes/correlation-from-statisti.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology university
Correlation from statistics to case outcomes
Details
Beyond simply aligning with professional opinion, a truly effective triage tool should have predictive utility—its initial assessment ought to correlate with future case developments. The study tested this through a series of chi-square analyses, examining the statistical relationship between the QuAIC-assessed level of concern and two key real-world outcomes: the length of time a case remained active and the severity of its final resolution. The results were highly significant.  
First, the analysis revealed a significant relationship between the QuAIC level and case length, finding that “the higher the level of concern, the lengthier the case” (x2=6.64, df=8, p<.001). This suggests that the QuAIC score at intake serves as a reliable indicator of the complexity and resource-intensiveness of a case.  
Second, an even stronger relationship was found between the QuAIC level and the severity of the case outcome. The analysis showed that “the higher the level of concern, the more punitive the outcome” (x2=127.17, df=8, p<.001). The specific patterns were clear:  


High/highest risk cases were most likely to result in an “external referral or a misconduct sanction.”


Moderate risk cases were most likely to lead to an “informal resolution or a misconduct sanction.”


Low risk/not applicable cases were overwhelmingly likely to be resolved through “informal resolution.”


These statistical correlations elevate the QuAIC from a simple triage instrument to a powerful prognostic tool. Its score is not just a label for the present but a statistically valid forecast of a case’s likely trajectory. A simple triage tool tells a case manager which file to open first. A prognostic tool, however, provides insight into what that case is likely to become. The chi-square results demonstrate that the QuAIC functions as the latter. A “High” concern rating at intake is a data-backed predictor of a complex, time-consuming case that is significantly more likely to require formal disciplinary proceedings or referral to external agencies like the police.
This has profound implications for strategic resource management. A university administrator can leverage this data to move from a purely reactive stance to a data-informed, proactive management model. By tracking the aggregate QuAIC scores of incoming cases over a semester, leadership can forecast demand on the SCU, student misconduct offices, legal counsel, and other support services. If a trend of higher-scoring cases emerges, they can proactively allocate additional staff time, budget for external assessments, or implement targeted preventative programming aimed at the specific behaviors being reported. The QuAIC thus provides the foundational data needed to manage institutional risk at a strategic, rather than purely case-by-case, level.

6---full-notes/courtesy-stigma-operating.content:

Courtesy Stigma operating via relational roles stereotypes
Details
In his theory, Goffman’s courtesy stigma also extends prejudice and discrimination towards individuals affiliated with a stigmatized person. The relational effects correlate with how closely affiliated the person is to the stigmatized individual. The effects differ for each role.
Parents would bear the brunt of onset blame, stereotyped as incompetent caregivers or historically labeled as causing psychiatric disorders. Whether through psychoanalytic frameworks or updated biomedical models, the blame still lies with the parents.
Siblings and spouses would then suffer offset blame, meaning they would be held responsible for the symptom relapse, treatment non-adherence, etc. For offspring, they would be at risk of contamination stereotypes, where peers and clinicians assume the child is tainted developmentally and psychologically.
Courtesy stigma operates along two axes: public avoidance and self-directed shame. Family members frequently report higher distress concerning the vicarious stigma borne by the patient than the direct discrimination directed at themselves.

6---full-notes/criticizing-society.title: Criticizing Society
6---full-notes/criticizing-society.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology psychology
Criticizing Society
Details
The collectivist society has always been marked by a particular, quieter counterpart to the nationalism of more individualistic ones: compliance. In this sense of compliance, I am not necessarily criticizing the broader architecture of political and social structures that allow us to function — that rests on a multitude of fields I am simply unqualified to synthesize or speak on with any real authority. Though, as someone whose academic interests sit firmly in psychology and philosophy, I believe the claim still stands: compliancy is arguably the defining characteristic of how certain collectivist societies (like my own) operate, and more importantly, how they self-perpetuate.
Now, why am I bringing this up? What does compliancy have to do with my critique of society? After all, I am not a sociologist, I have not personally experienced any society meaningfully different from my own, and I would not claim accuracy in perceiving their benefits and flaws from the outside. I largely concede that. But I do think I am entitled to an opinion on how our sociological structures bear down on our psyche and cultural perceptions — and crucially, I am speaking from inside the society I am critiquing, which grants a different kind of authority than an academic one. What I lack in comparative breadth, I make up for in proximity. Addressing the claim of criticizing society: I will be focusing primarily on academic environments, which are a miniaturized version of said society and are shaped by it through practically every available means.
Perhaps, as the means, conditions have been stated, I will no longer stall this essay for any longer and finally get to my arguments. The first argument I want to make about the current state of society is its overemphasis on community. Now, I am not arguing that we should abandon this emphasis; it is inherently what holds our society together. The reason that we are not a governed state or a part of another country is because of how communal relations have been emphasized throughout our history. Nonetheless, it is a new age, and I contend that we would be a fool to continue this tradition so harshly. Though there are arguments for its preservation, it has recently proven impractical, perhaps even self-defeating in our own society. To signify this claim, I want to bring forth stigma. Stigmas are inherently a sociological concept, and it is strongly determined by the bonds of a society as they cast out outsiders depending on their differences to the main group; I believe that because of such a strong bond in our society, we strengthen stigma even further, effectively constraining our ideologies that are strictly outdated, unscientific, illogical, and of course harmful (to ourselves!). Research on mental illness stigma in Pacific Rim collectivist societies, including those with strong Confucian and Vietnamese cultural influences, shows that psychological distress is frequently moralized as personal weakness, poor character, or a threat to family honor and “face,” leading to widespread avoidance of acknowledgment and professional help (Ran et al., 2021; Do et al., 2020). People inherently become blind or bias when having to engage in this problem, having to maintain their compliancy and relationship to the community and society. They are willing to condemn their own blood and people they care about to maintain their own framework of society that they have built for their whole lives, which society has cultivated throughout their lifetime. I can mention more mechanisms about how stigma restrains more than just society or the individual but relatives, friends,… but this is not a psychology course so I digress. Now, to the next point, how does this translate to academic environments?
Adult societies are consisted of people who have fully developed themselves and such, not necessarily their identity but the abilities that allow them to live and socialize in said society. For teenagers and children? Not so much, of course, in this society, we have learnt multiple social skills, or survival skills from a young age to survive scrutiny from our caretakers and adult relatives, it is still not enough for us to be prepared for the academic environment. The reason for this is that… well, they are teenagers, too. Now, that does not necessarily explain what I am getting at, but it provides us with a natural sense of safety or framework that would encourage us to interact and keep touching the fire despite how it may hurt us — through bullying, isolating, verbal/emotional abuse and so on. This is a real issue in academic environments. Because of how undeveloped every single individual in an academic environment is, with unresolved trauma, familial problems, or such, they are likely to be volatile as a “mob” or “group,” weaponizing the trauma and personal problems to other students that are…weaker socially. As an outcast, or just a radically different individual myself, I have experienced countless experiences of people outright violating my boundaries, criticizing my moralities without understanding it fully, failing their own morals, and so on and so forth. The life of an outcast is inherently made difficult in a society alike this, and is even harder in one where the main “goal” is to fit in and be content. Again, this is only my own testimony, and should be taken with a grain of salt, but this is consistent with what research on adolescent social dynamics actually shows in dozens of psychological analyses—and with ethnographic work on Vietnamese lower secondary schools, where bullying is deeply embedded in institutional power relations and disciplinary frameworks (Horton, 2011). Now, one may use the developmental failings mentioned above to rationalize the actions of these individuals, but doing so would be ignorant of the unnecessary, unaccountable, and immoral harm that it produces for other innocent individuals. Additionally, the actions are also poor alternatives to what actually resolves said problems (therapy, counseling, mentalizing to name a few). To not further ruminate on one singular point, we will move on to the next argument.
This second argument addresses the cultural factors. Citing research on stigma in Southeast Asian countries, specifically Confucian values, we can further understand the cultural context that produces the trend and how we act towards actions and people. Confucian thought heavily emphasizes the character and moral values of a person and how it is connected to their actions; society integrates said idea to its core, judging a person’s identity based on a singular negative action rather than logically deducing from the amounts of evidence that would more accurately conjure who they are (Hu et al., 2024; Berkson, 2021). Now, because of how rooted this phenomenon is in previous generations, it is much more prevalent in teachers and adults in most environments rather than in the current generations. Nonetheless, it is still somewhat prevalent, only passively as people judge and assess someone’s identity behind their backs when discussing with someone without inadequate evidence. This phenomenon is inherently psychologically harmful and wrong, as it is considered more as a shaming tool for adults to discipline and educate their students and children rather than a defense mechanism for the perpetrator’s psyche and as an outdated and impractical value. But due to how embedded and respected Confucian is as a philosophy, people continue to ingrain it into their lives without actually justifying the benefits and worthiness of doing so. Because of how human functions, when faced with questions against this inherent incoherence, people often attempt to rationalize their position with rhetoric, or if push comes to shove, become defensive and attacking the values of the other person - the very thing they are being critiqued of doing.
There are additional concepts that strengthen these phenomena even further. I will not mention every single heuristic or psychological mechanism that contributes to these phenomena, as I have also exemplified the Fundamental Attribution Error in the previous paragraph, but I will proceed to list the most devastating ones which actually have a substantial amount of effect on the environment and individuals residing in it. The first mechanism in line is the bystander effect, it practically defines the diffusion of moral responsibility that people possesses when in a group. This effect effectively expands and compounds for every person that is in the group. The reason this is so devastating is due to how it encourages teenagers to act against what they may morally conceive as the right thing in exchange for social aptitude. Furthermore, it allows others to chime in on the matter, bringing in another psychological mechanism - conformity. Morally righteous individuals, or individuals who never actually participate in bullying, can certainly be compelled by the group to engage in it as to not be judged or separated from it. After all, it is in our basic evolutionary-based mind that we adhere to the group and society as to not be casted aside.  The argument is a goalpost-moving move itself, as the institutions that govern these teenagers develop rules and moral conduct system to inherently train the teenagers to act morally, yet adults can still rationalize for their immoral actions just cause those actions do not correlate to the rules ? Point in case, our inherent psychological heuristics further strengthens the injustice that our culture and societal allows to happen, and there is no justification that can account for the immorality of the actions of these teenagers.
This is not the endpoint of the mechanisms and moral implications of a collectivist society — it is, at best, a first cross-section. What I have tried to show is that the cultural, sociological, and psychological factors at play in these environments do not operate in isolation; they compound, and the compounding is what makes the injustice so difficult to name and resist. That difficulty is itself worth examining — and worth continuing.
Supporting Content
Though I will not philosophically establish a framework here, I will mention about the concept of moral responsibility. In the situations mentioned above, people have adequate epistemic conditions about what was happening, they had control of themselves (on a baseline level due to how every single human operates with psychological mechanisms yet can still make moral decisions), yet they acted immorally nonetheless, so one cannot argue that they are not responsible for their actions. Some points of argument against this situation may be that they are merely teenagers and cannot account for their actions and so it decreases their responsibility. This argument is poor, as these individuals demonstrate morality in other situations just fine, yet when placed under these circumstances, they act differently. Of course, we do not judge someone for not being unfailingly moral, but teenagers act consistently immoral in these situations, which is not justifiable.

6---full-notes/critique-against-descarte.content:

Critique Against Descartes
Details
While the initial premise (“thinking is occurring”) is widely accepted, Descartes’ move to posit a substantial “Self” behind the thinking faces significant challenges. For example, the “Hume’s Bundle Theory” which posits that Descartes proposition only meant that there is thinking rather than I am thinking. When we look inward, we do not find a stable form of a continuous soul or “thinker” but rather something that changes by time or by situation, and so perhaps we are just a “bundle” of souls having our perceptions transfer from one to another.
Georg Lichtenberg attacked the grammar of Descartes’ deduction. He argued that saying “I think” assumes the very conclusion it tries to prove (that there is an “I”). A more scientifically rigorous observation would simply be “It thinks” or “There is thinking,” much like we say “It rains.” We observe the event (rain/thought) without necessarily observing an agent (rain-god/thinker). The “I” is a grammatical convenience, not a proven fact.
Additionally, there may be also arguments on our subjective belief, even if we believe that something is true, it might not even be so !

6---full-notes/critique-of-aristotelean-.title: Critique of Aristotelean Logic
6---full-notes/critique-of-aristotelean-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
Critique of Aristotelean Logic
Details
Kant pays Aristotle a backhanded compliment. Aristotelian logic, he says, constitutes the “formal” foundation of all reasoning — it is the “vestibule of the sciences.” It enables us to form correct judgments and serves as a truth-preserving device: if your premises are true and your reasoning is valid, your conclusion is guaranteed to be true. But logic alone cannot generate new knowledge. It is a tool of consistency, not a tool of discovery.
This distinction matters enormously for Kant’s larger project. When reason attempts to use logical forms not merely as a method of checking arguments but as a mode of discovering truths about reality — when it tries to prove the existence of God, the immortality of the soul, or the infinity of the universe through pure logic alone — the result is what Kant calls the “antinomies of pure reason.” Logic spins out conclusions that appear valid but are actually illusions, because the logical machinery is operating without any grounding in possible experience. You end up “discovering” all sorts of things that are really just artifacts of the formal structure you’re using.
The real substantive knowledge, Kant insists, is to be found “only in the sciences, properly so-called” — the objective, empirical sciences like physics and mathematics that combine formal reasoning with content drawn from intuition and observation. Logic tells you whether your argument is valid. Science tells you whether your premises correspond to anything real. The vestibule is necessary for entering the building, but you cannot live in the vestibule.

6---full-notes/cross-paradigm-factors-in.title: Cross-Paradigm Factors in Psychopathology
6---full-notes/cross-paradigm-factors-in.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychopathology Clinical Psychology
Cross-Paradigm Factors in Psychopathology
Details
Understanding psychopathology requires looking beyond any single paradigm to consider factors that cut across theoretical lines. Three of the most critical sets of factors are emotion, sociocultural context, and interpersonal relationships, as disturbances in these areas are present in nearly all mental disorders.
1. Emotion and Psychopathology Emotion—a short-lived state comprising expressive (behavioral), experiential (subjective), and physiological components—is fundamental to the human experience and its disruption is central to psychopathology. For example, individuals with schizophrenia may show a lack of facial expression (expressive component) while internally reporting strong feelings (experiential component). People with panic disorder experience intense physiological fear without a present danger, while those with depression endure prolonged sadness. The concept of ideal affect—the emotional states a person desires to feel—also varies culturally. Western cultures often prize high-arousal positive emotions like happiness, which correlates with higher treatment rates for stimulants like cocaine. In contrast, East Asian cultures tend to value low-arousal positive states like calmness, which correlates with higher treatment rates for sedating drugs like heroin. This highlights how emotional values can shape behavior and pathology.
2. Sociocultural Factors and Psychopathology Environmental factors, including gender, race, culture, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, can trigger, exacerbate, or maintain mental disorders.


Gender: Certain disorders show marked gender differences. Depression is nearly twice as common in women, whereas antisocial personality disorder and alcohol use disorder are more prevalent in men. Although this has more nuance and can be attributed to a wide range of causes.


Poverty: Low socioeconomic status is a significant risk factor linked to antisocial personality disorder, anxiety disorders, and depression.


Culture and Ethnicity: While some disorders like schizophrenia appear globally (with similar concepts found in Eskimo and Yoruba cultures), others like hikikomori (extreme social withdrawal) are culture-specific (predominantly in Japan). Diagnosis rates and substance use also vary by ethnicity. For instance, schizophrenia is diagnosed more often among African Americans than Caucasians, and while Whites are more likely to abuse many drugs, African American smokers have a higher mortality rate from lung cancer. The lifetime prevalence rates for several DSM-IV-TR disorders show significant differences among ethnic groups, as seen below:











































DisorderWhite (%)Hispanic (%)Black (%)Alcohol abuse/dependence13.415.0*9.5Bipolar disorder3.24.34.9*Depression17.9*13.510.8Generalized anxiety disorder8.6*4.85.1An asterisk indicates the group with the significantly highest prevalence rate.
3. Interpersonal Factors and Psychopathology The quality of a person’s relationships profoundly influences their mental health. Theories like object relations and attachment theory emphasize how long-standing patterns in close relationships, particularly with early caregivers, shape an individual’s psychological well-being and sense of self (the “relational self”). Therapeutic approaches like Interpersonal Therapy (IPT) directly address this by focusing on current relationship problems. IPT identifies four key areas that can impact symptoms: unresolved grief, difficult role transitions, ongoing role disputes, and interpersonal/social deficits. By helping patients understand and resolve these relational issues, IPT provides an effective path toward reducing symptoms of psychopathology.

Cumulative Summer Gains

Sociologist Barbara Heyns research on schools came to a wall, which led her to start examining the summer activities that different classes of students do and how that helps them or form the difference between academic achievement gap.
During the school year, it is pretty clear that their growth and progress are remarkably similar, in fact, the low-income students may gain a bit of ground on their high or middle-income counterparts. The divergence happens from June to September.


High-Income Students: Continue to learn and gain skills over the summer, benefiting from enrichment activities like camps, museum visits, travel, and literacy-rich home environments.


Middle-Income Students: Tend to tread water, retaining most of what they learned but not making significant gains.


Low-Income Students: Often experience a “summer slide,” losing a significant portion of the skills and knowledge they gained during the previous school year.


This pattern of course repeats every single year, meaning the gap here only becomes wider and wider between the classes.

6---full-notes/dna's-unique-causal-statu.title: DNA's Unique Causal Status in Behavioral Science
6---full-notes/dna's-unique-causal-statu.content:
Status: baby

DNA’s Unique Causal Status in Behavioral Science
Details
The paper argues that DNA variation has a unique causal status compared to other biological correlates of behavior. While a correlation between brain activity and a behavior is ambiguous (does the brain state cause the behavior, or does the behavior cause the brain state?), the relationship with DNA is unidirectional. An individual’s behavior does not alter their inherited DNA sequence. Therefore, a confirmed association between a DNA variant and a behavioral trait can be interpreted causally: the DNA difference contributes to causing the behavioral difference, not the other way around. This provides a firm anchor for causal inference in the notoriously difficult “direction of effects” problem in psychology.

6---full-notes/dsm---a-tool-for-classify.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology
DSM - A tool for classifying mental illnesses
Details
To create a standardized language for diagnosing mental health conditions, the American Psychiatric Association developed the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM). The DSM provides a common set of criteria and classifications, allowing clinicians and researchers to communicate more effectively about specific disorders.
The manual (specifically the fourth edition discussed in the lecture) organizes its diagnoses across five distinct categories, or axes, to provide a comprehensive picture of a client’s condition:


Axis I: Clinical Disorders: This is for the primary psychological disorders that are the main focus of treatment, such as depression, anxiety disorders, or ADHD. These are generally seen as conditions that can be treated or managed.


Axis II: Personality Disorders and Mental Retardation: This axis is for long-lasting, pervasive conditions that are less responsive to treatment. This includes personality disorders (e.g., antisocial personality disorder) and intellectual disabilities.


Axis III: General Medical Conditions: This includes any physical health problems that could be relevant to the client’s mental health, such as a heart condition that might be affected by medication or a recent injury causing stress.


Axis IV: Psychosocial and Environmental Problems: This axis documents social or environmental stressors that could be impacting the client’s condition, such as a recent divorce, job loss, or lack of a social support system.


Axis V: Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) Score: This is a single score from 1 to 100 that provides an overall assessment of the person’s ability to function in daily life. A high score (90-100) indicates superior functioning, while a very low score indicates severe impairment and potential danger to self or others.

Dark adaptation

The eyes have this ability to be able to see faint light in the dark, as time passes of course, at first you will hardly see anything, but it will adapt.
Exposure to light chemically alters molecules called retinaldehydes, stimulating the visual receptors. In moderate light, these receptors regenerate the molecules as fast as the light alters them for the person to maintain that visual sensitivity. In darkness or dim light, these receptors regenerate without interruption (as they are not constantly altered) and so they can detect faint light.
Now cones and rods are also important in this, as they adapt at different rates, cones adapt faster than rods, but rods are more sensitive to faint light then cones, and so when rods finish their regeneration, we mostly see with rods.

Dealing with Stigma
Details
Similar to therapy, there are many ways that society can deal with stigma. The first and perhaps easiest to see is “Top-down”, which basically is the government implementing laws so that discrimination towards the stigmatized groups are essentially illegal. This approach, though straightforward, has not demonstrate much effectiveness. For example, the ADA legislation in 1990, which makes discrimination illegal. The efficacy has been limited for those with mental illness as exposing the fact that they have these things may pose a threat to their societal reputation and their life projection, making these individuals refrain from opening up. Perhaps it is also difficult to keep track of due to how mental health help may be extra hours or help with work rather than physical renovations like ramps for disabled people.
The other two approaches are “bottom-up” and “middle-out”, these are more suggestive of changing how these groups are perceived. Bottom up relies on the “contact hypothesis” which states how an individual who reveals their conditions to the world and well, act how they act, the perception people have on the group as a whole can change, to be more normalized, like the LGBTQ+ community (what a fucking hassle to type). Simultaneously, the middle out approach is for the media to have a hand in. Instead of reporting news and making it in a way to condemn and even judge people with mental illnesses, they can instead change how they present these images to be more understanding and fair.
Ultimately, the goal is to humanize these individuals and their differences from society. The “top down” approach and the education of the person’s condition may reduce blame yet it can dehumanize them, make them subhuman. To combat this, we need to focus perhaps on the other two approaches to make people understand these people rather than just their conditions.

6---full-notes/deconstructing-'love'-bey.title: Deconstructing 'Love' Beyond Simple Emotion
6---full-notes/deconstructing-'love'-bey.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology love
Deconstructing ‘Love’ Beyond Simple Emotion
Details
While folk psychology might categorize love as a simple emotion, it fails to fit this classification upon closer inspection. Unlike “atomic” emotions such as sadness or happiness, which possess a distinct and singular feeling, the experience of being in love is more complex. For instance, one can be happy in love or sad in love, whereas the experience of sadness cannot itself be happy; it is an irreducible state. Furthermore, love is almost always directed toward an object or person. It’s difficult to imagine waking up with a disembodied feeling of “love” in the same way one might wake up feeling a general, disembodied sadness. This object-directed nature makes it different from primary emotional states. While love certainly has cognitive aspects (“I am in a state of love”), it also possesses a powerful affective, or “feeling,” component that separates it from a simple thought, like recalling a fact. This complexity suggests love is not a simple emotion but a more multifaceted psychological phenomenon.

6---full-notes/defense-mechanisms-agains.title: Defense Mechanisms against acknowledgement
6---full-notes/defense-mechanisms-agains.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Freudian psychology
Defense Mechanisms against acknowledgement
Details
According to psychoanalytic theory, the ego must mediate the conflicting demands of the id, the superego, and reality. To cope with the anxiety that arises from these conflicts, the ego employs various unconscious strategies known as defense mechanisms. These mechanisms protect the individual from unacceptable thoughts, desires, and impulses by distorting reality in some way.
1. Repression This is the foundational defense mechanism. Repression is the motivated forgetting of unacceptable thoughts, desires, and memories by banishing them to the unconscious. For example, a person might forget a traumatic event. While central to psychoanalytic theory, the evidence for repression is debated; emotionally traumatic events are often highly memorable, not forgotten.
2. Denial Denial is the refusal to believe information that provokes anxiety. While repression is about forgetting, denial is about asserting that the information is incorrect. For example, a person with a terminal illness might refuse to accept the diagnosis, or someone with a drinking problem might insist, “I’m not an alcoholic.”
3. Rationalization When people use rationalization, they attempt to prove that their actions are rational and justifiable, thus worthy of approval. It’s a way of creating a logical excuse for an unacceptable behavior. For example, a student who wants to skip studying for a movie might say, “More studying won’t do me any good anyway.”
4. Displacement Displacement involves diverting a behavior or thought away from its natural target toward a less threatening one. This allows the person to express an impulse with less anxiety. For example, if you are angry with your boss, you might go home and yell at a family member instead.
5. Regression Regression is a return to a more immature level of functioning to avoid the anxiety of a current situation. By adopting a childish role, a person escapes responsibility. For example, after a new sibling is born, an older child might start crying or pouting more often.
6. Projection Projection involves attributing one’s own unacceptable characteristics or impulses to other people. By seeing one’s own faults in others, the faults may seem less threatening. For example, someone who is angry might accuse someone else of being angry.
7. Reaction Formation With reaction formation, a person goes to the opposite extreme to hide an unacceptable impulse or truth from themselves and others. For example, a man troubled by doubts about his religious faith might become an overly zealous missionary, or someone with strong aggressive tendencies might join a pacifist group.
8. Sublimation Sublimation is the channeling of unacceptable sexual or aggressive energies into socially acceptable, and even admirable, behaviors. According to Freud, this is a constructive way to express an impulse without consciously admitting its existence. For example, aggressive impulses might be sublimated into a career as a surgeon. Sublimation is considered the most mature and socially constructive defense mechanism.
