6---full-notes/defining-clinically-abnor.title: Defining Clinically Abnormal Behaviors
6---full-notes/defining-clinically-abnor.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology
Defining Clinically Abnormal Behaviors
Details
One of the foundational challenges in clinical psychology is simply defining what constitutes “abnormal” behavior. Official definitions, like those from the American Psychological Association (APA), often describe it as behavior that leads to distress, disability, or an increased risk of death, pain, or loss of freedom. While this seems clear on paper, applying it to real-world situations reveals profound ambiguity. The lecture highlights this through several key examples:


The Problem of Context (The Soldier): A man named John is hypervigilant, fears strangers, and lashes out in public. In a civilian setting, this behavior seems clearly abnormal and dangerous. However, if we learn John is a soldier serving in a combat zone, the very same behaviors can be reinterpreted as adaptive, necessary, and even skillful survival tactics. The context completely changes the meaning of the behavior.


The Problem of Belief (The Messenger): A successful mother and bank employee named Susan secretly believes she is the daughter of God and is transcribing His message to save mankind. This could be seen as a delusion requiring therapy. Yet, in a society with strong religious traditions, where many people believe God communicates with them through prayer, where is the exact line between extreme faith and a clinical disorder? Her behavior doesn’t harm anyone and doesn’t impair her ability to function in her job or family life.


The Problem of Socially Sanctioned Abnormality (The Athlete): Professional football players engage in behaviors that perfectly match the clinical definition of abnormal: they intentionally cause distress and physical pain to others and knowingly put themselves at an increased risk of death and disability. In any other context, this would be considered pathological. On a football field, however, it is celebrated and rewarded with millions of dollars.


The Problem of Social Deviance (The Iconoclast): The label “abnormal” can be applied to anyone who significantly deviates from the mainstream. The professor contrasts a controversial media figure like Glenn Beck with a historical figure like Martin Luther King Jr. At the time they introduced their ideas, both were seen by many as abnormal, promoting ideas that caused distress and social upheaval. This shows how the label can be used for both those we demonize and those we later idolize, highlighting the subjective and political nature of defining what is “normal.”


These examples illustrate that there is no simple, universal line between normal and abnormal. The initial assessment of a client is a complex task that requires careful consideration of the individual’s environment, circumstances, and cultural background before a diagnosis can be made.

Defining intelligence
Details
This is actually something that is difficult to do due to the fact that there are things like memorization which does not necessarily fit into this, or empathy/emotional intelligence which is the same case. Here are some attempts to define intelligence (Kanazawa, 2004;
Sternberg, 1997; Wolman, 1989):
•The mental abilities that enable one to adapt to, shape, or select one’s
environment.
•The ability to deal with novel situations.
•The ability to judge, comprehend, and reason.
•The ability to understand and deal with people, objects, and symbols.
•The ability to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with
the environment.
Note that these definitions use such terms as judge, comprehend, understand, and think rationally—terms that are just as poorly defined as intelligence. To advance our understanding, we need research on intelligent behaviors. Psychological researchers have followed a circuitous route: They began with tests of intellectual abilities, defined as the ability to do well in school. Then they conducted research to find out what the tests measure. Do they measure a single skill or a variety of separate skills? It may strike you as odd to measure something before figuring out what it is. However, physicists used the same approach with electricity, magnetism, gravity, and other phenomena.

Because of all this emotional dysregulation, people might even dissociate themselves to get away from these situations and refuse to feel it all because it is just simply too overwhelming. They then will lose their sense of self, goals, and so on.

Degenerate State
Details
To live in a degenerate state is to live in a state of thinking without action. In this state, humanity becomes a mere thinker, or even worse, a parrot of other men’s thinking.
Emerson said that once we collectively exist under this state, society puts a lid upon itself, it stops us all from building any higher, of reaching higher heights. And all of the flashy exertions of skills are mere useless knowledge-academia for the sake of academia, not for the sake of intelligence or knowledge itself.
A society in the degenerate state severs its pieces from its whole. The worker, the tradesman, are boxed into their roles. These people are not understood or even considered by anyone of true societal power. Their efforts are not really applauded, and their perspectives are not really considered. The individual accordingly resigns himself to this role. He becomes subject to his own toil, sectioned off from the rest of a society. The farmer becomes the hands, while the academic becomes the brains. But in reality, Emerson notes that a society is one body. We are all connected. 6---full-notes/deindividuation.title: Deindividuation
6---full-notes/deindividuation.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Social Psychology
Deindividuation
Details
This concept is quite relative to the The Selves of Schopenhauer and Nietzsche as it constitutes the Will of Schopenhauer. And by Will I do mean the fact that these individuals that are in a group who experience deindividuation tends to do less responsible things rather than the opposite, as they are less accountable and are able to reason less.
Originating with Le Bon’s 1895 concept of the “group mind,” it describes what happens when a person stops experiencing themselves as a distinct, identifiable individual.
Zimbardo identified key inputs: anonymity, lack of accountability, physiological arousal, large groups, sensory overload, and altered consciousness (drugs, alcohol). These inputs produce specific psychological consequences: minimized self-awareness, reduced concern for social evaluation, impulsivity, time distortion (present dominates past/future), diminished differentiation from others, and poorer subsequent memory.
But how does this actually come into practice ? When experimenting on the differences between individuated and deindividuated people, it was recognized that people are to be less caring about how they shock an unidentifiable, unknown individual even if they know partially who they are and individuals who they can identify and that have shown them who they are. But Gergen’s dark room study showed deindividuated participants becoming more affectionate, intimate, and connected — and evaluating the experience positively afterward.
And so its not necessarily that deindividuation would cause us to act one way over the other, rather, it strengthens the situational context of whatever was happening (as the groups all believed it was an activity that they believed others would do).

Demarcation
Details
When doing science, we must be able to establish what is and what is not science. Following the epistemology of Karl Popper, scientific inquiries must be refutable. Domains like religion, art, and politics exist outside this boundary, while subjective experiences (like consciousness) remain on the very edge of our scientific capabilities. Furthermore, Popper noted that science never definitively “proves” a hypothesis; it only provides supporting evidence.
However, we just cannot rely on empirical experimentation, we must also have a theoretical framework to work off of. A hypothesis tested via experimentation without an underlying mechanism is often indistinguishable from pseudoscience. For instance, testing whether Mozart’s music improves cognitive abilities is mediocre science if the explanation relies on “magical” qualities of the music. We must explain the phenomenon using whatever has already been framed and confirmed within neurobiology. Alike any spiritual framework, those could also turn into bad science as well.

6---full-notes/depressed-people-are-wise.title: Depressed people are wiser...
6---full-notes/depressed-people-are-wise.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology
Depressed people are wiser…
Details
Depressive realism is the paradoxical phenomenon where individuals with depression, despite their cognitive distortions, sometimes have a more accurate perception of reality than non-depressed individuals. Sapolsky frames this with the phrase “sadder but wiser,” highlighting a key nuance in how depression affects cognition.
The paradox is resolved by understanding the context of the judgment being made:


When evaluating personal, emotionally charged events, a negative cognitive distortion dominates. A person with depression will overgeneralize a single failure into a narrative of lifelong incompetence. They will interpret neutral social cues as negative and see their future as inevitably bleak. In this personal realm, their thinking is distorted.


When evaluating external, emotionally detached situations, they often lose the “optimism bias” that characterizes most healthy individuals. The average person tends to be mildly delusional in their optimism, underestimating risks and overestimating positive outcomes. People with depression are often stripped of this bias. As a result, they can be more accurate in assessing risks, probabilities, and the state of the world at large.


This doesn’t mean depression is a “better” way of seeing the world. The loss of a healthy optimism bias comes at the cost of hope and well-being. However, it demonstrates that the cognitive effects of depression are complex. The illness doesn’t simply make a person think negatively; it fundamentally alters their relationship with reality, removing a protective layer of optimism that, while not strictly “accurate,” is crucial for psychological health.

6---full-notes/depression-is-a-medical-d.title: Depression is a medical disease
6---full-notes/depression-is-a-medical-d.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology biology psychopathology
Depression is a medical disease
Details
Major depression is fundamentally a biological disease, not a failure of character or a lack of willpower. The suffering is rooted in quantifiable, physiological malfunction. To treat it as anything less is analogous to telling a person with diabetes to simply will their pancreas to function correctly. The biological basis can be understood through three interconnected domains.
First, depression involves profound neurochemical dysregulation. This goes far beyond a simple “serotonin deficiency.” The entire system of neurotransmitters is disrupted. A deficit in norepinephrine contributes to psychomotor retardation—the overwhelming physical and mental exhaustion that makes basic tasks feel impossible. A failure in the dopamine system, which governs reward and motivation, leads to anhedonia, the core symptom where the capacity to feel or even anticipate pleasure is lost.
Second, the body’s stress response system is chronically activated. In healthy individuals, the release of stress hormones like cortisol is a short-term survival mechanism. In depression, this system becomes stuck in the “on” position, leading to hypercortisolism. The brain’s negative feedback loop, which normally shuts the response down, is broken. This constant exposure to stress hormones is neurotoxic, causing brain regions like the hippocampus (vital for memory and regulating stress) to atrophy.
Third, these processes result in altered brain structure and function. The prefrontal cortex, the seat of executive function and emotional regulation, often becomes underactive, impairing one’s ability to break cycles of negative thought. Concurrently, the amygdala (the brain’s fear center) can become overactive, intensifying feelings of anxiety and dread. The brain becomes physically locked in a self-reinforcing loop of negativity, where a sad thought is not just a feeling but a biological event that perpetuates the disease state.
Ultimately, psychological pain manifests as and causes tangible biological damage. This understanding is the foundation for effective treatment and the most powerful tool against social stigma.
Supporting Content
The thoughts of depressed patients usually centers on a significant loss. They perceive that they have lost something they consider essential to their happiness or tranquility; and so they anticipate negative outcomes from any important undertaking; as well as regarding themselves as void of the attributes required to accomplish their goals. This theme can be formulated in terms of the cognitive triad: a negative conception of the self, of life experiences and a nihilistic view of the future.
And so after that these senses can lead to typical emotions associated with depression: sadness, disappointment, and apathy. Furthermore the feeling of being trapped in unpleasant situations or insoluble problems increases, spontaneous constructive motivation dissipates. The patient, moreover, even feels compelled to escape via suicide.

6---full-notes/deriving-demand.title: Deriving demand
6---full-notes/deriving-demand.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Deriving demand
Details
Lecture 1 drew demand and supply curves and promised to explain where they come from. Lectures 2 and 3 built the pieces: preferences and the budget. This lecture puts them together. A demand curve shows how much of a good you want at each price. You get it by solving the consumer’s problem again at each price
The method is the one from Lecture 3, and Gruber warns you’ll repeat it until you’re sick of it. Take U = √(C·S), income Y = 24, a slice at 4 and a cookie at $2. Two equations give the two unknowns:
• Tangency: MRS = −S/C must equal −Pc/Ps = −½, so S = C/2.
• Budget: 4S + 2C = 24.
Substituting gives C = 6 and S = 3.
Now raise the cookie price to 3. The tangency becomes S/C = ¾, and the budget becomes 4S + 3C = 24. Substituting S = ¾C gives 3C + 3C = 24, so C = 4 and S = 3. (Gruber first said the new slope was −⅓; a student corrected it to −¾.) If you lower the cookie price to 4/3 instead, you get C = 9 and S = 3.
Plot the cookie price against the cookies you choose: (2, 6), (3, 4), (4/3, 9). That is the demand curve. Graphically, each price gives a new budget line, pivoting around the pizza intercept. A higher cookie price shrinks the opportunity set, and you end up with fewer cookies.
The general version is the formula from the Lecture 3 note. With this utility function you spend half your income on each good, so C = Y/(2Pc) = 12/Pc. That’s the whole demand curve in one line.
A student noticed that pizza stayed at 3 slices whatever the cookie price. That’s a quirk of this utility function, not a law: S = Y/(2Ps) doesn’t depend on the cookie price. Gruber calls the line through the chosen bundles a flat price-consumption curve. In general, changing one price changes the demand for both goods.
His homework runs the other way: change the pizza price, and cookies stay put while pizza moves. At $6 a slice, S = 24/12 = 2 and C stays at 6. The next note explains why the line is flat: two effects cancel.
ε = (ΔQ/Q) ÷ (ΔP/P), or with derivatives, ε = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q)
Gruber loosely calls it the derivative of quantity with respect to price. But the slope dQ/dP alone changes with the units, such as cookies per dollar or per cent. Multiplying by P/Q turns it into percent per percent, which doesn’t depend on units. ε is zero or negative, because people buy less when the price rises. The one theoretical exception is in the next note.
Two extremes don’t exist, but they fix the idea:
• Perfectly inelastic (ε = 0): a vertical demand curve, where quantity doesn’t respond to price at all. Students suggested gas and water. Gruber pointed to the substitutes (a bus, a bike, other drinks), so neither is perfectly inelastic. Insulin is the classic near-case: a diabetic won’t skip it over an extra 1. Even insulin is only inelastic within a normal price range, since at 1 million some people couldn’t buy it.
• Perfectly elastic (ε = −∞): a horizontal demand curve, where any tiny price rise wipes out demand. The near-cases are things you don’t really need, or goods with close substitutes. If McDonald’s charged twice what Burger King does for a burger, almost everyone would switch.
The lesson is that elasticity comes down to substitutability. The more substitutes a good has, the more elastic its demand. Every real good sits somewhere between the extremes.
Gruber also warns that the course cheats with straight lines. A demand curve with the same elasticity everywhere has to be curved, and he leaves the reason as homework. On a straight line the slope is fixed, but P/Q changes as you move along it. For Q = 10 − P, ε = −P/Q:
• At P = 8, ε = −4.
• At P = 5, ε = −1.
• At P = 2, ε = −0.25.
The cookie demand curve C = 12/Pc is the opposite case. Its elasticity is (−12/Pc²) × (Pc/C) = −1 at every price, and the curve bends. You can check this without calculus. Spending on cookies is 12 at every price (2 × 6, 3 × 4, 4/3 × 9). Spending that stays the same when the price changes is exactly what an elasticity of −1 means. So when the course gives one elasticity for a straight line, read it as true near one point.
Changing income instead of price traces a different curve. Raise income from 24 to 32 with prices fixed. The tangency stays at S/C = ½, since prices and tastes haven’t changed. Only the budget moves out in parallel, to 32 = 4S + 2C, so C = 8 and S = 4. Cut income to $16, and C = 4 and S = 2.
The relationship between income and quantity is the Engel curve; here it’s C = Y/4 for cookies. Its version of elasticity is the income elasticity of demand:
γ = (ΔQ/Q) ÷ (ΔY/Y), or γ = (dQ/dY) × (Y/Q)
Unlike ε, γ can take any sign, and its value sorts goods into types:

Normal goods (γ > 0): you buy more as income rises.

Luxuries (γ > 1): quantity rises faster than income, so the good takes a growing share of your budget. Examples are restaurant meals and nice watches.
Necessities (0 < γ < 1): you buy more, but the share of your budget falls. Examples are groceries for eating at home, clothes and rent. A poor household might spend 60% of its income on housing and a rich one far less, even though the rich one has the nicer flat.


Inferior goods (γ < 0): you buy less as income rises, because you only bought it for being cheap. Ramen is Gruber’s example.

Luxury and necessity are defined by income, not price. The curve is named after the statistician Ernst Engel. His 1857 study of household budgets found that the share spent on food falls as income rises, which makes food the original necessity.
For this note’s cookies, γ = (¼) × (Y/C) = 1 exactly. Both goods always take half the budget, which puts them right on the line between luxury and necessity.

6---full-notes/deriving-supply.title: Deriving supply
6---full-notes/deriving-supply.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Deriving supply
Details
A price-taking firm produces where p = MC. So the example firm makes 3 units at a price of 30, 4 units at 40, and so on. The firm’s supply curve is just its marginal cost curve: for any price, find the quantity where MC equals that price. For C = 10 + 5q², that’s q = p/10.
The intuition mirrors demand. The demand curve and the supply curve basically meet where the market settles: what someone will pay for the next unit equals what it costs to make. Gruber develops what that means for welfare in a couple of lectures.
The full definitions:

Short-run firm supply: the MC curve above the shutdown point, which is the minimum of average variable cost. Below that price, the firm makes nothing. In the example, AVC = 5q bottoms out at zero, so there’s no shutdown point, and supply is q = p/10 at any positive price.
Long-run firm supply: the MC curve wherever profit isn’t negative, meaning wherever the price covers average cost. In the long run, fixed costs can be changed, so a firm that would lose money leaves.

Market supply adds up the firms:

With one firm, the curve is S1: 1 unit at 10, 3 at 30.
Add a second identical firm, and the market makes 2 units at 10 and 6 at 30.
With n identical firms, market supply is n times firm supply: Q = n × p/10.

So each extra firm makes the market curve flatter. Gruber calls market supply a more elastic version of firm supply. He leaves a teaser: if a competitive market can have an unlimited number of firms, what does that imply for the supply curve?
He then rebuilds the whole market from scratch. Most universities leave this for intermediate micro. Gruber credits Paul Samuelson, who once taught this course, with bringing the math in; before him, intro courses taught the graph and stopped. Gruber says his students only ever complain about too little math.
Step A: one firm’s supply curve. Start with:

The production function, q = √(L·K).
Input prices, w = 5 and r = 10, still taken as given.
Capital fixed in the short run at K̄ = 1.

From these: with K = 1, q = √L, so L = q². Cost is rK̄ + wL = 10 + 5q². Marginal cost is 10q, and p = MC gives the firm’s supply curve, q = p/10. Then check the shutdown condition, which never applies here.
Step B: market supply. Assume n = 6 identical firms; where n comes from is next lecture. Market supply is Q = 6 × p/10 = 0.6p.
Step C: market demand. Assume Q = 48 − p. Gruber made this one up for the example, but you could derive it from preferences, prices and incomes, as in Lectures 2–4.
Step D: equilibrium. Set demand equal to supply: 48 − p = 0.6p, so 1.6p = 48 and p* = 30. Then Q* = 48 − 30 = 18.
Now check the firms. Six identical firms sharing 18 units means each makes 3. At p = 30, each firm’s own rule, 10q = 30, also gives q = 3. Everything is consistent at once:

Consumers who want 18 units at $30 get them.
Firms together supply 0.6 × 30 = 18.
Each firm is maximizing profit, at p = MC.

Gruber calls this the magic of the market.
For supply, all you needed was the production function and three numbers. Each given gets explained later:

w and r come from the input-market lectures.
K̄ comes from Lecture 6’s long-run cost minimization.
n comes in the next lecture.

6---full-notes/describing-distribution-s.title: Describing distribution shape
6---full-notes/describing-distribution-s.content:
Status: adult
Tags: statistics psychology
Describing distribution shape
Details
Before quantifying anything, you can describe a distribution’s shape in words along three axes.
Modality = number of peaks. Unimodal has one peak; bimodal has two (treat small wiggles as noise); a flat distribution with no peak, where every value is about equally likely, is rectangular or uniform. A bimodal shape is diagnostic: it often means two subgroups are mixed together (e.g., men and women), hinting that you should split the data by some underlying variable.
Symmetry / skew. A symmetric distribution’s two halves mirror each other (the bell curve is the type case). An asymmetric one has a tail stretching to one side, and that asymmetry is called skew, named for the direction the tail points. Positive (right) skew: the long tail runs toward high values — income is the classic case, because a floor effect at $0 blocks the left side while the right can run on to the very rich. Negative (left) skew: the tail runs toward low values — e.g., years of education or an easy test, where a ceiling bunches most scores high. (Mnemonic: point your fist’s finger along the tail; the axis direction it points is the sign of the skew.)
Kurtosis = peakedness relative to the normal curve, holding variance fixed. High kurtosis (leptokurtic) is more peaked and has heavier tails; low kurtosis is flatter with lighter tails. The subtle part: two distributions can share the same variance yet differ in kurtosis. A past midterm asked students to draw a high-kurtosis curve on top of a normal one with the same variance and total area 1 — the trick being that you must move probability mass into both the peak and the tails while removing it from the shoulders (the intermediate values), so the area still integrates to 1.

6---full-notes/details-of-the-cognitive-.title: Details of the Cognitive Approach
6---full-notes/details-of-the-cognitive-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology therapy CBT 3 - Tags/environment
Details of the Cognitive Approach
Details
As we understand in the depressed patients, they have a negative regard on themselves, in the future, as well. To be more specific, he regards himself as a loser, meaning he has lost something of value to his domain. Secondly, he expects the outcome of anything he takes part in to be negative, and so he does not do anything, which ruminates him. Furthermore, he can regard himself to be deficient in achievements, as well as worth.
This is the core idea, and it will lead to other symptoms, so to solve it, we must make the patient see himself as a “winner” rather than a “loser,” as masterful rather than useless.
First of all, we will separate the syndrome of depression into its specific components. We start with any of the symptoms cluster, such as emotional, motivational, cognitive, behavioral, or physiological and concentrate on solving that first. Each cluster may be conceptualized as a problem and a potential target for intervention. As the symptoms are connected, solving one will make the other better as well. It is actually advised for us to broaden our focus to many clusters of symptoms as it is extremely effective.
The specific problems under consideration are complex and consist of more than the particular difficulty verbalized by the patient. A problem generally can be formulated in terms of three “levels”: (a) The observable abnormal behavior or symptom, for example, easy fatigability, crying spells, suicidal threats; (b) the underlying motivational disturbances (if any), such as the wish to avoid activities or to escape from life; (c) underlying the motivation, a cluster of cognitions, such as the belief that striving toward a goal is futile, that there are no satisfactions ahead, and that he is defeated, deprived, and defective.
As said, in each case, we will focus on specific problems with according techniques depending on a variety of factors. Then we will have to reach a consensus with the patient. Of course, several targets and methods may be focused on concomitantly, and trial-and-error and ingenuity is necessary.
The approach to a presenting symptom should encompass the less obvious components of the problem. For example, a project to mobilize the patient into activity not only involves increasing his motivation but also improving his self-esteem. The patient’s own observation that he is successful in reaching a goal provides crucial information that affects his attitudes about himself. As he thinks better of himself in terms of his ability to control his environment and to be effective in everyday situations, he begins to expect that the outcome of his efforts might be of some avail. Consequently, his optimism is increased. As has already been pointed out, an increase in positive expectancies improves motivation. The increased motivation leads to still better performance. And so we can see a cycle appearing here, a cycle of improvement.
Lastly, even though the patient is doing better and is supposed to feel better, because of his tendency to downgrade or discredit positive happenings, he may screen out many of those events. We must then focus on this selective inattention and help him remove it.

6---full-notes/details-of-the-synapse.title: Details of the Synapse
6---full-notes/details-of-the-synapse.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience
Details of the Synapse
Details
There are two neurons that are in this process, called the presynaptic neuron and the postsynaptic neuron, they are the consequently the neuron that sends the message and the one that receives it. To begin, it starts in the tiny knoblike axon terminals of the presynaptic neuron. In these swellings are numerous tiny saps, or synaptic vesicles that are filled with neurotransmitters. When the presynaptic neuron fires, these vesicles burst and eject their chemicals through the terminal’s membrane into the synaptic gap in between the two cells. These molecules then diffuse across this gap and impinge upon the membrane of the other.
One the chemical is across, the transmitters activate specialized molecular receptors in the postsynaptic membrane. When these receptors are active, it opens or closes certain ion channels in the membrane. Which basically makes the voltage difference across the membrane decrease, rendering it less stable. As more and more transmitters molecules do this, the more the difference in voltage is, and when it reaches the excitation threshold, the action potential is triggered and the impulse speeds down the post-synaptic cell’s axon.

6---full-notes/determining-the-intensity.title: Determining the intensity of treatment and types of skills
6---full-notes/determining-the-intensity.content:
Status: adult
Tags: therapy Clinical Psychology
Determining the intensity of treatment and types of skills
Details
Another assessment necessary to be done is to see if the person needs more than just DBT. There are many options and intensities of care such as standard outpatient DBT; DBT skills training plus intensive case management; DBT skills integrated into individual DBT; DBT added to non-DBT case management or psychotherapy; and inpatient, residential, and day treatment DBT. This will depend on the patient’s “level of disorder,” which is defined by characteristics of the patient’s current conditions. Each stage relates to different symptoms and different goals.
The basic rundown for Stage 1 are a current severe mental disorder, behavioral dyscontrol, and/or imminent threat to life. Therapists will have to work on these conditions before others to ensure the client has suitable control. In the subsequent stages, the treatment are to replace “quiet desperation” with nontraumatic emotional experiencing; to achieve “ordinary” happiness and unhappiness, and to reduce ongoing disorders and problems in living; and to resolve a sense of incompleteness, to achieve a sense of freedom and joy. The stages can be jumped between each other, and there is no requirement for a person to go through all of them.
There is also the problem of evaluating progress. Many uses the DBT diary card to track the problem behaviors, changes in mood, self-efficacy, use of skills, beliefs that they are improving. However, it isn’t optimal for data analysis as it is a diary, so one must transfer it to a data list or something instead to keep easier track of.

6---full-notes/determining-the-terms.title: Determining the terms
6---full-notes/determining-the-terms.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
Determining the terms
Details
From marking these words, you now have two main possibilities. Either the words are in a single sense throughout or two or more, shifting the meaning depending on the context.
Your first instinct should be to try and determine if they have one or many meanings, then to see how they are related. At last, you can note the contexts of how they are used to determine the reason for the shift in meaning and so on, equalizing the flexibility of the author.
But, I hear you ask, or not. How does one find out what the meanings are ? The answer, though simple, may appear unsatisfactory, it is that you have to discover the meaning by using the meanings of all the other words in the context that you do understand. (The words surrounding the special words are the contexts.).
To illustrate this, consider definitions, stated in words. If you do not understand any of the words used in the definition, you will not be able to understand the word. But huh ? How does this help ? We know that a complex sentence has many parts, and the opposite of complex is simple, when we understand that a sentence has many parts of complex words and such, we know that that is what the author had intended. The more parts of a sentence, piece of writing you can put together, the easier it is to find the remaining parts, because there are fewer of them. (Like a jigsaw puzzle)
Usually, a good puzzle is one that always fits everything. The same should be for a perfect book, but such book doesn’t exist. The better a book is, the more fruitfully the reader can interpret it. The opposite applies for bad books.

6---full-notes/determinism-and-free-will.title: Determinism and Free Will
6---full-notes/determinism-and-free-will.content:
Status: baby
Tags: philosophy physics
Determinism and Free Will
Details
The famous Laplace demon example states how something, a being can completely predict what happens in the future without fail, as we are made of physical matter, we too can be predicted. Determinism asks if that even allows moral responsibility if everything in the universe is already set in stone.
There are two positions regarding this question, obviously so, in completely opposite ends of the spectrum. The libertarians argue that free will exist so determinism must be false while the hard determinists argue the opposite. But there also exists a third view of the compatibilists, which constitutes that even though we have rules that govern over us, we are still free beings that can decide for ourselves in ways that matter morally.
Supporting Content
It may even be the case that determinism is false due to quantum mechanics still being unproven.

6---full-notes/determinism-in-psychology.content:
Status: teen
Tags: statistics psychology
Determinism in Psychology
Details
Science necessitates determinism and the assumption of order in the universe so that it can truly function and predicts what will happen in the future. Classical determinism stated that absolute predictions could be made about physical bodies, but modern science has shifted towards probabilistic or statistical determinism. A clear biological example of this is the quantum release of neurotransmitters at the synaptic cleft: an identical presynaptic input does not guarantee an identical postsynaptic output, but rather a mathematically predictable probability distribution of vesicle releases.
We cannot predict human behaviors with 100% accuracy, but this is more about the confounding variables that have to be controlled. We cannot do this, and so statistics and determinism helps us to move through those variables.

6---full-notes/deterministic-autonomy-an.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Deterministic Autonomy and Second-Order Desires
Details
To understand second-order desires, we must understand the former “first-order desires” which are immediate impulses or cravings. However, as we have autonomy, it implies our capacity for “second-order desires,” which are desires about what desires one wants to have. A smoker may have a first-order desire for nicotine but a second-order desire to be healthy and free from addiction. Agency wouldn’t exist when someone fails to control their “first-order desires.” Conversely, “deterministic autonomy” states when an agent is able to reflect critically on their commitments and modify their first-order desires to align with their higher-order volitions.
And again, even if it can be explained that our “deterministic autonomy” states that we are inherently choiceless in reviewing our thought process and thoughts in general, it does not strip away the fact that we can still rationally act through our values, logic, and purposes.

Distinguishing Appearance from Reality
Details
This problem is related to how a child might try to understand how a ball is still white even after it is put through a blue filter, as children in the preoperational stage usually have this problem. They fail to understand that objects conserve such properties after changes in the shape or arrangement of the objects. Their brain cannot yet comprehend and perform the mental operations necessary to understand these transformations.
For example, when you get a thin and tall class of water, filled to the brim and pour it into a wide but short glass, the child most likely will not understand that the amount of water in both glasses are the same. Instead, they will say the wide and short glass probably has more water in it.

Development of Asylums

The original definition for asylums were safe places. These buildings would be located in the countryside far from the places where it was dirty and just overall worse. A lot of people were getting better living in those asylums, although some did not, they were still in safe places.
Furthermore, these asylums usually housed people for a long time, or for their whole lives, rather than just resting for a period of time and then getting back to work. The result of this was that asylums started getting overcrowded as more and more people came, which meant the countryside ran out of space to build asylums, and they had to do so in the cities, where conditions weren’t exactly fulfilling for the recovery of mental illnesses.
The fact that asylums were in cities also made patients there become entertainment for others, they were being used and abused. These places turned into bedlams, which were horrible places for the mentally ill to rest in. Luckily, there was Philippe Pinel who wanted to treat these people better, and started hospitals which were a new version of asylums… which still turned overcrowded as well.

6---full-notes/developmental-psychopatho.title: Developmental Psychopathology
6---full-notes/developmental-psychopatho.content:
Status: teen
Tags: developmental psychology
Developmental Psychopathology
Details
This field of psychopathology is quite new due to its nature. For the most of history, children have been seen as miniaturized forms of adults, not completely different type of humans that have different functions, systems than adults.
This utilitarian view meant there was little societal or scientific framework for recognizing or studying the unique mental and emotional struggles of the young. The first academic text on children wasn’t written until the mid-16th century, and concepts like adolescence were not formally defined until the early 20th century. The recognition of child abuse as a specific societal problem, with the coining of the “battered child syndrome” by radiologists in 1962, is shockingly recent. It took the observation of physical injuries that could only be intentionally inflicted to formally acknowledge children’s vulnerability.
The first edition of DSM even only had 2 conditions related to developmental psychopathology, but nowadays there are hundreds. The reasons for this is not that all of these disorders are new, but rather because now we can see all of the problems that children have that concerns them rather than adults.

6---full-notes/developmental-trauma-diso.title: Developmental Trauma Disorder
6---full-notes/developmental-trauma-diso.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology trauma
DTD
Details
The diagnosis of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) has been instrumental in understanding the aftermath of acute, terrifying events. It aptly describes a psyche fractured by an experience, like a deep crack forming in an otherwise solid road. However, this framework reveals its limitations when confronted with a different kind of suffering: the experience of a child for whom the road was never solid, but was instead built during a perpetual earthquake. For individuals whose childhood was defined by chronic abuse, neglect, and profound insecurity, trauma is not a disruptive event but the very atmosphere of their development. It is this diagnostic gap that Dr. Bessel van der Kolk and his colleagues sought to fill with the proposed diagnosis of Developmental Trauma Disorder (DTD).
The central argument for DTD is that the PTSD model, designed primarily for adults with a developed sense of self, is inadequate for capturing the pervasive impact of early-life, interpersonal trauma. A child growing up in a chronically dangerous environment does not experience a disruption to a baseline of safety; they learn from the outset that the world, and particularly the people meant to protect them, are sources of threat. This ongoing trauma fundamentally shapes the architecture of the developing brain, personality, and capacity for connection. DTD, therefore, is not merely a list of symptoms but a framework for understanding a systemic failure in development. It encompasses profound dysregulation across interconnected domains: the physiological and emotional inability to manage internal states; the attentional and behavioral difficulties often misdiagnosed as ADHD or Oppositional Defiant Disorder; and the deep wounds to self-perception and relational capacity, resulting in a core sense of worthlessness and an inability to form trusting bonds.
Despite its clinical resonance, the proposal to include DTD in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) was ultimately rejected. The decision was not based on a denial of the devastating effects of childhood trauma, but rather on methodological and political grounds. The primary objection cited was significant symptom overlap; committee members argued that the features of DTD were already covered by a constellation of existing diagnoses, such as ADHD, Reactive Attachment Disorder, and Borderline Personality Disorder. The concern was that adding DTD would muddy the diagnostic waters rather than clarify them. This rejection, however, is viewed by many in the field as a failure to recognize that these scattered symptoms are often manifestations of a single, underlying cause.
Even without official status, DTD persists as a revolutionary and vital clinical framework. Its true value lies in its power to re-contextualize a child’s struggles. By applying the DTD lens, a collection of disparate behavioral problems and emotional difficulties can be understood not as a list of co-morbidities, but as the coherent and predictable outcome of a childhood spent in survival mode. It fundamentally shifts the therapeutic inquiry from the pathologizing question of “What is wrong with you?” to the compassionate and clarifying question of “What happened to you?” In doing so, DTD provides the necessary language to describe the holistic impact of a traumatic childhood and guides clinicians toward integrated treatments that address the whole person, rather than merely managing a checklist of symptoms.

Dialetics and Therapy
Details
When developing DBT, Marsha Linehan referred to her personal experience about how BPD consists of two distinctly different parts of a person, and how they needed to accept each other to live finely. And so using the world “dialectical” to describe how it is like a push and pull game to lead them to the middle, she would incorporate it into the name of the method she created as well.
Different from CBT, DBT instead emphasizes on the behavioral part more, the skill building such as stress tolerance, problem solving, mindfulness, and so on. Still the cognitive modification to think differently and from another perspective may be helpful, it is not the focused part. When the environment becomes unsafe though, therapists may directly intervene rather than encourage to prevent the patient from endangering themselves, which is also another focus of DBT. Another part that becomes more important is the bond between the therapists and their patients, since BPD is so heavy on relationships, it is generally advised for therapists to become even more mindful and vigilant when helping the patient. Moreover, reinforcing this relationship may even encourage the patient to work on themselves to get better.

6---full-notes/difference-between-anxiet.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Difference between Anxiety and Fear
Details
These two words’ definitions have been confounded with each other a lot throughout the times which vitiates the advantages of using two distinct words to designate related but separable phenomena. And so we will define it simply: Fear is a particular kind of ideation; anxiety is an emotion.
This definition will derive from dictionaries mostly, as they all emphasize the meaning of fear as appraisal of an actual or potential danger. And so fear becomes a cognitive function in which people identify something undesirable that may occur.
A clear example of this may come when someone says “I have a fear of thunderstorms”. Which he is referring to a set of circumstances that are not present yet may occur some time in the future. In this sense, it is clear that fear is a predisposition to perceive a certain set of conditions as a threat and anxiety being the reaction if exposed to these conditions.
And so when a thunderstorm does happen, the fear is activated. The person reacts in words and actions, indicating the appraisal of potential harm, which is fear. The concept evolves from the possible consequences of the thunderstorm; namely, the possibility that he may be killed. And so “latent fear” which is the inner fear that is not showed to the outsider, is activated and anxiety is aroused, resulting in shakiness, jitteriness, and so on.
Fear is activated when the person gets closer to the dangerous situation. Or in some cases, merely talking about it may do the same as he may think and imagine it. Dwelling in such thoughts may make the threatening situation more salient and imminent as the person brings it into his “here and now”, and so he projects himself into it.
Supporting Content
This helps us have a clear indicator on how we define the irrational and rational anxiety. When the fear is realistic, it would become rational anxiety, when it is not, the opposite is true.

6---full-notes/difference-between-realit.content:

Difference between reality and brain states
Details
Brain states are normally categorized by its complexity, by how many neurons our brain has, the reactions that happens, the complex chemical gradients that happen in it to then produce a brain state. Yet, said complexity is only used to then attribute to something so simple in reality like the redness of a rose. And so it is a significant hurdle for physicalists theorists about the “commensurability problem”.
The discrepancy raises a question about how all that complexity can produce the sensation of redness. It seems impossible to logically derive the simple sensation from the complex mechanism; they appear to be different categories of reality. Same as the fact that no amount of complexity of an equation can generate a shade of blue.

6---full-notes/difference-in-genetics.content:
Status: adult
Tags: genetics
Difference in Genetics
Details
A human has 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) and each is made up of hundreds or thousands of genes that contain DNA. Different forms of the same gene are called alleles. These alleles are found at the generally same location. A genetics polymorphism refers to a difference in DNA sequence on a gene that has occurred in a population of a chromosome.
The DNA in genes is transcribed to RNA. In some cases, it turns into amino acids, which then form proteins, and such proteins make cells. These particular types in gene expression are called promoters. These promoters are recognized by proteins that are called transcription factors.
An area of molecular genetics that has been studied extensively the last decade has been single nucleotide polymorphisms or SNPs (pronounced snips). These things are differences between people in a single nucleotide in the DNA sequence in a strand of DNA. Another are of interest between the differences in people in gene structure are copy number variations (CNVs). A CNV can be present in a gene or multiple genes. These are abnormal copies of one or more section of the DNA in genes. Sometimes these CNVs can come in form of extra copies, or less copies than there actually should be.
SNPs contribute to about 90% of the differences of genes in people whilst CNVs make up the other 10%, but do not be fooled, the 10% is very substantial as people with schizophrenia, autism, and ADHD have been found to have CNVs.

6---full-notes/different-flavors-of-depr.title: Different flavors of depression
6---full-notes/different-flavors-of-depr.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Different flavors of depression
Details
Depression is not a single, uniform illness but a family of related disorders with distinct biological profiles. The existence of these different “flavors” of depression underscores that it is a biological phenomenon, not a singular emotional state. Each subtype has a different presentation and likely a different underlying neurochemical signature.
Key subtypes include:


Reactive vs. Endogenous Depression: This is a classic distinction. Reactive depression is triggered by a major external stressor or negative life event. In contrast, endogenous depression appears to arise from internal factors, without an obvious external cause. After several reactive episodes, the brain can become “kindled,” and the depression can begin to run on its own endogenous rhythm.


Atypical Depression: This subtype is dominated by vegetative symptoms, particularly psychomotor retardation and a feeling of “leaden paralysis.” The intense exhaustion and physical slowing are more prominent than the anhedonia or rumination. Sapolsky notes its biochemical similarities to chronic fatigue syndrome.


Psychotic Depression: A severe form where the individual experiences delusions and thought disorder. These delusions are not random but are typically extensions of the depressive mood, often centered on extreme, irrational guilt. The case of Andrea Yates, who believed she was saving her children from damnation, is a tragic example.


Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD): A rhythmic depression where episodes are tied to a specific time of year, most commonly the winter months. A person with SAD can be perfectly fine in the summer but fall into a major depression each winter, regardless of external circumstances. This is strongly linked to biology, specifically light exposure and the hormone melatonin.


The fact that a person can cope with a major stressor in July but become incapacitated by an internal rhythm in January demonstrates that depression is a collection of distinct biological diseases.

6---full-notes/different-kinds-of-attent.title: Different kinds of attention
6---full-notes/different-kinds-of-attent.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Zettelkasten writing learning
Different kinds of attention
Details
As discussed before, writing is never a single act of “focusing.” It is a dance among several kinds of attention, each suited to a different step in the process. Sustained attention lets us sit with a draft long enough to finish a thought, while selective attention helps us tune out the buzz of email pings and stray ideas so we can polish a single sentence. When we jump from outlining to fact‑checking we rely on alternating attention; when we keep an eye on reference material while shaping an argument we call on divided attention; and over all of this hovers executive attention, the internal stage‑manager that decides which spotlight to turn on next.​
Experts are able to slip between these modes without friction because they have practiced “variable attention.” Oshin Vartanian’s 2009 study on creative problem solving showed that high performers don’t stay broadly defocused or narrowly locked in; instead, they tighten or loosen their focus as the task morphs in front of them. In writing, that means knowing when to drill into the cadence of a paragraph and when to lean back to see if the story arc still holds. Such flexibility is an embodied skill, not a set of rules; it grows from countless cycles of noticing a mismatch between the attention being used and the attention the moment actually needs.​
Structures that expose us to those cycles—daily drafting sessions, slip‑box note taking, timed micro‑edits—become training grounds for the attentional repertoire. Finished pages are not the only reward; each conscious switch from one attentional gear to another thickens our intuition. Over time the writer’s inner stage‑manager learns to fade lights up or down without conscious orders, and what once felt like juggling becomes a single, fluid performance.

6---full-notes/difficulties-as-a-necessi.title: Difficulties as a Necessity
6---full-notes/difficulties-as-a-necessi.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning neuroscience
Difficulties as a Necessity
Details
Learning is at least a three-step process: initial encoding of information is held in short-term working memory before being consolidated into a cohesive representation of knowledge in long-term memory. Consolidation reorganizes and stabilizes memory traces, gives them meaning, and makes connections to past experiences and to other knowledge already stored in long-term memory. Retrieval updates learning and enables you to apply it when you need it.
Learning always builds on a store of prior knowledge. We interpret and remember events by building connections to what we already know.
Long-term memory capacity is virtually limitless: the more you know, the more possible connections you have for adding new knowledge.
Because of the vast capacity of long-term memory, having the ability to locate and recall what you know when you need it is key; your facility for calling up what you know depends on the repeated use of the information (to keep retrieval routes strong) and on your establishing powerful retrieval cues that can reactivate the memories.
Periodic retrieval of learning helps strengthen connections to the memory and the cues for recalling it, while also weakening routes to competing memories. Retrieval practice that’s easy does little to strengthen learning; the more difficult the practice, the greater the benefit.
When you recall learning from short-term memory, as in rapid-fire practice, little mental effort is required, and little long-term benefit accrues. But when you recall it after some time has elapsed and your grasp of it has become a little rusty, you have to make an effort to reconstruct it. This effortful retrieval both strengthens the memory but also makes the learning pliable again, leading to its reconsolidation. Reconsolidation helps update your memories with new information and connect them to more recent learning.
Repeated effortful recall or practice helps integrate learning into mental models, in which a set of interrelated ideas or a sequence of motor skills are fused into a meaningful whole that can be adapted and applied in later settings. Examples are the perceptions and manipulations involved in driving a car or in knocking a curveball out of the ballpark.
When practice conditions are varied or retrieval is interleaved with the practice of other material, we increase our abilities of discrimination and induction and the versatility with which we can apply the learning in new settings at a later date. Interleaving and variation build new connections, expanding and more firmly entrenching knowledge in memory and increasing the number of cues for retrieval.
Trying to come up with an answer rather than having it presented to you, or trying to solve a problem before being shown the solution, leads to better learning and longer retention of the correct answer or solution, even when your attempted response is wrong, so long as corrective feedback is provided.

Difficulties in reading scientific books
Details
One of these is to respect the arguments. Science is mostly inductive, and so the main arguments will be general propositions to evidence. There are obviously deductive arguments as well, which a proposition is proved from others that are already established.
This first difficulty arises because, in order to understand the inductive arguments in a scientific book, you must be able to follow the evidence that the scientist reports as their basis. Unfortunately, this is not always possible with nothing but the book in hand. If the book itself fails to enlighten him, the reader has only one recourse, which is to get the necessary special experience for himself at first hand. He may have to witness a laboratory demonstration. He may have to look at and handle pieces of apparatus similar to those referred to in the book. He may have to go to a museum and observe specimens or models.
Anyone who desires to acquire an understanding of the history of science must not only read the classical texts, but must also become acquainted, through direct experience, with the crucial experiments in that history. There are classical experiments as well as classical books. The scientific classics become more intelligible to those who have seen with their own eyes and done with their own hands what a great scientist describes as the procedure by which he reached his insights.

Difficulties of reading social sciences

The very factors that make this seem easy to read also makes it difficult. Many readers fear that it would be disloyal to their commitment to stand apart and impersonally question what they are reading, but as we know, we have to do this to read good.
Moreover, the familiarity of the words used in these writings also makes it difficult. Although a lot of these writers object  to using more or less specialized terms, those that they use sometimes are too wide, and they do not fully understand what it means. This makes it so that the reader may also be confused of the exact terms.
Why not combat this with stipulation ? Well, social sciences are not mathematicized. It is simply harder to stipulate social sciences terms, something like an isosceles triangle can be easily stipulated but it is another thing to define an economic depression or mental health.
The most important source, is the fact that it is mixed, rather than pure, kind of expository writing. The most important source of difficulty in reading social science derives from the fact that this field of literature is a mixed, rather than a pure, kind of expository writing. We have seen how history is a mixture of fiction and science, and how we must read it with that in mind. We are familiar with this kind of mixture; we have had a great deal of experience with it. The situation in social science is quite different. Much social science is a mixture of science, philosophy, and history, often with some fiction thrown in for good measure.
If social science were always the same kind of mixture, we could become familiar with it as we have with history. But this is far from the case. The mixture itself shifts from book to book, and the reader is confronted with the task of identifying the various strands that go to make up what he is reading. These strands may change in the course of a single book as well as in different books. It is no easy job to separate them out.

6---full-notes/discomfort-of-children.title: Discomfort of children
6---full-notes/discomfort-of-children.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Discomfort of children
Details
Human discomfort with viewing or handling children’s genitals—especially in caregiving contexts like diapering or washing—is a profound, evolutionarily adaptive signal of interpersonal boundaries, not a marker of deviance. This aversion protects vulnerability, enforces gender norms, and starkly differentiates normative psychology from pedophilic attraction. Far from warranting knee-jerk judgments like divorce, such unease calls for empathetic dialogue and therapeutic unpacking to foster secure parenting dynamics.
At its root, genital exposure triggers a visceral “too close” reflex for most people when it involves non-intimate others. This isn’t mere prudishness; it’s a wired safeguard against boundary violations. Dopamine circuits, which reward sexualization of “desirable” adults through pleasure and novelty, flip to aversion for the “undesirable”—children, the elderly, or even strangers—evoking nausea, embarrassment, or ethical recoil. Here, the brain prioritizes protection over titillation: Seeing a child’s genitals, even consensually during necessary care, can feel profoundly uncomfortable because it collides innocence with exposure. Personal testimony underscores this: Even mandated tasks like bathing a child can provoke “I can’t” paralysis, not from malice, but from an overload of empathy-fueled awkwardness. It’s the psyche’s way of screaming, “This vulnerability demands distance unless trust is absolute.”
This discomfort amplifies in cross-gender scenarios, reflecting entrenched social scripts. Same-gender interactions often normalize casual genital talk or exposure—think locker-room banter among men or intimate chats about bodies among close female friends—as extensions of communal bonding. Yet cross-gender? It’s taboo territory, laden with risks of misinterpretation, objectification, or cultural purity myths. Friends, regardless of gender, rarely breach this; platonic relationships thrive on unspoken walls around nudity. A father hesitating to change his daughter’s diaper isn’t “weird”—he’s navigating that minefield, perhaps compounded by unfamiliarity with the child’s rhythms or his own unexamined hang-ups from upbringing. Psychology here isn’t pathology; it’s the friction of norms clashing with necessity.
The glaring misstep in public discourse (e.g., viral rants equating unease with pedophilia) ignores this dopamine divide. Pedophilia thrives on eroticizing the forbidden—deriving pleasure from sexualizing children, hijacking reward pathways for harm. Normative discomfort? The polar opposite: a hard “nope” born of repulsion, not relish. If anything, aversion signals health—a father’s reluctance might stem from fierce protectiveness (“I love her too much to risk feeling off”) rather than sinister intent. Conflating the two erodes trust, pathologizes parenting, and silences real abuse signals. Better metric: Does the unease lead to abandonment, or adaptation? The former warrants scrutiny; the latter, support.
Responses like “divorce immediately” weaponize vulnerability for clicks, but they betray the nuance of human bonds. Instead, pivot to therapy—couples or individual—as the compassionate corrective. Unpack the roots: Is it cultural conditioning, attachment wounds, or simple inexperience? Tools like cognitive reframing or exposure hierarchies (gentle, guided) can normalize caregiving without shame. This isn’t “fixing” the uncomfortable parent; it’s fortifying the family unit, modeling boundaries for the child. In a world quick to judge, discomfort deserves decoding, not discard.

6---full-notes/discrepancy-model-and-bia.title: Discrepancy Model and Bias
6---full-notes/discrepancy-model-and-bia.content:
Status: teen
Tags: developmental psychology
Discrepancy Model and Bias
Details
The traditional method for diagnosing learning disorders relies on the “discrepancy model,” which requires a significant gap between a child’s intelligence (IQ) and their academic achievement. Under this model, a child with a high IQ (e.g., 150) who reads at an average level (120) qualifies as having a disorder because they are underperforming relative to their potential. Conversely, a child with a slightly below-average IQ (e.g., 85) who reads at a correspondingly low level (80) does not qualify, as there is no discrepancy; their poor reading is attributed to their lower cognitive ability. This model was historically supported by the Isle of Wight studies by Rutter and Yule, which suggested that high-IQ poor readers (“Specific Reading Retardation”) were distinct from low-IQ poor readers (“General Reading Backwardness”). However, modern research argues that the underlying phonological deficit is identical in both groups, challenging the validity of the discrepancy requirement.
This reliance though, may precipitate a bias in who gets treated. Imagine middle-high class kids who have a higher-than average IQ due to them having environmental advantages, they are viable for the diagnosis as their IQ is much higher than their reading score. Children of lower socioeconomic backgrounds may score lower due to the systematic factors, denying them of a diagnosis and not letting them getting the help that they need due to their reading score corresponding with their “IQ”.

Dissociative Disorder
Details
There are three dissociative disorders including dissociative amnesia, depersonalization/derealization disorder, and dissociative identity disorder. These disorders are all presumed to be caused by dissociation, resulting in some aspects of memories and cognitive ability becoming inaccessible. And this means that our consciousness is failing to integrate the information in our awareness. Both psychodynamic and behavioral theorists consider that dissociation is a method for the person to avoid overwhelming events. Which can also be seen in PTSD.
Dissociative amnesia is when a person completely loses their memories of being someone (perhaps even their sense of self) and then proceed to assume a new identity with new everything. These amnesia periods can last from several hours to years, but they generally do not reoccur after the period is done. Depersonalization/derealization disorders patients usually retain their memories, but they lose their sense of self, wanting to be someone else.
Lastly is dissociative identity disorder (DID). This diagnosis usually requires someone to have at least two separate personalities, or alters - different modes of being, thinking, feeling that exist independently and comes out at certain times. These personalities usually have one primary one who seeks out therapy to gain self-control back, although they generally do not have memories of the other actions.

In formulating his approach to depression, it is important for the therapist to distinguish among symptom, technique, and underlying attitudes. For example, the symptom may be affective, such as crying spells, sadness, loss of gratification, loss of sense of humor, apathy. The therapeutic approach may be behavioral, for example, mobilizing the patient into more activity and positively reinforcing certain types of activity. The underlying attitude, however, is the component that needs to be changed ultimately if the totality of the depression is to be influenced. Thus, the goal is cognitive modification.
Simply focusing on solving the symptoms without changing the attitude of the patient may lead to only temporary results. It may be even deceptive as a characteristic is changed, but the central core is not. And so we must be perceptive in recognizing the signs of change in fundamental attitude as well as symptomatic improvement.

6---full-notes/diverse-developmental-pat.content:

Diverse Developmental Pathways
Details
Developmental psychopathology rejects simplistic, single-cause explanations for mental disorders, instead embracing the concepts of equifinality and multifinality to explain the complex relationship between risk factors and outcomes. These principles acknowledge that developmental pathways are rarely linear or predictable.
Equifinality explains that a single end may have many ways or methods of getting to it. Depression, as an example, the first time a person experience this may be due to their genetics and a bad day, the second time maybe because of childhood neglect, third is severe trauma, and fourth is due to a consistent negative cognitive style. This makes it so that there is not an all-encompassing method to deal with every single depressive case and rather a tailored approach would be more effective (Tailored approach to mental illness).
Multifinality, on the other hand explains how individuals with the same risk factors can have radically different outcomes depending on their other factors. For example, two people both having grown up with a difficult temperament may all have different futures. The first one may have conduct disorder and become inducted into the juvenile system whilst the second can transform it into a drive and go on to become a successful entrepreneur. The factors like protective factors and environmental differences made these two outcomes possible, and so all of that must be taken into account.

6---full-notes/do-firms-maximize-profits.title: Do firms maximize profits? CEO pay, the separation of ownership and control, and the limits of incentive pay
6---full-notes/do-firms-maximize-profits.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Do firms maximize profits? CEO pay, the separation of ownership and control, and the limits of incentive pay
Details
The model assumes firms maximize profits, and the logic seems airtight. But CEO pay often looks unrelated to performance:

Amgen, 2010: lost 3% of its market value that year and 7% over five years, yet paid its CEO $21 million.
Abercrombie & Fitch, 2008: stock fell 71%, yet the CEO was paid $72 million.
Hewlett-Packard: Leo Apotheker was fired after a disastrous 11 months as CEO and still made $13 million.

If firms maximize profits, how can they pay so much to people who don’t seem to be doing a good job?
Of course we can’t know that; we have to view it in terms of opportunity costs. In other words: what would the company have lost if they didn’t have that CEO? We couldn’t know; only the people inside the company would.
But a clever test suggests this isn’t the whole story. When oil prices rise, oil company profits rise, yet no CEO controls the world oil price. So CEOs shouldn’t be rewarded for those gains. In fact, oil company CEOs get big raises when oil prices go up. That can’t be a reward for good work.
What we are looking for is “agency.” In the modern US economy, companies aren’t actually owned and governed by the same people. In fact:

The owners are a scattered crowd of stockholders.
The decisions are made by managers they employ.
Managers don’t automatically have an incentive to do what maximizes the owners’ profit.

Bengt Holmström, Gruber’s former MIT colleague, shared the 2016 Nobel with Oliver Hart for work on this tension, which economists call contract theory.
Gruber’s illustration is a manager at a large company that doesn’t yet have a private jet. The manager’s friends at bigger companies all have jets and mock them for it. The honest math says flying first class is cheaper. So the manager reruns the numbers assuming only peak-time flights on the priciest airlines, makes a slide deck showing that a jet “saves money,” and the owners don’t bother checking. The manager gets the jet; profits are lower. What’s best for the manager isn’t what maximizes profit.
Firms try to fix this with a board of directors: about 20 people elected to represent shareholders and watch the managers. But boards often fail:

Their members are largely picked by the managers they’re meant to watch.
Many are retired CEOs who like private jets too.
They do the job part-time, while the manager’s pay is the manager’s full-time focus.

Gruber’s example is Richard Grasso, who rose from the shipping department to run the New York Stock Exchange. On retiring he received a $187 million package. When the press asked, the board said it hadn’t understood what it had approved.
Another fix is stock options: the right to buy the company’s stock at a set “strike” price. Suppose you join when the stock is at 100 and get the right to buy 1,000 shares at 100. If the stock rises to 200, you buy at 100, sell at 200, and make 100,000. If it falls to $80, you simply don’t use the option, so it’s worth nothing.
In symbols, the payoff is max(stock price − strike, 0) × shares. The idea is that if the manager’s wealth is tied to the company’s, he will maximize the company’s profits, since that benefits him. There is a risk issue, though, because his payoff would never be zero while the potential for insane profits is high.
The deeper problem is that managers can raise the short-run stock price without raising long-run profits. Enron’s managers had large option holdings. Gruber describes Enron selling to subsidiaries it also owned, so that it looked like it was booking big sales. The stock soared, some managers cashed out, and the company went bankrupt once it all came out.
Supporting Content
Corporate finance is the field that studies how to write contracts that line up managers’ incentives with owners’. Gruber adds that workers’ interests belong in that design too. So far this has been a story of one rich group against another.

6---full-notes/dominance,-the-prisoner's.title: Dominance, the Prisoner's Dilemma, and why cooperaation needs enforcement
6---full-notes/dominance,-the-prisoner's.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Dominance, the Prisoner’s Dilemma, and why cooperation needs enforcement
Details
A situation becomes strategic when the outcomes depend on other people’s actions as well as your own. Perfect competition involves no strategy because firms would simply dominate or be comfortable with what they have. Everything in between these two outcomes, however, is strategic.
The first factor is dominance. Strategy X strictly dominates strategy Y if X pays you strictly more than Y whatever the others do. And, well, in the market, or strategy in general, one should never play a strictly dominated strategy, as switching to the dominant strategy is better.
Polak’s grade game shows how this works. Each student secretly writes α or β. α against β gets you an A and your partner a C, two αs get B− each, and two βs get B+ each. Here are the payoffs for someone who cares only about their own grade (A = 3, B+ = 1, B− = 0, C = −1; your payoff first):
α beats β whether the partner picks α (0 > −1) or β (3 > 1), so α dominates. Two students picked α for different reasons. One predicted her partner would pick α and replied to that. The other saw that α was better whatever the partner did. The second argument is stronger. It needs no prediction about the other person, only your own payoffs, and it contains the first as a special case.
Lesson 2 is the Prisoner’s Dilemma’s point: individually rational choices can produce an outcome that’s bad for everyone. The term is Pareto-inefficient, meaning another outcome would leave someone better off and nobody worse off. Both players choose α and get 0 when both could have had 1. This only needs saying because economics long held that self-interest adds up to efficiency. That is true under perfect competition, which is the non-strategic case.
Of course, it could become efficient the other way around, but achieving that efficiency is practically unachievable because people have different goals and lines of reasoning. Furthermore, if everyone picks Beta, then the dominant strategy becomes picking Alpha.
So, the obstacle to mutual benefits is enforcement. If the two players can promise each other that they won’t take advantage of each other’s absence, and that doing so would warrant betrayal.
The most obscure way this shows itself is through morality, as it makes the person experience guilt and indignation as payoffs.

Dopamine in relationships

Dopamine reward systems also plays a part in this, reinstating the fact that it is the anticipation of pleasure rather than pleasure itself. And so we can get a melancholic saying from this: “The price of a relationship is the loss of all anticipation from it.”, roughly translates to the price of love is the loss of reward from chasing it. When someone is trying to get their feelings reciprocated, they always have a huge maybe connected to the person that they are trying to have their feelings reciprocated. The larger that maybe is, the more dopamine they get from it, and so when it eventually flourishes, they come to the height of the pleasure, as it slowly dips down (according to scientific studies). There are also different types of dopamine receptors that serves different purposes. In monogamous species, two receptors are key: D1 and D2.
• D2 receptors are associated with the rewarding, anticipatory aspects of forming a new pair bond. The initial mating and attachment process requires their activation.
• D1 receptors appear to mediate the maintenance and pleasure of an established monogamous relationship.
Immediately after a pair bond is formed in monogamous voles, D2 receptor levels are down-regulated while D1 receptor levels are up-regulated. If this chemical shift is blocked, the pair bond does not last. This suggests that the brain has distinct mechanisms for the excitement of forming an attachment versus the contentment of maintaining one.

Industrial and commercial functions, which throw the door “wide to every sort of adventure,” furnish a high number of suicides because they are characterized by this lack of regulation. This condition is exacerbated by a modern belief that suffering is life itself and it should be accepted and integrated into our lives. In fact, he argues that it has become the ideal of swift, ruthless progress has become an article of faith. The data confirms this, showing higher suicide rates in industry and trade compared to agriculture, where older regulative forces persist. Education matters
Details
Depending on the perspective and the range that we are talking about, education can have completely different effects and results. Seeing the big picture (macro), education generally reduces inequality. Those who get an education are going to have more chances at a job and have higher salaries than those who don’t. Consider the examples in works such as Inequality by Design. During the post-WWII period until 1973, the U.S. aggressively expanded its higher education system, building new universities and creating more college slots than population growth demanded. This massive public investment led to a decline in overall social inequality as more people gained access to the advantages of a college degree. After 1973, when public investment in higher education slowed, the number of available places shrank relative to the population. This reduced overall opportunity, widened the wage gap between college-educated and non-college-educated workers, and contributed to rising inequality.
But on the other hand, viewing the lives of the primary and secondary school students, we can see that the difference in education (private or public school) and so on does not actually matter as much. In a school, there is more inequality than anywhere depending on their results, those who are good are grouped up there and those who get bad grades are in another group. These grades though depend little on the quality of these teachings, instead it is about the child’s background, family, for example.
