6---full-notes/educational-attainment-an.title: Educational Attainment and Family Life
6---full-notes/educational-attainment-an.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
Educational Attainment and Family Life
Details
Statistics have shown interesting correlations between these two values, specifically about how stable a family is with the level of education a person receive. The divergence is no longer subtle; it is a chasm. Data on adults nearing the end of their primary child-rearing years (ages 46-54) shows that 61% of those with a bachelor’s degree or higher are still in their first marriage. This figure plummets to just 30% for those with less than a high school diploma, with other educational groups falling in between. The stability of marriage, once a more broadly shared norm, is now increasingly correlated with higher education.
This pattern is further reflected in the experiences of children. Since the 1980s, the rate of children living with a single parent has remained low and relatively stable for college-educated families. For every other group, it has risen dramatically. For white families with only a high school education, the rate has more than doubled to around 20%, and for non-white families without a high school degree, it approaches 40%. This fracturing of family life is not a result of differing moral values but is deeply tied to the economic shifts that have eroded the foundation of the working class. The disappearance of stable, well-paying manufacturing and industrial jobs—the kind that could support a family with only a high school diploma—has left less-educated individuals, particularly men, with precarious employment, making the long-term commitment of marriage a far riskier proposition. Consequently, the stable, two-parent household is becoming a marker of class privilege, accessible primarily to those with the educational credentials to secure a place in the modern economy.

6---full-notes/effect-size.title: Effect size
6---full-notes/effect-size.content:
Status: teen
Tags: statistics psychology
Effect size
Details
A raw difference between two means tells you almost nothing on its own. Bay Area kids scoring 60 against a US mean of 50 is a gap of 10, but this 10 might be meaningless. If US scores cluster at 49-51 and Bay Area scores at 59 to 61, that gap is enormous; if scores scatter all over the place, it’s nothing. Effect sizes solve this problem by introducing scaling the gap to the spread: d = (μ₁ − μ₂)/σ. The trap worth flagging in red is that this σ is the standard deviation of scores, not of the distribution of sample means. The result is unitless, it says how many standard deviations the two means are apart.
Supporting Content
A lot of times effect size is confused with statistical significance. However, the latter asks “could this be chance?” while effect size asks “how big is it?”. Push n to 10000 and the distribution of sample means narrows a hundredfold, so even a trivially small true effect lands far out in the tail and returns a microscopic p.

6---full-notes/elasticity-and-change.title: Elasticity and Change
6---full-notes/elasticity-and-change.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Elasticity and Change
Details
Elasticity is the variable to determine how strongly quantity responds to price and the changes between the two. Its core driver is substitutability. Goods with many substitutes tend to have elastic demand because consumers can switch away easily. Goods with few substitutes, such as insulin, tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have fewer practical alternatives. But it is also psychological and institutional as well, as people will only change and substitute if they perceive it as a viable alternative. Institution-wise, it influences how policymakers make their decisions.
The other graph to consider is the Engel curve, where quantity changes depending on the income. Of course this is simple to understand as we already have the Consumer Choice, perhaps it may practically mirror the concept meaning-wise. Nonetheless, it is more varied than price elasticity because it can be positive, negative, greater than one, or between zero and one. A normal good is one where consumption rises as income rises. A necessity is a normal good whose consumption rises slower than income, so it takes up a smaller budget share as people get richer. Rent or basic groceries fit into this pattern while luxury goods fit the normal good pattern.
Inferior goods on the other hand are things that are consumed less when people become richer. Instant noodles is the simplest example: people like it, but they generally only do it because of budget constraints. And so when they have money they will purchase more high quality ramen from restaurants and such. The Engel curve then helps us understand how demand changes when constraint relaxes, which is essential for understanding poverty, welfare, development, and consumer behavior.

Elasticity and market shocks

So what decides how these two variables split? Elasticity. Take a supply shift that raises costs:

Normal demand: the price rises and the quantity falls (Figure 9-3).
Perfectly inelastic, vertical demand: quantity can’t change, so the price rises by the whole shift (Figure 9-4). Insulin is the example, for those who can afford it.
Perfectly elastic, horizontal demand: the price can’t change, because charging a penny more drives everyone away, so all the adjustment comes through quantity (in this case mostly dropping). Evaluating McDonalds vs Burger King. If McDonalds raised its price, it would lose a ton of customers because they’d just go to Burger King.

Electroencephalography (EEG) in Brain Research
Details

Methodology: Records electrical activity of neuron groups via scalp electrodes; amplifies and digitizes signals. Typically measures responses to stimuli (e.g., viewing images or sounds) over multiple trials to average out noise and correlate activations to tasks. Applicable to healthy/unhealthy subjects in labs or hospitals.
Advantages: Excellent temporal resolution. Detects unconscious processing and brain abnormalities (e.g., depression, schizophrenia). Inexpensive, widely available, minimally invasive. Allows long experiments with many trials.
Disadvantages: Poor spatial resolution (only gross brain areas). Noisy signals (e.g., from eye blinks, muscles, or room electricity) require multiple trials to average out noise, but noise isn’t fully eliminated.

6---full-notes/elevating-your-body-tempe.title: Elevating your Body Temperature when waking
6---full-notes/elevating-your-body-tempe.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sleep
Elevating your Body Temperature when waking
Details
Deliberate cold exposure, such as taking a cold shower for one to three minutes upon waking, serves as a potent physiological tool for rapidly inducing a state of alertness. This practice leverages multiple biological systems to send a powerful wake-up signal to the brain and body, effectively setting the tone for the day. The effectiveness of this method is not merely due to the uncomfortable shock, but rather to specific, predictable neurochemical and thermoregulatory responses.
The primary mechanism is a significant release of adrenaline (epinephrine) from both the brain and the adrenal glands. This hormonal surge is a core component of the body’s stress and readiness system, immediately increasing heart rate and energy availability. This is complemented by a sustained increase in dopamine, a neurotransmitter crucial for motivation, focus, and drive. This combination provides both an immediate jolt of alertness and a prolonged enhancement of mental focus.
Furthermore, cold exposure triggers a paradoxical thermoregulatory effect. While the skin’s surface cools, the body’s internal thermostat compensates by actively working to increase core body temperature. This rise in core temperature is a fundamental biological signal for wakefulness, directly opposing the drop in temperature required to initiate and maintain sleep. For this reason, this practice is recommended exclusively for the morning. Using cold exposure at night would directly counteract the body’s natural sleep-initiation process, making it a powerful but time-dependent tool for managing one’s state.

Emotion as an Act of Perception
Details
Understanding another person’s emotional state is fundamentally an act of perception; we observe their behavior and infer their internal world. More surprisingly, understanding our own emotions is also an act of self-perception that requires interpretation. This ability is not innate but develops over time. A young child, for example, may not correctly perceive their own bodily signals (like the need to use the bathroom), while their parents can perceive it clearly from external cues. This leads to a fascinating developmental shift: before early adolescence, a majority of children will assert that their parents know their inner emotional states better than they do themselves. It is only as they mature that they come to believe they are the primary authority on their own feelings. This process highlights that even our most intimate feelings are not simply “had,” but are actively perceived and understood through a developing cognitive lens.

Emotional Processing Theory
Details
This theory is the main model that covers PTSD. It posits two necessary conditions for emotional processing: the fear structure must be activated to modify it, and new info must be incorporated into the fear structure. This new information is encoded during the exposure and leading to a general pattern of reduction in negative effects as similar stimuli are encountered yet results are positive instead of negative.
The way one can get access to this emotional processing and be able to reduce their trauma symptoms include activation of the fear, within-session extinction (symptoms reducing in sessions), or between-session extinction. All of the improvement in the degree of fear activation, reduction, and peak responses with positively correlate with the improvement in PTSD symptom severity. Of course, there are also the reduction in negative cognitions, which proves the improvement of emotional processing and the resultant recovery.
In more recent times, the role of within-session extinction has been discouraged mostly, for it has been ineffective whilst the other, between-session extinction has. This has made it so current treatment directions are more towards that outcome, with emphasis on emotional engagement, disconfirmation.
In fact, research has even shown that higher fear expression shows superior treatment outcome after PE (Prolonged Exposure).

6---full-notes/emotions.title: Emotions
6---full-notes/emotions.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology biology
Emotions
Details
Emotions emerge through multiple interconnected pathways within the human body, encompassing learned responses, cognitive processes, phenomenological experiences, and biological mechanisms. Rather than originating from a single source, emotions represent a full-system process where each component influences and is influenced by the others.
This systemic nature of emotions fundamentally shapes human behavior. Emotions don’t simply color our experiences—they affect decision-making, social interactions, memory formation, and even basic physiological functions like heart rate and immune response. When we encounter a situation, our emotional response emerges from the convergence of:

Biological substrates: neurotransmitter activity, hormonal fluctuations, and autonomic nervous system activation
Cognitive appraisals: how we interpret and make meaning of situations based on past experiences and current context
Phenomenological dimensions: the subjective, lived experience of feeling that cannot be fully reduced to neural correlates
Learned associations: conditioned responses developed through personal history and cultural conditioning
Social-contextual factors: interpersonal dynamics and cultural norms that shape emotional expression and regulation

This complexity presents significant challenges for understanding emotional dysregulation in mental disorders. When someone experiences depression, anxiety, or emotional instability, clinicians cannot simply target a single “broken” component. The dysregulation might stem from neurotransmitter imbalances, maladaptive thought patterns, traumatic associations, or disrupted social relationships—more likely, it involves dynamic interactions among all these factors.
This multi-system involvement explains why treatment approaches often require integration: medication addresses biological substrates, therapy targets cognitive and learned patterns, mindfulness practices engage phenomenological awareness, and social interventions modify environmental contexts. The challenge lies not just in identifying which systems are involved, but understanding how they dynamically interact to maintain dysregulation patterns, creating self-reinforcing cycles that resist simple interventions.

6---full-notes/empathy-as-a-motivation.title: Empathy as a motivation
6---full-notes/empathy-as-a-motivation.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology
Empathy as a motivation
Details
To understand the full scope of human behavior, we must move beyond basic drives and consider social emotions and the conflict between motivations. Empathy, or emotional contagion, is a prime example of a social emotion. When we see an emotion in another person, we tend to reflexively mimic it (e.g., via our facial expression), which in turn helps us to “feel” their state. This mechanism helps bind social groups, allowing for shared experiences of joy or fear.
However, motivations are often in conflict. A person is not just hungry or thirsty or tired; they are a composite of many competing drives at once. And so we use the metaphor of a “vector field,” where an individual is pulled in multiple directions by various motivations (to eat, to sleep, to socialize, to study). Our ultimate behavior is the resultant vector of these competing forces. This explains why we act in complex, sometimes seemingly irrational ways—our actions are a compromise negotiated between the many different, and often conflicting, demands of our internal motivational systems.

6---full-notes/encoding-memories.title: Encoding memories
6---full-notes/encoding-memories.content:
Status: baby

Encoding memories
Details
Encoding is the initial process of learning, where sensory information from the environment is translated into a construct that can be stored within the brain. It is the crucial first step that determines whether information will be remembered. The effectiveness of encoding often depends on the level of processing applied to the information.
Shallow processing involves superficial characteristics, like the visual appearance of a word, and leads to weak, short-lived memories. In contrast, deep processing involves semantic analysis—focusing on the meaning of the information and how it relates to existing knowledge. Deeper, more meaningful encoding results in more durable and easily retrievable memory traces. For example, simply repeating a phone number (shallow) is less effective than associating the numbers with a memorable date (deep).

Details
Environments shape behavior, but an environment is not just physical space and physical cues; it is also the people within it. You can radically alter your habits by surrounding yourself with people who already possess the mindsets, characteristics, or methodologies you want to acquire. Your brain is wired for social mimicry and naturally absorbs the characteristics of the “tribe” you belong to. By embedding yourself in a culture where your desired behavior is the normal behavior, you will naturally adopt their traits and methodologies. This results in significant personal improvements that happen almost entirely unconsciously, requiring far less willpower than trying to change in isolation.

6---full-notes/epistemic-condition-for-m.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Epistemic Condition For Moral Responsibility.md
6---full-notes/epistemic-condition-for-m.title: Epistemic Condition For Moral Responsibility
6---full-notes/epistemic-condition-for-m.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
Epistemic Condition For Moral Responsibility
Details
Basic philosophy entails that for a person to be able to be responsible for something that they did, they would have to satisfy two conditions: the condition of knowledge and the condition of control. To quickly explain, the former is one pertinent to the fact that one needs to have certain information on the variables of the act; the latter depends on the assumption that one has control over said action.
From these two points, there are many views that attempt to define them. First is the awareness of action, it is the principle that one has to be aware of what they are doing: If John falsely believes that the button is a light switch, then he isn’t aware that by pressing it he will start the treadmill and so it seems that he can’t be blamed for Mary’s fall and for her injuries. Similarly, if John correctly believes that pressing the button will start the treadmill but isn’t aware that Mary is standing on it, it seems that he isn’t blameworthy either. These seemings have to be refined, of course, since John’s ignorance of the button’s function or of Mary’s location can itself be blameworthy, in which case (most think) it fails to exculpate (Ginet 2000: 271). (For the classic discussion of what it takes for ignorance to be culpable see Holly Smith 1983 and ++sect. 2++ below. For discussions of whether culpable ignorance excuses, see Holly Smith 1983 and 2017; Montmarquet 1995.) And so for one to be able to be morally responsible in this situation irrespective of their previous actions (the moral responsibility of ignorance) they would have be aware of the fact that they are performing.
Secondly is the requirement for awareness of moral significance. This is where it may perhaps be a bit confusing as the path diverges into two. On the one hand, there are philosophers who believe that John would be required to know the whole moral significance of the act itself in its entirety; on the other hand, other philosophers believe that John only needed to be aware that the factors in it could be wrong or could make it wrong in entirety, then he’s still responsible. The position according to which the relevant awareness is de dicto awareness entails that moral knowledge (or at least moral beliefs) is necessary for responsibility (Sliwa 2017), whereas the position according to which the relevant awareness is de re awareness denies the necessity of moral knowledge (Harman 2011 & 2015; Talbert 2013; Weatherson 2019: ch. 5). We’ll see below (++sect. 3.3++) that this is a key dispute concerning the epistemic requirements on praise-/blameworthiness.
Thirdly is the awareness of consequences. Of course this is quite simple so I will refrain from over-analyzing it, nonetheless, it is still important in the sense of which type of knowledge is actually required here: the exact knowledge of what will happen, or the general understanding that what will happen is wrong and bad. It’s worth noting that the requirement of awareness of consequences is usually stated in terms of “reasonable foreseeability” rather than actual foresight (Vargas 2005; Fischer & Tognazzini 2009; Sartorio 2017; cf. Zimmerman 1986; Nelkin & Rickless 2017a).
Fourth and finally, the requirement of awareness of alternatives. Some philosophers argue that an agent can’t be blameworthy for a wrong action unless she believes that there is at least one alternative (and permissible) course of action open to her. For instance, Levy writes (see also Wieland 2017a: 2; Guerrero 2007: 89):
Perhaps it need not be the case … that agents need genuine access to alternative possibilities when they choose and act, but they do need epistemic access to a range of alternatives: they can only appropriately be blamed for performing an action if they believed that alternatives were available to them, and understood the significance of these alternatives. (Levy 2011: 111)
Applying this idea to our example, John would be blameworthy only if he believed that he could have pursued an alternative and permissible course of action, such as refraining from pressing the button. However, not everyone agrees that this is a genuine epistemic requirement on responsibility. For instance, Sartorio (2017) argues—on the basis of a variation on the classic Frankfurt cases (Frankfurt 1969)—that an agent can be blameworthy even if she believes, or even knows, that she couldn’t have done otherwise, as long as this belief doesn’t interfere with her own deliberation about whether to perform the wrong action.

6---full-notes/essential-terms-for-psych.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Essential Terms for Psychological Statistics.md
6---full-notes/essential-terms-for-psych.title: Essential Terms for Psychological Statistics
6---full-notes/essential-terms-for-psych.content:
Status: adult
Tags: statistics psychology 3 - Tags/reading
Essential Terms for Psychological Statistics
Details
Core basics

Sample vs population: The people actually studied (sample) vs everyone we care about (population).
N (or n): How many people/observations. Bigger N = more precise.
Variable types:

Continuous (height, score),
Categorical (male/female; yes/no),
Ordinal (Likert 1–5).



Describing data

Mean: Usual “average.”
Median: Middle value; ignores extreme outliers.
Standard deviation (SD): Typical spread around the mean. If M=70, SD=10, most scores are ~60–80.
Range/IQR: Range = max–min. IQR = middle 50%; both describe spread.
z-score: How many SDs a value is from the mean (z=1 = one SD above average).

Significance and uncertainty

Null hypothesis (H0): “No real effect/difference.”
p-value: If H0 were true, how surprising are these data? Smaller p = more surprising. p<.05 is the common “significant” cutoff, not a magic truth machine.
Alpha (α): Your chosen cutoff for “significant” (often .05).
Type I error: False alarm (saying there’s an effect when there isn’t).
Type II error: Miss (failing to spot a real effect).
Power (1−β): Chance to detect a real effect (aim ~80%). Bigger samples = more power.
Standard error (SE): How wobbly an estimate is. Smaller SE = more precise.
Confidence interval (CI): Estimate ± wiggle room. A 95% CI is a plausible range for the true value. Narrow = precise. If a 95% CI for a difference doesn’t include 0, that’s typically “significant.”

Effect size (how big is it, in practical terms?)

Cohen’s d: Difference between two group means in SD units.

~0.2 small, ~0.5 medium, ~0.8 large (rough guides).


Correlation (r): Strength of a relationship (−1 to +1).

~.10 small, ~.30 medium, ~.50 large.


R-squared (R²): Percent of outcome variation a model explains (e.g., R²=.25 → 25%).
Eta-squared (η²): Percent of variation explained by a factor (ANOVA version of R²).
Odds ratio (OR): For yes/no outcomes. OR=1 no difference; OR=2 = double the odds; OR=0.5 = half the odds.
Beta (β): Regression slope. Standardized β says “how many SDs Y changes per 1 SD change in X.”

Common tests you’ll see

t-test: Compare two means.

Independent: two different groups.
Paired: same people twice (pre/post).


ANOVA (F-test): Compare 3+ means or multiple factors.

One-way, two-way, repeated-measures, or mixed.
ANCOVA = ANOVA while adjusting for a covariate.


Chi-square (χ²): Are categorical variables related? (e.g., treatment vs improved yes/no)
Correlation:

Pearson’s r: linear relation between continuous variables.
Spearman’s ρ: rank-based (for skewed/ordinal data).


Regression:

Linear: predicts a continuous outcome (test score).
Logistic: predicts a yes/no outcome (quit vs not).


Nonparametric stand-ins (when assumptions fail):

Mann–Whitney/Wilcoxon, Kruskal–Wallis, etc.



Assumptions (quiet rules the tests rely on)

Normality: Data roughly bell-shaped (mostly matters for small samples).
Equal variances: Groups have similar spread (you’ll see “Levene’s test”).
Independence: One person’s score doesn’t depend on another’s (watch for clustered data like students in classes).
Sphericity (repeated-measures ANOVA thing): Variances of differences are similar (“Mauchly’s test”). If broken, papers use corrections like Greenhouse–Geisser.

If assumptions are shaky, researchers might transform data, use robust/nonparametric tests, or switch models.
Multiple tests problem
Running many tests inflates false positives (p-hacking risk). Fixes:

Bonferroni, Holm, FDR: Adjust p-values or the cutoff.
Pre-registration: Promises the analysis plan ahead of time.

Measurement (super important in psychology)

Reliability = consistency.

Cronbach’s alpha (α): Internal consistency for a questionnaire; ~.70+ is often acceptable; >.95 can mean items are redundant.
Test–retest: Stable over time.
Inter-rater (e.g., Cohen’s κ, ICC): Raters agree with each other.


Validity = are we measuring what we think?

Construct validity (overall), convergent (agrees with similar measures), discriminant (not the same as different constructs), criterion (predicts outcomes).


Factor analysis:

EFA: Explore how items group into factors.
CFA: Confirm a factor structure; common fit indices: CFI/TLI (>.90–.95 good), RMSEA (<.06–.08 lower is better), SRMR (~<.08 lower is better).


Latent variables: Unseen traits (like “anxiety”) estimated from items.
Mediation and moderation:

Mediation: X affects Y through M (indirect effect; often tested with bootstrapped CIs).
Moderation: The effect of X on Y depends on Z (an interaction).



Designs you’ll read about

Between-subjects: Different people in each condition.
Within-subjects: Same people in all conditions (more power; watch order effects).
Mixed design: Both together.
Random assignment vs random sampling: Assignment = who goes to which condition; sampling = who gets into the study in the first place.
Covariates/confounds: Extra variables adjusted for (ANCOVA, regression).
Clustered data: People nested in groups (classes, clinics). Use multilevel/mixed models with random effects.

Bayesian terms (when you see them)

Prior: What you believed before the data.
Posterior: Updated belief after seeing data.
Bayes Factor (BF): How much data favor one model over another (e.g., BF10=5 means data are 5× more likely under the alternative than the null).
Credible interval: Bayesian version of an interval—“there’s a 95% probability the true value is in here” (different philosophy than CI).

Meta-analysis and replication

Meta-analysis: Combines many studies to estimate an overall effect.

Fixed vs random effects: Assume one true effect vs effects vary across studies.
Heterogeneity (I²): How much effects differ (25% low, 50% moderate, 75% high).
Publication bias: Missing null studies; checked with funnel plots.


Replication: Re-do the study to see if it holds up.

How to read a result quickly

Look for the effect size (d, r, OR, R²) + its 95% CI. That tells you “how much” and “how sure.”
Check N (was it big enough?) and power if reported.
p-values: Treat p<.05 as “worth a look,” not “truth.” Many tests? Look for corrections.
Measurement: Are the scales reliable/valid? (α reported? CFA fit ok?)
Design: Within vs between? Randomized? Any obvious confounds?
Assumptions/robustness: Did they check them or use appropriate methods?
Practical meaning: Would this matter in real life, not just on paper?

Supporting Content

6---full-notes/establishing-credibility.title: Establishing Credibility
6---full-notes/establishing-credibility.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology relationship CBT
Establishing Credibility
Details
To resolve the problem of trust, the therapy must establish some common ground, find some point of agreement, and then extend the area of consensus from there. They may start with something like empathizing with the patient, not necessarily agreeing or disagreeing, but encouraging the patient to express his distorted ideas to understand and really hear the patient. After that, he may send some signs, or trials to determine if the patient is ready to examine the distortions in his thoughts.
These delusions, though thought to be impermeable by psychotherapy, can still eventually become amenable to modification if the therapist is sensitive and patient (Beck, 1952; Davidson, 1966; Salzman, 1960; Schwartz, 1963). Studies have even shown that dogmatism tends to widen the gap between persons with different opinions, making them more extreme in their views of the subject to simply distance themselves from the other. The therapist must then be vigilant to any clues that indicates the patient’s disagreement, to not be deceived by their inexpressiveness as agreement.
Many patients appear to agree with the therapist due to their fears of challenging the person of authority and trying to please them instead. And so when in therapy, one must have an admixture of their own humility to trial-and-error and lead the patient to find the best approaches or formulations for his own illness.
Delusional thinking is a way that the confidence between the two is tested. It is generally wise for us not to attack it directly, but rather help the patient cope with it. For example, an elderly man believes his wife is cheating on him, his wife is subsequently annoyed and may really leave him. This is when the therapist steps in to make the man realize that if he continues to berate his wife, he might not have someone to take care of him anymore, which makes him stop.

Establishing Relationships
Details
In therapy, it is necessary to almost “market” the treatment and also the person doing it. Clients must understand/trust that the person has the expertise and ability to guide them through to solve their problems.
Expertise, credibility, and efficacy can be conveyed in a variety of ways. Skills trainers’ neatness, professionalism, interest, comfort, self-­ confidence, speech style, and preparation for therapy sessions are no less useful in skills training than in individual psychotherapy. It is especially important in conducting groups to have the group room prepared before the group members arrive: Handouts and worksheets should be distributed; chairs should be in place; and the refreshments should be made and available (if refreshments are provided). The key to the credibility problem, in my experience, is that many clients—­ particularly those with severe and chronic disorders—simply do not believe that learning the skills presented will in fact be helpful. This disbelief detracts from any positive motivation to learn the skills, and unless clients learn the skills and obtain positive rewards, it is difficult to change this attitude. Indeed, this dynamic can become a vicious circle.
In fact, DBT is quite like a shotgun, some pellets may hit, some may not, depending on the target. It is good for people to know about this inherent nature, as people can become distrusted in the therapist and question their credibility.

6---full-notes/estrogen's-underappreciat.title: Estrogen's Underappreciated Benefits
6---full-notes/estrogen's-underappreciat.content:
Status: teen
Tags: biology
Estrogen’s Underappreciated Benefits
Details
Estrogen, often sidelined in hormone discussions, wields powerful, protective effects on the brain and body in both sexes—far beyond stereotypes of “feelings and empathy.” Physiologically, it enhances cognition by stimulating hippocampal neurogenesis, improving glucose and oxygen delivery, and reducing inflammatory damage. This shields against dementia, Alzheimer’s, and cardiovascular issues, making high estrogen levels a boon: it decreases oxidative stress on blood vessels and bolsters neural resilience.
Contrast this with testosterone’s potential to worsen these (e.g., inflammation), and estrogen shines as a guardian. Yet, it’s dose- and timing-dependent: physiological levels protect, but abrupt shutdowns (e.g., menopause) harm; restarting via therapy yields mixed results, emphasizing continuity. The transcript urges “go for having a lot of estrogen” if choosing—it’s neuroprotective, countering age-related decline.
Misconceptions persist: estrogen isn’t just “sensitivity”; it’s a cognitive enhancer, predicting Alzheimer’s protection. In males, low levels correlate with decline, suggesting broader relevance. Implications for health: women post-menopause might benefit from timely replacement, but consult physicians to avoid pitfalls. For all, lifestyle factors (e.g., exercise) that sustain hormones matter.
This reframes estrogen as essential for vitality, challenging gender biases and highlighting its role in resilience. In a hormone-obsessed culture, recognizing its strengths promotes balanced views.

6---full-notes/euphoria-and-excitation.content:

Euphoria and Excitation
Details
Just as said before about paradoxical sadness linking to loss and such, the condition for euphoria or excitation is the perception or expectation of gain. This effectively means the person will increase his evaluation in his own domain.
But not only does this produce euphoria but the anticipation of achieving euphoria may also lead to pleasure. In fact, it can even have an escalating effect. For example, someone posting his work on a recognized journal and it doing well will lead to him thinking to himself that he is also important as people appreciate his work, then he thought of the people that would see it, his euphoria increased. And so on…
Whether one experiences pleasure or not heavily depends on the meaning that he attributes to the object or activity that is being linked to. As said above, the man attributed his work being mentioned as it being recognized, and so he was ecstatic.
This pleasure does not need to have a source before it, meaning that it isn’t necessary for there to be a need for it before, the only thing necessary is for it to be pleasurable. But, once someone has felt this pleasure, they might develop an active desire for more of it.
This leads us to feedback loops, which will help depressed patients to become motivated and eventually be treated.

Europe and China
Details
Revisionist historians, most notably those associated with the “California School” such as Kenneth Pomeranz and R. Bin Wong, fiercely challenge the notion of an inherent Western miracle or deep-seated European exceptionalism. Historians actually argued that these colonies could be equal to each other economically and technologically, and that they only really diverged in the 19th century onward. Europe with England’s abundance of coal and the massive influx of wealth and resources extracted from European overseas colonies. From this perspective, modernity is less a profound, localized structural shift and more a toolkit of surface-level economic and technological changes that spread across a globally level playing field.
England’s role in all of this is actually quite profound, it isn’t coincidental that it is perhaps marked as the origin of the modern world. It did not have strong academic prowess or innovative power as other nations combined but it was the main distributor. It would bring back inventions from certain areas of the world and formalize and distribute it to other nations, consequently allowing everyone to grow alongside.

Evidence Based Practices
Details
When studying at school, teachers are usually given materials that they will use their own methods and own teaching styles to teach the classes that they are assigned to. This can be ineffective for some due to the fact that these methods can be suitable to some learners whilst others none at all. When confronted with these facts, the teachers may often dismiss and scold the students as if it was their fault, affecting them not only academically but also mentally as well.
This is where EBP comes in. Evidence-Based Practices (EBPs) are instructional strategies and methods that have been proven effective through rigorous scientific research. Instead of relying solely on tradition or individual observation, EBPs provide teachers with a toolkit of validated approaches. By grounding instruction in research, EBPs reduce the guesswork involved in teaching. This shifts the focus from a teacher’s abstract sense of what should work to a concrete set of strategies that are proven to work for diverse learners.

6---full-notes/evidence-and-proof.content:
Status: baby

Evidence and Proof
Details
When distinguishing between evidence and proof that is central to rhetorical practice, we have to understand what these two terms entail: Evidence is raw material — it exists, but it doesn’t yet mean anything. It requires interpretation, assembly, arrangement. It must be made to fit an argument. Proof, by contrast, implies something settled, something that compels assent by its very nature. Evidence can be interpreted in many ways, which is why data is sent to many analysts. Even though this is the case, not every interpretation is good or accurate. Nonetheless, the fact that this exists is enough for rhetoricians, as they only need to understand how the same set of facts can support radically different conclusions depending on how they are framed, sequenced, and contextualized.

6---full-notes/evolutionary-mismatch-of-.content:
Status: baby
Tags: habits Evolutionary Psychology
Evolutionary mismatch of Delayed Gratification
Details
As humans, we did not evolve for the delayed-return environment that characterizes the modern world. For thousands of years, our ancestors operated in an immediate-return environment. Hunting and gathering required immediate gratification to push humans to continue performing tasks necessary to sustain vitality and survive. However, as society progressed—starting with the agricultural revolution (farming) and evolving into modern economic structures (bi-weekly salaries, long-term investments)—delayed gratification became the norm. Because our brains are still wired for immediate returns, we naturally feel dissatisfied with delayed tasks. Our biology fights our modern goals. To counter this evolutionary mismatch and sustain motivation for long-term projects, we must artificially inject immediate stimuli and short-term rewards into our routines to appease our ancient neurology.

6---full-notes/example-on-supply-and-dem.title: Example on Supply and Demand
6---full-notes/example-on-supply-and-dem.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Example on Supply and Demand
Details
The supply-and-demand model explains market prices by combining the behavior of buyers and sellers. A market is a setting where buyers and sellers interact to make transactions, whether physically in an old-style marketplace or abstractly through modern institutions and platforms. Demand represents the relationship between price and quantity from the consumer’s perspective. In the rose example, demand is written as q = 1,800 − 400p, which means that as the price rises, the quantity demanded falls. This downward slope is explained by opportunity cost: when roses become more expensive, buying roses means giving up more other goods, so consumers want fewer roses. The specific numbers in the equation are not the main point at this stage. The important point is the negative relationship between price and quantity demanded.
Supply represents the relationship between price and quantity from the producer’s perspective. In the same example, supply is written as q = 200p, meaning that as price rises, suppliers are willing to produce more roses. This upward slope is also explained by opportunity cost. Land, labor, and capital used to produce roses could be used for something else. When the price of roses is low, producing roses may not be worth giving up those alternative uses. When the price is high, producing roses becomes more attractive relative to the next best use of the same resources. Supply and demand therefore both follow from scarcity and opportunity cost, but they move in opposite directions because consumers and producers face different margins of decision.
Equilibrium is the point where these two curves meet. In the rose example, solving the two equations gives an equilibrium quantity of 600 and an equilibrium price of 3. At this point, buyers are willing to buy exactly the amount sellers are willing to sell at that price. The system has “come to rest” because there is no immediate pressure, within the model, for price or quantity to change. If the price were too high, consumers would demand fewer roses than suppliers want to sell. If the price were too low, consumers would want more roses than suppliers provide. This does not care about the moral or social implications but rather only the economic implications of it.
This relationship is easily illustrated by diamonds and water: though one is essential to life and the other is used mainly for jewelry, the scarcer one is more expensive, not the more practical or meaningful one.

6---full-notes/exercising-to-wake-up.title: Exercising to wake up
6---full-notes/exercising-to-wake-up.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sleep
Exercising to wake up
Details
Physical exercise is a powerful, non-photic (non-light-based) tool for influencing the body’s circadian clock and promoting alertness. Its primary mechanism of action is the elevation of core body temperature. An increase in body temperature serves as a potent biological signal for wakefulness and activity, directly counteracting the state of sleep, which requires a temperature drop. However, the ultimate effect of exercise on the sleep-wake cycle is critically dependent on its timing.
When performed in the morning (within the first few hours of waking), exercise acts to advance the circadian clock. It amplifies the natural morning rise in cortisol and temperature, strongly anchoring the body’s sense of “daytime.” This not only enhances alertness and focus throughout the day but also makes it easier to fall asleep earlier that night, reinforcing a consistent schedule. This effect is magnified when combined with other levers, such as viewing morning sunlight during an outdoor walk or run.
Conversely, when performed in the late afternoon or evening, vigorous exercise can delay the circadian clock. The significant increase in core body temperature close to one’s typical bedtime can interfere with the natural cooling process required to initiate sleep. This pushes the entire sleep-wake cycle later, causing a desire to fall asleep later and wake up later. While this can be a useful tool for intentionally shifting one’s schedule (e.g., for travel or social reasons), it can be disruptive for those trying to maintain a regular sleep pattern. Therefore, the timing of exercise determines whether it functions to solidify an existing schedule or to actively shift it.

6---full-notes/exogamy-to-group-selectio.title: Exogamy to Group Selection
6---full-notes/exogamy-to-group-selectio.content:
Status: teen
Tags: behavioral biology
Exogamy to Group Selection
Details
The social structure created by female exogamy provides a direct pathway for group selection to occur. When females leave their birth troop, the resident males are all highly related (brothers, cousins). This kin structure fosters intense cooperation and transforms the entire group of males into a cohesive, coordinated unit.
This “band of brothers” now has a collective trait: organized, lethal inter-group aggression (warfare). Evolution can now act on this group-level trait. When one such chimp group encounters another, the conflict is not between individuals, but between two organized armies. The group with the more effective collective strategy (better coordination, more aggression) will win, eradicating the other group and taking their territory and resources.
This is a modern, viable model of group selection: selection is not acting “for the good of the species,” but on the relative fitness of one group versus another, based on an emergent, collective behavior that is itself built upon a foundation of kin selection.

6---full-notes/experimental-and-observat.title: Experimental and Observational Designs
6---full-notes/experimental-and-observat.content:
Status: teen
Tags: statistics
Experimental and Observational Designs
Details
In scientific research, experimental design and observational studies serve distinct, essential, and sometimes conflicting purposes. Experimental design includes random sampling, control groups, and identical exposure; it is also the only methodology that can definitively prove a cause-and-effect relationship. Observational studies on the other hand may yield correlational data but are frequently required due to ethical constraints, practical limitations, or the need for naturalistic validity.
The dangers could be easily exemplified by the medical history of Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT). Prior to 2002, observational data suggested that HRT was mostly beneficial, reducing hear disease and improved longevity in postmenopausal women. However, later, as the Women’s Health Initiative performed an experimental design, they had to halt the study due to participants experiencing increases in heart attacks, strokes, and breast cancer. Eventually, it was found out that this discrepancy was caused by the category of participants: in the observational study, the main group was women who tended to be healthier, wealthier, exercise more and was advised by their doctors.

6---full-notes/extending-minds-everywher.title: Extending Minds Everywhere
6---full-notes/extending-minds-everywher.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Extending Minds Everywhere
Details
Fritz Heider’s 1944 video of geometric shapes — triangles and a circle moving around a rectangle — is perhaps the most elegant demonstration of a cognitive tendency so deep it feels like perception rather than inference. When audiences watch the video, they don’t see shapes moving. They see a bully chasing a victim, a romantic rivalry, parents protecting children. They attribute intentions, desires, emotions, and personality traits to pieces of felt that have never met each other.
We are quite literally designed to interpret the movement of patterns as mental states. We see and we interpret, not that we actively figure and assign roles and stories to it. But of course there are exceptions to this. Children and adults with severe autism describe the video in purely physical terms: “The triangle moved left, then the circle moved right.” People with early amygdala damage do the same. For everyone else — including very young neurotypical children — the automatic attribution of mental states to moving objects is inescapable.
This is where psychology lies, it is one of, if not the most important leg that social psychology stands on; we need to explain things that cannot be reducible to the physical, which are what we interpret from whatever situations that we are in as hard sciences do not have a good explanation for it.

6---full-notes/externalist-against-skept.title: Externalist Against Skepticism
6---full-notes/externalist-against-skept.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Externalist Against Skepticism
Details
Internalism against skepticism would only result in a Cartesian circle, as one would have to constantly wonder about “do I know that I know” again and again infinitely. This is why many philosophers turn to Externalism, which instead proposes that we need not to “know” about the mechanics behind something but rather just that it works.
Millican uses the example of a dog knowing its master is approaching. The dog relies on its nose. The dog cannot write a philosophical treatise proving its nose is accurate, but if the nose is in fact reliable, the dog knows. This perspective rehabilitates G.E. Moore’s famous anti-sceptical argument (“Here is one hand, and here is another”). From an internalist view, Moore proves nothing. But from an externalist view, if Moore’s eyes are working, he does know he has hands, effectively ignoring the sceptic’s demand for proof.
Externalism though, still fails when it doesn’t address the specific anxiety of the inductive sceptic. Let’s say a sceptic asks, “How do you know the sun will rise tomorrow?”, the Externalist replies, “If the universe is uniform, then my belief is justified.” The sceptic is asking if the world will be the same, telling that person that “if it does, you’ll be fine” is a tautology, not comfort.

6---full-notes/eye-for-an-eye-as-an-opti.title: Eye for an Eye as an optimal method for the Prison Dilemma
6---full-notes/eye-for-an-eye-as-an-opti.content:
Status: teen
Tags: behavioral biology
Eye for an Eye as an optimal method for the Prison Dilemma
Details
In computer tournaments run by Robert Axelrod, the strategy that consistently won the Prisoner’s Dilemma game was Tit-for-Tat. Its rules are simple:


Be Nice: Cooperate on the first move.


Be Retaliatory: If your opponent cheats, you cheat on the next move.


Be Forgiving: If your opponent returns to cooperation, you do too.


Be Clear: Your strategy is simple for your opponent to figure out.


This strategy “may lose the battles, but it wins the war.” It is not exploitable and fosters long-term cooperation. Remarkably, this is not just a theoretical model. Biologists have found real-world examples in species from vampire bats (who refuse to share blood with bats that have “cheated” in the past) to stickleback fish (who refuse to “cooperate” with their own reflection if it appears to be lagging behind in a territorial defense).
Supporting Content
Thanks to the Axelrod’s tournament, we can understand thoroughly why it is the optimal strategy. As the TfT users are able to help each other quadratically gain points whilst the naive nasty (instantly just manipulating) initially wins in one interaction, they would lose in the long run due to the both betraying situation giving less points than the both sharing. And this would be even worse when two “nasties” are pitted against each other.

6---full-notes/factors-that-affect-confo.title: Factors That Affect Conformity
6---full-notes/factors-that-affect-confo.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/Social Psychology
Factors That Affect Conformity
Details
Asch’s research and subsequent studies have identified key factors that influence the likelihood of conformity:


Group Size: Conformity increases as the size of the majority grows, but it levels off quickly. The pressure exerted by a group of 3 or 4 people is just as strong as the pressure from a much larger group.


The Presence of an Ally: The most significant factor in reducing conformity is having an ally. If just one other person in the group gives the correct answer, the pressure on the participant is dramatically reduced, and they are far less likely to conform. Being in a minority of two is much easier than being a minority of one.


Anonymity: When participants can give their answers privately (e.g., by writing them down) instead of publicly, conformity drops sharply. This removes the fear of social ridicule.


Task Difficulty and Ambiguity: Conformity increases when the task is difficult or the correct answer is ambiguous. When we are uncertain, we are more likely to look to others for information and assume they are correct.


Group Status: People are more likely to conform to groups they perceive as having high status or being attractive. The desire to be accepted by or associated with such a group increases the pressure to align with their views.


Culture: Rates of conformity can vary across cultures. Studies have shown higher rates in collectivist cultures (e.g., in many Asian countries), where maintaining group harmony may be valued more highly than individual expression. In contrast, rates have generally decreased in individualist cultures like the United States since the 1950s.

Fear and Phobia

In our daily lives, it is clear that there are many things in our environment that are logically a threat to us. Accidents consistently happen - automobile crashes, fires, explosions - or illnesses that result in death. A person who avoids interacting with things that clearly are dangerous can hardly be accused of being neurotic.
But that raises the question, how do we distinguish between normal fears and phobias ? This can simply be explained and tackled in basic terms of psychology: “Nearly always, excessive fear of some particular type of object or situation; fear that is persistent and without sound grounds, or without grounds accepted as reasonable by the sufferer” (English and English, 1958).
Some important components of a phobia are the urgent desire to avoid the situation and, as the patient approaches it, he may accumulate more anxiety and try to escape. Frequently, it is observed that even though the phobia can interfere greatly with his life, the phobic patient has no problem navigating and maintaining one. It is significant that even though he acknowledges that his phobia is unreasonable, he cannot erase his fear or desire to avoid it.

6---full-notes/feature-detectors-as-the-.title: Feature Detectors as the Building Blocks of Vision
6---full-notes/feature-detectors-as-the-.content:
Status: baby
Tags: neuroscience
Feature Detectors as the Building Blocks of Vision
Details
The brain begins to process visual information by breaking it down into simple components. This is accomplished by feature detectors—specialized neurons in the visual cortex that respond to specific, simple features such as lines, angles, or movement in a particular direction. One neuron might fire in response to a horizontal line, while another fires for a vertical line.
Evidence for feature detectors comes from two primary sources. First, neurophysiological studies (notably by Hubel and Wiesel) recorded activity from individual neurons in the visual cortex of animals, showing that cells responded selectively to specific patterns. Second, psychological phenomena like the “waterfall illusion” demonstrate sensory fatigue. Staring at a consistent motion (like a waterfall) fatigues the feature detectors for that motion. When you look away, the unfatigued neurons that detect the opposite motion create an aftereffect illusion.

Feedback loops

Moreover, the most reliable predictor for long-term success is having a “growth mindset”. To actively seek and welcome feedback, be it of any kind, is one of the most important factors. This is inherently present in the gifted and talented individuals, who are constantly praised for what they are rather than what they do, and so they tend to try to keep this impression intact, rather than exposing themselves to new challenges and possibly learning from failure.

6---full-notes/feedback-we-choose-and-fe.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Feedback we choose and feedback we enjoy.md
6---full-notes/feedback-we-choose-and-fe.title: Feedback we choose and feedback we enjoy
6---full-notes/feedback-we-choose-and-fe.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Social Psychology
Feedback we choose and feedback we enjoy
Details
There are two competing theories that attempt to explain what kind of feedback people seek about themselves. The first is Self-Enhancement Theory, rooted in Freud and has been dominant for decades, which posits that people universally want positive feedback, and that they only care about the good stuff, not the truth stuff. Self-Verification Theory, developed by Bill Swann, says that people want feedback that may already confirm what they believe about themselves. Its not necessarily that you want the truth, but you want to know what’s already known about yourself.
Swann and Pelham’s studies revealed something that neither theory alone could explain. When subjects chose which attribute to hear about, they picked their best one, which would confirm both theory as the best usually correlates with people thinking positively of it. The distinction only came when people were asked about the negative trait. People in these situations wanted to hear negative feedback because that would correlate to what they already think about themselves, that they are not good at the task.
Nonetheless, the results of these studies confirm both theories, as people DO want feedback that makes them feel good, the negative feedback does make them feel awful, but they also want consistent feedback, as it is accurate and real. The word “want” is doing double duty. People want (choose) consistency. People want (enjoy) positivity. These are two different systems producing different outputs.
And so we come to the point of a shared reality, something that is perhaps the most important concept in a relationship. Accepting negative feedback that matches your self-view creates the feeling that someone genuinely understands you. Rejecting it to feel momentarily good costs you the sense that your relationships are built on real knowledge rather than comfortable fictions.

6---full-notes/feeling-better-instead-of.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Feeling better instead of being better.md
6---full-notes/feeling-better-instead-of.title: Feeling better instead of being better
6---full-notes/feeling-better-instead-of.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Zettelkasten learning 3 - Tags/reading
Feeling better instead of being better
Details
Many students tell themselves they’re “studying” when, in reality, they are only looping through the same pages over and over. Re‑reading, massed review the night before an exam, or flipping passively through highlighted notes does something powerful—but mostly to their emotions, not to their memory. Each exposure makes the material feel easier to process (psychologists call this processing fluency). That ease is misread by our brains as “I must really know this,” a classic illusion of competence. Surveys of college learners show that the vast majority list “rereading my notes” as their default strategy even while admitting it rarely changes their test scores.
Experimental work confirms the metacognitive trap. When students reread a text twice in a row they do score higher on an immediate recall test, but once 48 hours pass the benefit shrinks to almost nothing; in contrast, a single read followed by self‑quizzing or free‑recall writing produces far larger gains a week later. A 2023 systematic review covering health‑sciences, engineering and humanities courses found that retrieval‑based techniques (practice tests, flash‑card recall, teaching the content aloud) outperformed rereading in 80 % of the comparisons and did so with minimal extra study time.
Why does retrieval beat familiarity? Learning happens when a memory is re‑assembled from scratch, not when it is merely re‑exposed. Each act of recall strengthens the neural pathways needed to find that idea later and reveals what you don’t yet know, guiding smarter subsequent study. Rereading, by contrast, leaves the difficult connections untested, so the material collapses under the stress of an exam despite the warm feeling of, “Yes, I’ve seen this.” Follow‑up lab studies show that students who rely on rereading also predict higher future scores than their quizzing peers—an error that grows the more familiar the text becomes.

6---full-notes/female-counterstrategies-.title: Female Counterstrategies to Infanticide
6---full-notes/female-counterstrategies-.content:
Status: baby
Tags: behavioral biology
Female Counterstrategies to Infanticide
Details
To deal the infanticide that males do, female develop defensive strategies, either physical (which is not inherently effective in a tournament-bonding species) or psychophysiological responses.
One of the most remarkable is pseudo-ovulation. When a new, potentially infanticidal male arrives, a pregnant female can develop the external physiological signs of being in heat (estrus), even though she is not ovulating. The new male, seeing these signs, will mate with her. When she gives birth a short time later, the male is tricked into “believing” the infant is his own premature offspring and will not harm it. These males usually do not have the ability to cognitively think about how his children are being birthed way faster than the usual time of his species.

6---full-notes/first-impressions.content:
Status: teen
Tags: 3 - Tags/Social Psychology
First Impressions
Details
In both folk psychology and social psychology, we often regard this as the most important aspect of an interaction between people as it often will dictate how they treat each other further down the line. This is known as the primacy effect (same as the one we studied in Primacy Effect). Though it may come as a surprise, we actually form first impressions with amazing speed and more accuracy through many researches and experiments. This concept can dictate and influence our decisions throughout our daily lives as we encounter many situations requiring the use of it.
These first impressions can manifest themselves into something worse though, referred to as self-fulfilling prophecies, which are the expectations that change the behavior of a person to increase the probability of those expectations becoming true. Suppose a psychologist hands you a cellphone and asks you to talk with someone, while showing you a photo supposedly of that person. Unknown to the person you are talking to, the psychologist might hand you a photo of a very attractive member of the opposite sex or a much less attractive photo. Not surprisingly, you act friendlier to someone you regard as attractive. Furthermore, if you think you are talking to someone attractive, that person reacts by becoming more cheerful and talkative. In short, your first impression changes how you act and influences the other person to live up to (or down to) your expectations (M. Snyder, Tanke, & Berscheid, 1977).

6---full-notes/five-modalities-of-approa.content:
Status: teen

Five Modalities of Approaching Marxism
Details
In approaching Marxism, one must view it not a monolithic subject but a complex intellectual and historical phenomenon that can be studied through at least five distinct lenses. First, one can approach it as an intellectual biography of Karl Marx, who was a fallible figure whose views evolved, developed, and even contradicted themselves as he too grew as a person. Second, scholars can perform a rational reconstruction, isolating Marx’s most fruitful concepts to build a maximally coherent and fully elaborated theoretical system, optimizing his thoughts and ideas. Thirdly, it can be viewed as something like Darwinism, where the focus of the theory is its most updated form rather than its origins. Fourth, one might examine it as a pluralistic historical phenomenon, exploring the fragmented and diverging projects of later thinkers like Lenin, Gramsci, or Adorno without assuming a unified theoretical mainstream. Finally, because Marxism fundamentally insists on the unity of theory and practice, it can be studied empirically by analyzing the actual historical societies that attempted to implement it, examining the friction between their ideological constitutions and their material realities.

Flow, Deindividuation
Details
Csikszentmihalyi’s concept of flow (1974) describes complete immersion in an activity where the self disappears. Its psychological features — time distortion, absent self-evaluation, poor subsequent memory, present-moment dominance, effortless-feeling control — are virtually identical to deindividuation’s.
And the difference is rooted in the evaluative nature of the flow, if it produces socially condemned behavior (riots, aggression), we call it deindividuation and pathologize it. The underlying mental state is likely the same.
Zen meditative states represent a third framing: deliberate, disciplined self-dissolution pursued as a spiritual ideal. Herrigel described the Zen state as “purposeless and egoless” — language that Western culture would treat as pathological in any non-spiritual context. This reveals that society’s evaluation of self-loss depends entirely on the cultural framework applied to it, not on the phenomenology of the experience itself.

Fodor’s mind model
Details
The model of the mind that Fodor thinks of is one that is also an information-processing device, but rather it operates on the premise that they operate on specific classes of information, are mandatory, and are fast. They also allow no to little inference from other modules, and produce shallow outputs. The development of modules exhibits a characteristic pace and sequencing, and they have
regular patterns of breakdown or malfunction (Weiskopf, 2002). Finally, according to Fodor, modules are associated with a stable neural architecture (for a more extensive review of Fodorian modularity, see Fodor, 1983).
Moreover, only input systems (responsible for perception and language processing) and output systems (responsible for actions) are plausible for modularity. In contrast, central systems (responsible for “higher” cognitive processes such as reasoning, problem solving and belief-fixation) are likely to be nonmodular. It should also be mentioned that the modular components are peripheral parts of the mind.

Folk Psychology
Details
Folk psychology is the common-sense, intuitive understanding of the mind that people use in everyday life without formal training. It’s the psychology that “folk know,” encompassing a vocabulary of terms like memory, emotion, learning, and personality that we use to navigate our social world. Unlike many science courses where students begin with zero knowledge of the topics, an introductory psychology course starts with subjects about which everyone already has pre-existing beliefs and notions. The term was originally coined in the 19th century to distinguish this everyday knowledge from the psychology one would learn in an academic setting. The goal of academic psychology is to move beyond this surface-level, often anecdotal understanding. It seeks to scientifically investigate the mechanisms, structures, and true nature behind these familiar concepts, often revealing that our intuitive or “folk” theories are incomplete or incorrect.
This sub-subject of psychology is often what people use in their daily life. As we could see at times, it can be quite helpful as it connects people together and may even help them empathize and help each other, but at other times, when problems get more specific and academic, it can backfire and instead harm the person in need.

6---full-notes/frameworks-for-difference.content:

Frameworks for differences
Details
The statistical framework of psychopathology defines abnormality in a logical way, meaning that a deviation from the norm. A behavior or trait is considered disordered if it falls in the extreme tails of a normal distribution, typically two or more standard deviations from the mean. It is clear about how this functions due to the amount of tests that exists nowadays, DASS, K-12, so on and so forth. They all are dependent on the person taking the test or someone else that knows them well. However, this model has two glaring drawbacks, one is about how easy it is to change the norm and deviation and how much it can affect; the other is that it is value-neutral, meaning we cannot understand if it is a positive or negative deviation. How we deal with the latter is that we apply our own social values and understandings into it so we can distinguish them.
The social deviance model on the other hand depends on what is regarded as a societal (not mathematical) norm and then identifying abnormalities from that norm. This model can be and is highly hurtful, as it can be used to make people feel “left out” and “isolated” from society. In fact, it has been used like this before, like how people with mental illnesses are considered weak and pathetic in Eastern societies or how mental disorders were known as possessions in the 20th century. Even worse, it was used as a political tool by the Soviet Union by defining those who does not believe in communism to have a mental illness.
Moreover, this model even includes the morals of the human beings, it stops being political or cultural and rather goes into the morals. When a person does activities to cope with or are symptoms of their mental disorders, it can be regarded as a moral failing.

6---full-notes/framing-effects.title: Framing Effects
6---full-notes/framing-effects.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Framing Effects
Details
Kahneman and Tversky demonstrated that mathematically identical choices produce opposite preferences depending on whether outcomes are framed as gains or losses. Given 600 people threatened by an earthquake: “200 will be saved” (gain frame) versus “400 will die” (loss frame) yield identical outcomes, yet 72% choose the sure option under gain framing while 78% choose the risky option under loss framing. This shows that for gains, we are risk-averse; for losses, we are risk seeking, we would prefer the gamble that might prevent the bad thing from happening. This shows that anyone, and anyone at all, can change the way they frame their words and propositions to reverse public preference. The deeper principle from prospect theory is that psychological distance is nonlinear: the subjective difference between 0 and 1 death is far greater than between 100 and 101 deaths, explaining Stalin’s observation that “one death is a tragedy, a hundred deaths is a statistic.” Even when people see both framings simultaneously and recognize they’re identical, the feeling differs—gain and loss frames activate different emotional responses that resist logical override.

6---full-notes/frankfurt-cases-and-the-p.title: Frankfurt Cases and the Principle of Alternate Possibilities (PAP)
6---full-notes/frankfurt-cases-and-the-p.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Frankfurt Cases and the Principle of Alternate Possibilities (PAP)
Details
The concept of PAP, or Principle of Alternate Possibilities asserts that an agent is morally responsible for a situation if there existed a world where they could have acted otherwise. Harry Frankfurt challenged this via thought experiments now known as “Frankfurt Cases,” which attempt to separate responsibility from the ability to do otherwise. In a typical scenario, an agent (Jones) chooses to perform an action A. However, a manipulator (Black) is monitoring Jones’s brain and would have intervened to force Jones to do A had Jones shown any sign of hesitating. Jones does A on his own, so we intuitively hold him responsible, yet he could not have done otherwise due to Black’s presence. This suggests moral responsibility stems from the action flowing from the agent’s own will, not from the metaphysical possibility of an alternative. But, there still exists an argument against this, being if Jones were to choose B but then diverted to A, then he still showed a flicker of freedom, and that itself shows some nuance about the responsibility that he has.

6---full-notes/free-floating-anxiety-fal.title: Free-floating anxiety fallacy
6---full-notes/free-floating-anxiety-fal.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Free-floating anxiety fallacy
Details
The term “free-floating anxiety” evokes a powerful and unsettling image: a pervasive sense of dread, untethered to any specific cause or object, that drifts through one’s consciousness like a phantom menace. Coined in the era of early psychoanalysis, this concept has long been a descriptor for the hallmark symptom of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD). However, modern psychology increasingly reveals the fallacy of this notion. The anxiety in GAD is not, in fact, “free-floating” but is deeply anchored in a web of underlying cognitive distortions, habitual negative thought patterns, and a heightened sensitivity to perceived threats. The feeling of untethered worry is a symptom, not the source, of a more complex psychological process.
The historical roots of “free-floating anxiety” can be traced back to Sigmund Freud, who used the term to describe a diffuse, non-specific apprehension. This psychoanalytic perspective suggested that the anxiety was a result of repressed conflicts or impulses, its true origins obscured from the individual’s conscious mind. While this was a foundational step in understanding persistent anxiety, it inadvertently created the impression of a causeless emotional state. This idea persisted for some time, even as the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) evolved to more precisely define GAD.
Contemporary understanding, heavily influenced by cognitive-behavioral models, presents a more nuanced picture. It posits that the anxiety in GAD is not an ethereal mist but a product of specific, albeit often automatic and unrecognized, cognitive processes. Individuals with GAD tend to exhibit a cognitive bias towards interpreting ambiguous situations as threatening. Their minds are constantly scanning the horizon for potential dangers, a state of hypervigilance that transforms everyday concerns about health, finances, or relationships into sources of chronic and excessive worry. This “what if?” thinking becomes a deeply ingrained habit, a seemingly constant hum of apprehension that feels disconnected from any single trigger because it is, in reality, connected to so many potential ones.
Therapeutic modalities like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) have been instrumental in deconstructing the fallacy of free-floating anxiety. The core of CBT for GAD lies in making the patient aware of these underlying and often subconscious thought patterns. Through techniques such as cognitive restructuring, individuals learn to identify their automatic negative thoughts, challenge their validity, and replace them with more balanced and realistic appraisals. In essence, CBT helps to give the “free-floating” anxiety a name and an address, tracing it back to its roots in maladaptive beliefs and cognitive habits. This process demonstrates that the anxiety is not a random, inexplicable force but a learned response that can be unlearned.
In conclusion, while “free-floating anxiety” remains a potent descriptor of the subjective experience of GAD, it is a misleading one. The unease is not adrift without an anchor; it is tethered to a complex network of cognitive biases and ingrained patterns of worry. Recognizing this is more than a semantic distinction; it is a fundamental shift in understanding that empowers both clinicians and those who suffer from this debilitating condition. By moving beyond the myth of causeless anxiety, we can focus on the tangible, cognitive roots of the distress, paving the way for effective, targeted interventions that can help individuals reclaim their mental peace from the seemingly nebulous grip of worry.

6---full-notes/freud's-stages-of-psychos.title: Freud's Stages of Psychosexual Development
6---full-notes/freud's-stages-of-psychos.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Freudian psychology
Freud’s Stages of Psychosexual Development
Details
Sigmund Freud proposed that personality develops through a series of five psychosexual stages. During each stage, a child’s psychosexual energy, or libido, is focused on a different erogenous zone. Freud believed that if a child’s needs at a particular stage were either over-gratified or not met, they could become fixated, leading to personality traits and behaviors that persist into adulthood.
1. The Oral Stage (Birth to ~1.5 years)


Erogenous Zone: Mouth.


Focus: The infant derives intense pleasure from oral activities like sucking, biting, and breastfeeding.


Potential Fixation: An unresolved conflict at this stage could lead to adult behaviors centered on the mouth (e.g., smoking, overeating, excessive talking) or issues related to dependency and independence.


2. The Anal Stage (~1.5 to 3 years)


Erogenous Zone: Bowel and bladder control.


Focus: The child gets psychosexual pleasure from the sensations of controlling and eliminating feces. The major conflict is toilet training.


Potential Fixation: Freud suggested that overly strict or lenient toilet training could lead to an “anal-retentive” personality (orderly, stingy, stubborn) or an “anal-expulsive” personality (messy, wasteful).


3. The Phallic Stage (~3 to 6 years)


Erogenous Zone: Genitals.


Focus: Children become aware of their genitals and, according to Freud, develop a sexual attraction to the opposite-sex parent (the Oedipus complex for boys and the Electra complex for girls). This stage is marked by controversial concepts like “penis envy” in girls.


Potential Fixation: Fixation at this stage could lead to long-term difficulties with relationships and authority.


4. The Latent Period (~6 years to puberty)

Focus: Sexual impulses are suppressed and dormant. The child’s energy is redirected toward social interactions, schoolwork, and developing friendships, primarily with same-sex peers. This is not a psychosexual stage in the same way as the others.

5. The Genital Stage (Puberty onwards)


Erogenous Zone: Maturing sexual interests.


Focus: The individual develops a strong sexual interest in people outside the family. If the previous stages have been successfully navigated, the person can form healthy, mature sexual relationships.


Potential Fixation: Freud believed that individuals with significant fixations in earlier stages would have less libido available for this stage, leading to difficulties in forming satisfying relationships.


Evaluation of the Stages While the basic observations are undeniable (infants suck, toddlers are toilet-trained), the core Freudian concept of fixation is very difficult to test scientifically. When researchers have attempted to test these ideas, such as the link between toilet training and an “anal” personality, they have found little to no supporting evidence.

6---full-notes/from-terms-to-message.content:

Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
From terms to message
Details
In the book, a proposition is also a declaration, but of the author’s judgement about something. He affirms something he thinks is true, or denies which is not, and so it is a declaration of knowledge, not intentions. He may tell us intentions at the beginning in a preface, and the rest is throughout the book.
This leads into the sixth and seventh rule, which I am including both because they are closely connected. As the author declares himself on his own knowledge, we usually trusts him or maybe even parrot his opinions, but we should not be satisfied by this. These propositions are merely personal opinions unless they are supported by scientifically reasons, or logical ones. And if we are also interested in both the author and the book, we should also ask why and how did he come to be persuaded by these ideas.
And the seventh rule, therefore, deals with arguments of all sorts. Every sort of argument consists a number of statements in any way, and we can choose to argue that is it true; but sometimes only a probability can be defended.
The presence of these arguments are by words that relate statements, such as: if this is so, then that; or since this,… and we must observe this, because there is no one to guide us completely through the book, it is an absent teacher. The parts of these arguments conclude a series of statements which provide the grounds on what is to be concluded. And therefore, a paragraph, is necessary to express an argument. It may not be stated first, but it is the source, and if it is valid, the conclusion will follow so. This does not mean that it is true, as the supporting anchors can be false.

6---full-notes/functions-as-relational-m.title: Functions as Relational Machines
