Functions as Relational Machines
Details
A function is formally defined not as a dynamic process, but as a static logical structure: specifically, a subset of a Cartesian product. A function f from A to B is a set of ordered pairs <a, b> such that for every input a, there is exactly one unique output b. While formally a set, it is intuitively understood as a machine that deterministically maps inputs (Domain) to outputs (Range).
Functions can be combined through Composition (g \circ f), where the output of f becomes the input of g. This is analogous to connecting two hoses; the flow (data) moves through the first to reach the second. This operation is associative, allowing complex chains of transformations to be built from simple mappings.

6---full-notes/fundamental-attributional.title: Fundamental Attributional Error
6---full-notes/fundamental-attributional.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Social Psychology
Fundamental Attributional Error
Details
In our daily social lives, what do we do ? We get into a lot of situations, and define them by our subjective interpretations, not their objective self. Not only that, but we also have a bias to ourselves, thinking that our interpretation and our rules is the bible. And so when we see someone acting different, driving faster than us for example, they’re “crazy”, if they’re slower then they’re “stupid” so there’s really no winning there. This is called FAE by social psychologists, a phenomenon that happens when we attribute anything to someone’s traits rather than the situations that they’re in, giving an unfair judgement of them as a whole, while rarely applying that same judgment to ourselves.
Same as the situation presented in the lecture, you who know the situation that happened already (giving the middle finger to the lecturer), wouldn’t feel the anxiety that the new students know, which could be called an Empathy Gap.
Now let’s take an example the Game Theory and the Prisoner’s Dilemma, name it “Wallstreet Game” and the “Community Game”, keep everything else the same and distribute it randomly. Depending on the context, those who were in the “Wallstreet Game” cooperated much less (30%) compared to those in the latter (70%).
Supporting Content
When we try to explain someone’s behavior, we often make a common mistake: we overestimate the influence of their personality or internal disposition and underestimate the power of the situation. This tendency is known as the fundamental attribution error, or the correspondence bias. We assume a person’s actions directly correspond to who they are, even when there are clear external pressures influencing them.
A classic experiment powerfully illustrates this bias. Participants were asked to read an essay, either praising or condemning Fidel Castro, the former leader of Cuba. Crucially, the participants were told that the student author had been assigned their position and had no choice in the matter.
Despite knowing this powerful situational constraint, when asked to guess the author’s true attitude, most people still assumed that the student who wrote the pro-Castro essay was genuinely pro-Castro. They failed to fully account for the external influence (the assignment) and instead made an internal attribution (the author’s personal belief).
This error appears in many contexts. For example, even though we know celebrities are paid large sums of money for endorsements, we still tend to believe they genuinely favor the products they promote. The fundamental attribution error shows how difficult it is for us to separate a person’s actions from their character, leading us to misjudge the true cause of their behavior.

6---full-notes/further-than-drives-and-e.content:
Status: teen

Further than drives and emotions
Details
Moving beyond simple reward-seeking, a more complete model of motivation must account for the complexity of drives and the role of emotions. A key distinction is between consummatory and appetitive behaviors. Consummatory behaviors involve the direct satisfaction of a need (e.g., eating the food), while appetitive behaviors are the actions involved in seeking out that satisfaction (e.g., the hunt). For complex organisms, the seeking behavior must itself be motivating to ensure survival; one cannot wait until starvation is imminent to begin looking for food.
Emotions serve as a higher-level system to manage these drives. They act as a kind of internal shorthand that helps us mobilize resources, generalize from past experiences, and, crucially, communicate our motivational states to others. An expression of fear, for instance, can signal danger to the entire group. Emotions allow for a more flexible and social response to the world than simple, isolated drives would permit. They are the language through which we understand and express our internal motivational landscape.

6---full-notes/glp-1-as-a-weight-loss-su.content:
Status: teen

GLP 1 as a weight loss substance
Details
The origins of GLP are quite interesting, coming from the Gila Monster connection (Exendin-4) was discovered by Dr. John Eng. He found a hormone in the venom of the Gila monster that mimicked GLP-1 but lasted longer in the body. This became exenatide (Byetta), the first GLP-1 drug approved in 2005.
The drug is an agonist of the receptor well, GLP. It allows the person to be able to eat though to a much less extent as they will feel as if they are full. It basically makes it physically and neurologically impossible to eat an absurd amount of food. It stimulates POMC neurons (which tell you “stop eating”) and inhibits AgRP neurons (which tell you “eat now”). And a multitude of other mechanisms.

Game Theory and the Prisoner’s Dilemma
Details
The dynamics of reciprocal altruism can be mathematically modeled using game theory, particularly the Prisoner’s Dilemma. In this scenario, two individuals can either “Cooperate” or “Cheat” (Defect). The payoffs are structured such that:


Temptation (You Cheat, They Cooperate): The highest payoff.


Reward (You Both Cooperate): The second-highest payoff.


Punishment (You Both Cheat): A low payoff (a loss).


Sucker (You Cooperate, They Cheat): The worst possible payoff.


While cheating on a cooperator gives the best single-round outcome, if both players do this, they end up with a poor result. This model formalizes the central conflict of reciprocal altruism and allows for the testing of different behavioral strategies to find the optimal solution.

6---full-notes/gender-difference-in-deve.content:

Gender difference in psychopathology
Details
There is a striking developmental reversal in the gender ratio of psychopathology. In the first decade of life, boys are significantly more vulnerable, acting as “canaries in the coal mine” for neurodevelopmental disorders like Autism, ADHD, and early-onset Conduct Disorder. Being male is a risk factor during this period, potentially due to the vulnerability of the Y chromosome or slower maturation. However, in the second decade of life, the pattern flips. Starting around puberty, which occurs earlier for girls, females show a surge in internalizing disorders. By age 15-16, rates of depression, anxiety, and eating disorders skyrocket in girls, becoming 2-3 times higher than in boys. Thus, being female shifts from a protective factor in childhood (where girls are more verbal and socially connected) to a significant risk factor in adolescence.

Gene Duplication
Details
In the process of evolution, an entire gene or a large stretch of DNA can be duplicated. This creates redundancy, which allows for evolutionary experimentation. One copy of the gene can continue to perform its essential, original function, while the second copy is can mutate and change itself and combine with other copies whilst it does not ruin any function in the organism. Over time, this second copy can evolve a completely new function. This helps explain how complex features (the “what good is half an eye?” problem) can evolve, as the necessary components can be built and refined in a duplicated gene without breaking the existing system (Basically people who opposed the theory of evolution thought that since the body could not just accept half an eye because it is useless, evolution just could not just happen).

6---full-notes/gene-environment-interact.title: Gene-Environment Interaction in Depression
6---full-notes/gene-environment-interact.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Cognitive Psychology biology genetics 3 - Tags/environment
Gene-Environment Interaction in Depression
Details
Genes do not cause depression; they create vulnerabilities. Sapolsky emphasizes that genes are not deterministic blueprints for disease but are highly context-dependent, meaning the same gene can have different effects in different environments. This gene-environment interaction is the ultimate bridge between biology and psychology.
The most powerful illustration of this is the study on the 5-HTT gene, which codes for the serotonin re-uptake pump. This gene comes in different variants, or “flavors.” One variant is less efficient and was considered the “bad news” or vulnerability variant. However, simply having this variant did not increase a person’s overall risk of depression.
The risk only emerged when the genetic vulnerability was combined with a specific environmental trigger: childhood adversity. Individuals who had the “bad news” gene variant and experienced significant stress or abuse in childhood had a much higher likelihood of developing major depression later in life. Those with the same gene but a stable childhood had no increased risk.
This demonstrates that a genetic predisposition for depression may lie dormant until it is “activated” by a stressful environment, particularly during the critical developmental periods of childhood and adolescence. The psychological experience of stress directly influences how a person’s genetic blueprint is expressed, leading to the biological changes that constitute the illness. This is not just a human phenomenon; Sapolsky notes that the same interaction between this gene variant and early-life stress is observed in monkeys, reinforcing the biological reality of this principle.

6---full-notes/genealogy-as-entanglement.title: Genealogy as Entanglement
6---full-notes/genealogy-as-entanglement.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Genealogy as Entanglement
Details
Nietzsche’s Genealogy of Morality radically departs from the 19th-century tendency to write “Origin Stories.” Traditional histories (like Christian or Marxist narratives) trace a phenomenon back to a single, pure source—such as the teachings of Jesus or primitive communism—and view history as a linear development or degeneration from that point. Accordingly to his account of The Myth of Moral Coherence, Nietzsche argued that history is rather a contingent convergence of distinct, unrelated causal lines.
This explains the structure of the book itself. The three essays in Genealogy do not tell a continuous story.


Essay 1 traces the origin of “Good and Evil” to Aristocratic/Slave conflict (Resentment).


Essay 2 traces the origin of “Guilt” (Schuld) to commercial contract law and debt (Schulden).


Essay 3 traces the origin of “Ascetic Ideals.” Crucially, the concept of “Guilt” (Essay 2) did not arise from the concept of “Evil” (Essay 1). They have completely different origins—one in class warfare, the other in marketplace economics. The genius of Christianity was to accidentally or forcefully entangle these separate strands, fusing “debt” with “moral badness” to create the “Bad Conscience.” Therefore, genealogy is the study of how disparate historical accidents knot together to form the present, rather than a search for a singular “meaningful origin.”

Combinatorial Explosion for EP
Details
This is the concept that ‘‘with each degree of freedom added to a system, or with each new dimension of potential variation added, or with each new successive choice in a chain of decisions, the total number of alternative possibilities faced by a computational system grows with devastating rapidity.”
Domain-specific architectures can deal with this explosion of possibilities, because they contain cognitive structures that organize information, such as domain-specific databases, domain-specific decision rules, and rules that constrain the inputs into a system. A domain-general system, in contrast, lacks such structure and as a result “must evaluate all alternatives it can define. Permutations being what they are, alternatives increase exponentially as the problem complexity increases’’ (Cosmides & Tooby, 1994, p. 94). Consequently, combinatorial explosion will paralyze any system that is truly domain general.

6---full-notes/generalized-anxiety-disor.content:
Status:

Anxiety Disorders
Details
Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by a persistent and excessive state of anxiety that is not tied to any specific object or situation. Unlike other anxiety disorders that are triggered by particular stimuli, individuals with GAD experience a “free-floating” sense of tension and worry that permeates all aspects of their lives. From academic performance to social interactions, everything becomes a source of apprehension. This constant state of heightened arousal means there are no moments of relief, distinguishing it from the episodic nature of panic attacks or phobias.
Diagnostically, GAD is identified through intake interviews that assess the breadth of a person’s worries and through physiological measures like a heightened startle response. Affecting a significant portion of the population (around 5-6%), it is often treated with a combination of medication (antidepressants or tranquilizers) and therapy. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is particularly effective, as it helps individuals reinterpret situations and manage their anxious responses, providing them with tools to cope with the pervasive sense of worry.

6---full-notes/generalized-other.content:

Generalized Other
Details
George Herbert Mead’s concept of the “generalized other” describes the crucial mental step we take when we move beyond understanding individual roles (like “mommy” or “teacher”) to internalizing the abstract expectations of society as a whole. This isn’t about any specific person, but rather the composite attitude of our entire social group. We develop this by participating in organized activities, like games, where success requires us to anticipate the actions and expectations of every other player simultaneously. By taking the perspective of this “team,” we learn to see ourselves through the eyes of the community. This internal viewpoint becomes our guide for social conduct, allowing us to coordinate our actions with others and, most importantly, to form a stable sense of self judged against the norms and values of our society.
Supporting Content
Babies do not inherently have self-awareness, instead hey have “other-awareness,” which is imitation and monitoring of their caregivers and other people. And so we build our concept of ourselves not through reflection but from other people’s reaction to our being. According to sociologist George Herbert Mead, this is “reflected appraisal.” Over time, this generates a construct for who we are known as the “generalized other.” Whenever we engage in any societal endeavors, we are engaging with what other thinks of us and values in us.

Gestalt Psychology
Details
This school of psychology is dedicated to perception, as “Gestalt” is German for it. The founders of Gestalt argued that “the whole is different from the sum of its parts.” and that something cannot be understood completely just by breaking its parts down.
This approach does not reject the existence of feature detectors but insists they are insufficient to explain perception. It highlights the importance of top-down processing, where the brain actively organizes sensory input into a meaningful whole. The ability to distinguish an object from its background (figure and ground) or to see an ambiguous image in multiple ways (reversible figures) are core examples that support the Gestalt view that perception is an act of imposing order on sensory information.
There are many groups that Gestalt argued to have existed, principles that organize perception into wholes which the brain uses to structure sensory information.

6---full-notes/glial-cells.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience
Glial cells
Details
These cells fill the nervous system, in some areas they even outnumber the neurons ten to one. These things function are crucial to neuronal communication. They act as guidewires for growing neurons, and later, they provide a scaffolding for neurons to assist in the repair process.
But more than even that, they increase the speed at which neurons can communicate. The specialized glial cells that can do this is known as myelin. Shortly after birth, they wrap and spiral themselves around neurons that have long axons, which eventually they will cover the whole axon. The uncoated gaps between the wrappers, called the nodes of Ranvier, are also crucial in speeding up nerve impulses along these type of axons.
Myelin is white, which is why the brain is made up of both white and gray matter. Gray matter are cell bodies, dendrites and unmyelinated axons and the interneurons that comprise of the nervous system’s circuitry.

6---full-notes/glucocorticoids-and-the-s.title: Glucocorticoids and the Stress-Depression Cycle
6---full-notes/glucocorticoids-and-the-s.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology biology
Glucocorticoids and the Stress-Depression Cycle
Details
The body’s primary stress hormones, glucocorticoids (cortisol in humans), play a central role in the biology of depression. In a healthy stress response, cortisol levels rise to meet a challenge and then fall once the challenge is over. In major depression, this system is broken.
Individuals with depression often exist in a state of hypercortisolism, meaning they have chronically elevated levels of cortisol. This is because the brain’s negative feedback loop, which is supposed to detect high cortisol levels and signal the adrenal glands to stop producing it, is impaired.
This creates a destructive, self-perpetuating vicious cycle:


Psychological stress (sad thoughts, rumination) triggers the release of cortisol.


High levels of cortisol contribute to the neurobiological changes of depression (e.g., hippocampal atrophy).


The state of depression itself acts as a powerful, chronic stressor, which keeps cortisol levels pathologically high, further damaging the brain and deepening the depression.


This constant internal state of emergency helps explain the profound exhaustion and vegetative symptoms of the illness. The body is always “on,” fighting a battle that has no external cause and no clear end as the MPFC is overdosing on cortisol, making the amygdala constantly report threats back to the body.

Goldbach’s Conjecture and the Trap of Conceivability
Details
Goldbach’s Conjecture (the idea that every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes). As of now, it cannot be proven, but it can still be conceived as true or false. True by induction as the past numbers have not shown anything different, false by imagining a counter-example. But mathematical truths are necessary; if the conjecture is true, it is necessarily true, and its falsity is impossible. If the Conceivability Principle held, the fact that we can conceive of it being false would imply it is “possibly false,” which is absurd for a necessary mathematical truth. This suggests that what we can “conceive” is often just a measure of our ignorance (“Epistemic Possibility”) rather than a guide to the structure of reality (“Metaphysical Possibility”).

Goodness of Fit of Environment

Decades ago, Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess wrote extensively about “goodness of fit” in families. This means that a family may be fitting to raise or take care of the children of said family. This “fit” requires similar levels of emotionality between the two or it might result in a discrepancy and the child being hurt. An emotionally sensitive child born into a family of people who are less emotional may feel different from the beginning. Though the family may not realize that the child is different, or not know how to react even if they do know she is more emotional, they may still cope well with their own level of emotionality. However, they do not teach the more emotional child how to regulate more intense, long-lasting emotions. They’re simply flabbergasted by them—or, worse, mortified by them, a message of unacceptability that they pass on to their child.
At the worst possible situation, this can result in something like a “fake life” of the child. They grow up fully catered to what parents tell and want them to be and are chronically unsatisfied with their situations and try to find catharsis per suicide.

Gothic Architecture
Details
So, what is Gothic Architecture ? This type of architecture is basically a style that originated in the mid-12th century in the Ile-de-France region. Originally called “Opus Francigenum” (French work), it evolved from Romanesque architecture and was succeeded by the Renaissance. The defining characteristics of these works are their pointed arches that channel weight more directly downward, allowing taller structures. Ribbed vaults, also, which reduce roof weights and allow for thinner walls. Flying buttresses to allow walls to open up for huge windows and support weight of the massive walls. An artistic and perhaps defining characteristic of this type of style are massive stained glass windows which are installed to flood interiors with “divine” light. And lastly, verticality, as belief in God was still very strong during these times, people believed that God was up there, and so verticality was also a feature, drawing the eyes upward to heaven.

When thinking about how long it takes to build a habit, people often ask, “How many days does it take?” (e.g., the myth of 21 days). This evaluates habits by the wrong metric. Instead of time, it makes much more sense to determine habit formation by the frequency of performing the habit. This is justified by the neuroscientific principle of Long-Term Potentiation (LTP). LTP states that the connections between our neurons are reinforced and strengthened based on the sheer amount of times they fire together. Therefore, a habit becomes automatic not because a certain number of days have passed, but because you have performed the repetitions enough times to physically rewire the brain’s circuitry.

6---full-notes/handling-math.title: Handling math
6---full-notes/handling-math.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading 3 - Tags/math science
Handling math
Details
Two reading modes: There are two key approaches, depending on your goal . If you’re reading a math textbook for its own sake, read actively front-to-back, with pencil in hand, working through proofs and problems. But if you’re reading a science text that uses math, it’s often better to skim the heavy details on a first pass. As a rule of thumb: “skipping is often the better part of valor” when the math isn’t the main goal .
Case study – Newton’s Principia: Adler & Van Doren give a strategy story with Newton’s Principia: do not solve every construction. Instead, read the statements of propositions, glance over proofs to get a sense of the methods, and focus on the lemmas, corollaries, and scholia (Newton’s explanatory discussions). This way, you see the overall architecture of Newton’s system (what builds on what) without getting lost in every diagram or algebraic detail . Notice their advice: even avoid diagrams on first read if they confuse you . The payoff is big: understanding the structure lets you grasp the “general scholium” that summarizes Newton’s grand conclusion , which is the treasure of the whole book.
Skipping vs solving – heuristics:  A useful heuristic is “Understand before you calculate.” In practice, that means you can often understand a science text without mastering every equation . Math provides precision and clarity, but your first goal is to get the narrative or concept. Adler & Van Doren show that in Newton’s Optics, diagrams look complex but the math is minimal . Conversely, lacking math can muddle understanding: Galileo’s Two New Sciences is famous but hard, because its dialogue form (no equations) hides its logic.
When math isn’t there: Not all science classics use math. Works by Hippocrates, William Harvey, or Gilbert (on blood and magnets) are readable without math, as long as you remember: your job is “not to become competent in the subject matter but instead to understand the problem” . This means focus on the ideas, not on doing math like a scientist.

6---full-notes/healing-trauma-beyond-the.title: Healing Trauma Beyond Therapy
6---full-notes/healing-trauma-beyond-the.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology trauma
Healing Trauma Beyond Therapy
Details
Even with access to therapy and the presence of compassionate individuals, many people struggle to fully grow past their trauma. While there can be numerous reasons for this, one critical aspect is often overlooked: the creation of a social environment truly conducive to healing.
When a survivor’s support system actively offers empathy and understanding, it creates a profound sense of safety. In this environment, the constant fear of being judged, of making a mistake, or of angering others begins to recede. This frees the individual to interact more openly with the world and engage with the difficult work of healing.
It is understandable why this factor is so frequently missed, as widespread knowledge about mental health is still lacking and the stigma surrounding therapy persists. Yet, the power of a healing environment has been demonstrated in practices like therapeutic theatre, which Dr. Bessel van der Kolk used with traumatized individuals. The therapeutic power of that setting, however, was not rooted solely in the acting. Van der Kolk observed that teenagers, overwhelmed by anxiety, would often flee the group. The pivotal moment of healing occurred when they chose to return. Instead of facing judgment or exclusion, they were consistently welcomed back with compassion by their peers.
This recurring cycle of rupture and repair proved the group’s safety in the most tangible way possible. It became a secure base where members learned that connection could withstand stress and that they would be supported, not abandoned, in their most difficult moments. This illustrates a fundamental truth: healing doesn’t just happen in an office; it happens in a community that has learned to hold space for our shared humanity.

6---full-notes/heart-rate-variability.title: Heart Rate Variability
6---full-notes/heart-rate-variability.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology physical
Heart Rate Variability
Details
Every time we breathe, our body balances between two nervous systems. When we inhale, the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) speeds up the heart. When we exhale, the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) slows it down. These small, steady fluctuations in heart rate are called heart rate variability (HRV).
Good HRV means the heart adjusts easily to changes. It helps us stay calm when faced with frustrations and small setbacks. With good HRV, we can assess situations clearly without panicking or rushing into impulsive reactions. It keeps both mind and body flexible and stable.
Poor HRV shows up when these fluctuations are missing. People with poor HRV often feel mentally scattered, overreact emotionally, and make poor decisions under pressure. Studies have found that low HRV is linked to greater risks of anxiety, depression, and physical illness.
The good news is that HRV can be improved. Simple practices like slow breathing, meditation, or mindfulness training help strengthen the natural rhythms between the SNS and PNS. In time, this builds a more stable emotional core—and a stronger, healthier heart.

Tags: environment Cognitive Psychology
High Heritability is not 100%
Details
A common view is that high heritability means that it would be fixed, unchangeable which is completely incorrect as proven by PKU or Phenylketonuria. PKU is a metabolic disorder that is 100% heritable. It is a simple Mendelian condition caused by inheriting two recessive genes, one from each carrier parent. An individual with this “double recessive” genotype cannot produce the enzyme needed to metabolize an amino acid called phenylalanine.
In cases without intervention, the toxic chemicals build up in the brain and impairs the cognitive functions, effectively reducing the patient’s IQ. But in cases where it is taken into account and dealt with from a young age by intervening with medications, and a phenylalanine-restricted diet, which helps the child’s brain develop normally, their average IQ returning to above/around 100.
Even if high heritability is present in a trait/condition, that does not mean that it is completely unavoidable. It only describes the variation of a population within its given environments, when introduced with interventions, it can be prevented.

6---full-notes/high-self-esteem-and-fail.title: High Self-Esteem and Failure
6---full-notes/high-self-esteem-and-fail.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
High Self-Esteem and Failure
Details
High self-esteem is quite a defensive trait as it allows people to buffer against failure. Dodgson and Wood showed that immediately after failure, high self-esteem individuals become faster at recognizing their strengths and slower at recognizing their weaknesses, while the opposite is true for low self-esteem individuals. Moreover, they also are better at mood-repairing, selecting funny videos over neutral ones after failure, and they increase volunteering. However, high self-esteem creates vulnerability when threatened. Baumeister and Heatherton showed that ego-threatened high self-esteem individuals take reckless gambling risks (losing everything) and administer more aggressive noise blasts to others. The higher the standard is, the more desperate the response is.
When their ego is threatened, these individuals become the most dangerous people in the room - more aggressive, more reckless, more willing to harm others if it provides relative advantage. Baumeister’s gambling studies show them losing everything through risky strategies; his aggression studies show them delivering the most intense noise blasts to opponents.
The baseline of self-regard that self-esteemed people create is so high that, when disrupted, produces an urgent need for restoration, and so they will do anything for that, even if it includes the suffering of others. This inherently challenges the assumption that self-esteem is a prosocial concept, as people are willing to act to be estimable, to look as if they have high self-esteem rather than actually having it.

6---full-notes/hippocampus-in-memory.title: Hippocampus in Memory
6---full-notes/hippocampus-in-memory.content:
Status: adult
Tags: neuroscience
Hippocampus in Memory
Details
The story of patient H.M. is one of the most important in the history of neuroscience. In an attempt to cure his severe epilepsy in the 1950s, surgeons removed the medial temporal lobes of his brain, including a crucial seahorse-shaped structure: the hippocampus. The surgery was a partial success for his seizures, but it came at a staggering cost: H.M. was left with a profound and permanent inability to form new long-term declarative memories (severe anterograde amnesia).
H.M.’s case provided the first definitive proof that memory is a distinct biological function, separate from general intelligence. He could hold a conversation, solve problems, and retain his short-term memory for about 30 seconds. Yet, moments later, he would have no recollection of the conversation or the person he spoke with. He was, in essence, living in a permanent present, unable to anchor new experiences in time.
Crucially, H.M.’s non-declarative memory remained functional. He could learn new motor skills, like mirror-reading, and improve with practice, despite having no conscious memory of ever performing the task before.
This taught us that the hippocampus is not the storage site of long-term memories, but rather the essential manager responsible for consolidating them. It takes fragile, short-term experiences and processes them for permanent storage in distributed networks across the cortex. Without the hippocampus, new experiences can never “stick,” and the bridge from the present moment to the permanent record of the past is broken.
Supporting Content
Moreover, there are other parts of the brain that are responsible for emotions that also stores memory, which is why emotions can hyper affect memories and make them a lot more memorable due to the brain wanting to study and avoid it the next time.

History of Abnormal Psychology
Details
The earliest instance of abnormal psychology have been demons and ghosts that affected humans in negative ways which we nowadays call schizophrenia and other mental illnesses. The solutions to these problems at those times were literally drilling holes into their skulls, this obviously sometimes resulted in brain damage and would make people change personalities.
Continuing, Hippocrates, who was considered the father of medicine, also took a dive into these illnesses and came up with terms such as melancholia, and mania, which we now call depression and mania, respectively. Furthermore, he also suggested about how the brain might be involved in these mental disorders.
With the coming of the dark ages, the dominance of Christian religions came, and instead of evil spirits now, the people with mental illnesses were thought to be possessed by Satan and sent to be baptized. After that, came the age of witches, which followed with hundreds of years of unstable economy, together with illnesses like the black plague. This of course led to mental illnesses.
Some interesting developments came in Switzerland when Paracelsus had a theory that when the moon misaligned with the stars, it made people go crazy and mentally ill. These tests in lunacy were conducted to see if it truly caused all of the illnesses, or if the person was truly mentally ill to take care of them. All of the explanations of these trials were about things like “having children, brain injuries,…” the other explanation was TRAUMA.
At about the 18th century, neurological illnesses such as hysteria popped up, this prompted an Austrian physician named Mesmer to come up with ways to treat with it. He theorized that this was caused by a universal magnetic fluid inside the person… and used magnets all over their body to help them with this. Since this was quite a hassle, he turned to hypnotism, mesmerizing such patients, and a lot of them got better. Moreover though, he set the basis for what is also known as hypnosis therapy nowadays.
Freud was an apprentice of Mesmer, and he was interested in treating people with hysteria. In fact, he was so interested that he ditched hypnosis and developed his own methodology, known as psychoanalysis.
Continuing with the times came John Watson with behaviorism, Pavlov, and so on… Until the 19th century when people came to genetics studying and the rise of psychological models and methodologies for therapy, neuroscience came roaring back, culture came into consideration in these factors.

History of Logic
Details
Logic has been seen in the earliest instances of civilization, as the Egyptian people of the past has used it to triangulate and re-establish property lines after the Nile floods. The Greeks, particularly Euclid and Aristotle, had used it to systemize it into a rigorous framework of axioms and theorems. For centuries, this geometric model—building complex truths from “self-evident” axioms—was viewed as the ultimate form of scientific theory.
But with the coming of the modern times, these claims of the “self-evident” was abolished due to how it could be wrong as people moved to epistemology, testing and experimenting to see if it is truly correct or not. And so logic was left in the dust and confines of linguistics until Boolean revived the field by reinstating it in mathematics instead. This shift transformed logic from a philosophical tool into a mathematical science, mirroring the revolutions of Copernicus and Newton in physics.

Tags: ADHD neuroscience
How Fidgeting Enhances Mental Focus
Details
The constant need to move, fidget, and shift—a hallmark of hyperactivity in ADHD—is not just random restlessness. It stems from a high level of “reverberatory activity” in the brain’s premotor circuits, which are constantly sending out commands to move. Trying to suppress this powerful neural drive requires immense mental effort, which then depletes the resources available for cognitive focus. This creates a paradox where sitting perfectly still can make it harder to concentrate.
A highly effective behavioral tool is to provide a controlled outlet for this motor activity. Engaging in a small, repetitive, and often subconscious physical action—like tapping a foot, bouncing a knee, pacing, or using a fidget toy—channels some of this excess premotor signaling. By giving the restless circuits a simple task to perform, it liberates the rest of the brain’s cognitive resources to be directed toward the primary task at hand, whether that’s listening, reading, or problem-solving. This is why surgeons learn to tap a foot to steady their hands, and why pacing can help with public speaking. It’s not about “getting energy out”; it’s about giving the brain’s motor system a simple, rhythmic job to do so that the mind can achieve a state of stillness and clarity.

How much does it hurt
Details
In order to reasonably reject a principle, I must have some objection to it. This objection may begin with some direct harm I suffer as a result of the principle. So far, if the harm involved is pain or suffering, contractualism mirrors utilitarianism. However, the fact that a principle impacts negatively on me is not sufficient. To know whether I can reasonablyreject the principle, I must also ask how it impacts on others. If a principle imposes a certain burden (b1) on me, but every alternative imposes a greater burden (b2) on someone else, then b1 does not give me a reason to reject the principle. If I am reasonable, then I withdraw my objection when I see that your reason is more pressing. (By contrast, it would make no sense to say that a utilitarian has ‘withdrawn her pain’ because she has noticed that someone else’s pain is greater.) So we conclude that the principle imposing b1 on me cannot be reasonably rejected. And we reach this conclusion without having to aggregate anything.
But unlike utilitarianism, however, this is not the only rational attitude towards morality. Contractualism can also accommodate deontological intuitions: such as the views that could be reasonably rejected. Among these principles might be ones that involve “accepting a certain view of the reasons one has: that the positive value of saving others does not justify killing someone” (Scanlon 1998, p. 84).

6---full-notes/how-to-train-focus-with-y.content:
Status: teen
Tags: ADHD focus
How to Train Focus with Your Eyes
Details
The simple act of blinking is profoundly connected to our state of attention and our perception of time, all of which is regulated by dopamine. Each eye blink serves as a neurological “reset,” segmenting the continuous flow of our experience into discrete moments, much like the shutter of a camera. The rate at which we blink is a direct reflection of our internal dopamine levels. When dopamine is high, we are aroused and focused, and our blink rate decreases. This causes our brain to process more “frames” of information per second, making time feel as if it’s slowing down. Conversely, when dopamine is low, as in ADHD, our blink rate increases, and our perception of time speeds up, causing us to underestimate how long things take.
This mechanical link provides a direct, behavioral tool for training focus. Studies show that a practice called fixation-focused training can significantly improve attention in both children and adults. The exercise is simple: you fix your visual attention on a single object for a short period (30-60 seconds) and consciously try to inhibit the desire to blink. This act of overriding the impulse to blink and maintaining a steady gaze directly engages and strengthens the neural circuits that control both the physical “shutters” of your eyes and the mental “aperture” of your attention. It’s a way of using a physical action to directly train the cognitive skill of sustained focus.

6---full-notes/how-to-read-lyric-poetry.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
How to read lyric poetry
Details
Many people believe that they cannot read lyric poetry because it is obscure and complex. But often, it is very much worth it and not as hard as you may think if you read it in the right way (bias to attract attention haha).
And so we start with the first rule, same as others, read continuously, do not stop under any conditions, this is even more important in this than others medias we have talked about.
Why ? You may ask, and it is because when you encounter a line or a part that is particularly difficult, it can be resolved after you’ve understood the unity of the piece, never because you extensively researched it like a puzzle. This process makes poetry unenjoyable and would demotivate you rather than anything else.
The meaning of these things can only be found in unity, when all layers are eventually connected, we cannot expect from a single line or a stanza that the meaning be present.
The second rule is this: Read the poem through again - but out loud, as said before in Shakespeare’s poetic dramas. This is essential compared to the helpful nature of it in those. Here, speaking those words forces you to understand them better. You cannot glide over such things if you are speaking it, and so you are forced to confront it. All of the context clues derived from the piece will also help with this as well. Last rule is immersion, which won’t be elaborated further.
The questions you ask of an expository work are grammatical and logical. The questions you ask of a lyric are usually rhetorical, though they may also be syntactical. You do not come to terms with a poem; but you must discover the key words. You discover them not primarily by an act of grammatical discernment, however, but by an act of rhetorical discernment. Why do certain words pop out of the poem and stare you in the face? Is it because the rhythm marks them? Or the rhyme? Or are the words repeated? Do several stanzas seem to be about the same ideas; if so, do these ideas form any kind of sequence? Anything of this sort that you can discover will help your understanding.
Also try to find the conflict in good lyrics as they are part of the other helpful clues.
The final advice is to understand the author, as poetry reflects him more than any other genre, and so it will help you understand the work further knowing the time period it was in and what kind of man the author was. Knowing extensively all this does not necessarily guarantee you would read the piece better, only rereading and putting effort in it will ensure that.

6---full-notes/how-to-read-plays.title: How to read plays
6---full-notes/how-to-read-plays.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
How to read plays
Details
Most of the rules that applied to reading stories should be done so here. The difference is when reading a play, you are not experiencing everything, in a play there is music, expressions, and so on.
This leads me to the suggestion that you should try to make a pretense of seeing it acted. After you’ve answered all the questions and understood what the play is about, you should then try to direct it. Imagine if you had a dozen actors under guidance, try to tell them How to say, act certain scenes. Explain the importance of these few words and how certain actions are the climax and such. Not a guarantee but this process is a lot of fun.
Earlier, we suggested that there were interesting exceptions to the rule that the playwright cannot speak directly to the reader as the author of a novel can and often does. (Fielding, in Tom Jones, is an example of this direct addressing of the reader in one great novel.) Two of these exceptions are separated by nearly twenty-five centuries of time. Aristophanes, the ancient Greek comic playwright, wrote the only examples of what is called Old Comedy that survive. From time to time in an Aristophanic play, and always at least once, the leading actor would step out of character, perhaps move forward toward the audience, and deliver a political speech that had nothing whatever to do with the action of the drama. It is felt that these speeches were expressions of the author’s personal feelings. This is occasionally done nowadays—no useful artistic device is ever really lost—but perhaps not as effectively as Aristophanes did it.
The other example is that of Shaw, who not only expected his plays to be acted but also hoped that they would be read. He published them all, at least one (Heartbreak House) before it was ever acted, and accompanied them with long prefaces where he explained and dissected.
The last advice I want to give is to read slowly at a puzzling passage, and aloud and expressive too. This simply will make you be able to clear up many difficulties, and only after this has failed should you turn to glossary or notes.

6---full-notes/how-to-read-“canonical”-b.title: How to read “canonical” books
6---full-notes/how-to-read-“canonical”-b.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading philosophy
How to read “canonical” books
Details
There is one very interesting kind of book, one kind of reading, that has not yet been discussed. We use the term “canonical” to refer to such books; in an older tradition we might have called them “sacred” or “holy,” but those words no longer apply to all such works, though they still apply to some of them.
The notion of a canonical book can be extended beyond these obvious examples. Consider any institution—a church, a political party, a society—that among other things (1) is a teaching institution, (2) has a body of doctrine to teach, and (3) has a faithful and obedient membership. The members of any such organization read reverentially. They do not—even cannot—question the authorized or right reading of the books that to them are canonical. The faithful are debarred by their faith from finding error in the “sacred” text, to say nothing of finding nonsense there.
These are the definitions that J.Adler and Van Doren came to, and I think it describes these works perfectly. How I would say it is that there is only one right way to read any of this. And so the faithful reader of books like this is obliged to make sense out of it and to find it true in one or another sense of “true”. If he cannot do this by himself he must ask help from another who can. So he reads without any freedom but in turn he gains a kind of satisfaction tjqt is possibly unattainable in other nooks.
This is difficult, perhaps of all genres of books, because it does not require a skill, but rather - faith. Someone who believes in the Word of God knows that this is the hardest piece of literature to read bur also the most important.

6---full-notes/how-to-syntopically-read.title: How to syntopically read
6---full-notes/how-to-syntopically-read.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
How to syntopically read
Details
Step 1: Surveying the Literature
This first step focuses on identifying and selecting relevant texts. Unlike analytical reading, where you read one book thoroughly, syntopical reading requires you to scan many texts quickly to judge whether they are worth deeper study. This is not about reading for full comprehension yet—it’s about discovering which works address your chosen topic, and how. You may not rely solely on titles or summaries; you look for structure, central themes, and relevance to your inquiry. For example, if you’re studying “human nature,” you might briefly look into works from psychology, philosophy, and theology to find those that present strong, differing views.
Step 2: Formulating Questions
Once you’ve selected a set of texts, the next step is to develop specific questions that will guide your comparative analysis. These questions act like a lens—focusing your reading across multiple texts. Importantly, they are created by you, not provided by any one author. They arise from your purpose for reading and reflect what you want to learn or clarify. For example, rather than asking “What does this author say about freedom?” you ask, “What are the common assumptions about freedom in these works?” or “How do authors disagree on the limits of freedom?” This shifts your role from passive reader to active investigator.
Step 3: Identifying Terms and Concepts
This step requires you to define and standardize the key terms used across the texts. Different authors often use the same words differently, or different words to mean the same thing. If you fail to clarify these terms, your comparison will be inaccurate. For instance, if one author uses “liberty” to mean legal protection and another uses it to mean personal autonomy, treating those as equivalent would distort their arguments. Your task is to understand each usage and then create a neutral framework for comparison. This step ensures conceptual clarity and avoids misunderstanding rooted in language.
Step 4: Comparative Analysis
Here, you look at how each author answers your questions and how they relate to one another. This means actively comparing arguments, tracing patterns, identifying disagreements, and understanding the foundations of those differences. You’re not merely noting who said what—you are asking why they said it that way, what assumptions underlie their views, and how their reasoning holds up in light of others. This process creates a map of the intellectual landscape around your topic.
Step 5: Synthesizing Insights
The final step is to bring all of this work together into a coherent synthesis. You’re not choosing sides, nor simply summarizing. Instead, you build your own perspective that draws from all the material you’ve read, showing how ideas interact and how a new understanding emerges. The result is an original insight, based not on isolated reading, but on broad and critical engagement.
Syntopical reading teaches us to think with—not just about—books. It is the foundation for deep learning, scholarly research, and intellectual independence.

6---full-notes/how,-nature.title: How, Nature
6---full-notes/how,-nature.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy science
How, Nature
Details
Kant was born in a time where Newton has just published a world-changing work on physics and such, to which Hume (Hume’s Fork) came back with a response that basically attempted to discredit all of physics in the sense that it was simply inductive reasoning and that it couldn’t be… explanatory completely. Kant heard this and so he wanted to offer up his own interpretation and his own arguments against Hume for it, with his main question being: “how is nature possible?” Now, in this time, Newtonian physics basically explained that our world is chaotic, its random, and that the variables that constituted it shouldn’t have birthed a functional universe in the first place, and so Kant’s question here could be interpreted as follow: how does a law-governed, ordered world emerge from sensory chaos? His answer is that we bring the order. The knowledge we have reflects on this world rational and perceptual principles we impose on experience as we confront it.
But this kinds of circles back to the point of it being inductive… a circular reasoning chain, so to say. And so Kant believes that even if we can interpret something different from another species, something objective is still being traced; and that our own personal stamp on things contribute to the objectivity of it, not separate from its objectivity.

How ? New World
Details
Normally, sciences would more often than not make the evolution of past societies into current one seem more seem-less and rational than it really was. Frankly, the industrial revolution happening was an unprecedented part of history compared to what was happening at the time and the dynasties involved in said eras.
The spread of modernity unfolded in distinct temporal and geographic waves, which in turn continually shifted the prevailing explanations for its cause. Initially, around the mid-eighteenth century, England was the sole nation to escape agrarian constraints, leading contemporary observers to view this unprecedented industrial shift as a uniquely English miracle. By the nineteenth century, as these structures spread to proximate nations like Belgium, Germany, and France, the narrative expanded to describe a broader Western European phenomenon, often attributed by thinkers like Max Weber to cultural factors such as the Protestant work ethic. The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries saw North America and Japan successfully adopt this blueprint, proving that Asiatic societies could also industrialize and expanding the concept into a Euro-American-Japanese miracle. This progression continued through the mid-twentieth century with the rapid rise of the “Four Little Tigers” in Asia, culminating in the late twentieth century when massive economies like China, India, and Brazil began their own modernizing transformations, effectively globalizing what was once an isolated regional anomaly.

6---full-notes/hume's-fork.title: Hume's Fork
6---full-notes/hume's-fork.content:
Status: adult

Hume’s Fork
Details
Completely different from Descartes arguments, Hume takes a completely different approach. In his book, “Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding”, he divided knowledge into two categories known as relations of ideas, truths that are known by a priori and are necessarily true. These are meanings of the words, not exactly the world. On the other hand, there’s matters of facts, which are truths that cannot be contradicted, perhaps objectively true.
But how do we measure cause and effects ? How do we understand that one thing leads to another ? It has to be a habit, we have to have had seen it before one time, and so. But of course, then so, we would meet the problem of induction reasoning, which states that we assume that the future will resemble the past, but we cannot justify it necessarily.
(- Is it self-evident? No.


Is it demonstrative (logic)? No, because we can conceive of a chaotic universe where gravity stops tomorrow.


Is it experimental? No, because any argument from experience (“It has always happened before, so it will happen again”) is circular. It uses induction to prove induction.)’


Supporting Content
This could then be applied into Descartes arguments about God, as it is very much just a priori and induction.
Everyone has pretty much agreed that Hume’s fork is inarguable, but even Hume himself doesn’t reject inductive reasoning, in fact, he thinks that it is the ONLY way to move forward as it is the way that we think and we cannot prevent it from happening. We have to accept the probability of it being true, even if its not 100%. Then, when it eventually fails us, then we would change our approach, improve it perhaps, to combat said errors.

6---full-notes/hume's-judicious-spectato.title: Hume's Judicious Spectator
6---full-notes/hume's-judicious-spectato.content:
Status: adult
Tags: morals philosophy
Hume’s Judicious Spectator
Details
The first to ground moral philosophy in social sciences and society in general rather than by natural law or through God. Hume wasn’t interested in why property ought to exist morally but why it came to serve social purposes. To do this, he introduced the concept of the “judicious spectator.” This is an imaginative, reasoning perspective we learn to adopt through socialization, where we evaluate actions based purely on a shared principle of humanity. It is an explanation of the psychological mechanics of morality rather than a judgment of it.
Supporting Content
Decades later, John Stuart Mill inherited this empirical, utilitarian lineage, but his approach to it was deeply colored by his unique, traumatic upbringing. Raised as an intellectual prodigy by his father (James Mill) and Jeremy Bentham, Mill was deprived of a normal childhood, serving instead as a tutor to his siblings. This bred a deep, albeit repressed, resentment. Interestingly, Mill’s chosen vocation was not to be a pure, isolated scholar, but rather an “educator of advanced and enlightened opinion.” Influenced by Saint-Simon, Mill believed society was entering a secular, democratic, and industrial “organic age,” and he wanted to provide the foundational principles for this new era. However, because of his complicated psychological relationship with his father, Mill could never bring himself to openly break from classical utilitarianism. Instead, he constantly presented his own highly original—and often contradictory—revisions of moral philosophy under the guise of simply updating and defending the utilitarian tradition.

6---full-notes/hume's-stance-on-locke.title: Hume's Stance on Locke
6---full-notes/hume's-stance-on-locke.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy
Hume’s Stance
Details
Of course, aforementioned in The Contextual Divergence of Hobbes and Locke, we have seen how Locke wrote his framework to basically oppose what was happening at the time in his own life. Hume, however, was writing during a far more stable period in the 18th century, completely detached from the urgency of civil war. Because of this stability, Hume did not need to invent a defensive legal architecture; instead, he approached political philosophy as a detached, scientific observer. Moreover, he also adopted a more epistemological approach, trying to introduce the “experimental method” into “moral subjects.” In the 18th century, “moral” did not just mean ethics; it encompassed the entirety of psychology and social theory, while “experimental” referred to the Newtonian method of observation and empirical data. He was trying to look for something practical.
Hume disagrees with Locke on the grounds of consent, and basically does so by applying practicality to humanity’s history, positing how almost all existing governments were founded on usurpation or violent conquest, not peaceful agreement. Furthermore, neither the rulers nor the subjects actually believe a contract exists. Princes view subjects as property or inheritance, and ordinary citizens are entirely unaware that they are supposedly participating in a grand philosophical agreement. These citizens cannot “consent” when they do not have the view of other ways of living and the knowledge necessary to participate in such a decision.

6---full-notes/hyper-focus--and--dopamin.content:
Status: teen
Tags: biology ADHD neurology
Hyper-Focus & Dopamine
Details
The state of hyper-focus, where an individual with ADHD can achieve intense concentration on an enjoyable task, is not a psychological quirk but a direct manifestation of the brain’s neurochemistry. This phenomenon is driven by the neuromodulator dopamine, which is profoundly linked to motivation, reward, and the very mechanics of attention. When the brain encounters an activity it deems highly rewarding or intriguing, it releases a surge of dopamine. This chemical signal acts to narrow our perception, creating a “tunnel vision” that filters out external distractions and allows for deep engagement with the task at hand.
This process explains the central paradox of ADHD. The difficulty in focusing on mundane or uninteresting tasks stems from an underlying dysregulation of the dopamine system, making it hard to voluntarily trigger the release of dopamine needed to engage the brain’s focus circuits. However, when a task is inherently stimulating—like a captivating video game or a creative passion project—it naturally floods the relevant brain circuits with dopamine. This chemically-induced state of arousal and motivation is what allows for hyper-focus to emerge. It demonstrates that the capacity for intense focus exists within the ADHD brain, but its activation is critically dependent on dopamine-driven engagement, rather than sheer willpower.

6---full-notes/hypothesis-testing.title: Hypothesis Testing
6---full-notes/hypothesis-testing.content:
Status: adult
Tags: statistics psychology
Hypothesis Testing
Details
This method is basically arguing with yourself. You suspect two groups differ, but you cannot measure if theres an effect directly, because sampling error guarantees some difference every time. So you assume the null hypothesis, that they are one population, then compute how often chance alone would produce a result this extreme. The p-value is exactly that probability, it shows the chance of the data being at least this extreme if the null were true. It would then provide supporting evidence for the research hypothesis being true too via Occam’s Razor.
There are a few ways one can go at this: set a cutoff point. You’ll reject only if a result would occur less than alpha (usually 5%, sometimes 1%) of the time under the null, which for a one-tailed 5% test is z = 1.645. Then either compare statistics — z = 2.2 beats 1.645, so reject — or compare probabilities — P(Z ≥ 2.2) ≈ 0.014 is below 0.05, so reject. Same conclusion, mirror images across the table. In plain terms, the sample mean has to sit at least 1.645 standard errors above μ. You can draw that same line in raw score units by inverting the formula: x = μ + z·σ_x̄ = 50 + 1.645×5 ≈ 58.2, so any sample mean past 58.2 rejects, and 61 clears it. Alpha itself is convention, partly cultural: social science leans on 0.05, stricter fields use 0.01. A fair rule of thumb — cheap, repeatable experiments can drive p down just by adding data, so they should hold themselves to a stricter alpha.

Hypothetical Transgressions
Details
Now we step into the territory of the transgressions that happens when someone does not actually experience anything. In these situations, their reactions may be as strong as if it did happen to them. But why ? The common denominator is that the offender violated a rule regarded as important to the offended. For example, a motorcyclist passing a red light, a pedestrian gets mad, they might explain it as if they WERE walking or that they could’ve been walking there.
Although these situations are subtle, they account for a large proportion of the discord in our relations. The imposition of a value judgement points to the existence of an implicit code of laws, rules, principles, and standards. These rules are mostly applied to protect the protagonist from physical and psychological harm even though he and his domain are in no way involved with the interaction of the offender.
To justify and be the outer wall of this are the principles of fair play, justice. Anything that goes against these principles are regarded as a threat to the wall, and violate the rules. We can notice that these things are being affected thanks to the angry complaints that the offended may say such as: “They have no right to act that way.” “He should not have done that.”
Moreso, they themselves do not realize that their anger may seem inappropriate and unhealthy to others, but to the individual it seems appropriate as he has his own standards of right and wrong. He only cares that it violates his own code (may be idiosyncratic).
Moreover, social conventions can play a great role in specifying in which conditions is this anger justified, expected, or even demanded, but also set the limits when it becomes excessive. And of course those implications are present in statements such as “You’re over-reacting”, or “Why the temper tantrum?”.

6---full-notes/hysteria.title: Hysteria
6---full-notes/hysteria.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology physiology
Hysteria
Details
Hysteria is a pathological extension of the process of somatic imaging. The current most common form of it consists some kind of physical dysfunction that is not based on illnesses (meaning organic disease or physiological abnormality). The bodily ailment may be loss of power in a limb; loss of sensation in some part of the body; sensation of pain in the absence of any stimulation of the pain receptors; and overactivity of muscles, such as in hysterical choking or pseudo epilepsy. In hysteria the patient believes he has a physical disorder. Since the imagined disorder is not fatal, he tends to accept it without severe anxiety. Patients with hysteria are essentially “sensory imagers”; that is, they imagine the particular illness and then take the sensory experience as corroborative evidence of having the illness. The patient typically experiences sensory or motor abnormalities that fit the pattern of his erroneous concept of organic pathology.
When examining these kind of patients, the physician usually is able to identify that the pattern of the hysterical symptom conforms not to the actual anatomy of the body but to the individual’s conceptions of the manifestations of a physical disorder. Which means, following an injury to a part of their body, the patient may develop a “stocking-glove” anesthesia- which is a distribution of sensory loss that cannot be produced by anything. Similarly, if a patient sustain brain damage, they will experience paralysis of a limb on the same side of the presumed damage, although the anatomy of the nervous system would determine otherwise. The reason for this is vast, and there are many theories for it, witnessing it in childhood and then projecting it onto one self, Freud’s theory of sexual frustrations,…
To exemplify this, a patient had apparently suffered organic brain damage following a myocardial infarction (Stein et al, 1969). Testing the patient, they found out that he had suffered deficits in immediate recall and inability to concentrate. Yet in the process of psychotherapy, they found out that he had a cognitive distortion regarding the effects of his heart. He had believed that there was an “artery to the brain” arising from the heart at the point of his condition. He thought that the artery had become occluded, resulting in irreversible damage to the brain. When treated, cleared up, the damage disappeared.
The way to treat hysteria is alike any other conditions that have been discussed before like depression or phobias. At the end of the day it is still reframing a “pathogenic idea” of a patient into something correct so that he stops experiencing such symptoms from his psychophysiological illness.

6---full-notes/ideal-theory.title: Ideal Theory
6---full-notes/ideal-theory.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
Ideal Theory
Details
To understand the urgent necessity of Immanuel Kant’s philosophy—and specifically his later “Refutation of Idealism”—one must first understand the profound epistemological crisis inherited from his predecessors. The intellectual landscape of the time was dominated by what philosopher Thomas Reid critically called the “Ideal Theory.” This theory posited that humans have no direct contact with the objects of the external world; rather, we only ever have access to our own mental representations or “ideas” of those objects.
This representational wall began earnestly with John Locke, who divided the world into “primary qualities” (solidity, extension, figure, motion—things inherent to the object) and “secondary qualities” (color, sound, taste—powers in the object to produce sensations in us). However, Bishop George Berkeley brilliantly and devastatingly dissolved this distinction. Berkeley pointed out that all experience, whether of a primary or secondary quality, is mediated by the mind. He took this to its ultimate, radical conclusion: esse est percipi (to be is to be perceived). Berkeley championed “Dogmatic Idealism,” arguing that the very concept of a mind-independent material world is intellectually incoherent. For Berkeley, a mountain does not exist without a mind to perceive it (ultimately relying on the mind of God to sustain reality).
René Descartes, on the other hand, offered “Problematic Idealism.” Through his method of radical doubt, Descartes realized that the sensations he experienced could simply be the product of a dream state or the machinations of an evil demon. Descartes could only establish his own existence as a “thinking thing” (Cogito, ergo sum), leaving the existence of an external, spatial world entirely doubtful.
Finally, David Hume delivered the fatal blow of total skepticism. Hume argued that reason and experience are utterly impoverished when it comes to proving an external world. We only ever experience a succession of fleeting perceptions. We cannot prove cause and effect, nor can we prove that our internal perceptions are caused by external objects, because we can never step outside our own minds to verify the connection. If Kant could not refute these three thinkers, philosophy would remain trapped inside the subjective prison of the mind, completely unable to explain the remarkable objective successes of human understanding (like, in a modern context, using math and physics to navigate to the moon and back).

6---full-notes/identity-boundaries-and-t.content:

Tags: sociology
Identity Boundaries and the Provision of Public Goods
Details
One of the most significant consequences of identity politics is its profound effect on social cooperation. Compelling research from across the globe demonstrates a powerful inverse correlation: the sharper and more salient the identity boundaries within a society—whether racial, ethnic, or religious—the lower its provision of public goods. This pattern arises because people are systematically less willing to invest in collective resources like education, healthcare, and infrastructure if they perceive that the benefits will flow to a rival “out-group.”
And so in countries that have their own agendas and try to manage so that everyone shares one identity, the public amenities are generally better and more well-maintained than countries where the government supports to “out-group.” Like how in Kenya, they promoted tribal languages and culture, resulting in bad public goods.
An even more specific example is the AIDS epidemics in Brazil and South Africa. By uniting every culture and diversity in their place, Brazil successfully managed AIDS as everyone was cooperating and helping each other. Whilst in South Africa, AIDS turned into a “Black” disease and so the public health response was negative and so on.

Details
Marx views the entire project of political liberalism — including constitutional limits on power, the extension of the franchise, religious toleration, and equality of opportunity — as merely an ideological framework designed to regulate a system of “personal independence” that hides the exploitation behind it. These concepts generate a powerful form of “ideological consciousness,” which serves as an illusion that people are free and that the system is fair while the structure is extracting unpaid labor time.
Because of how these liberal rights are boundaries protecting egotistic individuals and their property within this illusory market system, Marx argues that it is not adequate merely to demand a “more just” economic distribution or “fairer rights” but rather to radically move beyond justice entirely, move beyond the needs for these rights entirely.

6---full-notes/implicit-measures-of-ster.title: Implicit Measures of Stereotypes and Prejudice
6---full-notes/implicit-measures-of-ster.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/Social Psychology
Implicit Measures of Stereotypes and Prejudice
Details
A lot of people may say aloud that they may not have anything against certain groups of people, or they may not admit their prejudices, but there is no certain way for us to believe these claims. Researchers have sought out methods of measuring subtle prejudices that people might not want to admit, even to themselves.
One of the most prominent methods is the Implicit Association Test (IAT), which measures prejudices and stereotypes by measuring the speed of our associations. The core principle is that it’s easier and faster to respond to two concepts that are strongly associated in our minds than to two that are weakly associated.
How the IAT Works The test requires you to rapidly categorize items. For example, you might be instructed to press a left key for an unpleasant word (e.g., “death”) and a right key for a pleasant word (e.g., “love”). Then, the categories switch to insects (left key) and flowers (right key).
The critical part comes when the categories are combined. Most people respond faster when the pairing is “unpleasant words or insects” (left key) and “pleasant words or flowers” (right key). The response time slows down when the pairing is switched to “unpleasant words or flowers” and “pleasant words or insects.” This difference in reaction time reveals an implicit association: we more easily link flowers with pleasantness and insects with unpleasantness.
Measuring Implicit Prejudice Researchers use this same logic to measure implicit racial attitudes. In a typical study with White participants:


Congruent Pairing: Participants press one key for a photo of a Black person or a pleasant word, and another key for a photo of a White person or an unpleasant word.


Incongruent Pairing: The rule switches. Participants now press one key for a Black person or an unpleasant word, and another for a White person or a pleasant word.


Key Findings


For White Participants: Most White college students, even those who explicitly state they have no racial prejudice, respond significantly faster to the “Black/unpleasant” and “White/pleasant” pairing. This suggests a subconscious, implicit bias. This effect is generally stronger in older White individuals.


For Black Participants: On average, Black participants show little to no implicit preference between Black and White faces on the IAT, responding nearly equally to both pairings.


Gender Attitudes: The IAT also reveals implicit attitudes about gender. Most women show a strong implicit preference for women over men. Men, however, tend to show an almost equal preference for both men and women.


These implicit biases can have real-world consequences. In one study, when White students evaluated job applicants with ambiguous or marginal qualifications, they rated the application more favorably if they believed the applicant was White than if they believed the applicant was Black. This demonstrates how unrecognized prejudices can influence important decisions, especially in situations that are not clear-cut.

6---full-notes/incompatibilist-and-the-c.content:
Status: baby
Tags: philosophy Evolutionary Psychology
Incompatibilist and the Cartesian Error
Details
The intuitive pull of incompatibilism often rests on an implicit, perhaps subconscious, commitment to Cartesian dualism. It presumes that a “Self” exists separate from the biological machinery, viewing the brain’s causal process to be whips and chains rather than the vehicle of the self. Neuroscience and evolutionary biology of course is completely rejects this as it perceives that there is no immaterial controller floating above the neural architecture. To wish to be released from this is alike, as Kant famously noted, like a bird wishing to fly in a vacuum to escape air resistance, failing to realize that the air is the very medium that allows it to fly. And so neural determinism is not a prison for our will; it is the very mechanism that allows our will to exist in the first place.

6---full-notes/indifference-curves-and-t.title: Indifference curves and tradeoffs
6---full-notes/indifference-curves-and-t.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Indifference curves and tradeoffs
Details
Indifference curves are the graphical maps of consumer preferences. They show combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction, meaning they will he indifferent between all points on the same curve. In Gruber’s example, the two goods are slices of pizza and cookies. A consumer may be indifferent between two slices of pizza and one cookie, and one slice of pizza and two cookies, while preferring two slices of pizza and two cookies to both. The first two bundles lie on the same indifference curve, while the third lies on a higher indifference curve. This graphical device turns subjective rankings into something that can be analyzed with geometry.
These curves have four main properties: the higher are preferred; they slope downward because they need to have to give up to have some more; they cannot cross because crossing violate transitivity and non-satiation; and lastly, there can only be one curve across a number of bundles.
The job market example makes the concept more intuitive. A graduate student choosing between Princeton and Santa Cruz might care about two dimensions: academic quality and location or weather. Princeton has higher academic quality but worse weather; Santa Cruz has better weather but lower academic prestige. If the student is indifferent between them, both options lie on the same indifference curve. If the IMF in Washington, DC offers a middle combination of somewhat lower academic quality than Princeton but better weather, and the student prefers it, then the IMF lies on a higher indifference curve for that person. There is no objective sense in which the preference is “right” or “wrong.” It is just a representation of that person’s trade-off between two valued dimensions.
Of course this would then depend on the person’s preferences for their curves to be different.

6---full-notes/individuality.content:
Status: teen

Individuality
Details
Individuality, at least in Mill’s sense, is “the permanent interests of a man as a progressive being.” Individuality combines two elements:


The Greek ideal of self-development: Cultivating all one’s natural powers — especially the higher faculties of intellect, imagination, feeling, and moral capacity — into some harmonious whole. Mill draws this from Humboldt’s work published around 1795. The idea is the full unfolding and cultivation of human powers rather than their suppression.


The Christian ideal of self-government: Recognizing and acting within the limits imposed by the equal basic rights of others. Mill insists in paragraph nine that recognizing others’ equal rights is not incompatible with individuality — it is essential to the self-government component of individuality. You cannot genuinely govern yourself while violating the equal standing of others.


Furthermore, he posits this as a psychological fact, as if people will, if they have the necessary faculties, try to achieve individuality and improve themselves.

And in no way will they find this in self-help books, another distraction, another offer for a “way out”.
