Inspectional Reading
Details

There are two steps to this activity, performed simultaneously but they will be described as two different things in this Zettel. So first assume that the reader doesn’t know if they want to analytically read but suspects that there maybe valuable information in it. This is when they must skim the book, to know what kind of book the author is writing and what his main contention may be.
To skim, try to read every piece of info that is not the main content, the preface, title page, index, blurb, and of course the table of contents, as the author most of the time puts a lot of effort into it to allow a more aided approach to reading the book.
Only after these steps then the reader should look for the pivotal chapters of the book, then going to those chapters, reading the closing/opening statements, summary statements as well. Try to read the 2-3 most important pages of the chapters to get a gist of what is important in the book.
Try to be as active as possible and spend less than an hour reading all of it.

After determining
This is when the difficulty of the book has been determined and the reader has deemed it worthy. If the book is hard, the reader should read it through without stopping at any difficult to understand concepts or words. This works because the author would want the main points of the book most clearly to the readers without having to analyze the book fully.
This skimming also gives the reader a better view of the book’s structure and altogether meaning as well (which is the first layer of comprehension to a book).
Supporting Content

What kind of book is it ?
What is it about as a whole ?
What is the structural order of the work whereby the author develops his conception or understanding of that general subject matter ?

6---full-notes/institutional-complexes.content:
Status: teen

Institutional Complexes
Details
If individual institutions like hospitals or law firms are the distinct organs of social life, then institutional complexes are the major systems—the anatomy—that connect these organs into a functioning ecosystem. These complexes represent the large-scale machinery that provides structure and order to modern society.
The primary function of these complexes is to establish a system of impersonal, predictable rules, which stands in contrast to societies governed by personal, arbitrary authority. To exemplify this, consider a community where rights and benefits are ensured by a single leader rather than by a systemic rule of law. In such a place, if the leader dislikes a resident, they can withdraw protection and access to resources at will. The resident’s security is based on a personal relationship, not on guaranteed rights.
However, this ideal of a purely impersonal system is not absolute. Traces of personal rule persist even within modern institutional complexes, often through networking. The ability to leverage personal relationships—“knowing someone”—can grant access to services or opportunities that are not available through formal channels alone, revealing a lingering tension between systemic rules and personal influence.

6---full-notes/institutions-shaping-iden.content:

Institutions shaping Identities
Details
In our society, something we take for granted is just how much our environment shape us to be. We underthink about how much it really does so much, we do not realize the sheer amount of influence it has on our lives, from our relationships to our education and so on. These ideas influence us in different ways, from our friends to our marriage choices. It bleeds in from education to your own families.
For example, a large scale example is the difference in the education of America and France. In America, you get second chances, you fail, you fail a lot, and you will learn from those mistakes and build upon it to get better. Unlike systems with rigid national exams, a person can change their trajectory late in life (e.g., decide to go to medical school at 24 after doing nothing since high school). This institutional design reinforces a core American belief in individual reinvention and the idea that one’s fate is not permanently fixed at a young age.
But in France ? In France people use high-stakes national examinations at young ages (11, 14, 18) to sort students into fixed educational and career tracks. Failure on these exams can permanently close off opportunities like university or medical school. This structure creates a different sense of self and fate, where one’s potential is officially evaluated and decided early on. It also fosters a culture where elite status is clearly defined and credentialed by the state.
Another would be friendship groups, in America, they would usually be a big group who would be incredible close with each other for a really long time, a lifetime perhaps. They would have normal disagreements sure but it would not define their relationship a lot. These people also invite each other to more personal activities.
What about Europeans ? These people have less friends in a group, rather just a few. They do not have obligations with each other, they don’t just invite each other to go to personal activities and such as well.

6---full-notes/internal-stressor.title: Internal Stressor

Internal Stressor
Details
These stresses are the kind that comes internally and consists of psychological phenomena as the demands the person places on themselves, their fears, and their self-reproaches. This self-stressing mechanism may be detected by one tapping into the “internal communication system.” In some respects it is analogous to Freud’s concept of the superego.
Most patients who consult a physician for a psychosomatic disorder do not present any evidence of specific external stress. They frequently appear “nervous” and often acquire the label “neurotic” or “psycho” (first in the physician’s eyes and then in their own). The physician often tells them they worry too much and take things too seriously. Such statements, instead of providing insight, generally reinforce the patient’s self-concept of being unstable and inferior.
The hard-driving businessman who develops a peptic ulcer provides a stereotypical example of proneness to psychosomatic illness. Although the same psychological configuration may lead to other psychosomatic syndromes such as hypertension or dermatitis, it is useful to consider this case as illustrative of psychosomatic disorders in general. The “executive ulcer” type sets high goals and drives himself and others in order to achieve them. His outward behavior reflects his system of goals and beliefs that lead to a constant state of tension. The momentum behind his work drive is his chronic concern that he will not reach his goals, or that he or his subordinates will make costly errors. He reacts to each new task with strong doubts. He usually exaggerates the importance and the difficulty of said task, and underestimates his capacity to deal with it.
Although as we can see there are absolutely no external pressure from the outside, his mere occupation is causing a detrimental amount of stress because of the way he is perceiving his work. As he interprets every tasks as a major confrontation with the result being failure, he is under continuous stress, causing his physiological systems to overload.
Even more so, these stresses do not just make the consequences much worse, but also increases the probability of them happening. There is no idea on why some develop these disorders whilst other only suffer psychologically.

The attribution theory was founded by Fritz Heider, who emphasized the differences between these two types of causes. External attributions are explanations based on the situations, including events that presumably would influence almost anyone.

Meaning if we do something bad, we attribute it to the situation or something out of our control, but if someone else does it, we attribute it to them being the kind of person who would do something like that, or them just being a piece of crap.

6---full-notes/internalization-of-bad-co.title: Internalization of Bad Conscience
6---full-notes/internalization-of-bad-co.content:
Status: teen

Internalization of Bad Conscience
Details
Accordingly to his methodology, Nietzsche locates the origin of “Bad Conscience” not in a divine command or a metaphysical realization of sin, but in a historical rupture, not in religions like Christianity and such, but rather from the transition from wilderness to civilization of humanity.
He posits that in their pre-civilized state, humans were aggressive, semi-nomadic predators, we had powerful instincts for hunting, fighting, and releasing aggression outwardly toward enemies. And so when we were forced into society and peace, either by conquest or urbanization. Suddenly, the external discharge of aggression was prohibited by law and social pressure.
From this, Nietzsche argued that this tension did not go away (a very Freudian idea) and instead internalized. People didn’t self mutilate, instead they pained themselves with negative thoughts and such rather. Before it becomes moral guilt, bad conscience is simply this structural stress—the suffering of an animal that must now rely on its “weakest organ” (consciousness) rather than its instincts.

6---full-notes/introspection-undermines-.title: Introspection Undermines itself
6---full-notes/introspection-undermines-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Social Psychology
Introspection Undermines itself
Details
The question: can thinking about what you like actually lead you to choose things you’ll like less?
Nisbett & Wilson (1977) — the paper the lecturer calls arguably the most important in social psychology over the last 40 years. People primed with “ocean” and “moon” preferentially choose Tide detergent. Not surprising given everything about priming. But when asked why they chose Tide, they confidently generate completely fabricated reasons: “my mom uses Tide,” “I like the box.” They aren’t lying or covering up — they genuinely believe these are their reasons. They have no access to the actual cause of their preference and don’t know they lack that access.
Wilson’s art print study — the lecturer’s centerpiece. People choose between a Monet print and a Garfield cartoon. Without introspection, people prefer the Monet (unsurprisingly). But when asked to write out reasons for their preferences before choosing, the preference shifts dramatically — the cartoon jumps in popularity. People take their print home. Two weeks later, those who chose the Monet without introspecting still like it. Those who introspected and chose the cartoon now say they chose badly and wish they’d taken the Monet.
But why does this happen ? Social Psychology posits that its the same thing for Controlled Processes, cartoon is really really easy to linguistically say why it it preferable, which makes us take the position that it is our favorite work of art when our gut feeling might be saying otherwise. Nonetheless, the thing is we are verbally suppressing our gut feelings.

6---full-notes/islands-of-safety.title: Islands of Safety
6---full-notes/islands-of-safety.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology trauma
Islands of Safety
Details
People aren’t comfortable with talking about their traumatic experiences. This is attributed to the rejection that they get from expressing themselves through talking this out. This is a reason why they withdraw themselves and why these stories become rote narratives, into a form least likely to provoke rejection.
We start by establishing inner “islands of safety” within the body. This means helping patients identify parts of the body, postures, or movements where they can ground themselves whenever they feel stuck, terrified, or enraged. These parts usually lie outside the reach of the vagus nerve, which carries the messages of panic to the chest, abdomen, and throat, and they can serve as allies in integrating the trauma. I might ask a patient if her hands feel okay, and if she says yes, I’ll ask her to move them, exploring their lightness and warmth and flexibility. Later, if I see her chest tighten and her breath almost disappear, I can stop her and ask her to focus on her hands and move them, so that she can feel herself as separate from the trauma. Or I might ask her to focus on her out breath and notice how she can change it, or ask her to lift her arms up and down with each breath—a qigong movement.
For some patients tapping acupressure points is a good anchor. I ask others to feel the weight of their body in the chair or to plant their feet on the floor. I might ask a patient who is collapsing into silence to see what happens when he sits up straight. Some patients discover their own islands of safety—they begin to “get” that they can create body sensations to counterbalance feeling out of control. This sets the stage for trauma resolution: pendulating between states of exploration and safety, between language and body, between remembering the past and feeling alive in the present.

6---full-notes/iterated-dominance.title: Iterated Dominance
6---full-notes/iterated-dominance.content:
Status: teen
Tags: economics
Iterated Dominance
Details
In a game about choosing the number that is two-thirds of the class average, a natural first thought is, “Since it’s random, the average would be about 50, so pick 33.” Now here’s the problem: you’re not assuming that the others are trying to win as well… and if they picked 33, well, now 22 is the two-thirds number.
Iterated deletion of dominated strategies makes this rigorous. Each round of deletion needs one more layer of knowledge:


Above 67. Even if everyone picked 100, the target would be 66⅔, so every number above 67 is weakly dominated by 67. Ruling those out needs only your own rationality, meaning you’re trying to maximize your payoff.


46–67. With 68–100 gone, the target can’t go above about 45, so 46–67 are now dominated. They weren’t dominated in the original game, only after the first round. Ruling them out also needs you to know that the others are rational (Polak’s “in shoes” step).


31–45. This slice needs you to know that they know it too (“in shoes in shoes”).


Getting all the way to 1 would need common knowledge of rationality: everyone is rational, they know it, so everyone knows it, and so on.
So, depending on the population, the number might be much lower than one might think because of the sophistication of the people around them.

6---full-notes/john-stuart-mill's-life.title: John Stuart Mill's Life
6---full-notes/john-stuart-mill's-life.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy history
John Stuart Mill’s Life
Details
John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) stands alongside Marx as one of the 19th century’s most significant philosopher-economist-social theorists. Unlike Marx, who devoted himself to producing rigorous academic works like Capital, Mill cast himself in a fundamentally different role: educator of advanced public opinion. Writing primarily around 1830, Mill believed he lived in an age of transition toward modern democratic-industrial society, and saw his vocation as conveying philosophical and political principles that ought to govern this emerging form of civilization. This explains why his texts appear loosely written with imprecise terminology — he was not attempting systematic academic philosophy but rather persuading educated, politically engaged readers.
Mill’s unusual educational background also shaped his intellectual character. Tutored exclusively by his father James Mill, he mastered Ricardo’s economics by age 12 through rigorous drilling and recitation, never attending school or university. This created a psychological constraint: he could not openly reject his father’s ideas or Bentham’s utilitarian framework. Throughout his work, Mill consistently represses his originality, never claiming novel ideas as his own, always presenting changes as clarifications rather than corrections. This makes reading Mill require active interpretive reconstruction — identifying the drift of his arguments rather than taking his official statements at face value.

6---full-notes/jung's-psychology.content:

Jung’s Psychology
Details
Carl Jung, once seen as Sigmund Freud’s heir apparent, broke away to develop his own influential theory of personality. While he agreed with Freud on the importance of the unconscious mind, he envisioned it differently. Jung proposed that beyond our personal unconscious, there exists a deeper, universal layer he called the collective unconscious.
This collective unconscious is not shaped by personal experience but is inherited from our ancestors. It is a repository of shared human memories, instincts, and predispositions that manifest as archetypes.
Archetypes are universal symbols, themes, or patterns that appear in myths, art, literature, and dreams across all cultures. They are innate tendencies that shape how we perceive the world and react to it. Jung identified numerous archetypes, including:


The Good Mother: A universally understood figure representing nurturing, warmth, and unconditional love.


The Shadow: The dark, repressed, and sometimes creative side of our personality.


The Animus/Anima: The masculine aspect within a woman and the feminine aspect within a man.


The Faithful Companion: Often represented by an animal (like a loyal dog), symbolizing guidance and unwavering support.


According to Jung, we are born with these archetypal frameworks, and they cause us to unconsciously seek out and project these roles onto people and situations in our lives. This idea represented a significant departure from Freud’s sexually-driven model, expanding the unconscious to include a spiritual and ancestral dimension.

Justification as Public, Practical, and Distinct from Moral Truth
Details
Similar to Scanlon’s Scanlon Contractualism, this is a feature of Rawls’s philosophy that addresses the justification of the citizens about their own selves and institutions.
There are three features to this account: the first is addressed to disagreement - “If there is no disagreement, then offhand there isn’t anything to justify.” One must convince or reconcile through reason, not rhetoric, manipulation, or coercion. Second, justification is not just a valid deductive argument. It must holds an internal role, it must also work in the public consensus of it. Third and most distinctively is the aim of it, it must be practical: “to preserve the conditions of social cooperation on a basis of mutual respect.” Realistically, one cannot use moral frameworks to inherently justify and apply it to politics or society, because there would simply be too many disagreements. The task of political philosophy then is to narrow said range of disagreement by constituting partial convergence.

6---full-notes/justification-for-the-dif.title: Justification for the Difference Principle
6---full-notes/justification-for-the-dif.content:
Status: adult
Tags: morals philosophy
Justification for the Difference Principle
Details
Using the The Original Position, Rawls believes that this proves the two principles of justice as superior to the pure principle of average utility. However, that does not fully justify The Difference Principle. And so, to rigorously test it, Rawls sets up a “Second Fundamental Comparison.” Here, the Two Principles are pitted against a much stronger alternative: a system where the First Principle (Equal Liberties) and Fair Equality of Opportunity are guaranteed, but the Difference Principle is replaced by a “Principle of Constrained Average Utility” operating above a guaranteed social minimum.
In this situation, as basic liberties and catastrophic outcomes are already protected from the citizens, one must evaluate the resulting “The Well-Ordered Society” that is inherently more desirable and stable. To effectively determine this, we must look to the Publicity Condition and the concept of Reciprocity. The Publicity Condition demands that a political conception of justice must function smoothly even when its foundational rules are fully known, publicly recognized, and internalized by all citizens. The Difference Principle inherently embodies reciprocity—it guarantees that those who gain more wealth only do so on terms that directly benefit those who have the least. When this principle is deeply understood and publicly recognized, it actively generates social harmony, trust, and civic friendship, while mitigating destructive forces like envy. On the other hand, a society operating on the Constrained Average Utility lacks the reciprocity, which breeds resentment and then instability in exchange for slightly higher aggregate wealth with the public knowledge of the principle out there.

6---full-notes/kant's-synthetic-unity-of.title: Kant's Synthetic Unity of Apperception
6---full-notes/kant's-synthetic-unity-of.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Kant’s Synthetic Unity of Apperception
Details
Immanuel Kant viewed David Hume’s “bundle of perceptions” as an inadequate explanation for human cognition. For Kant, the mere existence of a stream of disjointed sensations does not explain how we arrive at stable, unified thoughts. To solve this, Kant introduced the “supreme principle in relation to the understanding”: the argument that all sensory intuition must be subject to the “original synthetic unity of apperception.” This dense terminology refers to the mind’s active, a priori necessity to unify disparate sensory elements into a single, cohesive consciousness. Kant insists this is not a subjective psychological feeling, but an objective, logical precondition for knowledge. Without this unifying principle, the fragmented data of the senses could never rise to the level of a comprehensible object.
To not fallback onto Humean skepticism, Kant splits the concept of the self into two specific domains here. Firstly is the empirical ego, which constitutes the “I” of ourselves. It is subjective, variable, and entirely distinct from person to person (e.g., when you say “Let me tell you about myself”).
The transcendental ego, conversely, is a prior substrate - a foundational ground of the mind - that must exist for one to have thoughts in the first place.

6---full-notes/kant's-upbringing-and-mor.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Kant's Upbringing and Moral Framework.md
6---full-notes/kant's-upbringing-and-mor.title: Kant's Upbringing and Moral Framework
6---full-notes/kant's-upbringing-and-mor.content:
Status: adult
Tags: morals philosophy
Kant’s Upbringing and Moral Framework
Details
Coming from an impoverished background and deeply resenting the rigid, oppressive dogmatism of his early education, Kant did not set out to create an eccentric, inaccessible philosophical system just for the sake of complexity. Rather, Transcendental Idealism functions as a rigorous defense of “reasonable faith.” Kant basically designed this system in response to the rise of Newtonian physics to reconcile the knowledge of the physical world with the absolute necessity of human freedom. Crucially, Kant does not believe that philosophy’s job is to invent the moral law or teach ordinary people right from wrong. He explicitly argues that any person of sound, uncorrupted natural reason already intuitively understands the moral law. However, human innocence is fragile and easily deceived by the sophistry, cynical arguments, and temptations of high culture. Therefore, the purpose of moral philosophy is to strengthen our grip on the moral law by illuminating how it is fundamentally rooted in our own free nature.
Within this defense, Kant draws a vital architectural distinction between the Moral Law, the Categorical Imperative, and the Categorical Imperative Procedure. The Moral Law is an ultimate idea of reason that applies universally to all perfectly rational beings, including God or angels. However, God does not experience the moral law as a burden or a constraint because a divine being has no selfish inclinations to overcome. On the other hand, because we humans constantly experience this friction between what we want to do and what reason demands, the moral law comes to us in the form of a command or a duty—this is the Categorical Imperative. The Categorical Imperative is simply the Moral Law experienced by imperfect beings who are tempted to violate it. Finally, the Categorical Imperative Procedure is the deliberative mechanism by which fully rational human agents apply this absolute command to the messy, everyday circumstances of human life.

6---full-notes/kant’s-copernican-revolut.title: Kant’s Copernican Revolution
6---full-notes/kant’s-copernican-revolut.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
Kant’s Copernican Revolution
Details
The historical context matters. Copernicus was contacted by Pope Leo X because the Julian calendar, in use since Caesar’s time, had drifted so far from astronomical reality that Easter Sunday was wandering by two to three weeks. Mathematicians could not agree on the length of the year. Copernicus’s insight was to ask: what happens if we change the position of the observer? What if, instead of assuming the earth is stationary and everything revolves around it, we place the observer on a moving earth orbiting the sun? The result was not subjectivism — Jack and Jill observing from the sun would agree with each other — but a more accurate model of reality achieved by recognizing that the observer’s position is itself a variable that must be accounted for.
Kant proposes “another trial of the same sort.” Instead of assuming that our cognition passively conforms to objects, suppose that objects must conform to the conditions of our cognition. The pure categories of the understanding — causality, substance, unity — are not extracted from experience but are the framework through which experience becomes intelligible in the first place. Just as Copernicus’s repositioning of the observer produced better astronomy, Kant’s repositioning of the cognitive subject is meant to produce genuine metaphysics. The observer is not a passive recipient of stimuli but an active participant whose cognitive constitution shapes what counts as an objective observation. Crucially, this does not lead to subjectivism, because the cognitive framework is shared by all rational beings. Astronomy developed as a science on exactly this basis — accounting for the observer’s position made the science more objective, not less.

6---full-notes/kant’s-critique.title: Kant’s Critique
6---full-notes/kant’s-critique.content:
Status: teen

Kant’s Critique
Details
Against Hume, Kant argued that the very stance that Hume is taking also directly contradicts itself.
Hume puts billiard balls on a table. Ball one moves, hits ball two, ball two moves. Causation isn’t visible — granted. But notice what Hume does take for granted: that the events happen in space, that one happens before the other in time. Yet there are no sense organs for space. There are no sense organs for time. These aren’t given in the stimulus any more than causation is. Leibniz already argued there’s no such thing as absolute space (against Newton) — empty space is nothing, and nothing causes nothing. And Kant works in this space, clearly these mechanisms work, and so, what must already be the case for them to work ? The concepts that work don’t depend on our senses, so it cannot be that.

6---full-notes/kant’s-refutation-of-idea.title: Kant’s Refutation of Idealism
6---full-notes/kant’s-refutation-of-idea.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Kant’s Refutation of Idealism
Details
Kant introduced in his second edition of the Critique of Pure Reason the “Refutation of Idealism.” His goal was to basically rid the subjective traps of Cartesian doubt and immaterialism and instead distinguish his own framework of “Transcendental Idealism.” Kant agreed that we only have access to appearances (phenomena) and cannot directly know “things-in-themselves” (noumena). Space and time are merely the a priori, sensible forms of human intuition. However, Kant fiercely rejected the idea that this meant the external, material world is an illusion or unprovable. He set out to turn idealism against itself.
Kant’s masterstroke here was to argue that self-consciousness fundamentally relies on the existence of a feasible, permanent external world. Since as a conscious being, one is aware of their own existence as a sequence of thoughts, feelings flowing through time, or as so set in time.
And if it is set in time, it can then logically be inferred from time itself. However, one cannot measure the line of consciousness against itself. Because the inner landscape of the mind is in a constant, fleeting state of flux, this required “permanent” background cannot be internal. Therefore, for inner sense (the march of conscious events) to exist at all, there must be an external, permanent, spatial framework.

Karl Popper and the Myth of Deductive Science
Details
Karl Popper was one of the most influential philosopher of the 20th century, and his approach to Hume’s Fork was quite different. He did not try to argue that it was wrong or unagreeable, he accepted completely that there was no argument you could realistically make against it. However, Popper argued that this didn’t matter because science does not actually rely on induction. Instead, he proposed “Falsificationism”: science proceeds by making bold conjectures and then trying to refute them deductively. If a theory survives a test, it is “corroborated,” but never confirmed.
Peter Millican argues that this point of view is also inductive due to how it functions. Of course, according to Popper, we would prefer something that has withstood 1000 tests rather than a new theory or model. But that would be inductive, because we are assuming that the previous model will guide/dictate the future model, while it doesn’t.

6---full-notes/kernel-density-estimation.title: Kernel density estimation
6---full-notes/kernel-density-estimation.content:
Status: adult
Tags: statistics psychology
Kernel density estimation
Details
Histograms are a crude way to estimate a distribution because of edge effects: every subject in a bin is counted as if they sat at the bin’s midpoint. A grad student earning 31,000 in a 30–40k bin contributes exactly as if they earned 35,000; someone at 19,500 near an edge is likewise shoved to the bin’s centre. Each data point is “weighed in a weird way,” and the result is jagged and sensitive to where you happened to draw the bin boundaries.
And so to remove these bins, we can use kernel density estimation. Basically, we mark every point on the axis, and then we replace each point with a small identical bell curve (a kernel) whose area is 1/n, where n is the sample size. Because there are n of them, the bumps’ areas sum to n × (1/n) = 1, so the total is a legitimate probability density. Lastly, we can add the bumps together to see more accurately where the graph might have a group that has a lot of data points and such.
You would never build this by hand, but software does it instantly. In R you create the estimate with density(Prestigeincome)‘(the‘income) (the  income)‘(the‘ selects the income variable inside the Prestige dataset) and overlay it on a histogram with lines(). A practical learning tip from the same demo: drive R through the R Commander GUI, then read the command-line code it auto-generates in the script window and edit that — a gentle on-ramp to R as a programming language, which is what it originally was.

6---full-notes/kinds-of-awareness-of-mor.title: Kinds of Awareness of Moral Responsibility
6---full-notes/kinds-of-awareness-of-mor.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
Kinds of Awareness of Moral Responsibility
Details
Moving on from the question about the epistemic conditions, now we have to move on to the question about knowledge and beliefs. To start this section, I will propose an example: a person is putting poison in another person’s drink for them to be assassinated. Now, the other person doesn’t actually die, is the perpetrator still morally responsible for what happened even if it did not result in their wanted conclusion. This brings us into our first point on kinds of awareness, or the beliefs of the person who did the act. After all, they are the person who genuinely wanted and believed that it would have killed the other person, so, they should be guilty for the act regardless of if they had the knowledge or not of what was going to happen, correct ? 	Key point here is that, regardless of if he had the knowledge or not, he would have been responsible either way due to his beliefs and that said beliefs actually bad or not.
The second point addresses the timely component of moral responsibility. The main dispute here is between those philosophers who think that the pertinent beliefs must be occurrently entertained (Zimmerman 1997: 421–2; 2017: 79; Ginet 2000: 270; Rosen 2004: 309; Levy 2011: 141) and those who think that it’s enough if these beliefs are dispositionally entertained (Haji 1997: 531; Peels 2011: 580; Timpe 2011: 18; Levy 2013: 167; 2014: 34).[3] According to the ‘occurrentist’ camp, an agent satisfies the EC only if, at the time of action, she consciously believes that her action is right/wrong and consciously contemplates some of its possible consequences (Zimmerman 1997: 421). Otherwise, and for the purposes of attributions of responsibility, she is ignorant of relevant considerations and so, in principle (recall the possibility of culpable ignorance), she has an excuse for her wrongdoing (Zimmerman 2017: 79; see sect. 3.1 below for an argument in favor of this position). As we’ll see below (sect. 2), the occurrentist interpretation of the EC plays a central role in a revisionist argument against commonsense attributions of responsibility. On the other hand, the dispositionalist argues that this is too strict and would let people off the hook or open morals up to be manipulated. After all, a person could somehow shield oneself from blame simply by avoid thinking about the moral status of one’s action, and that’s implausible (Guerrero 2007: 74; Timpe 2011: 23; Robichaud 2014: 150; Levy 2014: 31) (though this does raise some questions about if one can ACTUALLY do that or not or are they just subconsciously hiding it ?).

6---full-notes/knowing-your-audience.title: Knowing your audience
6---full-notes/knowing-your-audience.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship psychology
Knowing your audience
Details
A speaker stands before a sea of faces, a mosaic of different lives, beliefs, and histories. The greatest challenge they face is not what to say, but how to find a single, unifying note that can resonate within every person present. A lesser speaker might resort to broad, impersonal platitudes, hoping a wide net will catch a few listeners. Michelle Obama’s genius, however, was in her profound understanding that you do not unite a diverse audience by skimming the surface of their differences, but by digging down to the emotional bedrock they all share. Her choice of material was a testament to this deep knowledge of who was listening.
Her strategy was to begin in the most sacred and universal space imaginable: the family. This choice was a masterclass in audience awareness. She knew that within that auditorium—regardless of political party, race, or economic status—were countless stories of fathers who worked too hard, mothers who sacrificed their own ambitions, and the inextinguishable hope that parents hold for their children. By opening with the story of her father’s illness and unwavering dedication, she was not just telling her story; she was holding up a mirror to theirs. She was speaking a language of love and sacrifice that requires no translation. She demonstrated that she knew her audience not by listing their demographic characteristics, but by appealing to their most fundamental human identity—as sons, daughters, parents, and providers.
The effect of this is profound. When an audience feels that a speaker truly understands the quiet, unpraised dignity of their private lives, they grant that speaker an immense measure of trust. Having proven she understood their personal world, Michelle Obama earned the authority to speak on the more complex issues of our public life. She could then build the bridge from her father’s struggle to the systemic injustices faced by Barack’s family, knowing the audience would follow because she had already validated their own experiences of silent struggle. She knew her audience was not a group to be lectured, but a collection of individuals yearning to see their own values reflected on a national stage. By the end, they were not just convinced by her argument; they were empowered by it, leaving with the feeling that the best parts of their own stories were, in fact, the very soul of the nation’s story.

6---full-notes/knowing-yourself.title: Knowing yourself
6---full-notes/knowing-yourself.content:
Status:
Tags: scholarship psychology
Knowing yourself
Details
Amidst the fervent research into a university’s soul and the strategic weaving of a personal narrative, lies a quieter, more perilous journey: the journey inward. An applicant can master the art of storytelling and understand an institution’s values with perfect clarity, yet still produce an application that feels hollow. This happens when the story they tell is not truly their own. In the immense pressure to impress, it is tempting to become a ghostwriter for an imaginary ideal candidate, assembling a patchwork quilt of borrowed ambitions and experiences that seem to fit the mold. The resulting application may look impressive at a glance, but it lacks a center of gravity. It is a carefully constructed mask that, upon closer inspection, reveals there is no distinct face behind it.
True self-knowledge, in this context, is the act of taking an honest and unflinching inventory of one’s own character. It is about sifting through experiences not just for the successes, but for the moments of confusion, the surprising detours, the failures that taught more than any victory, and the quiet curiosities that have persisted since childhood. It is the process of uncovering the unwavering through-line that connects these disparate points—the quiet ‘why’ that animates the ‘what’. This internal compass is the most valuable asset an applicant possesses. It allows them to write with a voice that is not just polished, but authentic. When you know why a certain subject fascinates you, or what core value drove you to a specific volunteer opportunity, your writing gains a conviction that cannot be faked.
This is where the magic truly happens. When a deep understanding of the self meets a deep understanding of the institution, the application transcends a mere submission and becomes an act of authentic alignment. The applicant no longer has to strain to fit their story into the university’s mission; they can see and articulate the natural, genuine resonance that already exists. The personal statement becomes a bridge, built from two strong and certain anchor points: “This is who I am,” on one shore, and “This is who you are,” on the other. For the admissions officer, reading such an application is an electric experience. The voice is clear, the motivation is undeniable, and the fit feels not just logical, but inevitable. It is the moment an applicant stops trying to be what a university wants, and simply demonstrates, with confidence and clarity, who they are.

Knowledge and Capitalism

In other words, they are politically realigning themselves with the values so that knowledge can be pushed further rather than economically conservating their own wealth and power. This suggests a growing disparity in between the societal elites.
This could be explained by examining the nature of knowledge. Knowledge inherently thrives on freedom, the more people know about it, the more people will become somewhat educated and be able to push it forward using their own expertise which is the complete opposite of what capitalism is. In contrast, capitalism makes knowledge private property, because as long as people do not know what makes them rich and powerful, they will retain all that to themselves. All of the information can be copyrighted or patented so that they can legally keep it to themselves.
But this of course comes as a cost, as said before about how knowledge thrives, the fact that these methods are private is a barrier to the potential of knowledge expansion as they are stifled by the legal system and private companies.

6---full-notes/knowledge-vs.-mechanism-a.title: Knowledge vs. Mechanism as a Trivial Distinction
6---full-notes/knowledge-vs.-mechanism-a.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Massive Modularity Hypothesis Evolutionary Psychology Cognitive Psychology
Knowledge vs. Mechanism as a Trivial Distinction
Details
A key critique of the Massive Modularity Hypothesis (MMH) is that arguments for innate cognitive structure (like the poverty of the stimulus argument) do not necessitate innate mechanisms (modules), but could instead point to innate bodies of knowledge operated on by general-purpose processors [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf]. However, from a fitness-functionalist perspective, this distinction is largely semantic and does not undermine the core of the evolutionary psychology project [cite: Frankenhuis_and_Ploeger_2007.pdf].
The central claim of evolutionary psychology is that the mind is not a “blank slate” but is richly and intricately structured by natural selection to solve adaptive problems. The “solvability arguments” are designed to argue against a truly domain-general architecture that “lacks any content, either in the form of domain-specific knowledge… or domain-specific procedures” [cite: Cosmides_and_Tooby_1994, as cited in Frankenhuis_and_Ploeger_2007.pdf]. Therefore, a model that posits innate, domain-specific knowledge (like the Library Model of Cognition) is, in this context, simply another form of adaptive cognitive specificity.
From the perspective of natural selection, the functional outcome is what matters. It makes no difference whether an organism avoids incest because of an innate piece of knowledge (“do not mate with those you were raised with”) or a dedicated cognitive procedure that produces the same aversion. In both scenarios, the organism exhibits an adaptive behavior resulting from innate, domain-specific cognitive structure [cite: Frankenhuis_and_Ploeger_2007.pdf]. Thus, the retort is that the debate over “knowledge vs. mechanism” misses the larger point: both are forms of adaptive specialization, and the arguments for MMH are fundamentally arguments for this kind of specificity in the mind.

6---full-notes/language-in-ptsd.title: Language in PTSD
6---full-notes/language-in-ptsd.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology trauma
Language in PTSD
Details
The reason it is hard to communicate the trauma that one has is that it effectively makes one relive the old scenes in one’s head, or communicate with the other what transpired. When the latter was chosen, the patient would quickly lose touch and start just focusing on what the other opinion is. The slightest hint of doubt or judgement would shut them down, and would shift the attention to regaining their approval.
A concept that we need to know is the distinct forms of self-awareness: one that keeps track of the self across time and the other in the present moment. The first, the autobiographical self, creates connections among experiences and makes a coherent story. It is rooted in our language. It can change with the change of our perspectives as others provide their own inputs. The other operates on a moment-to-moment basis instead, which is based in physical sensations, but if we feel safe and not rushed, we can also communicate these feelings into words. These two ways of knowing are localized in different parts of the brain that are largely disconnected from each other.
Now to the important part, one of these system creates a story for the public, and if we tell that story often enough, we are likely to believe it is the whole truth. But the other registers a different truth, of the feeling that we have towards the situation. It is this that needs to be accessed, befriended and reconciled.

6---full-notes/learning-from-those-who-s.title: Learning from those who succeed before you
6---full-notes/learning-from-those-who-s.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship university
Learning from those who succeed before you
Details
The journey toward securing a prestigious scholarship or gaining admission to a top university can often feel like a solitary trek into uncharted territory. While application guides and official websites provide a map, they cannot replicate the wisdom of a seasoned traveler. This is why one of the most powerful, yet often overlooked, strategies is to actively seek out and learn from those who have already walked the path and reached the destination you are striving for.
Connecting with past scholarship winners or university alumni provides invaluable tactical and strategic insights that cannot be found elsewhere. These individuals have successfully decoded what selection committees are truly looking for. They can offer a firsthand account of the interview process, share which aspects of their profile they believe were most compelling, and provide clarity on the “unwritten rules” of the application. They can tell you not just what they did, but why it worked, helping you to tailor your own story to resonate with the specific values and mission of the institution or foundation. This moves you from simply following instructions to strategically positioning yourself for success.
Beyond practical advice, connecting with successful predecessors offers a profound psychological advantage. It demystifies the entire process, transforming an intimidating, abstract goal into a tangible, achievable reality. Seeing someone with a similar background or set of experiences who has succeeded can powerfully combat feelings of inadequacy or “imposter syndrome.” Their success serves as living proof that the goal is within reach, providing a crucial boost in motivation and confidence when you need it most.
To find these mentors, leverage university alumni networks, professional platforms like LinkedIn by searching for past scholars, or even your own extended social circles. When you reach out, be respectful of their time, specific in your questions, and clear about your ambitions. You will often find that people are incredibly generous and willing to “pay it forward.” By learning from their journey, you are not just gathering tips; you are gaining a mentor, a role model, and a clearer vision for your own success.

Learning of new knowledge
Details
Assuming the rhetorician point of view, learning would not be something simple but rather extremely difficult because of how it functions under these circumstances. This goes against Socrates’ method in the sense that a person is trying to not teach their students about their point of view and such, but rather trying to get students to imitate different styles of thinking entirely from master thinkers like Nietzsche or  Foucault or Nabokov. This is because the style is not decoration, but rather the thought itself.
The rejection of Socrates also entails a rejection of the classroom drama of contradiction — the student who stands up, argues with the professor, and earns respect for their boldness. In a Socratic classroom, this dialectical opposition is the engine of learning. But contradiction, the lecturer insists, is “not interesting. It gets us nowhere.” Saying “you’re wrong” simply reverses polarity within the same circuit. What is interesting is making new things, being different — not negating the existing argument but escaping it entirely, taking the line of flight. The classroom should produce novelty, not opposition.

6---full-notes/legitimate-expectations-v.content:
Status: baby
Tags: morals philosophy
Legitimate Expectations versus Moral Desert
Details
A critical and often misunderstood element of Rawlsian justice is the complete decoupling of economic reward from the concept of moral desert. In ordinary, everyday life, humans have a natural tendency to conflate a person’s moral virtue with what they deserve to earn or achieve. However, Rawls argues that in a pluralistic democratic society, citizens hold fundamentally divergent, comprehensive moral and religious doctrines. Because we cannot reach a universal consensus on what constitutes a morally good character, basing a political economy on a disputed concept of moral worth is entirely unworkable.
Basically, in such a system, it is not that the morals or religious or philosophy of a person that determines their “deservedness” but rather the legitimate expectations that they have to the institutions and the entitlements that they subsequently deserve.

6---full-notes/limbic-system-therapy.title: Limbic system Therapy
6---full-notes/limbic-system-therapy.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology CBT trauma
Limbic system Therapy
Details
Have you ever wondered why no amount of logical thinking can simply “talk you out” of fear, sadness, or anger? Why telling yourself to “calm down” often doesn’t work at all?
The answer lies deep within the brain—in the limbic system, the center of our emotional lives. According to Joseph LeDoux, the only way we can consciously access this emotional brain is through self-awareness. Most of our waking thoughts are outwardly focused: solving problems, making plans, forming relationships. We rarely stop to check the weather inside ourselves. Yet, true emotional change—true healing—demands we turn inward.
Limbic system therapy is built on a simple, but revolutionary truth: you cannot fix what you are not willing to feel. You can’t command emotions like a machine. Instead, you must befriend them. To heal fear, you must first notice fear without judgment. To soothe anger, you must first sit with it, listen to it, and understand its root. Self-awareness becomes the doorway through which real change can occur.
Unlike the rational, logical neocortex, the limbic system changes through experience, not reasoning. It’s a part of the brain that learns by feeling safe, feeling loved, feeling heard. This is why therapies that only rely on talking or explaining can fall short. Real limbic healing requires creating new emotional experiences that reshape how the brain feels about the world—and about itself.
In the end, limbic system therapy teaches us that managing our emotions is not about control. It’s about connection. It’s about learning to sit quietly with ourselves, becoming allies to our inner world instead of its harshest critics. Only then can we gently rewire the emotional brain, not by force, but by compassion.

6---full-notes/limiting-entry.title: Limiting entry
6---full-notes/limiting-entry.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Limiting entry
Details
Before Uber and Lyft, taxis should have been a textbook competitive market. All you need is a car, which is a low fixed cost, and cabs are close to identical. Instead, cities capped the number of cabs. Only holders of a medallion (once literally a metal medallion, now a paper permit) could legally drive one.
Gruber’s Figure 10-3 has two panels: one cab on the left, the market on the right.

Free entry. Each identical cab runs where P1 = MC = minimum AC, giving q1 rides, its most efficient amount. At P1, riders want Q1 rides in total, so the number of cabs is n1 = Q1/q1. If there were fewer cabs, the price would be higher and profits positive, and new cabs would enter. So long-run supply, S1, is flat at P1.
A cap of n2 cabs. The new supply curve, S2, is flat at P1 up to n2 × q1 rides, because until then each cab can stay at its efficient q1. Past that point, extra rides have to come from the same cabs driving more than q1 — longer hours, more tired, at less convenient times — so marginal cost rises and S2 slopes up. S2 meets demand at a higher price P2, with fewer total rides Q2.
Each cab now sets P2 = MC, gives q2 > q1 rides, and earns a profit π = (P2 − AC) × q2.































Free entryn2 medallionsConsumer surplusA + B + CAProducer surplus0B (= n2 × π)Deadweight loss—C
Producer surplus under free entry is zero because long-run competitive profit is zero (Lecture 8). The cap moves B from riders to cab owners and destroys C. Unlike the gas cap, there’s no rationing cost here: the market clears at P2, so anyone who values a ride above P2 gets one.
Is the transfer B fair? If riders are rich bankers and drivers are poor immigrants, maybe it’s a good thing; if riders are poor people getting to work, maybe not. Gruber’s twist is that it doesn’t matter, because medallions can be sold. Someone wanting to drive would pay up to π for a medallion, since owning one earns π. So drivers who buy or rent medallions are back to zero profit. Competition still drives profit to zero — not through entry, but by selling the barrier to entry. The winners are whoever was originally handed medallions when the system began, back in the 1930s. Renting one cost about 12,000 a year in San Francisco; buying one cost about 400,000 in Boston. Gruber puts the lost consumer surplus at about $2 billion.
Why have such rules at all? Some regulation makes sense: you don’t want just anyone driving strangers around, and you want doctors licensed — otherwise you get Dr. Nick, the quack from The Simpsons who trained at “Hollywood Upstairs Medical College.” This is occupational licensing: rules that check people can do the job they claim to do. But licensing should test quality. A fixed cap on the number of cabs just hands money to medallion holders.
Then came Uber. Ride-hailing effectively restored free entry, so the price fell back toward P1. Taxi and Uber drivers earn a little less than taxi drivers did, but they were never making much. Medallion values fell about 90%, because the profits they capitalized on were gone. Gruber calls medallion owners not a sympathetic crowd. The big winners are riders: total surplus and consumer surplus both rose. It’s a case of a market innovation increasing both.

6---full-notes/long-term-potentiation.title: Long-Term Potentiation
6---full-notes/long-term-potentiation.content:
Status: adult
Tags:neuroplasticity neuroscience
Long-Term Potentiation
Details
Memory is not an abstract concept but a physical change in the brain’s wiring. The formation of a long-term memory is the process of sculpting the connections, or synapses, between neurons. This principle is elegantly captured by the concept of Long-Term Potentiation (LTP). When one neuron repeatedly stimulates another, the connection between them becomes stronger and more efficient. The receiving neuron becomes more responsive, creating a more robust pathway. In essence, “neurons that fire together, wire together.”
This process is remarkably dynamic. Imaging of living brain tissue reveals that the dendritic spines—the tiny protrusions on a neuron that receive signals—are in constant motion. They are actively reaching out, exploring, and seeking connections. When a spine connects with an active axon from another neuron, that connection can stabilize and strengthen, forming the basis of a new memory trace. If it finds no active partner, the connection may wither away.
This reveals the brain to be an organ of incredible plasticity, constantly remodeling itself based on experience. It is the ultimate “use it or lose it” system. The act of learning and remembering is not just accessing a file; it is a biological process of physically reinforcing and creating pathways in a dynamic, living network. An emotional input, for example, can create a strong synapse that helps a nearby weak synapse (like one for a name) become strong itself, explaining why we more easily remember things that have an emotional charge.

6---full-notes/long-run-competition.title: Long-run competition
6---full-notes/long-run-competition.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Long-run competition
Details
Producer theory is consumer theory plus one step. The production function is like a utility function, and input prices are like the prices of pizza and cookies. But there’s no income: the firm chooses how much to produce. So instead of one tangency between an isoquant and an isocost line, there’s one for every output level. Together those trace out the supply curve, which is the marginal cost curve above the shutdown point.
We did this in Short-run competition (and perfect competition), but now the long-run competition would introduce something else: free entry and exit. Firms can come and go as they please:

They enter when profits are positive.
They exit when profits are negative.

In the long run there’s no separate shutdown decision; only the sign of profit matters. That harmless-looking assumption has a stark implication: long-run profits are zero.
Gruber’s first example is the personal computer market around 1990 (Figure 8-1), with a few firms like Dell and Gateway, all assumed identical. The left panel shows one firm, Dell. Its marginal cost slopes up. Its average cost curve is U-shaped: the fixed cost gets spread over more units, and then rising marginal costs take over. MC crosses AC at AC’s lowest point. The entry would turn out:

At the market price P1, Dell produces q1, where P1 = MC. Its profit is the rectangle π1 = (P1 − AC) × q1.
Those profits draw in new firms. With more identical firms, the market supply curve flattens, from S1 to S2.
The flatter supply curve meets demand at a lower price, P2, and a larger market quantity, Q2.
At P2, Dell cuts back to q2, and its profit shrinks to π2.

Dell’s own output falls (q2 < q1) while the market’s rises (Q2 > Q1), because there are more firms. As long as any profit remains, more firms keep entering, until profits hit zero.
The mirror case is mainframe computers (Figure 8-2). At Gruber’s 1987 MIT graduation, the speaker was Ken Olsen, an MIT alum who founded DEC, then a giant of big computers. Olsen spent the speech on how wonderful he and DEC were. Within about a decade, PCs had wiped DEC out. (Compaq bought what was left in 1998.) Gruber’s lesson for graduation speakers: don’t spend the whole speech praising yourself.
Take IBM, which had bet heavily on mainframes:

As demand for mainframes collapsed, the price P1 fell below IBM’s average cost, so it was losing money.
It still covered its average variable cost, so it was above its shutdown point and kept producing (the Lecture 7 shutdown rule).
Losses drive firms out. Exit steepens the market supply curve and raises the price.
Exit continues until the price reaches P2, where P = MC = AC and profits are zero.

The proof that every firm ends up at minimum average cost (Figure 8-3) takes three steps:

Zero profit means P = AC.
Profit maximization means P = MC.
So MC = AC, which happens only at the minimum of average cost.

You might object that profits obviously aren’t zero: Apple makes enormous amounts of money. Short-run profits are allowed, but firms like General Motors have made profits for decades. Gruber gives three reasons long-run profits can stay positive, or at least why the simple model breaks.
1. Barriers to entry. Firms don’t enter freely, and the ultimate barrier is a sunk cost. Think of becoming a doctor as an economic decision. If being a doctor weren’t profitable enough to repay about $300,000 of medical school, you wouldn’t go. And well, if profits won’t cover the cost of entry, it isn’t worth it. Profits don’t need to be enormous but it can’t be zero either.
2. Firms aren’t identical. If firms differ in their minimum average cost, the cheapest ones can profit even in the long run. Gruber’s example, from an old empirical study, is cotton (Figure 8-4). Each country is treated as having a flat marginal cost per kilogram, up to some capacity:

Pakistan: $0.71
Argentina: $1.08
Australia: $1.15
…and so on, up to the United States at $1.56

The market supply curve is a staircase. If world demand is 1 billion kilograms, Pakistan supplies it all at $0.71. Price equals marginal cost equals average cost, so profit is zero.
If demand is 5 billion kilograms, the market has to reach the US step, so the price is 1.56. Every lower-cost producer now earns the gap on each kilogram: Pakistan 1.56 − 0.71 = 0.85, Argentina 0.48, Australia 0.41, and the US $0.
3. Input prices rise with output. So far the wage has been taken as given; now it comes from a labor market (Figure 8-5).

Demand for workers slopes down. At a higher wage, firms switch toward capital and hire fewer workers; that’s the isoquant–isocost logic.
Supply of workers slopes up. At higher wages, more people want to work, and to work more. This is only an assumption for now. A later lecture shows it can even slope down, through income and substitution effects.

Here’s the chain of events:

If people want more of a good, firms need more workers, so the demand for labor shifts out.
With supply sloping up, the only way to get more workers is to pay more, so the wage rises.
A higher wage raises every firm’s marginal and average cost (MC1, AC1 to MC2, AC2, Figure 8-6).
So the zero-profit price, minimum AC, is higher.

The long-run supply curve slopes up, yet every firm still makes zero profit at its minimum AC.
The key distinction: cases 1 and 2 give positive long-run profits, while case 3 gives an upward-sloping long-run supply curve with zero profits. So an upward-sloping long-run supply curve doesn’t by itself prove anyone is making profits.
A student asked how you’d tell the cases apart. First check whether long-run profits are zero. If they are, it’s the base case or case 3; if they’re positive, it’s case 1 or 2. Then, to separate the base case from case 3, ask whether wages rise as the industry grows. To separate cases 1 and 2, ask whether there are sunk costs and entry barriers, or whether firms simply differ in cost.
Another student asked about accounting versus economic profit. Apple’s roughly $18 billion a quarter is accounting profit. Economic profit subtracts opportunity costs too, which makes it much harder to measure. Even accounting profit is slippery. Gruber says Apple reports billions to shareholders but almost nothing to tax authorities, by claiming its profits come from intellectual property held by an Irish company with two employees. That’s one reason “just tax profits” is harder than it sounds: profits are hard to define.

6---full-notes/long-run-costs.title: Long-run costs
6---full-notes/long-run-costs.content:
Status:
Tags: economics
Long-run costs
Details
Moving on to long-run costs, we would have to expand the firm’s optimization problem. In the short run, capital had always been fixed at some level of K, and the firm could only adapt to demand swings by labor (hiring or firing workers). But in the long run, capital is fully flexible. This allows an essential economic rule: long-run costs will always be at the lower bound of short-run costs, because firms have more freedom in their decisions.
Graphically, the long-run average cost curve forms the lower envelope of all possible short-run average cost curves. Imagine a firm facing three potential plant sizes, each represented by a distinct short-run average cost curve: SRAC_1for small output, SRAC_2 for intermediate output, and SRAC_3 for massive production. If the firm anticipates low output q_1, building plant size 1 is optimal. If demand surges to q_3, running that small plant requires hiring enormous amounts of labor, forcing the firm deep into diminishing marginal returns and driving costs skyward. In the long run, the firm can construct plant size 3, lowering its average cost back down to the frontier. Gruber describes the long run as a sequence of short-run games: in every period, the firm picks a plant scale, operates along that short-run cost curve, and then evaluates whether to re-optimize its capital stock for the next cycle.
Gruber ties this envelope logic directly to Elon Musk and Tesla. When Tesla began ramping up manufacturing in 2013, management had to commit to a specific battery factory capacity, planning for a projected demand of roughly 20,000 vehicles by 2017. Musk had effectively locked the firm into SRAC_1. Instead, consumer demand exploded, producing a backlog of 200,000 reservations that the existing plant could not service efficiently. Operating on the upward-sloping limb of an undersized short-run curve, Tesla incurred major production bottlenecks. To solve this, Tesla transitioned to SRAC_3 by constructing the massive Gigafactory in Nevada, capable of supplying 500,000 vehicles annually. Yet Gruber notes the lingering risk: if consumer sentiment shifts and demand contracts, Tesla will find itself stranded on the steep left tail of an oversized plant, burdened by massive capital overhead until it can re-optimize again.
To formalize this concept in mathematical terms and work to cost minimization, producer theory constructs the isocost line, the direct analogue to the consumer’s budget constraint. An isocost line depicts all combinations of labor L and capital K that generate the identical total expenditure, C = wL + rK. Solving for capital gives K = (C/r) - (w/r)L, showing that the vertical intercept is C/r and the slope is -w/r. With input prices w = \5 and r = $10, the slope is -5/10 = -1/2$. This slope captures the economic opportunity cost of factors: along any given expenditure line, hiring one additional worker requires surrendering half a unit of capital.
Similar to consumer theory, where the market allows you to exchange goods and your own marginal utility, minimizing the cost of producing any targeted output requires finding the point where the isoquant is tangent to the lowest achievable isocost line. At this tangency, the slope of the isoquant (the marginal rate of technical substitution, or MRTS) must equal the slope of the isocost line (the negative input price ratio):
MRTS = -\frac{MP_L}{MP_K} = -\frac{w}{r}
For the lecture’s production function q = \sqrt{L \cdot K}, the marginal products derived in Lecture 5 are MP_L = K / (2\sqrt{LK}) and MP_K = L / (2\sqrt{LK}). Their ratio simplifies to MRTS = -K/L. Setting this equal to the input price ratio -w/r = -1/2 yields the optimal capital-labor ratio K/L = 1/2, or L = 2K. The firm should always employ twice as many workers as machines. Intuitively, the market dictates that labor costs half as much as capital (w/r = 1/2), while technological trade-offs dictate an exchange rate of K/L; cost minimization balances the two.
This is where they diverge however, because in producer theory, we don’t have a budget constraint. So now we have to learn how do we achieve the optimal budget constraint and product amount.

6---full-notes/loss-in-bpd.title: Loss in BPD
6---full-notes/loss-in-bpd.content:
Status: teen
Tags: therapy Clinical Psychology trauma
Loss in BPD
Details
People with BPD experience lots of loss in their lives, and so that accumulated loss can cause them to act like loss has happened even if it hasn’t yet. This can further show in two ways, one is that they become hypersensitized to it, even at the first sign of loss they can already react as if it had already happened as said before, or secondly, they can be indifferent to it. This second situation is something extremely similar to those who have PTSD, they become desensitized to any and all emotions, positive or negative to protect their own mental state from being overwhelmed. (Inhibited grieving. This can also be automated, like a reflex rather than a mindful decision).
Moreover, people can also alternate between these two states, feeling extreme grief to not feeling any. This can also manifest in them displaying emotions that are different from what they are actually experiencing in order to avoid facing what will eat them up and what they think would actually destroy them.

6---full-notes/loss-of-confidence-in-tra.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Loss of confidence in trauma.md
6---full-notes/loss-of-confidence-in-tra.title: Loss of confidence in trauma
6---full-notes/loss-of-confidence-in-tra.content:
Status: adult
Tags: trauma psychology
Loss of confidence in trauma
Details
Out of all the numerous debilitating effects that trauma can have on an individual, a loss of confidence is perhaps the most profound barrier preventing recovery and progression. Confidence is not merely an abstract concept; rather, it is deeply intertwined with the individual’s capacity to trust themselves, others, and the world around them. Trauma survivors frequently experience a drastic reduction in self-assurance, manifesting as persistent fear, anxiety, and hesitancy in engaging with everyday activities. This hesitancy arises from an entrenched fear of experiencing outcomes or sensations reminiscent of the initial traumatic event.
The loss of confidence can manifest subtly at first—individuals may withdraw from social interactions, hesitate before making routine decisions, or avoid certain environments entirely. Over time, these behaviors become entrenched coping mechanisms. Consequently, what began as understandable caution transforms into paralyzing fear. Activities as mundane as traveling to a store, interacting with peers, or attending a workplace meeting suddenly become fraught with anxiety. Survivors worry that these seemingly ordinary scenarios might trigger memories or sensations similar to those associated with their trauma. This chronic anxiety and self-doubt effectively immobilize survivors, perpetuating the cycle of trauma and hindering genuine healing.
Interestingly, research has illuminated a powerful psychological component in the treatment of confidence loss among trauma survivors. In one notable study, participants suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) were administered placebos alongside a control group receiving actual pharmacological treatments. Remarkably, the placebo recipients exhibited comparable improvements in confidence levels as the group receiving genuine medication. This underscores the extraordinary power of belief and perception in trauma recovery. Simply believing that they had received a helpful intervention enabled individuals to overcome previously debilitating fears. They reported feeling more capable of confronting situations that had once seemed impossible, highlighting how psychological reassurance significantly influences recovery.
This research does not diminish the importance of genuine medical treatments; rather, it underscores how central confidence is in the recovery journey. Boosting a survivor’s sense of self-efficacy and belief in their abilities, even through non-pharmacological means, is crucial for reclaiming agency in their lives. Therapeutic methods focusing specifically on enhancing self-confidence, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), exposure therapy, or supportive counseling, can therefore serve as powerful adjuncts or even alternatives to medication.

6---full-notes/love-as-a-motivation.title: Love as a motivation
6---full-notes/love-as-a-motivation.content:
Status: teen
Tags: love psychology
Love as a motivation
Details
A more fitting classification for love is as a motivation. Similar to biological drives like thirst or hunger, love has a strong affective component and motivates an individual to perform specific actions—in this case, to get closer to, bond with, or possess the object of desire. This framework prompts the functional question: what is love for? From an evolutionary psychology perspective, the primary purpose of this motivation is to solve the problem of gene perpetuation. While the sex drive ensures reproduction, the motivational state of love encourages long-term pair-bonding. This bond creates a stable environment for the intensive and lengthy process of raising human children, thereby increasing the likelihood that one’s genes will be successfully passed to the next generation. This evolutionary goal is so fundamental that it can even be served indirectly; by being a protective aunt or uncle, one helps ensure the survival of a niece or nephew who carries a significant portion of one’s own genes.

6---full-notes/love-as-an-evolutionary-e.title: Love as an Evolutionary Exaptation
6---full-notes/love-as-an-evolutionary-e.content:
Status: teen
Tags: love biology psychology
Love as an Evolutionary Exaptation
Details
The profound feeling of adult romantic love, according to Lisa Diamond’s model, has an evolutionary origin that is both surprising and deeply logical. The neurochemical system that creates pair-bonds between partners did not originally evolve for the purpose of mating. Instead, it is a remarkable example of an exaptation: a biological feature that evolved for one purpose and was later co-opted for an entirely new function.
The original function of this attachment system was to ensure the survival of helpless mammalian infants. Nature forged a powerful, neurochemically-driven system to create an unbreakable bond between an infant and its caregiver. This bond, characterized by a desire for proximity, distress upon separation, and feelings of profound comfort and security, is mediated by hormones like oxytocin and vasopressin. It is a fundamental mechanism for survival.
Later in our evolutionary history, this same ancient system was repurposed to also create long-term bonds between adult reproductive partners. This new function was highly advantageous, as it encouraged parents to remain together to collaborate in the difficult, long-term project of raising their vulnerable offspring. The love you feel for a romantic partner is, in essence, running on the same neurochemical hardware that first evolved to bond you to a parent, a testament to nature’s ability to adapt existing tools for new and complex purposes.

6---full-notes/love-vs-lust-systems.title: Love vs Lust systems
6---full-notes/love-vs-lust-systems.content:
Status: teen
Tags: love psychology biology
Love vs Lust systems
Details
In our common understanding of intimacy, romantic love and sexual desire are often treated as a single, unified experience. However, the influential framework proposed by psychologist Lisa M. Diamond argues for a crucial distinction: love and lust are governed by two functionally independent biobehavioral systems, each with its own unique evolutionary purpose and neurochemical foundation.
The first, the sexual desire system, is the more straightforward of the two. Mediated primarily by gonadal hormones such as estrogens and androgens, its evolutionary function is to create a powerful drive to seek out sexual partners and engage in reproductive acts. This is the system of lust.
The second, far more intricate system is that of romantic love, or attachment. This system is not driven by sex hormones but by neuropeptides like oxytocin and vasopressin, which act upon the brain’s fundamental reward circuitry. Its function is to forge a powerful emotional bond, creating feelings of infatuation, security, and lasting comfort with a specific partner. The functional independence of these systems is evident throughout human experience; it is what allows for the existence of deep, “platonic” love devoid of desire, and for casual sexual encounters devoid of romantic attachment. Recognizing that these two systems can and do operate separately is the first step to understanding the full spectrum of human connection.

6---full-notes/low-dopamine,-self-medica.title: Low Dopamine, Self-Medication, and Stimulants
6---full-notes/low-dopamine,-self-medica.content:
Status: teen
Tags: pharmacology ADHD biology
Low Dopamine, Self-Medication, and Stimulants
Details
The leading theory for ADHD, the “low dopamine hypothesis,” posits that the core symptoms arise because key brain circuits have insufficient levels of the neuromodulator dopamine. This chemical deficit creates “noisy” neural signaling, preventing the brain from properly coordinating its focus networks. This theory powerfully explains the common, and often unconscious, tendency for individuals with ADHD to self-medicate with substances that boost dopamine. The craving for sugary foods, the heavy consumption of caffeine, or even the use of illicit drugs like cocaine and amphetamine can be seen as the brain’s attempt to correct its own chemical imbalance and achieve a state of focus and calm.
This brings us to the paradox of treating a hyperactivity disorder with stimulant medications like Ritalin and Adderall. These drugs are effective precisely because they address this underlying dopamine deficit. By increasing the amount of available dopamine in the brain, they effectively “turn up the volume” on the weak signals that are supposed to regulate attention. For a person with ADHD, this influx of dopamine doesn’t cause more hyperactivity; instead, it provides the necessary chemical tool for the brain to organize itself. It allows the “conductor” (dopamine) to properly manage the brain’s networks, suppressing distracting internal chatter and enabling sustained focus on external tasks. This is why a substance that would make a neurotypical person feel jittery can make a person with ADHD feel centered and in control.

6---full-notes/low-self-esteem.title: Low self-esteem
6---full-notes/low-self-esteem.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Low self-esteem
Details
When the depressed patient reflects on adverse events (such as a separation, rejection, defeat), he usually ponders over what does it all say about himself. And more than often does he come to the conclusion that it is a heinous defect in himself. The deserted husband concludes, “I have lost her because I am unlovable.” This conclusion, of course, is only one of a number of possible explanations, such as basic incompatibility of their personalities, the wife’s own problems, or her desire for an adventure related more to thrill-seeking than to a change in her feelings for her husband.
This leads to a chasm being created in his personal domain, he suffers not only the loss but he finds out about a deficiency in himself. And of course, he would exaggerate this all. This becomes so imperative that it infiltrates every thought he has about himself, then it takes over his self-image, and then he could only describe and talk about himself of his “bad” traits. He would merely flow over his achievements and abilities, which means he will discount or gloss over the attributes he once highly valued.
Moreover, the tendency of comparing one self to others may lower the self-esteem even further.
The harshness and inappropriateness of self-reproaches in depression have either been ignored by writers or have stimulated very abstract speculations. Freud postulated that the bereaved patient has a pool of unconscious hostility toward the deceased loved object. Since he cannot allow himself to experience this hostility, the patient directs the anger toward himself and accuses himself of faults that actually are characteristics of the loved object. The concept of inverted rage has remained firmly entrenched in many theories of depression. The convoluted pathway proposed by Freud is so removed from information obtained from patients that it is difficult to test it.
