6---full-notes/mdma-(ecstasy)-in-ptsd.title: MDMA (ecstasy) in PTSD
6---full-notes/mdma-(ecstasy)-in-ptsd.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology trauma pharmacology
MDMA (ecstasy) in PTSD
Details
It is a controlled substance, classified in 1985 after being used as a recreational drug for some time. Like Prozac and other psychotropic agents, it is unknown how it truly works but it is known to increase concentrations in oxytocin, vasopressin, cortisol, and prolactin.
It increases people’s awareness of themselves as well, which is critical in treating PTSD, and those who take this drug usually report overall a better state of mind, more energy and so on. Moreover, Mithoefer and his colleagues also found that it decreases fear, defensiveness, and numbing, as well as help access the inner world. This helps patients stay in their window of tolerance for them to revisit their traumatic memories without becoming overwhelmed.
Nonetheless, psychedelic substances are powerful agents with high-risk side effects. It is highly warned to use them carefully to avoid worsening the conditions of patients.

6---full-notes/mmh-as-an-unwarranted-and.title: MMH as an Unwarranted and Unmotivated Commitment
6---full-notes/mmh-as-an-unwarranted-and.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Massive Modularity Hypothesis Evolutionary Psychology Cognitive Psychology
MMH as an Unwarranted and Unmotivated Commitment
Details
The commitment to the Massive Modularity Hypothesis (MMH) by many evolutionary psychologists is, at present, both unwarranted by the arguments and unmotivated by the needs of the research program [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].
The primary arguments for MMH, such as the optimality and solvability arguments, fail to provide a compelling reason to prefer a massively modular architecture over a competing model like the Library Model of Cognition (LMC). These arguments successfully demonstrate the need for innate, domain-specific cognitive structure, but they do not successfully argue that this structure must take the form of computational mechanisms rather than representational bodies of knowledge [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].
Furthermore, the existing empirical evidence, particularly for central cognition, is unable to distinguish between the two hypotheses. Plausible explanations for the same data can be generated from both frameworks, resulting in an empirical stalemate [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].
Finally, the rejection of LMC is unmotivated because the model is fully compatible with the core tenets of evolutionary psychology. An evolutionary approach to the mind requires a commitment to innate, evolved, adaptive specializations, but it does not require that these specializations be modules in the sense advocated by MMH [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf]. Therefore, if the case for massive modularity is to be made, it cannot rest on general, a priori evolutionary arguments. It will depend on the “successive accumulation of specific, empirical evidence for the existence of particular modules”—a project that is still in its infancy [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].

6---full-notes/magnetic-resonance-imagin.content:
Status: baby

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) in Brain Research
Details

Methodology: Uses magnetic fields and radio waves to align and detect hydrogen protons in brain tissue (e.g., water-rich areas). Protons realign after radio bursts, emitting signals that map tissue locations and types. Produces static images of brain structures.
Advantages: Excellent spatial resolution. Distinguishes tissue types based on proton alignment speeds.
Disadvantages: Patient discomfort (must lie still for long periods). Shows only static structures, no brain activity.

Supporting Content
In PTSD, people are put in MRIs and then asked to think about their traumatic event to see the neurobiological information.

Magnetoencephalography (MEG) in Brain Research
Details

Methodology: Records magnetic fields generated by brain activity (e.g., from ionic currents and synaptic transmission in neurons). Uses non-invasive scans to detect communication between brain areas by tracing waves of activity from origin to processing regions. Involves expensive machinery similar to PET.
Advantages: Excellent temporal resolution for tracking rapid brain activity. Non-invasive. Detects inter-area communication effectively.
Disadvantages: Poor spatial resolution. Very expensive equipment.

6---full-notes/major-updates-from-dsm-iv.title: Major Updates from DSM-IV to DSM-5
6---full-notes/major-updates-from-dsm-iv.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychopathology Clinical Psychology
Major Updates from DSM-IV to DSM-5
Details
The publication of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5) in 2013 represented one of the most significant revisions in the history of psychiatric classification. Moving away from the structure of its predecessor, the DSM-IV-TR, the DSM-5 introduced fundamental changes in its organizational framework, diagnostic criteria, and overall philosophical approach to mental health.
1. Elimination of the Multiaxial System
The most substantial structural change was the removal of the multiaxial diagnostic system. The DSM-IV used a five-axis system to provide a comprehensive picture of a client’s functioning. The DSM-5 integrated these axes into a single, nonaxial format. Axis I, II, and III disorders were combined into one list, called the clinical factors, with separate notations for psychosocial and contextual factors (formerly Axis IV). The GAF score (Axis V), which was criticized for its subjectivity and lack of reliability, was replaced by the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS) as a more standardized measure of disability. This change was intended to simplify the diagnostic process and remove the artificial distinction between different categories of disorders.
2. A Shift Towards a Dimensional and Developmental Approach
The DSM-5 made a concerted effort to move towards a more dimensional understanding of psychopathology, acknowledging that many disorders exist on a spectrum rather than as discrete, categorical entities.


Spectrum Disorders: This is most evident in the creation of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), which combined previous diagnoses like Autistic Disorder, Asperger’s Disorder, and Pervasive Developmental Disorder Not Otherwise Specified (PDD-NOS) into a single continuum.


Severity Specifiers: Many diagnoses now include specifiers for severity (e.g., mild, moderate, severe), allowing clinicians to capture the intensity of a patient’s symptoms more accurately.


Lifespan Perspective: The chapters in the DSM-5 were reorganized to follow a developmental lifespan approach. Disorders are now arranged chronologically, beginning with those typically diagnosed in childhood (e.g., Neurodevelopmental Disorders) and ending with those more common in older adulthood (e.g., Neurocognitive Disorders).


3. Key Changes to Disorder Categories
Numerous specific disorder categories were restructured, added, or removed:


Anxiety Disorders: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) were removed from the Anxiety Disorders chapter and placed into their own new chapters (“Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders” and “Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders,” respectively). This reflects the understanding that while anxiety is a core feature, these conditions have distinct neurobiological and psychological underpinnings.


Mood Disorders: The chapter on Mood Disorders was split into two separate chapters: “Bipolar and Related Disorders” and “Depressive Disorders.” This was done to highlight the significant differences between these two groups of conditions. Bereavement is no longer an exclusion criterion for a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder, acknowledging that grief can sometimes precipitate a major depressive episode.


Schizophrenia Spectrum: The classic subtypes of schizophrenia (e.g., paranoid, disorganized, catatonic) were eliminated due to their limited diagnostic stability and validity. Instead, the focus shifted to rating the severity of core “positive” and “negative” symptoms.


New Disorders: Several new disorders were introduced, including Hoarding Disorder, Binge Eating Disorder, and Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD), the last of which was added to address concerns about the overdiagnosis of bipolar disorder in children.


In conclusion, the update from DSM-IV to DSM-5 was not merely a revision but a reconceptualization of mental illness. By eliminating the multiaxial system, embracing a dimensional and developmental framework, and restructuring key disorder categories, the DSM-5 aimed to create a more clinically useful, flexible, and scientifically grounded guide for the diagnosis of psychopathology.

6---full-notes/manage-afternoon-dips-wit.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sleep neuroscience
Manage Afternoon Dips with naps and such
Details
Most people experience a natural dip in energy and alertness in the afternoon, often tied to the circadian rhythm of body temperature. To manage this, one can use traditional napping or protocols like Non-Sleep Deep Rest (NSDR), which are designed to induce states of deep relaxation without necessarily causing sleep.
Napping is a valid recovery strategy, but its effectiveness depends on timing and duration. To avoid disrupting nighttime sleep, naps should be kept under 90 minutes and not be taken too late in the day. It’s crucial to note that napping is not a requirement for optimal performance.
For individuals who wake up groggy from naps or prefer a non-sleep alternative, NSDR is a highly effective tool. This category includes several practices:


Yoga Nidra & NSDR Scripts: These are typically zero-cost, guided audio meditations found on platforms like YouTube. They systematically guide the body and mind into a state of profound rest, which can replenish energy in 10-30 minutes.


Self-Hypnosis Apps (e.g., Reveri): Specific, science-backed applications have been developed to facilitate deep relaxation and improve sleep. The Reveri app, for instance, was developed based on Stanford research and uses self-hypnosis scripts to help users fall asleep, return to sleep if awakened, and generally improve sleep quality. While these tools often carry a cost, they provide structured, goal-directed protocols.


The key advantage of NSDR-based tools is that they help replenish mental and physical energy without the risk of sleep inertia (grogginess). Furthermore, consistent practice can improve one’s overall ability to control their state of relaxation, effectively training the brain for better sleep.

When reviewing homework, the strategy is to validate the progress of practicing skills correctly and effectively and to then problem-solve when it is not done or not practiced correctly, and/or problems in using the skills are identified. Even for those who try their best to learn and collect these skills, they can still encounter the same problems. Thus it is important to not eliminate review time in favor of any other thing.

To understand these problems, it requires the person to highlight and define problems in using the skills, highlighting patterns and implications of current skills use, and developing hypotheses about factors interfering with effective use of the skills. The second stage, then, is to target change, providing feedback on correct implementation of skills when needed; and encouraging efforts to practice the skills by providing the rationale and such for the skills.

6---full-notes/marginal-rate-of-substitu.title: Marginal Rate of Substitution
6---full-notes/marginal-rate-of-substitu.content:
Status: teen
Tags:  economics
Marginal Rate of Substitution
Details
This is the MRS, basically the algebraic equivalent of marginal utility, where we can calculate the rate at which a consumer is willing to trade his good for another while remaining on the same indifference curve.  In the lecture’s setup, it is the rate at which the consumer is willing to give up the good on the y-axis, pizza slices, for the good on the x-axis, cookies. Even if no literal barter is happening, the idea still applies because of opportunity cost. If the consumer has a limited budget, spending money on pizza means not spending that same money on cookies, and vice versa. A purchase is therefore an implicit substitution. The MRS captures the consumer’s subjective willingness to make that substitution.
Mathematically, the slope of the indifference curve will give the MRS. If the consumer gives up a little pizza, they lose utility to the marginal utility of pizza. Accordingly, the same applies for them gaining cookies. And so these changes offset each other and stay on the curve.

6---full-notes/marginal-utility.title: Marginal Utility
6---full-notes/marginal-utility.content:
Status: teen
Tags: economics
Marginal Utility
Details
Truly taking in how most situations actually function, we can come to the assumption that additional units of good increase utility will have diminishing returns. We can then assume that yes it is true that a consumer would prefer more cookies to fewer cookies while also acknowledging that they will become less satisfying as we purchase more.
Gruber illustrates this by holding pizza slices constant and asking what happens to utility as the number of cookies rises. The first cookie adds a lot of utility. The second adds less than the first. The third adds less than the second, and so on. This pattern is not a universal law of human psychology, but it captures a very common structure of consumption. A starving person values the first portion of food intensely. A person who has already eaten several portions still might enjoy more, but the additional unit is much
less important. This is why diminishing marginal utility feels common-sensical: abundance reduces the urgency and value of the next unit.
Of course we have to also consider the implication of other factors like if it fits or not. If one has an abundant of pizzas and no cookies, adding another pizza may result in practically nothing more for their satisfaction at all. This all then relates back to opportunity costs.

Mario Odyssey
Details
Mario is one of the most influential and greatest game series of all time, created by probably the greatest gaming studio of all time - Nintendo. Though in recent years, Nintendo has been on a downhill trend with the corporate decisions that they have been making and the fact that their gaming studio hasn’t been dropping revolutionary games (bangers) like how they did in the 1980s throughout the 2010s, but they are still occasionally dropping complete masterpieces, that’s undeniable.
And with that introduction out of the way, I want to discuss about Mario Odyssey, just Mario Odyssey, not any other Mario games that it is usually compared with like Galaxy or Sunshine. This game means a lot to me, it was the first game I ever played from Nintendo, and basically was what got me to become a Nintendo fanboy. People usually discuss lots about the gameplay, the art direction, less about the story as the story is never the main focus of a Mario game. Though I want to give my two cents on the matter, I believe that it is much more efficient to talk about the other aspects of the game is lesser… discussed about. In particular, I want to talk about the music and story/moments of the game.
The mechanics and gameplay of Odyssey is already talked to death about how revolutionary it was as a 3D game, with how much they focused on the open-world aspect of the platformer, similar to how Mario 64 was for me. The level design was immaculate and puzzles were fun. Main criticism was of course how imbalanced finding Moons were, some were the easiest thing ever, others took hours. For me, of course I remembered the Moons that were just god damn pecking into holes or ground pounding, but the thing is, I was never particularly focused on how I got the Moons, of course the feeling and dopamine you get from completing a hard ass puzzle to get a Moon FEELS better than if you just found it randomly but I never had that problem. Every Moon had SOME work to get there, either it was smart or skillful, I genuinely cannot remember a moment from the game that there wasn’t some clue or hidden aspect to any Moon at all. That being said, for certain people, of course this criticism is justified (not in my books but that’s fine).
For Galaxy, I didn’t play it when Galaxy came out, and of course I’m not gonna understand what it meant to people and for Mario at the time, but from what I’ve seen and experienced, it was fire, the mechanics seemed nice, gravity and interactions with the environment, I love it. For Odyssey however, I felt like the interactions WERE the game, it was all about how you interacted with the entities around you and how that would affect and played differently from just Mario. Odyssey still had sections that I felt resembled Galaxy whilst building on that with even greater mechanics.
The soundtrack, now I’m not gonna derail further to talk about Mario Galaxy soundtrack and how it compares to Odyssey because I have heard both… and fuck it I cannot pick one over the other. But that is a topic for another day, for Odyssey man, a lot of the times the music is very much just in the background of whatever level you’re at, blending into the atmosphere and immersing you more into the game. But at times, when it makes itself known and makes it so that you HAVE to acknowledge it, oh does it do that effectively. I still, with all my heart, remember Pauline’s performance to commemorate and celebrate Mario as the savior of the city. That, I mean, the festival and “Jump Up Super Star” ? It made you feel so fucking hyped, you WERE THE SAVIOR, YOU WERE THE SUPER STAR, AND YOU’RE HER SUPERSTAR, together with the gameplay during that section, oh my goddddd, it was the core memory I have of that game. It was not only groovy but memorable, it showed itself, and dedicated itself to the player, to Mario. I normally do not go out of my way to search music and listen to it on repeat or on my way to work or doing stuff or whatever (except Minecraft music), but this is the SINGULAR song I play whilst doing all kinds of stuff. There is just so much stuff to talk about the music of this section and how it corresponded to all kinds of emotions and thoughts of the player whilst enjoying it (of course ignoring the inaccuracies and illogicalness).
Finishing with one of the two parts I wanted to discuss, moving onto the next is the story. The story and emotional connection that one may develop with Cappy, the other half of the game. I genuinely wondered how people did not discuss much about the relationship and bond they have with him along the way. Cappy is whatever he is, he is Mario’s companion, who is working with him to save his sister, or girlfriend, or whatever. Alongside the journey, you and Cappy does so many stuff with each other, so much work, so much efforts, and as a player, I genuinely developed a bond with Cappy and with the game. And so when the game neared its end, when I was collecting every single Moons possible so that I can go ahead and 100% the game, I felt so sad, so so damn sad because of the fact that this adventure, this game that made me so happy was about to end. I deadass cried over the ending when Mario and Cappy captured their last Moon… It was just so emotional and I was just so attached with the game. No other games have made me ever felt like this, and I had my fair share of experience, with Zelda: Breath of The Wild, Minecraft, and many more that I will not try to name, but no game has made me cried like Odyssey has. Maybe throughout the game, people don’t mention, don’t care about the relationships and all with the other characters perhaps, but this meant something to me, so much.
Now, to prevent this from becoming repetitive, moving on from this topic, yes I tricked you all, I have something new to talk about. Though having not played the new Donkey Kong game, I do know that it is allegedly made by the same studio that made Super Mario Odyssey. This does not change anything for me as I have completely changed my views on Nintendo due to the recent monopolies that the corporation has done. I love the studio, the games they make, but I hate the corporation. They have the talent of indie game studios like Team Cherry and the funding of AAA corporations, which is a perfect combination, allowing them to make so many revolutionary games. Though I hope they can disconnect themselves from the evil, greedy corporation, it is quite impossible because of how connected and how tied they are to said corporations. Even if they leave, they cannot just make Mario games due to how copyright and patent works as well as how Nintendo is not just going to let that happen. Personally, I do not think that it stops the creativity and love for games that these developers can create since the freedom that Nintendo probably gives them. I am not against them chasing the bag, people have families, hobbies, and lives to manage, though I do hope that if they do have the chance, they would choose game over the other (basically hoping that Nintendo becomes a shit corporation and puts too many restrictions to the studio and makes them leave).

6---full-notes/market-power-and-the-mark.title: Market power and the markup rule
6---full-notes/market-power-and-the-mark.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Market power and the markup rule
Details
Take MR = P + (dP/dQ) × Q and pull out P:
MR = P × (1 + (dP/dQ) × (Q/P)) = P × (1 + 1/ε)
where ε is the price elasticity of demand (a negative number). Setting MR = MC and rearranging gives
(P − MC)/P = −1/ε
The left side is the markup: how far price sits above marginal cost, as a share of the price. (Economists call it the Lerner index.) It depends only on the elasticity of demand:

With perfectly elastic demand (ε = −∞), MR = P and the markup is zero. The monopolist behaves exactly like a competitive firm.
The less elastic demand is, the bigger the markup.

In the example, at Q = 6 and P = 18, ε = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q) = −1 × 18/6 = −3. The markup is (18 − 12)/18 = ⅓, which is exactly −1/ε.
So why can’t a monopolist charge whatever it likes? Buyers can’t switch to another firm, but they can switch to another good. A competitive firm is disciplined by rival firms; a monopolist is disciplined only by the elasticity of demand. The only maker of spearmint gum can’t charge much if people are happy with peppermint. The only maker of insulin can charge a lot.
Gruber’s example: on Amazon, Huckleberry Finn costs about 4 in paperback and nothing on Kindle, while _Fahrenheit 451_ costs about 9 either way. Both are old high-school staples, and their costs can’t differ much. The difference is copyright. Mark Twain’s book is out of copyright, so anyone can publish it and competition pushes the price down to cost. Fahrenheit 451’s copyright still gives its publisher a monopoly. Even so, it can’t charge $100, because schools could assign a different book. Its demand is less elastic than Huck Finn’s, not perfectly inelastic.
One more consequence (not in the lecture): a monopolist always prices where demand is elastic, with |ε| > 1. If |ε| were below 1, then 1 + 1/ε would be negative and so would MR. Cutting output would then raise revenue and lower costs at once, so that couldn’t be the profit-maximizing point.
Welfare. The competitive outcome is where price equals marginal cost: 24 − Q = 2Q, so 8 units at 16. The monopoly sells 6 units at 18. Gruber’s Figure 11-5 areas:

























Competition (8 units at 16)Monopoly (6 units at 18)Consumer surplusA + B + CAProducer surplusD + EB + DDeadweight loss—C + E
B moves from consumers to the monopolist, which is a transfer. C + E simply disappears.
This is the course’s first market failure. Until now, deadweight loss came only from government interfering; left alone, a competitive market reached the efficient outcome. Here the market is left alone and still falls short. The monopolist’s private incentive (don’t cut the price) diverges from society’s (sell every unit worth more than it costs). That doesn’t yet show government can fix it; that’s Lecture 12.

Status: adult

Marx’s Dialectic of Power and Alienation
Details
At the core of Marx’s theory, there is a profound dialectical contradiction: as human history progresses, humankind becomes stronger, while the individual human being become progressively more powerless. This is the central idea, and tragedy of his model.
We can easily see this from examples of the feudalism to the capitalism society. The feudalism was constraint, we as humans function in our own countries, we were basically just locked, chained down by our connections, our relationships with our family, our language, nationality. But in capitalism, by cooperating, we have built marvelous things, invented numerous generational inventions all because of capitalism.
But on the other side, other problems arise, the alienation of the individual human, we do not have a choice for labor anymore, and that choice is not enforced by some knight or some government, instead, it is enforced by death. If we do not work, we will die, and our family does not have to help us legally, its just out a sense of pity, of moralities, perhaps. And our tasks at times are meaningless, repetitive, not worth our effort. We get manipulated, used, everybody tries to find loopholes to abuse their workers.
Thus, every advance in the power of humankind has been achieved through the increasing oppression and alienation of individual human beings. This growing tension between our collective strength and our individual powerlessness is the contradiction that Marx believed would ultimately lead to revolution.
Supporting Content
Moreover, Marx also argues that this integration of the human being into society and the group takes away their ability to produce the conditions of their own social life over time and takes away their ability for self-realization.

Master Morality
Details
Nietzsche further extends his philosophical ideas to apply to his times. He believed that, alike Problem of Vitality and Decadence, the masters of the slaves are inherently healthy and vital people because they have self-affirmation. He believed that them comparing themselves to the slaves causes them to look inward and says, “I am powerful, I am beautiful, I am happy, I am beloved of the gods; therefore, I am Good.” This is basically an auto-valuation of their own vitality, they seize the right to define reality based on their own experience.
In contrast to this are the slaves, who doesn’t have any of the aforementioned power, and so in this system, they are viewed with a “Pathos of Distance.” This basically entails that people are at different hierarchical positions in the chain of power and so when looking at each other, or from the top down, the master would obviously feel a sense of superiority over the slaves and dismiss them as “Bad” (schlecht) which would equate to being a “loser” in today’s terms. It indicates that the slave failed to thrive and such, but not that they ought to be a master. The Master acknowledges this difference and feel no guilt or resentment towards those below him, as long as they stay that way.
Furthermore, Nietzsche compares this to the power of the priests and warriors at the time. Originally, these roles might overlap, but as society differentiates, a specific group becomes dedicated to ritual purity. Nietzsche cites the Roman example of the Flamen Dialis, the high priest of Jupiter, who was surrounded by extreme taboos: he could not touch the ground, he could not see a corpse, he could not touch iron.
And so this difference in how the two attribute power creates a sever psychological problem for the Priests. Nietzsche believes that because of their physical “Impotence” their Will to Power turns inward, causing them to become distinctively “evil” in a new sense, making them resent the warriors. This would then make them side with the slaves to overthrow everyone else.

6---full-notes/mastery-over-knowledge.title: Mastery over Knowledge
6---full-notes/mastery-over-knowledge.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning  neurology
Mastery over Knowledge
Details
The subjective experience of remembering is not a single, unified process. As cognitive science has robustly demonstrated, what we feel as “memory” is actually the product of two distinct and separable neural systems working in concert: recollection and familiarity. This dual-process model provides a powerful scientific framework for understanding the difference between deep mastery and shallow recognition. It moves the concept from a mere feeling to a biological reality, rooted in different brain regions and functions.
Familiarity is a fast, intuitive, and more global sense of knowing. It’s the feeling that a face, a name, or a fact has been encountered before, without the retrieval of any specific context. In the brain, this process is thought to be supported by the cortical regions surrounding the hippocampus, such as the perirhinal cortex. It operates like a signal detection system, assessing the “memory strength” of a stimulus. This is the biological basis for the “illusion of fluency”; passive re-reading strengthens this familiarity signal, making material feel known even when it hasn’t been truly learned.
Recollection, on the other hand, is the slower, more effortful process that defines true mastery. It is the conscious retrieval of qualitative, contextual details about a specific event—remembering where you learned a fact, who you were with, or the specific thoughts you had at the time. This is a threshold process, meaning it either happens or it doesn’t; you either retrieve the specific details or you fail to. This more demanding form of memory is critically dependent on the hippocampus, a brain structure essential for binding together the arbitrary elements of an event into a cohesive episodic memory. When we engage in active recall or retrieval practice, we are specifically training this hippocampal, recollection-based system, forging the strong, context-rich memories that constitute genuine understanding.

6---full-notes/mathematics-and-the-pure-.content:

Mathematics and the Pure Intuitions of Space and Time
Details
Kant argues that math itself is also dependent on synthetic propositions: alike how arithmetic additions, subtractions, so on and so forth presupposes an existent of time so that the calculations can actually happen and change: the same also applies for geometry, which depends on space.
Kant illustrates this with the story of Thales (or whoever first demonstrated the properties of the isosceles triangle). The discoverer did not simply meditate on a figure in front of his eyes or in his mind. He constructed the properties through a positive act — producing them “in accordance with his own concept.” He attributed to the object only those properties that necessarily followed from what he himself had placed in the object conceptually. This is the model of mathematical knowledge for Kant: the mind constructs the object according to its own rational resources, and then discovers necessary truths about it — truths that are both synthetic (genuinely informative) and a priori (knowable independently of particular experience).

Measuring Relationships
Details
Something as abstract as relationships is objectively difficult to measure. After all it is a concept, and to measure it, we would need to operationalize (finding variables that we can measure the “relationship” that reliably predicts it). And the answer here is interdependence: the ability between two people to affect each other’s situations.
The definition is embarrassingly overinclusive on purpose. Lecturer and class are interdependent. Students competing for parking spaces are. Through global warming, you and a stranger in Australia are. The move here is that once everything is on one continuum, narrowing can be done by specifying coordinates rather than by fiat.
The coordinates we are talking about will come from Kelley and colleagues — five dimensions along which interdependence varies: frequency of contact; duration, meaning how long a given level of contact persists; diversity of the interactions shared; direction of influence, from unidirectional (my relationship with a film star) to fully mutual; and strength of influence. Any relationship in the world is a point in that five-dimensional space.

6---full-notes/mechanics-of-cognitive-re.title: Mechanics of Cognitive Reorganization
6---full-notes/mechanics-of-cognitive-re.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology CBT therapy
Mechanics of Cognitive Reorganization
Details
As we have talked about, in depression the patient may act on a “closed system.” A system where they reject any and all information that contradicts what they believe is true currently. And so we just question these assumptions, which consists of: eliciting the patient’s reasons for believing the depressogenic assumption, and then marshaling the evidence in favor of or contradictory to the assumption, as if an argument, to help them find the truth.
Another important approach to testing these beliefs is through empirical demonstration. It is possible for us and the patient, as collaborators, to set up an experimental situation in which our assumptions can be tested and an answer can be obtained. Beck has carried out analog studies of this procedure with particular tasks and even has a clinical derivation of these experimental paradigms, to name is the Graded Task Assignment. Success improved the performance of the depressed group, and failure improved the nondepressed group (Loeb et al., 1971).
Further in his experiments, the patient was seen to react positively to tangible evidence of his superior performance, which can further provide clues for cognitive restructuring. Furthermore, to see the patient overgeneralize their own successes will mean that their cognitive distortions are malleable.

6---full-notes/mechanisms-of-cognitive-d.title: Mechanisms of Cognitive Dissonance
6---full-notes/mechanisms-of-cognitive-d.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Mechanisms of Cognitive Dissonance
Details
Festinger proposed a specific chain of events inside the “black box” of dissonance reduction. Firstly, the conflict between two cognitions triggers physiological arousal, which includes your autonomic nervous system activating. Second, you become consciously aware of this discomfort. Thirdly, you start attributing that discomfort to the cognitive conflict and then lastly you change your attitude to eliminate the inconsistency and discomfort.
Zanna and Cooper tested this model with a placebo study. Before going through a counter-attitudinal essay paradigm, subjects received one of three pills, all of which were placebos. One group was told that it was a pill that would make them aroused, another that it was relaxed and a control group which received none.
The no-pill group showed standard dissonance effects. The Relaxin group showed amplified effects — they expected to feel calm, found themselves aroused instead, and concluded the conflict must be even more intense than usual, warranting greater attitude change. But the arousal-pill group showed no attitude change at all. When they noticed their physiological arousal, they had a ready explanation: “That’s just the pill.” With the arousal attributed to a pharmacological source rather than a psychological conflict, there was no motivation to change attitudes.
This study effectively proves the attribution step inclusion, as it does not just require conflicting cognitions but also the person connecting their discomfort to the conflict.

6---full-notes/medications-in-ptsd.title: Medications in PTSD
6---full-notes/medications-in-ptsd.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology trauma pharmacology
Medications in PTSD
Details
Drugs are usually used to deal with traumatic stress, but replacement for those when they can’t legally obtain drugs like gin, vodka and such are much more popular. It makes sense, people are desperate to get anything to feel calmer and more in control.
The thing is, these cannot “cure” trauma; they can only dampen the expressions of a disturbed physiology. They do not teach patients how do deal with the effects that trauma has the body and the mind. They can help to control feelings and behavior, but at a price, they work by blocking the chemical systems that regulate engagement, motivation, pain, and pleasure.
Practically every group of medications have been used to treat some aspect of PTSD.
SSRIs are the one that have been studied the most, they make feelings less intense and life more manageable. But some report that it blunts them, that they feel like they’re “losing their edge”. If one SSRI does not work, it is advised to try another as they normally have different effects. Van der Kolk has experimented with this in comparison with EMDR, the result turned out that EMDR was more effective than the SSRIs.
Continuing with the theme, medicines that target the autonomic nervous system, can help decrease hyperarousal and reactivity to stress. This family of drugs helps block the physical effects of adrenaline, the fuel of arousal, and thus reduces nightmares, insomnia, and reactivity to trauma triggers.
Next up, tranquilizing drugs, benzodiazepines. They work like alcohol somewhat, in which they make people feel calm and keeps them from worrying. But also, they work like alcohol in the negative sense, making people less careful, say more hateful things even to their love ones. It’s generally ill advised to prescribe these drugs, as they have high addiction potential and interfere with trauma processing. Patients who use the drugs also report to have withdrawal reactions after stop using them.
Lastly, anticonvulsants and mood stabilizers, can have mildly positive effects, taking the edge off hyperarousal and panic. The most controversial medications are the second-generation antipsychotic agents. These can calm down combat veterans and women with PTSD related to childhood abuse. It is important to keep in mind that these medications block the dopamine system, so no pleasure, motivation. But moreover, these antipsychotic medications can dampen the emotional brain, which may interfere with being able to appreciate subtle signals of pleasure, danger, or satisfaction.

6---full-notes/method-of-emdr.title: Method of EMDR
6---full-notes/method-of-emdr.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology trauma
EMDR
Details
Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy involves a structured, eight-phase process aimed at helping clients process traumatic memories and reduce emotional distress.
Phase 1: History-Taking and Treatment Planning
In the initial phase, therapists collect comprehensive histories, assess client readiness, and develop personalized treatment plans. Therapist and client collaboratively identify potential targets for EMDR processing, such as distressing memories, current triggers, and related past incidents. Emphasis is placed on building necessary skills and behaviors to manage future emotional challenges.
Phase 2: Preparation and Stress Reduction Techniques
Before initiating deep trauma processing, therapists ensure clients have adequate coping mechanisms to manage emotional distress. Clients learn imagery and stress-reduction techniques, ensuring they maintain emotional equilibrium during and between sessions. EMDR aims for rapid, effective change while minimizing emotional disruption.
Phases 3-6: Target Identification and Reprocessing
These phases form the core EMDR processing sequence:


Target Identification: Client identifies a vivid visual image associated with a traumatic memory, a negative belief about themselves, and associated emotions and physical sensations. A positive belief is also chosen as a goal to replace negative associations.


Reprocessing: The therapist facilitates sets of bilateral stimulation (e.g., eye movements, auditory tones, tactile tapping) while the client focuses on the traumatic memory, negative belief, and physical sensations. The client is instructed to notice spontaneously emerging thoughts, feelings, or sensations after each set. This iterative approach continues until distress decreases significantly.


Positive Cognition Integration: Once the distress related to the target memory diminishes, clients revisit the previously identified positive belief, modifying it if necessary, reinforcing it during subsequent processing.


Therapists employ established interventions to manage distress, keeping clients effectively progressing through trauma reprocessing.
Phase 7: Closure
At session closure, therapists assign clients to maintain logs during the week, documenting emerging thoughts or related experiences. This log reinforces self-calming skills learned earlier, supporting emotional self-regulation outside therapy sessions.
Phase 8: Reevaluation
Subsequent sessions begin with reevaluation, assessing progress made and adjusting future interventions accordingly. EMDR systematically processes historical traumas, current distressing incidents, and anticipates future scenarios requiring new emotional responses and coping strategies.
EMDR’s structured phases guide clients safely and effectively from traumatic emotional intensity to resilient emotional self-management.

6---full-notes/methodological-breakthrou.title: Methodological Breakthrough of Stratification
6---full-notes/methodological-breakthrou.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology
Methodological Breakthrough of Stratification
Details
Peter Blau and Otis Dudley Duncan’s book, The American Occupational Structure, revolutionized the study of social mobility by overcoming the flaws of earlier research. Their approach had three key innovations:


Massive, Continuous Data: They used a national sample of over 20,000 men, which allowed them to move beyond discrete class boxes to a continuous scale of occupational prestige. This solved the problem of categorizing individuals who didn’t fit neatly into predefined classes.


Synthetic Cohorts: Instead of trying to track families over generations, they asked men of all ages about their father’s occupation when the son was 16. This created “synthetic cohorts” of men who started from the same point (e.g., all men whose fathers were laborers). By comparing the eventual outcomes of these different cohorts, they could measure the advantage or disadvantage conferred by one’s starting point.


Isolating “Circulation” Mobility: This method effectively controls for “structural” mobility—changes caused by economic shifts (e.g., the decline of farming, the rise of white-collar work) or demographic events. It isolates the degree to which the system allows individuals to move up or down, independent of these larger structural changes.

6---full-notes/micromutations.title: Micromutations
6---full-notes/micromutations.content:
Status: teen
Tags: genetics
Micromutations
Details
Genes are basically a sequence of letters, and these micromutations are the singular changes of the letters in the sequence. There are three primary types of micromutations, each with different consequences for the resulting protein:


Point Mutation: A single DNA letter is changed to another.


Neutral: The change results in a triplet that codes for the same amino acid (due to redundancy in the code). The protein is unchanged.


Minor Consequence: Codes for a different but similar amino acid. The protein’s shape and function are only slightly altered.


Major Consequence: Codes for a very different amino acid, dramatically changing the protein’s shape and function.




Deletion: A single DNA letter is lost. This causes a frameshift, where the three-letter reading frame is shifted for the rest of the gene. The result is a completely garbled sequence of amino acids and a non-functional protein.


Insertion: A single DNA letter is added or duplicated. This also causes a frameshift, with the same catastrophic result as a deletion.


The key takeaway is that micromutations typically alter the efficacy of a single protein, making it work slightly better, slightly worse, or not at all. And this is the basis for gradualism, the slight incremental changes of genes for it to be better.

6---full-notes/mill's-utility.title: Mill's Utility
6---full-notes/mill's-utility.content:
Status: adult
Tags: morals philosophy
Mill’s Utility
Details
The most philosophically important revision Mill makes occurs in Chapter Two. Classical Benthamite utilitarianism faces a fundamental difficulty: if we abstract entirely from the kind of activity producing pleasure, the object the activity aims at, and the relations between persons involved, why should pleasures estimated solely by intensity and duration be the only thing that matters? Mill felt this acutely after his mental crisis of 1829–1830.
Mill addresses this through what can be called the decided preference criterion. He distinguishes higher pleasures — arising from intellectual, moral, and imaginative capacities — from lower pleasures arising from physical and bodily needs. Rather than attempting precise measurement, Mill argues that those acquainted with both categories, under conditions of free choice, without moral obligation pushing them either direction, demonstrate a decided and stable preference for a life giving central place to higher pleasures. This preference is strong enough that at some point individuals would not exchange any further exercise of higher pleasures for any quantity of additional lower pleasures.
The asymmetry between the two threshold points is important: the lower bound on lower pleasures reflects biological necessity — we cannot indefinitely defer food, sleep, shelter without undermining our capacity to engage in higher activities at all. The lower bound on higher pleasures reflects something different — to entirely abandon them violates one’s sense of dignity. This appeal to dignity is significant and potentially non-utilitarian in character, a tension worth tracking throughout Mill’s work.
The result is that instead of calculating aggregate pleasure minus pain, Mill ultimately asks us to choose between modes of existence — manners of life — rather than comparing discrete pleasurable states. This shifts the utilitarian calculus significantly toward something resembling a conception of human flourishing.

6---full-notes/minds-of-children-and-par.title: Minds of children and parents
6---full-notes/minds-of-children-and-par.content:
Status: baby
Tags: psychology philosophy
Minds of children and Parents
Details
Children are naturally inquisitive. They ask questions born out of genuine wonder—not merely seeking confirmation of facts, but exploring deeper reasons (“why” rather than just “what”). This inherent curiosity is pure, profound, and often limitless. Yet, as children grow older, this innate wonder tends to diminish, not because curiosity itself dies, but because it becomes degraded by external influences. Parents and caregivers play a crucial role here. Frequently, adults—tired, overwhelmed, or burdened by their own unresolved issues—unintentionally suppress this instinct by scolding children’s incessant questioning or discouraging exploration through rigid, rote-learning educational environments.
When children sense that their natural curiosity or emotional needs are unwelcome, their instinct to attach compels them to adapt. In situations where parents are emotionally unavailable or distant, children subconsciously sacrifice their authenticity, suppressing genuine feelings or questions to meet parental expectations or simply to avoid rejection. They learn, tragically, to become “the mother’s idea of what a baby is,” diminishing their true nature to better align with the adult’s capacity for caregiving.
This process creates two distinct coping styles: avoidant and anxious attachments. Children with avoidant attachment appear indifferent, suppressing emotional expression externally while internally experiencing heightened anxiety. On the other hand, anxiously attached children amplify their emotional demands through tantrums or constant neediness, mistakenly believing only dramatic displays can garner care. Both attachment types reflect a fundamental insecurity that originates in early interactions with caregivers.
Connecting these two insights reveals a troubling cycle. A child’s naturally profound curiosity and emotional authenticity—the foundation for imagination, creativity, and psychological resilience—can be unintentionally eroded by the tiredness, stress, or unresolved trauma of parents. Such adults, trapped within their own limitations, inadvertently shape children who either detach from genuine emotional and intellectual expression or anxiously cling, demanding attention without fully experiencing emotional security.
Understanding this cycle allows recognition that the curiosity, imagination, and creativity lost in childhood can be rediscovered. As adults, acknowledging the connection between our early attachment patterns and current limitations enables healing and renewed openness. Ultimately, nurturing curiosity in children—and rekindling it within ourselves—requires a balanced perspective: we must ask with childlike wonder, yet respond with mature understanding, breaking cycles of trauma and reclaiming the creativity and emotional health that were our birthrights.

Minimal Brain Dysfunction
Details
ADHD actually started out from a plague, the influenza plague, which killed 80 million people worldwide. Though in survivors, particularly children, physicians found out that they were displaying a specific cluster of behavioral symptoms: severe impulsivity, an inability to pay attention, and unregulated hyperactivity. Because these symptoms appeared in the wake of a known viral infection that attacked the central nervous system, doctors termed the condition “Minimal Brain Dysfunction” (MBD). This of course is extremely wrong or “affirming the consequent.” They thought that since brain damage causes hyperactivity then if hyperactivity appears it must be brain damage, not considering or lacking the knowledge of other possible causes.
The condition evolved through various names, shifting from the neurological “MBD” to the behavioral “Hyperkinetic Reaction of Childhood,” then to “Attention Deficit Disorder” (ADD), and finally to the current “Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder” (ADHD).

6---full-notes/mirror-neurons.content:

Mirror neurons
Details
Mirror neurons fuel our ability to “feel into” someone else. It is the base for many functions of the human mind that are fairly unexplainable such as empathy, imitation, synchrony and even the development of language. We pick all these up not only from another person’s movement but their emotional state and intentions as well. This means that people who are mirroring each other have a tendency to mirror how they walk, sit, the rhythm of speaking, and so on. But also, they will mirror each other’s negativity, which can have a bad effect on both. 6---full-notes/mischel's-cognitive-affec.title: Mischel's Cognitive-Affective Theory
6---full-notes/mischel's-cognitive-affec.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology Cognitive Psychology
Mischel’s Cognitive-Affective Theory
Details
Walter Mischel expanded on the social cognitive perspective by emphasizing how our thoughts and interpretations shape our personality. He argued that in addition to learning behaviors, we also learn expectations about the outcomes of those behaviors and develop personal constructs or ways of interpreting situations. This leads to the development of unique competencies—skill sets we use to navigate different social situations.
For example, an extrovert and an introvert interpret a party with strangers very differently. The extrovert sees an exciting challenge, while the introvert sees a threatening situation. Each then deploys learned behaviors (competencies) to achieve their desired outcome in that context (e.g., being the center of attention vs. avoiding embarrassment).
The Marshmallow Test and Delay of Gratification Mischel’s most famous research is the “marshmallow test,” a study on delay of gratification.


The Experiment: Young children were placed in a room with a marshmallow and told they could eat the one marshmallow now, or, if they could wait a few minutes without eating it, they could have two marshmallows later.


The Findings: The study revealed that children had developed different competencies for resisting temptation. Some distracted themselves, some turned away, and some couldn’t resist at all.


Long-Term Correlation: The most groundbreaking finding was that this early ability to delay gratification was a powerful predictor of long-term life outcomes. Decades later, the children who were able to wait for the second marshmallow reported higher rates of college graduation, more stable marriages, and greater overall life satisfaction.


Mischel’s work showed that cognitive skills like self-control are core components of personality that have a profound and lasting impact on our lives.

Moderators, Mediators, and Confounders in Psychopathology
Details
Basically, these are the types of risk factors in how they lead to an outcome. Studying how one led to the other inherently birth the existence of these three:
Firstly, moderators, a variable that alters the direction or strength of the relationship between a risk factor and outcome. The effect varies at different levels. Secondly is a mediator, a variable that explains the mechanism through which the risk factor causes the outcome. (e.g., Poverty \rightarrow Harsh Parenting \rightarrow Delinquency. Here, harsh parenting mediates the link between poverty and delinquency). And lastly, a confounder, a third variable that causes both independent and dependent variables, creating a false association. For example, the statistical link between Race and Delinquency often disappears when controlling for Social Class (Poverty). Poverty is the confounder that drives the association.
The effects that risk factors have also depends on the socioeconomic and cultural factors, for when tough parenting is presented in white households and black households. The former resulting in delinquency or just more aggressiveness overall in childhood and the latter found no correlation at all, even slight reductions in aggressiveness even.

The type of knowledge that is untested by any real-life situation. We are only reading and thinking about the interpretation, the thoughts of something rather than the thing itself.
We become supposed scholars of shadows, the mere images of the objects that reflects those images. We are trapped debating, building upon that shadow, unbeknownst to the vast and beautiful knowledge of the object itself.
Academia, in all its beauty, is inherently finite. We may regurgitate and republish work forever, but it is still finite. It can only provide us a facsimiles of our own ability, it can only copy the work of reality at its best. Emerson tells us that we have always the resource of life. Modern types of economies
Details
I would consider these “models” of how different economies function. The most extreme of them can be simply divided into two: the command and the capitalist models. These basically never exist in practice due to how…impractical these extremes maybe. A pure laissez-faire capitalist economy would let individuals and firms decide what to produce and consume without government interference. In reality, even the United States is not pure capitalism. It is market-driven but constrained by government rules, taxes, regulations, and social norms. Firms may decide how many cars to produce, but they face safety standards, emissions standards, labor laws, taxation, and legal constraints. The market decides much, but it operates inside institutional boundaries. The bowling analogy captures this: in constrained capitalism, individuals throw the ball, but government and social rules act as bumpers that keep the system within acceptable limits.
The command economy is the opposite. In this model the government makes the production and allocation decisions. This was pretty much the idea of Karl Marx and how he wanted to run the government with his philosophy of communism. In practice, however, as many economists argue, it is simply too overwhelming a burden for the people governing to make, and they will eventually use it to further their own prospects. It is also overwhelming in the sense that there are simply too many decisions to be made and the government simply cannot make these decisions all by themselves and correctly.

6---full-notes/modernity-as-a-splitting-.title: Modernity as a Splitting of Factors
6---full-notes/modernity-as-a-splitting-.content:
Status: teen
Tags: history sociology
Modernity as a Splitting of Factors
Details
A precise anthropological definition of modernity requires looking beyond surface-level indicators like advanced technology, industrialization, or urbanization, recognizing that a nation can possess modern technology without being fundamentally modern in its social structure. The core of true modernity lies in the radical separation of human society’s four primary institutional spheres: economics, religion or ideology, politics, and kinship or society. In pre-modern tribal societies, these spheres are entirely unified, meaning the tribe simultaneously functions as the family, the economy, the religious body, and the government. As early civilizations developed, a partial separation occurred, typically leaving the economy bound to the family unit and politics tethered to religion. Western modernity, however, functions like a sociological nuclear fission. It violently splits all four of these spheres entirely apart from one another. In a truly modern framework, economic life is divorced from familial obligations, and political governance is strictly separated from religious authority. This total institutional separation is highly unnatural in the broader context of human history, yet it is the very engine that generates the immense energy, freedom, and structural openness characteristic of modern societies.

Molecular Shorthand and Structural Similarity
Details
To have an effect on the brain, substances usually try to mimic the shape and function of neurotransmitters. For example, by comparing the visual structure of Amphetamine to Dopamine, one can see they share a distinct hexagonal ring and carbon tail. This structural similarity allows the drug to interact with the same biological machinery (receptors and transporters) as the natural neurotransmitter. Small structural changes can then result in a completely different substance altogether: adding a methyl group (CH_3) to Amphetamine creates Methamphetamine, a more potent psychostimulant.
This elicits a line in between medicine and drugs, even a singular miniscule change can turn a medicine into a substance that has insanely high drug abuse potential. Methamphetamine (a potent, illegal stimulant) and Ephedrine (or Pseudoephedrine, a decongestant) are nearly identical in molecular structure. The only difference is the presence of a single Oxygen atom on the Ephedrine molecule.

6---full-notes/monopoly-pricing.title: Monopoly pricing
6---full-notes/monopoly-pricing.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Monopoly pricing
Details
Perfect competition was an extreme; no real market is perfectly competitive. The next few lectures relax it for two reasons. Other structures are more realistic, and they introduce market failures—cases where a market left alone doesn’t reach the efficient outcome. That’s where government stops being only an agent of chaos and can sometimes improve things.
The opposite extreme is monopoly: one firm being the whole market’s output. The key change is that a monopolist is a price maker, not a price taker (it doesn’t take from the market; it decides the market). For now, Gruber adds one assumption: no price discrimination. The monopolist sets a single price for every unit it sells.
Marginal revenue: A competitive firm faces a flat demand curve at the market price, so one more unit always adds exactly P to revenue. A monopolist’s demand is the whole market’s demand, which slopes down. To sell one more unit, it must cut the price—and with a single price, it cuts it on every unit, not just the extra one. Going from Q units at P1 to Q + 1 units at the lower P2:
MR = P2 − (P1 − P2) × Q
The first term is what the new unit sells for. The second is what the price cut costs on the Q units it was already selling. Gruber calls this the poisoning effect: each extra sale poisons the earlier ones. In calculus, with revenue R = P(Q) × Q:
MR = dR/dQ = P + (dP/dQ) × Q
For a competitive firm dP/dQ = 0, so MR = P. For a monopolist dP/dQ is negative, so MR < P. The marginal revenue curve lies below the demand curve everywhere.
Gruber’s example. Demand is Q = 24 − P, so P = 24 − Q and revenue is R = 24Q − Q², which gives MR = 24 − 2Q. For a straight-line demand curve, MR starts at the same intercept and falls twice as fast. (The shared intercept is special to straight lines; MR lying below demand is general.) Cost is C = 12 + Q², so MC = 2Q.
Profit maximization is MR = MC in every market structure. Here 24 − 2Q = 2Q, so Q = 6*.
The price is not 12, where MR and MC cross; that’s the classic mistake. The monopolist sets the price but has to stay on the demand curve, because buyers won’t pay more than it allows. So P = 24 − 6 = 18*. Average cost at 6 units is 12/6 + 6 = 8, so profit is (18 − 8) × 6 = 60.


















































UnitsPriceRevenueExtra revenueCostExtra costProfit519953758618108+1348+1160717119+1161+1358816128+976+1552
Look at the 7th unit. Its buyer would pay 17, and it costs only about 13 to make. Yet the monopolist won’t sell it. Selling 7 means charging 17 to everyone, which raises revenue by only 11 while cost rises 13, so profit falls from 60 to 58. The gain on the extra unit doesn’t cover the price cut on the first six.

6---full-notes/moral-reasoning.content:
Status: adult
Tags: morals philosophy
Moral Reasoning
Details
Moral reasoning follows similar principles to moral responsibility in that the person exercising it must have sufficient control over their thinking to actually perform it deliberately. It also categorizes itself neatly into reasoning about what to do: how we recognize moral considerations, cope with conflicts among them, and how they move us to act. Moreover, we also tacitly morally reason, though said thoughts never actually lead to a conclusive point; nonetheless, it might be wrong in certain situations to try and explicitly reason, like when you’re driving a car, just do it bruh.
A counterpoint to this neat categorization is the pull toward meta-level questions — “are there moral truths, and if so what are they?” and “what makes those truths true in the first place?” (metaethics). So moral reasoning doesn’t sit in isolation; it bleeds into questions about the very nature of morality itself. A further challenge to its practicality is how badly we actually perform it. This may be a result of our dual thinking systems — we default to fast, intuitive processing even for moral problems that genuinely require the slower, more deliberate one. The former point mentioned in this paragraph also leads to another one, one that substantiates that we cannot use moral reasoning to collapse it into either “perceive the facts” or “apply the correct theory” because of our intuition and theoretical limits.
But nonetheless, a practical point that we can draw from moral reasoning is the rationalization that it allows people to perform. People do not actually apply their ability to morally reason just because they become better at it, in fact, it just gives them the ability to rationalize whatever they already believed in and such.

6---full-notes/mortification-of-the-self.title: Mortification of the Self
6---full-notes/mortification-of-the-self.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
Mortification of the Self
Details
The engine driving the inmate’s transformation within a total institution is what Erving Goffman terms “mortification.” This is not random cruelty but a systematic series of “abasements, degradations, humiliations and profanations of self” designed to methodically dismantle the inmate’s pre-existing, civilian identity. This process is often a functional by-product of the need to manage large groups through impersonal routines.
The mortification begins with “role dispossession.” The new inmate is stripped of the multiple roles that defined them—parent, worker, friend—and is left with the single, all-encompassing role of “inmate.” This is physically enacted through the confiscation of their “identity kit”: the personal possessions, clothing, and grooming tools used to maintain a specific personal front. Replacing these with standardized institutional issue inflicts a “personal defacement,” erasing their unique identity.
A key technique is “contaminative exposure,” a violation of the boundaries of the self. This includes informational contamination, where discreditable facts from an inmate’s past are made public; physical contamination, where the body is profaned through public and intrusive procedures; and social contamination, where one is forced into unwanted intimacy and their degradation is witnessed by outsiders.
Furthermore, the institution employs “looping”: an inmate’s defensive reaction to a humiliation (e.g., anger) is itself interpreted by staff as another symptom of their pathology. This traps the inmate in a self-reinforcing cycle of control.
This entire architecture is a direct assault on the dramaturgical principles of everyday life. Mortification systematically deconstructs the resources—roles, props, and a private “backstage”—that an individual requires to project a coherent self. The process reveals that the self is an ecological phenomenon, requiring a specific environment of social and material supports to thrive. The asylum’s grim experiment shows that the self rapidly collapses when that ecology is deliberately poisoned, revealing our own sense of identity to be far more fragile and socially dependent than we imagine.

Motivational changes
Details
The reversals in major objectives are incredibly puzzling as they experience a sudden change and avoidance in experiences that formerly gratified him or represented the mainstream of his life, and he is drawn toward a state of inactivity. This may even result in him withdrawing from life via suicide.
He would no longer be attracted to such activities and rather  have to fight his inner urges to do the things that he feels like “is the right thing to do,” because others urge him to do it, not cause he wants to.
In the most extreme cases, the patient experiences “paralysis of the will”: He is devoid of spontaneous desire to do anything except to remain in a state of inertia. Nor can he mobilize “will power” to force himself to do what he believes he ought to do.
Everyday experiences—as well as a number of well-designed experiments—demonstrate that when a person believes he cannot succeed at a task, he is likely to give up. He adopts the attitude, “there’s no use trying,” and does not feel any spontaneous drive to work at it. Moreover, the belief that the task is pointless and that even successful completion is meaningless, minimizes his motivation.
Since the depressed patient expects negative outcomes, he does not experience any internal stimulation to make an effort; he sees no point in trying because he believes the goals are meaningless. People generally try to avoid situations they expect to be painful; because the depressed patient perceives most situations as onerous, boring, or painful, he desires to avoid even the usual amenities of living. These avoidance desires are powerful enough to override any tendencies toward constructive, goal-directed activity.

Multi-Systemic Therapy (MST)
Details
Before this existed, there was no effective way anyone could treat people who had severe ADHD, CD,… And so psychologists saw a need for a method to deal with said problems and developed well… this. Individual talk therapy or group therapy have been relatively ineffective, sometimes outright backfiring as the teenagers copy each other’s bad behaviors. Pharmacology also lacks a “magic bullet”; while stimulants help with comorbid ADHD, they may simply allow a “pure bully” to be more calculated, and antipsychotics or mood stabilizers often come with sedating side effects.
As evidence has shown, MST is the most effective treatment with a reduction to long-term delinquency rates of 30-60%. It is quite rigorous as dealing with these disorders require the person’s environment to be monitored and intervened 24/7 for 6 to 12 months, in which the same time the family has to be caring and empathetic and enduring as well.

6---full-notes/multi-tiered-system-suppo.content:
Status: adult
Tags: university psychology
Multi-tiered System Support
Details
The MTSS is a system that implements EBPs effectively, and a data-driven system that has been proved to work incredibly well. Its philosophy is to group all of the extra classes that a student might have to take if they fall behind their peers into the school’s system, improving the connection between these classes to the main ones by allowing the school to have control over them. Moreover, there are also scientific evidence to prove that they help students socially and mentally as well.
Within this system, there are three tiers which will be summarized accordingly. The first tier is the overall education offered to all of the students regardless of their level of learning. The education is different from others by that it uses EBPs alongside it, which has proven effectiveness due to 75-80% of students of this tier passes their tests. Moving onto the second tier is where specialized classes are necessary, students are grouped together into special classes that utilize other EBPs to supplement the main education, about 10-20% of students overall needs this. After evaluations, tier 2 students are either returned to tier 1, continue having another set, or move into tier 3, which is individualized education. At this tier, it is no longer a teacher managing the class but rather a interventionist, they apply even more specialized EBPs, with more time and resources, and also an overview of the process.
The other framework for this system is SWPPBIS (School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports), which handles the social and behavioral skills of students. Applying with the same principles that the former does, but with different EBIs, notably, the SEL. The SEL aims to improve the student’s emotional intelligence originating from the EQ tests (The one that we researched in summer), basically implementing methods to overall improve student’s skills. Each tier goes on the same, with the higher tiers requiring students to get even counseling or mental health providers. It has even been further proven that these methods can be performed by those in the school system, not necessarily outsiders. It has been proven to improve the overall positivity of the environment, mental health, reduction in distress,… but also the academic performance of students.

Rather than that, all the previously mentioned principals matter more, the fact that you learn actively, consolidate and build mental models truly matter.
In 2008, cognitive psychologists Harold Pashler, Mark McDaniel, Doug Rohrer, and Bob Bjork were commissioned to experiment and prove this claim and see if it was true. They set out to answer two questions. First, what forms of evidence are needed to justify basing their styles on students or employees. They did this by seeing how much more or less effective different people and different learning methods would do. Second question was if the evidence for this all existed, they found that very few studies were designed to test the validity of learning styles theory in education, and of those they found that virtually none validate it and few even contradicted it. In fact, more importantly is the method of instruction to the subject.
This does not mean that these do not exist, it is mostly cause of the fact that they have not done many rigorous studies to confirm it all and the cost to do so would cost way too much.

Naive Realism

As understood in social psychology, we usually interpret things subjectively from our point of view but think of it as the objective situation. This can then lead to Naive Realism, which states that we would then misjudge the difficulty and the state of the situation and everything alongside that. For example, in the Game Theory and the Prisoner’s Dilemma, observers of the experiment had a Reasonable Person Bias of themselves that they would have stopped at 150-volt when the person in the other room started showing reactions rather than be the 255-volt “killers” and considering those people as stupid, evil, etc., not realizing that they would have likely done the same in said situation (68%).

Nature-Based Interventions
Details
This is a type of intervention that focuses on the mental wellbeing rather than the symptom reduction, allowing the person access to psychoeducation and understanding the method, which actually encourages people to work on their mental wellness.
Recently, a trial pilot examining the “Roots and Shoots” NBI saw how truly effective this method was. Including all kinds of mindfulness activities such as psychoeducation, habit wheel, coping tool, honeycomb challenge, mood and nature connection tracking, expressive writing, nature videos, meditations and breathing exercises), users were found to all find them easy to do and quite effective as they saw improvement in their wellbeing.
Most of the results were medium-sized (in terms of Hedge’s g), larger ones were seen in relative increases in mindfulness, stress reduction and increased nature connection (g = 0.7; -0.67; 0.61). Sleep disturbance change was small (g= -0.17). The average scores on PHQ8 and GAD7 decreased so much that they moved from clinical caseness to non-caseness after 4 weeks. Not only that but the completion rate was surprisingly high, with 88.2% of participants with more than 50% of the 4 week period.

Also this could be integrated in therapy as another step for it or additional to the traditional psychotherapies.

6---full-notes/negative-coercion.content:

Negative Coercion
Details
This concept comes from Gerald Patterson’s work with aggressive children. Now, negative reinforcement doesn’t necessarily mean “bad” reinforcement but rather “taking something away.” Negative reinforcement is when a behavior is strengthened because the forces making that situation that the person is in go away.
To exemplify this in the parent-child relationship, we can take when a parent is demanding their children to do homework. Now because the child refuses to do said homework, the parent instead changes to shouting, insulting them, which results in the child eventually complying because they’re scared. After that, the parents think that if they simply scream loud enough, the child will do their work, they will continue to do that the next time. Now this is a failure in reasoning because they fail to account for the pent up feelings the child is likely experiencing and their plan to rebel the next time.
This cycle continues on and on, escalates further and further which morphs it into a strong indicator of future aggression due to how children might bring this to other environments like school or in their relationships.

6---full-notes/negative-dreams-in-depres.title: Negative dreams in depression
6---full-notes/negative-dreams-in-depres.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology dreams
Negative dreams in depression
Details
For individuals with depression, sleep often provides no escape. Instead, their dreams frequently become a nocturnal theater for their waking suffering, characterized by intensely negative themes and emotions that can worsen the illness. This phenomenon highlights how depression permeates every aspect of a person’s experience, even their subconscious.
The dream content of depressed patients is consistently bleak. Common narratives revolve around themes of failure, rejection, and personal inadequacy. Dreamers often find themselves as victims of misfortune or as the cause of a catastrophic event, mirroring the feelings of worthlessness and guilt that are hallmarks of depression. Themes of death are also significantly more frequent. These are not merely unpleasant dreams; they are emotionally potent, dominated by overwhelming sadness, anxiety, and fear. This emotional intensity is believed to be linked to dysregulated REM sleep, the primary dream stage, which is often altered in depression.
This cycle of negative dreaming has a tangible impact on waking life. Waking from a distressing nightmare can leave a residue of negative emotion that colors the entire day, reinforcing feelings of hopelessness. This aligns with the “continuity hypothesis,” which suggests our dreams are an extension of our waking thoughts and concerns. The anxieties of the day seep into the night, creating tormenting dreams that, in turn, feed the depression upon waking. In this way, the negative dreams of depressed individuals are not just a symptom but a perpetuating part of a vicious cycle, making the fight for mental wellness even more challenging.

Neglected Children

These children don’t understand the needs and emotions of other children, often resulting in them misbehaving or not fitting in with others, eventually being pushed out of groups and activities that others would be allowed to indulge in. Thing is this is not inherently their fault, this is the fault of not being taken care of correctly in their childhood (referenced in Attachment Theory) when their caretaker does not acknowledge their needs and emotions, prompting them to respond to it the same way when they grow up.
These children instead of reacting to faces, tones and such as cues to their actions, they automatically assign those things as danger, and respond to it like so, defensively, scared, different from how others normally would. They can’t stand being alone, as any human can’t. And in so they would find connections in the worst places, gangs, getting themselves in trouble and into jail for those police officers,…

The study of Romanian orphans demonstrated that neglect has a “dose-response” relationship with development: children removed from institutions and placed in foster care before age 2 showed significant recovery, while those who remained longer suffered irreversible developmental harm.
