6---full-notes/nervous-system-in-sleep.title: Nervous System in sleep
6---full-notes/nervous-system-in-sleep.content:
Status: adult
Tags: neuroscience sleep
Nervous System in sleep
Details
The nervous system requires external cues or “levers” to regulate its state of wakefulness or sleep. These inputs are used to control the body’s internal 24-hour clock (circadian rhythm) and prepare it for either activity or rest. Optimizing sleep involves the strategic use of these levers throughout the day.
The primary levers that provide input to the nervous system for sleep regulation are:


Light and Darkness: This is the most powerful lever. Light, especially sunlight viewed early in the day, triggers wakefulness signals (e.g., cortisol release) and sets the circadian clock. Darkness allows for the release of the sleep-promoting hormone melatonin. The timing, intensity, and even angle of light are critical variables.


Temperature: A drop in core body temperature by 1−3∘C is a required physiological gate to fall and stay asleep. Conversely, an increase in core body temperature promotes wakefulness. This can be manipulated with tools like cold/hot showers, exercise, or smart mattresses. Exercising can make someone become awake for an extensive amount of time, consider a few hours before exercising.


Food: The timing, composition, and volume of food intake act as a cue for the body’s clocks. Eating sends wakefulness signals, while fasting or large meals can impact alertness and sleepiness.


Exercise: The timing and intensity of physical activity influence core body temperature and alertness. Morning exercise reinforces wakefulness signals, while intense evening exercise can delay the onset of sleep.


Caffeine: This compound acts as an adenosine antagonist, blocking the buildup of the natural sleep-pressure molecule (adenosine) in the brain. Its strategic use is crucial for maintaining daytime alertness without disrupting nighttime sleep.


Supplements: Certain compounds can directly modulate neurotransmitter systems to facilitate sleep. Key examples include magnesium threonate, apigenin, and theanine, which can help with falling asleep and improving sleep depth.


Digital Tools: These are primarily script-based methods that guide the brain into states of deep relaxation, making it easier to fall asleep, return to sleep if awakened, and improve overall sleep quality. Examples include Non-Sleep Deep Rest (NSDR) protocols and self-hypnosis.


Each of these levers can be adjusted to create a predictable daily rhythm, which helps anchor the body’s internal clocks and leads to more robust and restorative sleep.

Nervous system

All the things that we instinctively register during a conversation is linked up by a single regulatory system. Which is a synchrony between two branches of the autonomic nervous system (ANS): which acts as the body’s accelerator, and the parasympathetic, which serves as its break. These are the “reciprocals” that Darwin spoke of, so they play an important role for the body’s energy, releasing it and conserving it.
The sympathetic nervous system (SNS) is responsible for arousal, including the fight-or-flight response. It partly pumps adrenaline into the muscle strands. The second branch is the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) which is for self-preservative functions. It triggers the release of acetylcholine which puts a brake on the adrenaline, slowing down heart-rate and such. These are a part of the autonomic nervous system.
A measurement called heart rate variability (HRV) can be used to measure this system, a good one will have many fluctuations which means both of the systems are working well and are in balance.

6---full-notes/neural-circuits-in-adhd.title: Neural Circuits In ADHD
6---full-notes/neural-circuits-in-adhd.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neurology ADHD
Neural Circuits In ADHD
Details
The neurological underpinnings of ADHD can be understood as a dysfunctional relationship between two of the brain’s major operating systems: the Default Mode Network (DMN) and Task-Related Networks. In a neurotypical brain, these networks operate like a seesaw; they are anti-correlated, meaning when one is active, the other is suppressed. The DMN is the brain’s “idle” state, responsible for mind-wandering and self-referential thought, while Task-Related Networks engage when we need to focus on a goal-oriented, external task. This opposition allows for a clean switch between internal reflection and external focus.
In the ADHD brain, this critical anti-correlation is broken. The two networks are often active at the same time, creating a state of internal conflict and neural noise. It’s akin to trying to listen to an important lecture while a loud, distracting conversation is happening right next to you—except the distracting conversation is coming from inside your own head. This makes it incredibly difficult to filter out internal chatter and sustain focus on the outside world. The neuromodulator dopamine acts as the “conductor” responsible for orchestrating this delicate seesaw balance. In ADHD, the weak or dysregulated dopamine signal means the conductor can’t keep the two networks in their proper, opposing rhythm, leading to the core symptoms of distractibility and an inability to stay on task.

Neurobiology of reward
Details
This is where the behaviors of us doing stuff that makes us feel good and stuff that makes us feel bad gets explained. Basically, as we evolved, as human beings, our brain developed systems for pleasure and rewards, but more than that, it also encoded information into our brain about stuff that we SHOULD feel rewarded after doing it.
These systems are called “pleasure centers” or, more accurately, reward pathways in the brain. These pathways are intrinsically linked to fundamental survival drives. Further research has shown that different areas correspond to different rewards; stimulating one spot might be as rewarding as eating when hungry, while another might be linked to the reward of mating. This suggests that we are motivated to act in order to activate these specific neural circuits. The satisfaction we get from eating, for instance, is not just about the food, but about the activation of this pre-programmed, hardwired system that tells us “this is good for survival.” In this sense, our motivations are a direct extension of our biology.

6---full-notes/neurofeedback.title: Neurofeedback
6---full-notes/neurofeedback.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology trauma
Neurofeedback
Details
The core mechanism of neurofeedback involves monitoring the brain’s electrical activity and providing immediate feedback based on specific parameters. It begins with placing non-invasive sensors on the individual’s scalp. These sensors detect the faint electrical signals produced by neuronal activity, collectively known as the electroencephalogram (EEG) or brainwaves.  
These real-time EEG signals are then amplified and processed by computer software. The software analyzes the incoming brainwave data, identifying patterns associated with different states of arousal, focus, or relaxation (e.g., the prevalence of specific frequencies like alpha, beta, theta, SMR. These waves correspond to certain activities like, sleep, drowsiness, focus,…)
Based on predetermined therapeutic goals for the individual (often aimed at reducing patterns linked to PTSD hyperarousal or instability), the system translates the relevant EEG activity into a perceivable feedback signal. This feedback might be visual (e.g., a video game that progresses, a bar graph that changes) or auditory (e.g., tones that sound, music that plays smoothly). Crucially, this feedback is contingent – it changes directly in response to the fluctuations in the targeted brainwave patterns, signaling to the brain how its current activity aligns with the desired state.

Neuromodulators
Details
Neural communication extends beyond simple, direct excitation or inhibition into a more subtle and powerful domain known as neuromodulation. In this form of signaling, a substance does not directly cause or prevent an action potential, but instead alters a neuron’s response to other incoming signals. This creates a sophisticated system of conditional, “if/then” logic that dramatically increases the brain’s computational power by making communication context-dependent. The effect of a neuromodulator is contingent on the presence of a primary neurotransmitter, changing how the pre- or post-synaptic cell responds to it.

Neurons
Details
These are the building blocks of the systems of the nerves, or the nervous systems, together with nerve impulses of course. There are many different types of neurons.
The neuron is a singular cell with three subdivisions: the dendrites, the cell body (soma), and the axon. The first of whom are usually branched, so they resemble a Medusa like bush. The axon, which extends like a wispy thread (looks weird as heck like it has nodes and stuff), may fork out into several axonal branches at its end. The dendrites receive nerve impulses from other neurons and the axon transmits that impulse.
The diameter of a neuron is very small; cell bodies can go from 5 to about 100 microns in diameter (1 micron = 1/1000 millimeter). The average hair has a diameter of 100 microns. Dendrites are typically short, only a few hundred microns, but axons can be longer.

6---full-notes/neuroscience-of-autism.title: Neuroscience of Autism
6---full-notes/neuroscience-of-autism.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience developmental psychology
Neuroscience of Autism
Details
Autism is quite a heritable disease, genetic factors explaining a vast majority of variance in the condition. While severe autism is rare, a “broad autism phenotype” consisting of mild social awkwardness or rigidity can run in families with autism. A huge finding is that a subset of children with autism exhibit head circumferences significantly larger than norms. This macrocephaly is linked to a failure of synaptic pruning. Typically, the brain sheds half its neurons between ages one and two to become efficient; in autism, this pruning process may fail, leaving the brain with an overabundance of noisy, inefficient connections, which correlates with the clinical phenomenon of developmental regression often seen around that age.
Simon Baron-Cohen proposes the “Extreme Male Brain” theory, suggesting that autism represents an extreme version of “systemizing” behaviors-traits typically associated with males-such as logic, analysis, and order, at the expense of “empathizing.” This aligns with the “Silicon Valley Syndrome” hypothesis, which posits that the mating of highly analytical, technically minded individuals may concentrate these genes, increasing the prevalence of autism. This may additionally explain why autism abundance hasn’t decreased, because these traits may contribute to evolution.

Neurotransmitters
Details
Now, there’s a whole lot more neurotransmitters than two that is excitatory and inhibitory, in fact there are about a hundred or so and more of course. We will mention just a few of these neurotransmitters here.


Acetylcholine (ACh) is released at many synapses and at the neuromuscular junction (itself a kind of synapse); the release of ACh makes muscle fibers contract.


Serotonin (5HT) is a transmitter that is involved in many of the mechanisms of sleep, mood, and arousal.


Glutamate is a critical neurotransmitter in the retina of the eye and appears to be important for long-term memory as well as for the perception of pain.


GABA (or to give its full name, gamma-amino butyric acid) is the most widely distributed inhibitory transmitter of the CNS.


Still others are norepinephrine (NE) and dopamine (DA), to which we will refer in later discussions of drug effects and certain mental disorders (see Chapters 3, 18, and 19).

6---full-notes/newton-and-the-death-of-i.content:
Status: baby
Tags: physics philosophy
Newton and the Death of Intelligibility
Details
With Newton’s findings, we could finally understand mathematically that vortices could not create elliptical orbits, and such, but rather, gravity. While Newton’s equations were miraculously predictive—unifying the fall of an apple with the orbit of the Moon—they were philosophically baffling. How can two objects affect each other across a vacuum without any mechanical connection? Newton famously refused to speculate on the mechanism (“Hypotheses non fingo”), settling instead for the mathematical success. This marked a profound shift in science: the goal moved from “rendering the world intelligible” (making sense of how things happen, like gears or fluids) to “predicting phenomena” via equations, even if the underlying forces (like gravity) seemed like spooky, occult magic. This gave the explanation for Kepler’s improved astronomy and such.

No Safe Smoking

Definition
Typically you would note things done then build connections, after that you would have ideas from those connections and start continue building from that, then you review it, notice some holes or missing info in your arguments. By the nature of science and psychology, established habits are inherently automatic. Because of this, we are often incapable of changing how we behave because we lack an indication of what we are actually doing. 6---full-notes/obedience-to-institutions.title: Obedience to Institutions
6---full-notes/obedience-to-institutions.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
Obedience to Institutions
Details
In society, it is quite common for people to obey to a certain authority figure and to perform whichever tasks or requests they might ask them. This may create a large hole/vulnerability as a lot of the times these people do it without questioning the authenticity of the person of authority, rather just follow their sentiments if they “sound like” a person of authority.
An example that shows this is the Stanley Milgram’s Obedience to Authority Experiment, conducted in the early 1960s. Positions were: Teacher, Learner, Experimenter. These people were of course applied the rules of an RCT so that the test would be truly random. The teacher and learner were placed in separate rooms but they could still listen to each other. The experimenter then would command the teacher to shock the learner, of course it was a fake but the learner would try to act the corresponding effects they would get from the shock. The rate of obedience of the Teacher was surprisingly high, about 60% in the United States and even more in other countries.
The reason the experiment is so famous is because of its horrifying results. Before the study, psychologists predicted that less than 1% of participants would go all the way to 450 volts. The reality was that approximately 65% (nearly two-thirds) of the participants obeyed the experimenter and delivered the full 450-volt shock, even when the Learner was screaming in agony and then fell silent.
This experiment showed us many things, it showed us that morally normal people who normally would not shock another person to death, a lot of them would do so under the presence of an authority. But moreover, it also showed us how we, as a society, could not function without the obedience to authority.
Supporting Content
A part of why people did this is because of the consistency, even if 15-volt in normal context wouldn’t kill anyone, the line of it killing and not is fairly thin. And because people followed through since 0 til the killing amount, they feel compelled/misjudge how easy it is for the voltage to kill people, eventually resulting in them crossing the line without much realization.

Objective Dangers
Details
It is quite difficult to differentiate rational and normal fears from phobias. But there is a general rule which states that “The greater the anxiety and disability compared to the actual risk, the easier it is to justify applying the term.” This means that it should be easy to make the diagnosis when the content of the fear is far-fetched. Like the person who avoids all outdoor activities as he is afraid a thunderstorm would happen and he’d get stricken and die.
In clinical practice, it has also been shown that phobias are quite easily distinguishable, and so there is often no need for us to analyze. In most cases, the phobic seeks help due to him not being able to live with the conditions that his phobia is preventing him from anymore, as the pain of such things are too much.
Supporting Content
But furthermore, a lot of people, specialists so to say, have been able to buffer or extinguish their fears of situations that are said to be dangerous by the normal human being. Experimental studies by Epstein has also showed us how parachutists have reduced anxiety as they become more experienced. As well as troops who experience less anxiety than fresh recruits. They use the method that these specialists do to help phobic patients deal with their own situations.
We also know that phobic patients may be fearless in a situation that would make others anxious, whilst doing the opposite with their phobia. This shows that even if a person seems to deal with a situation better than the normal person, it does not mean it is the same for every other.

6---full-notes/objective-self-awareness.title: Objective Self-Awareness

Objective Self-Awareness
Details
Proposed by Robert Wicklund, this theory suggests that whenever we are thinking inward, we are inherently evaluating ourselves as a social object meant to be judged by others. This can be exemplified by the actor-observer effect, which constitutes that people usually judge themselves depending on external situations, but when rewatching footage of themselves they instead treat themselves as something to be scrutinized personally and emotionally. Environmental triggers, such as sitting in front of a mirror or hearing a recording of one’s own heartbeat, force this objective perspective, activating the generalized other and compelling the individual to evaluate themselves against societal standards (so its not just rewatching footage but perhaps whatever increases self-awareness).
This comparison usually creates extensive aversion and anxiety, which people adapt with conformity or escape. On the Apollonian side of things, we will conform to morals and society, whilst individuals cannot conform to the standard, they will actively seek Dionysian escape from the self. This explains why people generally report higher self-esteem when engrossed in a television show rather than looking in a mirror; the television absorbs their attention outward, shutting down the reflective, critical voice of the generalized other and providing profound psychological relief.

6---full-notes/objectivity-in-syntopical.title: Objectivity in Syntopical reading
6---full-notes/objectivity-in-syntopical.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
Objectivity in Syntopical reading
Details
The good analysis of a discussion of a problem or subject matter identifies and reports the major issues, or basic intellectual oppositions. This does not imply that disagreement is always the dominant feature of every discussion. On the contrary, agreement in most cases accompanies disagreement; that is, on most issues, the opinions or views that present opposite sides of the dispute are shared by several authors, often by many. Seldom do we find a solitary exponent of a controversial position.
This means that there exist situations where none of the opinions are wholly true. Or that one is and others aren’t, or that all of them are true in some way; or that all the conflicting opinions may be false, and so on. Some opinion as yet unexpressed may be the truth or nearer to it.
And so we can say the rule is never to answer all the questions, but rather dogmatic, we are trying to just be the discussion, not be a voice in it. We will try to take a look at all sides and take none of it. We will fail at this as it is absolute, but we may succeed in a lot of it, particularly in taking no sides. We can never, though, take a look at all sides.
Taking no sides is easier than looking at all sides, we say, but it remains difficult even so. The syntopical reader must resist certain temptations and know his own mind. Perfect dialectical objectivity is not guaranteed by avoiding explicit judgments on the truth of conflicting opinions. Partiality can intrude in a variety of subtle ways—by the manner in which arguments are summarized, by shades of emphasis and neglect, by the tone of a question or the color of a passing remark, and by the order in which the various different answers to key questions are presented.
In order to avoid some of these dangers, the conscientious syntopical reader may resort to one obvious device and use it as much as possible. That is, he must constantly refer back to the actual text of his authors, reading the relevant passages over and over; and, in presenting the results of his work to a wider audience, he must quote the opinion or argument of an author in the writer’s own language. Although it may appear to do so, this does not contradict what we said earlier about the necessity of finding a neutral terminology in which to analyze the problem, and so when it is presented, we will still have to do so in such languages, though we will source and quote the author’s.

Obsessions and Compulsions
Details
The content of obsessions is concerned with some remote risk or danger expressed in the form of a doubt or a warning. The person may continue to doubt whether he has perform an act to ensure his safety adequately.
Compulsions consists of attempts to allay excessive doubts or obsessions through action. A hand-washing compulsion, for example, is when the patient believed that he has not removed all the dirt or contaminants from his body. As he regards the dirt as a source of danger, a cause of illness or general dirtiness. We often see the triad of phobia-obsession-compulsion. For instance, a patient afraid of being harmed by radiation, his phobia manifested from him avoiding things that might emit radiation, after a necessity to interact or come into contact with something of the sorts, he becomes obsessed about contamination, and so he acts on it by bathing long period to remove the contaminants (compulsion).
There are some neurobiological activities that have been studied in people with OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder), specifically different neurological activity in the occipital lobe. This does not show us that this maybe the cause or a symptom of it though. Moreover, the cingulate cortex is also active in situations where there is a conflict, something like the conflict between the reading comprehension and visual comprehension of a task, forcing the inhibition of one of the two parts.
Further cognitive testing has shown that thought suppression in anyone is impossible. Studies have shown that when a person is shown or is told something and then told they should not think about that thing, they will not be able to stop themselves from thinking of that thing. This applies closely to OCD.

6---full-notes/official-and-real-story.content:
Status: teen

Official and Real story
Details
There is a profound tension in Nietzsche’s account between the “Official Story” (the surface-level myth) and the “Real Analysis” of what occurred.
The Official Story depicts Masters as “active/creative” and Slaves as “reactive/sterile.” However the analysis reveals that it is the Slaves that are actually creative as they gave meaning to their internal struggles and selves through inventing new conceptual categories that are different from previous interpretations like Evil, Free Will, The Soul, Responsibility, and Inferiority. And so Nietzsche argues that Slave Morality may be something that is genuinely a contributing factor into society as it prevents it from falling back to the Greek aristocracy times.
Moreover, if we look at the last 2000 years of European history, we would see that the “Weak” have utterly defeated the “Strong.” Europe was dominated by Christian morality at that time, which according to Master Morality, would be Slave morality. The values of the weak have become the hegemonic standard. And so, in a dialectical twist, the Slaves proved to be stronger, not physically but conceptually and institutionally. They successfully made man interesting by introducing depth, guilt, and inferiority where previously there was only surface and action. And so in changing this power dynamic, they also changed how power could be interpreted as well, not just someone beating another person but being better morally.

6---full-notes/old-philosophical-culture.content:

Old Philosophical Culture of the Analytic Mainstream
Details
The dominant strand of modern analytic philosophy is a direct descendant of what Marx would categorize as the “old philosophical culture” of the 18th-century Enlightenment. Championed by thinkers like Descartes and Kant, and later revived by Frege and Russell, this paradigm is fundamentally individualistic, ontological, and ahistorical. It conceptualizes the human being primarily as a cognitive entity, a res cogitans operating within an internal theater of the mind that processes propositions or psychological states. In this framework, society is viewed merely as a secondary aggregate of these pre-existing, isolated individuals. Furthermore, this tradition assumes that human cognition and logical structures can be studied in a vacuum, entirely abstracted from the historical, linguistic, and social conditions in which the thinker is embedded.

6---full-notes/oligopoly.title: Oligopoly
6---full-notes/oligopoly.content:
Status: teen
Tags: economics market
Oligopoly
Details
Most real markets are oligopolies: a small number of firms supply the good and compete against each other. That’s more than one firm, but too few for entry to push profits to zero. Cars are the standard example. Most cars sold in America come from fewer than 20 companies. That’s probably not enough competition to drive profits to zero, but it’s enough that no company can simply pick its point on the demand curve.
With only a few firms, there are two ways to behave:

Cooperatively, by forming a cartel: otherwise competing firms agree to act as one monopoly, maximize the joint profit and split it. OPEC, the oil exporters’ cartel, is the classic case.
Non-cooperatively: each firm does what’s best for itself. This is the more realistic case, and Lecture 14 shows why cartels rarely last.

Since there still needs to be competition between the firms, we need something else to understand how these guys will compete when the game is this seated and set. That is called game theory.

6---full-notes/omega-3s-and-the-crucial-.title: Omega-3s and the Crucial Distinction Between Modulation and Mediation
6---full-notes/omega-3s-and-the-crucial-.content:
Status: teen
Tags: biology 3 - Tags/environment
Omega-3s and the Crucial Distinction Between Modulation and Mediation
Details
Omega-3 fatty acids, particularly EPA and DHA, are well-known for their broad health benefits, and they also play a significant role in brain function related to focus and mood. For ADHD, studies show that their effect is modest but significant. The data point to a key threshold of consuming over 300mg of DHA per day, which is typically achieved when taking a higher dose of fish oil (over 1g of total EPA+DHA) for its mood-elevating effects. This supplementation can help individuals function well on lower doses of medication and, in some cases, may help eliminate the need for it entirely.
This highlights a critical concept in biology: the difference between mediation and modulation. A process is mediated by a substance that directly causes it to happen; for instance, dopamine directly mediates motivation and focus. In contrast, a process is modulated by a substance that influences or adjusts the primary process. Omega-3s, like proper sleep or a healthy diet, are powerful modulators. They don’t directly cause focus, but they create a biological environment where the brain’s focus circuits can function more efficiently. They might make dopamine more available or help receptors work better. Understanding this distinction is vital for setting realistic expectations for treatments. While a drug like Adderall mediates focus, supplements and lifestyle changes modulate it, playing a crucial supportive role in the overall treatment plan.

6---full-notes/on-being-a-father.title: On Being A Father
6---full-notes/on-being-a-father.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy sociology
On Being A Father
Details
“To beget is not to be a father, a father is he who begets and proves himself worthy of it.” — Fetyukovich, The Brothers Karamazov
During the reading of Brothers Karamazov, this was one of the most interesting points that I encountered perhaps because of how it was used. Fetyukovich wields this idea not as an admission of guilt — he maintains his client’s innocence throughout — but as a philosophical argument to mentally reclassify the alleged crime from a horrific parricide to a mere homicide. This argument echoes a fundamental question about the definition of “family”: can we accept a definition of parenthood based purely on biology when the functional, visceral reality of that bond is entirely absent? In other words, if a parent abandons their child from birth and practically refuses to acknowledge their existence, can and should they still be considered a “father” — not just in the court of law, but in any morally serious sense of the word?
I. The Societal Meaning of A Father
But to contextualize this and justify its weight in Fetyukovich’s closing argument, we must understand what fatherhood meant in 19th century Russia. Russia was a deeply religious country at the time, and the father was treated as an institution - God ruled the universe, the Tsar ruled the empire, and the father ruled the family. As they were all linked together, parricide was essentially viewed as an unnatural abomination - a spiritual treason, so to say.
And the prosecutor Ippolit Kirillovich, by all means, epitomizes what this version of Russia represents. His troika metaphor — Russia galloping out of control, Europe stepping aside in horror — frames Mitya’s alleged crime not as an individual act but as a symptom of national moral collapse. Fetyukovich rejects this view, he puts the case of Mitya’s supposed murder of his father as evidence to question the opinion on parricides at the time and in of itself - the very structure of Russia at the time: “The prosecutor was pleased to terrify us with the Russian troika, at the galloping flight of which ‘all the nations stand aside in disgust and horror.’ Well, let them stand aside, gentlemen of the jury… but I submit to you that a chariot is not a troika. To drive a chariot, one needs a firm foundation, a reliable road.”
Dostoevsky is careful to undercut Fetyukovich here, as if reminding us that this is a rhetorician doing what rhetoricians do, working the jury’s emotions toward acquittal. But that is precisely what makes the argument worth rescuing. The rhetorician was right, by accident or not. And so the purpose of this essay is to take Fetyukovich’s point seriously on its own terms and grounds to substantiate why it holds.
II. The Moral Nature of A Father
Prior to addressing the argument proposed above, it is necessary to define the term “father” in the classical sense, so that the argument is able to meet the concept at its strongest, rather than a diminished version of it.
As the religious dimensions of 19th century Russia may not translate directly to contemporary society, I will refrain from anchoring the definition there. We will instead attempt to define the classical conception of fatherhood on its own terms. In this sense, we must understand that it is not simply a biological designation. Across the major traditions of the West and the East alike, fatherhood has always been understood as a tripartite structure: origin, authority, and formation.
The first layer — origin — is the biological fact of fatherhood. But, naturally, this would be too bare a foundation, and the ancients did not stop there. Aristotle, in the Nicomachean Ethics, treats the father-child relationship as one of natural inequality ordered toward the child’s good. The father is not merely the other half of the child’s birth, but also a person whose role is fundamentally defined by what follows from that cause. The relationship is not symmetrical, and it is not optional. It is somewhat similar to partiality, in the sense that the origin generates the role and does not only precede it.
The second layer is authority. In the classical sense, this does not necessarily mean domination but rather stewardship. Across virtually every major cultural tradition, the father has been the breadwinner of the household: providing protection, structure, and an orientation toward society and the world. As such, he is the child’s first encounter with the fact that power can be directed towards care rather than arbitrary imposition. In Confucianism, it is among the highest of virtues because of the role of the father as the primary moral educator; for he is the person who the child essentially learns the obligations of social life from. In the Abrahamic traditions, the father is involved in a chain of authority that runs down from God — which is why, in the context of 19th century Russia, parricide carried a meaning that exceeded the merely murderer.
And lastly, the third layer, which I personally consider the deepest one as it practically justifies the other two: formation. A father, in the fullest classical sense, is the first experience that a child has of that of authority, but also love. Psychology can attest to this as the father is the child’s first model of how to be somebody in relation to others. Philosophy would say that the father is the ground of the earliest of moral formation, of how to inhibit the world alongside other people. Dostoevsky himself understood this, specifically through Zosima. Zosima’s entire spiritual philosophy rests on the idea that the experience of being loved unconditionally is what makes the expansion of love outward possible at all. Such personal relation is the very foundation for the universal version of it.
The entirety of the argument above was to justify for why the charge of parricide was considered to never merely be a legal category. To kill your father was not merely to kill a man. It was, in the deepest sense the culture could articulate, to destroy the very axis of your own formation — perhaps even your own soul.
And, only after coming to this point, after understanding what the word was designed to mean, can we truly feel Fetyukovich’s question: What if the axis was never there?
III. The Word Without the Substance
It is clear from the former section that the inherent structure of the word “father” is quite understandable, and perhaps even defensible on its own terms. But this is precisely where the relationship between Fyodor Karamazov and Dmitri Karamazov becomes relevant.
Fyodor Karamazov did not raise Dmitri. He did not protect him, know him, or want him in any meaningful sense. He outright forgot about Dmitri’s existence — and had it not been for Grigory, his butler, Dmitri would have died in neglect. Could we, in any meaningful sense, call that fatherhood? I do not think so. What Fyodor gave Dmitri was not fatherhood but its hollow precondition — a biological fact barely sufficient to install the title permanently, regardless of what followed from it.
In this particular case, we can see clearly how the word “father” is truly being used: normatively, not descriptively. And yet it carries within it the entire tripartite structure outlined above. When we call someone a father, we are not simply naming a genetic link, rather, we are invoking a role, and with it, the accumulated weight of every expectation that role entails. Parricide is uniquely horrifying for precisely this reason: it is understood as a violation of something sacred, something foundational to human development, committed by the very person that relationship was supposed to form. But the case of the Karamazovs exemplifies what actually happens when that foundation was never laid, being that the sacredness was never there, the authority was never exercised, the formation never occurred.
And yet the horror does not recalibrate accordingly. The charge does not diminish. Society still reaches for the full weight of the word, as the word has become self-justifying. It does not require the father to prove his fatherhood to activate its consequences for the son. The title alone is sufficient. The substance is simply assumed.
This is, I would argue, a profound moral error.
IV. The Cathedral Around a Word
From the argument above, I believe we can come to the conclusion that society has built a cathedral around the world — completely forgot to check whether there was actually anything inside.
The word “father” in its classical/philosophical fullness is genuinely one of the most morally loaded terms in the human language. As demonstrated above, in its fullest form, it is arguably the most formative force in the human life. But that is not where the problem belies. The problem does not lie in whether the meaning of a “father” is extensive enough or not; it lies in the child that is abused by his dad but then demanded by relatives and society to care for the same person; it lies in the son that has never had a father for a singular moment yet suffers a punishment as if he had one. The problem is the assumption of equivalence between the biological fact of a father and the relational reality that goes with it when the history of human experience has offered us endless evidence that they may not correlate.
What Fetyukovich gestures toward, and what this essay has attempted to make explicit, is that this assumption is not merely philosophically sloppy. It is harmful in a specific and predictable way: it extends the protections of the full concept to those who hold only its biological shell, while simultaneously placing the full burden of the concept onto those who never received its substance. And so perhaps it is not just a matter concerning common knowledge or nature, but rather a concern of morality as well. For if we may look upon a person who has not ever in their life received care and love from their father and yet demand them to reciprocate feelings that they were never given access to in the first place then what are we ?
V. Additional Remarks
I have a certain feeling that one may suggest a common counterargument to that proposed above that the framework allows the absent father to be able to argue that he does not have obligations to his child as he never acted alike one.
This argument basically commits the exact same moral error that we have spent the essay discussing about, merely in reverse. The societal “cathedral” assumes that the biological fact automatically generates the moral reality. The absent father, in this sense, assumes that the absence of the moral reality somehow also erases the biological fact. Both of these perspectives sever the fundamental connection between origin and relation. Both of them reduce fatherhood to a mere convenience for one to treat accordingly to their own whims. To recognize that biology alone is insufficient to make a father is not to say that the biological act carries no inherent obligation; rather, it is to say that abandoning that obligation does not free a man from the title, but rightfully condemns him for leaving the cathedral empty.

6---full-notes/on-familial-bonds.title: On Familial Bonds
6---full-notes/on-familial-bonds.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
On Familial Bonds
Details
As sciences developed throughout history, I believe that the term “family” has become something worth questioning. Most of us laypeople recognize it as a societal default, something that is already accepted to be rather than thinking about the definition of it. The priori that most people go by is the biological implications of it, which is usually about the blood relatedness of one person to another. Furthermore, I also contend that people have also taken the functionality of a family for granted, depending on basic human morals or societal values rather than implicating their own.
While this approach may allow society to function steadily, it’s not something that is exactly satisfying for academics or just thinkers. The term “family” being purely biological becomes substantially more ambiguous as people mature as they take into account adoptive, foster families and so on. The definition no longer satisfies the generality and variability of people using the term, alongside its function as well. In the following essay, I will attempt to redefine the word in a way that allows it to be utilize across more situations, make it better fitting and more sensical as well.
When examining the literature on this problem, the models I stumbled upon were mostly top-down in their approaches, depending on a preexisting framework rather. I would personally argue that these models are unsatisfying, most of them. Instead, I was more intrigued by the idea of a “bottom-up” approach, a family defined by its members’ actions rather than any pre-conceptual frameworks. Though this was an interesting idea, it isn’t exactly equipped to deal with situations where it is pushed to its limits. A “bottom-up” approach to defining families may sound compelling at first, but for example, when a child is birthed into an abusive family when its parents do not want anything to do with it, the model collapses on itself, requiring a certain top-down framework for it to fall back upon. For example, even if the family is hostile, a developmental psychopathology approach detailing how the hostility would negatively impact the child’s overall life would entail the parents to act differently.
I believe that the hybrid model still falls short in the sense that it overcompensates and perhaps overrides the model. Combining with the sociological definition of a family, I instead moved to a certain top-down approach. This approach would fit the bottom-up framework of depending on the members’ experiences with each other whilst eliminating the dependence on the individuals. A family’s definition would still depend on the actions, experiences, and emotions that people have inside their times together, but these factors would have a certain threshold relative to the effectiveness or positivity of said factors. Unfortunately, this would require an additional definition of the positivity, but I believe it is much simpler than my former proposition.

6---full-notes/on-morality.title: On Morality
6---full-notes/on-morality.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy morals
On Morality
Details
“Helping is not, as conventionally thought, a charitable act that is praiseworthy to do but not wrong to omit. It is something that everyone ought to do.” — Peter Singer
Introduction
Imagine you are walking past a pond on your way to work. Suddenly, you see that in the water there is a young girl who is drowning. You could easily wade in and pull her out, your clothes would be ruined, you would be late to the bank, but these are trivial and justifiable costs against a child’s life. Almost no one would hesitate. Almost no one would say you had done anything beyond what morality demands. Here, Singer and societal intuition correlate.
Now change the scenario. The child is not in a pond no longer, she is in a village seven thousand miles away, starving slowly to death because her family cannot afford grain. You could help her just as easily, Singer argues - through a modest donation, a few minutes of your time - and the moral arithmetic would still be the same: a trivial sacrifice against a human life. Distance, as he insists, is morally irrelevant. If helping the drowning girl is obligatory, then helping the distant child must be equally so. From this foundation, Singer constructs the imperative captured in the quote above: helping is not charity, but duty, and failing to help is not merely ungenerous but wrong.
It is some of the most powerful moral argument ever conjured. Even so, I believe that there exists a fault line in Singer’s framework that goes even deeper than the question of distance. That fault line is partiality - the moral significance of our particular relationships, our situated knowledge, and the psychological mechanisms that enables us to experience, understand and feel emotions. In the following paragraphs, I will argue that Singer’s imperative, that obligation is universal and impartial, is fundamental inconceivable on the very moral grounds it is attempting to address. The argument will be developed in three stages: the epistemic asymmetry between proximate and distant helping; next, defending the psychological mechanisms that happen due to the information given priorly - something Singer would dismiss - by justifying their moral implications; and lastly, by drawing on Benard Williams to show how the moral framework Singer argues is fundamentally unjustifiable due to the impossible impartiality it demands in situations of deep personal attachment.
Understanding Singer
Singer’s quote can be distilled into three claims:

Helping is not a charitable act—that is, not a supererogatory good, something admirable but optional.
It is wrong to omit helping—not helping is a moral failure, not merely an absence of virtue.
Everyone ought to help—the obligation is universal and there are no exemptions.

The line of argument here effectively transform helping from a praiseworthy generosity into a binding moral duty. And crucially, Singer’s broader philosophical work makes clear that this duty is impartial: it does not matter whether the person who needs help is your neighbor or a stranger on another continent, your daughter or someone else’s. Suffering is suffering, and a unit of suffering alleviated is equally valuable regardless of who is alleviated or who does the alleviating.
And it is that exact impartiality that I wish to challenge.
The Epistemic Argument
Let us return to the two children - the girl drowning before your eyes and the child starving across the world. Singer claims that the moral obligation to help is practically identical. The basic epistemic position against this has been dependent on the geography and distance which is a point that Singer have rigorously retorted, and perhaps effectively as well. My position aims to address other epistemic categories rather than just the geography and uncertainty of said distance.
When you see the girl in the pond, you possess immediate, rich, first-hand knowledge of her situation. You can see that she is drowning. You can see the depth of the water, her inability to rectify herself from the situation, and the sheer emotional desperation that she shows. This inherently compels one to act to rectify the girl from her unfortunate situation and, with the epistemic conditions available, would likely bring about an excellent result.
The distant child’s case is fundamentally different - not because her suffering is any less real, but because the person’s epistemic knowledge of it is drastically impoverished. One may know abstractly that the child suffering, but there is no more information about their circumstances, not the visceral feeling that one may get from seeing suffering that is realer than anything their imagination can conjure. In addition to that, the epistemic conditions are not ideal in this situation, possibly leading to more harm being done rather than alike the situation of the girl in the pond as you are acting with far less information in practically every category.
This is not to say we have no obligation to the starving child, rather, this is to say that the differences between the two cases is morally relevant in a way Singer’s framework does not adequately knowledge. When Singer flattens these situations, he is effectively arguing for the separation of moral obligation and moral action, but the information, or lack thereof, prompts psychological mechanisms and visceral feelings that we cannot ignore.
In Defense of Psychological Mechanisms
At this point, one can anticipate Singer’s reply. He might attack the problem of the practicality of the human’s psychological mechanisms, arguing that these mechanisms are unreliable and ineffective moral tools due to their evolutionary backgrounds. And so the reason that we feel a stronger pull toward the drowning girl than the distant child is actually morally arbitrary. They are mere artifacts of our evolutionary history, calibrated for small tribal groups rather than a globalized world  in which we have the power to affect lives thousands of miles away. And so he might argue that the rational thing to do is to override these instincts and act on the nature of impartial reason.
This is a seductive argument, but I believe it is wrong by definition: psychological mechanisms are, by definition, what constitutes our morality in the first place, rather than roadblocks to achieving it. I will demonstrate so promptly.
Consider the following case - A building is on fire. Inside are two children—your own daughter and a stranger’s child. You can only save one. Who do you save?
Almost universally, people would not only understand but expect one to save their own child. Furthermore, they might even find it deeply troubling—perhaps even morally abhorrent—if you paused to perform an impartial calculation, weighing the two children’s future expected utility before deciding. The overwhelming intuition, shared across cultures and historical periods, is that you are not merely permitted to prioritizes your child but obligated to do so—that the bond between parent and child generates a special duty that no impartial calculus can override.
Singer’s framework, however, cannot accommodate this intuition. From his point of view, the values of these two children’s lives are the same, and the mere fact that one of them happens to be yours should carry no more moral significance than the color of her eyes. Alike the situation with psychological mechanisms, you should also ignore the biological implications in this one too, as Singer would claim. If you can only save one, you should—in theory—flip a coin, or perhaps choose whichever child has the greater life expectancy. The psychological agony you feel at the thought of abandoning your daughter is, on this account, just another evolutionary mechanism: powerful, perhaps, but morally irrelevant.
This is precisely where Singer’s framework begins to fall apart due to how our humanistic mechanisms conjure the love, loyalty, and fierce protectiveness that means to be a parent. These are not obstacles to our moral reasoning but what effectively constitutes them: that humans are not interchangeable units of welfare but particular persons standing in particular relationships, and that these relationships generate genuine moral obligations that an impartial framework cannot capture.
Williams, “One Thought Too Many”
It is here where Bernard William’s famous critique becomes decisive. Williams argues that if a man standing before his drowning wife and a drowning stranger must first consult his moral theory to determine whom to save—if he must think, “It is permissible to save my wife because impartial morality, properly calculated, allows for some degree of agent-relative preference”—then he has had, as Williams puts it, “one thought too many.”
This argument attacks the very structure of Singer’s framework. Williams is pointing out that Singer’s framework of impartial deliberation fails in the most basic situation that makes up our moral life and morality. Our deepest moral commitments - our children, partner, family - are not conclusions we arrive through calculation but rather ground where our moral reasoning begins. A theory that asks us to treat them as mere inputs and values to weigh against other competition is one that, in of itself, has misunderstood morality.
For me, the point can be pressed even further. Singer’s framework does not merely undervalue partiality but rather is structurally incompatible with it. This matters massively due to partiality not being an incidental feature of our closest relationships but a constitutive factor. To be a parent does not just have evolutionary or genetical implications, but also because it just is, in part, to regard your child’s welfare as carrying a weight that no impartial calculus could assign it. To be a friend just is to show up for this person in ways you would not for a stranger. Removing this partiality would fundamentally destroy the relationship itself - imagine a parent who only allocated her care to where it did the most aggregate good rather than the child in front of her - that is not parenthood at all, that is a being that has based its own life on utilitarianism caretaking.
Singer’s imperative, then, does not merely ask us to override our humanistic tendencies but asks us to inhabit a moral world where the relationships that structure human life are, at bottom, illusions—sentimental attachments to be overridden whenever impartial reason demands it. But he misunderstands that those relationships are not luxuries laid on top of morality but part of morality’s grounds. In cutting into the partial nature of relationships, Singer has, effectively, amputated the very legs that his framework stands upon.
Conclusion
None of this is to say that Singer is entire wrong. In fact, I agree with him that the conventional view of helping as mere charity is too comfortable, convenient and allows itself to too easily be used as an excuse to indifference to suffering we could alleviate. He is right that distance alone does not justify ignorance of obligation. And he is also right that we have become far too complacent with our own moral activities and the suffering of strangers.
But he is still wrong to conclude that his framework is a universal, impartial imperative. Morality is not mere math where everyone’s suffering carries a quantifiable coefficient. It derives from lived practice, shaped by relationships, knowledge, proximity and such. The psychological mechanisms that make us rush to save a drowning girl while hesitating over a distant donation are not irrational biases to be corrected but are moral responses grounded in the epistemic realities of our situation and the relational bonds that precipitate our deepest moral obligations.
To insist, as Singer does, that we ought to always help, and a failure to do so is always wrong, is to demand a kind of moral sainthood that is not only impractical but incoherent as it asks us to abandon what constitutes our morality in the first place - our partiality. And as Williams reminds us, a morality that requires us to think our way out of loving our own children is not a morality worth having. Perhaps the argument is not to unfailingly help, but to help well, to help effectively with what we know, to whom we are, and to the particular human beings whose lives are entangled with our own.

6---full-notes/on-reading-classical-scie.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading science
On reading classical scientific books
Details
You should, with no hesitation try to read at least some of these. None of them is impossibly difficult if you’re willing to put in the effort.
The most helpful advice is to state what the author has tried to solve, this has been relevant to all expository works but it is more relevant in these kinds of books rather than any else.
There is another way of saying this. As a layman, you do not read the classical scientific books to become knowledgeable in their subject matters in a contemporary sense. Instead, you read them to understand the history and philosophy of science. That, indeed, is the layman’s responsibility with regard to science. The major way in which you can discharge it is to become aware of the problems that the great scientists were trying to solve—aware of the problems, and aware, also, of the background of the problems.
To follow the strands of scientific development, to trace the ways in which facts, assumptions, principles, and proofs are interrelated, is to engage in the activity of the human reason where it has probably operated with the most success. That is enough by itself, perhaps, to justify the historical study of science. In addition, such study will serve to dispel, in some measure, the apparent unintelligibility of science. Most important of all, it is an activity of the mind that is essential to education, the central aim of which has always been recognized, from Socrates’ day down to our own, as the freeing of the mind through the discipline of wonder.

6---full-notes/on-the-definition-of-read.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading history
On the definition of reading history
Details
First of all, there is the difference between history as a fact and the history as a written record of facts. We are saying it in the latter sense, as we cannot read facts. But because of this, we made it so that there are many kinds of written records that are historical. Like a transcript of an interview or a diary, both of these reflect events that has happened and therefore a record of facts.
The sense in which we use the word “history” in what follows is both narrower and broader than any of those. It is narrower because we want to restrict ourselves to essentially narrative accounts, presented in a more or less formal manner, of a period or event or series of events in the past. This is a traditional use of the term, and we do not apologize for it. Again, as with our definition of lyric poetry, we think you will agree with us that this is the ordinary meaning of the term, and we want to stick to the ordinary here.
But our meaning is also broader than many of the definitions of the term that are current today. We think, although not all historians agree with us, that the essence of history is narration, that the last five letters of the word—“story”—help us to understand the basic meaning. Even a collection of documents, as a collection, tells a story. That story may not be explicit—that is, the historian may try not to arrange the documents in any “meaningful” order. But it is implicit in them, whether they are ordered or not. Otherwise, we think the collection would not be called as such.

6---full-notes/optimal-self-testing.title: Optimal Self-Testing
6---full-notes/optimal-self-testing.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning
Self-Testing
Details
Knowing that testing is a powerful learning method is the first step; the next is understanding how to implement it effectively. The period immediately following a learning session is a critical window for memory consolidation. Engaging in distracting activities, especially the rapid context-switching encouraged by smartphones, can actively inhibit this process and degrade what you’ve just learned. Instead, dedicating this time to immediate self-testing is a potent strategy to begin cementing knowledge and offsetting the natural curve of forgetting. The most effective forms of self-testing are not about mimicking a final exam, but about creating frequent, low-stakes opportunities for active retrieval.
The best methods are those that force you to pull information from your memory without the aid of external cues, thereby moving you from mere familiarity to true mastery. This is why open-ended, short-answer formats are so powerful. While multiple-choice questions can be useful, they sometimes only require you to recognize the correct answer, which engages the less effortful familiarity system. In contrast, having to generate the answer yourself engages the deeper, recollection-based memory system.
Excellent methods for this include:


The Blank Sheet Method: After reading a section or watching a lecture, put away your materials and write down everything you can remember on a blank sheet of paper. This is pure, un-cued recall. When you’re done, compare your sheet to the source material to identify and fill in the gaps.


The Feynman Technique: Try to explain the concept out loud in the simplest terms possible, as if you were teaching it to a child. This forces you to move beyond jargon and confront the areas where your understanding is weak. If you get stuck or have to use complicated language, you’ve found a gap in your knowledge that needs to be reviewed.


Self-Generated Questions: As you study, actively formulate questions about the material. Later, use these questions as your quiz. The act of creating the question itself is a form of learning, and answering it later solidifies the memory pathway.


The goal of these techniques isn’t to achieve a perfect score, but to embrace the struggle of retrieval. That effort is the mechanism that builds strong, durable, and flexible knowledge.

6---full-notes/optimized-repetition.title: Optimized Repetition
6---full-notes/optimized-repetition.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning
Optimized Repetition
Details
Here’s a quick rundown of what we know today about massed practice and its alternatives. Scientists will continue to deepen our understanding.
We harbor deep convictions that we learn better through single-minded focus and dogged repetition, and these beliefs are validated time and again by the visible improvement that comes during “practice-practice-practice.” But scientists call this heightened performance during the acquisition phase of a skill “momentary strength” and distinguish it from “underlying habit strength.” The very techniques that build habit strength, like spacing, interleaving, and variation, slow visible acquisition and fail to deliver the improvement during practice that helps to motivate and reinforce our efforts.
Cramming, a form of massed practice, has been likened to binge-and-purge eating. A lot goes in, but most of it comes right back out in short order. The simple act of spacing out study and practice in installments and allowing time to elapse between them makes both the learning and the memory stronger, in effect building habit strength.
“How big an interval, you ask? The simple answer: enough so that practice doesn’t become a mindless repetition. At a minimum, enough time so that a little forgetting has set in. A little forgetting between practice sessions can be a good thing, if it leads to more effort in practice, but you do not want so much forgetting that retrieval essentially involves relearning the material. The time periods between sessions of practice let memories consolidate. Sleep seems to play a large role in memory consolidation, so practice with at least a day in between sessions is good.
Something as simple as a deck of flashcards can provide an example of spacing. Between repetitions of any individual card, you work through many others. The German scientist Sebastian Leitner developed his own system for spaced practice of flashcards, known as the Leitner box. Think of it as a series of four file-card boxes. In the first are the study materials (be they musical scores, hockey moves, or Spanish vocabulary flashcards) that must be practiced frequently because you often make mistakes in them. “In the second box are the cards you’re pretty good at, and that box gets practiced less often than the first, perhaps by a half. The cards in the third box are practiced less often than those in the second, and so on. If you miss a question, make mistakes in the music, flub the one-touch pass, you move it up a box so you will practice it more often. The underlying idea is simply that the better your mastery, the less frequent the practice, but if it’s important to retain, it will never disappear completely from your set of practice boxes.
Beware of the familiarity trap: the feeling that you know something and no longer need to practice it. This familiarity can hurt you during self-quizzing if you take shortcuts. Doug Larsen says, “You have to be disciplined to say, ‘All right, I’m going to make myself recall all of this and if I don’t, what did I miss, how did I not know that?’ Whereas if you have an instructor-generated test or quiz, suddenly you have to do it, there’s an expectation, you can’t cheat, you can’t take mental shortcuts around it, you simply have to do that.”
“The nine quizzes Andy Sobel administers over the twenty-six meetings of his political economics course are a simple example of spaced retrieval practice, and of interleaving—because he rolls forward into each successive quiz questions pertaining to work from the beginning of the semester.
Interleaving two or more subjects during practice also provides a form of spacing. Interleaving can also help you develop your ability to discriminate later between different kinds of problems and select the right tool from your growing toolkit of solutions.
In interleaving, you don’t move from a complete practice set of one topic to go to another. You switch before each practice is complete. A friend of ours describes his own experience with this: “I go to a hockey class and we’re learning skating skills, puck handling, shooting, and I notice that I get frustrated because we do a little bit of skating and just when I think I’m getting it, we go to stick handling, and I go home frustrated, saying, ‘Why doesn’t this guy keep letting us do these things until we get it?’ ” This is actually the rare coach who understands that it’s more effective to distribute practice across these different “skills than polish each one in turn. The athlete gets frustrated because the learning’s not proceeding quickly, but the next week he will be better at all aspects, the skating, the stick handling, and so on, than if he’d dedicated each session to polishing one skill.
Like interleaving, varied practice helps learners build a broad schema, an ability to assess changing conditions and adjust responses to fit. Arguably, interleaving and variation help learners reach beyond memorization to higher levels of conceptual learning and application, building more rounded, deep, and durable learning, what in motor skills shows up as underlying habit strength.
Something the researchers call “blocked practice” is easily mistaken for varied practice. It’s like the old LP records that could only play their songs in the same sequence. In blocked practice, which is commonly (but not only) found in sports, a drill is run over and over. The player moves from one station to the next, performing a different maneuver at each station. That’s how the LA Kings were practicing their one-touch pass before they got religion and started changing it up. It would be like always practicing flashcards in the same order. You need to shuffle the deck.
Spacing, interleaving, and variability are natural features of how we conduct our lives. Every patient visit or football game is a test and an exercise in retrieval practice. Every routine traffic stop is a test for a cop. And every traffic stop is different, adding to a cop’s explicit and implicit memory and, if she pays attention, making her more effective in the future. The common term is “learning from experience.” Some people never seem to learn. One difference, perhaps, between those who do and don’t is whether they have cultivated the habit of reflection. Reflection is a form of retrieval practice (What happened? What did I do? How did it work out?), enhanced with elaboration (What would I do differently next time?).

6---full-notes/optimizing-learning-with-.title: Optimizing Learning with Spaced, Interleaved, and Varied Practice
6---full-notes/optimizing-learning-with-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning neuroplasticity
Enhancing Spacing with Interleaving and Variability
Details
To achieve durable and flexible learning, one must move beyond massed practice (cramming) and embrace a trio of more effective, albeit more difficult, strategies: spaced practice, interleaved practice, and varied practice. These principles introduce “desirable difficulties” that challenge the brain, leading to more robust and accessible knowledge.
1. Spaced Practice: The Principle of Timing Spaced practice involves reviewing information at increasing intervals over time. It directly combats the “forgetting curve,” the natural decay of memory. Each time you are about to forget something, forcing yourself to recall it sends a powerful signal to the brain that this information is important. This effortful retrieval strengthens the memory trace, making it more durable and easier to access in the future. The goal is not to review constantly, but to review at the optimal moment of near-forgetting.
2. Interleaved Practice: The Principle of Mixing Topics Interleaving involves mixing practice on several different skills or topics within a single study session. Instead of practicing AAA, then BBB, then CCC (blocked practice), you practice ABCABCABC. This prevents the mind from settling into a comfortable, automated routine. Each switch forces the brain to abandon the previous context and actively discriminate which strategy or information is needed. This process feels harder and slower than blocked practice, but it leads to superior long-term retention and the ability to apply knowledge outside the structured context in which it was learned.
3. Varied Practice: The Principle of Mixing Contexts Varied practice applies to learning a single skill but practicing it under a variety of different conditions. For example, instead of practicing a tennis serve from the exact same spot every time, a player would practice from slightly different locations, with different levels of fatigue, or under different weather conditions. This helps the brain develop a more robust and flexible “schema” for the skill, rather than a rigid motor program. It allows the learner to adapt and apply the skill effectively in novel situations that don’t perfectly match the initial training environment.
Together, these three practices build knowledge that is not just memorized, but deeply understood, flexible, and readily available when needed.

6---full-notes/optimizing-the-sleep-envi.title: Optimizing the Sleep Environment with Cool Temperatures
6---full-notes/optimizing-the-sleep-envi.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sleep 3 - Tags/environment
Optimizing the Sleep Environment with Cool Temperatures
Details
Maintaining a cool sleeping environment is a foundational element for achieving high-quality, uninterrupted sleep. The principle is based on a critical physiological requirement: to fall and stay in the deeper stages of sleep, your core body temperature must drop by approximately 1 to 3 degrees Celsius. A cool room directly facilitates this necessary process.
The body has specialized portals for efficient heat exchange located on the glabrous (hairless) skin of the palms, the bottoms of the feet, and the upper half of the face. Sleeping in a cool room allows you to use these portals for thermoregulation throughout the night. If you become too warm under blankets, you can instinctively expose a hand or foot to the cool air, rapidly releasing heat and maintaining the optimal temperature for sleep.
Conversely, if the room itself is too warm, there are very few effective ways to cool down once you’ve pushed off the blankets. This often leads to overheating, which is a primary cause of waking up in the middle of the night. Therefore, creating a cool ambient temperature (e.g., with a fan, open window, or smart mattress cover) and using blankets for insulation provides a far more dynamic and effective system for thermoregulation than sleeping in a warm room.

Origin of Guilt
Details
Nietzsche further challenges the assumption that “Guilt” is a fundamentally moral or religious concept. Instead, through etymological analysis, he asserts that it originates from the material concept of Debt, which originated from the relationship of the buyer and seller. Nietzsche posited that the most primordial, aboriginal human relationship is commercial exchange, which is an empirical mistake, referenced from David Graeber’s book: Debt: The First 5000 Years, where people mostly engaged in unequal exchanges.
As mentioned in The Phenomenology of Bad Conscience, we as humans are able to make deals and bind ourselves to the future, and this arises in the relationship between creditor and debtor, if the latter cannot pay the former, how is the balance restored ? Nietzsche argues that early justice was based on an equivalence principle: Pain is a currency. If the debtor is insolvent, the creditor is granted the right to inflict a specific quantum of pain on the debtor’s body (e.g., cutting off a pound of flesh, torture, imprisonment). This pain provides the creditor with a psychological “repayment”—the pleasure of cruelty, the “festival” of exercising power over another.

Other Dementias
Details
Other than Alzheimer’s, there are some other types of dementia out there such as frontotemporal dementia, vascular dementia, and dementia with Lewy Bodies. The following paragraphs below will offer a quick explanation for each of them.
First off, the frontotemporal dementia, or just FTD. It is caused by a loss of neurons in the frontal and temporal regions of the brain, this causes the deterioration to mainly be in those areas. It can start to as early as in the 30s, to the mid-late 50s, and unlike Alzheimer’s which patients can live for a couple decades, people with FTD only live 5-10 years, though the effects are much less annoying in this type of dementia. Unlike Alzheimer’s, people with this dementia only experience deterioration in their empathy, executive function, ability to inhibit behavior, hyperorality, and apathy. Usually, this type of dementia damages others relationship and emotional processes more than Alzheimer’s. Physical illnesses and diseases can cause this type of dementia.
Vascular dementia, similar to FTD, is caused by diseases as well, specifically cerebrovascular disease. Most commonly, the person has had a sequence of strokes forming a clot, impairing circulation and causing cell death. And then with the strokes repeating, the person gets more and more chances of getting vascular dementia.
Last but not least, dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), which can be divided further into two subtypes, depending on the presence of Parkinson’s disease in the patient. About 80 percent of people with it will develop DLB, but some people without it can develop DLB as well. The symptoms are difficult to differentiate from Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s.

6---full-notes/other-ways-of-administrat.title: Other ways of administrations
6---full-notes/other-ways-of-administrat.content:
Status: adult
Tags: pharmacology biology
Other ways of administrations
Details
The term “parenteral” literally translates to “beyond the intestine,” defining a category of pharmacological administration that fundamentally alters the efficiency and experience of a substance. Unlike the common oral route, which forces a drug to navigate the hostile acidity of the stomach and the metabolic gatekeeping of the liver, parenteral pathways offer a direct line to systemic circulation. When a substance is swallowed, the liver’s “first-pass metabolism” can neutralize a massive percentage of the active dose before it ever reaches the brain, creating a delayed and often unpredictable onset. By sidestepping this biological filter, parenteral methods ensure that the drug arrives faster, cleaner, and with significantly higher potency.
The most immediate of these pathways utilize the body’s highly vascularized mucous membranes. Intraoral or sublingual administration capitalizes on the rich capillary networks lining the mouth and under the tongue. Here, a substance diffuses directly into the bloodstream, draining into the superior vena cava and bypassing the liver entirely. This results in a sharp, distinct onset within roughly three minutes, avoiding the gastrointestinal distress often associated with oral ingestion. Similarly, intranasal insufflation leverages the moist, blood-vessel-rich nasal mucosa to achieve a comparable speed. Contrary to the popular myth that snorting sends substances directly to the brain via the olfactory nerve, the drug actually travels a rapid systemic loop through the heart and lungs before reaching the brain. Despite this detour, the massive surface area for absorption creates a characteristic “rush”—a spike in plasma concentration that oral dosing simply cannot replicate.
For situations where these routes are unviable, rectal administration offers a potent, albeit socially stigmatized, alternative. The anatomy of the rectum is unique; while the upper veins drain to the liver, the middle and lower veins bypass it, offering high bioavailability and an onset of approximately three minutes. This makes it invaluable when oral intake is impossible due to vomiting. In stark contrast to these rapid-onset methods, transdermal administration utilizes the skin not for speed, but for sustainment. Patches allow drugs to slowly permeate the lipid layers of the skin, providing a steady, plateau-like release over hours rather than minutes. Ultimately, the distinction between enteral and parenteral is the difference between a winding scenic route and a direct highway; by removing the variables of digestion, these pathways transform the physiological experience from a slow accumulation into an efficient, immediate shift.

6---full-notes/ovarian-hormones-and-fema.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology biology
Ovarian Hormones and Female Depression
Details
Fluctuations in ovarian hormones, specifically estrogen and progesterone, are strongly linked to the higher incidence of depression in women. Women are roughly twice as likely as men to be diagnosed with major depression, and this risk is not constant throughout life. Instead, it spikes during periods of significant hormonal change.
Key periods of vulnerability include:


Puberty


The perimenstrual phase (the time before and during menstruation)


Perimenopause


Postpartum (after childbirth)


The link is most stark in postpartum depression. The dramatic crash in progesterone levels immediately following childbirth is a major biological trigger for a depressive episode in susceptible individuals. Sapolsky highlights that this connection is so clear that new antidepressant medications have been developed to specifically target this hormonal pathway.
This hormonal link provides powerful evidence that the sex difference in depression rates is not merely a social or psychological phenomenon, but is rooted in fundamental biological differences.
