6---full-notes/overcoming-attentional-bl.title: Overcoming Attentional Blinks with Open Monitoring
6---full-notes/overcoming-attentional-bl.content:
Status: teen
Tags: ADHD focus
Overcoming Attentional Blinks with Open Monitoring
Details
A significant barrier to sustained focus is a cognitive glitch known as an “attentional blink.” This occurs when, after successfully identifying a target of our focus, our brain momentarily shuts down its attention, causing us to miss information that appears immediately afterward. This phenomenon is a key reason why we feel distractible; our focus isn’t just wandering, it’s actively blinking off. Individuals with ADHD may experience these blinks more frequently, but it is a universal aspect of how our attention system works. It’s as if our brain celebrates finding what it’s looking for with a brief pause, during which we become blind to new information.
A powerful, non-pharmacological method to counteract this is to consciously shift our mode of visual processing. Typically, we focus with a narrow, “soda straw” view of the world. The alternative is to engage in open monitoring, also known as panoramic vision. This involves deliberately dilating your gaze to take in your entire visual field at once—the walls, the ceiling, the floor—without focusing on any single point. This wide-angle view activates a different neural stream in the brain that is better at processing information over time, effectively increasing its “frame rate.” By practicing this open-gaze state, you can train your brain to reduce the frequency and duration of attentional blinks, leading to a more stable and continuous state of focus.

6---full-notes/pet-method.title: PET method
6---full-notes/pet-method.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neurology Cognitive Psychology
PET as a method
Details
Positron Emission Tomography records blood flow and brain metabolism, specifically glucose. A radioisotope is a chemical element that emits radiation, including positrons, as it decays into a more stable form. These emitted positrons combine with nearby electrons, resulting in the emission of gamma rays which can be detected by a machine. In a typical procedure, the subject’s head is surrounded by gamma ray detectors. When two gamma rays are recorded at the same time by opposing detectors, the point of origin is pinpointed as the spot halfway between them. This method produces a multitude of observations, particularly in research experiments where numerous events are recorded. All of these responses are then averaged to acquire a single, consolidated dataset that is used for statistical analysis. Many PET research experiments involve many subjects or many trials to get more reliable results.

Status: teen

PTSD as a violation of Human’s Rights
Details
Dr. Darren Richiter’s lecture reframes Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) not merely as a medical diagnosis but as a direct, measurable damage resulting from a crime. Unlike most psychiatric disorders in the DSM, PTSD is one of the few that requires a specific external cause (Criterion A). In the context of Dr. Richiter’s work with refugees and survivors, this cause is invariably a human rights violation such as torture, genocide, or other war crimes.
This crucial link between the crime (the cause) and the psychological injury (the effect) allows for a powerful shift in legal strategy. It enables the use of psychiatric epidemiology—population-level data on mental health—as formal evidence in international criminal tribunals. By demonstrating a statistically significant increase in PTSD prevalence in a post-conflict population, such as in Cambodia after the Khmer Rouge regime, prosecutors can quantify the immense psychological harm inflicted upon an entire people. This approach transforms the abstract concept of “suffering” into concrete, scientific evidence that can influence judgments, strengthen the case for crimes against humanity, and contribute to sentencing, as was successfully done in the Khmer Rouge tribunal.

Pairs and Cartesian Products
Details
Mathematics also requires structure where order matters, this is achievable for the Ordered pair <a, b>. Unlike sets, where \{a, b\} = \{b, a\}, an ordered pair strictly distinguishes the first element from the second. The Law of Ordered Pairs states that <a, b> = <c, d> if and only if a=c and b=d.
This is the bridge between abstract algebra and geometry. By associating the geometric points with ordered pair of numbers, distinct mathematical fields can merge. This concept scales up to ordered n-tuples. The set of all possible ordered pairs between two sets A and B is the Cartesian Product (A \times B). If set A has 2 elements and set B has 3, their Cartesian product contains 6 ordered pairs, creating a “grid” of all possible combinations.

6---full-notes/panic-disorder.title: Panic Disorder
6---full-notes/panic-disorder.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology
Panic Disorder
Details
Panic Disorder is defined by the experience of recurrent, unexpected panic attacks—sudden, intense episodes of terror that manifest in severe physical symptoms like shortness of breath, chest pain, and a feeling of impending death. Initially, these attacks are not directed at a specific trigger. However, the debilitating and frightening nature of the attacks often leads to a secondary, learned fear. There are physical symptoms such as labored breathing, heart palpitations, nausea, upset stomach, chest pain, feelings of choking and smothering, dizziness, lightheadedness, sweating, chills, heat sensations, and trembling. Other psychological symptoms may include depersonalization and derealization; and fears of losing control, going crazy. All of these symptoms mean that people will likely try to escape the situation they are in. They also come rapidly and reach a peak of intensity in about 10 minutes of the panic attack.
This is due to a misunderstanding of the fear system, it misidentifies that it is in danger and causes the sympathetic nervous system to arouse and makes the whole body go into panic mode. There are also things called cues, which are signs that triggers the panic attacks, cued panic attacks usually relate back to a phobia.
The complication of the panic disorder can bring phobias into the equation, they will become fearful of the situations where they get panic attacks, like situations of being seen, like being in public when it happens, which is called Agoraphobia. These fears only gauge the feeling of panic more, creating a debilitating cycle where the person avoids public life to prevent a potential panic attack. Treatment often involves antidepressants to reduce the frequency of attacks and cognitive therapy to break the association between public spaces and the experience of panic.

6---full-notes/paradoxical-sadness.title: Paradoxical Sadness
6---full-notes/paradoxical-sadness.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology CBT
Paradoxical Sadness
Details
Although sadness is ubiquitous, it is also at times puzzling as we cannot fully understand why one is sad. Similarly in situations where people actually gained something in their domain by attaining some long-awaited goal, their dominant interpretation was that they actually lost something.
It is actually simple to observe how these situations can be interpreted at a lost and can lead to a devaluation of the domain. Some of the kinds of events that may do so can be categorized as follows:
Loss of a tangible object that is considered a source of gratification or is valued.
An intangible loss such as the diminished self-esteem produced by an insult or disparagement.
A reversal in the value of a component of the domain; for example, what was regarded as an asset is now judged negatively.
A discrepancy between what is expected and what is actually received.
A fantasy or expectation of a future loss: They ten to live through this loss as if it was actually happening in the moment, so they experience the sadness before it occurs.
Hypothetical loss: “Loss that could happen”
Pseudo loss: The person incorrectly perceives an event as subtracting from his domain.
Moving on, actual loss may refer to the deprivation of something tangible and definable. An intangible loss, like the loss of another person’s affection, may produce the same feeling. Similarly, a reversal in a person’s evaluation of their own attribute may also result the same way.
The intensity of the sense of loss is proportional to the devaluation of the attribute rather than its “max value”. The ideation in unfulfilled expectations and disappointment also incorporates the theme of loss and triggers sadness. When a person expects something to be given to him, he takes a title to it, as it were his. If he doesn’t actually receive it though, the he may experience as much sadness as if he did receive it and lost it. Intense disappointment happens despite the unrealistic expectation.
And so on, so on…

6---full-notes/paranoid-state.title: Paranoid state
6---full-notes/paranoid-state.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology
Paranoid state
Details
The paranoid patient perseverates in assuming that other people are deliberately abusing him or interfering with his objectives. Unlike the depressed patient who feels that supposed insults or rejections are justified, the paranoid patient is preoccupied with the idea that an injustice has been done. The main theme in his thinking is “I am right, he is wrong,” in contrast to the depressed patient who follows the theme, “I am wrong, he is right.” Unlike depressed patients, the paranoid patient does not experience any lowering of his self-esteem. He is more concerned with the injustice of the attack on his domain than with the actual loss to his domain.
Differences among anxiety neurosis, neurotic depression, and paranoid state may be summarized as follows: The anxious patient focuses on the possibility of an attack; the paranoid patient concentrates on the injustice or malevolent motives behind a supposed attack or infringement on his boundaries; the depressed patient focuses on the presumed loss he attributes to some inadequacy of his own.

6---full-notes/payoffs-define-the-game.content:
Status: adult

Payoffs define the game
Details
Choices and outcomes alone don’t make a game. The game’s outcome matrix says who can choose what and which grades follow. It cannot be analyzed and strategized until you know the payoffs: what each player is trying to achieve, selfish or not. Once the payoffs are fixed, then the questions can change to what people should do. Then game theory is purely a tool to tell you how to get it.
Keep the same outcomes, change the payoffs, and you get a different game. Polak’s “indignant angels” still like good grades, but two things cost them:

An A won at a partner’s expense costs them guilt, so 3 becomes −1.
A C caused by a partner’s defection costs them indignation, so −1 becomes −3.

Now nothing dominates. α is the better reply to α, and β is the better reply to β. This is a coordination problem. Both (α, α) and (β, β) are stable, since at either one neither player gains by switching alone, and both players prefer (β, β). The class split along two sensible rules. α protects the worst case (−1 rather than −3), while β goes for the best case (1 rather than 0). So moral feeling doesn’t guarantee cooperation. It removes defection’s dominance, which makes cooperation depend on what you expect the other person to do.
And so, in this situation, you would have to take into account the other person’s perspective and work out what they will do. And so we will be able to see why:

A purely self-interested player (an “evil git”) facing an angel still plays α. α still dominates for them, so the partner’s payoffs don’t matter.
An angel who knows they face a git has no dominant strategy. But they can see that the git’s α dominates, so they expect α and reply with α.

6---full-notes/penalty-kick-game.title: Penalty kick game
6---full-notes/penalty-kick-game.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics math
Penalty kick game
Details
In Polak’s penalty-kick game, the shooter kicks Left, Middle or Right, and the goalie dives Left or Right (for now the goalie can’t stay put). The shooter’s payoff is the chance of scoring, written in tens, so 4 means 40%. The goalie’s payoff is the negative of the shooter’s. Rows are the shooter’s kicks and columns are the goalie’s dive; the table shows only the shooter’s payoff:
Goalie dives Left	Goalie dives Right

Kick Left	4	9
Kick Middle	6	6
Kick Right	9	4
Nothing is dominated. Compare within each column:
•	Against a goalie diving Left, Right is best (9), then Middle (6), then Left (4).
•	Against a goalie diving Right, the order flips.

So Middle beats Left in the first column but loses to it in the second, and the same goes for Middle against Right. The class split roughly evenly among the three kicks.
Best responses get further. Let p be the chance you give the goalie diving Right. Each kick’s expected payoff is then a line in p:
•	Left: 4 + 5p, rising from 4 to 9.
•	Middle: 6, flat.
•	Right: 9 − 5p, falling from 9 to 4.

Chance goalie dives Right (p)	Left	Middle	Right	Best response
0	4	6	9	Right
1/2	6.5	6	6.5	Left and Right tie
1	9	6	4	Left
Left and Right cross at p = ½, where each is worth 6.5. Whichever of the two is higher is never below 6.5, while Middle is stuck at 6. So Right is the best response when p < ½, Left is the best response when p > ½, and Middle is the best response to no belief at all.
So the lesson? Don’t kick to the middle cause it’s never the best. Threshold is always fulfilled by the two options anyways.
What the model leaves out, per the class:
•	Footedness. Kicking across your body, to your "natural side," is easier. For a right-footer, that's the goalie's right.
•	The goalie can stay in the middle. This is left for the problem set.
•	Height. The kick can go high or low.
•	Power versus placement. See below.

One suggested gap isn’t a real one: timing. Whenever the decision is made, neither player sees the other’s choice in time, so the game works as simultaneous.
Real data come from Chiappori and co-authors (AER, 2002), drawn half from the Italian league and half from the French. The sides are relabeled as the kicker’s natural side and the other side:
Goalie dives to kicker's natural side	Goalie dives to other side

Kick to natural side	63.6%	94.4%
Kick to other side	89.3%	43.7%
The natural side is easier. When the goalie guesses correctly, a natural-side kick still scores 63.6% of the time, against 43.7% for the other side. But nothing is dominated:
•	Against a goalie diving to the natural side, kicking the other way is better (89.3 vs 63.6).
•	Against a goalie diving the other way, the natural side is better (94.4 vs 43.7).

Polak’s made-up numbers were close. But again, there are many more factors affecting the chances such as the player’s habits and abilities.

Pendulation
Details
The adrenaline that the body pumps out during stressful situations usually help the person to do something to deal with a disaster. But those who are traumatized, the adrenaline usually just fuels their reactions to trauma, tiring them out completely, leaving them unable to do anything.
In order to return to proper functioning, this has to stop, the body needs to be restored to its normal state of safety and relaxation and then it can mobilize to take action in response to danger.
To deal with this issue, treatments usually include approaching what has happened and taking a backseat to explore the physical sensations and the imprints of trauma on the body. Patients are helped to build up their resilience to safely access these sensations and emotions that overwhelmed them at the time, which helps them expand their window of tolerance. Moreover, allowing the actions that patients did at the time to protect themselves to finish is a good way for them to be able to transform the energy from adrenaline that fuel their traumatic responses into energy for them to utilize and fight back.

6---full-notes/perceived-brightness-is-r.title: Perceived Brightness is Relative, Not Absolute
6---full-notes/perceived-brightness-is-r.content:
Status: baby
Tags: neuroscience psychology
Perception and Recognizing Patterns
Details
Our perception of how bright an object is does not depend solely on the intensity of the light it reflects. Instead, the brain determines brightness through comparison with the surrounding environment. This phenomenon is known as brightness contrast. An object can appear lighter or darker depending on the brightness of the objects or background it is compared against.
For example, two bars of the exact same color and light intensity will appear to have different brightness levels if one is placed against a dark background and the other against a light one. This demonstrates that perception is an active calculation based on context, not a passive reception of raw data. The brain interprets the pattern of light by considering past experiences and contextual clues to infer the most likely reality.

6---full-notes/personalization.title: Personalization
6---full-notes/personalization.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology
Personalization
Details
In the argument of humanity in philosophy, the inevitable egocentricity of man has been debated for ages. In a sense, everybody seems to have a private world of which he is the axis. Nonetheless, people are still generally capable of making judgements that are separate, objective from their relevancy and emotions in the event. In psychiatric disorders though, these thoughts become unusually compelling and may completely displace the objective judgements. That is what we call “personalization.”
This process can be illustrated by a few extreme examples: specifically, patients who fall into the loose category of “psychotic.”. A paranoid schizophrenic patient believed that the images he saw on the television screen were talking directly to him, and he did so to them. A psychotic depressive heard about an epidemic of an infectious disease in a distant land and blamed himself for having caused it. In conclusion, psychotic patients consistently interpret events totally unrelated to them as though it was caused by them or at least directed at them.
Neurotic patients on the other hand experience less extreme forms of self-reference. They tend to overestimate and be excessively absorbed in it. For example, a mother blames herself for every single error that is apparent in her children, a man seeing another expressing disgust for him interprets that everyone will feel the same way as well.

There are always multiple, often opposite, perspectives from which to view any given problem or obligation. Merely taking a moment to consciously change that perspective can result in a dramatically better mood and provide more encouragement to do the work. For example, changing the internal narrative from “I have to wake up early to work out” to “I get to wake up early and build my physical strength” shifts the task from a burden to an opportunity. This simple cognitive reframe can be enough to overcome initial resistance.

Persuasion in practicality
Details
Propaganda exists in every book, this is because your judgement of if a practical book is good or not is if it solves your problems. And so the author must be able to persuade you that his method is achieving the goal that you are trying to get to. This is not wrong, although it is not optimal in your reading, it isn’t wrong. But we still are trying to read the best as possible, and so we must recognize it.
The method to not fall for propaganda is to recognize it, as usually it is made for you to not even know that you’ve swallowed it. Now comes to the propositions and terms, if someone who has good use of these, he will know which passages that make an “emotive use of words”. And so he can do something about those appeals. This is good, but the opposite can also be detrimental, being too harsh and removing all emotive context of a piece of writing is being deaf to all appeals, which is the whole point of practical books.
A further point (still relative), is that these “emotive use of words” also projects the author’s personality. It allows us to see what kind of man he is through his moral treatise, a political tract,…

6---full-notes/pessimism-in-depression.title: Pessimism in Depression
6---full-notes/pessimism-in-depression.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology
Pessimism in Depression
Details
In one way or another, we as humans, are living in the future. We interpret our experience not just by what the event means in the current state but as well as its possible results/consequences. For example, a young man just received a compliment from his girl, he would look forward to receiving more, might even think “she likes me,” and he foresees a more intimate relationship with her. But if he is disappointed or rejected, he will likely anticipate future relationships alike this one.
Depressed patients have this even worse, as they tend to overgeneralize and be extreme. Since the patients regard the future as an extension of the present, they expect a deprivation to continue permanently, as it is always in absolute statements. Another way depression can develop pessimism is in the presumed deficiency of the self, which he also likely regards as a permanent defect.
Pessimism can engulf not only the future, but also the present of the patient. As they already expect themselves to not have the ability to do it before even indulging in it. It may even become so strong that the patient, even experiencing the success in something, still thinks they cannot do it the next time, ignoring the small “wins.”

6---full-notes/philosophical-methodologi.title: Philosophical methodologies
6---full-notes/philosophical-methodologi.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading philosophy
Philosophical methodologies
Details
Philosophy is not just “pure” speculation, which means thinking without experience. There are stringent tests of the validity of these answers. Although these tests are based on common experience alone - the experience you have because that you are a human being, not a philosopher.
The only difference is that philosopher has thought about these questions extremely well and formulated the most penetrating questions that could be asked about and took their time developing answers. And they’ve done so by thinking more profoundly about the experience than the rest of us.
Understanding this is not enough. We must also realize that not all of the questions that philosophers have asked and tried to answer are truly philosophical. They themselves were not always aware of this, and their ignorance or mistake in this crucial respect can cause unperceptive readers considerable difficulty. To avoid such difficulties, it is necessary to be able to distinguish the truly philosophical questions from the other questions that a philosopher may deal with, but that he should have waived and left for later scientific investigation to answer. The philosopher was misled by failing to see that such questions can be answered by scientific investigation, though he probably could not have known this at the time of his writing.
And so to distinguish between these things we merely have to differentiate between problems that can be tested and do in our normal lives and those that we must only think about to do so.
A good theoretical book in philosophy is as free from oratory and propaganda as a good scientific treatise. So that you will not have to worry about the author’s personality, or investigate his background. Though it may be of great use still so see other points of view of people who have tried to tackle the same problems as they will usually converse.
It should not trouble you if philosophers disagree, for two reasons. First is that even if they disagree, they persistently do so, may point to a great unsolved or even insolvable problem. (Which is good). Secondly, the disagreements of others are relatively unimportant, your responsibility is to make up your on mind, so don’t get swayed by others, make up your own mind.
The grounds of philosophy is that everyone must answer for himself. Taking side with the opinions of others (without evidence), is evading the question. And so your answers must be solidly grounded, with arguments to back them up. This is different from science as you cannot rely on experts, only yourselves.
The reason is that these questions are more important than the questions of anyone else, except children.

6---full-notes/philosophy-as-a-science.content:

Philosophy As A Science
Details
Philosophy isn’t necessarily the first subject, even as all subjects have derived from it. Philosophy is still governed by the laws of our universe which means the studies of said variables would at the end, rule above it. But nonetheless, it is where all the other sciences are born. As J.L. Austin metaphorically described, philosophy is the “initial central sun,” a tumultuous body that throws off cooled, regulated planets that become independent sciences. When a subject is unrecognized, people do not have the vocabulary and such for it, the subject will likely reside in philosophy, but when it does, they will separate into a distinct science, as happened with mathematics, psychology, physics, and linguistics. Logic is a unique case in this sense, as it is seeing its migration out of philosophy, though only part of it, deductive reasoning, while inductive logic remains distinct.

Phobia

The anticipation of physical or psychological harm is confined to definable situations. If the patient can avoid such situations, then he does not feel threatened and may be tranquil. But if he may enter these situations perhaps out of necessity or their own desire to overcome it, he will experience the general effects of the anxiety-neurotic. The symptoms may include: intense anxiety, rapid breathing, palpitations, abdominal pains, difficulty in concentration and recall. Yet some find that their distress is milder than they expected - much less than what their avoidance warranted. Despite this very bland expression, they may still try to avoid it nonetheless. And reintegration or attempts to face the phobia does not help reduce any of the symptoms nor avoidance.
As said before of the anxiety-neurotic, a patient can experience these symptoms anywhere from mere verbal form or in some form of imagery. 6---full-notes/photoreceptors-=-cones.title: Photoreceptors = Cones
6---full-notes/photoreceptors-=-cones.content:
Status: baby

Photoreceptors = Cones
Details
In stark contrast to rods, cones are the photoreceptors that give our visual world its vibrancy and sharpness. They are responsible for our vision in bright light, allowing us to perceive both fine detail and the full spectrum of color. Though they are far less numerous than rods, with only about 6 million in each retina, their influence is immense. Cones are densely concentrated in the center of the retina, particularly in the fovea. Their ability to perceive color comes from three distinct types, each tuned to a different wavelength of light, corresponding roughly to blue, green, and red. This specialization for detail and color makes them essential for tasks like reading and recognizing faces.

6---full-notes/photoreceptors-=-rods.title: Photoreceptors = Rods
6---full-notes/photoreceptors-=-rods.content:
Status: baby
Tags: psychology neuroscience
Photoreceptors = Rods
Details
Rods are the workhorses of our visual system, responsible for our ability to see in low-light conditions. These photoreceptors, numbering around 120 million and making up about 95% of all receptors in the retina, are incredibly sensitive to faint light. They are most abundant in the periphery of our vision, which is why we can often detect a dim star at night by looking slightly to the side of it. However, this sensitivity comes at a cost: rods do not detect color and provide poor detail. Their strength lies in their collective action, as many rods pool their signals to a single downstream neuron to detect even the faintest glimmer of light.

Physical Abuse to Externalizing Problems

Physical abuse usually leads to externalizing problems alike ODD, traits like aggression. 6---full-notes/physical-disorders-with-a.title: Physical Disorders with a psychological overlay
6---full-notes/physical-disorders-with-a.content:
Status: adult
Tags: physiology psychology
Physical Disorders with a psychological overlay
Details
A compelling body of research demonstrates that a significant psychological overlay can influence the onset, exacerbation, and experience of physical disorders. This psychosomatic perspective, which gained considerable traction in the mid-20th century, posits that emotional states are not merely secondary reactions to illness but can be integral to its physiological manifestation. Pioneering studies from that era, such as those by Dudley, Martin, and Holmes (1964) on respiratory function and Katcher (1969) on cardiovascular conditions, laid the groundwork for our current understanding of the intricate relationship between the mind and body.
The work of Dudley, Martin, and Holmes was groundbreaking in its direct observation of how psychological stimuli could elicit profound physiological changes in the respiratory system. Their research, which included inducing emotional states and pain through hypnosis, revealed that subjective experiences could directly alter respiratory patterns, including ventilation and gas exchange. This provided empirical evidence that feelings and thoughts could have a tangible and measurable impact on the body’s vital functions. For individuals with underlying respiratory conditions, this suggests that psychological distress could be a significant factor in triggering or worsening their symptoms.
Similarly, research into cardiovascular disorders has consistently highlighted the detrimental effects of psychological stress. While Katcher’s 1969 work contributed to the broader understanding of hemodynamic changes, subsequent and more extensive research has firmly established that chronic stress, anxiety, and depression are significant risk factors for heart disease. These psychological states can lead to a cascade of physiological responses, including increased heart rate, elevated blood pressure, and higher levels of inflammatory markers, all of which contribute to the pathogenesis of cardiovascular ailments.
These examples underscore a fundamental principle of psychosomatic medicine: the artificial separation of mind and body can be a significant impediment to holistic health. A physical disorder with a psychological overlay is not to suggest the illness is “all in one’s head,” but rather to acknowledge that emotional and psychological factors can be powerful modulators of physiological processes. This integrated perspective is crucial for developing more effective treatment strategies that address both the physical symptoms and the underlying psychological contributors, ultimately leading to more comprehensive patient care.

6---full-notes/physicalism-is-about-bodi.title: Physicalism is about bodies, not persons
6---full-notes/physicalism-is-about-bodi.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy death
Physicalism is about bodies, not persons
Details
This clarification that carries all the weight: “just a body” is not “just any old body.” Chalk, a phone, and a person are all material objects with wildly unequal repertoires. The physicalist is not saying persons are as inert as chalk; he is betting that nothing in the human repertoire requires a second kind of stuff. So the thesis is ambitious about matter and what it can do, not deflationary about persons.
This matters because the instinctive resistance — I am not just meat — is aimed at a deflationary reading nobody defends. Whatever is genuinely hard about physicalism (consciousness, the felt quality of experience) has to be stated as a claim that some specific capacity outruns what any physical system could do. For whatever reason something that we possess are different, basically.
Two branches Kagan names and sets aside: idealism (minds and their ideas exist; matter is a way of talking about them) and the dual-aspect view (mind and body are two views of an underlying reality that is neither). Worth registering that this is a pragmatic narrowing, not a refutation. Both of these can be true, its just not argued in the course.

6---full-notes/piaget's-stages-of-cognit.title: Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development
6---full-notes/piaget's-stages-of-cognit.content:
Status: adult
Tags: developmental psychology Cognitive Psychology
Piaget’s Developmental Theory
Details
Jean Piaget’s influential theory proposes that children progress through four distinct stages of cognitive development. He believed that children are active “little scientists” who construct their understanding of the world through their experiences. Each stage is characterized by a qualitatively different way of thinking and perceiving the world.
1. Sensorimotor Stage (Birth to ~2 years) During this initial stage, infants and toddlers build their understanding of the world primarily through sensory experiences (seeing, hearing) and physical actions (touching, moving). Children in this stage may think that their parents disappear from the world if they close their eyes.

Key Achievement: The most significant milestone is developing object permanence—the understanding that objects continue to exist even when they cannot be seen, heard, or touched. Before this, it’s “out of sight, out of mind.”

2. Preoperational Stage (~2 to ~7 years) This stage is marked by the development of language and symbolic thought, but the child’s logic is not yet fully developed.


Symbolic Function: Children begin to use symbols (words, images) to represent objects and ideas. This is evident in their pretend play.


Egocentrism: The child has difficulty taking the perspective of others. They assume that other people see, think, and feel exactly as they do.


Centration: They tend to focus on only one aspect of a situation at a time, ignoring other relevant features. This leads to errors in logic, such as failing to understand conservation.


Lack of Conservation: This is a classic hallmark of the stage. A child will believe that a tall, thin glass holds more water than a short, wide one, even after seeing the water poured from one to the other. They are centering on the height of the water and ignoring the width.


3. Concrete Operational Stage (~7 to ~11 years) Children’s thinking becomes much more logical and organized, but it is still limited to concrete, physical objects and events.


Logical Thought: They can now reason logically about concrete events and understand the concept of conservation (the idea that quantity remains the same despite changes in appearance).


Reversibility: They understand that actions can be reversed (e.g., 2 + 3 = 5 is the same as 5 - 3 = 2).


Decentering: They can consider multiple aspects of a problem at once, which allows them to solve conservation tasks.


Limitation: Their reasoning is still tied to the physical world. They struggle with abstract or hypothetical concepts.


4. Formal Operational Stage (~12 years and up) This is the final stage, where adolescents and adults develop the ability to think about abstract concepts and reason hypothetically.


Abstract Reasoning: They can think about abstract ideas like justice, morality, and freedom.


Hypothetical-Deductive Reasoning: They can systematically think about multiple variables, formulate hypotheses (“what if…”), and consider all possible outcomes to solve a problem. This allows for advanced scientific reasoning and problem-solving.

Pluralist Theory
Details
As a direct critique to the Power Elite Theory, this argues that the power is distributed amongst groups as they compete against each other, with different views, needs, and so on.
Pioneered by Robert Dahl in his study of New Haven (Who Governs), the research methods start from the political decisions then tracing back to those who make such decisions and understanding them. Dahl found out that different groups had parts in different kinds of politics, for example, parents and teachers mattered in school politics; real estate developers and banks were central to urban renewal; and party activists were key in selecting political candidates. There was no single group that dominated across all issue areas.
Most people don’t care about most political issues. People and groups mobilize around issues that directly affect their interests (“whose ox gets gored”). The group that cares the most about a specific issue (e.g., gun rights advocates, abortion opponents) will have a disproportionate influence on that issue because of their intense focus and mobilization.
Same with Power Elite Theory, there are drawbacks. Changes cannot be made easily as acceptance needs to be gained from many groups, but they can also be stopped easily because of the same nature. These people also only care about what really matters to them and mobilize to do so, and then so would vote for those who are going to mobilize and promise to manage their causes.

6---full-notes/polarized-thinking.title: Polarized Thinking
6---full-notes/polarized-thinking.content:
Status:
Tags: psychology
Polarized Thinking
Details
The neurotic patient may be prone to thinking in extremes in situations that impinge on his sensitive areas, which is in his domain. Events are labeled very simply, it is all in black and white, Good or Bad. This characteristic has been termed “dichotomous thinking” or “bipolar thinking”. But in these patients, the absolute terms that couch this kind of thinking are “always” and “never.”
An example is of a Valorant player, in a game, if he scores less than 500 points on his tracker score or even less, he might scold himself for being so bad and that he cannot rank up, but if he scores 600 or more consistently, he will regard himself as having the ability to climb through the ranks and that he is not deserving of the current predicament he is in. This is like a loop, as he will inevitably have bad and good games, but he will never label them as mildly good, mildly bad, or just OK.
Sometimes this kind of thinking may even be unipolar: for example, events may be perceived as totally bad or neutral or irrelevant. “Catastrophizing,” a common characteristic of anxious patients, illustrates anticipation of extreme adverse outcomes. Regardless of evidence, of aspects, the patient will always think of the worst possible situation.
As this way of thinking impinge on the patient’s sensitive areas, it will apply so as to tangible objects as well. For example, a man seeing a mere scratch of his wooden table, he might dwell on it for hours, thinking that it is a permanent defacement, it cannot be repaired, it ruins the whole aesthetic of the whole room. But as he gives it time and view the damage more objectively (that is, as trivial). Also the degree of his exaggerations may even present in his self-criticisms.
Supporting Content
Moreover, other types of thinking can also lead to distortions and misinterpretations, such as selective abstraction, arbitrary inference, overgeneralizations. These examples illustrate how aberrant thinking is aroused in situations that impinge on specific vulnerabilities of the patient’s domain.

6---full-notes/policies-and-constraints.title: Policies and Constraints
6---full-notes/policies-and-constraints.content:
Status:
Tags: economics
Policies and Constraints
Details
Moving into economic laws, this is where we understand more about how different types of constraints may be affected by policy. For example, one particularly popular question is the policy question is the question of how people will spend their budget on certain things if donated or given to.
So food stamps would change the budget constraint differently. If the benefit can only be spent on food then the budget line becomes flat over the initial food range and then rejoins the ordinary budget constraint. This creates a kinked or piecewise budget constraint. For someone who would have spent more than five hundred dollars on food anyway, SNAP may function almost exactly like cash. Because money is fungible, they can label the first five hundred dollars of food spending as SNAP and free up their original cash for other uses. Their final consumption may be the same as if they had received cash.
But for someone who would have preferred to spend most of the transfer on shelter, SNAP constrains choice. If they would have chosen more shelter and less food under a cash transfer, the food-only benefit forces them to consume more food and less shelter than they personally prefer. They may still be better off than with no transfer, but they are worse off than they would have been with equivalent cash. Economically, cash weakly dominates in-kind benefits from the recipient’s perspective because it allows at least the same choices and usually more. Restricting the form of aid can only reduce or leave unchanged the recipient’s attainable utility, never improve it relative to cash of equal value under standard preferences.
Nonetheless, policymakers may believe that poor people will spend cash badly on alcohol, drugs, other goods that society does not wanna subsidize. As such, this method would be effective to get these people to spend it on what matters. This reveals the tension between paternalism and autonomy in welfare policy. Cash respects local knowledge and individual preference; in-kind aid expresses social control over what counts as acceptable need. The model therefore shows why the same dollar amount can have different welfare effects depending on whether it is given as cash or restricted to a specific use.
Practically, these policies are stripping away people’s potential to spend their money in a way that allows them to further their income in an even better way to ensure the mutual benefit of everyone else in similar situations. Nonetheless there is a possibility that people will just try harder to find loopholes which would be counter-productive and heavily backfire the purpose of these policies.

6---full-notes/political-justification.title: Political Justification
6---full-notes/political-justification.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy
Political Justification
Details
Rawlsian justice aims to develop a critical, normative conception of justice. It does not describe people as they are, but interprets them as representatives of free and equal citizens. Therefore, the arguments do not rely on predictive psychology, but on structurally embedded moral premises.
The central premise of this theory is that people have incommensurable and irreconcilable conceptions of the good, and so we cannot prove one conception clearly enough for it to secure universal public agreement. Consequently, it should be known that a political conception of justice cannot be based on a single comprehensive doctrine. Even if fulfilling these conditions, it would also need to be able to be recognized by the public and mutually accepted by all members of society. If a political system relies on keeping its foundational principles a secret from the masses to function—resembling the Marxist concept of ideological or “false consciousness”—it fails this essential test of rightness. Finally, the “Primary Goods” distributed in this framework are not merely things people psychologically desire. Instead, they are objective, fundamental needs derived directly from the conception of citizens as free and equal persons (which basically are reasons that they will be reasonable people).

Polyvagal Theory
Details
Neuroception, the term describing the capacity to evaluate one’s danger and safety in an environment. Traumatized patients usually have a faulty neuroception, the challenge is the find ways to reset this so that their survival mechanisms stop going against them. There is a spectrum of responses: focused, collapsed and frantic. Porge’s theory suggests that there are 3 fundamental physiological states. When we feel threatened, the first level is social engagement, we try to find help from others, this is the work of the “ventral vagal complex”. But if no one tries to help us, or we’re in danger, we revert to fight or flight, the second stage, fighting off, running to a safe place. And when that also stops working, we preserve ourselves by shutting down and using the least amount of energy as possible, also known as freeze or collapse, this is of the “dorsal vagal complex”.

6---full-notes/poor-morality,-poor-world.title: Poor Morality, Poor World
6---full-notes/poor-morality,-poor-world.content:
Status: adult
Tags: morals philosophy
Poor Morality, Poor World
Details
“‘I have done that,’ says my memory. ‘I cannot have done that,’ says my pride, and remains adamant. At last — memory yields.” - Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, §68
Rarely, and I do mean it, rarely, do I ever quote or engage with Nietzsche at all due to my strong disagreement with his philosophical views. Yet, under these certain circumstances, I find that this quote strongly reflects how I feel about the world of which I will address how the world as it operates, and why that operation constitutes a moral failure that most people are structurally prevented from recognizing in themselves. This essay may be less academic and less rigorous than previous essays that I have written due to it not being a critique off of rationality but a genuine discontentment and indictment of how the world operates.
I. The Gap Everyone Admits
For the first gap, and perhaps the most discussed gap in moral philosophy - the theory and practical gap. Ever since Aristotle, who named it akrasia - weakness of will - and gave it formal philosophical treatment in Nicomachean Ethics. Ovid dramatized it centuries before systematic philosophy could categorize it: “I see the better and approve it, but I follow the worse.” Paul, writing to the Romans, rendered it with the particular anguish of a man who experienced it as spiritual rupture: “I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do I do not do, but what I hate I do.”
The gap is clear, ancient, well-documented — and in Western moral consciousness, perhaps that is precisely the problem. Familiarity has made it comfortable. To name akrasia is to normalize it, to file it under ‘human nature’ and move on without self-examination. But in Eastern collectivist societies, the failure runs deeper - the gap is not named at all, not because people are less moral, but because the gap was never addressed in the first place. It feels like no one ever revises or tries to understand and see morality for its limits, only for the practicality that is applied in their own lives. Confucianism is the most prevalent philosophy here in Eastern Asia, and people here takes morality less scientifically and more socially. Specifically, they mistake morality for socially-preferred values. And furthermore, mistake the information that actually show those values. A mother who criticizes her son for not being virtuous, being irresponsible, having empathy merely for not having a flawless room fundamentally already is misunderstanding and misusing the very moral framework that she is trying to operate from. This effectively shows that people are entirely unaware of the gap between theoretical moral frameworks and what they themselves or the people around them constitutes. But I also feel like this is not merely akrasia, as the mechanism is not that the person - the mother - sees the weakness of her own reasoning, rather she is not aware of it at all.
II. The Gap No One Sees
This is the gap that I want to address. The gap that perhaps has more effect on practical morality than any other gap. It exists between the existence of the first gap and the individual’s awareness of it in themselves. It is the gap that you are failing to live according to your own values and your complete inability to see that this is happening. Why and how does this gap exists ? I would argue that it is alike heuristics, that we fundamentally have to allow this gap to exist to ensure functioning. After all, if one were to ever notice that they themselves commit so many immoral acts in their everyday lives, how would one feel about themselves ? The question is in of itself already disturbing, and I myself cannot imagine what the actual experience actually is like.
This is not akrasia. The akratic person may see, approve, and does the worse nonetheless, but they see. There exists a conscious thought in their mind that they are failing their own morality, no matter how small and buried it may be. But the mechanism I describe is more corrosive: it is the constant failure mentioned previously, yet the recognition is not present. Not because the information has been hidden in any way, but because the architecture of the self has demanded that it be discarded.
The quote mentioned at the beginning captures this mechanism. Memory yields. Not that it is overruled, not that it is suppressed by our conscious acts; but rather, because it restructures itself to accommodate whatever the mind demands. It is not dishonesty in any ordinary sense — the person never intended the lie. But some part of them decided to perform the trick before consciousness arrived to object.
Dostoevsky, through Father Zosima in The Brothers Karamazov, articulated this with a precision that I find almost unbearable:
“Above all, don’t lie to yourself. The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to a point that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others.”
Zosima here is not merely describing something singular, he is talking about the existence of a process that terminates the capacity of one to detect the lie, and also terminates the ability to do so in every other human being.
III. The Machinery of Invisibility
This passage will serve to identify and provide psychological evidence for the mechanism mentioned above, even if the moral implications of these mechanisms are rarely followed to their conclusions.
The first is self-serving bias. When I do well, it reveals who I am. When I do poorly, it reveals what I was up against. This example is all that one needs to know to understand the bias: that people attribute failings to situation and successes to character. And so when we apply this across a life, it produces someone who is, by definition, unable to ever recognize and incorporating the possibility of a deep moral failure to themselves.
The second is moral licensing (Thank you Dad for mentioning this mechanism in an offhanded conversation). Moral licensing allows the performance of smaller virtues to rationalize large vices. People donate to charity, use the right language, perform acts of conscience and care - these people believe that there is a “psychological credit” that they have accumulated and therefore can spend on moral failures that never reach the ledger. Worst of all, they believe that it is fair and balanced when in reality - they virtually commit more wrongs than rights.
But more corrosive than all is, perhaps, the mechanism of theatrical function. La Rochefoucauld again: “Hypocrisy is the tribute vice pays to virtue.” This quote practically alludes to the fact that even the language of virtue itself has been captured by this mechanism. People who are fluent in moral discourse may already be precisely the ones using it as currency, rationalizing their failures whilst maintaining the most moral seriousness in comparison to their behaviors.
T.S. Eliot described the human cost of this machinery with devastating accuracy:
“Half the harm that is done in this world is due to people who want to feel important. They don’t mean to do harm — but the harm does not interest them. Or they do not see it, or they justify it because they are absorbed in the endless struggle to think well of themselves.”
This goes further than the quote mentioned in the previous section, as it is the project of maintaining self-regard, one that is so consuming that the harm that they cause becomes inherently uninteresting. The mind is now prioritizing the maintenance of its own moral self-image rather than the moral self-image itself.
IV. The World That Results
So, one may wonder: What does a world look like when it is populated by people who are, in this specific way, morally blind?
It looks like this one.
It looks like a world where moral language exists in every social media post, in every conversation, yet the behavior itself is scarce. It looks like a world where people will argue passionately about justice in the theoretical and fail to apply it in the practical. Where cruelty is not performed by people who think of themselves as cruel individuals but rather people who have made it so that they never see their cruelty as cruelty. The world’s suffering is not maintained by villains who delight in suffering but by ordinary people who have organized their attention so that the harm they cause never arrives as harm at all.
Solzhenitsyn understood this:
“If only it were all so simple! If only there were evil people somewhere insidiously committing evil deeds, and it were necessary only to separate them from the rest of us and destroy them. But the line dividing good and evil cuts through the heart of every human being. And who is willing to destroy a piece of his own heart?”
And the answer that we have come to is: almost no one.
So I look at the world and I see people who will weep over injustice in a film and perpetuate it in their homes. People who will share an article about understanding and treat the waitress with contempt. People who will preach forgiveness from a position of power and practice vengeance from a position of insecurity. None of these people recognizes the inherent contradiction in their being, ever, because the machinery that requires so requires them to destroy their own pride.
People have access to moral knowledge. Every ethical tradition, framework in human history has told them substantially the same things: Be honest. Do not harm others needlessly. Treat people as you wish to be treated. It is not rooted in the knowledge, it is rooted in the application. It is rooted in the act of treating oneself with the same rigor and the same lack of mercy that one might direct at a murderer.
And that is the most damning feature of this moral blindness: it is asymmetric. The same person who cannot see their own failures can see that of others with clarity that the other person themselves do not see. The judgment that is never applied inward is applied outward with surgical precision. Yet this asymmetry is never asymmetry, it is objectivity, it is: Naive Realism - the belief that one sees the world as it is, in all of its objectivity; and that others are clearly biased.
V. The Impossibility of This Essay
Of course, I am aware of the meta-problem that is residing in the grounds of my writing.
C.S. Lewis observed: “If you think you are not conceited, it means you are very conceited indeed.” The belief that one has escaped the trap is, in of itself, the very evidence of one being inside it. This applies to me. It applies to this essay. It applies to the very act of writing about moral blindness, which is itself a form of moral performance as a substitute for the moral practice that it is describing.
I cannot exempt myself from the indictment. Not because I do not want to, but because to do so would to instantiate the very mechanism I am describing. The only honest position is that I am almost certainly as blind in my own personal ways as how I have described other people and that this essay may not be evidence to the contrary, but rather evidence in its favor.
But that was never the point, the point was that the people who most need to read this essay are the ones who are structurally least capable of receiving it. What I have described in the previous passages will, with perfect efficiency, prevent the morally blind from realizing themselves in the description. These people will read and think of someone else. They will nod along and believe that this only confirms their morality. Perhaps they would even share it, which would function as another deposit in the moral licensing account.
Upton Sinclair wrote: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends upon his not understanding it.” We can use this quote for ourselves, substitute self-image for salary and you have the whole process. One’s self-image is not a luxury. It is, for most people, the legs, and if you pull the legs, you will collapse.
Which is why people don’t pull it out. Which is why the gap persists. Which is why memory yields.
Supporting Content

Pre-Reflective and Reflective Consciousness

When referring to consciousness, there are usually two definitions that people can come to that results in them disagreeing with each other, those being the pre-reflective and reflective stream of consciousnesses (as William James named them). Pre-reflective is what we share with many other animals, as if life was a film that is constantly rolling and showing. In contrast, reflective consciousness is an ability that we possess in tandem with some other animals having a weaker level of it that is strictly characterized by “aboutness” or intentionality; thoughts are always about an object, memory, or concept. Reflective thought requires effort, interferes with other cognitive tasks, relies heavily on linguistic symbols, and operates like a movie critic actively analyzing the film rather than merely experiencing its projection.
Supporting Content
The lecturer pushes back against Freud’s conscious/unconscious divide. He thinks the important split isn’t between conscious and unconscious but between pre-reflective and reflective — both conscious and non-conscious processes operate under similar principles on one side, while reflective processing operates under fundamentally different principles on the other.

6---full-notes/precipitating-event.title: Precipitating event
6---full-notes/precipitating-event.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Precipitating event
Details
This is when the experience of loss has a substantial significance to the patient. It does not have to always be a discrete event unlike trauma, insidious stresses such as the gradual withdrawal of affection by a spouse may also erode the personal domain sufficiently to make it vulnerable for a depression.
Experiences just prior to the onset of depression are often no more severe than those who reported by those who do not become depressed. They only differ in the conceptualization or the attachment of meaning to the event or experience.
The manner in which traumatic circumstances involving a loss lead to the constellation of depression may be delineated by an illustrative case: a man whose wife has deserted him unexpectedly. The effect of the desertion on the husband may not be predictable. Obviously, not every person deserted by a spouse becomes depressed. Even though he may experience the desertion as a painful loss, he may have other sources of satisfaction—family members and friends—to help fill the void. If the problem were simply a new hiatus in his life, we would expect that, in the course of time, he would be able to sustain his loss without becoming clinically depressed. Nonetheless, we know that certain vulnerable individuals respond to such a loss with a profound psychological disturbance.
The impact of the loss depends, in part, on the kind and intensity of the meanings attached to the key person. The deserting wife has been the hub of shared experiences, fantasies, and expectations. The deserted husband in our example has built a network of positive ideas around his wife, such as “she is part of me”; “she is everything to me”; “I enjoy life because of her”; “she is my mainstay…” Though positive, these thoughts can range from unrealistic to realistic. The more extreme and rigid they are, the greater the impact of loss.’
If the damage is big enough, it may set off a chain reaction. The depressed man will go through every lost he can possibly experience in his domain, leading to more sadness. This chain can then go on to become full-blown depression if left unattended to.

We must view this as an ability that can be used in a short amount of time before its effectiveness drops, one can allocate this tension into their forearm, wrist or arm to increase control in that area. And different scenarios will require different amounts of tension.
When flicking, it is important not to do it too fast nor explosive, and instead focus on trying to read the movement, not react to it fast.

6---full-notes/prefrontal-cortex-in-togg.title: Prefrontal Cortex in Toggling Stress Perception and Hierarchies
6---full-notes/prefrontal-cortex-in-togg.content:
Status: baby
Tags: neurology biology
Prefrontal Cortex in Toggling Stress Perception and Hierarchies
Details
The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is a marvel, toggling stress from harmful to beneficial via context and choice, influencing primitive systems like the amygdala and hypothalamus. It can rewire autonomic responses—type-A personalities dilate blood vessels in high-stress scenarios due to motivation, reversing typical constriction. This “switch” changes event polarity: voluntary challenges energize, involuntary ones drain.
Humans uniquely juggle hierarchies, using PFC to prioritize (e.g., excelling in softball despite a lowly job). It excuses our flaws situationally (“I was stressed”) while judging others constitutionally, enabling self-deception. Individual differences are vast: optimal stress ranges from birdwatching to mercenaries. You can judge someone who is doing something rotten, then assume that they will always be rotten, has always been. Yet when you do the same thing, you may excuse yourself as it being situational, under the circumstances, so that you don’t merge lanes with the person that you perceive as a rotten and bad person.
Toggling potential is enormous—reframe threats as opportunities, but it requires effort. The PFC abstracts over space/time, unlike animals, allowing infinite fear/love plug-ins. Harness via therapy or mindfulness to direct this power wisely.

6---full-notes/prenatal-risks-for-retard.title: Prenatal Risks for Retardation
6---full-notes/prenatal-risks-for-retard.content:
Status: teen
Tags: developmental psychology biology
Prenatal Risks for Retardation
Details
The prenatal period is a critical window for cognitive development, characterized by an explosive rate of neurogenesis where the fetus creates approximately 10,000 to 12,000 new neurons every second. This rapid development makes the developing brain highly susceptible to environmental insults. Maternal malnutrition, alcohol consumption, smoking, and stress can disrupt this delicate process, leading to lifelong cognitive deficits. For women in poverty, the lack of prenatal care exacerbates these risks, contributing to the higher prevalence of sociocultural retardation in lower socioeconomic groups. Conversely, organic causes are increasingly being managed through prenatal screening technologies like amniocentesis.
The rise of prenatal screening introduces profound ethical and statistical dilemmas regarding false positives and false negatives. In medical screening for fatal diseases like cancer, the goal is to avoid false negatives at all costs; however, in prenatal screening for conditions like Down Syndrome or Trisomy 18, a false positive can cause unnecessary trauma, while a true positive forces parents to make difficult choices about abortion. As screening becomes more universal, the prevalence of severe organic retardation is decreasing, raising questions about how society values lives that deviate from the cognitive norm. This touches on the broader issue of stigma, where the worth of a human being is often unjustly equated with their intellectual output or economic productivity.
Supporting Content
This may also be able to affect by exposing the fetal to FASD or FAE. In these cases, they will not show the signs of mental retardation but rather suffer from neurodevelopmental deficits that manifest as inattention, impulsivity, and learning disabilities.

6---full-notes/preventing-suicides-from-.title: Preventing Suicides from Machine Learning
6---full-notes/preventing-suicides-from-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology
Preventing Suicides from Machine Learning
Details
Suicide is the most lethal outcome of mental disorders, and much of the field have been dedicated to finding effective ways to prevent this outcome from happening. Due to recent technological advancements, people are using EMA (Ecological Momentary Assessment) to record the responses of surveys of participants to up to 6 times per day for up to 3 months.
The questions include the below with others about their emotions at the time throughout the day.


Suicidal Urges: “Right now, how strong is your urge to kill yourself?” (Rated 0–10).


Suicidal Intent: “Right now, how strong is your intention to kill yourself today?” (Rated 0–10).


They split the patient’s data in half. They trained the model on the first 50% of the responses and tested it on the last 50% to see if early data could predict later data. This would then result in them using Gaussian models, which will learn upon the response that it predicts. This allowed the model to continuously learn and update as the patient’s symptoms changed over time.
Surprisingly, the questions about moods did not help the model become more accurate in predicting, only the answers about urges and intents did help. Also, the best performing model was the simple Gaussian model, significantly outperforming the base models (machine learning).


Suicidal Urges: GP models explained ~17% of the variance (R^2 = 0.17) vs. 10% for baseline models.


Suicidal Intent: GP models explained ~12% of the variance (R^2 = 0.12) vs. 8% for baseline models.


Supporting Content
The model did though, not help with those who didn’t report any suicidal intentions, urges.

6---full-notes/price-changes-and-differe.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Price Changes and Different Goods.md
6---full-notes/price-changes-and-differe.title: Price Changes and Different Goods
6---full-notes/price-changes-and-differe.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Price Changes and Different Goods
Details
We have already established how the price change may affect demand through the mechanisms of substitution effect and the income effect. The substitution effect comes from the change in relative prices. If cookies become more expensive relative to pizza, cookies are now a worse deal, so the consumer substitutes away from cookies and toward pizza. This effect always moves opposite the price change: when a good becomes more expensive, substitution pushes demand down; when it becomes cheaper, substitution pushes demand up.
The income is on the purchasing power. If the price of cookies rises while income stays the same, the consumer is effectively poorer because the same money buys a smaller opportunity set. For normal goods, this reinforces the substitution effect. Cookies are both relatively less attractive and less affordable, so demand falls. For inferior goods, however, the income effect goes the other way. As an example, if potatoes price increases, you’d still need to purchase potatoes, but you cannot purchase as much steak… so what does one do ? They would have to abandon the steak money to use it for the potatoes.
Supporting Content
This creates the possibility of a Giffen good: an inferior good that has an income effect so powerful that it overwhelms the substitution effect, causing demand to rise when the price rises. But this effect can also be skewed by data, like how rich people leaving and not purchasing the inferior goods anymore may superficially increase the income effect.

References
Elasticity and Change
Marginal Rate of Substitution
Deriving demand

6---full-notes/price-ceilings-and-ration.title: Price ceilings and rationing
6---full-notes/price-ceilings-and-ration.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Price ceilings and rationing
Details
The market is always right has shown us how a competitive market maximizes total surplus. Now we come to the interventions part of it. In a world of perfectly competitive markets, the market knows best, and government can only make things worse (as Gruber says). Later lectures show when government isn’t the bad guy.
First, a shock that isn’t an intervention (Figure 10-1). A war in the Middle East (he’s speaking in October 2023) raises the cost of getting oil. The supply curve for gas shifts up, and the market moves from E1 to E2 at a higher price. Measured against E1:

Consumer surplus falls from A + B + D + E to just A.
Producers gain B from the higher price but lose F + G on the gallons no longer sold, so producer surplus goes from C + F + G to B + C.
Total surplus falls by D + E + F + G.

That loss is real, because oil has genuinely become harder to get. But it isn’t a market failure. Once the war has happened, E2 is the best the market can do.
Now politics. Voters’ sense of inflation is shaped heavily by gas prices, and President Biden faced re-election in about a year. Suppose the government caps the price at the old level, P1 — in Gruber’s numbers, 3.60 a gallon instead of letting it rise toward 4 or $4.50 (Figure 10-2).
At P1, consumers want Q1 gallons, but producers will only supply Q3, the amount on their supply curve at that price. Since the price can’t adjust, the quantity will be set by whichever side wants to trade less. Which means here the suppliers decide, and so the market sits at E3 with excess demand. The right comparison is E3 against E2, not E1. The war has happened; E1 is gone. Gruber’s areas:

























E2 (no cap)E3 (cap at P1)Consumer surplusV + YV + WProducer surplusW + Z + XX

W is a transfer from producers to consumers: the lower price on the gallons still sold.
Y + Z is deadweight loss: the gallons between Q3 and Q2 that buyers and sellers would both gladly trade but aren’t allowed to. Gruber’s analogy is two kids who each want the other’s playing card while a parent forbids the swap. Both are worse off.

That’s the first cost. The second is new: allocative inefficiency from rationing. In equilibrium, the price decides who gets the good. Everyone who values a gallon above the price buys it, and nobody else does. Under the cap, Q1 is wanted but only Q3 exists, so something other than price has to decide who gets it. In the 1970s, after the OPEC cartel cut oil supplies (cartels come later in the course), the US capped gas prices. The result was long lines at gas stations, with waits of 15–20 minutes or more. That waiting is pure waste: time that could have gone to work or leisure. There was a smaller second waste too: cars that got about 8 miles to the gallon burned gas idling in line for gas. So what is it? Utility in Economics
The supposed benefit is the transfer W to consumers, whether you call it equity or political calculation. But with welfare defined as consumer surplus plus producer surplus, transfers count for nothing, so the cap is pure loss. In reality, we might accept some inefficiency to get goods to people we think deserve them more. That’s the equity–efficiency trade-off, which the course returns to later.
Supporting Content
Prices without money: Feeding America distributes donated food to food banks across the US. Allocating it without prices, it ended up doing things like sending potatoes to Idaho, the country’s potato capital. So it built a virtual market. Each food bank got a budget of points and bid for the loads it wanted; a bank that badly needed potatoes could spend more of its points on them. No real money changes hands, and the food stays free, but the bidding reveals who values what most. That’s the job prices do in a market.

Where demand comes from
Producer surplus

6---full-notes/price-discrimination.title: Price discrimination
6---full-notes/price-discrimination.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Price discrimination
Details
The single-price assumption is not only unrealistic but also inefficient. So what do monopolists do? They learn the needs of each potential customer and then price accordingly. And that actually posits quite an interesting welfare situation:

Consumer surplus is zero. Nobody pays less than what the good is worth to them.
Deadweight loss is zero too. With no single price, there’s no poisoning effect: selling the 7th unit doesn’t force a price cut on the first six. So the monopolist sells every unit worth more than it costs.
The whole surplus goes to the firm: 96 in the example, the same total as perfect competition.

That’s uncomfortable. By the course’s welfare measure, total surplus, perfect price discrimination is exactly as good as perfect competition, because both give 96. Yet in one world consumers get 32 and in the other nothing. Hardly anyone is truly indifferent between those. This is the course’s first hint that economics has to care about who gets the surplus, not just its size.
But of course they aren’t mind readers, so how do they do this? Well, they just look for signs that correlate people into these groups.

Airlines charge more for last-minute tickets. Someone booking late (a business meeting, a sick relative) has few options; someone booking four months ahead is clearly shopping around. The seat costs the same to fly either way.
Movie theaters charge less for matinees. People free in the daytime, such as retirees, could easily come another time, so they’re more price-sensitive. (A student suggested lower demand; Gruber’s point is that it’s elasticity that matters.)
McDonald’s charges little extra for a large drink over a small one (from an earlier lecture), because the upgrade faces more elastic demand than the small drink does.

The markup rule from the monopoly note says how far apart the prices should be. An illustration (not in the lecture): if an airline seat has a marginal cost of $100, business travelers have ε = −1.5 and leisure travelers ε = −4. Setting P = MC/(1 + 1/ε) for each group:

Business: P = 100/(1 − 1/1.5) = $300.
Leisure: P = 100/(1 − 1/4) ≈ $133.

Sometimes firms deliberately make a worse version of the same product to sort their customers:

Tesla sold a cheaper Model S with less range, using the same battery limited by software. When a hurricane hit Florida in September 2017, Tesla unlocked the extra range so owners could evacuate, which revealed the trick.
IBM’s cheaper home laser printer was the office printer with something added to slow it down.
Amazon, Gruber says, tried pricing by IP address — charging more to orders from, say, Goldman Sachs than from a homeless shelter — and was stopped.

The logic is the same each time. One high price would lose the lower-income buyers. One low price would give away money on buyers willing to pay more. Two versions capture both groups.
Why were people outraged at Amazon? In the standard framework, discrimination like this raises efficiency: it sells units that wouldn’t otherwise be sold and shrinks the deadweight loss C + E. People object because they don’t value consumer surplus and producer surplus equally—another sign that fairness matters.

6---full-notes/primacy-effect.title: Primacy Effect
6---full-notes/primacy-effect.content:
Status: baby
Tags: Cognitive Psychology
Primacy Effect
Details
The primacy effect is a cognitive bias where items presented at the beginning of a list or sequence are recalled more accurately than items in the middle. This phenomenon is a component of the serial position effect.
The leading explanation for the primacy effect is that the initial items receive more cognitive rehearsal. When the first few items are presented, there is ample time and working memory capacity to repeat them, which facilitates their transfer from short-term memory into more stable long-term memory. As more items are added to the list, attention becomes divided, and the opportunity for rehearsal diminishes, making subsequent items harder to encode into long-term storage.

When helping a patient identify and correct his own distortions, we will need to apply certain principles of epistemology (justified belief from opinion): the nature, limits, and criteria of knowledge. The therapist will have to convey these principles to the patient. Firstly, a perception of reality is not the same as reality itself; only something close to it. The patient’s sampling of reality is restricted by inherent limitations of their sensory functions - meaning seeing, hearing, smelling, etc. Second, his interpretations of his sensory input are inherently dependent on his ability to distinguish and interpret stimuli, which means that these states can significantly affect his perception. 6---full-notes/principles-underlying-syn.title: Principles underlying Syntopical reading
6---full-notes/principles-underlying-syn.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
Principles underlying Syntopical reading
Details
Some argue that we need to treat authors’ terminologies as sacrosanct, as books should never be read “out of context”, and also it is dangerous when we translate terms to other of other books as we can lose meaning in translation. They support this further by expressing the fact that these works are radically different in style and in space and time, and so it would be hard to make it so that they are discussing together. Finally, they say that the subjects that they discuss are not as important as the ways they do so.
Of course, we disagree with literally everything. First, we can translate that of course, and also treating something as sacrosanct is merely saying that it is difficult to translate to others. Sure it may be hard, but it is not impossible.
Second, let’s take an example. For example, if Aristotle, walked into our office right now, and accompanied by an interpreter who knew both of our languages, we would be able to understand him and his points. There may be recurring difficulties about us discussing philosophical questions but it would still be possible.
Finally, to the point about manner or style. This is like saying we communicate at the same level, all of us, no differences whenever, whoever, whatever. Like even if someone tells us to “fuck off” in a nice tone, he’s still telling us to fuck off, and maybe we should leave him alone.
Believing, then, that translation is possible (because it is done all the time), that books can “talk” to one another (because human beings do so), and that there is an objective, rational content of communication between human beings when they are trying to be rational (because we can and do learn from each other), we believe that syntopical reading is possible.
