6---full-notes/probability-density.title: Probability density
6---full-notes/probability-density.content:
Status: teen
Tags: statistics psychology
Probability density
Details
Arguably the most difficult thing you can put on a histogram. Probability density is represented by the area of the graph, of each bar, so to say. It may sound simple and purely cosmetic, but it actually has quite the defect.
The defect: with relative frequency, a bar’s height depends on how wide you made the bins. Take a graduate-income bin of 10–15k holding 30 of 200 students = 15%. Split it into 1k sub-bins and those same 30 students spread out as (say) 7.5%, 5%, 1.5%, 1%, 0% — still summing to 15%, but every bar is now far shorter. Keep subdividing and the bars shrink toward zero. So you cannot compare two histograms drawn with different bin widths, and you certainly cannot lay a smooth theoretical curve (which effectively has infinitely small bins) on top of relative-frequency bars.
To fix this, before dividing, just make sure equals the actual probability by separating the two variables before you divide them to get a clearer picture.
Supporting Content

6---full-notes/problem-reduction.title: Problem Reduction
6---full-notes/problem-reduction.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Problem Reduction
Details
Most of the time when going to a therapist, the patient has a host of symptoms and problems. We cannot help them with all of this as it is inefficient as well as probably impossible. And so we must identify the problems with similar causes and group them together to solve the cause behind them.
Let us take as an example the patient with multiple phobias. A woman described in Chapter 7 was greatly handicapped by a fear of elevators, tunnels, hills, closed spaces, riding in an open car, riding in an airplane, swimming, walking fast or running, strong winds, and hot, muggy days. Treating each phobia separately with the technique of systematic desensitization might have required innumerable therapeutic sessions. However, it was possible to find a common denominator for her symptoms: an overriding fear of suffocation. She believed that each of the phobic situations presented substantial risk of deprivation of air and consequent suffocation. The therapy was focused directly on this central fear.
The principle of problem reduction is also applicable to a constellation of symptoms that comprise a specific disorder such as depression. By concentrating on certain key components of the disorder, such as low self-esteem or negative expectations, the therapy can produce improvement in mood, overt behavior, appetite, and sleeping pattern. One patient, for instance, revealed that whenever he was in a gratifying situation, he would get some kind of “kill-joy” thought: When he began to feel pleasure from listening to music, he would think, “This record will be over soon.”, etc…
Another form of problem reduction is identification of the first link in a chain of symptoms. An interesting fact is that even though the first of the chain may be minimal, the problems that it can lead to may be detrimental. This can be done by us painstakingly reviewing the patient’s symptoms and past history to delineate the causal sequences. An example could be seen in a student who has depression, when looked further, this is because he has a phobia of going outside, interacting with people as he thinks they are all bad. Though it was resolved by him going out with someone he trusts or his friend, when he went abroad, he had no one, and so he mostly stayed at his place, which in turn made him develop depression.

6---full-notes/problem-of-vitality-and-d.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Problem of Vitality and Decadence
Details
According to his philosophy, Nietzsche believed that there was a certain problem in the late 19th century being Nihilism, or a catastrophic loss of vitality. Because of the lost of hope and a set “framework”, humanity risks losing the “will” to continue. Of course, now looking back, people would scold him for being so wrong, but in the context of the time, it would be logical why he would think that. Nonetheless, Nietzsche adopts “Vitality” as his primary axiomatic criterion for judgement, rather than Justice, Happiness, or Holiness.
Initially, Nietzsche believe that health, reproductive power, and physical energy was the definition for Vitality, traits where he didn’t have as he had syphilis. However, as his thoughts matured, he moved away from purely biological definitions and toward Self-Affirmation. Self-Affirmation is basically the concept of one being able to judge one’s life as good and meaningful without needing external justification.
Supporting Content
Interestingly, Nietzsche complicates this dichotomy by acknowledging that vitality and decadence are often implicated in one another; great cultural breakthroughs (like his own insights) may arise from states of physiological sickness, suggesting a complex relationship between biological decay and cultural potency. He also argued that the levels of Vitality could differ in the structure, a society of Vitality may include citizens who aren’t all vital and so can the opposite exist.

6---full-notes/problems-and-controversie.title: Problems and Controversies of the DSM
6---full-notes/problems-and-controversie.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology
Problems and Controversies of the DSM
Details
While the DSM is an essential tool for standardizing diagnoses, it is not without significant problems and controversies.


The Categorical vs. Dimensional Debate: The DSM uses a categorical approach, meaning a person either has a disorder or they do not. Many critics argue that mental health is more accurately represented on a spectrum, or dimension. This “all-or-nothing” system struggles to account for individuals who have significant symptoms but don’t meet the full, rigid criteria for a diagnosis.


Arbitrary Criteria: The criteria for diagnosis—such as the number of symptoms required or the duration they must be present—can seem arbitrary. This can lead to situations where two people with very similar levels of distress are treated differently simply because one falls just short of the official diagnostic threshold.


The Influence of Culture and Time: The contents of the DSM are not fixed and can be influenced by shifting social and cultural norms. Homosexuality, for example, was listed as a mental disorder in the DSM for many years before being removed. This shows that what is considered “pathological” can be a product of its time.


External Influences: Diagnostic changes can sometimes be driven by non-clinical factors. For instance, the decision to merge Asperger’s syndrome and autism into a single “autism spectrum disorder” in the upcoming DSM-5 was partly influenced by the fact that insurance companies would cover treatment for autism but not for Asperger’s. This highlights how economic and political pressures can shape the diagnostic manual.


Supporting Content

DSM - A tool for classifying mental illnesses
The falsity of Psychiatry

Problems with Empiricism, Rationalism
Details
When arguing against Hume, there are two arguments: empiricist and rationalism, which both fail to come to a complete conclusion - something that Kant is trying to resolve.
For the empiricist, the problem is that you will get a thickening book of observations with nothing to pull together, as you have to depend on your own posteriori again to act a certain way and feel a certain way. For example, a man bleeding out in front of a bank where a robbery has clearly occurred. Do you feel like it’s a wrong thing because of life and because it’s an objective thing or it is internally, of yourself ? Kant argues here that even though it’s the latter, there has to be something that constitutes that feeling in the first place, so what is it ?
For rationalist, Leibniz and Wolff try to render experience intelligible through reason alone. Leibniz argues that with fully developed knowledge, all propositions — even factual ones — would turn out to be analytic, everything is what it is necessarily. This produces the conclusion (mocked by Voltaire in Candide) that this is “the best of all possible worlds.” Rationalism overreaches — it deduces content it has no business claiming.
Leibniz attributed to Locke scholastic maxim “nihil est in intellectu quod non prius fuerit in sensu” which means that nothing is in the mind that wasn’t in the senses…but Leibniz added “nisi intellectus ipse” - except the intellect itself. The mind is not just a blank state, it interprets the senses in a certain way that makes it intelligible, the question is so: what ?

6---full-notes/problems-with-homework.title: Problems with Homework
6---full-notes/problems-with-homework.content:

Problems with Homework
Details
If problems are reported about using the skills, we then would use problem-solving strategies to help the client analyze what happened, what went wrong and how to use the skills better. It is important to lead them through an examination of what happened. Though it can be torturous since they are afraid of the trainers’ judgements. Many cannot come to the conclusion of what objectively stopped them, rather, they automatically just blame their own inability or saying that it will just not work for them.
Another problem one may encounter is difficulty with homework (as with not practicing). Do not take this statement at face value, most of the time, they did practice, its that they just didn’t solve the problem necessarily. Then the conversation after this, turns to discussing to help the client have a fuller understanding of the skills. For example, a client may enter a situation where they are going to practice relaxing, but it doesn’t give them anything, no reduction in anxiety or tension. In these situations, both sides must be understanding and try to tackle the problems to see if its truly because it isn’t working or that they are doing it wrong. At any point, the trainer should be thinking about how to solve a problem rather than what would work.
The last problem is that of noncompliance and of refusal or failure to engage in skills training activities. Reject anything (excuses, such like that), and try to tackle why they would not practice, like if they don’t want to, don’t remember, not having an occasion to do so. Try to help them to tackle their problems in a gentle way, don’t punish or anything like that, maybe one can even take advantage of the situation to practice skills as clients usually are ashamed in these situations (emotional regulation).
Here are some questions to start and deal with these problems:

Did doing your homework get into short-term memory: if no, then non-awareness must be dealt with. This may stem from inattention in the session, absence from it, and/or not reading or getting the reminder of the homework.
Were you willing to do the needed or expected effective behavior: if no, ask what got in the way.
Did the thought of doing homework get into mind: if no, find ideas to get it into mind.
What got in the way: Continue to problem solve.

Something to keep in mind is motivation. Now, most of the time we do not need to be judgmental with the client, they are already judgmental enough about themselves. Instead, we have to go ahead and try to see what negative thoughts would be making them having negative reactions. Though it is fine for them to have these thoughts, it is probably not effective to withhold them, and so one should try to tackle them.

6---full-notes/producer-surplus.content:
Status: teen
Tags: economics market
Producer surplus
Details
Producer surplus is basically the gap between the price and the producer’s willingness to supply, which is its marginal cost. One gas producer facing 3 and making 100 gallons (Figure 9-10) earns surplus on every gallon whose marginal cost is below 3. That’s the area above its supply curve and below the price. Gruber says this is basically profit, which makes producer surplus easier to grasp than consumer surplus: it’s just dollars.
For the whole market (Figure 9-11), the supply curve slopes up because firms differ in cost. It’s Lecture 8’s cotton example, smoothed into a straight line. The most efficient producer has nearly zero marginal cost, so it keeps almost the full $3 on each gallon. Moving right along the curve, costs rise, and profit per gallon shrinks. At the marginal producer, A, price = marginal cost = average cost, so its profit is zero, and nobody further right enters. In this market, producer surplus is exactly the profit of the lower-cost firms.

6---full-notes/production-functions.title: Production functions
6---full-notes/production-functions.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Production functions
Details
This is the first variable we will discuss regarding production theory. It is basically where products come from. Similar to how consumers want to maximize how much they get from products, manufacturers do the same.
Profits depend on three things: consumer demand, the costs of production, and competition. In the standard model, demand and competition are out of the firm’s hands. (How advertising can shape demand, and how monopoly changes competition, come later.) What the firm controls is its costs, so Gruber treats maximizing profit as minimizing cost. Strictly, minimizing cost only tells you the cheapest way to make a given amount. How much to make also depends on revenue, which comes in later lectures.
Now we will treat the firm as a black box; that means we can only know what goes into the firm and what comes out. Whatever they do with it? We won’t know. The course uses two inputs:

Labor (L): hours worked at the firm. Its price is the wage.
Capital (K): everything else, such as machines, buildings and land. Its price is the rental rate.

Think of both as rented. The wage is the rent on an hour of a worker’s time, and the rental rate is the rent on a machine. (Firms owning machines comes later.) And we will now make it as. If these two are cookies and pizza slices.
The production function is q = f(L, K). It plays the role the utility function played for consumers: it turns inputs into output instead of goods into happiness. It’s easier to picture than utility, because it’s just technology. Lowercase q is one firm’s output; uppercase Q is the whole market’s.
Inputs are either variable (easy to change) or fixed (hard to change soon):

Short run: the period in which some inputs are fixed.
Long run: the period in which all inputs can change.

(Of course, in practice it isn’t like this, but for simplicity). In the short run, q = f(L, K̄), with capital fixed at K̄. The key number is the marginal product of labor, MPL = dq/dL: the extra output from one more worker. The assumption is diminishing marginal product: each extra worker still adds output, but less than the one before. In symbols, dq/dL > 0 (local non-satiability) but d²q/dL² < 0.
His example is digging a hole with one shovel. A second worker might nearly double the pace by taking shifts, but a third probably doesn’t triple it. By the hundredth worker, people mostly wait their turn. Rotating faster still helps a little, so 100 workers beat 90, but the hundredth adds far less than the second. In the long run you’d buy more shovels and wheelbarrows. The pattern isn’t guaranteed (the second worker might be as good as the first), but it’s the normal case.
Here’s the math with the lecture’s function and one shovel. With K = 1, q = √L. One to four workers produce 1, 1.41, 1.73 and 2 units, so each worker adds 1, then 0.41, 0.32 and 0.27. The derivative says the same thing in general: MPL = ½√(K/L), which falls as L rises.
And of course, just the same as consumer theory, we also have indifference curves, which are called isoquants in this case. They behave just like those curves and display all possibilities you can get one result.
The shape of an isoquant depends on how well the inputs substitute for each other, as a student guessed:

Perfect substitutes, q = L + K: straight-line isoquants, since only the total count of units matters. Gruber’s joke example is Harvard graduates and Beanie Babies.
Perfect complements, q = min(L, K): L-shaped isoquants. Think of cereal and cereal boxes: every unit of cereal needs a box, and extra cereal without boxes just sits there. These are the production version of left and right shoes.
Real cases fall in between, with curved isoquants (Figure 5-3).

And similar to Marginal Rate of Substitution, we also have the marginal rate of technical substitution (MRTS): the rate at which you can swap labor for capital and keep output the same. It comes from the same proof as the MRS. Moving along an isoquant, output doesn’t change, so the output gained from extra labor cancels the output lost from less capital:
MPL × dL + MPK × dK = 0, so MRTS = dK/dL = −MPL/MPK
MPK, the marginal product of capital, also diminishes: with one worker, each extra shovel adds less. For q = √(L·K), MPL = K/(2√(L·K)) and MPK = L/(2√(L·K)), so the MRTS is −K/L. On the q = 2 isoquant:

At A (1 worker, 4 shovels), the MRTS is −4. At the margin, a worker can stand in for four shovels.
At B (2, 2), it’s −1.
At C (4 workers, 1 shovel), it’s −¼. At the margin, a shovel can stand in for four workers.

Supporting Content
One difference isn’t in the lecture. Output is a real quantity, so 4 units really is twice 2 units, whereas utility numbers only rank bundles. That’s what makes returns to scale, below, a meaningful question.

6---full-notes/productivity.title: Productivity
6---full-notes/productivity.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Productivity
Details
The idea of productivity comes from a famous application of diminishing marginal product. In 1798 Thomas Malthus looked at farming, where the two inputs are people and land. Unlike machines, land is fixed even in the long run; there’s only one Earth. So as population grows, each extra worker adds less food on the same land. Eventually, output per person falls below what it takes to stay alive.
Malthus predicted cycles. Population grows, food runs short, and people die. The smaller population can then feed itself again, and the cycle restarts. His own framing was that population grows geometrically while food grows only arithmetically. Gruber notes that Malthus didn’t call it diminishing marginal product, but that’s the logic.
A simple version of the math shows the squeeze. With land fixed at 1, let food be q = √L. Food per worker is √L/L = 1/√L, which falls as L grows. Double the workforce and total food rises only by a factor of √2 ≈ 1.41, so food per worker drops by about 29%.
Malthus was wrong. World population has grown roughly eightfold since he wrote, from about 1 billion to about 8 billion. And people are fatter than ever: Gruber says world food consumption per person has risen since 1950. Starvation still exists, but he cites Amartya Sen’s observation that there has never been a famine in a democracy. Famines happen when governments fail to get food to people. They are political failures, not technological ones.
What Malthus missed was technology. Land is fixed, but how much each acre yields isn’t: fertilizers, machines, disease-resistant seeds and better land management keep raising it. So the production function should be written
q = A × f(L, K)
What is A? A is technology, which is the factor that determines how much output you get from given inputs (a variable from the black box, so to speak).
In the example above, food per worker stays level when the workforce doubles only if A rises by about 41% (a factor of √2). That’s the kind of gain farm technology delivered.
When news reports cite “productivity,” they usually mean output per hour, which rises with both A and the number of machines per worker. A is the narrower part: the output growth that more inputs don’t explain.
It isn’t just farming:

Henry Ford’s assembly line. Before 1900, cars were built one at a time by a few craftsmen. Ford used interchangeable parts and a line where each worker did one task over and over. Gruber says it cut the cost of making a car roughly in half almost overnight: the same workers and machines made far more cars. The moving line Ford introduced in 1913 cut the time to build a Model T from over 12 hours to about an hour and a half.
The Tata Nano. An Indian car priced around $2,500. It’s lighter and smaller, it pushes the wheels out to the corners to make room inside, and it uses fewer parts so it’s easier to repair.
Electric cars. Gruber calls electrification one of the biggest innovations in cars in decades. Whatever you think of Elon Musk, he says, a Tesla is a pretty cool car.

Productivity is the main driver of living standards, meaning how much stuff each person gets. Three things set that:

how hard we work (L)
how many machines we have (K)
how productive we are with them (A)

But of course the first two are costly, either financially or in terms of effort. What does that mean? That means A is suddenly magical, at least for the normal workers, as they are inheriting the work from innovations of other researchers and such.
Small differences in growth rates compound into big ones. At 2.5% a year, output per worker multiplies by 1.025^25 ≈ 1.85 over 25 years, nearly doubling. At 1% a year, it rises by a factor of only 1.01^25 ≈ 1.28. A handy rule is that something growing at g% a year doubles in about 70/g years: 28 years at 2.5%, and 70 years at 1%.
US productivity growth has gone through phases, by Gruber’s figures:

World War II to 1973: about 2.5% a year. Working just as hard with just as many machines, each person could consume 2.5% more every year.
1973 to the 1990s: under 1% a year. More stuff now meant working harder or building more machines. The IT revolution started in the late 1980s, yet productivity didn’t move. You could see IT everywhere except in the productivity numbers.
Mid-1990s to mid-2000s: a burst back to about 2.3% a year, and economists thought IT had finally arrived.
After 2005: back down to a little over 1% a year.

Supporting Content
Gruber draws four questions from this:

Why did IT give only a brief burst? Life is radically different from 25 years ago, yet the economy isn’t much more productive. His half-joke is that maybe our innovation goes into watching TikTok rather than making stuff.
Where does A come from? It isn’t actually free or magic. It comes from education, which makes people more creative and better at new ideas. It comes from firm research and development, which is mostly applied: turning ideas into products. And it comes from public research funding like the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health, which pay for much of the basic research. So society can raise A on purpose, through more education and more R&D.
How should we spend productivity? Higher A can mean more output with the same hours, or the same output with fewer hours. Gruber jokes that the hardest thing about teaching at MIT is that in the real world, people don’t like work.

Since World War II, the US has mostly taken its gains as more goods, and Europe as more leisure.
A new worker in Europe gets six weeks off, against two in the US.
Europeans work from about 25 to 60 and Americans from about 20 to 65, and Americans work more hours per week.This wasn’t necessarily a conscious choice. Gruber says the young him would have picked stuff, and the older him might pick time off. The pandemic may have shaken things up: labor supply dropped, many people retired early, and people started valuing leisure, better jobs and working from home.


Who gets A? From World War II to 1973, every group’s income grew about 2.5% a year, poorest and richest alike. Since the mid-1970s, nearly all the gains have gone to the richest, who own the capital, rather than to workers.

A typical wage buys little more than it did in 1980, because prices rose along with wages.
The top 1%‘s share rose from 26% in 1989 to 35% today. (Gruber says “wealth” and then “income” in the same breath.)
In 2021, coming out of the pandemic, the top 1% of earners saw their incomes rise 9%, while everyone else’s fell as inflation ate into wages.A more productive economy doesn’t lift everyone automatically. Who benefits depends on choices by individuals and by government. Gruber returns to this as economic fairness near the end of the course.

6---full-notes/propositions-against-skep.title: Propositions against Skepticism
6---full-notes/propositions-against-skep.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
Propositions against Skepticism
Details
In the 20th century, philosophers like Roy Harrod and Simon Blackburn tried to solve Hume’s problem using probability. They used the analogy of a traveler crossing a desert of unknown length.
If the traveler constantly predicts “The desert will continue for another 10% of the distance I’ve already traveled,” they will be right 10 out of 11 times. (e.g., at mile 100, they predict 10 more miles. If the desert ends at 110, they are right until the very last prediction). Since this method has a 10/11 success rate, induction is rationally justified.
Some argue against this that the probability is sequential, as a probability of a former group that was being evaluated would naturally not be useful after that group has “expired”. Its as if buying lottery tickets for weeks and weeks, but of course, those of the previous week would have expired once you get to evaluating for the current week.
One other prominent attempt, championed by Max Black, is the “Inductive Justification of Induction.” This argument suggests that while we cannot use an inductive premise to justify induction (which would be circular), we might be able to use an inductive rule.
Professor Millican argues that this distinction is essentially semantic hair-splitting that misses the sheer radicalism of Hume’s attack. Hume is not merely pointing out that induction lacks the certainty of deductive logic (like mathematics); he is arguing that we have absolutely no reason—deductive, inductive, or sensory—to believe that the past is a reliable guide to the future. Whether you call it a rule or a premise, any attempt to validate induction by pointing to its past success is circular. It assumes the very thing in question: that the “success of the past” has any bearing on the “success of the future.”

Psychoanalysis

Psychoanalysis, developed by Sigmund Freud, is a distinct method for explaining and dealing with personality. Its central principle is that human personality and behavior are shaped by the dynamic interplay between conscious and unconscious forces.

6---full-notes/psychological-stress-and-.title: Psychological Stress and Loss of Control
6---full-notes/psychological-stress-and-.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology
Psychological Stress and Loss of Control
Details
Psychological stress is a primary pathway to depression, and its intensity is determined not by an external event itself, but by our perception of it. Sapolsky identifies several key psychological factors that amplify the biological stress response, the most crucial of which is the loss of control.
When an individual feels they have no agency or control over a negative situation, their stress response becomes pathologically elevated. The brain and body react as if the threat is more severe simply because it is perceived as uncontrollable. Sapolsky illustrates this with studies showing that even the illusion of control (e.g., having a lever to press that does nothing) significantly dampens the stress response to an identical physical stressor (like an electric shock).
This feeling of powerlessness is a core component of what leads to learned helplessness. When repeated attempts to control a situation fail, the individual learns that their actions are futile and gives up trying. This transition from active coping to passive resignation is the psychological model for how chronic, uncontrollable stress can lead directly to a depressive state. The other key factors that constitute psychological stress—a lack of predictability, a lack of outlets for frustration, and a lack of social support—are all variations on this central theme of losing control over one’s environment and well-being.

Psychological Tests
Details
These are some other methods of assessing if a person has a mental illness or not. For example, an IQ test may help a diagnostician understand and see the symptoms of a child who has ADHD, as they can see the child has a learning disability or something of the sorts. Another is schizophrenia, which we can apply the same IQ test to see if they have symptoms of it, learning disability. It may of course help further stuff like determining neurological injuries.
Another is a projective test where the patient is incredibly guarded in telling the diagnostician about the things they believe, and it would help them gauge out those hidden beliefs and such. An example of this is the Rorsarch’s test (Thematic Apperception Test) which are LITERALLY INK BLOTS, there’s nothing more to it, and it helps to find out stuff that are hidden behind the patient’s wariness. They will then evaluate the way they say and what they are saying to determine the above mentioned items. We can also gauge out stories from them and see the theme in their responses to determine the hidden information.
More are the personality tests, an example is the MMPI, or the Minnesota Multi-phasic Personality Inventory, which can be used to detect a number of psychological problems. These are also known as a personality inventory, where the person is asked to complete a self-report questionnaire indicating whether the questions conform to him or her. Something of worry is that people may lie about these things, and of course there is a built-in items to see if people are faking it.
Talking about some cognitive-behavioral assessments, which are observing people activities when they are at home, or at school to see what they might do that may be related to the diagnosis. There may also be interviews and self-report inventories like the other assessments.
There are of course also neurobiological assessments which are just looking at the brain to see what is happening or if their brain is healthy to diagnose the effects.
Lastly, assessments of course can also get affected by cultural and sociological biases. Since a lot of these psychological assessments were developed for the western populations, it is quite hard to get accurate information in other cultures. Forms that this can come in are differences in religions, beliefs, alienation or timidity, and so on.

Psychological stress to physical abnormalities
Details
As experimental evidence has shown that individuals overreacts under stress in a particular physiological system, it is crucial to set the terms to understand what “stress” truly is. In most interpretations, stress means external conditions that presumably produce internal strains that lead to physical disorders. These internal strains are manifested by states of excitation experienced subjectively as anger, anxiety, or euphoria.
Emotional arousal is accompanied by increased activity of the autonomic nervous system. One or more physiological systems or organs may be affected by this. The system that is activated is not necessarily predictable based on what emotion is being felt, but there appears to be a characteristic reaction for a given individual: Depending on which system that is overly reactive, the somatic manifestation may be a lesion or disturbance of the gastrointestinal tract, skin, bronchioles or cardiovascular system.
This formulation may appear plausible, even though it jumps over many links in the chain. We can identify the variables that we have jumped by examining the nature of stress and the interaction of the cognitive and emotional systems in response to it. Various of stress-inducing situations have been implicated in the precipitation of psychophysiological disorders.

Psychology Experiments

Diving deeper into experiments, we can see things such as the internal validity which refers to the extent that the experimental effect (the difference between the control group and the group manipulated by the independent variable) to the independent variable. Having a control group does not ensure internal validity, the control group has to be truly random as well. For example, a group of people with the same base characteristics (like all being this age, or all doing this certain thing), and then a coin is flipped so that they can be sent to one group or another, and then we can choose which group is the control which is the influenced group.
The other characteristic is the external validity which is how generalized this study can be compared to our daily lives. For example, knowing the result of a treatment tested in an experiment like this does not guarantee it will work with other groups in the outside world. Sometimes psychologists will use groups from the outside to perform experiments on them, this instead sacrificed the internal validity, its a tradeoff, basically.

Psychophysiological problems
Details
The problems of these two things against each other becomes more complex than ever when we consider the etiology of the psychophysiological disorders. In these cases, although it is possible for us to observe symptoms, such as peptic ulcer or dermatitis, or to see evidence of a disturbed physiology. Moreover, the doctor can wisely propound that “hyperactivity of the autonomic nervous system” is responsible for the trouble. Being able to see this disorder proves that it is indeed real - an opinion dramatized by the knowledge that the person experiencing the illness may die. But when we try to see further what cause or produces the disturbance, our knowledge that it is exclusively physiological is shaken.
Those who suffer from these kind of conditions usually report a sequence of emotional upsets to the symptom. Whenever someone is angry or worried, they may experience pain and such in their systems and organs. Yet, these emotions cannot be put into a test tube for us to measure and acknowledge, but they can clearly be seen when we treat it with therapy or medicine to reduce the emotional factor rather than the physiological factors.
We can divide these disorders which have been closely linked to emotional disturbances into three groups: (1) Physiological disturbances or structural abnormalities in which psychological and constitutional factors combine to produce the disorder. These conditions are generally triggered or aggravated by states of emotional arousal. (2) Primary physical disorders that are exacerbated by psychological processes. This category includes cases of “psychological overlay,” such as cardiac invalidism and severe dyspnea based on mild chest pathology. (3) Aberration of sensation or movement, but with no demonstrable tissue pathology or disturbed physiology. This category includes a broad spectrum of conditions ranging from “somatic imaging” and the hysterias to somatic delusions. In many aspects, this group is probably the most interesting out of the ones mentioned.

Qualia and Epiphenomenalism
Details
“Qualia” is the technical term used to describe the qualitative, subjective characters of experience—the redness of a rose, the pang of a headache, or the taste of wine. If Jackson’s argument holds, these qualia are real but non-physical. This leads to the position of Epiphenomenalism. If the physical sciences already provide a complete account of the causes of behavior (e.g., neurons firing cause muscles to move), then there is no causal work left for qualia to do.
And so when we “think” that we are making a decision consciously, it is at the end just our mind having us feel the visceral experience, not that we are actually having a choice necessarily. Simpler, take the advantage of Pong, we push the ball around, and it makes it as if we feel that the pixels are hitting the ball and making it bounce. But rather, there is a chip that is calculating the trajectory and physics of the ball and simply letting the pixels visualize it all.

Quantitative Genetics
Details
Quantitative genetics is a field that addresses the first-order questions of genetic influence: whether and how much genetic factors contribute to individual differences in psychological traits. It partitions the variance of a trait within a population into genetic and environmental components. Its primary methods are twin studies (comparing identical and fraternal twins) and adoption studies. The main statistical output is heritability, which represents the proportion of phenotypic differences attributable to genetic differences. This approach does not identify specific genes but establishes the overall importance of genetic influence, which has been found to be ubiquitous across nearly all psychological traits.

Quantitative Trait Loci (QTLs) and the Genetics of Complexity
Details
The QTL perspective is fundamental to modern molecular genetics. It posits that complex traits and common disorders are not the result of a single gene, but of the cumulative, additive effects of many genes, each with a small impact. This means there is no single “gene for” a complex trait like intelligence or personality. Instead, we all inherit a unique combination of alleles that contribute probabilistically to our traits. This perspective suggests that many disorders are simply the quantitative extremes of dimensions that vary across the entire population, blurring the line between normal and abnormal.

Questioning “The life after death”
Details
The cheap objection, which Rosenberg presses and Kagan takes seriously enough to answer: death is the end of life, so “life after death” unpacks as “life after the end of life,” and “will I survive my death?” unpacks as “will I be alive after I stopped being alive?” Both answer themselves. On this reading the question that has occupied religion and philosophy for millennia is a grammatical accident — the same joke as asking which country buries the survivors of a crash on the border.
Kagan’s response is not to dispute the definition but rather change the subject that is being questioned. Instead of “the life after death,” we can simply restrict the subject to our body instead. Now, this doesn’t entirely comicalize the question as no can still be an answer, but now it has to be earned rather than be assumed through language.
Though the reformulation is not perfect, due to how the question is now defined, it is stipulated that the answer is rooted in dualism as it is assuming the body and soul are now two different things.
From then on the question also enters the realm of philosophy of mind: the substance of someone and how to know they are the same version of themselves that lived.

6---full-notes/questions-that-philosophe.title: Questions that philosophers ask
6---full-notes/questions-that-philosophe.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading philosophy
Questions that philosophers ask
Details
These questions are not simple even when we write them down because answering them is so difficult. Nevertheless, they are initially simple in the sense of being basic or fundamental.
For example, a question about being or existence: What is the difference between existing and not existing? What is common to all the things that do exist, and what are the properties of everything that does exist? Are there different ways in which things can exist—different modes of being or existence? Do some things exist only in the mind or for the mind, whereas others exist outside the mind, and whether or not they are known to us, or even knowable by us? Does everything that exists exist physically, or are there some things that exist apart from material embodiment? Do all things change, or is there anything that is immutable? Does anything exist necessarily, or must we say that everything that does exist might not have existed? Is the realm of possible existence larger than the realm of what actually does exist?
These are typically the kind of questions that a philosopher asks when he is concerned to explore the nature of being itself and the realms of being. As questions, they are not difficult to state or understand, but they are enormously difficult to answer—so difficult, in fact, that there are philosophers, especially in recent times, who have held that they cannot be answered in any satisfactory manner.
Another set of philosophical questions concerns change or becoming rather than being. Of the things in our experience to which we would unhesitatingly attribute existence, we would also say that all of them are subject to change. They come into being and pass away; while in being, most of them move from one place to another; and many of them change in quantity or in quality: they become larger or smaller, heavier or lighter; or, like the ripening apple and the aging beefsteak, they change in color.
Such questions are asked by the philosopher who turns his attention from being to becoming and also tries to relate becoming to being. Once again, they are not difficult questions to state or understand, though they are extremely difficult to answer clearly and well. In any case, you can see how they begin with a childishly simple attitude toward the world and our experience of it.
All these questions are speculative or theoretical in the sense of those terms that we have employed in distinguishing between the theoretical and practical realms. But philosophy, as you know, is not restricted to theoretical questions only.
The two groups of questions that we have discussed determine or identify two main divisions of philosophy. The questions in the first group, the questions about being and becoming, have to do with what is or happens in the world. Such questions belong to the division of philosophy that is called theoretical or speculative. The questions in the second group, the questions concerning good and evil, or right and wrong, have to do with what ought to be done or sought, and they belong to the division of philosophy that is sometimes called practical, and is more accurately called normative. Books that tell you how to make something, such as a cookbook, or how to do something, such as a driver’s manual, need not try to argue that you ought to become a good cook, or learn to drive a car well; they can assume that you want to make or do something and merely tell you how to succeed in your efforts. In contrast, books of normative philosophy concern themselves primarily with the goals all men ought to seek—goals such as leading a good life or instituting a good society—and, unlike cookbooks and driving manuals, they go no further than prescribing in the most universal terms the means that ought to be employed to achieve these goals.

6---full-notes/questions-to-ask-of-a-his.title: Questions to ask of a historical book
6---full-notes/questions-to-ask-of-a-his.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading history
Questions to ask of a historical book
Details
Literally same as everything before this, we have to variate the questions of the former to this form.
The first question, we must classify it carefully with its limitations, so that we do not accidentally mistake it with something it is not. Certainly, if we are to criticize it, then we must know this well as the author cannot be blamed for not doing what he did not try to do.
For the second question, the historian is trying to tell a story, and so there are general outlines and we need not to search for them. But we must know something else, how he is presenting his story, his formatting, his writing must all be taken into account.
Criticism of history takes two forms. We can judge—but only, as always, after we understand what is being said—that a historian’s work lacks verisimilitude. People just do not act that way, we may feel. Even if the historian documents his statements by giving us access to his sources, and even if to our knowledge they are relevant, we can still feel that he has misunderstood them, that he has judged them in the wrong way, perhaps through some deficiency in his grasp of human nature or human affairs. We tend to feel this, for example, about many older historians who do not include much discussion of economic matters in their work. People, we may be inclined to think now, act out of self-interest; too much nobility ascribed to the “hero” of a history may make us suspicious.
On the other hand, we may think, especially if we have some special knowledge of the subject, that the historian has misused his sources. We may be indignant to discover that he has not read a certain book that we have read. And he may be misinformed about the facts of the matter. In that case, he cannot have written a good history of it.
With regard to the last question, since history has the largest effects on man, often lead us to make changes, to try to be better, and so the answer lies in the direction of practical, political action.

Radical Empiricism
Details
Modern science operates under a materialist mythos (worldview) that often dismisses subjective mental states as secondary to brain physiology. William James, the father of American psychology, countered this with Radical Empiricism: the rigorous study of all phenomena, including internal, introspective states.
James argued that “rational consciousness” is only one type of consciousness, separated from other potential forms by the “filmiest of screens.” He posited that a complete scientific account of the universe cannot ignore these altered states (often induced by chemical stimuli/nitrous oxide), as they represent distinct types of mentality with their own adaptations.

6---full-notes/rationality-and-the-logic.title: Rationality and the Logical Impossibility of Absolutism
6---full-notes/rationality-and-the-logic.content:
Status: adult
Tags: morals philosophy
Rationality and the Logical Impossibility of Absolutism
Details
This brings us to the exact mechanism of the social contract, which hinges entirely on Locke’s specific understanding of human rationality. In Locke’s framework, being rational does not mean modern economic profit-maximizing; rather, it means taking prudent, far-seeing steps to secure, protect, and improve one’s baseline condition. The things we rationally seek to protect are our lives, our liberties, and our estates. When free, equal individuals living under Natural Law decide to form a government, they are making a calculated risk-assessment. They are choosing to trade the volatile, unpoliced freedom of the state of nature for the security of a neutral judge, a codified legal system, and a collective enforcing power that can better protect their fundamental rights. The entire purpose of the contract is an upgrade in security and stability.
From this rational starting point, Locke elegantly and devastatingly destroys the argument for absolute monarchy. He argues that surrendering all power to a singular, unchecked sovereign fundamentally violates this rational calculus. If you give one person absolute power, that monarch remains in the unregulated state of nature relative to their subjects, but they are now armed with the entire military and legal force of the state. It is a wildly asymmetric power dynamic where the subject has absolutely no recourse, no neutral judge to appeal to, and no protection against the sovereign’s whims. Locke argues that the standard state of nature is actually vastly preferable to absolute tyranny. Because no rational person would ever willingly sign a contract that leaves them far less secure than they were wandering in the wild, an absolute monarchy cannot logically originate from a valid social contract. Therefore, any absolute regime is illegitimate by default, making armed resistance against such a regime not just a political right, but a moral imperative.

6---full-notes/rationalization.title: Rationalization
6---full-notes/rationalization.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Social Psychology
Rationalization
Details
Fritz Heider’s Balance Theory established that people are uncomfortable when their beliefs conflict with someone else’s, as if you like Jim but Jim does or like something you find morally objectionable, the triad is unbalanced and psychologically distressing. But, another breakthrough happened when Festinger removed the second person and only left you yourself. Two of your own cognitions can clash, producing cognitive dissonance, an aversive internal state analogous to dissonant musical notes. Three paths exist for reduction: change an attitude, change a behavior (often impossible since the act already happened), or justify and minimize the conflict. This third path is what everyone recognizes as rationalization.
Festinger’s most famous demonstration, and best, is the insufficient justification paradigm, which made the mechanism viscerally clear. Subjects did an excruciatingly boring task for an hour, then were asked to tell the next subject it was fun. Half were paid 1 for this lie, half were paid 20. Counterintuitively, the 1 group later reported enjoying the task _significantly more_. The 20 group had sufficient external justification — “I lied for a large sum, that’s reasonable, I can live with that.” The dissonance between “lying is bad” and “I lied” was resolved by the payment itself. The $1 group had no such escape. A dollar doesn’t justify lying to someone’s face. And so, with no justification available, the only remaining route was internal, you have to change how you feel about the task.

6---full-notes/raven's-progressive-matri.content:

Raven’s Progressive Matrices as a Culture-Reduced Test
Details
Raven’s Progressive Matrices is a non-verbal test designed to be a “culture-reduced” or “culture-fair” measure of intelligence. It aims to minimize the impact of language and cultural knowledge, which can bias results in tests like the Stanford-Binet and Wechsler scales. This helped psychologists to achieve better results at understanding intelligence.
The test consists of a series of matrices (visual patterns) with one piece missing. The test-taker must choose the missing piece from a set of options, a task that requires abstract reasoning and rule inference—key components of fluid intelligence. Because it is non-verbal and requires simple instructions, it is considered fairer for individuals from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Its main limitation is that it provides only a single score for abstract reasoning, without identifying other cognitive strengths or weaknesses.

6---full-notes/reading-and-understanding.title: Reading and understanding the university
6---full-notes/reading-and-understanding.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship 3 - Tags/reading
Reading and understanding the university
Details
Many applications arrive as monologues, passionate broadcasts sent into an imagined void. The student speaks at length about their own achievements, their personal journey, and their future ambitions, assuming the sheer force of their credentials will be enough. But a university is not a void; it is a living community with a distinct character, a specific soul forged over decades or even centuries of its own history. To submit an application without first understanding this soul is like giving a beautiful speech to an empty room. The words may be eloquent, but they will never connect, because they were never tailored for the listener.
To truly understand a university requires an act of deep and dedicated listening. It means treating the institution’s website not as a simple brochure, but as its autobiography, filled with clues to its core identity. The mission statement is its constitution, the foundational document declaring its most cherished values—be they innovation, social justice, community service, or interdisciplinary inquiry. The course descriptions and faculty profiles are not just lists; they are windows into its intellectual heart, revealing the questions it deems important and the conversations it wants to host. Even past application forms or student project showcases are artifacts, remnants of a culture that reveal what is truly celebrated within its walls. This process is a form of academic archaeology, digging beneath the surface to decode the institution’s DNA.
Armed with this profound understanding, the applicant can finally craft a statement that is no longer a monologue, but the beginning of a dialogue. They no longer need to list their achievements like items on a resume; instead, they can weave their own narrative into the larger tapestry of the institution. They can demonstrate how their passion for scientific research aligns with the university’s specific emphasis on collaborative labs, or how their volunteer work is a direct continuation of the school’s long-standing commitment to community outreach. The statement of purpose transforms from a plea for entry into a compelling proposition: “My journey has prepared me to contribute to the very mission you cherish.” In the hands of the admissions officer, the application then ceases to be just another file. It becomes a shock of recognition—the exhilarating discovery of a candidate who not only wants to attend their university, but who truly understands and belongs to it.

6---full-notes/reading-on-current-events.title: Reading on current events
6---full-notes/reading-on-current-events.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading history
Reading on current events
Details
Although we do not have to analytically read everything, it is still necessary for us to answer the 4 questions that it presents.
Of course same as history, we have no chance to absolutely know if news are true, we can only depend on the reporter whose job is to reflect reality that they research about. Ideally, a reporter, of whatever kind, is a clear glass in which reality is reflected—or through which it shines. But the human mind is not a clear glass. It is not a good reflector, and when reality shines through it, the mind is not a very good filter. It separates out what it considers to be unreality, untruth. That is proper, of course; a reporter should not report what he thinks is false. But he may be mistaken.
Thus the most important thing to know, when reading any report of current happenings, is who is writing the report. What is involved here is not so much an acquaintance with the reporter himself as with the kind of mind he has. The various sorts of filter-reporters fall into groups. To understand what kind of filter our reporter’s mind is, we must ask a series of questions about it. This amounts to asking a series of questions about any material dealing with current events. The questions are these:

What does the author want to prove?
Whom does he want to convince?
What special knowledge does he assume?
What special language does he use?
Does he really know what he is talking about ?

The last question is especially hard to confirm as there are private matters that one has no right to dabble in and won’t know as it is classified information. We can’t criticize him for that.

6---full-notes/readings-of-the-project.title: Readings of the Project
6---full-notes/readings-of-the-project.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Readings of the Project
Details
Karl Ameriks identifies four possible readings of what Kant is doing in the First Critique:

Systematic metaphysics — building a proper metaphysical system at a time when metaphysics was considered wreckage.
Refutation of skepticism — specifically Humean empiricist skepticism, which showed that if all knowledge comes through the senses, and senses only give us mediated access to reality, we can never be sure our reports are faithful. You can’t check the accuracy of your senses without using your senses — “that’s the box you can’t get out of.”
Ontology — answering “what is there?” against Locke’s claim that we only ever know nominal essences (how we label things based on experience) never real essences (the ultimate nature of things, which on Newton’s corpuscular theory lies beyond perception).
The transcendental option (what Ameriks and the lecturer favor) — uncovering the necessary conditions for both scientific knowledge and ordinary experience to be possible at all. Not defending common sense, not doing psychology, but asking: what must already be in place for any experience or knowledge claim to get off the ground?

Kant recognizes the stunning success of Newton, Galileo, the whole 17th-century scientific project — and insists this cannot rest on the “stunningly chancy” deliverances of fallible human senses. There must be a deeper foundation. The transcendental argument asks: given that science works, what does that tell us about the necessary structure of experience and reason?

Recency Effect
Details
The recency effect is the tendency to have superior recall for items at the end of a list compared to those in the middle. This is the second component of the serial position effect, complementing the primacy effect.
This effect is typically explained by the items’ presence in short-term or working memory. When recall is tested immediately after the list is presented, the last few items are still actively being held in this limited-capacity store, making them readily accessible. Unlike the first items, they haven’t been displaced by subsequent information. If a delay or a distracting task is introduced between the end of the list and the recall test, the recency effect often disappears because the contents of short-term memory decay or are interfered with.

Recognizing automatic thoughts
Details
As mentioned before, automatic thoughts are generally hard to be recognized, and so people must be trained to, well, recognize them. These thoughts usually appear in between an event happening and the actions or emotions evoked by it. View it like a sequence: “A, B, C.” “A” is the event, and “C” is our emotion to it (which is the irrational thing here). “B” then is the automatic thought, filling in the space between A and C, and so we must recognize B.
One patient outlined the sequence of A, seeing an old friend, and C, experiencing sadness. Another patient reported the sequence: A, he heard a report about somebody being killed in an automobile accident, and C, felt anxiety. In these instances the patients were able to replay the events in slow motion, as it were, and could then successfully recall the thoughts that had occurred in the gap. Seeing the old friend had elicited B, the following sequence of thoughts: “If I greet Bob, he may not remember me…He may snub me…It’s been so long, we won’t have anything in common. It won’t be like old times.” These thoughts evoked the sad feelings. The patient who felt anxious after witnessing the auto accident was able to fill in the blank when he recalled having had a fantasy image of himself as the victim.
The A B C sequence may be illustrated by the common fear of dogs. A person may assert that although he has no reason for fearing dogs, he experiences anxiety whenever he is exposed to them. One such patient was puzzled by the fact that he became frightened when near a dog even when there was no possibility of being attacked. He then recognized that he was thinking “Every dog will bite me” and when he examined the thought again and see it was irrational, he didn’t feel anxious anymore.

Recognizing relatives
Details
In the realms of identifying who is similar to you, animals have two ways of going at this, either innate or imprinted. The innate mechanism includes a unique protein that is called the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC). Every individual has a different MHC, and they let it out in pheromones like sweat or pee. The brain, then, has olfactory receptors that can recognize these scents. In fact, we all have these abilities to smell and identify MHC, but when giving birth, the olfactory part of our brains are actually being renovated by the body increasing hormones like prolactin and such through neurogenesis. The increase in oxytocin and vasopressin also makes the new system more sensitive to recognizing the baby’s smell.
The other way of recognizing relative is imprinting. This is quite simple, if a child smells like my vaginal fluids, its mouth smells like my milk, etc. that would mean that it is my child. Same for the siblings, if the siblings smell like mom, then they are my relative. The innate part here is the learning process, the recognition is still imprinted.
There is actually a third method for doing this, and it is cognitive, and of course it is most prevalent in humans. We recognize who our mother is because she is holding us at birth or taking care of us and such, not because we have some innate ability or imprinted stuff. Same as how the mother recognizes the father, “I had sex with this dude in my ovulating stage.”… God that sounds weird. Of course there also exists this system in primates although their abilities are quite weak from that of the humans.

6---full-notes/references-for-applicatio.title: References for applications
6---full-notes/references-for-applicatio.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship
References for applications
Details
A compelling scholarship application is more than just grades and a personal statement; it’s a multi-faceted portrait of your potential. One of the most critical components of this portrait is the letter of recommendation. A generic, lukewarm reference can stall an otherwise strong application, while a powerful, personalized one can be the deciding factor. Securing this kind of endorsement requires a strategic approach centered on choosing the right people and empowering them to be your best advocates.
The foundation of a stellar recommendation is selecting the right referee. This isn’t about choosing the person with the most prestigious title, but rather the one who can provide personalized and detailed insights into your abilities. Your goal is to have references who can speak to different aspects of your profile—one might highlight your academic excellence, another your professional capabilities or leadership, and a third your personal character. Consider the context and relationship you have with each potential referee. A professor from a small seminar who witnessed your intellectual curiosity firsthand is often a more suitable choice than a department head who only knows your name from a transcript.
Once you’ve chosen your referees, your job is to equip them to write a detailed and impactful letter. This is where you must provide them with the necessary tools. Share your application essays, your resume, and, most importantly, information about the specific scholarship. Explaining why you believe you are a strong fit for the scholarship allows them to tailor their letter to the sponsor’s values, whether they be leadership, community service, or academic research. Don’t be shy about reminding them of specific examples of your achievements and impact—the research project you excelled in, the team you led, or the insightful analysis you presented in class. These details are the evidence that transforms a good letter into a great one.
Ultimately, the most crucial element in this process is respect for your referee’s time. A thoughtful, detailed letter cannot be written overnight. You must allow them plenty of time—at least three to four weeks is a standard courtesy. By choosing your referees wisely, providing them with comprehensive information, and giving them ample notice, you create a partnership that results in a powerful, authentic endorsement that will make your scholarship application shine.

6---full-notes/reflective-equilibrium.title: Reflective Equilibrium
6---full-notes/reflective-equilibrium.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy morals
Reflective Equilibrium
Details
This is Rawls’s method and ideal endpoint of justification. It begins from the assumption that every citizen carries a capacity for a sense of justice. Evidence of this developed capacity is that adults routinely make justice judgments across an enormous range, “extending from basic institutions… to the law of nations to all the way down to particular standards, principles, practices, the actions of individuals and their characters.”
Rawls then select it in two stages. First, we isolate political judgements of justice concerning the basic structure. Then we identify considered judgements which are ones made depending on adequate information, impartiality, freedom from threat… these occur at all levels of generality, from particular assessments of individual actions to abstract constitutional principles.
Among these, some serve as “fixed points” — convictions so firm they are effectively non-negotiable. Rawls’s examples include the wrongness of slavery, religious persecution, and inflicting unnecessary suffering. Other judgments — such as views about income distribution — are far less settled, involving “a variety of criteria” applied inconsistently. Rawls observes that internal inconsistency among one’s considered judgments is the normal human condition: “if you’re not internally inconsistent, you’re either probably unreflective or insensitive or maybe mad” — meaning in the grip of a doctrine that enforces artificial consistency “at the cost of ordinary human feeling.”
None of these principles are exempt from being scrutinized, any and all of them can realistically be seen and viewed so unlike other frameworks that has a set of first principles.

6---full-notes/reid,-common-sense,-and-w.title: Reid, Common Sense, and Why Kant Dismissed It
6---full-notes/reid,-common-sense,-and-w.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
Reid, Common Sense, and Why Kant Dismissed It
Details
Thomas Reid was a person of first principles, he was a person that above all, cared about how something, how everything has a reason, or reasons. You can’t prove the law of contradiction because all proof presupposes it. Likewise, in physics, you also assume that it always apply, if your car doesn’t start tomorrow, then its the car not working, not that the laws of combustion has been suspended.
Reid turned Hume against himself. Hume argued causation is just a mental habit from repeated experience — “anything may be the cause of anything” — then admitted he thinks like an ordinary person once he leaves his study. Reid’s response: a philosophy that contradicts everything required for functioning life will have a very brief shelf life. People will smile at the clever philosopher and get on with things.
Even though this closely resembles Kant’s transcendalism, Kant still criticized Reid nonetheless as consulting the wisdom of the herd, of the masses rather than something that he figured out himself. The lecturer argues, following Manfred Kuehn, that this dismissal is strategic rather than philosophical: Kant was fighting a war within German philosophy between serious systematic philosophy (Schulphilosophie) and accessible popular philosophy (Popularphilosophie). Reid’s common sense approach looked too much like the popular side, so Kant needed distance from it — even though the actual arguments have significant overlap.
In this sense, Kant was blind in the sense that these were not exactly arguments, but rather presuppositions that rational people would have to believe, which corresponded more strongly to his transcendalism than he admits.

Rejection of Philosophical Social Roles
Details
The traditional view of philosophy entails a fixed social role for philosophers who address a permanent set of questions, alike a doctor, or a cook, or whatever, as they don’t have a set social role throughout the times but rather a fluid function that changes based on historical context. He takes this from the example of philosophers throughout the time-a king’s advisor, a doctor of culture, a theologian, or a free thinker. Furthermore, there are no eternal philosophical questions, only questions arising from specific historical conflicts or events during those times. The Greeks asked about rhetoric because of the Sophists; Kant asked about determinism because of Newtonian science, and the Stoics were the one who created Will. Nietzsche derides the belief in eternal questions as “Egyptianism”—the fallacy of treating historically contingent concepts as immutable pyramids.

Validity is aboutness: does the measurement actually capture the thing you intend to measure?

Measuring stress hormones (corticosteroids) in the blood is highly valid. This is because we are drawing the chemical directly from the source. 6---full-notes/remarks-of-an-author’s-po.title: Remarks of an author’s points
6---full-notes/remarks-of-an-author’s-po.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
Remarks of an author’s points
Details
The first is saying that he is uninformed, which means to say he lacks a piece of knowledge that is relevant to the problem he is trying to solve. And so one must point this information out to state what he is lacking and how it is relevant to his conclusions.
A few illustrations here must suffice. Darwin lacked the knowledge of genetics that the work of Mendel and later experimentalists now provides. His ignorance of the mechanism of inheritance is one of the major defects in The Origin of Species. Gibbon lacked certain facts that later historical research has shown to have a bearing on the fall of Rome. Usually, in science and history, the lack of information is discovered by later researches. Improved techniques of observation and prolonged investigation make this the way things happen for the most part. But in philosophy, it may happen otherwise. There is just as likely to be loss as gain with the passage of time. The ancients, for example, clearly distinguished between what men can sense and imagine and what they can understand. Yet, in the eighteenth century, David Hume revealed his ignorance of this distinction between images and ideas, even though it had been so well established by the work of earlier philosophers.
Next is to say he is misinformed, which means what he is asserting is not the case. The error this presents is that the author himself made assertions contrary to the fact. He is proposing that something is true or probable although it is in fact false and less probable. This should be pointed out only if it is relevant to his conclusions, and you must be able to argue about the truth with that of the author.
These two points are extremely relevant to each other, and you are right, lack of information means misinformation most of the time. The difference comes when we consider the conclusions made from these two, lack of information makes the author leads to conclusions that might not be what he was trying to get at, but misinformation fully leads us to wrong conclusions.
The third point is illogicality in the reasoning of points to ideas. This is when the conclusion does not simply follow the line of thoughts presented, it is the occurrence of inconsistency, meaning the two things the author tried to connect were incompatible. And so the reader must be able to show the precise respect in where the author’s argument lacks cogency.
This is also related to the previous two points, they all lead from one to another. Poor grounds, evidence leads to poor conclusions even with good reasonings. Good grounds, poor reasonings also does the same, different destination but around the same location.

6---full-notes/reproductive-effects-and-.title: Reproductive Effects and Warnings of Tobacco
6---full-notes/reproductive-effects-and-.content:
Status: teen
Tags: pharmacology
Reproductive Effects and Warnings of Tobacco
Details
The toxicity of tobacco extends beyond the user to the developing fetus, leading to specific medical classifications. “Fetal Tobacco Syndrome” is one of the few medically diagnosed syndromes caused by drug consumption during pregnancy (alongside Fetal Alcohol Syndrome). Tobacco use during pregnancy correlates with a 50% decrease in fertility, a 50% increase in spontaneous abortion (miscarriage), and a higher incidence of premature birth and perinatal mortality.
The mechanism is largely attributed to the hypoxic effects of carbon monoxide and the vasoconstrictive effects of nicotine, which starve the developing fetus of oxygen and nutrients. Consequently, infants are often born with significantly lower birth weights. Furthermore, there is a strong statistical association between environmental/maternal tobacco smoke and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS).
Public policy attempts to mitigate these risks through warning labels, though the efficacy and implementation vary globally. In the United States, warning labels have historically been small, text-based, and placed on the side of packaging (e.g., warning of CO or low birth weight). In contrast, European and other international regulations often mandate large, graphic warnings that cover a significant portion of the package (e.g., “Smoking Kills”). This disparity highlights the ongoing tension between public health advocacy and the entrenched political and economic power of the tobacco industry, a legacy stretching back to the American colonies.

Resource Mobilization Theory
Details
The contemporary understanding of how social movements emerge is dominated by Resource Mobilization Theory, a framework pioneered by sociologists like Charles Tilly. This theory is radically different from the The Collective Behavior Theory in that instead of these protests just being collective behavior that happen because people are so out of touch with society, it is instead led by those who are educated and intelligent.
The people involved in these protests are not the alienated and helpless members of society but often those who believe that they have political efficacy, that they have the power to change things, which motivates them psychologically. Leaders of these protests are educated because they need to be able to handle many things that a leader is required to do such as financial, or public speaking to incite people to fight, and prior organization. Prior organization is extremely important because these uprisings do not just appear out of a vacuum, but rather from existing political institution. They are almost always built upon pre-existing organizational structures—churches, unions, student groups, community associations—that can be repurposed for political action. This existing network provides the communication channels, leadership, and trust necessary to mobilize people effectively. In history, there have been so many examples of this, the French Revolution is one of the most obvious.

6---full-notes/respiration-restoration-t.title: Respiration-Restoration Theory
6---full-notes/respiration-restoration-t.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sleep neuroscience psychology
Respiration-Restoration Theory
Details
One of the primary theories of why we sleep is that it serves a vital restorative function, allowing the brain and body to repair themselves from the wear and tear of waking life. While it feels like a period of shutdown, deep sleep is actually a time of intense biological housekeeping.
During the day, the brain’s high metabolic activity produces waste products, such as beta-amyloid (a protein linked to Alzheimer’s disease). Research suggests that during sleep, the space between brain cells increases, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to flush out these toxins more effectively. This is the brain’s “cleaning cycle,” essential for maintaining healthy neural function.
Beyond cleaning, sleep is crucial for:


Energy Replenishment: The brain replenishes its stores of glycogen, the primary energy source for neurons, which are depleted during wakefulness.


Cellular Repair: The body increases its rate of cell growth and repair, producing molecules that are essential for fixing damage caused by stress and ultraviolet rays.


It’s important to view this restorative process alongside the active processing of memory consolidation. The brain isn’t just turning off; it’s shifting its priorities. It reduces its processing of external stimuli to dedicate energy to these two critical, simultaneous tasks: repairing the hardware and organizing the software.

6---full-notes/retinal-processing-and-bi.title: Retinal Processing and Bipolar Cells
6---full-notes/retinal-processing-and-bi.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology neuroscience
Retinal Processing and Bipolar Cells
Details
The journey of a visual signal does not end at the photoreceptor. Once a rod or cone transduces light into an electrical impulse, the signal begins a complex process of refinement within the retina itself, starting with the bipolar cells. The wiring between photoreceptors and bipolar cells is a masterpiece of biological engineering that explains their different functions. For rods, many converge their signals onto a single bipolar cell. This ‘pooling’ of information creates a system highly sensitive to dim light, as weak signals can combine to trigger a response. The trade-off is a loss of spatial detail. For cones, especially in the fovea, the connection is much more direct, with very few (or just one) connecting to a bipolar cell. This preserves the precise location of the stimulus, enabling the high-acuity vision for which cones are known. From the bipolar cells, the signal continues to other retinal neurons before being sent to the brain via the optic nerve.

6---full-notes/retrieval-as-a-powerful-l.content:
Status: teen
Tags: learning
Retrieval as a Powerful Learning Tool
Details
For most of us, tests are viewed as tools of assessment—a stressful final step to measure what has been learned. However, a robust body of cognitive science reveals that this view is fundamentally incomplete. The act of testing is, in itself, one of the most powerful methods for learning and consolidating information. This phenomenon, known as the testing effect or retrieval practice, demonstrates that the process of actively pulling information out of our memory is far more effective for long-term retention than simply putting information in.
When we reread notes or highlight a textbook, we engage in passive review. This creates an illusion of fluency; the material feels familiar, but this familiarity does not equate to true mastery. In contrast, when we force ourselves to recall a fact, concept, or process without looking at the source material, we are engaging in active retrieval. This effortful act strengthens the neural pathways associated with that memory, making it both more durable and more easily accessible in the future. The struggle to remember is not a sign of failure; it is the very mechanism of deep learning. Even when a retrieval attempt is unsuccessful, it primes the brain to better encode the information once the correct answer is revealed. Therefore, low-stakes testing, such as using flashcards, answering practice questions, or simply closing a book and summarizing its contents aloud, should be reframed as a primary method of study, not just a final judgment of it.
