6---full-notes/returns-to-scale.title: Returns to scale
6---full-notes/returns-to-scale.content:
Status: teen
Tags: economics
Returns to scale
Details
The first wrinkle is returns to scale: what happens to output when you scale all inputs up by the same factor. That’s what we mean by a firm getting bigger.

Constant returns: f(2L, 2K) = 2f(L, K). Double the inputs and you double the output.
Decreasing returns: f(2L, 2K) < 2f(L, K). Gruber says this is the usual assumption: two people with two shovels on one hole get in each other’s way.
Increasing returns: f(2L, 2K) > 2f(L, K). A bigger firm can specialize and get better at what it does.

Returns to scale sit at the core of every model of economic growth in macroeconomics. Economists usually think returns increase at first, as a firm specializes, then decrease as it matures. If they increased forever, one firm would end up producing everything. Gruber suggests search engines might come close. He points to the then-ongoing antitrust trial, in which Google might be broken up.

6---full-notes/rewiring-focus-permanentl.title: Rewiring Focus Permanently with a Single 17-Minute Practice
6---full-notes/rewiring-focus-permanentl.content:
Status: teen
Tags: ADHD focus psychology
Rewiring Focus Permanently with a Single 17-Minute Practice
Details
One of the most remarkable and efficient tools for enhancing focus requires no special equipment and, according to research, can create a lasting improvement after just one session. This practice, lasting about 17 minutes, works by rewiring the brain’s attentional circuits to significantly reduce the occurrence of “attentional blinks.” The technique is a form of simple meditation focused on interoception—the perception of your body’s internal state.
The practice involves sitting quietly with your eyes closed and turning your attention inward. Instead of trying to clear your mind, you simply pay attention to the physical sensations of your body: the rhythm of your breathing, the feeling of your heartbeat, the contact of your skin against the surface you’re sitting on. When your mind inevitably drifts, you gently guide it back to these internal signals. This brief, one-time investment in consciously attending to your inner world has been shown to produce a durable change in how the brain allocates attention to the external world. It appears to train the brain to maintain a state of readiness, offsetting the natural tendency to “blink” and miss information, and may even help counteract age-related cognitive decline.

6---full-notes/rhetoric-as-an-approach.title: Rhetoric as an Approach
6---full-notes/rhetoric-as-an-approach.content:
Status: adult
Tags: rhetoric
Rhetoric as an Approach
Details
Rhetoric, as mentioned in Debating as a Sport, is a radically different approach from any other kind of approaches in any other subject because of its uniqueness to be able to approach ANY subject at all. When someone asks “Are you for or against abortion?”, the rhetorician’s first instinct is not to answer but to interrogate the question itself. The question has already done enormous work before you even open your mouth: it has framed the issue as binary (for/against), it has named the act as “abortion” (a termination rather than, say, a restoration of menstrual flow, as 19th-century medicine once framed it), and it has positioned you as someone who must choose a side within those prefabricated terms. The rhetorician refuses this positioning. The approach of the rhetorician is to question any and everything rather than accept the premises and go on.
Rhetoric, because of its very nature, has no home, it is merely an approach that applies Karl Popper and the Myth of Deductive Science. It can challenge a field and question its validity and purpose but that’s its only function, which may not be productive overall. This may extend to the proof of arguments, as historical documents may be questioned by rhetorician if the evidence are real, not compelling, but rather real. This has profound methodological consequences. If you can never get behind the document to the thing itself, then what you are always doing is reading documents — not recovering history, but interpreting texts. The lecturer’s undergraduate thesis argued essentially that history, as traditionally conceived, is impossible. Each text is a particular moment, and the leap from individual texts to a unified historical event (“all these texts equal the War of 1812”) is never justified — it is an assumption smuggled in before the research even begins. This is why the course focuses on learning to read texts carefully, as singular objects, rather than treating them as transparent evidence of something beyond themselves.

6---full-notes/rumination.title: Rumination
6---full-notes/rumination.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology
Rumination
Details
Rumination is the state of being cognitively “stuck” in a loop of negative thoughts. It’s a defining feature of depression where the mind compulsively replays sad memories, perceived failures, and feelings of guilt, unable to break free. This is not simply “thinking sad thoughts”; it is a pathological process where negative cognitions become self-perpetuating, like a cow endlessly chewing its cud.
The biological basis for rumination involves a critical imbalance in brain circuitry. The Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (DLPFC), a part of the brain’s executive control center, is responsible for cognitive flexibility and suppressing unwanted thoughts. In major depression, the DLPFC is often underactive and can even atrophy over time. It loses its ability to say “stop” to the negative thought patterns.
Simultaneously, brain regions that generate these thoughts become overactive. The Default Mode Network (DMN), which is active during self-referential thought and mind-wandering, gets hijacked by negativity. The amygdala (fear center) and anterior cingulate cortex (emotional pain) feed this network with a steady stream of distressing signals.
The result is a vicious cycle: the overactive DMN generates a negative thought, and the underactive DLPFC fails to suppress it. The thought then resonates through the network, reinforcing the negative emotional state, which in turn fuels more rumination. This cognitive quicksand is exhausting and makes it nearly impossible to focus on neutral or positive information, directly contributing to the cognitive deficits and persistent low mood seen in depression.

Sartre
Details
Sartre had the view that the self is not continuously present, that there is no “I” and that there is only consciousness of the streetcar-to-be-caught. The self is like a refrigerator light: on when you open the door, off when you close it. We assume it persists, but during unreflective living there’s no evidence it does. This directly challenges Descartes: cogito ergo sum works only because Descartes was actively engaged in reflective doubt. Had he been busy chasing a streetcar, would he still exist as a self ? Sartre thinks no, or that there wouldn’t be any evidence of that happening.
What this extends to is the objectiveness of our identities, because we never are able to exactly perceive ourselves and rather only understand that perception from other people. Each person is a “drain hole” through which the universe flows into a unique, private experience. With billions of such drains, almost everything knowable is unknowable to any one person. And so this develops anxiety, as it develops selfhood: us thinking about who we are, how we will be judged, and so on and so forth.

6---full-notes/schemas-to-learn-quicker.title: Schemas to learn quicker
6---full-notes/schemas-to-learn-quicker.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience learning Cognitive Psychology
Schemas to learn quicker
Details
Learning is not always a slow, trial-and-error process. The brain dramatically accelerates the acquisition of new information when it can fit that information into a pre-existing knowledge structure, or schema. A schema is a mental framework or map for a particular concept or activity. Schemas can be big or tin depending on things that one interacts with the world.
This was demonstrated in an experiment where rats learned the location of a food reward in a complex environment. The first time, it took many trials. However, when presented with a new food in a new location days later, the rats learned the new layout in a fraction of the time. They had developed a schema for “how this game works,” which made subsequent learning far more efficient.
This explains why an expert golfer can remember every shot of a round while a novice remembers almost none. The expert has a rich, detailed schema for the game of golf, providing a mental scaffold upon which to hang each new memory. The novice has no such framework, and the experiences remain a disorganized blur. Building these schemas—through education, practice, and experience—is fundamental to developing expertise and allows for the rapid, almost effortless, encoding of new, related knowledge.

Even if we have a schematic understanding of minds alien from our own, like understanding that a person might feel urges, hunger, thirst, we cannot feel how that feeling actually is. A bat must scream loudly to get an echo, but to avoid deafening itself, it must switch off its hearing implies during the scream, then immediately amp it up to catch the echo, all while flying at high speed. We can describe this mechanism computationally. We can map the brain cells involved. But we cannot simulate the phenomenology—the actual feeling—of that sensory stream. Schizophrenia
Details
A story about the term “schizophrenia” which comes from Greek roots meaning “split mind,” but the “split” in the term schizophrenia refers to a split between the intellectual and the emotion aspects of a person. Someone suffering from this may express strong inappropriate emotion or just fail to do so. It is no longer the defining symptom of it, but nonetheless it still occurs.
The main symptoms with schizophrenia are hallucinations and delusions, if these symptoms are severe, no other secondary symptoms may be necessary for it to be diagnosed. Some other symptoms also include, grossly disorganized behavior, or a loss of normal emotional responses and social behaviors. Before diagnosing a patient that could possible have this, the psychologist must rule out all other illnesses that can cause the symptoms.
These symptoms can be distinguished between positive and negative. Positive meant that the symptoms are present symptoms that normal human beings do not have. Negative symptoms means symptoms that humans are supposed to have.
Now we will go into detail about the symptoms. Hallucinations are perceptions that do not correspond to anything in the objective world. The most common examples are people seeing things, hearing voices, and such like that, these hallucinations do actually show brain activity in the auditory cortex and related brain areas (spooky). Now, consistency here does matter, if you do not hear these voices often, rarely only, then that does not mean you are schizoid.
Moving onto delusions, these are the unfounded belief that are strongly held despite the lack of evidences for them. There are three common types of this, which are persecution, grandeur, and reference. Persecution meaning there are fucking people chasing me ! Grandeur meaning I’m god basically. Reference meaning, oh the news are talking about Michael Jordan… it must be a sign for me.
The last big symptom to talk about is disordered thinking, which is basically people just functioning worse cognitively than others, people with schizophrenia I mean. Sometimes people with schizophrenia may suddenly stop talking and wait for you to talk although it is clear that their speech hasn’t end, sometimes they may even be able to sit in a singular position for extended periods of time which is completely abnormal to the human being.

Semantics and Symbols
Details
According to Searle, the fundamental misconception that the computer model of mind is the confusion between Syntaxes and Semantics. They think that just because the computer have and is able to move syntaxes around in its internal system that means that it understands them. The understanding of these symbols is semantics.
Just as a calculator can multiply “12 x 3” by flipping binary switches without knowing what the number “12” is, a computer can process the word “Apple” without knowing what an apple is. Functionalism tries to build a mind entirely out of syntax (rules and shapes), but Searle argues that “Syntax is not sufficient for Semantics.” No amount of symbol shuffling will ever add up to the conscious experience of meaning. Therefore, the scientific study of the mind based on the computer analogy is fundamentally mistaken because it ignores the semantic content that defines human thought.

In Propositional Logic, “meaning” is detached from the real-world significance of the words used. Instead, it derives entirely from Truth Assignments, binding them to a binary value of 1 or 0 (true or false). Logic is unconcerned to what the constant represents; only to how the truth values propagate through it.
The semantic rules defining this propagation are rigid, while operators like conjunction (AND) and disjunction (OR) align relatively well with intuition, Material Implication (\Rightarrow) presents a unique conceptual challenge. This is defined by the condition of falsifiability: an implication is considered false only when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false.

6---full-notes/sense-of-loss-in-depressi.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology emotional disorders
Sense of loss in Depression
Details
The first thing when encountering something like this is to consider the requirements and criteria of it first, try to read it carefully and such. This can also vary from subject to subject and field to field, and so the information and criteria may be different. In exploring the theme of loss, the psychological disorders revolves around a cognitive problem. This is in which the patient shows specific distortions, he has a negative view of his world, of himself, and a negative appraisal of the future which we call the cognitive triad.
These evaluations concern shrinkage of his domain, and lead to sadness. As said before, this is because it affects heavily on his domain of the self. When he considers his present position, he sees a barren world; he feels pressed to the wall by external demands that cheat him of his meager resources and keep him from attaining what he wants.
The term “loser” captures the flavor of the depressive’s appraisal of himself and his experience. He agonizes over the notion that he has experienced significant losses, such as his friends, his health, his prized possessions. He also regards himself as a “loser” in the colloquial sense: He is a misfit—an inferior and an inadequate being who is unable to meet his responsibilities and attain his goals. If he undertakes a project or seeks some gratification, he expects to be defeated or disappointed. He finds no respite during sleep. He has repetitive dreams in which he is a misfit, a failure.
In considering the concept of loss, we should be sensitive to the crucial importance of meanings and connotations. What represents a painful loss for one person may be regarded as trivial by another. It is important to recognize that the depressed patient dwells on hypothetical losses and pseudo losses. When he thinks about a potential loss, he regards the possibility as though it were an accomplished fact.
Supporting Content
Granted that the perception of loss produces feelings of sadness, how does this sense of loss engender other symptoms of depression: pessimism, self-criticism, escape-avoidance-giving up, suicidal wishes, and physiological disorders?
In order to answer this question, it would be useful to explore the chronology of depression, the onset and full development of symptoms. This sequence is most clearly demonstrated in cases of “reactive depression,” that is, depression in which there is a clear-cut precipitating factor. Other cases of depression, in which the onset is more insidious, show similar (although more subtle) patterns.

6---full-notes/sets-and-the-axiom-of-ext.content:
Status: teen
Tags: logic
Sets and the Axiom of Extensionality
Details
A “set” is rock bottom basic modern mathematics; it is a primitive notion that cannot be defined by simpler terms, only described by synonyms such as class, collection, or totality. A defining feature of a set is its indifference to the relatedness of its members, for example something like Socrates’ nose, the number 19, and Mark Twain’s sense of humor without contradiction.
This identity is extended by the Axiom of Extensionality, which dictates that it is solely defined by its members, not by the method used to describe it. This distinguishes sets from properties. For instance, the property “creature with a heart” is conceptually distinct from “creature with kidneys.” However, if every creature with a heart also has kidneys, the set of creatures with hearts is identical to the set of creatures with kidneys. Consequently, because identity is tied strictly to membership, the order of elements and the repetition of names in a list are irrelevant; \{a, b\} is identical to \{b, a, a\}.

Sexual Totemism as an Intermediator
Details
Between the collective totem of the clan and the personal totem of the individual lies a curious intermediate form: sexual totemism. Here, the entire male population of a tribe is mystically linked to one animal species, and the entire female population to another. All men are “brothers” to their totem (e.g., the bat), and all women are “sisters” to theirs (e.g., the nightjar). This system partakes of both other forms. Like clan totemism, it is collective and implies a relationship of descent from a mythical ancestor. Yet, like individual totemism, the bond is so intimate that the death of a single totemic animal is thought to endanger the life of a corresponding human, and the cause should be punished and hunted for accordingly. This structure reflects the profound social reality of the separation of the sexes, creating two distinct corporations within the tribe, yet also uniting them together somewhat, each with its own sacred protector, demonstrating again how religious classifications mirror social organization.

Shaping Behaviors
Details
Mastery is the goal of shaping, and is something that is complex and unlikely to be understood easily or all at once. And so a process need to be derived, a process that slowly but surely shapes into the act that we want to achieve, in this case mastery. This can also be applied to reinforcing and shaping the approximate actions of animals for us to achieve a behavior that we want from them.
The process begins by identifying a behavior the subject already does naturally. If the goal is for the pigeon to peck a key, the trainer might first reward the pigeon simply for turning toward the wall where the key is located. Once that behavior is established, the reinforcement criteria are raised: the pigeon is now only rewarded for moving closer to the wall. This continues incrementally—rewarding for looking at the key, then for touching it, and finally, only for pecking it.
This same principle applies to human behavior. A professor’s jokes are shaped by the audience’s laughter; jokes that get a positive response are repeated and refined, while those that fall flat are dropped. By rewarding small steps toward a desired outcome, shaping makes it possible to cultivate complex and precise behaviors that would be highly unlikely to occur spontaneously.

6---full-notes/short-term-vs.-long-term-.title: Short-Term vs. Long-Term Stress
6---full-notes/short-term-vs.-long-term-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology physiology
Short-Term vs. Long-Term Stress
Details
Stress is a fundamental biological response, but its value hinges on duration, as illustrated by two conceptual graphs. Short-term stress yields a cascade of benefits, such as enhanced focus, energy mobilization, and adaptive physiological changes. For instance, in a brief crisis—like evading danger or tackling an urgent task—the body ramps up cortisol and adrenaline, sharpening senses and boosting performance. This acute phase can foster resilience, improve memory consolidation, and even promote growth in neural pathways, making it evolutionarily advantageous.
However, as stress extends into chronicity, we can experience detrimental effects from stress instead. Prolonged exposure—think daily traffic jams, an abusive boss, or unrelenting financial worries—erodes health. Chronic stress suppresses immunity, elevates blood pressure, disrupts sleep, and contributes to conditions like anxiety, depression, and cardiovascular disease. The body’s systems, designed for quick bursts, become overwhelmed: glucocorticoids that aid short-term survival start damaging the hippocampus, impairing learning and emotional regulation.
Stress isn’t monolithic; its perception varies. We must conceptualize stress not as an enemy to eradicate but as a tool with a tipping point. Chronic stressors dominate modern life, often psychological rather than physical, making them insidious. For example, a 20-year grind in a toxic job isn’t a saber-toothed tiger chase—it’s a slow drip of cortisol that atrophies well-being.
To apply this: prioritize interventions that keep stress acute and purposeful. Exercise, hobbies, or challenges can harness short-term benefits, but unchecked chronicity demands lifestyle audits. This framework shifts the narrative from “stress is bad” to “timing is everything,” encouraging proactive management before the downhill slide. Ultimately, understanding these dynamics empowers us to reframe everyday pressures, turning potential drawbacks into controlled stimulation.

6---full-notes/short-run-competition-(an.title: Short-run competition (and perfect competition)
6---full-notes/short-run-competition-(an.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Profit Maximization under perfect competition
Details
Finally, we move on to how we decide how much of a product to make.
Market structures run between two extremes:

Perfect competition: many firms selling identical goods. The course starts here.
Monopoly: a single firm. This comes next.
Oligopoly: a handful of firms. Gruber calls it his favorite word in economics, and it describes most real industries: there’s more than one car company, but not a thousand. It comes after the midterm.

The technical definition of perfect competition is that every firm is a price-taker: nothing one firm does can move the market price, because each firm is tiny relative to the market. So the demand curve facing a single firm is perfectly elastic, horizontal at the market price p.
This is about one firm’s demand (little q), not market demand (big Q). Demand for Eiffel Tower keychains overall isn’t perfectly elastic, but demand for one seller’s keychains is. If one firm’s costs shift, its output changes but the price doesn’t.
Three assumptions make firms price-takers:

Identical products.
Full knowledge of prices: every buyer knows every firm’s price.
No transaction costs: buyers can easily shop at any firm.

No real market fits exactly; the extreme is a benchmark. eBay looks close for a standard item, like a particular chip or a shirt in a given size and style: the products match, prices are listed, and shopping is easy. In practice, it falls short in two ways:

For years, eBay ranked listings by price without shipping. That makes shipping a shrouded attribute, a hidden part of the price.
Few products are truly identical, so comparing them takes time, which is itself a transaction cost.

Gruber’s favorite near-example is the hundreds of sellers on blankets around the Eiffel Tower, all offering the same keychain within sight of each other. After he taught it online, a student mailed him a bag of the keychains. The student reported that sellers right by the tower all charged exactly the same price, while those further away charged differently. A different location makes it a different product.
A firm chooses quantity to maximize profit, π(q) = R(q) − C(q): revenue minus cost. Setting the derivative to zero gives
dR/dq = dC/dq, or marginal revenue = marginal cost (MR = MC)
That’s profit maximization in one equation, and it holds in any market. Under perfect competition, every extra unit sells for the market price, so MR = p and the rule becomes
p = MC
Gruber’s example uses the cost function from Lecture 6, C = 10 + 5q², with a price of $30. The 10 is the fixed cost, which you pay whatever you produce. The 5q² is the variable cost, which grows with output. Marginal cost is MC = dC/dq = 10q, so p = MC gives 10q = 30, and q* = 3.
The unit-by-unit view shows why. Each extra unit brings in $30; the last column is what that unit adds to cost:















































UnitsRevenueCostProfitCost of that unit0010−10130151552603030153905535254120903035
The first three units each cost less than the 30 they sell for, so each one raises profit. The fourth costs 35, so it lowers profit.
Gruber’s image is climbing a mountain in the clouds. You can’t see the top, only whether your next step goes up or down, and you’re at the top when the next step goes down. The table steps in whole units. The derivative is the same test for a tiny next step, which is why the method also works with fractional amounts, as Gruber told a student.
Profit shows up on the cost-curve graph as a rectangle. Write profit as (revenue per unit − cost per unit) × number of units:
π = (p − AC) × q
Here AC = C/q is average cost, which works out to 10/q + 5q. At q = 3, AC = 10/3 + 15 ≈ 18.33. Each unit sells for 30 and costs 18.33 on average, so profit per unit is 11.67. The rectangle is 11.67 tall and 3 wide, so profit is 35. Gruber says 40 in class, but 11.67 × 3 = 35, which matches revenue of 90 minus cost of 55.
He then asked what a 10-per-unit tax does. The new cost function is C = 10 + 5q² + 10q. The common first answer, 20 + 5q², treats it as a single flat 10, which is wrong because the tax is paid on every unit.

Marginal cost rises to 10q + 10, so p = MC gives 10q + 10 = 30, and q* = 2.
The price hasn’t changed. Output falls because each unit now costs more to make.
Both sides of the profit rectangle shrink: fewer units, and less profit on each, since average cost rises too. In numbers (not given in the lecture), AC at q = 2 is 5 + 10 + 10 = 25, so profit falls from 35 to (30 − 25) × 2 = 10.

A flat $10 tax, by contrast, wouldn’t change output at all. It doesn’t touch marginal cost, so the firm still makes 3 units and simply earns 25 instead of 35.
The last short-run complication is whether to shut down. Losing money isn’t, by itself, a reason to stop. Suppose the price falls to $10 (no tax). Then 10q = 10 gives q = 1. Revenue is 10 and cost is 10 + 5 = 15, so profit is −5. But if the firm produces nothing, it still owes the fixed cost and loses 10. Losing 5 beats losing 10, so it keeps producing.
In the short run, the fixed cost is sunk: you’ve already paid it whatever you do, so it shouldn’t affect the decision. Staying open also keeps the option to fix your costs later, in the long run.
So the shutdown rule compares revenue with variable cost only. Shut down if
p × q < VC, or, dividing by q, p < AVC
where AVC = VC/q is average variable cost. Keep producing as long as the price covers average variable cost.
In this example the firm never shuts down. AVC = 5q²/q = 5q. A profit-maximizing firm produces q = p/10, so AVC = 5 × p/10 = 0.5p, which is always below p.
In the long run nothing is fixed, so there are no sunk costs to ignore. A firm that has fully re-optimized and still loses money should leave the industry.

6---full-notes/short-run-costs.title: Short-run costs
6---full-notes/short-run-costs.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Short-run costs
Details
Suppose a firm rents capital at rate r and hires labor at wage w. In the short run with capital fixed at \bar{K}, total expenditure as a function of output q is C(q) = r\bar{K} + w L(q). The only choice variable in the short run is labor, and Gruber notes that he treats hours of labor and the count of workers interchangeably as the measure of labor input unless specified otherwise. To obtain the explicit cost function C(q), you invert the short-run production function to express the required labor L in terms of output q, and then substitute that expression directly into the cost equation.
Using the lecture’s working example, let the production function be q = \sqrt{L \cdot K}, with input prices set at wage w = \5 and rental rate r = $10. Holding capital fixed at \bar{K} = 1, the production function simplifies to q = \sqrt{L}, which inverts to L = q^2. Substituting this into the expenditure relationship yields the short-run total cost function C(q) = 10(1) + 5(q^2) = 10 + 5q^2$. The function maps the technological requirements of production straight into dollars: producing twice as much output does not merely double labor costs, but quadruples them because of diminishing returns to the single variable input.
From this cost function, Gruber constructs several foundational metrics. Fixed costs (FC) are expenses that do not vary with output in the short run, which in this case equals the 10 spent on fixed capital. Variable costs (VC) are the expenses that fluctuate directly with production, represented here by 5q^2. Total cost (TC) is simply their sum, 10 + 5q^2. Marginal cost (MC) is the differential of total cost with respect to quantity, dTC/dq. Because fixed costs do not change when output shifts, dFC/dq = 0, meaning marginal cost is identical whether differentiated from total cost or variable cost: MC = dVC/dq = 10q. Average cost (AC or ATC) is total cost divided by output, which breaks down into average fixed cost (AFC = 10/q) plus average variable cost (AVC = 5q).
This U-shape explains why marginal cost must cross average cost precisely at its minimum point. The intuition is purely mathematical and mirrors a grade point average. When the marginal cost of producing the next unit is below the current average cost, that additional unit pulls the overall average downward. Once the marginal cost of producing the next unit exceeds the current average cost, that next unit pushes the average upward. It follows that the turning point—the absolute minimum of average cost—must occur exactly where marginal cost equals average cost. Setting 10q = (10/q) + 5qleads to 5q = 10/q, which simplifies to q^2 = 2, or q = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41, which Gruber rounds to roughly 1.5 in lecture.
Marginal cost and the marginal product of labor are two sides of the same coin. Starting from the short-run cost relation C = r\bar{K} + wL and differentiating with respect to quantity gives dC/dq = w \cdot (dL/dq). Because the marginal product of labor is MP_L = dq/dL, the inverse function rule establishes that dL/dq = 1 / MP_L. Substituting this in yields MC = w / MP_L. The economic intuition is immediate: producing one extra unit of output requires 1 / MP_Ladditional hours of labor, and each hour costs the wage w. When workers are highly productive, an additional unit requires very little labor, keeping marginal cost low. As diminishing marginal returns set in and MP_L falls, each subsequent unit demands progressively more labor hours, causing short-run marginal cost to rise.
We are then introduced to sunk costs. They are basically costs that once you buy, you never get it back regardless of what happens. Its quite an essential and yet difficult concept to understand but yeah it’s just gone bro. But at the end it is still separate from opportunity costs rather than as if we are saying the opportunity cost is also zero in this situation.
The fundamental decision rule of economics is that sunk costs are sunk, meaning they must be entirely ignored in forward-looking decisions. Because past expenditures cannot be altered by any present or future choice, factoring them into a decision is irrational. To illustrate how counterintuitive this is, Gruber shares his experience buying two tickets to see the rock band Journey in Mansfield, Massachusetts, for \125 each ($250$ total) to see their replacement vocalist discovered on YouTube. After reviewing the concert setlist, he realized he only cared for three songs and decided that sitting through a ninety-minute show was not worth his evening.
He considered selling the tickets on StubHub, raising the question of how the \250 purchase price should influence his listing price. The instinctive human response—which a student in the audience offered—is to try to recover the $250. Gruber stresses that this is textbook sunk-cost fallacy. The $250 is gone whether he attends, resells, or burns the tickets. The rational floor on his selling price depends entirely on his opportunity cost of going. If his subjective value of attending is zero because he would genuinely rather sit on his couch, he should be willing to part with the tickets for anything above zero dollars. If he values attending at $50 a ticket, he should set $50 as his reservation price: if the market pays more than $50$, he sells; if it pays less, he attends. What he paid in the past does not enter the arithmetic.
When a student asked whether intent separates fixed costs from sunk costs, Gruber acknowledged that the line can feel fuzzy. If you buy a building intending from the outset to hold it as an asset and eventually resell it, the expense is an avoidable fixed cost. If you buy a non-transferable service or an asset with zero salvage value, it is sunk immediately. He recalled being reprimanded by his own graduate school advisor when agonizing over non-refundable plane tickets: his advisor reminded him that the money was spent, and the only relevant consideration was the utility of taking the trip versus staying home.

6---full-notes/simple-is-big.title: Simple is Big
6---full-notes/simple-is-big.content:
Status: adult
Tags: creativity Zettelkasten
Simple is Big
Details
We often imagine that great ideas or breakthroughs come in a flash—a spark of genius, a sudden insight that rewrites the rules. But in truth, they rarely arrive fully formed. Most transformative ideas are not the product of sudden inspiration, but the culmination of slow, layered thinking: observations, failures, habits, and small questions gradually compounding over time.
Big ideas have deep roots.
What seems like an “aha!” moment is often just the final click in a long sequence of unnoticed gears turning. A scientist may suddenly “discover” something after years of failed experiments. A writer’s striking line might emerge only after hundreds of discarded drafts. Behind every apparent leap is a quiet, patient build-up.
This process is often invisible. We don’t see the pages of notes, the walks taken in silence, the unanswered questions held for months. But it’s in these small acts—what seems trivial or even boring—that the ground is prepared for insight. Breakthroughs aren’t made from thin air; they crystallize out of background work we often forget or dismiss.
Simplicity is deceptive.
When something finally makes sense, it feels obvious. But this is hindsight. Clarity doesn’t mean the path was easy. It means someone distilled complexity into a form that now feels natural. The deeper the idea, the simpler it often appears at the surface—because it’s been refined through time, error, and persistence.
“Simple is big” means that foundational, basic-looking things often carry immense conceptual weight. A small change in habit can remake your mental landscape. A basic question can birth a whole discipline. The key is not to underestimate small steps, or wait for some dramatic epiphany. Every slow, thoughtful moment counts.
Creativity is cumulative.
Whether in science, art, philosophy, or daily living, progress grows out of attention to detail. Seeds are sown long before they bloom. You can’t always trace the origin of a good idea—it might have been planted by a stray comment, a line in a book, a moment of stillness.

6---full-notes/skill-acquisition.title: Skill Acquisition
6---full-notes/skill-acquisition.content:
Status: adult
Tags: therapy Clinical Psychology learning
Skill Acquisition
Details
Depending on the difficulty of the skills, we can try to teach anywhere from 1-3, although it is of course better to acquire mastery in one skill over the others. Presenting many skills may overwhelm the client and suggests that the skills are easy. Secondly, teaching a large amount of skills then saying nothing works can make the client deflated as their resistance and motivation would run out before the amount of skills does.
Moreover, knowing what the task it, the person’s role, and what one can expect from the other person facilitates learning enormously. This is orientation, and it called for each specific skill and each homework assignment. Some clients though, may have skill deficits and fear acquiring new ones. It can be useful to point out that learning it doesn’t mean using it. A person can acquire then choose whether to use it or not. Also, it may help to reinforce them that the skill will work, but also to say that not every skill is gonna be useful.
Another point to bring up is about assessing the client’s abilities. When assessing a client’s ability, it is most difficult to determine if they are incapable of doing something or emotionally inhibited or constrained by environmental factors. These people don’t have the metacognitive ability to assess their own abilities so it might be more difficult. For instance, they may confuse the inability to do something than being afraid to do it. Not only that, this stems from their own dissociation with themselves, being unable to tell their own thoughts/emotions, or rather, being afraid to do so. They don’t wanna be vulnerable, and also their family have completely destroyed that part of them down to the ground. To more effectively see this, trainers can orchestrate situations or role play situations, emotional regulation can be assessed by interrupting (ragebaiting) then seeing if the client can change their state, and so on.
Instructions, this can vary anywhere from general guidelines to specific suggestions of the client’s actions. Try to make it as clear and easy to understand as possible, for adolescents, it might help to make them read the instructions out loud. You may even get those who have done it before to make examples. Furthermore, they should try to explain all dimensions of it, when, why, and what. This helps so that they can deal with problems before clients encounter it in practical situations. Lastly, it is also important to get the client to understand that the immediate relief of pain is not the goal but rather the long-term relief and all.
Modeling can be provided by trainers, or other clients. It is basically supporting materials for the people who hasn’t understand how to do it yet, and it can also be fitted into how people perceive it all. There are also many ways to model and help the person further understand.

6---full-notes/skill-generalization.title: Skill Generalization
6---full-notes/skill-generalization.content:
Status: adult
Tags: therapy Clinical Psychology learning
Skill Generalization
Details
The last step in skill teaching, which is to help people use their skills in situations outside of therapy. There are a few ways that a trainer can go by this, firstly is to have between-session consultation, being with them and talking to them about performing such actions. Another way is to review session video recordings, which provide benefits such as allowing an easier way to review their actions out of sessions, as well as helping them to calm down if they are unable to cope and so on in between sessions. Moreover, people can also go online and app stores to find DBT apps/sites that allow them access to resources for them to learn and practice their skills.
Another big one is diary cards, which is how trainers check on their clients’ behavioral progress between sessions, providing necessary feedback and coaching. This though does not replace any of the skills reviewing in the session, as it is only seeing if the person has remembered to do their skills, not seeing if they are doing it effectively. Any forgetting or such of the diary cards may be marked as self-management problems to be analyzed and discussed so that it can be solved by the skills being taught.
In managing an environment so that clients can reinforce their behavior, it is necessary for them to create structure, public commitments, finding communities to support their new behaviors, and how to elicit reinforcement from others. More than that, the problem with clients is that they sometimes hold such high expectations that it is impossible for them to reach it, so trainers then need to deal with this. Another help in the environment building can be family members, who can help them train their skills. Last but not least, trainers also have to learn how and when to start fading out from the skills training procedures of the clients. They have to follow an intermittent schedule and provide less help to the clients which helps them to become independent of the influence.

6---full-notes/skill-strengthening.title: Skill Strengthening
6---full-notes/skill-strengthening.content:
Status: adult
Tags: therapy Clinical Psychology learning
Skills Strengthening
Details
Happening after Skill Acquisition, then comes skill strengthening as it helps us to shape, refine, and increase the likelihood of its use. We have to have reinforced practice so that we can learn the skills, as it includes effortful behavior which counteracts the passive behavior of the emotionally-dysregulated patients.
Practice of skills can be “overt” or “covert”. Covert is practicing the requisite response in the imagination whilst overt is behavioral rehearsal, like roleplaying. Covert response may be more effective than overt methods for teaching more complex skills and also useful for when clients refuse to engage in overt rehearsal. To practice emotional behavior, clients have to practice specific components of emotions, like their faces, inner systems, muscles, and so on. When clients refuse to engage in roleplay/behavioral rehearsal, the trainers would then have to try to talk them through a dialogue or something of the sorts.
The next step is response reinforcement, which is like Classical conditioning, meaning they have to be positive reinforced for their actions and growth. Many individuals have lived in environments that overuse punishment, this makes them expect negative, punishing feedback from the world (including their therapists) which also makes them punish themselves to shape their own behavior. Over the long run though, this reinforcement can increase their self image in a positive way, which enhances the sense of control they have over their lives. A reinforcer though can also be negative, meaning it can take away or discourage the response of people, and so one must be careful to not accidentally negatively reinforce the clients. Lastly, trainers also have to completely be sure about their decisions and reinforcing, not skipping over analyzing failures and so on.
Lastly, bringing our views to feedback, which is necessary for these people whose actions and feedback that they get are so uncontaminated with interpretations about their presumed motives and intent. By trying to judge their motives and getting it wrong, this would discourage the clients from listening and absorbing the feedback. So instead, one should focus on their behaviors, not thinking about their intent. Also, the amount of feedback has to be optimal so that it won’t lead to stimulus overload and/or discouragement. But again, these feedback may be interpreted as negative and so people need to surrounding it with positivity like talking about people’s own inability to do it, as it isn’t just them. In addition, there is “coaching”, which is combining feedback with instructions.

Slave Morality
Details
This is the other side of Nietzsche’s arguments, which he describes as a profoundly creative act that is poisonous. He originally argues in Ressentiment: a specific physiological and psychological state where a subject is oppressed but lacks the power to react physically. If a Master is insulted, he strikes back immediately, but if a Slave is insulted, he must swallow it. And so slaves would then act inwardly and conceptually.
They do this by taking the very qualities that define the Master—strength, pride, violence, wealth, sexual confidence—and conceptually reframes them as “Evil.” This is the birth of the concept of “Evil” as a moral category. They weaponize this redefinition of the word to be reactive and aim at the evilness of the Masters.

6---full-notes/slave's-evilness.title: Slave's Evilness
6---full-notes/slave's-evilness.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
Slave’s Evilness
Details
Nietzsche furthermore argued about the reversal of attribute of slaves. We have established in Slave Morality how they were considered “Good.” Now, this goodness doesn’t address the useless suffering that these slaves have to endure without ending, and so the priests have two solutions to this. They either do therapy to the slaves by making them confess and such and so on (Innocent Means) which numbs the pain, or they give the slaves’ suffering meaning (Guilty Means). To give them meaning, the Priest fuses the psychophysical pain of Bad Conscience with the moral concept of Evil in Nietzsche previous essays and turns it into the Slave interpreting their own instincts as evil. This saves the Slave from suicidal nihilism (the suffering now makes sense), but it traps them in a pathological narrative where their own natural instincts are the enemy.
Furthermore, as mentioned in The Phenomenology of Bad Conscience, us humans have the ability to perform “Ascetic Practices” which are activities that we do to refrain ourselves from making it more difficult for us to reach a higher goal (this is a theory similar or primitive to Deterministic Autonomy and Second-Order Desires).
The Priest’s idea pushes this to the extreme, by forcing an Ascetic Ideal instead, universally claiming every turn of the will to be extremely evil and a failure of morals. But in conclusion, this does not solve the problem fully, it instead introduces a descending spiral of Vitality.
The “cure” the Priest prescribes for the “sin” of willfulness is to crush the will—to engage in self-abnegation, fasting, guilt, and penance. However, the Slave is already sick and weak; that is why they are suffering in the first place. The Priest’s cure (attacking the self) attacks the very reservoirs of energy the Slave needs to get better. By turning aggression against their own remaining instincts, the Slave becomes sicker and weaker. As they become sicker, their suffering increases. As their suffering increases, the Priest interprets this as a need for more penance and self-flagellation. Thus, the remedy aggravates the disease. Christianity, in Nietzsche’s view, is a systematic machine for maximizing degeneration by turning the human animal against its own biological foundations.

6---full-notes/snowballing-of-sadness-an.title: Snowballing of sadness and apathy
6---full-notes/snowballing-of-sadness-an.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Snowballing of sadness and apathy
Details
Although the onset of depression may be sudden, its full development spreads over a certain timeframe. The symptoms of the depressed patient may gradually increase in intensity until he “hits rock bottom.” This gradual development is due to the repeat of the sense of loss being repeated and constituting a fresh experience which is added more.
The depressed person tends to extract elements suggestive of loss and to gloss over other features that are not consonant with, or are contradictory to, this interpretation. As a result of such “selective abstraction,” the patient overinterprets daily events in terms of loss and is oblivious to more positive interpretations; he is hypersensitive to stimuli suggestive of loss and is blind to stimuli representing gain. He shows the same type of selectivity in recalling past experiences. He is facile in recalling unpleasant experiences, but may “draw a blank” when questioned about positive experiences. This selectivity in memory has been demonstrated experimentally by Lishman (1972).
This “tunnel vision” makes it so that the patient becomes impermeable to stimuli that can arouse pleasure. Though he might be able to recognize his achievements, he might still not feel happy, or angry, or any emotions other than sadness. The same applies to any other distortion in thinking  from depression.
Whilst this usually results in sadness, the passive resignation may lead to apathy, as they feel like there is no point in trying so they stop trying.

6---full-notes/social-comparison.title: Social Comparison
6---full-notes/social-comparison.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Social Psychology
Social Comparison
Details
Perhaps the most common mechanism in people to protect and evaluate their own standings in society (but perhaps also one of the most inaccurate). We do not have an exact measurement for how good we are, so we have to compare it to other people. But the entire process is rigged by who we choose to compare ourselves to, and we almost never question that choice because we are our own standard of reasonableness.
Festinger identified two functions of social comparison that pull in opposite directions. Downward comparisons and upward comparisons, which are basically comparing ourselves to people who are worse off and people who are better than us, but both makes us feel bad or dissatisfied one way or another. This is the core relationship of these mechanisms: the comparisons that are the most informative are the most emotionally expensive, and the comparisons that feel best are informationally empty.
Cialdini’s research emphasizes how people bask in reflected glory - basically how people usually want to identify with a group when they succeed - wearing school insignia after a team win, but saying “we won” and “they lost.” But Tesser’s Self-Evaluation Maintenance Theory revealed sharp limits. When someone close to you succeeds in a domain central to your identity, their success becomes threatening. Your brother winning a cooking competition feels wonderful if cooking means nothing to you, but agonizing if it’s your life’s passion. He demonstrated this with a gameshow survey.
But, as a way of life, it is quite anomalous. In the world, there is a practically infinite amount of people that you can compare yourself to, and so its a losing game, or more accurately, an unwinnable one. We might (as a hypothesis) have to abandon this comparison standards if we want to be happy.

6---full-notes/social-hierarchy-and-logi.title: Social Hierarchy and Logical Aspirations
6---full-notes/social-hierarchy-and-logi.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology
Social Hierarchy and Logical Aspirations
Details
According to Durkheim, a healthy society provides a “regimen” that regulates desires. This happens through the “moral consciousness of societies,” which establishes a hierarchy of social functions and assigns a corresponding degree of well-being that each class may legitimately aspire to. They will be assigned to needs that are fair for what they were born as, their inheriting, their abilities, their statuses.
This creates a scale, though not immutable, that sets an upper limit on the ambitions for each person within their sphere. If an individual has a “wholesome moral constitution,” they accept this collective authority and feel “that it is not well to ask more.”
This limitation is what allows for contentment. It sets a defined end and goal for the passions, which “make men contented with their lot while stimulating them moderately to improve it.” This creates a “calm, active happiness” because one’s happiness is secure and defined, not dependent on an infinite and unattainable goal.
For this system to work, however, individuals must not only accept the hierarchy of functions but also believe the distribution of those functions is just.

Social Media’s Impact on Human Hierarchies and Self-Perception
Details
Humans repurpose ancient biology for novel contexts, and social media exemplifies this, expanding hierarchies infinitely and often detrimentally. We use the same hormones and circuits as baboons but abstract them—feeling belittled by a stranger’s luxury car or an uninvited party in Singapore. Feeds bombard with mishmash contexts (meals, bodies, intellects), eroding self-esteem via endless comparisons.
Evolved for limited interactions, our PFC now navigates vast landscapes, triggering stress from abstract inadequacies (e.g., envying Bezos’s space flight). This fosters novel misery, using dopamine-testosterone loops for virtual status chases. Mitigate by curating feeds or limiting exposure, reclaiming constrained hierarchies for well-being.

Durkheim argues this force cannot be physical, as “hearts cannot be touched by physico-chemical forces.” It must be a moral force that individuals recognize as just and yield to spontaneously. He argues further that humanity needs a higher force, a force that will make them follow codes, rules of their own restrictions so that they understand their limits and can be happy. He also argued that people will follow these rules out of respect, not fear. And that force is society. Therefore, the bond that regulates humanity is not physical, but moral and social. Society as a Social Union of Social Unions
Details
A social union differs from The Private Society and Human Nature by two features. The first is that its participants have identically the same end and that the social institutions and cooperative activities are ends in themselves, not just means.
And so a well-ordered society governed on this philosophy would govern the smaller social unions of families, friendships, and so on. The end that they all share is the basic structure of a society to be just and that everyone be treated justly and do their part accordingly.
Crucially, acting from a sense of justice is not merely an obligation imposed from outside. Given the moral psychology Rawls relies on, the exercise and realization of one’s moral powers — including the capacity for justice — is part of one’s good. The good of exercising complex, subtle, and discriminating powers is greater than simpler exercises of capacity. The sense of justice is among citizens’ most important powers, and its realization in a successful cooperative life organized around just principles is part of what makes that life go well for the person living it.

Society as a System of Social Cooperation
Details
John Rawls posits that the most fundamental intuitive idea in justice as fairness is the concept that society itself is a system of social cooperation between citizens as free and equal persons. He also does not force this concept to be the definitive idea or that it is required, but rather that it is a model that will be used and reflected upon.
This idea of course has to include some prerequisites from the relationships: Firstly, citizens do not see their social order as something fixed but rather something that can change and be justified depending on the context of discussion.
From this, Rawls distinguishes three features of cooperation. First is the separation of cooperation from mutual coordinated activity to an unquestionable central authority as this authority cannot be questioned and people would be obligatory to follow. Secondly, he states that cooperation would involve fair times that are publicly recognized and embody some sense of reciprocity or mutuality. Lastly, he believes that both parties engaged in this act would be looking to increase their own wellbeing and achieve personal benefits.
And so justice acts as a definition, it has the role of setting the grounds and the principles on which cooperation happens in a certain way with the purpose of that way leading to fairness.

Sociometrics and Peer Rejection as a Risk Factor

Sociometrics defines the likeness of a particular student in a class or group by asking their classmates to nominate how they feel about the other students. 6---full-notes/solubility-principles.content:

Solubility Principles
Details
How a drugs behave is usually accredited to its interactions with the human body. Molecules are generally classified as hydrophilic or hydrophobic, which simultaneously means water-loving and water-hating. Chemically, that means hydrophilic substances are polar or charged, allowing them to dissolve easily in blood and urine, excreted quickly. On the other hand, hydrophobic means they prefer oily or fatty environments, and will dissolve slower.
This is critical in drug testing as THC (the active compound in cannabis), dissolve into the body’s fatty tissues. Because they are stored in fat rather than staying in the water-based blood, they are eliminated from the body very slowly. This all explains how a user of cannabis may still test positive weeks after use whilst those who use water-based substances won’t.

Somatic Imaging
Details
In a person’s domain, some other essential components of the self-concept is the “bodily self,” “somatic self,” or “body image”. This conception of the self may dictate someone (as normally the personal domain does) whether he feels pleased or pained, strong or weak, energetic or listless. This may be even more important than the true physical conditions that the person finds himself in.
Visual stimulation is something that could affect the body image and thus lead to multiple physical sensations. Like how a curved screen with motion pictures may lead the person feeling that they are moving very fast on a vehicle of some sorts. Same with one who is watching gore, they may feel pain or anxiety. These feelings have been documented by Sir Francis Galton (1883). Some of his subjects experienced somatic sensations that were so vivid that they often wondered if it was imagination or reality.
Moving on to fantasies or daydreams (without any external visual stimuli as mentioned above) may also do the same thing. Psychiatric patients usually report this kind of somatic imaging. For example, a patient reported seeing a needle and imagining it being injected into his penis (which I am also experiencing the emotional repercussions of writing that).
The thought of a physical injury may also do this. A young adolescent reacted with anxiety to blood, as he was sensitive to any stimulus that suggested bones breaking. When his therapist showed him a bone, he thought, “My leg could be broken” and felt pain in his leg and the sensation of the bone protruding through his skin.

6---full-notes/somatosensory-cortex.title: Somatosensory cortex
6---full-notes/somatosensory-cortex.content:
Status: baby
Tags: neuroscience psychology
Somatosensory cortex
Details
The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) is the main receptive area in the cerebral cortex for the sense of touch and other bodily sensations. Located in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe, it receives sensory information from the skin, muscles, joints, and internal organs.
Its primary functions include processing tactile information such as pressure, vibration, texture, temperature, and pain. It is also crucial for proprioception, the sense of the relative position of one’s own body parts and the effort being employed in movement.
The somatosensory cortex is organized somatotopically, meaning that adjacent areas of the skin are represented by adjacent areas in the cortex. This organization is famously depicted as the sensory homunculus, a distorted representation of the human body where more sensitive areas (like the lips and hands) have disproportionately larger regions of cortical tissue devoted to them.

6---full-notes/some-common-depowering-ru.title: Some common depowering rules
6---full-notes/some-common-depowering-ru.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Some common depowering rules
Details
There is something called the pleasure-pain rule: One is often converse of the other. Certain of these rules are so gross that they are at a complete variance with reality or have a long term effect that will inevitably affect the goals of the patient. For example, an attitude like: “It is wonderful to be famous.” The converse will be: “I can never be happy if I’m not famous.” People can be dominated by these rules and so they will constantly hold themselves to it: chalking a point up when they gain fame, subtracting if they lose relevancy. Slavishly following these rules will interfere with the person’s own goal of living a fulfilling life or something of the similar nature.
Even more crucial is that certain people are likely to become depressed by overemphasizing these rules, they will constantly judge themselves and confine themselves to this one definition of happiness, and so they won’t be able to find happiness at all once the fame isn’t there anymore.
Some of the attitudes that predispose people to excessive sadness or depression are listed below:

In order to be happy, I have to be successful in whatever I undertake.
To be happy, I must be accepted (liked, admired) by all people at all times.
If I’m not on top, I’m a flop.
It’s wonderful to be popular, famous, wealthy; it’s terrible to be unpopular, mediocre.
If I make a mistake, it means that I’m inept.
My value as a person depends on what others think of me.
I can’t live without love. If my spouse (sweetheart, parent, child) doesn’t love me, I’m worthless.
If somebody disagrees with me, it means he doesn’t like me.
If I don’t take advantage of every opportunity to advance myself, I will regret it later.

Rules such as the above are likely to lead to misery. It is impossible for a person to be loved totally, at all times by all his friends. The degree of love and acceptance fluctuates considerably. The rules are framed in such a way, however, that any diminuation of love is likely to be regarded as a rejection.
Another problem posed by excessive reliance on acceptance, admiration, or love is that we do not possess a reliable gauge that another person is, indeed, rejecting, reproaching, or critical of us. As pointed out previously, we can verify objectively when somebody has attacked us physically by examining the site of the injury. But when somebody seems to be rejecting us, how do we know that we have not misinterpreted his behavior? Our subjective feelings of distress cannot be used to validate our interpretation because such feelings can occur whether the interpretation is right or wrong. This lack of validating information makes it immensely more difficult to deal with psychological trauma than physical injury.
A major technique of cognitive therapy consists of making the patient’s attitudes explicit and helping him decide whether they are self-defeating. Moreover, it is essential that he learn from his own experience that because of certain attitudes he ends up with less happiness and more misery than if he were guided by more moderate or realistic rules. The therapist’s role should be to suggest alternative rules for the patient’s consideration—not to “brainwash” him.
Related to the pleasure-pain rules are the set of rules called the “tyranny of the shoulds” (Horney, 1950). If a person has the rule, “In order to be happy, I need to be loved by everybody,” he is likely to implement this by another rule, “I should make everybody love me.” The “shoulds” and “should nots” have a slave-driving quality and have much in common with Freud’s conceptualization of the superego. Some of the common “shoulds” are:

I should be the utmost of generosity, considerateness, dignity, courage, unselfishness.
I should be the perfect lover, friend, parent, teacher, student, spouse.
I should be able to endure any hardship with equanimity.
I should be able to find a quick solution to every problem.
I should never feel hurt; I should always be happy and serene.
I should know, understand, and foresee everything.
I should always be spontaneous; I should always control my feelings.
I should assert myself; I should never hurt anybody else.
I should never be tired or get sick.
I should always be at peak efficiency.

6---full-notes/some-other-pain.title: Some other pain
6---full-notes/some-other-pain.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy morals
Some other pain
Details
3.2 extends the rejection mechanism beyond welfare: my grounds for rejecting a principle include not just how much it burdens me but what it implies about me. Two principles can impose identical welfare costs yet one remains rejectable — because the basis of treatment, not just its magnitude, is morally relevant.
The racist distribution example makes this clean: I cannot reject the racist principle on welfare grounds alone (the random principle burdens someone equally). I reject it because it treats my race as a legitimate distributive criterion — which constitutes a failure to recognize my status as a person. The wrong is epistemic and relational before it is material.
This is where contractualism most sharply diverges from utilitarianism, which has no native vocabulary for “this wrongs me because of what it says about me” independent of welfare impact. Scanlon is quietly installing something like dignity as a moral primitive here — without naming it as such. The mechanism of reasonable rejection just allows it in through the back door.
Connection to my framework: “unnecessary intentional suffering” already gestures at this gap. The intentional component isn’t welfare-tracking — a racist distribution that hurts you identically to a random one still wrongs you more. The intention behind the principle, and what it implies about the person subjected to it, carries independent moral weight.

6---full-notes/space-and-time,-intuition.content:
Status: teen
Tags: physics  philosophy
Space and Time, Intuitions
Details
Space and time are not physical realities we discover through sensory experience, nor are they mere concepts derived from rational deduction. Instead, they are pure intuitions, meaning they are the foundational, a priori frameworks that human consciousness imposes upon the world. Kant uses the concept of incongruent counterparts, such as chiral objects like right and left hands, to prove this. A mirrored hand maintains all internal rational logic, yet cannot fit into the opposite glove, proving that spatial orientation relies on an inherent aesthetic intuition rather than pure deduction. Space acts as the necessary precondition for organizing our external reality, while time provides the framework for ordering our internal mental states. Otherwise, other explanations for this would be us crafting everything from prior experiences, which neurologically might mean that we will not live long enough for this way of processing.

6---full-notes/specialized-techniques-of.title: Specialized Techniques of Therapy
6---full-notes/specialized-techniques-of.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology therapy CBT
Specialized Techniques of Therapy
Details
Scheduling activities with the patient: As the patient see themselves as ineffective, we must enable him to be active for him to observe himself in a different, more positive light. Any activity that is scheduled can help the patient structure their day. As these patients often resist attempts to get them to be “busy,” it is essential to use a variety of incentives, such as the notion that doing this will make him feel better.
Graded Task Assignment: This is a method that is used to give the patient a series of successes, and is sometimes called “success therapy.” The therapist starts with a simple assignment that they know the patient will succeed in. Then they will together, design more activities that gets more complex and longer.
Mastery and Pleasure Therapy: The essence of this kind of therapy is to help the patient keep tracks of their “wins.” It is used to bypass the inability of the patient to be satisfied in situations that they are successful.
Cognitive Reappraisal: Has been discussed before, it is finding the faulty cognitions and also the faulty basic premises and assumptions to change them.
Alternative Therapy: This method consists of two different approaches: (1) Considering other views for experiences when the depressed patient shows a systematic negative bias in his interpretations. By thinking of other explanations, he will be able to substitute it with more accurate ones. (2) Considering alternative ways of dealing with such situations. This is to help the patient find ways to deal with his problem that he considers insoluble.
Cognitive Rehearsal: This technique is used to expose the patient’s problems that are keeping them from carrying out their activities. They will imagine themselves doing the activity and find the “obstacles” that are interrupting them, then those obstacles will be the main topic of discussion.
Homework Assignments: This is of course an essential part as the patient has to integrate therapy into his life as well. They are expected to carry out certain activities that will counteract their symptoms. In addition, they will keep a log of negative thoughts and then figure out the logical response to it.

6---full-notes/standards-for-evaluating-.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Standards for evaluating systems of psychotherapy.md
6---full-notes/standards-for-evaluating-.title: Standards for evaluating systems of psychotherapy
6---full-notes/standards-for-evaluating-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology psychopathology therapy
Standards for evaluating systems of psychotherapy
Details

The system procedures should be well-defined and clearly described.
The general principles of treatment should also be the same so that different therapists dealing with the same problem among similar patients will have the same methods, relatively. Furthermore, the blueprint of therapy should be sufficiently clear and comprehensive so that the neophyte therapist is not forced to proceed like an automaton following the same formula for each patient.
There should be empirical evidence to support the validity of these principles. For example, if a therapy is based on “reliving” an alleged traumatic memory, there should be evidence that (a) such episode occurred; (b) it was traumatic; (c) it is currently contributing to the patient’s problem; and (d) reliving it will enable the patient to solve it.
The efficacy of the treatment should also have empirical support, such as: (a) analog studies in which certain procedures identical to or analogous to those used in therapy are applied to experimental subjects under highly controlled conditions; (b) carefully investigated single cases in which quantitative measures are used to demonstrate improvement at various stages of the treatment and at follow-up; (c) well-designed therapeutic trials, including quantitative measures, control groups, ratings by independent judges, and long-term follow-ups. In view of the well-known phenomena of spontaneous remission and “cures” based on suggestion, we need more than the claims of the therapist or testimonials from his patients in order to judge the value of a therapy.
At the time CBT was created, only a few popular therapies met the requirements. Rogerian, was one of them, client-centered, therapy is reasonably specific in its processes but not a comprehensive model of psychopathology. Instead, it focused on the few theoretical postulates; the principles of therapy and the model that are readily testable.

Standards for evaluating theories
Details

As it is scientific, the theory should satisfy the requirements of any good scientific theory, namely, that is should explain the phenomena within its domain with ease. According to the law of parsimony, the best theory has the most data but uses the simplest of concepts. Moreover, it should logically have no internal contradictions and its basic assumptions and hypotheses should be consistent.
The theory should be closely related to its allied psychotherapy so that it is obvious how the methods derived from it.
The theory should provide the basis for understanding why the methods are effective. The rationale and mode of operation should be implicit, it should provide reasons for why it is more effective than other theories.
The theory should also be flexible enough for it to be the foundations of developing new techniques without being so loose or complex that it can obligingly dispenses a justification for any procedure a therapist might want to improvise.
The last thing is the fact it must have sufficient evidence, tests and such, or axioms, hypotheses, and assumptions that can be verified through experiments and investigations.

States of Socialization

Milgram argued that we have two states of working, the first is autonomous, when we can do our actions for ourselves and we are sure, in this state we usually work quite quickly and automatically as we can clarify and check our actions by ourselves. Another is the agentic state, which is a psychological state where an individual no longer sees themselves as responsible for their actions. 6---full-notes/stereotype-threat.content:

Stereotype Threat
Details
Stereotyping doesn’t just have social effects, it also has cognitive effects that can impair performance on tasks relative to stereotypes. Claude Steele demonstrated this through an observational study pertaining to SAT scores between races. The mechanism is quite elegant, when Black and White students were told a test measured intelligence, Black students’ performance dropped dramatically. Plotted against a control group where they were told it was just some piloting items, no racial gap appeared. The mechanism operates through distraction and anxiety: fearing that one’s performance might confirm the group stereotype consumes working memory resources. This mechanism is entirely culture-dependent as the relevant stereotypes vary by society. But the implication is sound: if everyone believes that the SAT measures intelligence, and there exists a stereotype linking group memberships to said intelligence, the act of taking the test under those beliefs may bring systematic disadvantages to the stereotyped group, creating the gap it describes.

6---full-notes/stereotypes,-prejudice,-a.title: Stereotypes, Prejudice, and Discrimination
6---full-notes/stereotypes,-prejudice,-a.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Stereotypes, Prejudice, and Discrimination
Details
These three terms are usually conflated alongside each other but they all refer to separable psychological phenomena along the cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions. Stereotype is easy to define, prejudice is affective: they are negative feelings or attitudes toward individuals because of their group membership. Discrimination is behavioral: they are actions that people take against others group memberships. These often co-occur but are logically independent—one can hold a stereotype without feeling prejudice, or feel prejudice without discriminating. A critical distinction regarding stereotypes: they can be statistically accurate when applied to groups (NBA players are indeed tall) but become problematic when applied to individuals, because overlapping distributions mean many individual members of the “lower” group exceed many members of the “higher” group. The distributions’ means may differ while their ranges largely overlap. A second problem arises when people make causal attributions for group differences, citing “nature” when confounding variables (socioeconomic status, diet, culture, historical oppression) make such claims scientifically unsupportable.

6---full-notes/sternberg's-triarchic-the.title: Sternberg's Triarchic Theory of Intelligence
6---full-notes/sternberg's-triarchic-the.content:
Status: baby
Tags: Cognitive Psychology intelligence
Sternberg’s Triarchic Theory of Intelligence
Details
Spearman’s The Psychometric Approach has been criticized to be “monarchic” as it proposes “g” as a monarch above all the specialized ability. In this department, Robert Sternberg attempted to go beyond it by proposing a triarchic theory with three processes in mind: (a) cognitive processes, (b) identifying situations that require intelligence, and (c) using that intelligence in practical ways.
This model improves upon the Gardner’s theory of multiple intelligences by actually having empirical research to back it up. In the studies, it was found out that children in rural Kenya were found out to have incredibly informal knowledge of herbal medicines. The children who performed best on these tests of knowledge of their world did worst relative to the tests of formal academic subjects. This is because their families probably valued these knowledge and skills much more than the formalized knowledge. Moreover, since tests did not account for this type intelligence or the fact that the mastery of the academic intelligence was simply undeveloped compared to the others.
And from that example, Robert Sternberg introduced his theory of intelligence. Analytical intelligence, which is the ability to complete problem-solving tasks such as those in tests; creative intelligence is the ability to synthesize and apply existing knowledge to deal with unusual and new situations; practical intelligence is our ability to adapt to everyday life, or streets smarts.

6---full-notes/stigma-as-a-threat.title: Stigma as a Threat
6---full-notes/stigma-as-a-threat.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology sociology
Stigma as a Threat
Details
Stigma is not only a cognitive labeling mechanism, but an existential threat within a local moral world. Drawing on Arthur Kleinman’s anthropology, stigma directly undermines an individual’s personhood by jeopardizing the core lived values needed to preserve social standing.
In socioeconomically marginalized communities (e.g., Fuzhounese immigrants in New York City), what matters most centers on labor participation, income generation, and remitting money to discharge debts and support families. Stigma intensifies drastically when mental health symptoms prevent work, prompting accusations of uselessness, abandonment, and social death.
Furthermore, this cultural mechanism also precipitates stigma resistance. Because people must possess these factors to preserve “what matters most,” they will do whatever they can to keep their lives, including adhering to treatment without meaning it.
Holding a psychiatric diagnosis does not automatically produce irreversible social degradation. If an individual maintains the functional capacity to work and earn money, their moral standing and personhood are preserved, buffering against employer and community discrimination. Treatment adherence is viewed instrumentally: medication is embraced primarily when it restores work performance, not merely for psychological symptom relief.

6---full-notes/stigma-in-asian-cultures.content:
