Stigma in Asian Cultures
Details
In today’s society, scholars have argued that the impact that stigma has on PWLES (people with lived experiences of mental illnesses) are far worse than the symptoms of the conditions itself. Particularly in Asia where mental illnesses tend to be highly moralized and connected with the person rather than with the condition. This has been proven throughout thousands of scientific studies, proving that stigma against PWLEs is much stronger in Asia rather than Western contexts.
Theories have been made to explain why this is the case, with results showing how historical context of governmental and religious institutions and country-specific power elites and individuals shape these conceptions of cultural stigma. They then continue to permeate through society by word-of-mouth (facilitated by collectivism) and media turning into public stigma, which causes distrust between the public and PWLEs. Individuals in society further perpetuate stigma by shunning, interpretating and discriminating PWLEs based on the preconceived cultural prejudices about the stigma, activating during social interactions, further reinforcing the public stigma. Finally, PWLEs turn this into learned helplessness as they anticipate stigma and then self-stigmatize due to internalization of cultural and public stigma.

Stopping of suicidal behaviors
Details
Addressing the first priority, of stopping any life-threatening threats in the process. For example, if something like an interpersonal problem between the client and trainer appears, the first priority of course is to resolve it. Although the skills that we teach (mindfulness, interpersonal effectiveness, emotional regulation, distress tolerance) skills are necessary, we still can use other strategies may the need come.
Skills trainer behaviorally defines what client is doing to destroy therapy.
Skills trainer conducts a brief analysis of destructive behavior.
Skills trainer makes contingencies very clear for continued destructive behaviors.
Skills trainer adopts a problem-­ solving plan with client.
When client refuses to modify behavior:
Skills trainer discusses goals of skills training with client.
Skills trainer avoids unnecessary power struggles.
If client has an individual primary provider, skills trainer refers client to primary provider for an in-depth behavioral analysis of the destructive behavior.
If client does not have an individual primary provider, skills trainer considers either requiring client to obtain a primary provider, or—in extreme cases—putting client on vacation from skills training until there is evidence that behavior has come under control.
Continuing is about managing one self about attacking the clients or becoming judgmental of them:


Observe what a difficult client is actually doing, and describe it nonjudgmentally in your own mind before commenting on the behavior.


Practice radical acceptance of clients who engage in repetitively annoying behaviors, but who are corrigible if you make the effort.


Practice opposite action with a matter-of-fact or light tone of voice when you want to withdraw.


Practice opposite action, using irreverence or humor with a light tone of voice, to avoid attacking and to lower tension between you and the individual and in the room.


Use the DEAR MAN, GIVE FAST skills (see Interpersonal Effectiveness Handouts 5, 6, and 7) to ask a person to stop behaviors that distract you or others. Use the “broken record” and negotiate (Interpersonal Effectiveness Handout 5) if necessary.


Put problem behaviors on an extinction schedule (see Interpersonal Effectiveness Handout 21), and plunge in where angels fear to tread by acting as if clients are cooperating even when they are not.

6---full-notes/story-instead-of-telling.title: Story instead of Telling
6---full-notes/story-instead-of-telling.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship writing
Story instead of Telling
Details
At its core, the principle of “show, don’t tell” is about immersing the reader in an experience rather than simply stating facts. For a scholarship essay, this means translating your personal attributes—be it resilience, leadership, or intellectual curiosity—into a vivid narrative that allows the reader to witness these qualities in action.
Think of it this way: a statement like, “I am a dedicated and hardworking student,” is a claim. A story about the time you spent weeks painstakingly researching a complex historical event for a school project, the late nights you spent perfecting your arguments, and the thrill of finally presenting your findings—that is evidence. The first tells the committee what you want them to believe; the second allows them to draw that conclusion on their own, making it far more impactful.
Scholarship committees are not just looking for students with impressive GPAs and a long list of extracurricular activities. They are seeking to invest in individuals—people with unique perspectives, demonstrated character, and the potential to make a positive impact. A story is the most effective vehicle to convey this.
Here’s why focusing on a story is more important than telling them who or what you are:

It Creates an Emotional Connection: Stories evoke emotions. A narrative that details a personal challenge you overcame or a moment of profound realization will resonate with the reader on a human level. This emotional connection makes your application memorable long after they’ve finished reading.
It Demonstrates Your Qualities Authentically: Anyone can claim to be a leader. A story about how you rallied a team to achieve a common goal, navigated disagreements, and took responsibility for the outcome provides concrete proof of your leadership skills. It’s the difference between a resume line and a lived experience.
It Showcases Your Values and Character: The stories you choose to tell reveal what is important to you. A narrative about volunteering at a local shelter, for instance, says more about your compassion and sense of community than simply listing “volunteering” as an activity.
It Makes Your Application Unique: Many applicants will share similar academic profiles and extracurricular interests. Your personal stories, however, are yours alone. They are the unique threads that make up the fabric of your character and set you apart from a sea of qualified candidates.

6---full-notes/strategies-against-cultur.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Strategies against Cultural Bias in Assessment.md
6---full-notes/strategies-against-cultur.title: Strategies against Cultural Bias in Assessment
6---full-notes/strategies-against-cultur.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology
Strategies against Cultural Bias in Assessment
Details
The risk of cultural bias in psychological assessment is a critical concern in mental health, as standardized tools and diagnostic criteria developed primarily within a Western, Euro-American context can lead to misinterpretation and misdiagnosis when applied to individuals from different backgrounds. To counter this, the field has developed a multi-faceted approach rooted in education, self-reflection, and culturally-informed clinical practices.
1. Foundational Graduate Training and Self-Awareness
The process begins in graduate training, where future clinicians are taught that effective practice is not “culture-blind” but culturally aware. This education involves:


Multicultural Coursework: Dedicated courses on multicultural psychology, diversity, and social justice are now a standard part of most clinical programs. This training provides knowledge about the values, worldviews, communication styles, and family structures of various cultural and ethnic groups.


Understanding “Idioms of Distress”: Clinicians learn that psychological suffering is expressed differently across cultures. While one culture might express depression through sadness and guilt, another might express it through physical symptoms like fatigue or pain. Recognizing these “idioms of distress” prevents the misinterpretation of symptoms.


Clinician Self-Reflection: A crucial component of training is turning the lens inward. Clinicians are trained to examine their own cultural background, assumptions, and implicit biases. This process of self-awareness is essential to prevent their own worldview from becoming the default standard against which clients are measured.


2. The Shift to Cultural Humility
More recently, the field has moved from the idea of “cultural competence” (implying one can become an expert in another’s culture) to cultural humility. This is a career-long commitment that involves:


An awareness of the power imbalances inherent in the therapist-client relationship.


A posture of openness and learning, acknowledging that the client is the expert on their own experience.


A commitment to actively challenging one’s own biases and the systemic biases within the profession.


3. Using Culturally-Informed Tools and Frameworks
Recognizing that assessment tools themselves can be biased, several strategies are employed:


Culturally Validated Measures: Clinicians are trained to question the appropriateness of standard assessment tools (e.g., personality inventories, IQ tests) that were normed on a limited demographic. They seek out measures that have been validated for the specific cultural group of the client.


The Cultural Formulation Interview (CFI): The DSM-5, as noted in the document on its updates, made a significant step forward by including the CFI. This is a set of 16 questions that helps the clinician understand a client’s distress from the perspective of their own culture. It asks about their cultural identity, their cultural explanations of the problem, and the cultural factors related to coping and seeking help. This structured interview helps prevent the clinician from imposing a purely Western framework on the client’s experience.


4. Adapting the Diagnostic and Therapeutic Process
A culturally-aware clinician adapts their approach in real-time:


Avoiding Pathologizing Difference: They learn to differentiate between what is truly a symptom of a disorder and what is a cultural difference. For example, a lack of direct eye contact may be a sign of respect in some cultures, not a symptom of social anxiety or avoidance.


Contextual Understanding: The clinician considers the client’s sociocultural context, including experiences with discrimination, acculturation stress, and systemic barriers, all of which can profoundly impact mental health.


Language and Interpretation: When language barriers exist, using a professional interpreter is essential, as opposed to a family member who may edit information or have their own biases. The clinician must also be aware that many psychological concepts do not have direct one-to-one translations.


By integrating these strategies—starting with foundational education and continuing through a career-long commitment to cultural humility—clinicians can work to provide more accurate, ethical, and effective care, ensuring that a diagnosis reflects the client’s true condition rather than a cultural misunderstanding.

6---full-notes/stress-mitigation.title: Stress Mitigation
6---full-notes/stress-mitigation.content:
Status: teen

Stress Mitigation
Details
Mitigating stress requires understanding its psychological building blocks, but application demands nuance to avoid harm. Core elements include control, predictability, frustration outlets (e.g., exercise or, problematically, displacement aggression), social support, and positive reframing. These blunt the stress response: a rat gnawing wood during shocks fares better, mirroring human benefits from hobbies or venting. Social support, like confiding in friends, similarly buffers.
The rat wheel study exemplifies: voluntary running yields exercise benefits (e.g., neurogenesis), while forced running mimics severe stress, harming health despite identical exertion. Interpretation is key—control flips physiology from detrimental to adaptive.
Caveats abound: these aren’t universal prescriptions. Preaching control to the powerless (e.g., refugees or the terminally ill) is insensitive, potentially worsening despair. For privileged contexts, they work, but misplaced faith leads to backlash. Mitigation must be daily, not sporadic—20-30 minutes prioritizing well-being is 80% of the battle.
Culturally, encourage voluntary practices without coercion, fostering families and societies that build these blocks organically. The transcript warns of disaster from oversimplification; true efficacy lies in tailored, compassionate application.

6---full-notes/stress-as-stimulation.title: Stress as Stimulation
6---full-notes/stress-as-stimulation.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Stress as Stimulation
Details
Our relationship with stress is paradoxical: we demonize it, yet we crave it in the right form. The key insight is that stress isn’t always aversive; when calibrated correctly, it transforms into stimulation, something we actively seek and even pay for. Consider roller coasters, horror films, or competitive sports—these induce physiological stress (elevated heart rate, adrenaline surges) but feel exhilarating because they’re voluntary, controlled, and temporary. The goal, then, isn’t to “cure” stress but to embrace its stimulatory potential, recognizing that eliminating it entirely would dull life.
This reframing aligns with evolutionary biology: short bursts of stress historically aided survival, like hunting or fleeing predators, and our brains reward them with dopamine hits when perceived positively. We love the “right amount” of stress because it engages us—it’s what psychologists call eustress, fostering growth and joy. In contrast, distress arises from overwhelming, chronic variants. The transcript highlights how we “pay good money” for this: theme parks and thrill-seeking industries thrive on it, proving stress can be a commodity.
Yet, individual thresholds vary. What stimulates one person (a high-stakes negotiation) might overwhelm another. This subjectivity underscores the need for self-awareness: tune into what feels like “stimulation” versus strain. Culturally, we could promote this by designing environments—workplaces or education—that incorporate positive stress, like gamified challenges, rather than grinding monotony.
In essence, reconceptualizing stress as stimulation invites a healthier paradigm. It’s not about avoidance but curation: seek the roller coaster, not the endless traffic jam. By doing so, we harness stress’s upside, turning a biological imperative into a source of vitality and pleasure. This perspective is liberating, reminding us that stress, when chosen, enriches rather than erodes.

6---full-notes/stress-system.title: Stress system
6---full-notes/stress-system.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience
Stress system
Details
The endocrinology system of the human being is not just simply the hypothalamus sending a signal to the pituitary gland and to other glands to release stress hormones. There are different stress hormones and are mixed and combined depending on the situation of them being stressed. For example, having an existential crisis is different from being in front of a tiger, so those two situations would make the system release different stress hormones.
One key aspect of this complexity is the use of multiple releasing hormones to trigger a single pituitary hormone. The release of the stress hormone ACTH, for instance, is not solely dependent on CRH. It can also be stimulated by vasopressin, oxytocin, and norepinephrine. This is not a redundant system; rather, different types of stressors evoke different combinations, or “orchestrations,” of these releasing factors, creating what can be thought of as a unique “stress signature.” This arrangement provides two distinct advantages: it allows for precise control over the shape and duration of the ACTH secretory curve, and it couples ACTH release with other necessary physiological adjustments that are specific to the nature of the stressor. Furthermore, this regulation is bidirectional, with inhibitory factors like Delta Sleep-Inducing Factor providing a “brake” on the system to ensure precise control. Furthermore, these cells may react differently due to their neighborhood cells due to sensitivity and so on.

Structural Family Theory

On the other hand, enmeshed boundaries where parents may not have any boundaries at all may make the children develop internalization problems.

6---full-notes/structure-of-an-evaluatio.content:

Structure of an Evaluation Session
Details
Firstly, you should try to set the agenda and tell the patient what is going to happen, walk them through the generals of it, this may include: conducting the psychosocial assessment, set goals, relate to the treatment plan, set an Action Plan, set expectations for treatment, and then summarize everything.
Something you can start with is to ask them how they spend their day, understand their perspective and then work out from there. For example, if they are already doing well taking care of themselves, validate and encourage them to do further.
At times, there would be hopelessness and skepticism due to many reasons, like a previous therapy not working. When that happens, try to validate, understand, encourage them for that matter. Try to discredit their skepticism by proving your care and competence, also understand why it failed for the previous therapist and resolve it with them. When the period does come to an end, ask them important stuff you might have missed or haven’t got a chance to talk about.

“ACTION PLAN May 6
Put this Action Plan next to the coffee maker and read it every morning and again later in the day.
Therapy Notes: When I start to feel more depressed, remind myself that the therapy plan makes sense. With Judy’s help, I’ll be working toward goals every week, step by step. I’ll learn how to evaluate my thinking, which may be 100% true, or 0% true, or somewhere in the middle. The way I’ll get better is by making small changes in my thinking and behavior every day.

6---full-notes/studying-heritability.title: Studying Heritability
6---full-notes/studying-heritability.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology genetics biology
Studying Heritability
Details
To untangle the influences of genes and environment, researchers rely on clever natural experiments, most notably twin and adoption studies. Heritability is a statistical estimate of how much of the variation we see in a particular trait within a population can be attributed to genetic differences among individuals. These studies provide a direct route to estimating this value. The logic behind twin studies is straightforward: by comparing monozygotic (identical) twins, who share 100% of their genes, with dizygotic (fraternal) twins, who share on average 50%, researchers can infer the strength of genetic influence. Any differences observed between identical twins are generally assumed to be the result of environmental factors, as their genetic makeup is the same.
Adoption studies offer another powerful angle. When children are adopted and raised separately from their biological relatives, similarities between the child and their biological parents point strongly toward shared heredity. Conversely, similarities between adopted, non-biological siblings raised in the same household are believed to be the result of their shared environment. Together, these research designs have been fundamental in demonstrating that nearly every human trait has both a genetic and an environmental component, allowing scientists to move from philosophical debate to empirical investigation.

6---full-notes/studying-the-brain-in-psy.title: Studying the brain in Psychology
6---full-notes/studying-the-brain-in-psy.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology biology
Studying the brain in Psychology
Details
A newcomer to psychology might reasonably ask, “Why do psychologists study the brain? Isn’t that the job of biologists?” The answer lies in the fundamental difference in perspective between the two fields. While both disciplines examine the same physical organ, they ask fundamentally different questions and seek different levels of explanation.
The biological perspective, championed by neurobiologists and neuroscientists, is primarily concerned with the brain as hardware. It seeks to understand the brain’s structure and mechanics: the anatomy of its regions, the function of individual neurons, the chemical processes at the synapse, and the electrical signaling within neural circuits. The goal is to map the physical and chemical machinery itself.
The psychological perspective, in contrast, is concerned with how this hardware runs the software of the mind. Psychologists study the brain to understand how its physical processes give rise to subjective experience and observable behavior—phenomena like thought, emotion, memory, consciousness, and personality. The psychologist’s question is not just “How does the amygdala work?” but “How does activity in the amygdala relate to the feeling of fear and subsequent avoidance behavior?”
A useful analogy is studying a computer. A biologist or electrical engineer would analyze the motherboard, transistors, and flow of electricity to understand how the machine physically operates. A psychologist is like a software engineer who studies that same hardware to understand how it executes an operating system, runs programs, and creates a user experience. One cannot fully understand the software without knowing the capabilities of the hardware it runs on, and the purpose of the hardware is only fully realized through the software it enables. Thus, psychology studies the brain not merely as a biological organ, but as the substrate of the mind.

Suggestions for reading classical scientific books
Details
These are the books that report the findings or conclusions in some field of research. It is always to describe the phenomena as accurately as possible and trace connections from it to other phenomenas.
In the great works of science, there is no oratory or propaganda, though there may be bias in the sense of initial presuppositions. You detect this, and take account of it, by distinguishing what the author assumes from what he establishes through argument. The more “objective” a scientific author is, the more he will explicitly ask you to take this or that for granted. Scientific objectivity is not the absence of initial bias. It is attained by frank confession of it.
The leading terms in a scientific work are usually expressed by uncommon or technical words. They are relatively easy to spot, and through them you can readily grasp the propositions. The main propositions are always general ones. Science thus is not chronotopic. Just the opposite; a scientist, unlike a historian, tries to get away from locality in time and place. He tries to say how things are generally, how things generally behave.

Suicidal behaviors
Details
Suicidal wishes and suicide attempts may be regarded as the ultimate expression of the desire to escape. The depressed patient sees his future as filled with suffering. He cannot visualize any way of improving his lot; he does not believe he will get better. On the basis of these premises, suicide seems to be a rational course of action. It not only promises an end to his own misery but presumably will relieve his family of a burden. Once the patient regards death as more desirable than life, he feels attracted to suicide. The more hopeless and painful his life seems, the stronger his desire to end his life.
Another premise underlying the suicidal wishes is the belief that everybody would be better off if he were dead. Since he regards himself as worthless and as a burden, arguments that his family would be hurt if he died seem hollow to him. How can they be injured by losing a burden? One patient envisioned suicide as doing her parents a favor. She would not only end her own pain, but would relieve them of psychological and financial burdens. “I’m just taking money from my parents. They would use it to better advantage. They wouldn’t have to support me. My father wouldn’t have to work so hard, and they could travel. I’m unhappy taking their money, and they could be happy with it.

6---full-notes/superstitious-behavior.title: Superstitious Behavior
6---full-notes/superstitious-behavior.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Behaviorism Psychology
Superstitious Behavior
Details
This concept arises from the incorrect assumption from an accidental or non-contingent reinforcement, making the subject believe whatever they were doing was the cause of that result, and subsequently trying to repeat it to achieve such results. The reason for this is that our brains are powerful pattern recognizers, it craves patterns, even in things where patterns do not exist, it will hallucinate one.
B.F. Skinner first demonstrated this by providing food to pigeons at random intervals, regardless of what they were doing. The pigeons began to repeat whatever specific action they happened to be performing just before the food arrived—one might turn in a circle, another might bob its head. They had developed a personal ritual that they falsely associated with the reward.
This phenomenon is readily observable in humans. A baseball player who hits a home run after coincidentally tapping his shoes a certain way may develop a pre-batting ritual of tapping his shoes. A student who scores well on an exam after arranging their pencils in a specific way may feel compelled to repeat that arrangement for future exams. The behavior doesn’t actually cause the outcome, but the accidental reinforcement was strong enough to create a powerful, albeit irrational, learned association.

6---full-notes/supply-and-demand-shocks.title: Supply and demand shocks
6---full-notes/supply-and-demand-shocks.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Supply and demand shocks
Details
For the most part, we’’‘ve been discussing about positive economics (if you don’t remember its how things are). And for now we’d have to show how the market may be and the interactions between consumers and producers.
Gruber’s example is the gasoline market (Figure 9-1), with gallons on the x-axis and dollars per gallon on the y-axis:

Demand is consumers’ marginal willingness to pay: each point is what someone would pay for the next gallon. It slopes down because at higher prices, fewer people find the next gallon worth it.
Supply is producers’ marginal willingness to supply, which is their marginal cost. It slopes up because higher prices make more output worth producing.
Equilibrium (e1: P1, Q1) is where the two cross. At P1, consumers want Q1 gallons and producers want to sell Q1.

A demand shock (Figure 9-2). Suppose tastes shift toward big cars like SUVs and minivans, which feel safer and handle bad weather better. Big cars and gas are complements, since big cars burn more gas. So demand for gas shifts out, from D1 to D2.

If the price stayed at P1, consumers would want Q1′ while producers still supplied Q1. The gap is excess demand.
Sellers respond by raising the price. As it rises, consumers cut back a little along the new demand curve, and producers expand along the supply curve.
The market slides up the supply curve to e2, with a higher price and a higher quantity.

A supply shock (Figure 9-3). Now suppose a war in the Middle East raises the cost of producing gas: shipping gets more expensive, or supply has to come from higher-cost sources like the US. Supply is marginal cost, so the supply curve shifts up and in; at any price, producers offer less.

At P1, producers now offer only Q1′ while consumers still want Q1. That’s excess demand again, this time caused by costs rather than tastes.
The price rises, and the market slides up the demand curve to e2: a higher price but a lower quantity.

Gruber catches himself calling the new equilibrium “happy.” Equilibrium only means both sides are on their curves at that price; it says nothing about whether anyone is better or worse off. Consumers are clearly worse off in the second situation due to having to pay more and we’d then have to see how that is measured.
We were just demonstrated basically situations where the same thing happened yet for different reasons. So what do we learn from that? We need to see both demand and prices to make a conclusion about the market.

Syntax and the Structural Hierarchy of Logic
Details
Propositional Logic functions as another language to analyze the structure of truth preservation, independent of specific content. At its core, the syntax distinguishes between simple sentences (propositional constants) and compound sentences. A propositional constant acts as an abstract variable representing a single condition of the world that is binary, right or wrong, which is unlike natural language, which depends on so many other factors.
And so we have five fundamental operators to relate between these constants: negation, conjunction, disjunction, implication, and the biconditional. And to avoid ambiguity inherent in linear text, there’s a hierarchy in this logic. Negation binds most tightly, followed by conjunction, disjunction, and implication, with the biconditional being the loosest.

6---full-notes/synthesis-of-depression.title: Synthesis of depression
6---full-notes/synthesis-of-depression.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Synthesis of depression
Details
According to Aaron T. Beck’s seminal work, depression is not a spontaneous wave of sadness but a structured “chain reaction” of thought, initiated by a profound sense of loss. This cognitive model reframes the disorder, moving from a mysterious affliction to an understandable, albeit painful, process of distorted interpretation. The entire structure of depression, from self-loathing to a bleak view of the future, is built upon this initial foundation of perceived loss.
The triggering loss is not always obvious or dramatic, like the death of a spouse. While such events are clear catalysts, Beck highlights a more subtle and insidious form of deprivation: an internal imbalance. This “upset in his ‘give-get balance’” occurs when an individual perceives a chronic deficit between what they contribute emotionally and the gratification they receive, or when they consistently fail to meet their own demanding standards. This persistent sense of falling short or being emotionally short-changed creates a powerful feeling of diminishment.
Following this experience of loss, the depression-prone individual undergoes a critical cognitive shift. They begin to appraise all their experiences through a negative lens, overinterpreting neutral or even positive events as further proof of defeat or deprivation. This negativity pervades their entire worldview, creating the classic depressive triad: a negative view of themselves, their world, and their future. The initial sense of loss becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy; by viewing themselves as “deficient” and “inadequate,” they filter all incoming information to confirm this belief, locking themselves into the cognitive architecture of despair.

6---full-notes/synthetic-propositions.title: Synthetic Propositions
6---full-notes/synthetic-propositions.content:
Status: teen
Tags: logic philosophy
Synthetic Propositions
Details
Hume argued that there were only analytical reasoning or synthetic reasonings, which in both situations are incredibly lacking in one sense while fulfilling the other. For analytical reasoning, it holds up without a priori but does not bring any actual knowledge to the table, whilst the opposite is true for synthetic propositions (more like they’re logically correct but requires a priori).
Kant argued that synthetic propositions without a priori existed. His examples: “there is no number so large that one cannot be added to it” — you don’t discover this by counting, yet it says something real about numbers. “Every effect has a cause” — Newton’s laws, the principle of sufficient reason. These are substantive claims about the world, yet their truth doesn’t depend on checking every case empirically. The radical empiricist who denies this is, as the lecturer quotes, “one who believes the series of positive integers was discovered one at a time.”

6---full-notes/system-dependent-habits.title: System-Dependent Habits
6---full-notes/system-dependent-habits.content:
Status: teen
Tags: habits psychology
System-Dependent Habits
Details
Most people mistakenly use their habits and activities solely to achieve specific goals, which comes with a multitude of disadvantages. First, a goal-dependent habit is fragile; it might entirely lose its purpose and driving force the moment the goal is achieved, leading to regression (e.g., stopping exercise after running a marathon). Second, relying on goals means relying heavily on motivation or discipline—intrinsic qualities that are unfathomably difficult to intentionally increase and maintain on a daily basis. Rather than fixating on the finish line, people should think in systems. Focusing on the systems that govern the habits creates a sustainable foundation that doesn’t rely on fleeting emotional states.
Expanding on the idea of systems over goals, resting on robust systems is vastly more viable for long-term success. A good system does not require you to become a fundamentally better, more disciplined person overnight. Instead, a system improves your output by actively lowering the required threshold for performing tasks. When you have a system in place (like a set time, a pre-packed gym bag, a specific sequence of actions), it removes the cognitive load of decision-making. You don’t have to decide how or when to do something; the system dictates it. By lowering the energy barrier to entry, systems make consistent execution the path of least resistance

6---full-notes/taq.content:

TAQ
Details
This was an effort by van Der Kolk and Judy, as well as Chris Perry to find out the relation between BPD and childhood abuse. The questions ranged from relatively light then would dive deeper to understand the patient. Most traumatized patients gave surprising answers like “my dog” or “my therapist”… even “nobody” was an answer.
The most surprising was the answers to “Was there anybody who you felt safe with growing up?” One out of four patients did not recall anything along those lines. Imagine a child not having a source of safety, making their way into the world unprotected and unseen.
All of these patients have something in common, they did not have a safe space, a way, a place to run away or escape; they had nobody to turn to and nowhere to hide. Yet they developed ways to survive and manage their despair and terror. It was eventually realized that the BPD group’s problems-dissociation, desperate clinging to whomever might be enlisted to help-had probably started off as ways of dealing with overwhelming emotions and inescapable brutality.
“When children feel pervasively angry or guilty or are chronically frightened about being abandoned, they have come by such feelings honestly; that is because of experience. When, for example, children fear abandonment, it is not in counterreaction to their intrinsic homicidal urges; rather, it is more likely because they have been abandoned physically or psychologically, or have been repeatedly threatened with abandonment. When children are pervasively filled with rage, it is due to rejection or harsh treatment. When children experience intense inner conflict regarding their angry feelings, this is likely because expressing them may be forbidden or even dangerous.” - John Bowlby.

6---full-notes/target-being-inertia,-avo.title: Target being inertia, avoidance, fatigability
6---full-notes/target-being-inertia,-avo.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology therapy CBT
Target being inertia, avoidance, fatigability
Details
The signs in depression that has been regarded with passivity and apparent enervation are a form of neuropsychological inhibition: psychomotor retardation. But research has shown that they can get out of this state if their motivation is aroused by the experimenter or therapist. And so we will make a personalized schedule for them to do so.
There are many positive advantages from a well-developed program. To list some of them are: (a) The patient’s self-concept is changed as he will view himself to be more able and less inept. Concomitantly, with this improvement, he will become more optimistic. (b) He is distracted from his thoughts because he is focusing his attention on the activity instead. (c) Other people’s responses to the patient become more positive; their significant others will reinforce their development in a beneficial way. (d) There may be a change in the patient’s response, they may enjoy the activities and thus feel better.
Of course we will also have to be vigilant of the motivation necessary for the activity, and so we must stimulate it. The therapist doing this must be careful and meticulous in his methods to do so. There are some recommendations: Firstly, the therapist must elicit the patient’s reasons for his inactivity, by giving them something that is well in their ability to do and find the “reasons” that they state for not doing it. Then we will figure out an activity for the patient to do to contradict his reasons.
And now to nudge the patient, we must gently present the rationale for the particular procedure, and conveying to the patient that it is a less painful alternative to feeling as bad as he does by cooperating with us. Then we must make the patient realize how his thoughts are making him more vulnerable and miserable, and that by questioning these ideas, he is likely to feel better.
It is crucial that the therapist pose his questions and assertions regarding the patient’s self-defeating ideas and wishes in a nonjudgmental, reflective way. He should avoid the appearance of scolding the patient, and making him defensive. Because depressed patients generally respond to “criticism” with further self-criticisms and self-immobilization, the therapist should elicit the patient’s reactions to his statements; he should determine whether the patient is using the therapist’s comments “against himself.”
The therapist, furthermore, should be vigilant lest his statements be construed simply as a summons to invoke “the power of positive thinking.” He should indicate clearly that he and the patient are attempting to pinpoint a problem and provide a remedy for it. Global exhortations to “think positively” rarely help to correct unreasonable negative thinking and thus lead the patient to a further sense of failure.
After outlining his pragmatic approach, the therapist should encourage the patient to state his points of agreement and disagreement. This approach may seem fairly obvious and superficial, and one might reasonably wonder how it could be effective in counteracting the patient’s powerful regressive wishes and negative ideas. But this is not the purpose of this procedure yet, it is only here to help the patient recognize his thoughts without the therapist’s help.
When the therapist is able to penetrate the patient’s resistances and engage his interest, he then proceeds to the next stage in the therapeutic program. The therapist should not be content with simply producing cognitive dissonance, but must insure that whatever advantage is gained through discussion is followed immediately by action.
The therapeutic program may be formulated in terms of the following steps: (a) proposing a specific project to the patient; (b) eliciting his reasons for opposing the proposal; (c) asking the patient to weigh the validity of his “reasons” (or negative attitudes); (d) indicating to the patient why these reasons (or attitudes) are self-defeating and invalid; (e) stimulating the patient’s interest in attempting to perform the proposed assignment; (f) setting up the project in such a way that the patient’s performance will test the validity of his ideas. Thus, successful completion of the task will contradict the patient’s hypothesis that he is incapable of doing it; (g) after the successful experience, indicating to the patient how the favorable outcome contradicts his self-defeating predictions; (h) reviewing with the patient the “constructive” attitudes proposed previously by the therapist. These formulations may be used later by the patient to combat his negativity; (i) training the patient to give reasonable answers to these thoughts. This technique is implemented through home work assignments.
The homework is a three column worksheet where the patient writes down the situation that elicited an unpleasant feeling, the negative automatic thought, and then the correction to that thought.

6---full-notes/targeting-hopelessness-an.title: Targeting Hopelessness and suicidal wishes
6---full-notes/targeting-hopelessness-an.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology therapy CBT
Targeting Hopelessness and suicidal wishes
Details
The attitudes that can be related to hopelessness can be traced back here Details of the Cognitive Approach. In these situations, the patients usually regard that they are locked into an insoluble life situation and cannot get away from it. And so if hopelessness is the core of these suicidal thoughts, the therapist can use (a) alternative interpretations of his life situation and his future, and (b) that he has other choices rather than his current behavior, which is leading him down into a spiral.
The therapist should not evade probing for the reasons that the patient has for committing suicide. Most of the time the patient has attempted or considered these alternatives but have seen them as useless, the therapist should then help the patient reframe these solutions. By doing this, we may be able to shift his assumptions and hopelessness.
A teen-age girl reported that her future looked pretty grim and she was seriously considering suicide. She stated as her reason for suicide that she had felt unhappy during most of her childhood and that, “Childhood is supposed to be the happiest period of your life.” Thus, she could only look ahead to increased unhappiness as she grew older. I was able to discuss with her that most people I knew claimed that they were happier in their adulthood than in their childhood. The patient was surprised to hear this.
She also asserted that her future was bleak for her because she was not attaining the high standards that she had set for herself in her art work. She was amused when I pointed out to her that many people, including me, could not even draw a straight line and yet were happy. She was willing to consider setting more flexible standards for herself. Moreover, she was able to see that it was unwise to apply her subjective judgment of her performance to the over-all judgment of the value of life. More to the point, I indicated how she had identified herself with her work. Thus, if her work was a failure, she was a failure.
After this single discussion, she revamped her thinking. Several years later she told me that she had not had any recurrence of her hopelessness or suicidal wishes.
The assumptions underlying hopelessness and suicidal tendencies can be subtly undermined by skillful questions. By pointed, but friendly, questioning, the therapist can make the patient aware of the incongruity of some of his assumptions. Recognition of the incongruity helps to shake his faulty belief system. As a minimal goal, the questioning should be directed to encourage the patient to see that his assumptions are ideas that can be examined rather than indisputable reality or unshakeable facts.

6---full-notes/targeting-painful-effects.content:

Targeting Painful Effects
Details
This is extremely intense, and so it is important to alleviate the patient’s sadness and other affective disturbances as soon as possible. Depressed patients frequently report that none of their usual sources brings them pleasure anymore.
There are a variety of techniques we can use to solve this. Firstly, it is possible to make the patient feel sorry him self, be it crying or something else. This will make him thaw out of his frozen effect, it will make them feel more alive, and more like a “whole person” as Beck says. (Of course, some may feel worse after something like this, so it is advised to be used with caution.) The patient will feel sympathy for themselves in this,. and so his cognitive set will change from rejecting or derogatory to sympathetic.
Other methods are alike this, in which they also stimulate the patient and change them in a way so that they become more sympathetic for themselves.
Supporting Content
Feeling sorry for oneself can be analogized to the kind of empathy one experiences with characters who are portrayed as wronged or unfortunate in a movie. The people in the audience become dewy-eyed or sob because they care about the unfortunate character. Similarly, by feeling genuine pity for themselves, depressed patients are likely to be less self-critical (Efran, 1973). The process can be accelerated by a number of techniques. Telling the patient a story of another unfortunate person with a similar problem and with whom the patient can identify frequently evokes sympathy in the patient. Feeling sympathy for another person in the same situation helps the patient to regard himself sympathetically. Dramatic techniques such as role-playing, in which the therapist assumes the role of his depressed patient, may also help the patient to change his cognitive set from critical to sympathetic.

6---full-notes/targeting-self-criticisms.title: Targeting Self-criticisms and Self-blame
6---full-notes/targeting-self-criticisms.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology therapy CBT
Targeting Self-criticisms and Self-blame
Details
The depressed patient, most of the time tries to find a reason for his problems. And due to his causality, he is prone to regard his own self as the problem of his difficulties, maybe deriving from a social stigma as “take a look at your own mistakes before judging others.” His rules can then make him carry this notion to absurd extremes, like how when it is pointed out that his self-blame is maladaptive, he might blame himself for blaming himself, which can only make him feel even worse.
And so the cognitive approach to this would be to make the patient first be aware of the stream of self-criticisms. This is easy as the patient will feel worse when the criticism happens; thus when he experiences a spurt of dysphoria, he need only to “play back” his preceding thoughts to identify it.
The next is for us to increase his objectivity to his self-hate. This is crucial as the patient commonly believes his assumptions are justified (as always). One method is for us to ask something like, “Suppose a friend made the same mistakes that you did? Would you hate or encourage them and try to get them to feel better?” And this would make him realize his own exaggeratedness of his self-criticisms.
This process may sometimes be boosted by role playing. For example, the therapist would play the role of the person that the patient sees in themself. And the patient is then coached to become a critic to harshly judge and attack the therapist. The therapist would act accordingly to demonstrate the patient’s own conditions, his cognitive distortions. If the patient understands the role of the critic, he can then get out of that role and see its extravagance.
Same as we mentioned before, recognizing automatic thoughts here will also help, and the “three-column” task will help as well as we assign the patients homework.

6---full-notes/tension-between-utility-a.title: Tension between Utility and Basic Moral Rights
6---full-notes/tension-between-utility-a.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy
Tension between Utility and Basic Moral Rights
Details
Mill defines basic moral rights as having three distinct features: (1) they carry a special weight and urgency because they concern the absolute essentials of human well-being; (2) they have a peremptory character, meaning an individual has a justified claim to demand protection of these rights via state coercion or social pressure; and (3) they exist independently of whatever legal institutions happen to be currently established.
There are then two paths to take from this: justifying rights via a general teleological appeal to maximize utility, or, justifying rights by appealing to antecedent, absolute moral essentials (like freedom of speech). If Mill wants to be consistent, then these two paths cannot diverge, it must invariably result in general public rules that assign equal rights to everyone. The persistent critique against utilitarianism is that it could theoretically justify repressing a minority if it produced a massive aggregate pleasure for the majority (e.g., maintaining an oppressed underclass to support a “high culture”). Mill attempts to resolve this not by arguing that “each counts for one” (which he viewed as a mere measurement rule), but by fundamentally redefining utility. Which means he is including a need for individuality/autonomy in utilitarianism itself, thus disallowing the aforementioned situation from happening.

6---full-notes/terminology-in-sex-resear.content:
Status: baby

Terminology in Sex Research
Details
To move beyond colloquialisms like “libido,” behavioral scientists employ a more precise lexicon to deconstruct sexual behavior. A foundational framework consists of a triad of terms: attractivity refers to how appealing an individual is to others; proceptivity describes the active, soliciting behaviors used to initiate a sexual encounter; and receptivity is the readiness to engage in copulation in response to another’s advances. This triad allows for a detailed analysis of the dynamic, interactive process of courtship.
In parallel, particularly within clinical settings, researchers distinguish between motivation and performance. Motivation encompasses the psychological drive, desire, and arousal for sex, whereas performance relates to the physiological capacity to carry out the sexual act, such as erectile function. Recognizing that these two aspects can be dissociated is fundamental to diagnosing and understanding various forms of sexual dysfunction.

6---full-notes/the-active-interplay-betw.title: The Active Interplay between environment and genes
6---full-notes/the-active-interplay-betw.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Cognitive Psychology genetics 3 - Tags/environment
The Active Interplay
Details
The relationship between genes and environment is not a one-way street where a static environment acts upon a passive set of genes. Instead, it is a highly dynamic interplay where our genetic predispositions actively influence the very environments we encounter. This is known as gene-environment correlation, and it occurs in several distinct ways. A passive correlation happens when children receive both genes and a corresponding environment from their parents; for example, musically gifted parents are likely to pass on musical genes and create a household rich with musical influence.
The correlation can also be evocative (or reactive), where a child’s inherited traits evoke specific responses from their environment. A child who shows a natural talent for singing is more likely to be noticed by parents and teachers, who then provide music lessons, thereby creating an environment that nurtures the genetic talent. Finally, an active correlation occurs when individuals, partly because of their genotype, consciously or unconsciously seek out environments that align with their genetic tendencies. A child with an innate musical talent might actively choose to join the school band or spend their time with other musicians. This active shaping of our own worlds makes it practically impossible to ever fully disentangle the effects of nature from nurture, as our nature fundamentally influences the nurture we receive.

6---full-notes/the-all-or-nothing-rule.title: The All-Or-Nothing Rule
6---full-notes/the-all-or-nothing-rule.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience
The All-Or-Nothing Rule
Details
A neuron’s action potential operates on an all-or-none basis. This means that if a stimulus is strong enough to reach the threshold of excitation, the neuron will fire with its full, characteristic strength. If the stimulus is weaker than the threshold, the neuron will not fire at all.
There is no “half-fire” or “weak fire.” The intensity of the initial stimulus does not change the amplitude (strength) or velocity (speed) of the resulting action potential. The action potential is a binary, digital event: it is either on (1) or off (0).
Analogy: This is like firing a gun or flushing a toilet. Pressing the trigger harder does not make the bullet fly faster. Pushing the flush handle gently versus slamming it down both result in the same standard flush. The mechanism either engages completely or not at all.
This raises a question: If all action potentials are the same size, how does the nervous system encode the intensity of a stimulus? The answer lies in the frequency of firing. A strong stimulus (e.g., intense pain) will cause a neuron to fire action potentials more rapidly in succession compared to a weak stimulus (e.g., a light touch).

6---full-notes/the-amygdala-checkpoint-i.title: The Amygdala Checkpoint in stress
6---full-notes/the-amygdala-checkpoint-i.content:
Status: adult
Tags: physiology psychology biology
Physiological Overlap Between Stress and Excitement
Details
At a glance, the body’s response to stress and excitement looks identical: racing heart, rapid breathing, muscle tension, and heightened brain activation. This overlap reveals a profound truth about human biology—the difference often boils down to subjective valence, or how we interpret the event. A surprise party might spike adrenaline joyfully, while a sudden noise in the dark triggers terror, yet the autonomic nervous system fires similarly in both. This raises a fascinating question: what biologically distinguishes delight from dread?
The amygdala emerges as the critical checkpoint. This almond-shaped structure in the limbic system processes emotions, particularly fear. When activated amid physiological arousal, it biases the experience toward adversity—labeling it as threat. Without strong amygdala involvement, the same signals register as positive excitement. Mechanically, if you’re exerting yourself (e.g., running for fun versus fleeing), brain profiles align, but amygdala engagement flips the script to “terror.” This isn’t just abstract; neuroimaging shows amygdala hyperactivity in anxiety disorders, where neutral stimuli become stressors.
The implications are profound for mental health and daily life. Valence is malleable, influenced by context, mindset, and past experiences. For instance, athletes reframe pre-game nerves as “excitement,” reducing amygdala overdrive and enhancing performance. This subjectivity explains why one person’s thrilling hike is another’s panic-inducing ordeal. Biologically, it ties into the stress response’s evolutionary roots: quick threat detection saved lives, but in modern, safe environments, misfiring valence creates unnecessary suffering.
To leverage this, practices like cognitive reframing (e.g., mindfulness) can dampen amygdala responses, shifting stress to stimulation. The transcript’s insight—that physiology alone doesn’t dictate emotion—empowers us: by modulating perception, we control the narrative. In a world of constant stimuli, recognizing the amygdala’s role helps us engineer more positive valences, turning potential stressors into sources of wonder.

6---full-notes/the-antinomies-of-pure-re.title: The Antinomies of Pure Reason
6---full-notes/the-antinomies-of-pure-re.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
The Antinomies of Pure Reason
Details
While Paralogisms deal with the internal illusions of the self, the Antinomies of Pure Reason emerge when the mind attempts to comprehend the external “World” (defined as the absolute totality of all existing things). Kant outlines four antinomies where reason traps itself in irresolvable contradictions, presenting a thesis and an antithesis that both seem logically sound. These are divided into Mathematical antinomies (debating the limits of space/time and infinite divisibility) and Dynamical antinomies (debating determinism versus free will, and the existence of a necessary being or God).
To handle these deadlocks, Kant employs the Skeptical Method—provoking a conflict not to declare a winner, but to expose that both sides are vainly grasping at deceptive appearances beyond human knowledge. Crucially, this strict limitation of pure reason is exactly what opens the door to human morality. Reason cannot empirically prove human freedom or the existence of God. However, from a moral standpoint, one does not need to mathematically prove freedom; one simply must act on the supposition of their own agency. When an individual is faced with deeply consequential choices, they require an ultimate, flawless guiding principle to act justly. This ideal principle—the ultimate anchor of perfect moral reasoning—is what Kant conceptualizes as God. Therefore, God and human freedom are not secured by empirical science or theoretical logic, but are demanded by the innate architecture of human morality and practical reason.

The Architecture and Implications of Natural Law

And so in the process of conjuring such an argument, Locke came to establishing a framework of rules that exist above any earthly king, which brings us to the profound theological and philosophical mechanics of Natural Law. Locke draws a strict distinction between Divine Law, which requires religious revelation, and Natural Law, which is simply the will of God decoded through human reason by observing the natural order of the world. He effectively conjures that since God created us, he has legitimate authority over us and such. The fundamental law of nature dictates that all mankind is to be preserved, and when absolute preservation is impossible, the innocent must be given strict priority. This law governs human behavior entirely independent of any government; for example, we are forbidden from casually destroying nature, animals, or resources without a genuine need, laying the groundwork for how we interact with the world before the state even exists.
Furthermore, as God did not intend an earthly lieutenant, and as the capacity to reason exists in everyone,  the original state of nature is inherently a state of equal, reciprocal political jurisdiction. Every individual is essentially their own sovereign, possessing absolute jurisdiction over their own body and possessions.

The Architecture and Priority of Basic Liberties

But of course, Locke’s framework is way too loose and is merely operating on the possibility of contractualism. In this sense, John Rawls tries to harden this framework to something that people would accept. This means that he would have to build a far more rigorous machinery into the thought experiment, which is why the The Original Position and The Necessary Person exist.
When Rawls finally constructs his First Principle of Justice, he is not just praising some vague, abstract concept of “Liberty” like a modern libertarian might. Instead, he lists specific points of basic liberties-such as freedom of thought, conscience, political association. All of these are the conditions that allow people to develop and use their fundamental moral powers. And Rawls also place them at the top of the chain, as a first principle, so they could never ever be touched by any other factors.

6---full-notes/the-architecture-of-the-s.title: The Architecture of the Self
6---full-notes/the-architecture-of-the-s.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
The Architecture of the Self
Details
In the journey to understand who we are, we often focus on our conscious thoughts, feelings, and decisions. Yet, these are merely the visible peaks of a much deeper and more complex personal architecture. This underlying framework, which psychiatrists like Dr. Paul Conti refer to as our “character structure,” serves as the primary interface between our inner world and the external environment. It is not a collection of static personality traits, but a dynamic and operational “nest” of predispositions and potentialities that dictates how we react, engage, and ultimately experience our lives. Understanding this structure is fundamental to cultivating a healthier, more agentic self.
The foundation of our character structure lies in the interplay between three core components of the mind. The vastest and most influential of these is the unconscious mind, the submerged base of the proverbial iceberg. It is a supercomputer of biological predispositions, ingrained habits, automated thought patterns, and crucially, any unprocessed trauma. Rising from this deep reservoir is the conscious mind, the small, visible tip of the iceberg representing our immediate awareness—the “I” that we identify as our self. This conscious self is inherently vulnerable, susceptible to the fear, confusion, and despair that life can present. To shield it, a third element emerges: our defense mechanisms. These unconscious strategies, ranging from healthy responses like altruism and humor to unhealthy ones like projection, denial, and avoidance, arise from the unconscious to protect our conscious awareness from psychological harm. The unique combination of these defenses forms a critical layer of our character structure.
How this internal architecture functions determines its expression in the world. A healthy character structure is marked by flexibility and adaptability. It allows an individual to access a range of healthy defenses, enabling them to be trusting in safe environments and appropriately cautious when faced with danger. In contrast, an unhealthy character structure is often rigid and maladaptive. It might be defined by a chronic predisposition to mistrust, even in the absence of a threat, or by the habitual use of unhealthy defenses that distort reality. When we project our own anger onto others or avoid facing difficult truths, we are operating from a flawed character structure that perpetuates poor decision-making and often leads to repetitive, negative life patterns.
Ultimately, the “Self” we present to the world and experience internally is the product that grows from this character structure. Our actions, the narrative of our lives, and our phenomenological experience—how it feels to be us—are all direct results of this framework’s engagement with the world. Therefore, the path to meaningful change does not lie in simply willing ourselves to be different, but in a spirited inquiry into our own architecture. By examining our predispositions and identifying the defense mechanisms we unconsciously deploy, we can begin to understand why we act and feel the way we do. This understanding is the essential first step toward modifying our behavior, dismantling unhealthy patterns, and consciously building a more empowered, resilient, and truly agentic self.

6---full-notes/the-attitude-recall-error.title: The Attitude Recall Error
6---full-notes/the-attitude-recall-error.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
The Attitude Recall Error
Details
The brain does not just account for the change in attitude, it also convinces and reconstructs memories so that we would misremember and support that change in attitude. One of the most striking findings in dissonance research comes from Bem and McConnell’s counter-attitudinal essay study, where attitude change was measured not minutes but a week after the essay was written. Subjects who freely chose to write a pro-tuition-increase essay showed significant attitude shift toward favoring tuition increases a week later — demonstrating that dissonance effects persist beyond the laboratory session.
But the truly revealing measure came next. Subjects were asked to remember what their attitude had been a week earlier, before writing the essay. Their recall errors were almost perfectly proportional to their attitude change. If someone’s attitude shifted 10 points on a 30-point scale, they misremembered their original attitude by approximately 10 points — in the direction of their current attitude. They believed they had always held the position they now held. Subjects who wrote no essay and showed no attitude change were accurate in recalling their earlier attitudes.
The implications that this study shows are quite uncomfortable, it shows that our rationalizations and such are quite unreliable and fakeable, by our own mind no less.

The Availability Heuristic
Details
When estimating how common something is, we usually use the question “how easily can I think of examples?” which is based in availability heuristic. More words have K as their third letter than as their first, but nobody believes this because there’s an easy mental procedure for generating K-first words (king, kitchen, ketchup) and no corresponding procedure for third-letter-K words. Similarly, people estimate shark attacks as more lethal than failing airplane parts when it is 30 times less likely. Notably, this estimate reversed after 9/11, when falling airplane debris became the more available mental image. The heuristic works adequately when the items being compared are equally vivid or accessed through equivalent procedures (more S-words than J-words? Yes, and availability gives the right answer). The brain doesn’t distinguish between “I’ve encountered this many times” and “I’ve encountered this few times but it was unforgettable.”

The Background pillar in traits
Details
Other than just genetics or the environment, there also exists a chance factor in it. Biology is not a perfectly deterministic machine. Randomness, or stochasticity, is woven into its very fabric. Consider the mitochondria in a single cell. Because they have their own DNA and replicate independently, a cell contains a mosaic of slightly different mitochondrial genes. When that cell divides, which mitochondria end up in which daughter cell is a matter of random chance—where they happened to be floating at the moment of the split. Two genetically identical cells can thus give rise to genetically different offspring in a single generation, not because of a grand blueprint, but because of a cosmic dice roll. This principle applies to all the crucial molecules of life, like transcription factors. This inherent randomness is a fundamental source of variation, ensuring that even with identical genes and an identical environment, life will always retain an element of unpredictability.

The Basic Structure as the Primary Subject of Justice
Details
Concerning the third fundamental intuitive idea in justice as fairness is the notion of basic structure. The question is simple: what subjects should we apply the idea of society as a fair system of cooperation on ? The answer Rawls come to is in the way that the main political, legal, and social institutions hang together into one system and determine the division of benefits from cooperation. This includes the constitution, the judiciary, the legal system, the forms of property permitted (including private property in means of production), and the organization of the economy.
There are some limits to this though. First, the principles of justice discussed in TJ do not apply directly to particular institutions like churches or universities. Though they operate within the framework, they do not actually fulfill the requirements of the principle of toleration, which prevents them to use state power to engage politically. Second, the inquiry does not apply directly to the law of nations or relations between states. If the view works for the basic structure, one might later attempt to extend it (perhaps imagining a well-ordered international society composed of well-ordered constitutional states), but that extension is a separate project.
Rawls offers two reasons for this focus. Practically, it is to ensure that we have a view for the basic structure for it would be significant regardless of its extension. The deeper reason is to reemphasize how people’s identities are built upon this basic structure.

6---full-notes/the-better-than-average-e.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Social Psychology
The Better-Than-Average Effect
Details
Across virtually every measurable dimension, roughly 75%-80% of people rate themselves as above average. Of course this is statistically impossible and represents one of psychology’s perhaps…easiest findings or replicable findings: positive illusions. Coined by Shelley Taylor, these are illusions of people that makes them believe in the extent of their abilities to be much farther than it actually is. She also argues that it carries mental and physical health benefits. The only group, that can reliably produce accurate self-assessments is clinically depressed individuals. This creates a disturbing implication: psychological health may depend partly on self-deception, and accuracy about oneself may be a symptom of dysfunction rather than clarity. The debate over whether positive illusions are genuinely adaptive or merely feel good remains unresolved.
To explain why this exists, we have to look into two of the strongest arguments: motivational - as it protects our self-esteem (from an evolutionary standpoint) or that it is cognitive - as biased outputs can emerge from unbiased processing applied to unequal information. Ross and Sicoly’s household chores study illustrates the cognitive side: each partner claimed responsibility for 16 of 20 tasks, not from vanity but because each had fuller memory access to their own contributions than their partner’s. The database itself is asymmetric (this proves the latter).
Dunning’s work shows a deeper mechanism, the mechanism in which people emphasize and value traits that they themselves are expressive of. So a loyal person would value loyalty in friends and tell that to people who ask them questions relative to…friends, and so on. And so their comparisons will also shift to serve their selves.

6---full-notes/the-big-five-model-of-per.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
The Big Five Model of Personality
Details
Psychologists have devised questionnaires to measure belief in a just world, and hundreds of the other traits. They have examined the English dictionary and narrowed down, cut down the words that are similar to each other down to 35 words, then they mathematically narrowed it down even further, words that may be synonyms or antonyms of one another, but overlap. They looked for these clusters and then narrowed it down to the big five personality traits: neuroticism, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness to new experience (McCrae & Costa, 1987). The case for these five traits is that they correlate with many dimensions of our personality and none of them correlate with the other four as well. The traits are described accordingly:


Neuroticism: A tendency to experience unpleasant emotions frequently. Psychologists have proposed another term emotional stability. This can determine to the person’s anxiety, hostility, depression, self-consciousness, and frequent squabbles with other people.


Extraversion: A tendency to seek stimulation and enjoy the company of other people. This is what people usually call extraversion and introversion. Unlike Neuroticism, there are actually two sides to being high or low on this trait, the positives are warmth, gregariousness, assertiveness, impulsiveness, and a need for excitement. The unpleasant side is an increased chance in alcohol abuse and risky behaviors. In researches, this usually corresponded with happiness, so take that how you want to take it.


Agreeableness: The tendency to be compassionate towards others. It is very closely related to empathy or Adler’s concept of social interest. These people usually place a lot of trust into people and also expect the same amount of trust back. The also seem to have more stable marriages and stable employment (Roberts et al., 2007).


Conscientiousness: A tendency to show self-discipline, to strive for achievement and competence. People high in this scale works really hard and complete their tasks on time. They just tend to avoid risky and dangerous activities and tend to have successful jobs, marriages, and greater than average life expectancy (Roberts et al., 2007).


Openness to experience: A tendency to enjoy new experiences and ideas. People with this trait enjoy modern art, unusual music and though-provoking things, like films and books. They are just really open to everything, be it meeting people or doing something new.


There have been further research that suggested that this is still too many traits and it could be reduced down to three, which are neuroticism, extraversion, and agreeableness as the others correlate with each other in one way or another. The use of this depends on the purpose that it is being taken on for.

6---full-notes/the-biology-of-the-brain-.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience biology
The Biology of the Brain of Transexuality
Details
A landmark 1980s study by Simon LeVay provided the first major biological correlate for sexual orientation. He found that a specific hypothalamic nucleus, the INAH-3, was on average twice as large in heterosexual men as in heterosexual women. In gay men, the INAH-3 was, on average, the same small size as in heterosexual women. This finding, which has been replicated, suggested a biological basis for orientation rather than it being a “lifestyle choice.” Other, more subtle biological markers have also been found, such as differences in the ratio of the second to fourth finger length and in the frequency of the inner ear’s otoacoustic reflex. These markers are believed to be indicators of the prenatal hormone environment.
Neurobiological research suggests that transsexuality is a condition where a person’s brain structure aligns with their gender identity rather than their anatomical sex at birth. A key study focused on the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BSTc), a brain region that is reliably larger in men than in women. The study found that male-to-female transsexuals had a small, female-sized BSTc, while female-to-male transsexuals had a large, male-sized BSTc. Crucially, this was true regardless of whether they had undergone hormone therapy, indicating it was not a result of adult hormone levels. This reframes transsexuality not as a psychological issue, but as a biological one where the brain’s sex and the body’s sex are mismatched.

The Biopsychosocial Model of Mental Disorders
Details
In modern times, the prevailing view has moved on from single-cause explanations for mental illnesses (e.g., purely biological or purely environmental). The current dominant framework for understanding the causes of abnormal behavior is the biopsychosocial model. This model proposes that, rather than just one or two factors affecting the upcoming of mental illness in individuals, there are three factors that may altogether contribute to it.


Biological Factors: This includes an individual’s genetic makeup, brain chemistry, neurotransmitter levels, and overall physiological health. A biological predisposition might make someone more vulnerable to developing a certain disorder.


Psychological Factors: This encompasses an individual’s thoughts, interpretations, past traumas, learned behaviors, and coping mechanisms. Stress, low self-esteem, and negative thinking patterns can all contribute to the development of a disorder.


Social-Cultural Factors: This involves the influence of one’s environment, including cultural norms, societal expectations, family dynamics, and socioeconomic status. The roles we are expected to play and the support systems we have can either protect against or contribute to psychological distress.


A therapist using this model doesn’t look for a single “cause” but rather tries to understand how these three areas interact to produce and maintain a person’s specific symptoms or if it is truly a combination between the three factors at all.

The Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB)
Details
In the general circulatory system, capillaries have small pores or gaps in between them, allowing most small molecules to flow freely between blood and tissue. However, in the CNS, these blood vessels have no pores.
For a drug to be psychoactive, it has to be able to pass through this barrier. Meaning it has to pass by being actively transported or it has to be hydrophobic enough (The Lipid Bilayer Membrane). This principle explains the potency difference between Morphine and Heroin. Heroin is chemically modified morphine; the modification makes it more hydrophobic (oil-soluble), allowing it to cross the BBB much faster and in higher concentrations, creating a more intense “rush.” Conversely, antibiotics like penicillin are hydrophilic and cannot cross the BBB, making them useless for treating brain infections.

6---full-notes/the-brain-behavior-link.content:

The Brain-Behavior Link
Details
While functional brain imaging provides an unprecedented map of neural activity, the relationship between this activity and our actual cognitive processes is not straightforward. A brain scan is not a mind reading. For example, while the fusiform gyrus is strongly associated with face perception, we know that damage to this area is not the only cause of prosopagnosia (face blindness), indicating that cognition is the product of a distributed network, not a single isolated area. This tells us that behavioral measures—the end product of cognition—remain the gold standard for validating our theories. A brain imaging study without a clear behavioral outcome is less informative, as it’s difficult to know what the observed brain activity truly signifies.
A useful way to think about this is the artificial intelligence metaphor. One cannot understand the function of a computer program simply by looking at the electricity flowing through its circuit board. The operations are performed by algorithms (the software), which exist as relationships between the physical circuits (the hardware). Similarly, our cognition can be thought of as the “software” that runs on the “hardware” of the brain. The patterns of neural firing are the substrate, but the cognitive functions themselves—our thoughts, memories, and decisions—are the complex operations that this hardware performs. This distinction highlights why simply mapping active brain regions is only part of the story; we must also understand the computational rules and relationships that constitute the mind itself.
