The Central Ingredient of many Phobias
Details
Many people can have a wide variety of phobias, which may seem to have little or no correlation with each other. It is possible for us to find a central theme in all of these phobias that may seem disparate. It is usually concerned with a specific fear of the consequences of being in the apparent dissimilar situations.
A woman had a fear of flying, lying on the beach on a hot day, standing still in crowded places, riding in an open car on a windy day, riding in a closed car, elevators, tunnels, hills, and flying. After determining what the woman was afraid of in each of these situations, it was quite possible to find a common denominator.
She had the notion, based on certain superstitions or folklore or actual possibility, that she could suffocate under each of these conditions. The central fear, in this case, was being deprived of air. For example, the feared outcome of being in enclosed places was lack of sufficient air. She had also heard, as a child, that “The wind was strong enough to blow the air out of your mouth.” Also, she had been impressed by the notion, “It was so hot, you couldn’t breathe.” The patient’s fear of flying was based on the notion that the pressurized cabin might be punctured accidentally and that there would be a loss of oxygen.
It was also discovered that she had a latent fear of water, which she managed to handle by having someone going with her when she was swimming. If she did not, she would be afraid as she thinks she might drone and there would be no one to save her.
This shows us how important it is not to make a priori judgement regarding the ideational content of phobias. Just as how the meaning of a particular object or situation may vary from patient to patient, so a varied assortment of fears experienced by one may have a common underlying meaning.

The Challenge of Multilevel Accounts
Details
The ultimate goal of cognitive psychology and neuroscience is to create a grand, unified theory of behavior—one that can explain how we get from the most fundamental biological processes to the complexity of human experience. This requires generating multilevel accounts that bridge the enormous gaps between vastly different scales of analysis. The challenge lies in connecting the dots from the expression of DNA into genes, from genes to the production of proteins and molecules, from those molecules to the firing of single neurons, from single neurons to the coordinated activity of large neural populations, and from those populations to the function of gross brain structures, which finally results in observable behavior.
As our knowledge at each of these individual levels increases at a staggering rate, the primary challenge is no longer just about discovery within a single level, but about integration across them. How does a change in a single gene cascade up through the system to alter the function of a neural network and ultimately influence a personality trait or a decision? Answering these questions requires a deeply interdisciplinary approach, combining genetics, molecular biology, electrophysiology, systems neuroscience, and psychology. Creating these comprehensive, multilevel explanations represents the major frontier of brain science, promising to unravel the deepest mysteries of who we are and why we do what we do.

At times we will need to examine these data to change the intricate pattern of meanings. This must then be tried in real situations and reworked until it fits the patient’s conception of reality.

Although they are aware of this, they keep it hidden because revealing it would only bring more displeasure. Special meanings happen when the event touches an important of someone’s life, but of course are frequently kept hidden.

In fact, when patients reveal such meanings to therapists, it is usually the first time they get to examine these thoughts and consider their validity. The Combination of Fields in Behavioral Biology
Details
The study of behavior is not one field but at least three warring tribes, each with its own language, tools, and definition of truth. The evolutionary biologists tell grand stories of selection and adaptation. The molecular geneticists hunt for the precise mutations in the DNA. And the behavior geneticists look for patterns of inheritance in families and twins. From within one camp, the others look naive or misguided. The molecular biologist scoffs at the evolutionary theorist’s story, demanding to see the specific gene. The theorist finds the geneticist’s focus on a single molecule laughably reductive. This isn’t a sign that one field is “wrong.” It’s a demonstration of different levels of analysis. One discipline’s satisfying answer—“culture affects biology”—is another’s starting point: “Yes, but how? Which genes are turned on? What is the epigenetic mechanism?” The whole point is, all of this can exist with each other and none necessarily disproves the other, is just that they have to have a different view of it.

The Combined Treatment Paradox
Details
The logical clinical instinct is to combine treatments: “If CT works and Meds work, surely CT + Meds is best.” However, studies actually show that this can result in the drugs undermining the effects of CT. In a long-term trial, patients receiving a combined treatment expressed no greater benefit after withdrawal compared to those only using medications.
The mechanism likely relates to “Hebb’s Dictum”: neurons that fire together, wire together. Based on Steve Maier’s rat models, the cortex (vmPFC) needs to fire in response to the brainstem’s stress signal to build the inhibitory pathway. But because the medication dampens the brainstem’s stress response system, they’re not actually experiencing any stress. And as suggested in Why are treatments of Depression different, we NEED stress to teach the brain. Another study that reinforced this is Dave Barlow’s panic disorder study, in which patients using CT + placebo retained their gains whilst those with CT + medication lost them.

Status: teen
Tags: Cognitive Psychology biology genetics 3 - Tags/environment
The Complexity of Environment
Details
While it’s easy to think of the “environment” as a single entity, its influence is far more nuanced. Siblings growing up in the same family do not experience the exact same world. To account for this, scholars distinguish between shared and non-shared environments. A shared environment includes all the factors that siblings have in common as a result of growing up in the same family, which theoretically should make them more similar to one another. This includes things like the family’s socioeconomic status, the house and neighborhood they live in, their parents’ child-rearing style, family activities and diet, and the language and culture of the household.
However, the non-shared environment consists of all the unique experiences that individuals living together do not share, and these factors are what cause them to become dissimilar. This can include having different friends or teachers, participating in different activities outside the home, or even experiencing unique family events that affect one sibling differently than another. Counterintuitively, research consistently shows that these non-shared environmental factors tend to have a more significant influence on shaping an individual’s personality and traits than the shared factors. This finding complicates the simple nature-nurture equation, highlighting that even within the same family, individual experience is paramount.

6---full-notes/the-comprehensive-guide-t.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/The Comprehensive Guide to DBT.md
6---full-notes/the-comprehensive-guide-t.title: The Comprehensive Guide to DBT
6---full-notes/the-comprehensive-guide-t.content:
Status: adult
Tags: therapy Clinical Psychology
The Comprehensive Guide to DBT
Details
The structuring of session time is the primary factor that distinguishes Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) skills training from DBT individual psychotherapy. In individual therapy, the agenda is open and set by the client’s behavior since the last session. In skills training, the agenda is pre-set by the behavioral skill to be taught, creating a structured, classroom-like environment.
Pretreatment DBT
The Core Four-Part Session Structure
Every skills training session, regardless of length, adheres to a consistent four-part structure:


Beginning Ritual (Mindfulness and logistics)


Homework Review (Sharing of skills practice) Managing Homework


Presentation of New Material (Teaching new skills) Skills training Procedures


Closing “Wind-Down” (Emotional regulation and session closure)


Session duration varies by context. For adults with severe disorders (like BPD), sessions are typically 2.5 hours with a 15-minute break. This length is considered necessary; 1.5 hours is often insufficient, as it provides inadequate time for both homework review (50-60 mins) and new material (50-60 mins). Adolescent groups or groups for less severe disorders may last 90 minutes to 2 hours. Individual skills training is typically 45-60 minutes.
1. The Beginning Ritual
The session formally begins with a mindfulness practice led by the leader, often using a bell (three rings to start, one to end). The type of practice is varied weekly to cover all mindfulness skills. After the practice, each participant (including leaders) shares their experience, which provides an opportunity for the leader to offer corrective feedback.
This time is also used for logistics. Members who missed previous sessions can briefly share where they have been. Any group-level issues (announcements, lateness, not calling when absent) are addressed. This brief attention to therapy-interfering behaviors (no more than 5 minutes) is a crucial part of the session and should not be dropped.
2. The Homework Review
This phase is essential for skills acquisition. The leader goes around the circle and asks each member to share their efforts to practice skills during the week. This is not voluntary; waiting for volunteers wastes time. The “homework” (a term that should be discussed, as some clients find it demeaning) review is a powerful motivator. The sure knowledge that each client will be asked about their practice, and that not practicing will be analyzed, encourages effort. This part of the session takes precedence over any other task.
3. The Presentation of New Material
Following a 10-15 minute break, the next hour is devoted to teaching. The break is an important, unstructured time for clients to interact and fosters group cohesion independent of the leaders. Leaders should be alert during the break, as clients having a hard time may be at risk of leaving.
When a new module begins, the first 30 minutes of this teaching block are spent on the rationale for that module. The leader’s task is to convince clients that the skills are relevant, that learning them will improve their lives, and that they are capable of learning them.
A variation occurs in the final session of a module. No new material is presented. Instead, this time is used to:


Review all skills from the current module.


Review skills from previous modules.


Discuss pros, cons, and generalization of skills.


If clients are “graduating,” a positive sendoff ritual is held, which includes certificates, a card with personal notes from leaders, and an opportunity for each member to say goodbye.


4. The Closing “Wind-Down”
The final 5-15 minutes are critical for clients with emotion dysregulation. Skills sessions can be emotionally activating, and this period helps clients regulate their affect and “close up” the session before leaving. It also allows any clients who dissociated to “come back” to the room.


“Observe and Describe” Wind-Down: The most popular method. Each member shares one observation from the session. Leaders coach clients to describe just the facts (“I noticed the thought that I was angry”) rather than interpretations (“Bill was angry”).


“Process-Observing” Wind-Down: A more advanced method where members observe the group process itself. This is risky, as it can lead to critical comments, conflict, and members storming out. It is especially problematic when mixing new and advanced clients.


In both wind-downs, the leaders go last to repair any damage and pull the group together.

6---full-notes/the-conflict-between-libe.title: The Conflict Between Liberty and Equality
6---full-notes/the-conflict-between-libe.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy morals
The Conflict Between Liberty and Equality
Details
Within the democratic thought there resides a conflict between the competing claims of liberty and equality. Rawls frames this using Benjamin Constant’s famous distinction (Constant lived roughly 1770–1830). The Lockean tradition emphasizes what Constant called “the liberties of the moderns” - freedom of speech, thought, conscience, and various civil rights of equal citizenship. The Rousseauian tradition emphasizes “the liberties of the ancients” — the political liberties of participation, the values of public life, and active self-governance, modeled on the adult male citizens of Athenian democracy.
Both traditions recognize these values but they treat them very differently. This discrepancy is basically from how differently the people in these traditions view and think about these concepts and how it actually should be treated.
Rawls then maps two great philosophical traditions onto this divide: the social contract tradition (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Kant) and the utilitarian tradition (Hume, Bentham, J.S. Mill, Sidgwick). The latter is quite formidable due to its dominance over the English economists theorists from 1750 to 1900, making it not only a moral-political doctrine but a comprehensive social-scientific framework. It remains, in some form, the dominant view. And many philosophers have come to challenge this viewpoint, John Rawls included.

6---full-notes/the-contextual-divergence.title: The Contextual Divergence of Hobbes and Locke
6---full-notes/the-contextual-divergence.content:
Status: adult
Tags: morals philosophy
The Contextual Divergence of Hobbes and Locke
Details
Political philosophy is rarely a continuous timeline of abstract thinkers trying to answer a single, universal question; rather, it is a desperate attempt to solve the immediate, bleeding crises of their specific historical moments. To truly understand the friction between Thomas Hobbes and John Locke, we have to look at the visceral, physical realities they were surviving. Hobbes was writing under the shadow of the English Civil War, deeply traumatized by the horrific violence of sectarian factions tearing the country apart. For Hobbes, the absolute worst-case scenario for humanity was the total collapse of society back into the state of nature, which he viewed as a perpetual, chaotic war of all against all. Because his primary goal was to prevent this violent collapse, he argued that all rational people sharing a basic self-interest in preserving their own lives and securing a “commodious living” should willingly submit to an absolute sovereign. In Hobbes’s view, any effective sovereign—no matter how tyrannical—was a rational necessity because the alternative was violent death.
Locke, however, was in completely different political waters. Writing primarily during the Exclusion Crisis of 1679 to 1681, Locke was embedded in the radical Whig faction led by his patron, the Earl of Shaftesbury. They were actively, and often treasonously, conspiring to prevent Charles II’s Catholic brother, James, from succeeding to the throne, fearing he would establish a French-backed Catholic absolute monarchy. Locke was not an armchair philosopher writing abstract theory; he was a political operative living in Shaftesbury’s home, deeply involved in dangerous resistance efforts that eventually forced him into exile. Because Locke was personally invested in armed resistance against a monarch who was overstepping his bounds, his entire philosophical project had to be reverse-engineered to ethically justify rebellion, protect a mixed constitution, and mathematically prove that royal absolutism was fundamentally illegitimate.

6---full-notes/the-core-behavioral-featu.title: The Core Behavioral Features of ADHD
6---full-notes/the-core-behavioral-featu.content:
Status: adult
Tags: ADHD biology
The Core Behavioral Features of ADHD
Details
The experience of ADHD extends far beyond simple hyperactivity. It is defined by a collection of distinct behavioral and cognitive traits that reveal a fundamental difficulty in regulating perception and action. At its core is a struggle with both attention, which is the ability to direct one’s perception toward a specific goal, and impulse control, which is the equally important skill of filtering out irrelevant distractions. While it may seem that individuals with ADHD cannot focus, the opposite is often true. Many experience periods of profound hyper-focus, an intense, laser-like concentration on tasks they find deeply engaging or rewarding. This paradox reveals that the brain’s focus circuitry is fully functional but is difficult to engage voluntarily for tasks that are not inherently stimulating.
This regulatory challenge also manifests in a distorted perception of time. Individuals with ADHD often underestimate how long tasks will take, leading to chronic procrastination and lateness, a pattern that is only broken when the severe consequences of a deadline become imminent. Their physical world can reflect this internal disorganization through what is known as the “pile system,” where belongings are arranged in piles that follow a personal logic but ultimately fail as an effective organizational tool. Furthermore, while long-term memory may be intact, there is a significant deficit in working memory—the crucial ability to hold a piece of information, like a phone number or a short instruction, in the mind just long enough to use it. These traits together paint a picture not of a lack of ability, but of a fundamental challenge in directing and managing the brain’s powerful executive functions.
These issues can further lead to alienation, to aggression, just overall alienation from others in their lives, like family, like friends, at school, and so on like that. They would underperform academically a lot, due to their low attention span.

6---full-notes/the-core-of-active-passiv.title: The Core of Active-Passivity
6---full-notes/the-core-of-active-passiv.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology therapy
The Core of Active-Passivity
Details
People with BPD usually actually thinks that they are problem solving, just in a different way. They’re thinking that they are merely utilizing the tools at their disposal by requesting your assistance on help. But as always, BPD makes this get lost in translation, instead of “can you help me” it comes out as “YOU NEED TO HELP ME WITH THIS PROBLEM”. This makes it sounds very passive-aggressive but they’re not doing it intentionally, and they genuinely believe that they were actually reasonably requesting.
And because of that, you shouldn’t treat them harshly, and rather with empathy as you now understand why they act that way. Then, you can start helping them to develop said skills by basically assessing their problems with the current situation. The problems fall into the existing questions:
What is the problem, what needs to happen. To help them with this, work with them on clarifying the problem definition and helping her to problem solve along the way, make sure to validate her.
Are you afraid, or too angry to be effective, or too embarrassed of having to do it. If this is the problem, check the facts of situation, see if they genuinely will react in the way your loved one thinks they will, and proceed.
And if they do not believe in themselves being able to solve the problem. Try to role-play the situation with them to train their confidence on solving the problem (this is a method used in DBT therapy to help patients develop said skills).

6---full-notes/the-cultural-relativity-o.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology
The Cultural Relativity of Abnormality
Details
What is considered normal or abnormal behavior varies dramatically across different cultures. This concept of cultural relativity is a major challenge for creating a universal system of diagnosis.
Behaviors Normal in One Culture, Abnormal in Another:


Professional Wrestling (USA): In American culture, men in tight underwear simulating violence for entertainment is a multi-million dollar industry. In many other cultures, this behavior would be seen as bizarre and pathological.


“Demon Possession” (Sudan): In parts of Sudan, it is considered a normal and understandable reaction for a woman under extreme stress to become “possessed by demons,” acting violently and screaming obscenities. The “cure” is not medication, but a brief holiday away from her family.


“Brain Fag” Syndrome (Sub-Saharan Africa): In some African cultures, it is believed that studying too hard can cause debilitating headaches in children. The accepted treatment is to be excused from schoolwork.


Culture-Bound Syndromes: Some disorders appear to be created by or are unique to specific cultures.


Multiple Personality Disorder (USA): This disorder became rampant in the United States in the 1960s-80s but was virtually nonexistent in other countries. It has since almost completely disappeared, suggesting it may have been a culturally-created phenomenon.


“Running Amok” (China): A few years ago, there was a spate of incidents where overworked men in China would grab weapons and attack children in elementary schools. This specific expression of psychological breakdown was a temporary, culture-specific phenomenon that has since faded.


These examples demonstrate that culture not only defines what is abnormal but can also create unique forms of mental distress.

Huntington critiqued the common American belief that good, democratic institutions will spontaneously emerge once a population is given “freedom”—as if they were weeds in a garden. This was the flawed model applied in post-invasion Iraq, where the U.S. focused on writing a constitution but neglected to build the actual machinery of a functioning state. The same situation can be seen in Mexico (although one can argue how the US is tolerating Mexico and so on).
A few more examples would be the difference between Cuba and South Vietnam. Of course Cuba was the enemy of the US back then and South Vietnam was their ally. The US tried hard to get Fidel Castro to be assassinated, but they failed due to how the people in Cuba were so supervised (and also treated really nicely). At the end though, they had a rock solid foundation on their political landscape.
On the other hand, South Vietnam was the opposite, they did not have good politics, no structure, their political institution was practically fighting themselves for power. North Vietnam though, as authoritarian as it is, it still was a tighter political system which allowed them to win.

The Difference Principle
Details
Elaborating further on the Difference Principle made in The Architecture and Priority of Basic Liberties, we have to establish a certain concept for it: the optimality curve (OP curve). When economists or philosophers map social productivity like this, they are illustrating how variations in economic returns to the more advantaged groups can actively incentivize a system that ultimately produces a greater total yield for everyone. These greater returns are necessary to cover the costs of advanced training, to mark out positions of high responsibility, and to encourage necessary economic innovation.
Criticisms against this are the extreme mathematical possibilities of it and such. They worry that a society might justify massive, thousand-to-one wealth disparities if the optimality curve rises too slowly or tapers off infinitely without dipping. However, this is only because they are failing to consider that the Principle is subordinate to prior principles of justice, specifically the guarantee of fair equality of opportunity. This fairness in the background framework ensures that no matter what happens, in a just world, it will be certain that the resulting distribution of wealth will organically be just.

The Difference between Scientific and Psychological Explanations
Details
Simplifying these concepts altogether, scientific explanations are the mathematical and statistical algorithms that may help us determine a person’s tendencies to do something or the probability that they will do it. What this doesn’t explain though is their motive, the reason behind their decision, like how perhaps it is a past experience or memory that make them act that certain way.
Without the Imaginative Understanding, or empathy, the understanding is completely stripped of any humanity or warmth, which is something that is always needed.
For example, even if we act like a bat, trying to sleep in lockers (the dark) and eat like them, we can maybe perhaps know every physical fact there is to know about a bat’s neurophysiology. However, no amount of physical data will allow a human to truly possess an imaginative understanding of the bat’s inner life. We cannot know “what it is like” to be a bat. If physical facts are exhaustive, yet they leave out the subjective experience, then physicalism seems incomplete. This underscores the isolation of the mind: physics describes the hardware, but subjective experience remains inaccessible to outside observation.

6---full-notes/the-differences-in-instit.title: The Differences in Institutions
6---full-notes/the-differences-in-instit.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
The Differences in Institutions
Details
A foundational principle of sociology is that our sense of self—who we are, what we value, and how we relate to others—is not born in a vacuum. Instead, it is profoundly shaped by the social institutions that structure our lives. These institutions, from the family and the economy to the educational system, differ dramatically across time periods and geographical locations. Each distinct institutional arrangement carries its own inherent logic and core values, which in turn influence and foster a particular type of person.
We can see this contrast clearly when comparing a traditional, land-based economy with a modern, labor-market economy. In a traditional society where one’s fate is determined by land inheritance, the central institutional value is honor. A “good person” is one who dutifully performs their social obligations to their family and community. The self is external, public, and defined by one’s reputation for fulfilling these roles.
In contrast, a modern society organized around a competitive labor market promotes a different core value: individual human capital. Here, a person’s fate appears to rest on their internal collection of traits—their intelligence, talent, work ethic, and personality. The self becomes an internal, psychological project to be constantly assessed, managed, and improved for success.
This demonstrates that the very questions we ask about ourselves are products of our institutional context. Whether we define our worth by our honor and duties or by our talents and ambitions is not a timeless personal choice, but a reflection of the world we inhabit. Institutions provide the blueprint, and we are, in many ways, the buildings constructed from it.

The Different questions regarding Suicides
Details
Usually in the matter of morality and rationality, people conflate the two together and assume that they are relatively correlated. That, of course, does not apply to many situations, and suicide is one of them. Though that can also be debated as well.
The cultural default treats contemplating the act as evidence of either madness or wickedness, which means the question never gets asked as a question. Separating rationality from morality is what makes it askable at all. The two standards can diverge in both directions. Cheating on taxes may be prudentially rational — audit rates are low, penalties mild — and still impermissible: a moral requirement with no rational one behind it. Choosing a much worse university over a much better one violates no duty but may be irrational: a rational requirement with no moral one. Inside rationality, then, there’s a separate set of questions:

Could it ever be true that a person is better off dead?
Could a person ever be warranted in believing their own case is one of those?
Of course these questions are separate and can have separate answers.

6---full-notes/the-differential-structur.title: The Differential Structure of Valuation Tags
6---full-notes/the-differential-structur.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
The Differential Structure of Valuation Tags
Details
Nietzsche posits a structural theory of psychology: to value something is inherently an act of differentiation. Valuation is not a passive, one-place predicate (e.g., “I like tea”); it is a relational hierarchy (e.g., “I prefer tea to coffee”). To affirm “X” necessarily implies the subordination or rejection of “Y.” Therefore, valuation is fundamentally discriminatory.
A state of universal acceptance, or an inability to discriminate, represents a failure of valuation-a form of nihilism where everything is equal and therefore nothing matters. Nietzsche argue that the human soul can only find the world “good” if it is in a state of tension, constantly ranking experiences. This means that “preference” is the fundamental unit of value. Even if the comparison is tacit, every “Yes” to a value involves a “No” to its opposite. This psychological mechanism explains why Nietzsche is so hostile to egalitarianism; if you remove the hierarchy and the ability to distinguish “better” from “worse,” you destroy the very mechanism by which human beings find meaning and value in their existence.
Moreover, there exists a difference of level between passive valuation and active valuation. Nietzsche argue that the capability for someone to appreciate something needs them to be able to create something, the future. This is illustrated by an anecdote involving Richard Wagner and the Louvre during the Franco-Prussian War. Upon hearing a false rumor that the Louvre had burned down, Wagner supposedly remarked that if the French could not paint new pictures as good as or better than the old ones, they did not deserve the originals anyway. And so a pianist who plays Beethoven cannot truly value his work, only someone who creates a different kind/type of music.
Furthermore, this would even be used to justify how high culture functions, how it requires a hierarchical society, potentially even slavery. Unlike Aristotle, who defended slavery on economic grounds, Nietzsche defends it on psychological grounds about how Masters have to distinguish themselves from slaves to actually function and experience…Vitality.

6---full-notes/the-drug-abuse-potential.title: The Drug Abuse Potential
6---full-notes/the-drug-abuse-potential.content:
Status: adult
Tags: physiology pharmacology
The Drug Abuse Potential
Details
When assessing how easily a drug can be abused, we must look beyond the substance itself and evaluate a broader set of criteria, including pharmacology, dose, route of administration, and cultural context. In simpler terms, drug abuse potential—often referred to as abuse liability—is basically the likelihood that a specific substance will be sought out and used compulsively for non-medical purposes, regardless of the harm it may cause.
The most fundamental factor in this assessment is the drug’s pharmacology, or how it interacts with the brain. A drug has a high abuse potential if it acts as a powerful “reinforcer,” meaning it reliably produces euphoria or relief from distress. This usually happens because the drug triggers the brain’s reward system, specifically the mesolimbic dopamine pathway. If a substance can mimic natural neurotransmitters or force a massive release of dopamine, the brain learns to prioritize that substance above natural rewards like food or social interaction.
However, the “high” is heavily influenced by pharmacokinetics, particularly the speed of onset. There is a strong correlation between how fast a drug enters the brain and how addictive it becomes. This is why the route of administration is so critical. A drug that is smoked or injected reaches the brain in seconds, creating an intense, immediate “rush.” This rapid association between the action (taking the drug) and the reward (the high) reinforces the behavior much more strongly than a drug taken orally, which must pass through the digestive system and enters the bloodstream gradually.
Beyond the initial reward, physical dependence plays a crucial role in sustaining abuse. If a drug has a short half-life, the effects wear off quickly, leading to a “crash” or withdrawal symptoms. At this stage, the motivation to use shifts from positive reinforcement (seeking pleasure) to negative reinforcement (avoiding pain/illness).
Finally, we cannot ignore the environmental and cultural context. A drug’s abuse potential is not purely biological; it is also logistical. Availability, cost, and legal status act as gatekeepers. A drug that is potent but incredibly difficult to obtain has a lower practical abuse potential than one that is moderately potent but available in every medicine cabinet. When we combine high accessibility with powerful pharmacological effects, we see the highest rates of widespread abuse.

The Dunning-Kruger effect
Details
The definition for this phenomenon is basically that incompetent people overestimate their own competence and fail to sense a mismatch between their actual level of competence and their actual skill level. But these people have been shown to be able to raise their competence by improving their metacognition and skills that they are bad at.
Many experiments have shown this, testing students of their logic and rating their own performance, so on and so forth. Even after being shown others’ competence and answers they still fail to judge their own questions accurately. The last experiment which explored whether they could improve their judgement. Receiving training after the tests and such, and pitched against a part of the same former group who did something else rather than training, they did perform better than the group that did nothing.
There are quite a few theories on why these people fail to see their own unskillfulness. One is that people seldomly receive negative feedback on their own incompetence because others are too afraid of delivering bad news, and even if they do receive it, they still need to understand why it is that bad.
Supporting Content
At times, this incompetence in certain fields can be frank, like sports, where people who are clearly athletic are picked and those who are not are left out. And so students may have a bad view of their own capabilities from the start, preventing them from trying to improve in that field.

The Ecological and Medical Models
Details
The impairment model, aka an ecological model, argues that behavior is not inherently disordered but rather it is significantly impairing an individual’s life. This makes it so that the abnormality dependent on how good of a fit the behaviors are to the person rather than social norms or statistical norms. The model works profoundly correct in how it personalizes the feelings and personal suffering rather than just the data.
Next up is the medical model, which argues that mental illnesses are like biomedical illnesses, that it is a problem of the brain. The ultimate goal is to identify objective biological markers—lesions, neurotransmitter imbalances, or faulty neural circuits—that cause the disorder. This approach promises scientific objectivity and holds the hope of reducing stigma by framing these conditions as legitimate illnesses. However, it faces significant hurdles. First, for most mental disorders, we lack a definitive “lab test” like a blood test or a simple brain scan. Second, even in medicine, complex illnesses like heart disease are multifactorial, resulting from an interplay of genetics, lifestyle, and environment, not a single cause. And lastly, even if it is defined, it does not prevent stigma, it just changes from a moral one to a fundamental one.

6---full-notes/the-economic-model.content:
Status: teen

The Economic Model
Details
Usually, models in sciences explain through having exact universal constants or laws that apply perfectly everywhere. As it is a social science, it takes the characteristics of how models in other social sciences work, in the sense that it is not completely accurate. The aim is not to build a model that is literally complete, but one that is useful enough to explain something important while remaining simple enough to understand, teach, and solve. George Box’s line that “all models are wrong, but some are useful” captures the spirit of this method.
A major trade-off inside modeling is between explanatory richness and parsimony. A richer model may include many goods, many kinds of agents, uncertainty, institutions, habits, power, and imperfect information, but it can become impossible to solve or too complicated to see the core mechanism. A parsimonious model may reduce the world to two goods, two variables, or a simple linear relationship, which is obviously incomplete but can reveal the logic of the broader case. For example, introductory economics often models choices between two goods even though people actually choose among thousands of goods and activities. The defense is not that the two-good model is literally true, but that the intuition gained from two goods can often generalize to many goods with harder math and uglier graphs.

The Effects of Inhibition in Neurons
Details
As mentioned in Listening between Neurons, the presynaptic neurons can be louder in numerous ways, one of them is by silencing the other neurons around it or sending a more distinct signal using inhibition. The first type of inhibition is temporal inhibition, a neuron can inhibit itself to create a sharp, precise end to its own signal, like a musician using silence for dramatic effect. Through spatial inhibition (or lateral inhibition), a neuron silences its immediate neighbors, effectively shouting, “Pay attention to me, not them!” This is not an abstract concept; you can see it in the Hermann grid illusion, where your brain creates illusory dark dots at the intersections because the neurons there are being heavily inhibited. This process of active ignoring is what allows our brain to separate signal from noise, to detect edges, and to construct a coherent reality out of a chaotic flood of sensory information.

6---full-notes/the-empirical-stalemate-i.title: The Empirical Stalemate in Central Cognition
6---full-notes/the-empirical-stalemate-i.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Massive Modularity Hypothesis Evolutionary Psychology Cognitive Psychology
The Empirical Stalemate in Central Cognition
Details
While the theoretical distinction between the Massive Modularity Hypothesis (MMH) and the Library Model of Cognition (LMC) can be debated, the more pressing issue is whether empirical evidence can distinguish between them. Currently, for central cognitive processes like reasoning and belief-fixation, the evidence is ambiguous, leading to an empirical stalemate [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].
There is substantial evidence for modularity in peripheral systems, such as vision and language processing. This evidence, often from neuropsychological studies of selective impairment, is well-established [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf]. However, since the LMC does not deny the existence of these modular “input systems,” this data does not help differentiate it from MMH. The core of the disagreement lies in the architecture of central cognition.
The primary difficulty is that for any piece of evidence supporting a central module, a plausible counter-explanation can be constructed from the LMC framework. This is because both models predict innate, domain-specific structures. One model calls this structure a “module” (a mechanism), while the other calls it a “body of knowledge” (a representational system). Without a clear method for empirically distinguishing an innate specialized process from a general process operating on innate specialized data, the debate cannot be resolved by current experimental paradigms [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf]. This challenge is exemplified by the case of the “Theory of Mind” module.

6---full-notes/the-epicurean-form-of-ego.title: The Epicurean Form of Egoistic Suicide
6---full-notes/the-epicurean-form-of-ego.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology philosophy
The Epicurean Form of Egoistic Suicide
Details
Beyond the melancholic intellectual, Durkheim describes a more commonplace form of egoistic suicide, which he terms “Epicurean.” In this state, the individual does not reflect sadly upon their condition but instead accepts their egoism and its logical consequences cheerfully. They assign themselves the single, simple task of satisfying personal needs, living for sensual pleasure with a full and knowing awareness of their limited purpose. This philosophy, however, provides only a very slight link to life. The individual is always prepared to leave existence at the slightest stimulus, should the possibility of their easy, pleasurable life be threatened. The dreamy melancholy of the intellectual form is replaced by a sceptical, disillusioned matter-of-factness. The final act is passionless, performed with an “ironic tranquillity” and a matter-of-course mood, with the primary goal being simply to minimize pain. This, too, is a direct result of a lack of a higher social purpose, but it manifests as a pursuit of fleeting pleasure rather than an absorption in inner emptiness.

6---full-notes/the-epidemiology-of-smoki.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology statistics
The Epidemiology of Smoking
Details
Data from the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH) reveal the staggering toll of tobacco on public health. In the United States alone, tobacco is linked to approximately 430,000 deaths annually—roughly 20% of all mortality. Notably, 35,000 of these deaths are attributed to secondhand smoke, a toxicity level that surprised researchers and catalyzed litigation (such as the flight attendants’ lawsuit) to ban smoking in public spaces.
While overall prevalence has shifted, the data highlights a profound “education gap.” Educational attainment is arguably the strongest predictor of smoking status. Individuals who did not finish high school have a smoking prevalence of 35%, whereas college graduates have a rate of only 14%. This disparity has widened since 1965, suggesting that health education and socioeconomic factors play a critical role in cessation and prevention. Furthermore, the highest prevalence of use occurs in the 18–29 age bracket (peaking at ~41%), a critical developmental window where lifelong habits are often cemented.

The Euthanasia of Pure Reason
Details
Kant’s “discipline of reason” requires human reason to become its own pupil, identifying exactly where it unlawfully oversteps the boundaries of possible experience. Kant then divides transcendental logic into the Analytic and the Dialectic. Human reason naturally craves the absolute, leading to inevitable, structurally embedded illusions. The primary mechanism of this self-deception in rational psychology is the Paralogism. A paralogism is a formally fallacious syllogism that is transcendentally grounded in our cognitive apparatus.
Historically, rationalists like Descartes and Leibniz attempted to use pure reason to prove that the noumenal “Soul” is a simple, enduring, and indestructible substance. Kant doesn’t believe this as true, rather he believes that they are confusing what is required for one to have rational thoughts with the empirical discovery of something. Because pure concepts are completely empty without sensory intuition, trying to know the noumenal self is akin to operating a clinical diagnostic framework without any actual patient data

The Executive Control Circuit (DLPFC) in Depression
Details
The Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (DLPFC) is a key part of the brain’s executive control system. It functions like the brain’s “brakes,” responsible for cognitive flexibility, problem-solving, and, most importantly, suppressing unwanted thoughts and regulating emotional responses.
A critical feature of major depression is that the DLPFC becomes underactive. It loses its strength and can even atrophy with chronic depression.
This weakening of the DLPFC is what allows rumination to run rampant. The overactive Default Mode Network (DMN) generates endless negative thoughts, and the underactive DLPFC fails in its job to inhibit them. It cannot apply the brakes to the runaway train of negativity. This failure of top-down control is a core reason why individuals with depression feel powerless to stop their own painful thought processes.

The Fallacy of Categorical Thinking
Details
In our lives, to simplify thoughts and processes, we usually divide them into categories so that we can easier deal with them. This is a natural impulse, and like most natural impulses, it has quite some detrimental effects:


It makes us underestimate the difference between two facts that fall into the same category. For example, let’s say, the alphabet are all just letters right ? And if you switch a letter to another, most of the time it would not have a big effect. Right… so now if I tell you to fuckle up, what do you think I really mean ? Buckle up.


On the opposite side of the spectrum, it makes us overestimate as well. For example, the number 80 and 82.5, normally that’s not a very big difference right ? Only about 2.5 numbers, and yet, when we take it into context like rounding up to a test score. Suddenly the 80 stays an 80 and the 82.5 gets rounded to an 83 or 85 (depending on the teacher).


Lastly is the ignorance of us thinking about boundaries. Let’s say memorization of numbers as an example, if I told you a set of numbers resembling a phone number, you would catch it right ? Now I switch the tone and speed at which I say the number, and you get quite disorientated. Why ? Because you were expecting me to categorically say each pairs or group of numbers, not randomly spitting the numbers out.

6---full-notes/the-fallacy-of-psychologi.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy psychology
The Fallacy of Psychological Egoism
Details
Psychological Egoism is quite a popular philosophy in the space for certain groups of people, even if it isn’t considered an exactly “strong philosophy.” Basically, it states that people, human beings, are completely and utterly selfish, they only act in their self-interest, whatever can lead to their pleasures. This view is often supported by a seductive “a priori” argument: “When I act, I act to satisfy my desire. Satisfying my desire brings me pleasure. Therefore, I act to get pleasure.”
But this actually exposes certain flaws about the philosophy. For example, if a father buys life insurance to protect his children after his death, his desire is that “my children are provided for.” This desire is semantically satisfied if the children are actually provided for, even though the father will be dead and feel no psychological pleasure at that moment. To claim the father only pays the premium to avoid the “unease” of worry is circular; he would only feel unease if he already cared about his children’s future welfare independently of his own state. Thus, the argument that all actions are selfish is based on a linguistic trick, not psychological reality.
Furthermore, even as those who believe in this philosophy argues from an evolutionary perspective, it still falls apart. The gene itself that propagates us can be selfish while we can be altruistic. Not only that, the best way for a gene that wants to be passed on further is if it just jumped to empathy and love and care rather than a series of calculations running in our head to think about if we are “logically” deducting that we should do this. It would be an absurd view of psychology if we did !

6---full-notes/the-fallacy-of-substance-.content:

The Fallacy of Substance Dualism
Details
When faced with the difficulty of explaining consciousness in a physical world, a common reaction is to propose Substance Dualism: the idea that there is a physical world of atoms and a separate “mental world” made of “soul stuff” or “ectoplasm.”
Campbell argues this is a philosophical dead end. He uses the analogy of Martians investigating a television. If Martians understood the electronics but couldn’t explain the picture, postulating a magical “TV Stuff” that generates images doesn’t solve the problem; it just names the mystery.


It doesn’t explain how the “stuff” works.


It doesn’t explain how the “stuff” interacts with the physical parts.


Postulating a soul or “golden dust” (a la The Amber Spyglass) merely pushes the problem back one step. We are still left with the question: How does this substance sustain a mind? Therefore, we must solve the problem within the context of the brain and the physical world, not by fleeing from it.

6---full-notes/the-false-consensus.title: The False Consensus
6---full-notes/the-false-consensus.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Social Psychology
The False Consensus
Details
The False Consensus Effect describes the tendency for people to overestimate the extent to which others share their beliefs and preferences. In a study by Tom Gilovich, participants were asked whether they preferred music from the 1960s or the 1980s and then asked to estimate what percentage of their peers would share that preference. The results showed a clear projection bias: those who preferred 1960s music believed the majority of others would too, while those who preferred 1980s music believed the 80s were the popular choice. Essentially, individuals treated their own subjective preferences as a reflection of objective reality or the “reasonable person” standard, assuming that any rational person would naturally agree with them.
Gilovich’s research went a step further to identify why this happens, tracing it back to subjective construal. When asked to list specific bands they associated with each decade, the participants revealed that they were defining the categories differently. A 1960s fan might be comparing the Beatles (a high-quality 60s representation) to Mötley Crüe (a lower-quality 80s representation), whereas an 80s fan might compare the Police to a lesser 60s band. The disagreement wasn’t necessarily about the inherent quality of the decades, but rather that the two groups were mentally constructing different realities for the same terms. When a new group of subjects was shown the specific list of bands generated by a peer, the disagreement largely vanished; once the subjective construal was fixed and shared, people generally agreed on which music was better. This suggests that many social disagreements are actually failures to realize that we are talking about different things while using the same words.

The Forebrain
Details
The human being has a forebrain that covers all of our midbrain and half of our hindbrain. The part that is on the surface and all wrinkled as we see in models and such is called the mammalian cortex, and it is extremely important.
Like all the other parts, the forebrain is bilaterally symmetrical. It is obvious on the surface of it as it shows a deep front-to-back cleavage called the longitudinal fissure. On either side of this fissure, and underneath the cortex, there is the rest of the forebrain, including numerous subcortical structures. There are four that should be mentioned here:


The thalamus, buried deep inside the forebrain and shaped like a fist atop the midbrain. It contains a number of centers that act as relay stations for nearly all the sensory information going into the cortex.


Secondly, the hypothalamus, which is just beneath it, it is intimately involved in controlling behaviors like feeding, drinking, body temperature, sexual activities.


Astride the thalamus in each hemisphere is the basal ganglia. It is crucial in regulating muscular contractions during movement. There are many disorders that come from these cells dying and just not being sufficient like Parkinson’s and Huntington’s.


The last party that covers literally everything and lies beneath the cortex is the limbic system, which contains the amygdala and hippocampus, it has close ties to many of the parts of the brain. It is primarily involved in emotional and motivational activities, some aspects of learning and memory.

The Formality Problem
Details
A persistent objection to liberal political theory is that the basic liberties, even formally equal, are substantively unequal in practice. Even if citizens appear to be equal under the two principles of justice mentioned, because of background social and economic inequality, the wealthy can dominate legislation and social policy, thus rendering them as merely formal for everyone else.
Rawls’s response is to distinguish between the worth and extent of a basic liberty. The extent may be the same for everyone but the worth differs depending on the person it is affecting, which is a problem reserved for the The Difference Principle.
The solution introduced is the fair value of political liberties — the idea that whatever one’s economic or social position, everyone must have a sufficiently equal opportunity to hold political office and influence political outcomes. This parallels fair equality of opportunity in the second principle but applies specifically to the political domain.

6---full-notes/the-foundation-of-nature-.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Cognitive Psychology genetics
The Foundation of Nature and Nurture Genotype, Phenotype
Details
The age-old question of whether we are born as a “blank slate” or are predetermined by our biology is now understood to be a false dichotomy. To grasp why, we must first distinguish between genotype and phenotype. Our genotype is the specific set of genes encoded in our DNA, the underlying blueprint for a particular trait. The phenotype, however, is the actual physical expression or observable characteristic of that trait—our morphology, our development, and our behavior. The journey from the genetic blueprint to the final, observable person is where the simple idea of “nature versus nurture” breaks down.
Modern cognitive psychology has moved beyond this confrontational framing. It is now clear that who we are is not a battle between two opposing forces, but rather the result of a complex and continuous interaction between our genetic inheritance (nature) and our environmental experiences (nurture). Every characteristic, from our behavior to our susceptibility to illness, is an expression of both components to varying degrees. Anything with a genetic influence is considered heritable, while the remainder is attributed to the environment. This foundational understanding reframes the debate, asking not which one is more important, but how they work together to shape the individual.

Which means that anxiety appears in the second phase, as the person identify if the threat is too much or not.

6---full-notes/the-functionalist-view-of.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
The Functionalist View of society
Details
As mentioned in The People Needed for Society to Work, there exists a sociologist view that attempts to explain how society includes concepts, how it functions as an organism and how these concepts all contribute to the organism in some way, shape, or form.
The size of the reward for any given position is determined by two factors: its functional importance (how crucial it is to society) and the scarcity of personnel (how rare the talent and training for it are). A physician, for example, is highly rewarded because the role is vital and requires years of difficult training. These high rewards motivate capable individuals to make the necessary sacrifices.
However, this theory has significant flaws. First, it assumes rewards are based on value to society, but the market often rewards skills that serve the wealthy (like designing luxury watches) far more than those essential for public good (like ensuring water safety). This suggests rewards reflect market power, not just societal function.
Second, the theory wrongly assumes societies maximize competition. In reality, institutions like professional associations (e.g., for doctors or lawyers) and national borders actively limit competition to protect the privileges of insiders.
Finally, the model ignores how existing inequality in class and race creates unequal opportunities, preventing many talented individuals from ever competing for top positions. Despite these flaws, the theory’s vision of a merit-based system remains a powerful and intuitive model for understanding our own experiences of striving for success.

The Functions of QuAIC
Details
It is crucial to understand the QuAIC’s designated role within the broader threat management process. The authors are explicit that the tool “is not a validated formal risk assessment tool and should not be used to replace existing threat assessment protocols”. Its purpose is to function as a “decision-making aid” or “screening tool”. It is designed to achieve two primary goals at the earliest stage of a report: to help victims and witnesses decide when their concerns warrant a formal report, and to help institutional responders “prioritize cases and determine appropriate interventions and allocation of resources”.  
The tool’s output is not a definitive risk judgment but a categorized level of concern: Low, Moderate, High, or Highest/Critical. Each level is linked to a set of corresponding recommendations for both the target of the behavior and the first responder, outlining suggested actions and response timeframes. This action-oriented output transforms the tool from a passive measurement device into an active guide for immediate decision-making.

As Table 1 illustrates, the QuAIC provides a clear, escalating framework for action. It gives targets concrete, tiered guidance on how to proceed, and it provides responders with a standardized protocol for prioritizing their caseload and initiating an appropriate level of intervention. This structure is fundamental to its utility as a triage instrument.

6---full-notes/the-generalization-of-the.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology academia
The Generalization of the Modern Research University
Details
The holistic vision of the early Chicago school proved unsustainable. The pressures of professionalization and specialization—forces inherent in the research university’s DNA—quickly eroded the integrated ideal. Within two decades, the university that sought to bring coherence to society began to merely mirror its fragmentation. It became, in the author’s evocative phrase, a “multiversity cafeteria” or “Harper’s bazaar.” The institution ceased to be a community bound by a shared vision, devolving instead into a collection of individuals pursuing their own ends, held together only by the thin threads of bureaucratic administration. Instead of interpreting the world, it simply reflected its chaos.
The modern university is pulled in two opposing directions. On one hand, it is seen as the primary vehicle for socioeconomic advancement—the most tangible version of “the American dream.” It promises to equip individuals with the technical and professional skills needed to succeed in a complex industrial or postindustrial economy. On the other hand, this focus on individual success leaves unanswered the older, more fundamental questions about character, citizenship, and the moral fabric of society. By prioritizing education as a means to an occupational end, the university implicitly sidelines its role in fostering a shared moral or civic vision, contributing to the very fragmentation it once sought to mend.

Status: teen
Tags: economics
The Grounds of Microeconomics
Details
So, what is microeconomics ? As the name suggests, the science focuses on how individuals and firms try to make themselves as well off as possible under scarcity (meaning the current state already). People do not simply just choose how things are but rather that these choices happen inside constraints and conditions. Scarcity means that resources, time, attention, money, land, labor, and productive capacity are limited, so an action always displaces some other possible action. This is called opportunity cost: the cost of doing something in turn of the next best alternative that must be given up.
And so microeconomics can be described as constrained optimization. Economic agents face trade-offs, compare alternatives, and try to choose the best available option given the rules. The “dismal” side of economics is that it constantly points out that nothing is truly free, because any use of scarce resources rules out another use. The “fun” side, at least from an MIT-style perspective, is that this makes economic behavior analyzable with the same spirit as engineering: given constraints, what is the best solution? The economic way of thinking does not require assuming that choices are morally good, emotionally wise, or socially fair. It begins by asking what options exist, what constraints bind, what is sacrificed, and what decision follows from those sacrifices.

Toddlers (ages 1-2) are actually the most physically aggressive age group, frequently hitting to assert “mine.” Therefore, aggression only becomes a disorder when it harms others and represents a breakdown of internal mechanisms.

Within aggression, there is a crucial distinction between “Reactive Aggression” (explosive, retaliatory, often linked to ADHD and hostile attribution bias) and “Proactive Aggression” (calculated, instrumental bullying). While reactive aggressors are often rejected by peers, proactive bullies can be “controversial”—feared but respected for their social dominance.

6---full-notes/the-hindbrain.title: The Hindbrain
6---full-notes/the-hindbrain.content:
Status: adult
Tags: neuroscience psychology
The Hindbrain
Details
The hindbrain is the visible part of the brain that is at the back of it, connecting to the spine. At the bottom of it, there’s the medulla, which lies above the spinal cord. It is crucial in controlling many basic biological functions like the cardiovascular and respiratory systems, determining the functions of it. Moreover, it also incorporates functions like swallowing, coughing and sneezing. It also helps us to maintain balance and orientation of ourself.
Above it is pons. This part consists of special regions that will integrate movements of, and sensations from, the facial muscles, tongues, eyes, and ears. Other regions of it may also control the level of attention and initiate sleep and dreams.
The cerebellum, a large, cauliflower-like part of the hindbrain, acts as a specialized computer for the body. It processes information from balance sensors and your muscles and joints to coordinate movement. Different parts of the cerebellum have specific jobs:


One part controls overall bodily balance. Damage to this area results in a wide, staggering walk, which is why police check for this in suspected drunk drivers.


Another part manages the timing and precision of skilled movements, like a tennis swing or playing the piano. Damage here can cause tremors and an inability to perform rapid, alternating motions.


Studies on cats with their hindbrain surgically separated from the rest of the brain show that the hindbrain alone can produce basic movements for standing or walking. However, the animal cannot coordinate these movements to perform a complete action and will collapse without support.
In short, an animal with only its hindbrain “can move, but it cannot act.”

6---full-notes/the-hippocampus-in-depres.content:
Status: teen

The Hippocampus in Depression
Details
The hippocampus is a brain region primarily associated with learning and memory. It also plays a vital role in regulating the body’s stress response; specifically, it is one of the main structures that helps to turn off the release of stress hormones like cortisol.
Under the chronic stress of major depression, the hippocampus is known to be vulnerable. The constant exposure to high levels of glucocorticoids can cause neurons in the hippocampus to shrink and can inhibit the birth of new neurons, leading to a measurable atrophy or volume loss in the region. This damage likely contributes to the memory problems often seen in depression and further impairs the brain’s ability to shut down the stress response.
However, Sapolsky notes in his updated lecture that while this link is important, he now considers the hippocampus less central to the core symptoms of depression (anhedonia and rumination) compared to the dysregulation in the prefrontal cortex and mesolimbic circuits.

6---full-notes/the-history-of-psychophys.title: The History of Psychophysiological Disorders
6---full-notes/the-history-of-psychophys.content:
Status: adult
Tags: history psychology physiology
The History of Psychophysiological Disorders
Details
The 20th-century understanding of physical disorders with a psychological overlay has evolved dramatically, moving from personality-based psychoanalytic theories to a more integrated, evidence-based framework. This progression reflects a deepening comprehension of the intricate pathways connecting our psychological states to our physiological health.
The formal study of psychosomatic medicine gained traction in the 1930s-1940s, led by figures like Franz Alexander and Flanders Dunbar. Alexander’s “specificity hypothesis” proposed that specific unconscious conflicts led to specific diseases (e.g., repressed anger causing hypertension). Dunbar, in contrast, focused on “personality profiles,” suggesting certain temperaments were prone to specific ailments, a precursor to the “Type A” personality concept for heart disease. While groundbreaking for their time, these theories were criticized for their lack of empirical rigor and for creating an overly linear, almost blame-oriented, model of illness.
A pivotal paradigm shift occurred in 1977 with George L. Engel’s biopsychosocial model. This model revolutionized medicine by rejecting simple mind-body dualism and instead proposing that health and illness are the products of a dynamic interplay between biological (genes, physiology), psychological (thoughts, emotions, stress), and social (culture, relationships, economics) factors. This holistic framework became the dominant paradigm, acknowledging the complex, multifactorial nature of health.
The current era is defined by psychoneuroimmunology (PNI), the scientific field that maps the precise biological links between the psyche, the nervous system, and the immune system. PNI provides the mechanistic proof for the biopsychosocial model, demonstrating how psychological stress, via hormones like cortisol, can directly suppress immune function, thereby increasing vulnerability to illness. This evolution from broad psychoanalytic concepts to the molecular evidence of PNI marks a profound maturation in our understanding, leading to more effective, integrated treatments that address the whole person.

6---full-notes/the-human-as-a-machine.title: The Human as a Machine
6---full-notes/the-human-as-a-machine.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy psychology biology
The Human as a Machine
Details
Our understanding of the mind has never existed in a vacuum. Since early modern philosophy, attempts to explain consciousness and thought have consistently drawn upon the most advanced technology of the era as a guiding metaphor. These technological models provide a tangible framework for conceptualizing the brain’s intangible processes, and their evolution reflects our own changing scientific and cultural context.
This tradition began with thinkers like René Descartes in the 17th century. Living in an age of intricate clockwork automata and hydraulic systems, he envisioned the body as a complex machine. He proposed that “animal spirits” (cerebrospinal fluid) flowed through nerves to inflate muscles, creating movement much like water flowing through the pipes of a royal fountain. This mechanistic view, while rudimentary, established the powerful precedent of using contemporary technology to model the mind.
As technology progressed, so did the metaphors. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the advent of the telephone exchange led to the brain being conceptualized as a vast and complex switchboard, connecting sensory inputs to behavioral outputs. The mid-20th century’s cognitive revolution was inextricably linked to the invention of the digital computer. Psychologists adopted the information-processing model, describing the mind in terms of hardware (the brain) and software (mental processes), complete with memory storage (RAM and hard drives) and central processing units.
Most recently, the rise of the internet and artificial intelligence has prompted another shift, this time towards connectionist or “neural network” models. This view sees the mind less like a single computer and more like a massively parallel, distributed network. Cognition is an emergent property of simple, interconnected nodes firing together, much like the vast, decentralized structure of the internet. Each of these models, from hydraulic machine to neural net, reveals as much about the era that created it as it does about the timeless mystery of the mind itself.

6---full-notes/the-humanistic-perspectiv.title: The Humanistic Perspective
6---full-notes/the-humanistic-perspectiv.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
The Humanistic Perspective
Details
The Humanistic approach to personality, championed by theorists like Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow, offered a more optimistic alternative to the deterministic views of Freud. This perspective emphasizes conscious experience, free will, and the innate human potential for growth.
Carl Rogers and the Self Rogers believed that the core motive of personality is the drive toward self-actualization—the fulfillment of one’s unique potential. He proposed that our personality is structured around our concept of “self”:


The Actual Self: Our perception of who we are right now.


The Ideal Self: The person we aspire to become.


According to Rogers, psychological health and growth occur when we work to close the gap between our actual and ideal selves. When these two concepts align, we achieve a state of congruence and move closer to self-actualization.
Abraham Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs Maslow expanded on this idea by proposing that our ability to pursue self-actualization depends on the fulfillment of more fundamental needs. He organized these needs into a hierarchy:


Physiological Needs: Food, water, air, basic survival.


Safety Needs: Security, stability, a roof over one’s head.


Love and Belonging Needs: Intimacy, friendship, a sense of connection.


Esteem Needs: Self-respect, achievement, recognition from others.


Self-Actualization: Reaching one’s full potential, creativity, morality.


Maslow argued that if our lower-level needs are unmet, our personality and behavior will be dominated by the struggle to satisfy them. Only when these foundational needs are secure can we fully dedicate ourselves to the higher-level pursuit of self-actualization.

6---full-notes/the-importance-of-childre.title: The Importance of Children Language
6---full-notes/the-importance-of-childre.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning neuroplasticity neuroscience
The Importance of Children Language
Details
The development of literacy represents a transformative moment in human cognitive evolution, marking a distinct shift from purely oral communication to sophisticated symbolic interaction. Bruce McCandliss highlights that the human brain’s ability to decode written symbols is not innate but rather a relatively recent neurological adaptation that has occurred within approximately the last 8,000 years. This adaptation underscores the brain’s remarkable plasticity, demonstrating its capacity to reorganize neural pathways to process visual symbols and translate them into meaningful linguistic concepts.
One critical aspect of McCandliss’s research emphasizes the importance of phonological skills—the ability to identify and manipulate the sound structures within words—as central to successful literacy acquisition. The significance of phonological skills lies in their role as a foundational cognitive mechanism that enables readers to bridge visual inputs and linguistic comprehension effectively. Variations in these skills among learners explain much of the individual differences observed in reading proficiency, suggesting targeted educational strategies that emphasize phonological processing may substantially improve literacy outcomes.
Moreover, selective attention emerges as a pivotal cognitive function in McCandliss’s examination of learning. The act of intentionally directing one’s cognitive resources towards specific sensory information profoundly enhances brain activity within relevant neural circuits. For instance, deliberately focusing on phonological aspects of language stimulates increased neural activation in regions associated with language processing. This phenomenon illustrates the powerful role educators play in guiding students’ attention, thereby actively shaping neural development through strategic instructional approaches.
Educational neuroscience, the interdisciplinary field arising from these insights, represents a significant collaboration between cognitive neuroscience and educational practice. This field leverages neuroscientific discoveries to refine educational methods and interventions, directly addressing practical classroom challenges. McCandliss’s own experiments vividly demonstrate how structured phonological interventions, informed by neuroscience, lead to substantial improvements in students’ reading abilities, showcasing a tangible application of neuroscience in real-world educational contexts.
In conclusion, Bruce McCandliss’s research underscores the essential interplay between neural plasticity, phonological skills, and selective attention in literacy development. It further illuminates the potent collaborative potential between neuroscience and education, paving the way for innovative, empirically informed teaching practices that enhance human learning.

6---full-notes/the-inability-to-prove-a-.title: The Inability to Prove a Universal Question
6---full-notes/the-inability-to-prove-a-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
The Inability to Prove a Universal Question
Details
A core idea in the functionalist argument is about “Why is there inequality?” Due to the nature of scientific experiments, we need variation, but in our world, we cannot just find a society that does not have inequality, as it is practically impossible. That does not mean that we give up on the idea entirely, rather we ask a question that is more practical, and actually can be verified.
For example, the incest taboo, one cannot get a firm explanation on why this taboo exists because there are so many reasons that can be said, maybe because it is a genetical nightmare from the view of someone who is educated, or that is refrains a family from expanding their grasp on the overall community and power from society because they are only allowed to care for the people in their family.
To change this, we must turn the universal idea into a variable one. We do not try to force or find a society where taboo does not exist, we find the varieties of it, like how many bloodlines, or how far bloodlines should be for them to marry each other, is it completely forbidden to the sense that people in a family should literally not interact with each other (African societies).
This variation allows us to ask testable questions. We can now investigate why the scope of the taboo changes. Do societies with complex property inheritance rules have broader incest prohibitions to manage alliances? Does the taboo shrink as societies become more anonymous and less reliant on kinship? By focusing on the variation, we can test theories against evidence.
This same logic applies to inequality. Asking “Why is there inequality?” is a dead end. Instead, we should ask, “Under what conditions do societies become more or less unequal?” This reframing allows for real comparison and testing, moving beyond untestable stories and toward genuine social science.

6---full-notes/the-integrated-approach-t.content:
Status: teen
Tags: behavioral biology biology
The Integrated Approach to Behavioral Biology
Details
To avoid the fallacies of categorical thinking, behavior must be analyzed as a seamless process through time. The proposed method is to start with a behavior and work backward in nested layers of explanation:


A few seconds before: What neural activity caused the behavior?


Seconds to minutes before: What environmental stimuli triggered that neural activity?


Hours to days before: What hormonal states changed the sensitivity to those stimuli?


Weeks to months before: How has experience and environment reshaped the brain’s structure (neuroplasticity)?


From conception onward: How did genetics and fetal life shape the brain and body?


Centuries to millennia before: How did culture and ecology shape the pressures on the population?


Millions of years before: What evolutionary pressures shaped the genes?


In this model, there are no separate “buckets.” Each level is simply the most convenient way of describing the sum total of all the influences that came before it. A “hormone” is the physical manifestation of a “gene” being expressed, which itself is a product of “evolution.”

The Inverted Spectrum Thought Experiment
Details
One day you wake up and realize that everything is of a different color from previously before you were asleep, but even weirder than that, everyone else’s sense of color seemed to remain the same. So how would you respond to this ? Continue responding and talking to the others as if nothing changed so that you get used to calling everything by their “perceived” color ? Then would you “forget” what the color is from your perspective ?
The question is, do YOU still see the same qualia, the same difference from others ? Philosophers argue that if this is true, then Functionalism is false, because different processes has yielded different results (they should have been the same).
Supporting Content


This does not matter though, as the function is the same, identifying color, regardless of the result (counter-argument from Functionalism ?). Our mental states could be the same even if we get different experience. But nonetheless, the point is the same, the experience/qualitative aspect is missed in Functionalism.


Relative vs. Absolute: We can compare relative states (e.g., “I see this as larger than that”), but absolute comparisons between minds might be meaningless. It is like saying “My desire for a cookie is absolutely stronger than your desire for world peace.” We can only rank preferences relative to each other, not on an absolute scale between people.


Asymmetry: Colors have emotional associations (red is “hot” or “angry”). If you swapped red and blue qualia, you would likely feel “cold” when looking at fire, which would change your functional role (behavior). A perfect inversion that preserves all function might be impossible because color space is not perfectly symmetrical.
