The James-Lange Theory
Details
James Lange found out that we did not feel emotion due to the situation, but rather our body’s own response to it. He found out that our body acts faster than we feel emotions, the brain sends a non-conscious physiological response to our body for it to do an action, then our limbic system catches up and starts inciting the emotions that would be correlated with the situation.
At first, this theory was discredited due to the thought of such a theory being so inefficient feels wrong. An experiment that proved this was the Stanley Schachter’s classic experiment showed that subjects injected with epinephrine (adrenaline) did not feel a specific emotion, but rather amplified whatever emotion was being socially modeled for them, be it anger or joy. The epinephrine created a state of physiological arousal, and the brain latched onto the most available social cue to label that arousal.

6---full-notes/the-landscape-of-the-germ.title: The Landscape of the German Philosophy in the 19th Century
6---full-notes/the-landscape-of-the-germ.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy history
The Landscape of the German Philosophy in the 19th Century
Details
German Idealism, particularly in its Hegelian form, was intimately tied to a progressive view of history. It posited that history was rational and that the ideals of the French Revolution—specifically constitutional monarchy and liberal reform—would inevitably realize themselves in Central Europe, which means it was trying to stabilize and keep the status of Europe or the world as it is. However, this philosophical optimism faced a catastrophic reality check with the failure of revolutions of 1848-1849. And so because of this, Idealism lost its philosophical reputation, but not only that, it dragged the reputation of philosophy down to the dumps as well, being viewed as a failed enterprise that could not deliver on its promises of social reconstruction.
Nietzsche lived and wrote during the “interregnum” period, between the collapse of Hegelian Idealism and the rise of Neo-Kantianism. During this period, there was no unified framework of philosophy in Germany, it was a pariah discipline, mocked by established scholars to be magic rather than science. The intellectual landscape was instead populated by history of philosophy (scholarship rather than original thought), reductive materialism (e.g., Lange), and the belated discovery of Arthur Schopenhauer. Nietzsche is thus a product of a fragmented era, an autodidact who did not have to engage with a dominant academic orthodoxy because none existed at the time.
Unlike other great philosophers, Nietzsche had no formal academic training in philosophy. He was a classical philologist-an expert in the history of Greek and Latin languages and literature. He only knew Kant through the distorted lens of Schopenhauer, and of course pre-Socratics. Nietzsche method was strictly philological, taking ancient texts, or corrupt versions of them and using genealogical techniques to trace the errors back to the original source. And this was also his way of contributing to philosophy, by introducing the truth-finding factor into it, as people have to consider the cultural and societal context of the time and how certain versions of the text might have been altered from the original.

6---full-notes/the-library-model-of-cogn.title: The Library Model of Cognition is Compatible with Evolutionary Psychology's Core Commitments
6---full-notes/the-library-model-of-cogn.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Massive Modularity Hypothesis Evolutionary Psychology Cognitive Psychology
The Library Model of Cognition is Compatible with Evolutionary Psychology’s Core Commitments
Details
Given the failure of arguments for the Massive Modularity Hypothesis (MMH) to rule out the Library Model of Cognition (LMC), and the empirical stalemate between them, the strong adherence to MMH within evolutionary psychology seems unmotivated. This is especially true because LMC is perfectly consistent with the central theoretical and methodological commitments of the evolutionary psychology research program [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].


Conceptual Integration: Evolutionary psychology requires that psychological theories be consistent with the natural sciences, especially evolutionary biology. LMC, which posits innate, evolved structures, does not conflict with any established biological principles and thus meets this standard [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].


Universal Human Nature: A central tenet of evolutionary psychology is that there is a universal, species-typical cognitive architecture. LMC is compatible with this claim; the “library” of innate, domain-specific knowledge can be posited as a universal feature of the human mind [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].


Psychological Structures as Adaptations: Evolutionary psychology views our mental architecture as a collection of adaptations built by natural selection. Where MMH identifies modules as these adaptations, LMC simply identifies the innate bodies of information as the adaptations. Both are evolved solutions to recurrent ancestral problems [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].


The Utility of Evolutionary Analysis: A core methodological claim is that analyzing ancestral adaptive problems can help generate hypotheses about cognitive specializations. This method is equally useful for generating hypotheses about innate bodies of information (for LMC) as it is for innate computational mechanisms (for MMH). For example, analyzing the problem of social exchange could lead one to hypothesize an innate “social contract” body of knowledge just as easily as a “social contract” module [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].


Since LMC can accommodate all the foundational principles of evolutionary psychology, the field’s insistence on MMH specifically is not a logical necessity of adopting an evolutionary approach to the mind.

6---full-notes/the-limitations-of-bioche.title: The Limitations of Biochemical Treatments for Depression
6---full-notes/the-limitations-of-bioche.content:
Status: adult
Tags: pharmacology psychology
Drugs in Therapy
Details
While depression is a biological disease, the available biochemical treatments, though powerful, are significantly limited in their efficacy and reach. This highlights the vast gap that still exists in successfully managing the illness on a global scale.
The primary treatments and their limitations include:


Pharmacology (Antidepressants):


Standard Drugs (SSRIs, etc.): These medications, which target monoamine systems (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine), are miraculous when they work. However, Sapolsky emphasizes their shortcomings: roughly one-third of patients are treatment-resistant and do not respond to any conventional medication. Of those who do respond, about half must stop due to intolerable side effects.


Newer Drugs (e.g., Ketamine): While revolutionary for their rapid action on the glutamate system, these are still new and not a universal solution.




Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT):


For severe, treatment-resistant, and often hospitalized cases, ECT can be highly effective, metaphorically “breaking the back” of the depression.


However, it remains a last resort due to its history of misuse and the fact that its precise mechanism is still not fully understood.




Brain Stimulation (TMS, DBS):


Techniques like Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) and Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) are exciting, cutting-edge approaches.


They are still in relatively early stages of use and require much more research to become widespread, reliable treatments.




The most significant limitation, however, is diagnostic. Sapolsky states that an estimated 80% of major depression cases are never diagnosed. When combining this with treatment resistance and side effects, it becomes clear that only a small fraction of the people suffering from this disease are ever successfully treated with biochemical interventions. This underscores the desperate need for more effective treatments and, just as importantly, better systems for diagnosis and care.

6---full-notes/the-limitations-of-the-fr.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
The Limitations of the Free Will Defense
Details
Basically, this defense asserts that God allows evil because human freedom is more important than that of the costs of sin. However, this defense is logically contingent upon a libertarian (incompatibilist) view of free will. If compatibilism is true—as many philosophers and neuroscientists argue—then a free action is simply one that flows from the agent’s desires, even if those desires are determined. A compatibilist God could therefore create agents who are determined to always freely choose the good. The refusal to do so implies that God is either not omnipotent or not benevolent. Furthermore, the Free Will Defense fails to account for natural evil (suffering caused by disease, tectonic shifts, or predation) that existed for millions of years prior to human agency. To bridge this gap, theists must postulate “fallen angels” affecting physics, a violation of parsimony that complicates the God hypothesis significantly.

6---full-notes/the-limits-of-feature-det.title: The Limits of Feature Detectors
6---full-notes/the-limits-of-feature-det.content:
Status: baby
Tags: neuroscience psychology
The Limits of Feature Detectors
Details
While feature detectors are fundamental to vision, they cannot fully explain perception on their own. They represent a bottom-up process, where simple elements are combined to form a larger perception. However, this model fails to account for how context and expectation influence what we see.
For instance, an ambiguous symbol can be perceived as the letter ‘H’ in the word ‘THE’ and as the letter ‘A’ in the word ‘CAT’, even though the visual stimulus and the feature detectors being activated are identical. Similarly, reversible figures, which can be perceived in more than one way, show that perception is not a fixed output based on a given input. This indicates that a top-down process, where experience and expectations are applied to interpret sensory information, is also essential for perception.

6---full-notes/the-limits-of-quaic.title: The Limits of QuAIC
6---full-notes/the-limits-of-quaic.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology university
The Limits of QuAIC
Details
The study concludes that the “QuAIC provided a useful standardized framework to screen reported concerns” and recommends it as a “quick and simple tool to guide case prioritization and intervention,” particularly during the peak reporting periods that align with key semester activities. Its primary value lies in its ability to bring consistency and structure to the often-chaotic front end of the reporting process.  
However, the analysis also reveals a critical and nuanced limitation. Despite the tool’s innovative design, which intentionally balances aggression and intrusion, the study found that the assessed level of concern “was more strongly related to overtly aggressive behavior than to intrusion”. This suggests a form of systemic inertia. While the tool itself has evolved to formally recognize the significant harm caused by intrusive behaviors like stalking and harassment, the human and policy systems using the tool may still be preferentially wired to react more strongly to overt, physical threats.  
This discrepancy between the tool’s design and its practical application points to a gap between technological innovation and cultural adaptation. The QuAIC provides the means to properly weight the impact of intrusion, but this finding suggests that practitioners may still be conditioned by training, experience, or policy to prioritize aggression. University disciplinary codes, for example, often have clearer, more decisive, and more punitive pathways for responding to a physical altercation than for a persistent pattern of harassing emails. Therefore, the “aggression bias” observed in the results is likely not a flaw in the tool itself, but a symptom of this larger systemic context. It highlights that implementing an innovative tool is only the first step. The second, and arguably more difficult, step is to evolve the surrounding organizational culture, policies, and training to fully leverage the tool’s capabilities. This “aggression bias” identifies a critical area for future development and training for campus threat management teams.

6---full-notes/the-lipid-bilayer-membran.title: The Lipid Bilayer Membrane
6---full-notes/the-lipid-bilayer-membran.content:
Status: baby
Tags: physiology neuroscience
The Lipid Bilayer Membrane
Details
From ancient bacterial to braincells, they are all encased in a lipid bilayer membrane, which are formed from phospholipids, unique molecules that have a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail.
Because the environment inside and outside the cell is water-based, these molecules spontaneously arrange themselves into a “sandwich”: the heads face outward toward the water, and the tails tuck inward to hide from the water. This creates a stable, oily barrier that defines the cell’s boundary. For a drug to enter a cell passively, it usually needs to be lipophilic (hydrophobic) enough to dissolve through this oily interior layer.

Patients of trauma, when they shut down their emotions, their own thoughts it also makes them unaware of what has truly happened to them. So overwhelmed by the event their brain would make them forget, so that they can continue functioning. But the body remembers, the body keeps track of the trauma and reacts to it still. Her immune system, her muscles had all kept the score yet her conscious mind lacked a story that could communicate the experience.

When they try to find it from their parents they are met with an adult conspiracy of silence and disbelief. And so they eventually cope with by staying silent. Furthermore, children are programmed to be fundamentally loyal to their caretakers, even if abused by them. Terror increases the need for comfort, even when the source of comfort is the source of terror. And the feeling of rebelling, the feeling of getting out, it violates the very loyalty one has to their family-deep inside one still felt like they need it to protect them against their fears. A patient has one said “It is like hating your home, your kitchen and pots and pans, your bed, your chairs, your table, your rugs.” Nothing will ever feel safe-least of all your own body.
When asked about this later in life, most of these children would say that they are merely exaggerating it, or that it is supposedly their fault. Whenever a situation of this sorts happen, they shut down, their heads “goes into the clouds”. And they look down onto their mortal body, they were not looking down at themselves, but some other little girl.

6---full-notes/the-materialist-foundatio.title: The Materialist Foundation of Psychology
6---full-notes/the-materialist-foundatio.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology philosophy neurology
The Materialist Foundation of Psychology
Details
The core ideological assumption of modern psychology and neuroscience is materialism: the principle that the mind is what the brain does. This framework posits that all mental phenomena—thoughts, feelings, memories, consciousness—are the direct result of physical and chemical processes within the brain. It stands in stark contrast to dualism, an older philosophical position most famously articulated by René Descartes. Dualism argues that the mind (or soul) is an immaterial, non-physical entity that is separate from the physical body and brain. Descartes, for instance, searched for a single, non-symmetrical point in the brain (settling on the pineal gland) where this immaterial soul could interact with the physical body.
Materialism rejects this separation. It asserts that to understand the mind, we must understand the brain’s structure and function. If a thought exists, it exists as a pattern of neural firing. If a memory is stored, it is stored as a physical change in the connections between neurons. This foundation is not just a philosophical stance; it is the practical basis for all modern methods of brain study. It is the reason why studying lesions, stimulating brain tissue with TMS, or recording neural activity with fMRI can provide profound insights into our mental lives.

6---full-notes/the-melancholic-form-of-e.title: The Melancholic Form of Egoistic Suicide
6---full-notes/the-melancholic-form-of-e.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology
The Melancholic Form of Egoistic Suicide
Details
Durkheim identifies an ideal type of egoistic suicide characterized by a state of melancholic languor that relaxes all springs to action. In revulsion from the external world, the individual’s consciousness becomes self-preoccupied, taking itself as its sole object of study. This extreme concentration, however, only deepens the chasm separating the individual from others and from the very sources of life’s meaning. As the person detaches radically from the world, their inner life is deprived of its primary material, and it can find nothing to reflect upon but its own “wretched misery” and “inner nothingness.” The individual becomes addicted to this state with a kind of morbid joy, finding a perverse pleasure in the contemplation of non-existence. This condition is the direct individual expression of the over-individuation that defines egoistic suicide; it is the result of the slackening of social ties. The final act is not violent or hasty but is instead a calm, meditative process, where the sufferer analyzes their own state to the very end.

6---full-notes/the-metaphysics-of-person.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/The Metaphysics of Personal Identity.md
6---full-notes/the-metaphysics-of-person.title: The Metaphysics of Personal Identity
6---full-notes/the-metaphysics-of-person.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy psychology
The Metaphysics of Personal Identity
Details
Perhaps diverging a bit from the tracks of Kant’s project, we may now take a look at defining the continuity of the “self” over time. If a ship’s wooden planks are entirely replaced one by one over decades, is it still the same ship? Applying this to human biology—where our cellular makeup and sensory receptors are in a constant state of death and renewal—how can we claim to have a continuous, enduring identity? Classical and scholastic philosophers typically solved this through “essentialism,” positing a static, underlying substance or “soul” that undergoes accidental changes but remains fundamentally the same entity.
John Locke radically challenged this essentialist view by separating the concept of “man” (the biological entity) from “person” (the conscious self). Through his famous “Prince and the Cobbler” thought experiment, Locke argued that if the consciousness and memories of a prince were transferred into the body of a cobbler, the resulting entity would biologically be the cobbler, but personally be the prince. For Locke, personal identity is completely exhausted by the contents of consciousness and memory.
David Hume took empiricism even further, directing his skeptical gaze inward. Hume famously declared that when he introspected, he could not find a “self” at all; he found nothing but a “bundle of perceptions” passing in rapid succession, much like soldiers replacing one another in a marching formation. Because there is no single, permanent perception of a “self,” Hume argued the self is an illusion. However, this radical skepticism met fierce resistance from Scottish Common Sense philosopher Thomas Reid. Reid wryly pointed out the logical absurdity of Hume’s position: “for there to be treason, there must be a traitor.” In other words, a bundle of perceptions logically requires a unified perceiver to hold the bundle together, setting the stage for Kant’s revolutionary synthesis.

6---full-notes/the-methodology-of-ifs.title: The Methodology of IFS
6---full-notes/the-methodology-of-ifs.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology trauma IFS
The Methodology of IFS
Details
Firstly, one has to identify the parts of themselves, even the parts that they presumably hate the most. This makes them less intimidating and less overwhelming. Next, therapists are to help the patient to ask the protective parts to move back temporarily to see the Self that it is protecting. When this is done, the parts unblend themselves from the Self and allow it to be observed. And only then can patients open up to themselves and build their inner dialogues with their parts.
Next the therapist asks, “How do you feel toward that (sad, vengeful, terrified) part of you?” This sets the stage for mindful self-observation by separating the “you” from the part in question. If the patient has an extreme response like “I hate it,” the therapist knows that there is another protective part blended with Self. He or she might then ask, “See if the part that hates it would step back.” Then the protective part is often thanked for its vigilance and assured that it can return anytime that it is needed. If the protective part is willing, the follow-up question is: “How do you feel toward the (previously rejected) part now?” The patient is likely to say something like “I wonder why it is so (sad, vengeful etc.).” This sets the stage for getting to know the part better—for example, by inquiring how old it is and how it came to feel the way it does.
Once the patient has reached a point where they can talk to their parts without hating or being scared of any certain. It is important for the therapist to step to the side and just keep an eye for the parts that might interfere, make occasional empathetic comments, and trying to keep it all going altogether.

The midbrain also coordinates with the simple movements that the hindbrain creates to make larger wholes. The MSC states that for any proposed cognitive architecture to be considered a valid hypothesis, it must, in principle, be capable of producing the “minimally adaptive behavior in ancestral environments”. This means the proposed design must be able to solve all problems that were essential for survival and reproduction during the Pleistocene era. 6---full-notes/the-mixed-constitution.title: The Mixed Constitution
6---full-notes/the-mixed-constitution.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy
The Mixed Constitution
Details
As stated before, Locke is strongly against the way of forcing a person to serve under a political obligation merely due to the biological and geographical factors that they are born under. And so he instead structurally divides the concept of social compact into two totally distinct criteria: the fundamental legitimacy of the regime’s form itself, and the precise, individual conditions under which a person becomes morally obligated to obey it. But how does one manage its supreme legitimacy ? Well we can look to a country like England, where it is split between the Crown and Parliament. Locke designates these as coordinate, mutually dependent powers—neither is fully supreme over the other in a strictly commanding sense. Parliament cannot enact laws without the King’s consent, and the King cannot raise taxes or enforce laws without Parliament. And yet this proposes a terrifying vulnerability: if there is a chronic, systematic conflict between these two figures, then there is absolutely no mechanism to resolve it. From this, Locke argues that when such a persistent constitutional crisis occurs, there is an “appeal to heaven” for a justifiable righteous civil war.

6---full-notes/the-model-of-schizophreni.title: The Model of Schizophrenia
6---full-notes/the-model-of-schizophreni.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Clinical Psychology psychopathology
The Model of Schizophrenia
Details
This model posits that schizophrenia is not a sudden-onset degenerative disease, but the result of a chain of events starting before birth.
The foundation is a silent, static brain lesion or wiring abnormality that occurs during prenatal or perinatal development. This initial “hit” does not cause symptoms. It can be caused by genetic predisposition, maternal viral infections (e.g., influenza), malnutrition, or obstetric complications (e.g., hypoxia at birth). This results in subtle disruptions in neural migration and connectivity, particularly in regions like the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. The individual is born with a brain that is quietly vulnerable.
Throughout childhood, although people would not notice anything faulty or inherently wrong about the person who has these vulnerabilities, when checking back from an adult stance, they can clearly see the symptoms more, like how undeveloped their cognitive abilities are sometimes, their inability to express emotion, lack of empathy, so on and so forth.
This combination of a vulnerable brain undergoing faulty adolescent reorganization, often under environmental stress, “unmasks” the initial lesion. The brain’s circuits can no longer compensate, leading to the dysregulation of neurotransmitter systems (especially dopamine) and the emergence of positive (hallucinations, delusions) and negative (avolition, anhedonia) symptoms of schizophrenia.

6---full-notes/the-modern-mind-body-prob.title: The Modern Mind-Body Problem
6---full-notes/the-modern-mind-body-prob.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology neurology
The Modern Mind-Body Problem
Details
The ancient philosophical debate about the relationship between the mind and body continues today at the heart of cognitive neuroscience. The dominant scientific hypothesis is mind-brain reductionism, which asserts that the mind is the physical brain. According to this view, all mental phenomena, including consciousness itself, are ultimately reducible to neurochemical processes. The psychologist U.T. Place famously articulated this in 1956, proposing that “consciousness is a process in the brain” is a reasonable scientific hypothesis, the success of which depends entirely on future empirical discoveries.
However, this reductionist view runs into a persistent and powerful challenge: our own subjective experience. We have a profound and intuitive feeling that our mind is qualitatively different from our body. Our thoughts and emotions feel private and exclusively accessible to us, while our bodies are public and perceptible to others. Even young children understand this distinction. We have vivid dreams in the absence of any material stimulation, and people in life-threatening situations often report feelings of disassociation from their physical bodies. This persistent feeling of dualism raises a fundamental question that reductionism struggles to answer: how does the objective firing of neurons give rise to the rich, vivid, and private “whole” of our subjective experience? This gap between the physical brain and the felt quality of consciousness remains one of the greatest challenges in science.

6---full-notes/the-modern-toolkit-of-cog.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology biology neurology
The Modern Toolkit of Cognitive Psychology
Details
To make the invisible processes of the mind visible, modern cognitive psychology employs a diverse toolkit that moves beyond simple observation. The most traditional method involves measuring behavioral outcomes, such as recording the reaction time between a stimulus and a response, or tracking the accuracy of a participant’s performance on a task. Another powerful behavioral approach comes from neuropsychology, which examines the loss of a specific ability following brain damage from events like a stroke or injury, allowing researchers to infer the function of the damaged brain region.
However, recent technological advances have opened a direct window into the working brain. Tools like Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) allow researchers to temporarily and non-invasively stimulate or inhibit specific parts of the brain to observe the effect on behavior. Furthermore, sophisticated imaging techniques let us record brain activity in real-time. Electroencephalography (EEG) captures the rapid electrical rhythms of neurons, making it ideal for studying the timing of cognitive processes like language or attention. For mapping where activity happens, researchers use methods that track blood flow, such as Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and, most commonly, Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI). These tools allow us to see which brain areas become more active when a person is engaged in a specific mental task, giving us a geographical map of cognition.

6---full-notes/the-myth-of-errorless-lea.title: The Myth of Errorless learning
6---full-notes/the-myth-of-errorless-lea.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning Behaviorism Psychology neuroscience neuroplasticity
The Myth of Errorless learning
Details
Beginning in the 1950s and 1960s, B. F. Skinner, one of the most influential behavioral psychologists, advocated the “errorless learning” methods in education. He believed that encountering these errors would impeded learning processes instead of helping them learn.
Of course these days we now understand that errors, and subsequently adequate feedback, can help someone learn better rather than not making any errors at all. Like how letting someone struggle with a problem before eventually giving them the answer after they cannot figure it out will help them remember the answers and principles better. Moreover, these people will understand that learning takes a lot of effort and are more prompt to follow through the struggles and difficulties.
In fact, in experiments, it has shown that those who understand that failing is a part of the way of learning usually do tests better, with less anxiety as they do not have to dedicate a part of their cognitive function to thinking about if they are right or wrong, rather, they can just focus on the test before them. Another example comes in the form of the works of Carol Dweck and Anders Ericsson, they showed that people who believed their abilities to be hardwired, unchangeable from birth, usually shun away from challenges at which they may not succeed because they are scared/ashamed by it. Those who understand that their intellectual abilities lie in their control and they can grow and are not hardwired, are more likely to charge into difficult tasks and persist at them. This is a necessary trait, as any area of expertise requires someone to spend thousands of hours in it and fail a lot.

6---full-notes/the-myth-of-moral-coheren.title: The Myth of Moral Coherence
6---full-notes/the-myth-of-moral-coheren.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy history
The Myth of Moral Coherence
Details
Nietzsche also challenged the 19th century notion that society’s definition of morality is a single, seamless, and logical whole. Philosophers and historians often speak of “The Elizabethan Worldview” or “Christian Morality” as if these were monolithic structures where every intuition fits neatly with every other. Nietzsche argue that this presumption is false, suggesting that even the Christian Morality is a combination of antagonistic and disparate historical remnants.
To exemplify this, we can take a look at the 19th century as a conglomerate of chaotic Christian values, feudal aristocratic remnants, and modern utilitarian calculus. These values obviously do not fit together-feudal honor views the Roman concept of “glory” as supreme, while Christianity views it as sinful pride. Yet, they coexist in a state of historical tension.
Nietzsche illustrated this in his book Beyond Good and Evil with a striking metaphor. He posited that philosophers viewed Morality as a star that we rotate around, but in fact, it should be multiple stars that we are moving around without a certain direction or orbits. And so Morality at any time could be different due to the shade or point of view that we are standing from.
Furthermore, Nietzsche would also define the concept of “Good” as being univocal, multi-meaning, extending from his conceptualization as there is not a single unified worldview. For example, when viewed nobly, the word “good” is a self-description coined by the masters to refer to themselves. It implies vitality, power, wealth, and happiness. Its opposite, “Bad,” is an afterthought—a dismissive word for the “losers,” the commoners, or the weak. It carries no moral condemnation, only a recognition of low status. For the slave, “Evil” is the primary term. It is a projection of intense hatred toward the masters. The slave looks at the master’s power and violence and labels it “Evil.” “Good” is then created as a back-formation: “I am good because I am not like that evil master.”

6---full-notes/the-nature-of-rules.title: The Nature of Rules
6---full-notes/the-nature-of-rules.content:
Status:
Tags: psychology CBT
Changing of Rules
Details
Humans have a set of rules that they follow to go by their daily lives, these rules sometimes may be framed in absolute terms, are unrealistic, or are used inappropriately and excessively, which will make them produce maladjustment. And so it will lead to mental illnesses. Solving this problem will require the therapist to help the patient adjust their own rules. Though some therapists do look over the fact that if a patient’s incorrect assumptions or personal mythology are not related to their difficulties, it is not necessary to change them.
In recoding these rules, there are two main axes: danger vs safety and pain vs pleasure. The difficulties that most people encounter are in their assessments of risk and safety or in their conceptions of pain and gratification.
In order to minimize danger, people generally will apply rules to estimate the probabilities in degree of harm and the likelihood of them being able to deal with the threat. The ratio between these concepts can be labeled the risk. If a patient overestimates the risk, they are more likely to be anxious and be unable to function normally in their day to day life, if a patient underestimates the risk, they may be more prone to encountering accidents.
The complexities of interpersonal relations and the lack of a reliable index of another person’s intentions to cause hurt add a fuzziness to the rules used in interpersonal situations. Some people regard themselves as highly vulnerable in all interpersonal contacts and thus feel constantly on the razor’s edge. Conversely, those who are oblivious to signals from other people, of course, may regularly get into interpersonal difficulties.
Because most problems presented by patients seem to arise in the context of interpersonal relations, some of the common interpersonal attitudes will be considered first. Interpersonal dangers are epitomized by a rule such as the following: “It would be awful for someone to form a low opinion of me.” The other person might be a close friend, a parent, a peer, remote acquaintance, or a stranger. In clinical practice, we find that our patients are generally most afraid of being devalued by members of their peer group—their classmates, fellow workers, colleagues, or friends. Many patients, however, are even more afraid of the prospect of appearing ridiculous to strangers. They are apprehensive of the reactions of clerks in stores, waiters, taxi drivers, passengers on a bus, or passersby on a street. It is possible that the reactions from strangers are more threatening because they do not know what to expect. And most of the time, they cannot define why this is bad, only that it is bad.

The Nature of Thinking Disorders
Details
A thinking disorder has generally been considered a feature of schizophrenia. Whilst the opposite, depression, mania, and anxiety are generally considered emotional disorders due to the excessive emotions evoked in them. However, there is now considerable evidence that a disorder in thinking is less gross and more circumscribed than that in schizophrenia, which is an important component of the common psychiatric syndromes.
This symptom is apparent in the systematically misconstrued specific kinds of experiences. These can range from subtle inaccuracies in the mild neurotics to the fully grotesque misinterpretations of the psychotics. As said before, these thoughts appear in subjects that are relative to the patient’s problems.
Supporting Content
These thoughts and ideas have the characteristics of automatic thoughts, meaning they appear as if by reflex, without any apparent antecedent reflection or reasoning, being familiar and true to the patient even though implausible to others. And finally, they were less amenable to change by reason or contradictory evidence than other forms associated with the specific form of psychopathology

6---full-notes/the-necessary-person.content:

The Necessary Person
Details
When building a well-ordered society, the concept of the people in it is quite important, in which they must be “free and equal persons.” Rawls emphasized that this is political, of what people think about each other and such and in no way philosophical or metaphysical.
Within this framework, equality means that persons are equally capable of participating in social cooperation and equally capable of honoring the fair terms of cooperation specified by the principles of justice. This capacity is articulated through two moral powers that parallel the two elements previously distinguished within the concept of cooperation itself. In short, the powers are to understand and accept the principles of justice and the capacity to form, revise, and pursue a conception of the good.
And in this, even if it is somewhat circular, it is fine as long as we achieve the goal of fully realizing and making meaning to our well-ordered society.

6---full-notes/the-neurochemical-and-soc.content:
Status: teen
Tags: love psychology neuroscience
The Neurochemical and Social Dimensions of Love
Details
The motivational drive of love is not monolithic and can be distinguished from lust at a neurochemical level. Scientific evidence suggests that the brain pathways involved in romantic love are closely related to those involved in parent-child attachment, utilizing opioid chemicals that the brain naturally generates. In contrast, lust is more directly linked to sex hormones like testosterone and androgens. This distinction supports the idea that romantic love may have evolved as a social mechanism to channel the more primal sex drive in a way that is compatible with civilization. Unchecked lust, as seen in the reproductive behaviors of animals like spiders, is not conducive to building complex, stable social structures. Romantic love, by co-opting the powerful bonding mechanism seen between parent and child, provides a framework for the long-term, cooperative relationships that are foundational to human society. This echoes Freudian concepts where civilization is built upon the sublimation and channeling of basic drives.

6---full-notes/the-neurochemistry-of-sam.title: The Neurochemistry of Same-Sex Love
6---full-notes/the-neurochemistry-of-sam.content:
Status: teen
Tags: love psychology biology
The Neurochemistry of Same-Sex Love
Details
The framework of separate love and lust systems offers profound insights into the complexities of gender and sexual orientation. It helps explain the widely observed phenomenon that women, on average, tend to report a greater interconnection between their feelings of love and desire, a concept often termed “sexual plasticity.” Lisa Diamond posits a compelling neurochemical hypothesis for this difference.
The key may lie with oxytocin, a primary hormone in the attachment system. While crucial for bonding in both sexes, oxytocin also appears to play a more significant role in the female sexual response cycle than in the male’s. Diamond suggests this dual function in women—acting in both the love system and the desire system—may create a stronger biological feedback loop between the two.
This has powerful implications for understanding same-sex attractions. Because the attachment (love) system is independent of the desire (lust) system, a person’s sexual orientation does not necessarily restrict their capacity for romantic bonding. A woman, for instance, can form a deep, platonic, emotional bond with a female friend. For some, due to the tighter neurochemical link between love and desire, this powerful feeling of love can then trigger the desire system, leading to the emergence of sexual feelings that effectively “override” a previously established heterosexual orientation. This model provides a nuanced, bio-psychological explanation for why some individuals’ sexual feelings can be fluid and develop out of deep emotional connection.

6---full-notes/the-nuanced-decision-to-m.title: The Nuanced Decision to Medicate A Case for Early, Adaptive Intervention
6---full-notes/the-nuanced-decision-to-m.content:
Status: teen
Tags: ADHD neurology biology
The Nuanced Decision to Medicate A Case for Early, Adaptive Intervention
Details
The decision to medicate a child for ADHD with a powerful stimulant like amphetamine is fraught with complexity and concern. An anecdotal case study involving a pediatric neurologist who treats ADHD and is contemplating medication for their own child reveals a highly informed perspective. The core argument for early intervention, even before puberty, rests on the principle of neuroplasticity. The brain’s ability to remodel itself is at its absolute peak during early childhood (from ages 3 to 12). Waiting until after puberty, when the frontal lobes mature, means missing this critical window of accelerated learning.
The therapeutic strategy, therefore, is not simply to medicate but to use the lowest possible dose as a tool to guide the developing brain. The medication should be seen as a temporary support system that enables the child’s frontal circuits to come online and function correctly. This allows the child to learn the essential skills of focus and impulse control during their most formative years. A crucial part of this approach is that the treatment should be adaptive; the dosage should be modulated as the child grows and develops their own innate powers of attention. The ultimate goal is not lifelong dependency, but to use the medication as a catalyst to shape a more resilient and focused brain, potentially leading to a reduced need for the drug later in life.

The Nurture Assumption and Peer Influence
Details
In the late 1990s, Judith Harris challenged the hegemony of parenting research with The Nurture Assumption. She argued that parental influence is vastly overrated, particularly after age 5. Her thesis suggests that shared environment (parenting) accounts for very little variance in adult outcomes, while genes and non-shared environments (specifically peer groups and school culture) are the primary drivers of personality and behavior.
While controversial, this perspective forced a re-evaluation of developmental psychology, moving away from a “parent-centric” model to one that acknowledges that parents may influence children indirectly (by choosing neighborhoods/schools) rather than directly through day-to-day discipline.

The ODD Controversy
Details
ODD, also known as Oppositional Defiant Disorder, is one of the most controversial diagnosis in the DSM 5. Why is it so ? This is because many clinicians argue that it pathologizes normal childhood behavior and stigmatizes children with a permanent record for being merely “ornery.”
But on the other hand, many argue that it is necessary due to its predictive nature, as a warning system, so to say. About one-third to 40% of children with ODD progress to Conduct Disorder (CD), a much more severe condition involving violence and theft. And when it has developed to CD, the window for effective treatment has closed. ODD is a “heterotypic” risk factor, it changes its appearance overtime, what seems like merely defiance at age 6 can turn into delinquency at age 16.

The Opacity of the Self (Contra Descartes)
Details
Descartes argued that our mind is transparent, meaning we can always look inward to our mind and easily identify what we are actually thinking, but common sense and psychology actually disproves this. Most of the time, it is the other people that are able to understand and know what we are thinking before us.
For example, take into account a jealous person, they would rather contradict their own physical reactions and words when questioned about their true thoughts behind such reactions to protect their own mind and ego from admitting that they are indeed jealous. This suggests that the “Cartesian Theater”—where the self views its own thoughts infallibly—is a myth. We are often strangers to ourselves, and self-knowledge is a hard-won achievement, not a starting guarantee.

The Oral-Digestive Route and First-Pass Metabolism
Details
How do chemicals, drugs, substances actually have an effect on us ? Now, drugs do not actually get injected into our brain the moment we ingest them, contrary to popular belief (sarcasm). It rather travels through our blood, and yes, that would mean it travels all throughout the body and has an effect even though it is miniscule. Since blood travels through our brain multiple times again and again, the chemicals EVENTUALLY will be able to effect us through that transmission process, but not before going through the liver.
The liver is what everything our body consumes passes through before entering the blood and all. The reason for this is to eliminate any weird or harmful stuff from what we consume so that our body won’t shut down or go wrong. And so it biotransforms and often deactivates a portion of the toxins (drugs) before they reach the brain. Because of this process, the time to onset for orally ingested drugs is roughly 20 minutes.

6---full-notes/the-original-position.title: The Original Position
6---full-notes/the-original-position.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy morals
The Original Position
Details
The sequence of fundamental ideas develops through a natural progression. So now we have to understand how the fair terms of cooperation are determined.
Rawls offers three possibilities. First, the fair terms could be from an external authority, as was done with God in the former times. Second, they could be determined through common moral knowledge and intuition that derive from ourselves. Third is the alternative that Rawls pursues - the parties themselves determine the fair terms by agreeing in an appropriately characterized situation. This is where the social contract idea enters justice as fairness: the original position is offered as a way of specifying how this agreement might work.
Crucially, the parties can also choose from a somewhat menu of conceptions of justice drawn from the history of moral philosophy - two principles of justice, two forms of utilitarianism, intuitionism, and so on. The parties do not generate principles through their own reasoning; they select from a pre-existing list. The original position is thus a selection device, not a generative one. This means that we can only choose to use what is conceivably the best currently, not something superior in the future.

The Origins and Spread of Tobacco
Details
Tobacco is a member of the Solanaceae (nightshade) family, sharing lineage with both potent poisons and common food crops. Whilst there are over 50 species of Nicotiana, the main crop that we cultivate and use is Nicotiana tabacum.
Following Colombus’s arrival, tobacco spread the world with unprecedented speed. Within a century, it has spread from mere rituals to sailors, and then the world. Figures like Jean Nicot, for whom the genus and the molecule nicotine are named, popularized the plant in French courts as a medicine for migraines.
For the United States, this plant can be viewed as its parent plant. It was the cash crop par excellence for the English colonies, letting the early settlements have enough money to settle. Due to this, King James I of England hated the plant due to its economic and political dynamics, but even he declared it a royal monopoly.

Details
Excluding innate biological reflexes, the automaticity of human behavior originates from two distinct mechanisms of practice. Or, turning it into a habit through practicing (interesting its not like I have a whole series of notes on it). 6---full-notes/the-paradox-of-heritabili.title: The Paradox of Heritability
6---full-notes/the-paradox-of-heritabili.content:
Status:
Tags: genetics 3 - Tags/environment Cognitive Psychology
The Paradox of Heritability
Details
There is a central paradox in the findings of quantitative genetics. High heritability estimates are used to prove the importance of genes. However, the same data provides the strongest evidence for the importance of the environment. For example, if identical twins have a 45% concordance for schizophrenia, this means that in 55% of cases, these genetically identical individuals have different outcomes. This discordance can only be explained by non-genetic (i.e., environmental) factors. Therefore, heritability studies simultaneously establish the influence of genetics while also highlighting the profound impact of the nonshared environment.

The Paradox of Self-Blame and Helplessness in Trauma
Details
Inherently, self-blame is a defense mechanism of PTSD patients, it makes them feel as if they were in control of the situation and could have done something about it. But their inner world knows the opposite, it knows that they couldn’t have protected themselves in any capacity, and so is why it still hurts so much to self-blame.
And so you can’t exactly rewire it like an automatic thought in CBT, as it isn’t an illogical thought, it is a coping mechanism that has been developed to protect the self. If the self feels safe enough through emotional regulation, to gain back the control that it has loss, then this self-blame will go away by itself.
Of course, this does not mean that CBT or CPT won’t work on trauma patients, but rather that it works when the trauma patient experience self-blame not as a defense mechanism, but an automatic thought. Further pushing to recalibrate something that is not a thought but protecting the self will only further put pressure on and even damage the patient further.

6---full-notes/the-paradoxes-of-depressi.title: The Paradoxes of Depression
6---full-notes/the-paradoxes-of-depressi.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology emotional disorders
The Paradoxes of Depression
Details
In depression, there is a big “tell” of those who are suffering from it, it is the inconsistency in the individual’s previous behavior and values. Self-preserving actions usually vanish and thwarted. “Social instincts,” such as attraction to other people, love, and affection evaporate. The pleasure principle and the reality principle,… etc are turned around. Even the strong emotions that they usually convey when a specific event happens disappear.
Initially, the reason of this seems to defy logic, without an explanation. Any normal wanting or feelings are completely flipped onto their head. To understand this, we can attempt to arrange the various phenomena into some kind of understandable sequence. There exists a sequence that writers have assigned primacy to: intense sadness, wishes to “hibernate,” self-destructive wishes, or physiological disturbance.
In his seminal work, Cognitive Therapy and the Emotional Disorders, Aaron T. Beck challenges the foundational assumption that the painful emotion of sadness is the primary catalytic agent for the entire syndrome of depression. He questions whether a primary affective disorder can logically account for the complex cognitive and behavioral symptoms that characterize the condition. Through a compelling critique, Beck methodically deconstructs the idea that the unpleasant emotional state is a sufficient explanation for the debilitating changes a depressed individual undergoes.
Beck’s argument hinges on a crucial distinction between the emotional state in depression and other forms of human suffering. He observes that states such as physical pain, nausea, or intense anxiety, while deeply unpleasant, seldom produce the symptoms typical of a major depressive episode. These other forms of suffering do not ordinarily lead to a profound renunciation of life’s major goals, the erasure of affectionate feelings for loved ones, or a wish for death. On the contrary, Beck suggests that individuals enduring physical ailments often develop a heightened appreciation for the very aspects of life they find most meaningful. This contrast strongly implies that the negative emotion of depression is qualitatively different and that its downstream effects cannot be attributed to mere suffering.
Furthermore, Beck scrutinizes the nature of sadness itself, concluding that it lacks the specific properties required to generate the hallmark symptoms of depression. The pervasive self-castigation, significant distortions in thinking, and the profound loss of drive for formerly gratifying activities are not natural consequences of feeling sad. A simple state of sorrow does not inherently possess the power to warp one’s entire perception of self and the future so destructively.
In extending his critique, Beck also addresses alternative biological theories, such as the notion that the passivity and withdrawal seen in depression are an atavistic “hibernation” response designed to conserve energy. He skillfully points out a fundamental contradiction in this hypothesis: if the ultimate goal were energy conservation, it makes little sense for the individual to be simultaneously driven to engage in relentless and mentally exhausting cycles of self-criticism and rumination.

The Passive Learner
Details
As stated in Childhood Socialization, there are two groups about how children understand the socialization around them and adapt to it, the paragraphs below concerns the first group.
The effectiveness of simple conditioning can be overstated. Children often conform to societal roles not because they have been conditioned, but because they understand social expectations and are motivated by a fear of negative backlash. Consequently, when a child’s genuine preferences deviate from the norm, conditioning alone is rarely enough to force a change in their behavior.
Indoctrination is when new ideals are introduced into the child, usually at middle school, when they start questioning and when they start finding out new things about the world, about their own ideas and all. They still challenge these views though, and there is quite a bit of personal bias involved in it sometimes. So it does not do much for socialization as well.
Imitation is what children usually do, viewing others who are involved around them and try to imitate the way they act and such to learn from it and socialize the way that they do. In normal families where there are both parents, the child can learn from them, but in households with only one parent or both parents are the same gender, do they act like them instead ? The answer is no, the influence does not exactly come from them. When they get pass the age where they learn from their parents, they will instead start imitating the society and community around them.

6---full-notes/the-persistence-of-adhd.title: The Persistence of ADHD
6---full-notes/the-persistence-of-adhd.content:
Status: teen
Tags: ADHD developmental psychology
The Persistence of ADHD
Details
How well does ADHD persists throughout one’s life ? Well professor Susan Campbell answered that in her landmark study of testing children through 8 hours worth of test then repeating it when 6th grade came.
The result was that 50% of the original children remained with ADHD, but there were actually 2 main reasons playing into this. Firstly, biological cause, the severity of the initial symptoms. Children with “difficult temperaments” (high intensity, low effortful control) were more likely to remain ADHD. Secondly, though, was their environment, how their parents reacted with invalidation, sarcasm, unseriousness, resulting in them significantly more likely to have ADHD. This illustrates a “coercive cycle” or “reciprocal chain.” A child with a difficult temperament frustrates the parent; the parent responds with harsh control; this harshness increases the child’s stress and impulsivity, leading to worse behavior, which elicits more harshness.
The opposite of this environment was a “good holding environment” which allowed children to be energetic whilst protecting them from harms and also not escalating the situation due to the parents’ emotions. This allowed the children to develop self-regulation.

The Pharmacology of Nicotine
Details
The primary psychoactive substance in tobacco is nicotine, a pyridine alkaloid, an agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR). Unlike how The Solanaceae Family (Nightshades) are found only in muscles, these receptors are also found in the CNS, the ANS, and neuromuscular junctions.
As how shamans described the feeling as “grounding”, nicotine does this: it is a stimulant to the CNS and also an anxiolytic. They may feel increased focus and alertness whilst also feeling grounded, reduction of stress and anxiety. This precipitates a high The Drug Abuse Potential clearly. It also affects sleep, increasing REM sleep and dream intensity.
Nicotine also increase the basal metabolic rate, which explains why people who give it up gain more weight. It affects the ANS, which raises heart rate and blood pressure through brain-mediated pathways. The body builds up tolerance of nicotine extremely fast, even though negative side effects include nausea and vomiting.

6---full-notes/the-phenomenology-of-bad-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy psychology
The Phenomenology of Bad Conscience
Details
Before going into the history and function of Bad Conscience, Nietzsche defines it not just as a simple feeling, but as a complex compound of a raw physiological fact and a specific cultural interpretation. The lecturer breaks it down into four components that must all be present for it to exist. First is the somatic fact, which is the real, pre-moral state of internal psychic pain or “malaise.” Then it is the subjective interpretation of it as guilt. Then the guilt would turn into the cognitive awareness of having done something “wrong.” Lastly the transgression would have to be interpreted metaphysically, the subject would have to believe that they have Free Will and could have acted otherwise yet they weren’t strong enough to do so. Nietzsche argues that while the first step (internal pain) might be a universal result of civilization (internalization), the subsequent steps are not. The connection of pain to “Guilt” and “Free Will” is a specific Christian/Western interpretation of that pain. Therefore, one cannot simply “cure” bad conscience by changing one’s beliefs, because the underlying somatic pain (Step 1) remains even if the interpretation is removed.
Nietzsche then tries to exemplify this by projecting a possible future-the Sovereign Individual. Basically, they are an individual that is the most capable of humanity, they are autonomous, predictable, and possess the “right to make promises.”
Nietzsche believed that the ability to make promises is not a natural human trait but rather a hard-won artificial power that allows one to bind themselves to the future and be able to control both internally and externally to ensure they can perform the function they promised to do.
This continuity, as Nietzsche posits, which was something revolutionary for his time, was the “Mnemonics of Pain.” which is basically modern cognitive psychology about how memories get more integrated through strong feelings.

6---full-notes/the-plateau-of-latent-pot.content:
Status: baby
Tags: psychology
The Plateau of Latent Potential
Details
A major pitfall in habit formation is a fundamental misunderstanding of how progress actually works. We tend to think of work as compounding linearly over time, expecting steady, highly visible improvement day after day. When this doesn’t happen, we get discouraged. Instead, we must conceptualize habit building as the accumulation of latent potential. Think of it as building up energy to eventually cross a specific threshold, which then lets out a massive, sudden change. Like heating an ice cube from 25 degrees to 31 degrees, the work is happening, but the visible transformation (melting) doesn’t occur until you hit 32 degrees. Understanding this plateau prevents us from quitting during the early stages of habit formation when our efforts seem unrewarded.

6---full-notes/the-pleasure-and-motivati.title: The Pleasure and Motivation Circuit in Depression
6---full-notes/the-pleasure-and-motivati.content:
Status: baby
Tags: psychology neurology
The Pleasure and Motivation Circuit in Depression
Details
The loss of pleasure and motivation in depression (anhedonia) is directly linked to the malfunction of the brain’s mesolimbic dopamine system. This circuit is responsible for processing reward and, more importantly, the anticipation of reward.
In depression, this crucial circuit becomes underactive. It doesn’t fail on its own; it is actively suppressed by other overactive brain regions. The two main culprits are:


The Amygdala: The brain’s fear and threat-detection center.


The Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC): The center for processing emotional pain and empathy.


In a depressive state, the amygdala and ACC are in overdrive, constantly sending inhibitory, “negative” signals to the mesolimbic system. This barrage effectively shuts down the brain’s ability to anticipate or feel pleasure, leading directly to the profound apathy and anhedonia that define the illness.

The Power of Others
Details
When placed into difficult moral situations, people may look for social proof - how people around them act - to then act. If others act, you should act, if others don’t, then you shouldn’t. We look at them not to find if they are doing or not, but to find out if its right to do so or not (since if it is then the majority would do ?). Also, something that also heavily relates to this is the Diffusion of Responsibility, which states that well, the more people in the room who has to make the decision, the less each will bear the responsibility. This encourages people who you normally wouldn’t think would act a certain way to act that way because they carry less responsibility now.
For example, in a study done in the Reagan era by social psychologists to find out the effects of crowd cheering, they separated a recording of the presidential debate with the claps and laugh of the audience and one without. Now those who view the former version were significantly affected, believing Reagan to be suitable as a president because he is a funny person whilst the latter was not affected by his arguments/jokes without the audience (70% vs 45%). This shows that even if we don’t realize it, our mind is still being affected by these things nonetheless.

6---full-notes/the-problem-of-evil.title: The Problem of Evil
6---full-notes/the-problem-of-evil.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
The Problem of Evil
Details
Perhaps the most famous problem contrasting theists against atheists, and one that has been ongoing for such a long time even though it is possibly a never-ending argument (but again that’s inductive reasoning). The central tension in the philosophy of religion lies between the theoretical definition of God and the empirical observation of the world. Richard Swinburne argues that we define God as “Omni-Perfect” (infinite in power, knowledge, and goodness) not because of empirical evidence, but because of theoretical simplicity; postulating a single, infinite being is logically simpler (via Occam’s Razor) than postulating a complex, finite one. However, this theoretical elegance collapses when confronted with the Problem of Evil: the existence of profound suffering (pain) and sin (immorality).
David Hume has cited Epicurus to formulate the trilemma that is: If God is willing to prevent evil but unable, he is impotent; if able but unwilling, he is malevolent. While the “Logical Problem of Evil” (that God and evil cannot coexist) is generally considered defeatable, the “Evidential Problem” suggests that the quantity of gratuitous evil makes an Omni-Perfect God highly improbable.
There has been theodicies attempted against this, one being the “Soul-Making” theodicy (John Hick)—which argues suffering is necessary for character development—fails against the concept of Omnipotence, as an all-powerful being should be able to instantiate virtuous character without the inefficient mechanism of torture or pain. Another is the argument that God’s conceptualization of “goodness” is incomprehensible to us, and that perhaps we ARE in a world that is inherently good, but this also fails, as it would strip us of moral responsibility if everything that we do is good at the end of the day (working off the statement that God decides what is good and what is evil).

6---full-notes/the-problem-of-self-conti.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
The Problem of Self-Continuity
Details
How could you ever know that you are still the same person as you were yesterday or tomorrow ? Seemingly every piece of evidence we reach for, be it memories, photographs, witnesses, are in principle fakeable or fallible. Memory is quite reconstructive as it is already inherently glitchy and unstable currently for us. Joseph Butler pushed this further in the 1700s, arguing the self “lives and dies, begins and ends continually” — today’s self is merely a similar successor to yesterday’s, not the same entity. This is a concept that is imbued in our own lives: we apologize for our past selves, we sleep late without caring much about tomorrow’s tiredness, treating as if its a different person’s problem. We would need temporal (timely) difference and distance so that we can admit fault. John Locke further argued that our identity would then extend as far as consciousness can reach backward, and while amnesics prove this isn’t technically true, we feel it is. We only never question this due to the fact that it would be counterproductive form an evolutionary perspective.

6---full-notes/the-processing-of-the-scu.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology university trauma
The Processing of the SCU
Details
The core of the SCU’s method is a structured yet flexible case management system designed to handle reports from various sources, including students, staff, and external parties. Upon receiving a report through multiple channels such as a dedicated phone line, email, or an anonymous online form, the SCU conducts an initial triage. This critical first step ensures that emergencies are immediately escalated to police or security, while other matters are appropriately directed. For cases falling within its purview, the SCU employs a triage risk assessment to guide its response, which can range from simply recording the information to implementing more formal resolutions. This systematic approach allows for a tailored response to the specific level of risk and need presented by each case.
A defining feature of the SCU’s approach is its “victim/survivor-centered” philosophy. By prioritizing the needs and wishes of the person who has been harmed, the unit aims to mitigate the potential for re-traumatization throughout the reporting and resolution process. This ethos dictates the management actions taken, which are decided in consultation with the reporting party. The options are broad, encompassing informal advice for self-management, formal warnings, or escalation to other university bodies for disciplinary action. This empowerment of the victim/survivor marks a departure from purely punitive systems and aligns with contemporary best practices in trauma-informed care.

The synthesis would be a new mode of production, unalienated, where people would work, not because they are forced to and exploited to, but because they flourish from it.

6---full-notes/the-psychometric-approach.content:

The Psychometric Approach
Details
The psychometric approach is a method for studying intelligence that is based on the measurement of individual differences in performance. Pioneered by Charles Spearman, this approach uses statistical analysis of scores from various cognitive tests to identify the underlying structure of intelligence.
The core idea is that if performance on different types of tasks (e.g., arithmetic, spatial reasoning, vocabulary) correlates, it suggests these tasks share a common mental faculty. By analyzing these correlations, psychometricians aim to create a “map” of human intelligence, identifying its core components and how they relate to one another. This approach forms the foundation for most modern intelligence testing.

6---full-notes/the-revolutionary-role-of.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
The Revolutionary Role of the Bourgeoisie
Details
In a surprising twist, Karl Marx argues that the capitalist class—the bourgeoisie—“has played a most revolutionary part” in history. He doesn’t mean this as a compliment. He is thinking dialectically: capitalism, in its ruthless pursuit of profit, acts as a destructive force that unintentionally creates the conditions for its own downfall.
According to Marx, capitalism’s revolutionary role is to obliterate the old world. It “has put an end to all feudal, patriarchal, idyllic relations.” It tears away the sentimental veils of loyalty, family, religion, and nationality, leaving behind only one connection between people: “naked self-interest” and “callous cash payment.” A boss can no longer afford to be loyal to a worker; competition forces them to be ruthless. Family becomes a “mere money relation.”
This destruction is crucial. The old ties—to family, to a specific craft or skill, to a nation, to private property like a home—are what keep people attached to the existing system and divided from one another. By grinding everything down, capitalism performs a vital historical function: it erases these divisions.
It creates a “cosmopolitan character to production and consumption in every country,” breaking down national barriers. It drives small artisans out of business, forcing everyone into the same powerless position: the proletariat. By stripping people of their individual skills, their property, their national identities, and their family loyalties, capitalism forges a single, unified mass of humankind. This unified, property-less proletariat is the new force of production that capitalism creates within itself, and it is the class that will ultimately rise up to overthrow it.

6---full-notes/the-role-of-diet-in-manag.title: The Role of Diet in Managing ADHD Sugar, Allergies, and Elimination
6---full-notes/the-role-of-diet-in-manag.content:
Status: teen
Tags: ADHD
The Role of Diet in Managing ADHD Sugar, Allergies, and Elimination
Details
Dietary intervention represents a powerful, non-pharmacological approach to managing ADHD symptoms, acting as a modulator of the underlying neurochemistry. The most consistent and impactful dietary change observed across numerous clinical anecdotes and studies is the elimination of simple sugars. Given that individuals with ADHD often crave sugary foods to unconsciously boost their low dopamine levels, removing these items can have a dramatic and positive effect by stabilizing the brain’s reward and hyperactivity circuits.
A more targeted but controversial approach is the oligoantigenic diet, which involves identifying and eliminating specific foods to which a child has a mild allergy or sensitivity. A landmark, albeit debated, study in The Lancet showed that this method could produce dramatic improvements in ADHD symptoms, statistically equivalent to the effects of medication in some cases. The theory is that low-grade allergic inflammation contributes to brain dysfunction. However, this approach is complex, as some research suggests that avoiding potential allergens in childhood might increase the risk of developing more severe allergies later. Despite the controversy, the evidence strongly suggests that for many, diet—especially the management of sugar and potential food sensitivities—can be a significant leverage point for reducing the severity of ADHD symptoms, sometimes enough to lower medication doses or avoid them entirely.

6---full-notes/the-role-of-dopamine-in-d.content:
Status: teen

The Role of Dopamine in Depression
Details
Dopamine is a critical neurotransmitter in the biology of depression, but its role is more nuanced than simply “pleasure.” Sapolsky clarifies that dopamine is less about the experience of reward itself and more about the anticipation of reward. It is the chemical that drives motivation, goal-directed behavior, and the “happiness of pursuit.”
In major depression, the dopamine system is depleted. This deficit is the direct biological cause of anhedonia, the core symptom of the illness. When the brain cannot generate the necessary bursts of dopamine in anticipation of a positive outcome, the motivation to act disappears. Activities that once brought pleasure feel flat and unappealing because the neurological system that would normally drive a person towards them is offline.
This explains why anhedonia is not just a lack of joy, but also a profound loss of interest and drive. The individual doesn’t just fail to enjoy things; they lack the fundamental motivation to pursue them in the first place. This collapse of the brain’s reward and motivation circuitry is a key component of the paralysis experienced in depression.

6---full-notes/the-role-of-inflammation-.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology biology
The Role of Inflammation in Depression
Details
Chronic inflammation is another critical biological factor that has a bidirectional relationship with depression. This connection reveals that depression is not just a neurological disorder, but one that involves the body’s immune system.
The link works in two directions, creating a vicious cycle:


Inflammation Increases Depression Risk: Individuals with chronic inflammatory diseases (like autoimmune disorders) have a significantly higher risk of developing major depression. Furthermore, giving healthy individuals drugs that mimic an inflammatory response can induce a severe depressive episode.


Depression Increases Inflammation: The state of major depression itself acts as a stressor that activates the body’s inflammatory systems. Post-mortem studies of the brains of people with depression show clear markers of chronic neuroinflammation.


This feedback loop is similar to the one seen with stress hormones. An initial inflammatory state can trigger or worsen depression, and the resulting depressive state then fuels more inflammation, further entrenching the illness. This interplay between the immune system and the brain provides another powerful piece of evidence for the biological nature of depression and helps explain its systemic, whole-body effects.

6---full-notes/the-role-of-norepinephrin.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neurology psychology
The Role of Norepinephrine in Depression
Details
Norepinephrine (also known as noradrenaline) is a key neurotransmitter implicated in depression, primarily associated with the body’s energy levels, arousal, and vigilance. It was one of the first neurotransmitters targeted by antidepressants, long before the modern focus on serotonin.
The “norepinephrine hypothesis” of depression, which emerged in the 1960s, proposed that a deficit of this chemical was a root cause of the illness. This theory was based on early medications that worked by either blocking norepinephrine’s re-uptake or inhibiting the enzymes that break it down, both of which increase its availability in the synapse.
The most direct symptom linked to a norepinephrine deficit is psychomotor retardation. This is the profound physical and mental slowing, the overwhelming sense of exhaustion, and the inability to mobilize for action that characterizes many cases of major depression. When norepinephrine levels are low, the brain and body lack the necessary signals for alertness and energy, leading to a state of near-paralysis. This connection highlights how a specific chemical deficit can produce one of the most physically debilitating symptoms of the disease.

The Rumination Circuit (Default Mode Network) in Depression
Details
The Default Mode Network (DMN) is a collection of brain regions that is active when the mind is at rest and wandering, engaged in self-referential thought. It’s the network responsible for your sense of self and autobiography.
In major depression, this network is hijacked by negativity. Instead of neutral mind-wandering, the DMN becomes the engine of rumination, getting stuck in a persistent loop of sad memories, self-criticism, and feelings of guilt.
This pathological state is driven by the overactive amygdala and Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC), which constantly feed the DMN with distressing emotional information. The DMN then processes this information in a self-referential way, creating the inescapable internal narrative of failure and sadness that characterizes depressive rumination.

Status: adult

The SAT
Details
Within Victoria University’s intricate framework for managing student safety, the Safety and Triage (SAT) team operates as a critical, high-level body for addressing the most serious behavioral concerns. The SAT team’s work is distinct and highly specialized, functioning not as a primary investigative unit, but as a multi-disciplinary panel convened to make determinative judgments about student risk and recommend consequential sanctions.
The composition of the SAT team is one of its defining features, bringing together key stakeholders from across the university. It includes representatives from Human Resources, Occupational Health and Safety, Security, Legal Services, Student Counseling, and Student Misconduct, among others as needed, such as faculty or accommodation staff. This multi-disciplinary structure ensures that any student case referred to it is evaluated from a comprehensive range of professional perspectives—legal, clinical, safety, and academic. The team convenes on an ad-hoc basis, assembled specifically when a referral is made, indicating its role as a responsive, rather than a standing, committee.
Crucially, the text delineates what the SAT team does and, perhaps more importantly, what it does not do. Unlike similar “threat assessment teams” found in U.S. campuses, the SAT team at Victoria University does not conduct its own risk assessments or formulate threat management plans. Its function is more focused and adjudicative. Its primary purpose is to evaluate the evidence presented—including comprehensive reports from external threat assessors referred by the Safer Community Unit (SCU)—and determine whether a student meets the university’s specific definition of a “high risk person.”
The outcome of the SAT team’s deliberation carries significant weight. Based on its assessment, the team makes direct recommendations to the university’s leadership regarding appropriate management and sanctions. These are not minor disciplinary actions; they can include severe outcomes such as the suspension or complete exclusion of a student from the university. In essence, the SAT team serves as the university’s ultimate internal tribunal for cases where student behavior is deemed to pose a significant threat, acting on expert information to enforce policies and protect the wider university community.
