Tags: philosophy
The Same Application Fallacy
Details
The claim that synthetic a priori knowledge is impossible is in of itself: a synthetic proposition. Those who believe it is true and regard it as such is implicitly treating it as a priori.
More importantly, Kant argues, the existence of mathematics and Newtonian physics already demonstrates that synthetic a priori knowledge is actual. The propositions of geometry are necessarily valid and extend our knowledge of spatial relations — they are both synthetic and a priori. The laws of physics express necessary connections between events that go beyond mere observation. The question is therefore not whether such knowledge exists — it manifestly does — but how it is possible. What cognitive resources make it the case that we can know necessary truths about the structure of experience before any particular experience occurs?

6---full-notes/the-selves-of-schopenhaue.content:

The Selves of Schopenhauer and Nietzsche
Details
These two basically had the same internal division but assign opposite moral valuations to each side, and so they have different visions of human flourishing. Schopenhauer split the self into Will (animalistic drive, selfish, degrading) and Idea (reflective thought enabling transcendence). This meant that he believed that we were monsters, brutal, but the idea makes us noble. The idea is quite similar to Freud’s Id and Superego — unsurprisingly, since Freud denied reading Schopenhauer but was found posthumously to have annotated copies of his works hidden under his bed. Nietzsche, on the other hand, recast the duality as Dionysian (losing oneself, merging with the world, raw experience) and Apollonian (light, individuation, regulation, categorical thinking). The crucial difference is that he had a more balanced view, in that the Dionysian was required as it is the moments that we truly experience happiness and what we want (similar to when in a concert we may dance with everyone or such like that). The Apollonian, while necessary for civilization, produces an artificial, emotionally sterile existence when it dominates. It tells you what should make you happy through analysis and categories, but what we analytically decide should satisfy us rarely does — an insight echoed by Tim Wilson’s modern research on introspection (resembling the Spectacle as well).

6---full-notes/the-social-cognitive-pers.content:
Status: teen

The Social Cognitive Perspective
Details
The Social Cognitive perspective marked a shift toward a more scientific and empirical approach to personality. It posits that personality is not just an internal force, but is shaped through a dynamic interaction between our thoughts (cognition), our environment (social context), and our own behaviors. A key element of this theory is that we learn by observing others.
Albert Bandura and Modeling Albert Bandura was a pioneer of this view, arguing that much of our personality is learned through modeling—observing and imitating the actions of others. His famous Bobo doll experiment provided powerful evidence for this concept.


The Experiment: Children watched a video of an adult interacting with a large, inflatable “Bobo” doll. One group saw the adult act aggressively toward the doll—punching, kicking, and yelling at it—and then get rewarded. The other group saw the adult play non-aggressively.


The Results: When the children were later allowed to play in a room with the Bobo doll and other toys, those who had witnessed the aggressive model were overwhelmingly more likely to attack the doll themselves. They not only mimicked the adult’s specific actions but also devised new ways to be aggressive.


Bandura’s work demonstrated that personality traits like aggression are not just innate but can be learned through social observation. We learn not only how to behave but also what behaviors are likely to be rewarded by watching the people around us.

6---full-notes/the-society-of-the-specta.title: The Society of the Spectacle
6---full-notes/the-society-of-the-specta.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
The Spectacle
Details
Picture a baseball game: once a simple pastime, now a flashing billboard of ads, sponsored stats, and corporate-named stadiums. The game itself bends—rules tweaked to keep viewers hooked, not for love of play, but for profit. This is Guy Debord’s The Society of the Spectacle in action: a world where authentic life gets buried under a dazzling show put on by moneyed interests. What happens when the spectacle stops reflecting reality and starts replacing it?
“The Spectacle is not a collection of images, but a social relation among people, mediated by images.”
Debord saw the spectacle as more than just media—it’s the way consumerism and images hijack our relationships and existence. Think of your day: scrolling feeds, chasing trends, buying the next big thing because ads say it’s essential. The spectacle isn’t a sideline; it’s the main event. It tells us what matters—new cars, bigger houses—while quietly sidelining what’s real: connection, quiet, being. Baseball didn’t just get ads; it got remade to serve the spectacle’s hunger for attention and cash.
Today, this isn’t abstract. Social media turns hobbies into content, conversations into chats on corporate apps. The spectacle doesn’t coexist with life—it takes over, molding us into players in its endless growth game. We work to buy, buy to feel, and repeat, all while the raw, unscripted world fades. Debord nailed it: “The more his life is now his product, the more he is separated from his life.” We’re strangers to ourselves, and we are even more so to everyone else.  It ensures that we do not dip our toes into the water - it forces us to keep moving forward, like the man who commits suicide by walking into the ocean.
“That what the Spectacle shows is important, that what is important the Spectacle shows.”

The Stages of Sleep
Details
The process of sleep is studied by using things such as EEGs to elaborate the details and such of it. Upon falling asleep, a person will enter stage 1, this is when the eyes are nearly motionless and the EEG would show choppy, short waves. These waves indicate brain activity of some kind. Because these brain cells fire out of synchrony, they cancel each other out. In this stage, it is easy to wake someone up and they would say something like “I wasn’t sleeping.”
As sleep continues, a person would go into stages 2 through 4, which differs in the number of long, slow waves. Stage 2 has the fewest and stage 4 had the most. These waves indicated synchrony, which meant that there was decreased brain activity.
After this, they progress back through stages 3 and 2, then to REM sleep instead of stage 1 sleep. At the end of REM sleep, the sleeper again goes through 2,3,4 and the back through 3,2, and then REM. These cycles last for about 90 to 100 minutes on average in a healthy young adult.

The Stanford-Binet Test
Details
The Stanford-Binet IQ test is a foundational intelligence test that operationalized the psychometric approach through an age-scaled design. Items on the test are designated by the age at which a typical child can answer them correctly. This allows an examiner to determine a person’s mental age, which can then be compared to their chronological age.
The test uses an adaptive testing method, where the difficulty of questions is adjusted based on the test-taker’s performance, making the process efficient. The final score is an IQ score calibrated so that the mean at any age is 100. While it provides an overall IQ, it also yields subscores for more specific skills like visual reasoning and short-term memory.
This test was highly flawed for its time, and more effective tests have derived since its inception, although it is still the reason that this all started.

Status: adult
Tags: therapy CBT Clinical Psychology
The Structure of a Therapy Session
Details
In the first session of therapy, the main agenda is not to solve problems or figure out what to do and so on but rather elicit hope from the patient as well as psychoeducate them on anything that they haven’t understood or known about the process yet. First though, it always starts with a mood check.
Now, we can check by using public questionnaires such as the PHQ-9 or the GAD-9 or even using Beck’s item inventories to evaluate their hopelessness and so on. It may also be necessary to check on people’s medication use or other conditions that should be known. For this, it may be better to get in contact with the doctor, psychiatrist,… managing the patient.
Initially, we would obviously start by setting the overall agenda of the session, seeing what to do and everything. If anything arises during the session, we may discuss it collaboratively with the client to see if we should move to that idea instead.
After that, it’s a lot of psychoeducation as we reinforce the cognitive model, talking about automatic thoughts, making analogies for them to understand. We may even educate them on depression and why they should perceive it as a real and damaging illness like pneumonia or diabetes.
Moving on, we will try to understand and get what are the client’s values and aspirations to then be able to set goals from there. Then we will figure out how to achieve these goals with the given tools of CBT (and other therapies). Of course, all this should be documented in the action plan (summarized) to allow the client to have something to remind themselves about the process.
Last but not least, feedback is also important to know what has gone wrong and what needs to be changed from the process.

6---full-notes/the-synapse-and-neurotran.title: The Synapse and Neurotransmitter Re-uptake
6---full-notes/the-synapse-and-neurotran.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology neurology pharmacology
The Synapse and Neurotransmitter Re-uptake
Details
The synapse is the microscopic gap between neurons and is the primary site of action for many antidepressant medications. Understanding its function is critical to understanding the biological basis of depression treatment.
As Sapolsky explained, neurons communicate by sending an electrical signal down their length. To pass this message to the next neuron, the signal must cross the synapse. This is done by converting the electrical signal into a chemical one. The first neuron releases chemical messengers, called neurotransmitters (e.g., serotonin, dopamine), into the synapse. These chemicals then float across the gap and bind to receptors on the second neuron, delivering the message.
After the message is sent, the neurotransmitters must be cleared from the synapse to stop the signal. This happens in two main ways: degradation (enzymes break them down) or, more importantly, re-uptake. The re-uptake process involves specialized pumps on the first neuron that actively suck the neurotransmitters back in to be recycled.
This re-uptake mechanism is the key target for SSRI antidepressants. The theory of depression suggests a deficit of neurotransmitters in the synapse. By blocking the re-uptake pumps, SSRIs prevent the neurotransmitters from being cleared away too quickly. This allows them to remain in the synapse longer, stimulating the receiving neuron multiple times and amplifying their effect. This process demonstrates how medication can directly intervene in the brain’s fundamental communication system to treat the biological aspects of depression.

6---full-notes/the-synthesis-of-experien.title: The Synthesis of Experience
6---full-notes/the-synthesis-of-experien.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy psychology
The Synthesis of Experience
Details
At the very core of Immanuel Kant’s epistemology is the famous maxim: “Thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind.” This captures his foundational argument that human knowledge requires an inextricably linked partnership between sensibility (our capacity to receive sensory data) and understanding (our capacity to deploy concepts). Without sensibility, no object is ever given to us; without understanding, no object can ever be thought.
And so Kant starts with the breakdown. First, he begins with raw sensation, the biological triggering of sensory organs cause of external stimuli. Through the a priori pure intuitions of space and time, these are then converted into appearances. But this is not where it stops. Kant believes that the information received from external stimuli is a chaotic, unorganized mess of sensory input. For it to become a cohesive reality, it must undergo the “original synthetic unity of apperception.” This is basically the step where the mind goes through the concepts and what not (the understanding) to organize something cohesive.
Consider the everyday experience of a cup of coffee. The external world provides a disconnected manifold of sensations: a black color, a high temperature, a liquid viscosity, and a pungent aroma. The sensory organs receive these, but the synthesis of these elements into the unified object we recognize as “coffee” is an active imposition of the mind’s conceptual framework. The unification is ours, the material of it is the world’s.
Supporting Content
Additionally, Kant also argues that this is the “anthropology of knowledge,” in the sense that the rules governing the conceptual synthesis are universal and necessary for all rational human beings.

6---full-notes/the-theory-of-mind-case-s.title: The Theory of Mind Case Study
6---full-notes/the-theory-of-mind-case-s.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Massive Modularity Hypothesis Evolutionary Psychology Cognitive Psychology
The Theory of Mind Case Study
Details
The “Theory of Mind” (ToM) provides the most well-developed experimental case for a non-peripheral, central cognitive module, yet it perfectly illustrates the difficulty in distinguishing the Massive Modularity Hypothesis (MMH) from the Library Model of Cognition (LMC) [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].
The key evidence for a ToM module comes from dissociative studies. For instance, individuals with autism, even those with normal IQs, consistently fail standard false-belief tasks. Conversely, individuals with Williams syndrome, who often have low IQs and broad cognitive deficits, can pass these same tasks [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].
An advocate for MMH offers a straightforward explanation: there is a ToM module that is selectively impaired in autism but selectively spared in Williams syndrome.
However, an advocate for LMC can “mimic this explanatory strategy” [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf]. They can argue that what is impaired or spared is not a computational mechanism, but an innate, domain-specific body of knowledge about mental states. On this view, autistic individuals lack access to this crucial information, while Williams subjects retain it, allowing their general-purpose reasoning mechanisms to solve the task.
The situation is further complicated by findings that Williams subjects, while passing simple false-belief tasks, may fail more complex “higher theory of mind tasks” [cite: Tager-Flusberg_1997, as cited in Samuels_1998.pdf]. This pattern of results can be explained in at least three ways:


MMH Explanation: The ToM module is partially, not fully, impaired.


Mixed Explanation: A basic ToM module is intact, but the impaired general-purpose processors fail on the more complex tasks.


LMC Explanation: The body of ToM knowledge is intact, but the impaired general-purpose processors lack the computational power to solve the more demanding tasks.


Since none of these explanations is obviously more parsimonious or less ad hoc than the others, the currently available data does not provide a reason to prefer a modular account over an LMC-style account [cite: Samuels_1998.pdf].

6---full-notes/the-transcendental-deduct.title: The Transcendental Deduction
6---full-notes/the-transcendental-deduct.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy
The Transcendental Deduction
Details
After having established how the mind synthesizes data into unified experiences, Kant is not left with a massive burden of proof: how can we be sure that the concepts we impose on reality are actually valid and objective, rather than arbitrary fictions? This is the task of the Transcendental Deduction of the Categories. In 18th-century German jurisprudence, a “deduction” was a formal legal brief meant to establish the legal right, warrant, or legitimacy of a claim. Kant must provide epistemic justification rather than a simple logical deduction for his arguments.
After establishing the basic principles of metaphysics to outline the minimum, finite number of pure conceptual categories required for objective knowledge to exist, Kant gets to proving they are universally operative in the human cognition. He does this through differentiating between two concepts: “Judgments of Perception” and “Judgments of Experience.”
Perception is strictly subjective and phenomenological in the sense that different people can experience it differently, and as such, it is merely a statement about one’s internal state. A Judgment of Experience, however, transcends the individual. Because all rational humans share the same a priori categorical framework, when we subsume sensory data under these pure categories, we arrive at conclusions that are valid for everyone. For example, recognizing that a person walking toward you is not physically growing in mass—despite their retinal projection getting larger—is a concept-driven judgment of experience that overrides raw perception. This allows for non-absolute subjectivism, which is the whole point of Kant’s argument.

The Traumatized Parent
Details
Not only has research mostly shown that parents who are traumatized have a higher chance of getting hyper-aggressive or have emotional problems (which can affect their spouses as well), but they can also affect their children a lot from their actions and feelings.
A research done by Karlen Lyons-Ruth, observing children from “high-risk families” (poverty, single parents,…) showed that these parents either seem to be too preoccupied to their own problems to think or care about their children whilst the other often was helpless and fearful. Though both of these had something in common, they both wanted the comfort and the response to their needs, but through their own children. These mothers didn’t seem to be doing these things deliberately-they simply didn’t know how to be attuned to their kids and thus failing to respond to their cues and comforting, taking care of them. The hostile ones usually had a history of domestic violence and the dependent ones were more likely to have histories of sexual abuse.
When these kids eventually grow up, them developing mechanisms to cope, they would become more inconsolable, sullen or resistant to their misattuned mothers. This in turn would cause the mothers to see the child as not a part of her family, her love but as a stranger, and she gets mad, frustrated and sets the stage for subsequent abuse on the child.
Of course, these kids when they become adults all most likely cope with self-damaging impulsivity due to their unstable sense of self, inappropriate and intense anger, and recurrent suicidal behavior.
Supporting Content

6---full-notes/the-triune-brain-model-an.title: The Triune Brain Model and Depression
6---full-notes/the-triune-brain-model-an.content:
Status: adult
Tags: neurology psychology
The Triune Brain Model and Depression
Details
To understand the circuitry of depression, Sapolsky uses Paul MacLean’s triune brain model. This is not a literal anatomical map but a conceptual framework for understanding how different brain functions interact. It organizes the brain into three layers:


Layer 1: The Reptilian Brain (Hypothalamus, Brain Stem): This is the most primitive layer, responsible for automatic, regulatory functions essential for survival: body temperature, blood pressure, hunger, etc. It handles the body’s basic housekeeping.


Layer 2: The Limbic System (Amygdala, Hippocampus): This layer, more developed in mammals, is the seat of emotion. It processes feelings like fear, anger, anxiety, and pleasure.


Layer 3: The Cortex (especially the Prefrontal Cortex): This is the most recently evolved layer, responsible for cognition: thought, memory, planning, and abstract reasoning.


The critical insight from this model is that these layers are in constant communication, both top-down and bottom-up.


Top-Down Influence: A thought can trigger an emotion, which in turn triggers a physical response. For example, simply thinking about a past failure (Layer 3) can activate feelings of sadness and guilt (Layer 2), which then elevates stress hormones and heart rate (Layer 1). This is the mechanism by which psychological stress becomes a biological event, and it’s central to how rumination drives the physical symptoms of depression.


Bottom-Up Influence: Physical states can influence emotion and thought. For example, being hungry (Layer 1) can make a person more irritable (Layer 2) and lead to poorer, more impulsive decisions (Layer 3).


In depression, this system becomes pathological. The cortex (Layer 3) gets caught in a loop of negative thoughts, constantly sending “sad” signals to the limbic system (Layer 2), which then keeps the body’s stress systems (Layer 1) on high alert.

The Truth of Intelligence and Knowledge
Details
Emerson notes the way to discover oneness and to break down the walls of academia is to venture forth into the world, to exit the hallways of colleges and institutions, to find a more honest intelligence. Often, Emerson said, man thinking will play the role of the idiot. As he learns and discovers new things in the real world, he will be confronted by his own ignorance. It will be embarrassing, and it will result in admonishment rather than praise. The learned men of yesterday will look at him derisively as he stammers and stutters. Man thinking’s language will take the form of questions rather than answers. He will stand off in society, but that is fine. In doing so, he learns not what the world appears to be, he learns not what academics have proclaimed it to be; instead, he gains an intimate understanding of the world as he experiences it, as it is. The Two Classes of Hormones
Details
Basically these two classes of hormones that have different natures, characteristics, that’s really their only differences. Peptide Hormones (like Insulin) are built from amino acids that are hydrophilic. This allows them to travel freely in the watery bloodstream, but it does not allow them to pass through the membrane, meaning their receptors will be on the surface, these hormones usually have a part in modifying proteins. In contrast, steroid hormones (like cortisol and testosterone) are built from cholesterol and are hydrophobic (“water-hating”). They need a chaperone protein to travel through the blood, but once they arrive at a target cell, they can slip right through the membrane. Their receptors are located inside the cell, and their primary job is to march into the nucleus and directly change gene transcription. This makes their action slower to start but far more long-lasting.

6---full-notes/the-two-axis-of-quaic.title: The Two-Axis of QuAIC
6---full-notes/the-two-axis-of-quaic.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology university 3 - Tags/environment
The Two-Axis of QuAIC
Details
A central innovation of the QuAIC is its evaluation of problem behavior along two distinct axes: Aggression and Intrusion. This dual-axis model represents a significant departure from many traditional screening tools, which “focus largely on aggression” and may only trigger intervention when overt threats or physical violence occur. The elevation of “Intrusion” to an equal footing with “Aggression” is a deliberate and theoretically grounded design choice.  
The inclusion of the intrusion axis is explicitly informed by stalking research, which has highlighted that “the degree of intrusion and disruption to the lives of stalking targets cause as much, if not more, psychological harm as actual violence”. The QuAIC operationalizes this concept by assessing intrusion across three distinct facets:  
frequency (how often the behavior occurs), persistence (how long it has been going on), and disruption (its impact on the target’s life). This multi-faceted approach allows the tool to capture the cumulative and corrosive impact of behaviors that, when viewed in isolation, might appear “innocuous”. Behaviors such as “rudeness, passive aggression, repeated unwanted correspondence” may not meet the threshold for aggression but can, through their relentless and disruptive nature, create a profoundly unsafe and harmful environment for the target.  
This reframing of threat is uniquely suited to the specific context of Australian university campuses as described in the source material. The report notes that, unlike in the United States where campus threat assessment models were forged in response to mass casualty incidents, such events are exceedingly rare in Australia. Instead, the most commonly reported problem behaviors involve “bullying, inappropriate communication, cyber-abuse, stalking, physical altercations, sexual harassment, communicated threats, and threatening behavior”. These behaviors are characterized far more by their intrusive qualities—their unwantedness, persistence, and disruption to academic and social life—than by overt, targeted physical aggression.  
An assessment tool focused solely on a linear scale of aggression would be poorly calibrated to this reality. It would systematically fail to capture the severity and psychological harm associated with the most frequent types of campus concerns. The QuAIC’s dual-axis framework, therefore, represents a direct methodological adaptation to the specific threat landscape of the environment in which it is being applied. It is engineered to be sensitive to the actual problems that campuses like Victoria University most often face, not just the most extreme and feared scenarios.

The Two-Minute Rule
Details
The Two-Minute Rule is a powerful technique for establishing new behaviors. It involves aggressively dumbing down a desired habit until it takes less than two minutes to perform, thereby removing almost all friction and restricting the commitment required. But its power goes beyond just making things easy. When I talk about this as an “investment,” I mean that performing this two-minute action acts as a prior anchor. By showing up and doing the easiest possible version of the habit, we are putting investments into our identity. This forces our future selves to have an easier time committing to the larger, full-scale version of the habit later. It establishes the routine before optimizing it.

The Two-Person Hypothesis
Details
Philosopher Roland Puccetti argued that split-brain cases prove we are actually two people inhabiting one body (even in normal brains), and the corpus callosum just keeps the two people in sync.

Campbell’s Rejection: While Puccetti’s view is clear, it doesn’t survive scrutiny. In everyday life, split-brain patients are functionally integrated (walking, playing tennis). They do not act like two people fighting for the steering wheel.

The reality is more unsettling: There are not two souls, but zero “souls” (in the unified sense). The brain is a collection of mechanisms. Science can easily explain the wiring (The “How”), but it cannot explain how a unified subjective experience arises from these fragmented parts, nor can it help us imagine the fragmented experience of the patient.

6---full-notes/the-types-of-biases.title: The Types of Biases
6---full-notes/the-types-of-biases.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
The Types of Biases
Details
Explicit stereotyping—what people willingly self-report—has been the dominant research paradigm since the 1930s. Princeton studies tracking white Americans’ trait attributions about Black Americans from 1933 to 1993 show dramatic declines in endorsement of traits like “superstitious” and “lazy.” This could reflect genuine attitude change or merely increased awareness that such endorsements are socially unacceptable. There are problems with this methodology though: people may conceal their biases, or lack awareness about their own biases. The IAT (Implicit Association Test) addresses both problems by measuring reaction time differences when categorizing stimuli under compatible versus incompatible pairings (white+pleasant vs. black+pleasant). The classroom demonstration reveals the phenomenon experientially: pairing black names with pleasant words and white names with unpleasant words produces measurably slower responses for most participants, regardless of their conscious beliefs. Over 10 million people have taken online IATs, and the effects are robust across hundreds of studies controlling for order, side assignment, and stimulus type. Most strikingly, African Americans show attenuated but still present pro-white implicit bias—evidence that implicit associations are shaped by cultural exposure (shared media, shared teachers, shared imagery) rather than by group membership or personal endorsement.

6---full-notes/the-tyranny-of-the-majori.title: The Tyranny of The Majority
6---full-notes/the-tyranny-of-the-majori.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy
The Tyranny of The Majority
Details
As society moved towards democratic, industrial systems, Mill realized that the primary threat to individual liberty was no longer from individuals who simply had too much power, but rather from the majority and the moral coercion of the masses. To draw a definitive boundary between the rights of the individual and the authority of society, Mill introduces the Principle of Liberty, widely known as the Harm Principle. It posits that the only legitimate reason society can interfere with the liberty of an individual, to prevent the harm of others, so to say.
Mill’s principle functions by strictly excluding three specific categories of reasoning from public and legal justification. Paternalistic reasons (cannot coerce someone “for their own good”). You can’t force them even if you can advise or persuade them (though this line is fairly thin so to say). Second, society cannot affect or restrict an individual based on ideals of excellence of perfectionism. Third, society cannot restrict individuals based on mere preferences or disgust (repressing behavior simply because the majority does not like it). This effectively allows people to maintain their core liberties.

6---full-notes/the-underlife-and-seconda.title: The Underlife and Secondary Adjustments as Acts of Liberty
6---full-notes/the-underlife-and-seconda.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
The Underlife and Secondary Adjustments as Acts of Liberty
Details
Despite the totalizing pressure of the institution, Erving Goffman identifies a vibrant and secret social system he calls the “underlife.” This is a covert world of practices, relationships, and values that operates “in the cracks” of the official establishment, functioning as an underworld does to a city.
The building blocks of the underlife are “secondary adjustments.” These are the “unauthorized means” or “unauthorized ends” that inmates habitually use to get around the organization’s assumptions about them. Ranging from using a radiator to dry personal clothes to developing complex barter systems, these adjustments are how inmates reclaim a piece of the world for themselves.
These practices are more than simple rule-breaking; they are fundamental acts of self-preservation. By engaging in a secondary adjustment, an inmate obtains “important evidence that he is still his own man,” asserting that some part of his being remains under his own control. These are small but vital “movements of liberty” that allow an inmate to survive without total submission (“conversion”) or self-destructive rebellion (“intransigence”).
This dynamic reveals that the self is a dialectical entity that emerges through resistance. As Goffman profoundly observes, “it is… against something that the self can emerge.” Total commitment to any social unit implies a “kind of selflessness.” Secondary adjustments are the “little ways in which we resist the pull,” and it is this friction against the institutional machinery that generates a potent sense of personal identity. The underlife is the primary stage where the self is actively forged and defended.
This micro-sociological analysis complements macro-level theories of power, such as those of Michel Foucault. If the institution’s official structure is a Foucauldian network of power, the underlife’s myriad secondary adjustments are the points of resistance that are inherent to, and produced by, that very network. Goffman provides the ground-level, ethnographic texture for how these abstract power structures are lived, navigated, and subverted in everyday life.

6---full-notes/the-unnecessary-middleman.content:
Status: adult
Tags: morals philosophy
The Unnecessary Middleman of the Social Contract
Details
Hume now turns his argument to the purely philosophical, positing that this contract is unnecessary to justify political obligation. To do this, he separates human duties into wo categories: natural duties, which are spontaneous biological sentiments like the love of children or gratitude to benefactors, and artificial duties, which require a rational understanding of society’s general necessities. For Hume, both the duty to keep a promise (fidelity) and the duty to obey the government (allegiance) are artificial duties. Though from here he argues quite poorly.
He argues that we follow the king/sovereign because they ensure our survival and what not, so basically a Utilitarianism stance - one dependent on the utility of the sovereign depending on what they could do and not. This completely misses the point though. Hume attacks the social contract as if it were simply a historical claim about how governments start, completely ignoring the fact that Locke uses the contract as a strict, logical constraint on the form a government can legally take. For Locke, the real question is not whether a peasant actually signed a piece of paper; the question is whether the existing regime is structured in a way that free, equal, rational people could have contracted into it without violating their natural rights. Hume’s stance allows for an absolute, unchecked dictatorship could technically be justified if it happened to be highly efficient at managing the economy and maximizing overall societal pleasure or stability. This would be impossible under The Original Position because no rational person would want to advocate for this result.

6---full-notes/the-unworkability-of-util.title: The Unworkability of Utility
6---full-notes/the-unworkability-of-util.content:
Status: teen
Tags: morals philosophy sociology
The Unworkability of Utility
Details
Rawls believe that utilitarianism cannot be used as a foundational political philosophy for a modern democratic society because “utility” or “happiness” cannot be objectively measured and compared across an entire population. This is due to ideological pluralism, as people will naturally hold various frameworks of the “good life” that are conflicting or even incommensurable to each other. A devout religious ascetic, a hyper-competitive entrepreneur, and an introverted artist have radically different ultimate ends.
And because a comprehensive conception of the good is impossible to enforce without violating liberty, one must then rely on a partial conception of it, which is the framework of Primary Goods. Instead of attempting to maximize subjective psychological happiness, the state’s role is to ensure the fair distribution of objective, “all-purpose means.” Primary goods include basic rights and liberties, freedom of movement, free choice of occupation, income, wealth, and the social bases of self-respect. This is highly relative to From Utility to Liberty, which states that liberty is a necessity for people to find pleasure and happiness.

6---full-notes/the-use-of-non-prescribed.title: The Use of Non-Prescribed Stimulants and How Medication Teaches the Brain to Focus
6---full-notes/the-use-of-non-prescribed.content:
Status: teen
Tags: pharmacology biology ADHD
The Use of Non-Prescribed Stimulants and How Medication Teaches the Brain to Focus
Details
The drive to enhance focus is so pervasive that a significant portion of the population, particularly young adults, turns to stimulants without a clinical diagnosis. It’s estimated that up to 25-35% of college students and young professionals regularly use drugs like Adderall, obtained through a black market, to study, work, and manage the demands of daily life. This widespread use, which in some demographics now surpasses cannabis use, highlights a societal-level struggle with attention. This modern self-medication mirrors historical trends of using caffeine and nicotine to increase alertness and concentration. These substances all function by increasing levels of dopamine and norepinephrine, thereby engaging the brain’s focus circuits.
For a child diagnosed with ADHD, the mechanism of these stimulants goes beyond a simple chemical boost. Because a child’s brain is in a state of heightened neuroplasticity, the introduction of a stimulant like Adderall or Ritalin does something remarkable: it artificially creates the neurochemical state required for focus. This allows the child’s developing brain to experience what focused attention feels like, often for the first time. By chemically activating the frontal, task-related networks, the medication provides a scaffold that “teaches” the brain how to enter that state of concentration. The goal of this therapeutic approach is not just to manage symptoms in the short term, but to leverage the brain’s plasticity, allowing the child to learn and internalize the patterns of focus so that, ideally, they can access them later in life without chemical assistance.

The Wechsler Tests (WAIS)
Details
The Wechsler intelligence scales (WAIS for adults, WISC for children) are the most widely used IQ tests today. Like the Stanford-Binet, they produce an overall IQ score with a mean of 100.
Their defining feature is the emphasis on subscores, which provide a more detailed cognitive profile. The test is structured into four main indices:


Verbal Comprehension Index: Measures verbal reasoning and knowledge.


Perceptual Reasoning Index: Measures non-verbal, fluid reasoning.


Working Memory Index: Measures attention and short-term memory.


Processing Speed Index: Measures the speed and accuracy of simple visual scanning and discrimination.


This structure is clinically useful for identifying specific cognitive strengths and weaknesses, which can help diagnose learning disabilities or account for cultural factors affecting verbal scores.

6---full-notes/the-well-ordered-society.title: The Well-Ordered Society
6---full-notes/the-well-ordered-society.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy morals
The Well-Ordered Society
Details
This is John Rawls’s idea of a society where it is not only designed to advance the good of its members but is effective at regulating a publicly recognized conception of political justice. To be frank, it is not necessarily a novel or difficult definition of an ideal society, it has two defining features: that every citizen accepts and knows that the other accepts the same principles that they do. And that the society’s main political and social institutions actually satisfy, or are with good reason believed to satisfy, those principles.
The consequence is that a well-ordered society possesses a shared point of view from which citizens’ competing claims on institutions can be adjudicated. Unlike the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century religious conflicts — where no common basis for discussion existed — citizens in a well-ordered society can argue about justice in a principled, non-futile way. Rawls is careful to note that no set of principles resolves every question; what they provide is a framework within which discussion is possible and answers are reachable enough of the time.
Of course, there has not actually been a society that satisfies all of the conditions that Rawls stated above, and perhaps none can ever be in a precise sense. Nonetheless, it is usable as a tool and a comparison against other societies to see if one has dumped every principles in the trash and therefore cannot achieve this ideal or how close one is to it.

The Yuck Factor
Details
Humans pride themselves on being rational creatures who use logic and social rules to determine kinship. But beneath this cognitive surface lies a powerful, non-rational mechanism that shapes one of our most critical decisions: who we choose as a mate. Studies of individuals raised in Israeli kibbutzes and traditional Taiwanese households revealed a profound rule: if you are raised in close, domestic proximity with someone during the first six years of your life, you will not develop a sexual attraction to them later. They feel, irrevocably, like a sibling. This is known as the Westermarck effect. It’s not a conscious decision or a cultural taboo; it’s a deep-seated “yuck factor,” an imprinted sexual aversion. This shows that despite our large cortexes, we are still guided by ancient, subliminal rules. This very malleability—the fact that “family” can be defined by experience rather than blood—is what makes humans so susceptible to manipulations of “us” versus “them,” forming the psychological bedrock of both our greatest cooperation and our most horrific conf

6---full-notes/the-z-test.content:
Status: baby
Tags: statistics psychology
The Z-test
Details
This test asks whether a sample mean plausibly belongs to a population. To do so, take the gap between the sample and population means and standardize it: z = (x̄ − μ) / σ_x̄. The trap is the denominator. You’re placing a mean within the spread of means, not a score within the spread of scores, so you divide by the standard deviation of the distribution of sample means, σ_x̄ = σ / √n. Keep those two distributions distinct: scores scatter widely (σ = 20, individuals at 30, 70, etc.), but sample means cluster tighter around 50 because averaging smooths out variation. Here σ_x̄ = 20/√16 = 5, so z = (61 − 50)/5 = 2.2.

6---full-notes/the-advantages-of-the-syn.title: The advantages of the Syntopicon
6---full-notes/the-advantages-of-the-syn.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
The advantages of the Syntopicon
Details
The advantage also is that these books will most likely be what you want to read anyways. Therefore you can most likely skip to the point where you can think independently about it.
Useful as the Syntopicon is for that kind of reader, it is much more useful for the beginner. The Syntopicon can help such a reader in three ways: initiatively, suggestively, and instructively.
It works initiatively by overcoming the initial difficulty that anyone faces when confronted by the classical books of our tradition. These works are a little overpowering. We may wish that we had read them, but often we do not do so. We find ourselves advised from all sides to read them, and we are given reading programs, beginning with the easier works and proceeding to the more difficult ones. But all such programs require the reading of whole books or, at least, the integral reading of large parts of them. It is a matter of general experience that this kind of solution seldom achieves the desired result.
A syntopical reading of these major works with the aid of the Syntopicon provides a radically different solution. The Syntopicon initiates the reading of great books by enabling persons to read particular ones on the subjects in which they are interested; and on those subjects, to read relatively short passages from a large number of authors. It helps us to read in the great books before we’ve even touched them.
Syntopical reading in the great books, with the help of the Syntopicon, may also work suggestively. Starting from the reader’s existing interest in a particular subject, it may arouse or create other interests in related subjects. And once started on an author, it is hard not to explore the context. Before you know it, you have read a good portion of the book.
Finally, syntopical reading with the aid of the Syntopicon works instructively, in three distinct ways. This, in fact, is one of the major benefits of this level of reading.
First, the topic in connection with which the passage is being read serves to give direction to the reader in interpreting the passage. But it does not tell him what the passage means, since the passage may be relevant to the topic in several or many different ways. Hence the reader is called upon to discover precisely what relevance the passage has to the topic. To learn to do this is to acquire a major skill in the art of reading.
Second, the collection of a number of passages on the same topic, but from different works and different authors, serves to sharpen the reader’s interpretation of each passage read. Sometimes, they order it in context so that each becomes clearer. Sometimes the meaning of a series of contrasting or conflicting passages from different books is accentuated when they are read against one another. And sometimes the passages from one author, by amplifying or commenting on the passages from another, materially help the reader’s understanding.
Third, if syntopical reading is done on a number of different subjects, the fact that the same passage will often be found cited in the Syntopicon under two or more subjects will have its instructive effect. The passage has an amplitude of meaning that the reader will come to perceive as he interprets it somewhat differently in relation to different topics. Such multiple interpretation not only is a basic exercise in the art of reading but also tends to make the mind habitually alert to the many strains of meaning that any rich or complex passage can contain.
Because we believe that the Syntopicon can be useful to any reader wishing to read in the manner described in this chapter, be he a beginner or a mature scholar and researcher, we have taken the liberty of adopting its name for this level of reading. We hope the reader will forgive us what may seem to be a small self-indulgence. In return for that forgiveness, we would like to point out an important fact. There is a considerable difference between syntopical reading, with a small “s,” and Syntopical reading, where the latter phrase refers to reading the great books with the help of the Syntopicon. Syntopical reading, in the latter sense, can constitute a part of any syntopical reading project where the term is used in the former sense, and perhaps it would always be wise to start there. But syntopical reading with a small “s” is a term of much wider application than Syntopical reading.

Status: adult
Tags: psychology Evolutionary Psychology
The argument of Psychological Egoism and Retorts
Details
When discussing about the moralities of a person, the question of why people do things come up quite often. One viewpoint that is perhaps cynical is the stance of psychological egoism. Psychological egoism posits that basically everything that humans do are for their own self-interests, regardless of how altruistic it may seem. An argument in this stance is the observation that whenever a person gets what they want, they feel pleasure. Since helping someone makes you feel good, that is what one is chasing, not altruism. The philosopher Joel Feinberg proposes multiple arguments against this claim.
Feinberg first challenges the assumption that what we chasing is pleasure. Feinberg basically posits that even if pleasure accompanies successful action, positing it as the purpose of all action is a non sequitur. Feinberg thinks that pleasure is only something that goes with the desire-fulfillment, not because we are inherently and selfishly chasing it. The main feeling when we are finished with doing anything is satisfaction, regardless of the pleasure or nothingness that it might bring us. And so when a situation where we accomplish something and feel nothing, that would go against the psychological egoist’s argument.
The next argument is the argument of disinterested benevolence, where Feinberg turns the egoist’s own evidence against him. He brings this up with the example of Lincoln, when Lincoln says that his saving of a the pigs is only the result of his own pleasure for the peace of his mind. Feinberg argues that the only reason we have pleasure from the activity is because we desired the wellness for the person or the being in the first place, effectively turning the point that the psychological egoists made for themselves into one for altruism. In other words, the pleasure was, and always had been the result of concern for the pigs, not the selfish need of peace of mind after. He also argues the same for malevolence, in the sense that the person is ready to be benevolent to others, the same can be said for malevolence, as in both cases the person can also sacrifices his own wellbeing to achieve his malevolent goal.

6---full-notes/the-arguments-of-descarte.title: The arguments of Descartes
6---full-notes/the-arguments-of-descarte.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy psychology
The Argument from Certainty (The Cogito)
Details
The foundation of Descartes’ philosophy rests on a single, immovable point: the absolute certainty of one’s own existence. His method begins with radical doubt—skepticism applied to every aspect of reality. He proposes that we cannot trust our senses, as they often deceive us (e.g., optical illusions). He goes further to suggest that we cannot even trust the reality of the physical world or our own bodies, as it is logically possible that we are dreaming, or that a “malicious deceiver” (a god-like entity with bad intentions) is manipulating our perceptions to simulate a reality that does not exist.
In this scenario of maximum doubt, where the sky, the earth, and my own hands might be fictions, one truth remains unassailable: I must exist to be deceived. Even if my thoughts are hallucinations, the act of having them proves the existence of a thinker. The proposition “I am, I exist” (Cogito, ergo sum) is necessarily true every time it is conceived in the mind. This creates a fundamental asymmetry: the existence of the physical world is dubitable, but the existence of the self is indubitable.
The Nature of the “I” (The Res Cogitans)
Having established that he exists, Descartes asks what he is. Since he can doubt the existence of his body (it could be part of the dream), the “I” he has proven to exist cannot be defined by physical attributes. It cannot be an arm, a brain, or a human animal, as those are all dubitable.
He concludes that the only attribute inseparable from him is thought. He is a res cogitans—a thinking thing. This implies that the self is a non-physical substance, distinct from matter. If the self were physical, it would be subject to doubt; since it is not subject to doubt, it must be non-physical.

6---full-notes/the-balance-between-knowl.content:

The balance between knowledge and creativity
Details
Knowledge and creativity exist in a delicate, symbiotic balance. Knowledge provides the raw material—the “dots”—for creative thought. Without a deep well of information, concepts, and models, creativity is shallow and uninformed, unable to produce meaningful or robust insights. It becomes mere opinion.
However, an overemphasis on knowledge consumption is counterproductive. Constant information intake without dedicated time for synthesis leads to intellectual overload and stifles original thought. The mind needs periods of quiet “incubation” to process information, forge novel connections between disparate ideas, and allow for serendipitous insights to emerge. This is why the feeling of being “stuck” can often be solved by stepping away from the input.
The ideal process is not linear (learn then create) but cyclical. One must alternate between focused learning (input) and unstructured synthesis (output). The very act of creating—writing a summary, explaining a concept to someone else, or connecting notes—forces a deeper understanding of the knowledge consumed and is the primary engine of novel thought.

The brain identifying dangers
Details
Sensory information about the outside world arrives through all of our senses, eventually converging in the thalamus, which is an area inside the limbic system that outputs an integrated, coherent experience of what is happening to the body. The sensations are passed down to the amygdala (in the limbic, unconscious brain) and the frontal lobes, where they reach our conscious awareness.
The thing is, the time it takes for the info to reach the amygdala is several milliseconds faster than of the frontal lobes. This is bad, because the thalamus can also output dissociated fragments, which can create a feeling of danger, as time freezes, it will feel like it lasts forever. The amygdala identify input if it is relevant for our survival so fast and automatically that with the help of the hippocampus, a nearby structure that relates the new input to past experiences. If the amygdala senses a threat, it sends a message to the brain stem and hypothalamus, orchestrating a response from the body. And of course, because it processes the info faster than the frontal lobes, by the time we are conscious of what is happening, our body may already be on the move.
While the amygdala is usually very good at this, trauma can increase the risk of misinterpreting situations.

6---full-notes/the-brain's-negativity-bi.title: The brain's negativity bias
6---full-notes/the-brain's-negativity-bi.content:
Status: adult
Tags: neurology trauma
The brain’s negativity bias
Details
It is a common human experience that a single criticism can sting more than a dozen compliments, and a past failure can haunt us with more clarity than a string of successes. This isn’t a personal failing but a deep-seated feature of our brain’s architecture known as the negativity bias. From an evolutionary standpoint, this mechanism was a critical survival tool. For our ancestors, failing to remember the location of a predator, a poisonous plant, or a rival tribe had far more severe consequences than failing to remember a beautiful sunset or a pleasant meal. The brain, therefore, evolved to be like Velcro for bad experiences and Teflon for good ones, prioritizing the encoding of any information that could represent a potential threat.
The neurobiological machinery behind this bias involves a powerful partnership between two key brain structures: the amygdala and the hippocampus. The amygdala acts as the brain’s rapid threat detector or alarm system. When we experience something frightening, stressful, or socially painful, the amygdala becomes highly active. This activation triggers the release of stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, which essentially act as a “highlighter pen” for memory. These hormones send a powerful signal to the hippocampus—the brain’s center for forming long-term, episodic memories—effectively screaming, “This is important! Record this with high fidelity and make it easy to retrieve!” Which makes the brain reinforces its neurons connections extremely quickly and well, most of the time in only one trial.
As a result, negative memories are consolidated more robustly. They are encoded with greater detail, emotional intensity, and are given priority storage. This is why the memory of a car accident, a public embarrassment, or a harsh rejection can feel so vivid and intrusive, replaying in our minds with startling clarity. While this system was designed to protect us from physical harm, in modern life it can lead to rumination, anxiety, and a skewed perception of our own lives, where the weight of our negative experiences feels disproportionately heavier than the positive ones. Understanding this innate bias is the first step toward consciously counteracting it and giving more weight to the good.

6---full-notes/the-central-limit-theorem.title: The central limit theorem
6---full-notes/the-central-limit-theorem.content:
Status: teen
Tags: statistics psychology
The central limit theorem
Details
When the normal curve first arrived, people wondered why the bell curve existed in so much nature. And so this theorem was found out, the statement being: if a measured variable is the sum of many other random variables, that sum will be approximately normal. The pieces can be skewed, flat, exponential, anything; add enough of them and the total comes out normal.
This is exactly the case that happens in psychology. After all, in any situation, there are infinitely many factors contributing to how one acts. “How happy I am” is not driven by one thing but by many contributing factors — friends who called, cups of coffee, roses spotted, hours slept — each with its own odd distribution. Because your happiness score is their sum, happiness across people lands on a normal curve. A simulation makes it vivid: sum 50 skewed factors per person, repeat for hundreds of people, and the histogram of totals traces the bell curve.
However, for certain exceptions where the chance of something happening is so low, this theorem does not apply, e.g. “number of presidents in your family,” which is almost always 0. As the summing factors never yields a normal shape, we cannot apply the theorem.

6---full-notes/the-changes-of-the-rules-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
The law of the rules of the psyche
Details
As mentioned before, there exists a set of rules within a person to help him decipher and evaluate his experiences so that he can act accordingly to regulate his own behavior and others as well. The nature of these rules is that they are applied unconsciously. He completely just screens selectively, integrates, and sorts the flow of stimuli to form his responses. But this process is far from perfect.
When someone has not have enough experiences and such to prepare for a situation, they might infer incorrect meanings from the other person’s behavior; their underlying intentions, attitudes, their probable future towards him.
In anxiety, the rules are generally conditional: “If something occurs, it will probably have adverse results.” Hence, when it does, there is still a possibility of an innocuous outcome. In contrast, the rules in depression are absolute and unconditional: “My present deficiencies mean I shall always be a failure.”
In phobias, the rules are also conditional; which applies to situations the patient is successfully able to avoid. Though similar to anxiety in which the reactions are high probability, in phobia it can be fortified when a helpful person is with them.
In depression, the rules as formulated derive negative meanings and negative predictions from a present or past circumstance. There is no ‘escape clause’ as in anxiety and phobias.
In manic conditions, the content of the assumptions is opposite to that in depression. The rules are framed in such a way to exaggerate the gain and elevate self-esteem: “When people look at me, they admire me.”
In conclusion, when we question a patient about his ideas, he generally does not volunteer the rule that shapes his interpretation of events. Instead, he states his conclusion. We then have to work back to derive the rule, sometimes the patient is able to do this without difficulty.

6---full-notes/the-choice-in-fidelity.title: The choice in Fidelity
6---full-notes/the-choice-in-fidelity.content:
Status: adult
Tags: neuroscience genetics psychology
The choice in Fidelity
Details
Can the profound human experiences of love, loyalty, and fidelity be reduced to a simple neurochemical reaction? The question probes the very essence of our nature, pitting biological impulse against conscious will. Groundbreaking research, particularly in animal models, tempts us with a simple “yes,” revealing a clear, manipulable chemical pathway for attachment. Yet, human psychology and the complexities of our lived experiences demand a more nuanced answer. Fidelity is not a chemical switch to be flipped, but rather an emergent property that arises from a dynamic and often contentious dialogue between ancient biological systems and our uniquely human capacity for conscious choice.
The strongest case for a purely chemical basis for fidelity comes from the humble vole. Landmark studies revealed that monogamous prairie voles possess a higher density of receptors for the neuropeptide vasopressin (specifically, the V1a receptor) in key reward centers of the brain compared to their promiscuous meadow vole cousins. This was initially just a correlation, but the 2004 study by Lim et al. established a stunning causal link. By using a viral vector to increase the expression of this single gene in the brains of promiscuous voles, scientists were able to induce monogamous-like pair-bonding behavior. The mechanism is elegant: during intimacy, a flood of vasopressin and its partner hormone, oxytocin, activates these reward circuits, effectively conditioning the brain to associate a specific partner with a powerful feeling of security and pleasure. This research proves that a biological engine for attachment exists, providing the raw material for the feeling we call love.
However, the human story is not so simple. As psychologist Lisa Diamond outlines, the biological engine for attachment is not the only system at play. Humans operate with at least two functionally independent systems: the attachment system (love) and the mating system (lust). The attachment system, which we share with the voles, evolved from the infant-caregiver bonding mechanism and is governed by oxytocin and vasopressin. Its function is to create feelings of long-term union and security. The mating system, governed by sex hormones, evolved for reproduction and motivates sexual desire. The independence of these two systems explains a vast range of human experiences: the ability to feel deep, platonic love without desire, to feel sexual desire without love, and to have a sexual orientation that doesn’t strictly dictate who we can become romantically attached to. Fidelity, therefore, is not just about managing desire; it is about navigating the relationship between these two powerful, and sometimes conflicting, drives.
This brings us to the ultimate human factor: the cognitive system. Governed by the highly developed prefrontal cortex, our capacity for abstract thought, long-term planning, and value-based decision-making acts as a “CEO” or gatekeeper. This cognitive override is the critical difference between a human and a vole. It allows us to contextualize our feelings and make choices that may directly contradict our base-level chemical signals. The “friends with benefits” scenario is a perfect illustration. Two people can engage in intimate acts that release a cascade of bonding chemicals, yet one or both can consciously prevent an attachment from forming by framing the relationship as purely physical. Conversely, when one person in such an arrangement “catches feelings,” it is often because the repeated chemical exposure has overwhelmed their cognitive gatekeeper, allowing the attachment system to form a bond despite their initial intentions. This demonstrates that while the chemistry creates the potential for a bond, it is our mind that interprets, nurtures, or rejects it. Fidelity is ultimately a choice.
The complexities of this three-part system are thrown into sharp relief when we consider the thought experiment of a commercial “fidelity product.” Based on the vole model, a spray designed to enhance the V1a receptor pathway is scientifically conceivable. But it would be an “Attachment Spray,” not a “Fidelity Spray.” It could amplify the feeling of a bond, but it could not eliminate sexual desire for others nor could it prevent the conscious choice to be unfaithful. The ethical implications are a minefield, opening the door to chemical coercion and treating infidelity as a simple technical problem rather than a symptom of deeper relational issues.
In the final analysis, human fidelity resides in the space between impulse and intention. It is a testament to our complex nature that we are creatures of both profound biological drives and profound cognitive freedom. The chemistry of attachment provides the beautiful, powerful music of the bond, but it is the conscious mind that chooses to stay and listen.

The combining of the suicides
Details
Durkheim asserts that while the egoistic, altruistic, and anomic types of suicide are analytically distinct, they are not always found in a state of purity in actual experience. The different social causes of suicide can simultaneously affect the same individual, leading to composite varieties where the characteristics of several types are united in a single act. There is a peculiar affinity between egoism and anomy, as they are often two different aspects of the same social state; an individual detached from society (egoism) lacks the social hold needed for regulation (anomy). This can produce a mixed state where reflective sadness alternates with transports of desire. Similarly, anomy can be associated with altruism, as a single crisis may both disrupt an individual’s equilibrium and intensify their devotion to a collective cause, blending exasperation with a sense of duty. Even the contraries of egoism and altruism can combine, as seen in Stoic suicide, which blends the apathy of the egoist with the sense of duty of the altruist.

6---full-notes/the-cycle-of-suppression.title: The cycle of suppression
6---full-notes/the-cycle-of-suppression.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology creativity
The cycle of suppression
Details
Children are born with a natural spark of creativity, imagination, and deep emotional curiosity. However, many parents — instead of nurturing this spark — feel discomfort, irritation, or even anger when their children express these qualities freely. This reaction is not primarily because the child is wrong or problematic. Rather, it reflects an unhealed wound in the parent’s own history.
Many adults were once curious and imaginative children themselves. Yet at some point, through critical parenting, rigid schooling, social pressures, or emotional neglect, they were taught—often painfully—that their wonder, sensitivity, and playfulness were unwelcome. To survive emotionally, they internalized the belief that these vital parts of themselves were shameful, useless, or dangerous. They learned to suppress them.
When these adults become parents, they are confronted with their child’s wide-eyed questioning and open emotional expression. But instead of responding with joy, they often experience an unconscious pain. The child’s aliveness mirrors the parts of themselves they were once forced to abandon. Without awareness, they feel threatened and react defensively—through anger, annoyance, withdrawal, or even ridicule. Not because they hate their child, but because seeing that freedom reminds them of what they lost and never had the chance to reclaim.
Thus, the cycle continues:


The child’s creativity triggers the parent’s buried grief.


The parent, unable to tolerate that discomfort, suppresses the child’s creativity.


The child grows up, internalizes the suppression, and eventually repeats the same pattern.


This intergenerational chain can seem inescapable, but it is not. Recognition is the first step to breaking it. When a parent becomes aware of their emotional inheritance—realizing that their discomfort with their child’s wonder is a reflection of their own denied self—they can choose a different path. They can grieve their losses, begin reclaiming their suppressed vitality, and crucially, nurture the child’s curiosity instead of punishing it.

The details of automatic thoughts
Details
Guessing and asking about what one “must be thinking” made it possible to define with great precision what he was actually thinking.
These automatic thoughts actually had a great number of similar characteristics. They generally were not vague and unformulated, but specific and discrete. They were formed with only essential words in a sentence. Moreover, they did not occur as a result of thinking about an event or opinion, it just appeared, as if by reflex. And when they appeared, usually without effort and difficult to get out of one’s head.
In addition, the patient often considered these thoughts as reasonable, although others would say it doesn’t make sense. Most of the time there is no resistance in accepting the validity of these thoughts. And even if they did evaluate it all in a therapy session and eventually coming to the conclusion that it is illogical, later when they come again, they will revert to accepting the thoughts without second thoughts. And even when they external evidence directly object these thoughts, they will persist until the person stops having depression.
Also, the thoughts that were repetitive and seemed to be the most powerful, are idiosyncratic. They were closer to the patients’ problems, and not peculiar to a singular patient. They also involved more distortion of reality than other types of thinking.
All of this information of how someone thinks, functions to themselves will shed light on the inner workings of their emotional disorders. These thoughts prevailed more in depressed patients and less in ones who weren’t.

6---full-notes/the-detriment-of-bullet-p.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/The detriment of bullet point.md
6---full-notes/the-detriment-of-bullet-p.title: The detriment of bullet point
6---full-notes/the-detriment-of-bullet-p.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship writing neurology
The detriment of bullet point
Details
When we are presented with information, the mind can receive it in two fundamentally different ways. One path is sterile and direct, a transaction of data. The other is a living, breathing journey. Consider information delivered as a list of facts or bullet points. When the brain encounters such data, it performs a specific and limited task. The language centers, primarily Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas, get to work decoding grammar and assigning meaning to words. It is an intellectual exercise, a cool and clinical process of translation. The information may be understood, but it remains at a distance, an object to be analyzed rather than an experience to be felt. It rarely ventures beyond the analytical part of our consciousness, leaving the rest of our inner world untouched.
A story, however, invites the brain into a completely different kind of activity. It does not simply deliver information; it wraps it in a context of character, emotion, and sensory detail. As a narrative unfolds, something remarkable occurs. The brain of the listener does not just process words; it begins to simulate the experience being described. If a character runs through a forest, our own motor cortex, which coordinates movement, begins to light up. If the story details the aroma of freshly baked bread, our olfactory cortex activates. The brain ceases to be a passive observer and becomes an active participant. This phenomenon, known as neural coupling, even causes the listener’s brain activity to synchronize with the storyteller’s, creating a deep and powerful sense of shared understanding and connection.
This process extends beyond mere mental simulation into our very biochemistry. A compelling narrative, rich with relatable characters and emotional stakes, can trigger the release of oxytocin, the neurochemical responsible for empathy and social bonding. This fosters a sense of trust and connection with the storyteller and their message. As the plot builds tension and anticipation, our brains release dopamine, which heightens focus and aids in memory formation, making the embedded information more salient and memorable. During moments of conflict or drama, a touch of cortisol sharpens our attention, flagging the events as important. We are no longer just learning; we are feeling, and these feelings forge powerful neural pathways that anchor the information deep within our memory.
Ultimately, this is why a story is such a persuasive and enduring vessel for knowledge. When we are lost in a narrative, our critical defenses are lowered. We are not actively counter-arguing or fact-checking because we are busy living a vicarious experience. The information arrives not as a foreign object to be scrutinized, but as a natural part of a world we have come to inhabit and care about. This ancient mechanism, born from the evolutionary need to pass down vital survival knowledge through memorable tales, remains the most powerful tool for communication we possess. While facts may inform the intellect, it is the story that captures the whole person, transforming abstract data into a shared, and therefore accepted, human experience.

6---full-notes/the-development-of-the-li.title: The development of the Limbic Brain
6---full-notes/the-development-of-the-li.content:
Status: adult
Tags: ethology history neuroscience
The development of the Limbic Brain
Details
From the earlier days, neuroanatomists researched the brain of rodents and found that 40% of it was dedicated to olfactory functions, and so they called it the rhinencephalon, or the “nose-brain.” The more modern approach however, concluded that this part was the emotions of the brain, and so it would be the limbic system.
The perspective that settled this came from neither of the fields above, but of course ethology. Ethology proved that the reason the rat’s brain was so dedicated to olfactory functions is because that is its world of inciting emotions through processing the cues of its activities. Therefore, for a rat, the “nose-brain” is the emotional brain. This insight unified the two perspectives, showing that the limbic system’s primary inputs are whatever sensory information is most relevant to the emotional life of that particular species. In an auditory species like a songbird, the limbic system is more of an “ear-brain,” and in electric fish, it receives powerful inputs from electroreceptors. The limbic system is not fundamentally a “nose-brain,” but rather the brain’s hub for processing the most emotionally salient sensory information, whatever that may be.

6---full-notes/the-difference-between-th.content:
Status: adult

The difference between the two sides of the brain
Details
Back in the early nineties, some people divided the world between left-brainers, who were more logical, rational people and right-brainers, those artistic, creative one, this relates to the fact that when past trauma is present in the patients mind, the left deactivates and the right activates.
From this, we understand that the right brain is emotional, visual, spatial, intuitive, and tactual whilst the left is linguistic, sequential and analytical. As an example, when developing or learning a language, the left brain is more likely to be in use rather than the right, which is utilized for non-verbal communication mostly. Moreover, the two also perceives memories differently, the left remembers the vocabulary, words of description, perhaps dates, statistics whilst the right remembers the emotions evoked, the smell, perhaps.
Under normal circumstances both of these work together more or less smoothly. However, when one side shuts down, even temporarily can have a significant impact. The left hemisphere when deactivated will directly impact the capacity to organize experience into logical sequences and translate feelings and perceptions into words. Which means we cannot identify the cause and effect, or create plans for the future. A common case of this is when one is saying they are “losing their mind”, when their brain is overwhelmed and shuts down temporarily.
The other is when traumatized people remember of the past, their right brain reacts as if it is happening in the current moment. But because their left brain isn’t working well, they may not be aware that it is just a reenactment and feel furious, terrified, enraged, scared,… After this passes, they may look for someone to blame for it. Of course this can also occur in people who aren’t mature or something along those lines, but most of the time when they realize they will apologize and fix their mistakes, trauma directly affects the awareness of this matter.

6---full-notes/the-effects-of-neurofeedb.title: The effects of Neurofeedback

Status: teen
Tags: trauma psychology
The effects of Neurofeedback
Details
Building upon the real-time feedback mechanism, neurofeedback aims to induce lasting changes in brain function for individuals with PTSD. When the feedback system signals that the brain’s activity is moving towards a more regulated state (e.g., reduced hyper-arousal patterns, increased calm-alert patterns), this acts as a form of reinforcement.  
The brain, even operating below conscious awareness, tends to repeat actions or states that lead to positive or rewarding outcomes. This process mirrors principles of operant conditioning. By consistently receiving positive feedback for producing healthier EEG patterns, the brain gradually learns how to generate these states more readily and reliably.  
This learning is not superficial; it engages the brain’s neuroplasticity – its fundamental ability to modify its own structure and function in response to experience. Repeated neurofeedback sessions act like targeted exercise, strengthening the neural pathways associated with self-regulation, calm, and focus, while potentially weakening those associated with the persistent trauma response.  
The ultimate therapeutic goal is to enhance the brain’s intrinsic capacity for self-regulation. The aim is for the individual to maintain these more stable and adaptive neurological states naturally, outside of the training sessions and without reliance on the feedback device, leading to a reduction in core PTSD symptoms related to nervous system dysregulation.
