6---full-notes/the-elusiveness-of-histor.title: The elusiveness of historical facts
6---full-notes/the-elusiveness-of-histor.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading history
The elusiveness of historical facts
Details
In a jury, when determining a suspect if he is guilty or not, we must have witnesses and stories of it. But we are never sure that that was the fact, even if the witness was there, we have no way of knowing for sure if it is the truth, because we were never there. Even if we applied human psychology tricks to know if they are lying or not, then we still do not know the truth, and so there will always be doubt, although that doubt must exist with evidence on why it does.
In history, every witness is dead, all these facts are often guessed, estimated and so on, they are not cross-examined, there is no guarantee they know what they are talking about either. Then this now means that it’s even more difficult to be sure about a relatively simple matter if it is true or not, we can only trust the author is truthful.
Of course, about some kinds of historical fact we can be pretty certain. America was involved in a Civil War that began with the firing on Fort Sumter, on April 12, 1861, and ended with the surrender of General Lee to General Grant at Appomattox Court House, on April 9, 1865. Everyone agrees about those dates. It is not likely (though it is not totally impossible) that every American calendar was incorrect at that time.
But how much have we learned if we know exactly when the Civil War started and when it ended? Indeed, those dates have been disputed—not on the grounds that the calendars were wrong, but that the war really started with the election of Lincoln in the fall of 1860 and ended with his assassination five days after Lee’s surrender. Others have claimed that the war started even earlier—as much as five or ten or twenty years before 1861—and we know that it was still actually being fought in outlying parts of the United States, to which word had not yet come of the Northern triumph, as late as May, June, and July, 1865. And so on..
And we will continue to question everything from one singular fact, and a lot of those questions won’t be answered due to their restrictions of the truths.

6---full-notes/the-empirical-rule.title: The empirical rule
6---full-notes/the-empirical-rule.content:
Status: adult
Tags: statistics psychology
The empirical rule
Details
For a normal distribution it pays to memorize roughly how much of the data sits within a given number of standard deviations of the mean, because it lets you sanity-check any probability calculation at a glance. The area from the mean out to +1 SD is about 34%; by symmetry the same holds out to −1 SD, so ±1 SD captures ≈ 68% of scores. ±2 SD captures ≈ 95%, and ±3 SD captures ≈ 99% — so a z-score beyond ±3 is genuinely rare (you would be more extreme than ~99% of the population).
As these areas are quoted in deviation, you can apply them to any normal curve. You could even convert them into z-scores with x = μ + z·σ: on a test with mean 70 and SD 9, a score exactly 3 SD above the mean is 70 + 3×9 = 97. Use the rule as a reality check before trusting an exact figure pulled from a table
Supporting Content

References
This rule can obviously be applied to the table and z-scores themselves. The area of the curve can be calculated through the equation: (bigger slice) − (smaller slice); e.g. P(0.6 ≤ z ≤ 1.09) = 0.3621 − 0.2257 = 0.1364. A tail beyond z = 0.5 − (slice from 0 to z); e.g. P(z ≥ 1.09) = 0.5 − 0.3621 = 0.1379. Everything below a positive z = 0.5 + (slice from 0 to z); e.g. P(z ≤ 1.09) = 0.5 + 0.3621 = 0.8621. Negative z’s need no new numbers — by symmetry the slice from 0 to −z equals the slice from 0 to +z; the sign only says which side.

6---full-notes/the-falsity-of-psychiatry.content:
Status: baby
Tags: psychology
The falsity of Psychiatry
Details
Psychiatry is a subspecialty of medicine, aspiring to define mental illness as precisely as other physical illnesses. But given the complexity of the mind, brain and human attachment systems, we cannot even come close to that precision. It is usually diagnosed by the mindset of the practitioner rather than cold hard facts.
The first systematic manual of diagnoses, which was recognized by the American Psychiatric Association (APA). DSM-III warned explicitly that its categories were insufficient to be used in forensic settings or for insurance purposes. The fear of mathematics
Details
Most people think that they cannot read this at all. They all have their reasons for feeling such a way. But the problem is partly that math is a language, and we must learn it like one. Different from other languages, it only needs to be learnt once, not written and verbally but only written.
As so we should treat it like learning a language, we should search up syntaxes that we do not understand, concepts, expressions, everything.
Another point I want to make is about the beauty of math, which is not told enough, or because academic math is truly repetitive and boring. But if you start with an author like Euclid, you will be able to experience one of the most lucid and beautiful works of any kind that has ever been written (Elements of Geometry).
Moving on to propositions and their construction.
Constructions can be interpreted as serving another purpose. They bear an obvious similarity to postulates; both constructions and postulates assert that geometrical operations can be performed. In the case of the postulates, the possibility is assumed; in the case of the propositions, it is proved. The proof, of course, involves the use of the postulates. Thus, we might wonder, for example, whether there is really any such thing as an equilateral triangle, which is defined in Definition 20. Without troubling ourselves here about the thorny question of the existence of mathematical objects, we can at least see that Proposition 1 shows that, from the assumption that there are such things as straight lines and circles, it follows that there are such things as equilateral triangles.
Consider the difference between the argument of Proposition 5, as outlined here, and even the simplest of syllogisms, such as the following:
All animals are mortal;All men are animals;Therefore, all men are mortal. 
There is something satisfying about that, too. We can treat it as though it were a piece of mathematical reasoning. Assuming that there are such things as animals and men, and that animals are mortal, then the conclusion follows with the same certainty as the one about the angles of the triangle. But the trouble is that there really are animals and men; we are assuming something about real things, something that may or may not be true. But Euclid’s proposition does not suffer from this. He is saying if these things exist, then this is right.

6---full-notes/the-foundations-of-quaic.title: The foundations of QuAIC
6---full-notes/the-foundations-of-quaic.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology university
The foundations of QuAIC
Details
The development of the QuAIC was not an abstract academic exercise but a direct response to “organizational demands that sought a standardized approach to early reporting”. Institutions required a practical method for front-line personnel and potential targets of concerning behavior to report their concerns in a consistent and quantifiable manner. The primary function of the QuAIC is to serve as a screening tool that can be “used easily by non-clinicians to quantify their emotional responses to problem behavior”. This design principle is critical, as it effectively democratizes the initial stage of the threat assessment process, empowering individuals without specialized clinical or forensic training to contribute meaningful data.  
The core objective of the tool is to provide an “objective measurement and quantification of the ‘gut feeling’” that often accompanies experiences of concerning behavior. By translating subjective intuition into a structured output, the QuAIC aims to remove the “reliance on personal thresholds and biases for both targets and responders”. This addresses a fundamental vulnerability in many reporting systems. Without a standardized framework, the decision to escalate a concern can be highly variable, depending on the reporting individual’s temperament, cultural background, or tolerance for conflict, as well as the personal biases of the staff member receiving the report. A stoic individual might under-report a serious pattern of harassment, while a more anxious person might frame a minor issue in alarming terms. This inconsistency creates systemic risk, as genuinely dangerous situations may be overlooked if they are not articulated in a way that triggers an institutional response.  
The QuAIC’s intervention is therefore systemic in nature. It is designed to correct this flaw by creating a more reliable and equitable “front door” to the university’s safety and support apparatus. By prompting users to answer four specific questions about the behavior—its level of aggression, frequency, persistence, and disruptive impact—it channels subjective experience into objective data points. This structured data can then be processed, triaged, and acted upon with a degree of consistency that is impossible to achieve with purely narrative or ad-hoc reporting. This ensures that cases are evaluated based on the intrinsic characteristics of the behavior in question, rather than on the communication style of the person reporting it.

6---full-notes/the-g-and-s-factors-of-sp.title: The g and s factors of Spearman
6---full-notes/the-g-and-s-factors-of-sp.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Cognitive Psychology intelligence
The g and s factors of Spearman
Details
Based on his psychometric research, Charles Spearman proposed a two-factor theory of intelligence. He observed that performance across a wide range of seemingly unrelated mental tasks was positively correlated, leading him to infer the existence of a single, unifying intellectual capacity.


The g factor (general intelligence): Spearman argued that a “general” ability, which he labeled g, underlies all intelligent behavior. It represents a common mental energy or power that is required for any cognitive task. A person’s level of g is seen as the primary determinant of their overall intellectual ability.


The s factor (specific abilities): To account for the fact that correlations between tasks were not perfect, Spearman also proposed that each task requires a set of s factors, or “specific” abilities. These are abilities unique to a particular task, such as mechanical, musical, or logical skills.


In this “monarchic” theory, intelligence is a combination of one’s general ability (g) and various specific abilities (s). While g rules over all cognitive functions, the s factors explain why an individual might excel in one area but not another, despite having the same level of general intelligence.

6---full-notes/the-hybrid-brain.title: The hybrid brain
6---full-notes/the-hybrid-brain.content:
Status: adult
Tags: neuroscience psychology Evolutionary Psychology
The hybrid brain
Details
The contemporary understanding of brain function has moved beyond the historical debate of whether the brain is a collection of highly specialized modules or a single, general-purpose processor. The prevailing theory today is a hybrid model, which posits that the brain is a dynamic combination of both specialized components and generalist, flexible networks.
On one hand, there is clear evidence for modularity, or localization of function. Specific brain regions are reliably associated with particular tasks. Classic examples include Broca’s area for speech production or the fusiform face area (FFA) for facial recognition. These specialized modules are like expert tools, optimized through evolution to perform critical, recurring tasks with high speed and efficiency. They handle the predictable aspects of our interaction with the world.
On the other hand, no complex behavior relies on a single module in isolation. Higher-order cognition—such as reasoning, planning, and creative problem-solving—depends on general-purpose networks. These are large-scale, distributed circuits that connect and coordinate activity across different brain regions. Networks like the executive control network or the default mode network provide the computational flexibility needed to integrate information from different modules, manage novel situations, and orchestrate goal-directed behavior.
The synthesis of these two concepts forms the hybrid model. The brain is neither a set of isolated specialists nor a single jack-of-all-trades. Instead, it is best conceptualized as a team of experts (modules) managed and coordinated by a flexible, system-wide executive team (general-purpose networks). This architecture allows the brain to be both incredibly efficient at familiar tasks and remarkably adaptive and creative when faced with new challenges.

The illusion of learning
Details
Even though due to the ineffectiveness of cramming, people still continue to do this. One reason may be that it has become such a phenomenon of everyone who studies that they think that its effective because other uses it as well. But another theory can derive from it, a subtler way, is that this feel of familiarity with a text and fluency in reading can create the illusion of learning. Students usually try to capture everything that they listen, but the thing is they robotically copy everything back, not interpreting or anything else in their own words. This actually has no correlation between the significance of the ideas that they describe, their application, or their relation to what you already know.
Too common is the experience of a college professor answering a knock on her office door only to find a first-year student in distress, asking to discuss his low grade on the first test in introductory psychology. How is it possible? He attended all the lectures and took diligent notes on them. He read the text and highlighted the critical passages.
How did he study for the test? she asks.
Well, he’d gone back and highlighted his notes, and then reviewed the highlighted notes and his highlighted text material several times until he felt he was thoroughly familiar with all of it. How could it be that he had pulled a D on the exam?
Had he used the set of key concepts in the back of each chapter to test himself? Could he look at a concept like “conditioned stimulus,” define it, and use it in a paragraph? While he was reading, had he thought of converting the main points of the text into a series of questions and then later tried to answer them while he was studying? Had he at least rephrased the main ideas in his own words as he read? Had he tried to relate them to what he already knew? Had he looked for examples outside the text? The answer was no in every case.
He sees himself as the model student, diligent to a fault, but the truth is he doesn’t know how to study effectively.

6---full-notes/the-importance-of-a-contr.title: The importance of a control group
6---full-notes/the-importance-of-a-contr.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology
The importance of a control group
Details
The reason these groups are so important is that they isolate factors, variables that could have influenced the other group. So for example, a summer camp where campers played video games and only video games for a week, at the end of the summer camp, they have better attention span, is this really because of the video game ? Now we add a control group, a group that receives relatively the same treatments except they do not play video games, they do normal activities. Now we can identify if the independent variable that was the video game truly caused the result that attention span gets better.
In a treatment outcome research, which are experiments to determine the effectiveness of a treatment, more procedures are applied to validate the tests even further. Psychologists and psychiatrists evaluating the effectiveness will be subjected to a double-blind procedure, meaning they have no idea the person they are evaluating will be from which group, avoiding biases. The control group will also receive something called a placebo, which is basically nothing, just to make them think that they are receiving something. This helps validate the test even further as the control group will function as if they received treatment as the other group.
Supporting Content
However, as highlighted by Irving Kirsch’s meta-analyses on antidepressants, maintaining a true double-blind is frequently compromised by the physical reality of the medications. Kirsch’s analysis revealed that the placebo effect alone accounts for roughly 75% of the reported benefits in antidepressant trials. More troublingly, drugs prescribed for entirely different conditions (like sleep aids or anti-anxiety meds) produced similar improvements in depressive symptoms during trials. The likely culprit is the presence of side effects. Real medications have noticeable side effects, whereas standard sugar-pill placebos do not. When a patient begins experiencing dry mouth or lethargy, both the patient and the purportedly “blind” doctor can easily deduce that they are in the experimental group. This realization triggers an enhanced psychological placebo response and alters how the doctor interacts with the patient, effectively breaking the integrity of the experiment.

The importance of the Womb
Details
From the time that they are in the womb, fetuses are already keeping track of everything that is happening from their mother and indirectly from the environment (as the mother is reacting to it) and change adaptably to it. For example, the “Dutch Hunger Winter” provides a chilling case study. Fetuses whose mothers endured a sudden famine during WWII had their metabolisms permanently programmed for scarcity. When they grew up in a world of abundance, this “thrifty phenotype” led to soaring rates of obesity and diabetes. This was an environmental effect so powerful it was passed to the next generation, masquerading as a genetic legacy. This principle extends beyond nutrition. A mother’s stress levels can sculpt the developing brain of her fetus, predisposing it to anxiety. A fetus can even learn to recognize the rhythm of a story like The Cat in the Hat read aloud. To ignore the prenatal world is to ignore the first and perhaps most formative chapter of our lives.

6---full-notes/the-interviewing.title: The interviewing
6---full-notes/the-interviewing.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship
The interviewing
Details
If your written application is the blueprint of your potential, the interview is where you build the three-dimensional model. It is a crucial extension of the written application, offering a chance to breathe life into the words on the page and demonstrate the person behind the achievements. Success in this phase hinges on understanding that this is not a test of memory, but a demonstration of character, passion, and preparedness.
Your primary goal is to add new layers to your story; you must not just repeat your essays. The interview committee has already read your application; now they want to meet you. This is where the intangibles come into play. The clarity and confidence of your language, and the positive energy and vibe you project, are just as important as the content of your answers. This is your opportunity to convey enthusiasm for your field, resilience in the face of challenges, and a genuine passion for the opportunity the scholarship represents. These are qualities that can only be truly felt in a live conversation.
Thorough preparation is non-negotiable. The mantra to live by is: “Prepare, prepare, and prepare!” This involves more than just re-reading your application. Research the scholarship’s values and mission, and anticipate questions by studying examples from similar programs, such as the Chevening or NZ Manaaki scholarships. Conduct a mock interview with a mentor, professor, or friend to practice articulating your thoughts clearly and concisely under pressure. However, preparation also means cultivating your own questions for the interviewers. 6---full-notes/the-kinds-of-practical-bo.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
The kinds of practical books
Details
Any book that contains rules, prescriptions or maxims, or directions are practical books. But furthermore, it may contain principles that underlie those rules to explain why they work and how they do so.
From this insight, we can divide practical books into two main groups. One is primarily presentations of rules, the other is concerned with the principles that generate said rules. The distinction is not obvious as both of these things can be found in the same book. Thing is, the point is one of relative emphasis. The book of rules in any field will be recognizable as practical. The book of principles deals with theory of practicing rules, and so you can tell if it’s practical. All of the fields that practical books are about are usually fields which men can do better or worse.
The major propositions to look for in a rulebook are, of course, rules. It is expressed by an imperative rather than a declarative sentence since it is a little more emphatic, but not necessarily more memorably. It recommends you to do something as worth to gain a certain end. The book of principles on the other hand will try to show that rules are sound. They have to appeal and persuade you that they are good, in any way they can.
In the other kind of practical books, principles underlying rules will look exactly like those in a purely theoretical book. The propositions will state that something is the case, then the arguments will try to show that it is so.

The knowledge of living

The idling brain, or the “default state network” (DSN), is when we are not particularly focusing on imagining or thinking about anything really and rather just emptying our minds. It turns out that in this state, humans start working on ourselves, creating our sense of “self”. The midline structures are the most active during this process, and the posterior cingulate seems to work the most, it gives us a sense of where we are, like a GPS. It is also strongly connected to the MPFC, it is also connected with areas of the brain that registers sensations from the body.
In PTSD patients, the difference was that they had none of this, their midline structures barely worked, the only thing that did was the GPS, which is responsible for basic orientation of space. The explanation for this is that they have effectively shut down these areas, not allowing the brain to feel terror or fear, but in such they have also prevented it from feeling other emotions, deadening their capacity to feel alive. What this also explains is why traumatized people are so lost. How could they know what to do, what decisions to make when even them couldn’t define what they want, when they have already lost their sense of self ? 6---full-notes/the-library-model-of-cogn.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/The library model of cognition.md
6---full-notes/the-library-model-of-cogn.title: The library model of cognition
6---full-notes/the-library-model-of-cogn.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Cognitive Psychology Fodor’s mind model
LMC
Details
The Library Model of Cognition (LMC) is a cognitive architectural thesis proposed by Richard Samuels (1998) as an alternative to the Massive Modularity Hypothesis (MMH). LMC posits that the human mind contains few domain-specific computational mechanisms (e.g., Darwinian modules), especially for central processes like reasoning and belief fixation.
He instead proposes that Domain-specific structure arises from innate, domain-specific bodies of knowledge—truth-evaluable systems of mental representations (e.g., core principles for physical objects, number, or intuitive psychology). These bodies of knowledge are “inert” (representations manipulated by processes) and are operated on by domain-general computational mechanisms, which are not dedicated to specific domains but can flexibly apply knowledge across tasks. LMC denies that central cognition requires massive domain-specific modules (hardware or algorithms); innate knowledge suffices for specialization without modular encapsulation or dedication.
Key points:

Compatible with evolutionary psychology’s commitments (e.g., computationalism, adaptations, universal human nature, evolutionary analysis) but incompatible with MMH’s claim of “largely or entirely” modular central systems.
Addresses adaptive problems (e.g., social exchange, incest avoidance) via general mechanisms + specialized knowledge, avoiding MMH’s overcommitment to unproven modular hardware.
Critiques of MMH: Optimality and solvability arguments fail to prefer MMH over LMC, as domain-general mechanisms with innate knowledge can handle domain-dependent error, unlearnable relations, and combinatorial explosion without modules. Experimental evidence (e.g., Theory of Mind dissociations in autism/Williams syndrome) doesn’t distinguish LMC from MMH.

LMC is argued as more effective/parsimonious than MMH because it provides innate domain-specificity without requiring implausible massive modularization of central processes, making MMH “unwarranted and unmotivated” (Samuels, 1998, p. 576).

Newton’s discoveries were some of the first to ever prove the limits of priori and intuition. This trend reached the peak in modern physics with the Double Slit experiment. When light is fired through two slits, it behaves as a wave (creating interference patterns), but when detectors are added to see which slit a photon goes through, it behaves as a particle, and the interference pattern vanishes.
We can describe this behavior with mathematics (quantum probability distributions), just as Newton described gravity, but we cannot visualize it. Our natural, common-sense concepts of “waves” and “particles” fail to capture reality. This suggests that the universe is not obligated to be understandable to the human mind. 6---full-notes/the-liver-in-eating.content:
Status: teen
Tags: biology
The sign to stop eating
Details
The liver is a major source of information in this mechanic, as its job is to monitor and control the major nutrient used as short-term energy: glucose (blood sugar).
When a meal is done, there’s usually a lot of glucose, some of it is stored, some is converted into glycogen and various fatty acids which are used for later. When energy is required, these substances are used and burnt to be used as glucose (energy).
The liver manages this conversion process and informs other organs of where this process is going. If the balance tips toward storage (when we are eating too much), it will send a satiety signal to stop the animal from eating. Same for the opposite. The evidence of this came from injecting glucose into hungry dogs, only into the vein that was leading to the liver though.
Now though, we recognize that the process in between announcing that the body is low on glucose and when we actually get supply is really slow. To counter this, the liver must anticipate the body’s future needs, so that eating has already initiated.
It does this by responding to a characteristic drop and rise to the glucose level. Simply, when we’re low on glucose, glycogen turns into glucose, this indicates a drop and rise, characteristically, and that is what the liver responds to.

6---full-notes/the-market-is-always-righ.title: The market is always right
6---full-notes/the-market-is-always-righ.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market welfare
The market is always right
Details
The First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics says that competition maximizes welfare. Gruber credits the grand name to Paul Samuelson, “not a humble man.” Define welfare as consumer surplus plus producer surplus, weighting consumers and producers equally. Then the competitive equilibrium that Lecture 7 derived as a positive prediction is also the normatively best outcome.
Gruber shows it with a price ceiling (Figure 9-12). Someone argues that lower prices are always better for consumers and caps the price at P2, below the equilibrium P1. At P2, producers supply only Q2 because they must stay on their supply curve, so only Q2 is traded. The areas are:

R: consumer surplus that survives (above P1, below demand, up to Q2)
S: the rectangle between P2 and P1 on the Q2 units still sold
T: producer surplus that survives (below P2, above supply)
U: producer surplus on the units between Q2 and Q1 that are no longer made
V: consumer surplus on those same lost units

Before the cap, consumer surplus is R + V and producer surplus is S + T + U. After it:

Consumers lose V on trades that no longer happen, but gain S because they pay less on the units they still buy. Consumer surplus becomes R + S.
Producers lose S to consumers and U on lost trades. Producer surplus becomes T.

S is a transfer: it moves from producers to consumers. Since welfare is the sum of the two, transfers don’t change it. U and V simply vanish. That vanished amount is the deadweight loss: the net loss from trades that would have made both sides better off but don’t happen. The competitive equilibrium has no deadweight loss, because every trade that benefits both sides gets made. Any departure from it removes some of those trades and lowers welfare.
Here are worked numbers (not in the lecture), using Lecture 7’s market (Q = 48 − P, Q = 0.6P, P1 = 30, Q1 = 18) with a cap at $20:

Producers supply 0.6 × 20 = 12 units. The 12th unit was worth 48 − 12 = $36 to its buyer.
The areas are R = 144, S = 120, T = 120, U = 30 and V = 18.
Before the cap, consumer surplus is 162 and producer surplus 270, a total of 432.
After it, consumer surplus is 264 and producer surplus 120, a total of 384.
The deadweight loss is U + V = 48, which matches ½ × 6 × (36 − 20).

Consumers as a group gain here, from 162 to 264, because the transfer S outweighs the trades V they lose. A price ceiling can help consumers and still shrink the total.
Under these assumptions, Gruber says, we should even let people sell kidneys on eBay: the poor seller and the rich buyer are both better off. Lecture 1 covered why we might object: fairness, and markets that may not work well. Those are exactly the assumptions the course relaxes later. That’s why Gruber calls economics, at bottom, a right-wing science. Its starting point is that under perfect competition the market knows best and should be left alone. Everything after builds from there.

6---full-notes/the-masterplan-of-scholar.title: The masterplan of scholarship
6---full-notes/the-masterplan-of-scholar.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship
The masterplan of scholarship
Details
The ambition to win a scholarship is a powerful starting point, but without a clear plan, it can quickly become an overwhelming and chaotic pursuit. The key to transforming that ambition into achievement is to move from passive desire to purposeful Action. This requires architecting a Master Plan—a strategic, living document that turns the daunting marathon of applications into a series of manageable, intentional steps.
The foundation of your master plan is structure and preparation. It begins by creating a prioritized list of scholarship opportunities, focusing your energy on the awards that best align with your profile and goals. From there, you must implement a Scholarship Schedule, integrating the application process so it becomes one integral part of your life, not a frantic, last-minute rush. A critical component of this is to build a Scholarship “Toolbox”: a centralized collection of your core documents—transcripts, a master CV, draft essays, and lists of potential recommenders—that can be customized for each application, saving you invaluable time and effort.
However, a master plan is more than just schedules and documents; it is also a commitment to deep engagement. You must immerse yourself in the scholarship’s space, mentally and physically. This means understanding its mission, its values, and the community it has built. As you do this, inspiration will strike—be ready for it by taking notes of random ideas, capturing the authentic thoughts and connections that will make your essays stand out. This immersive preparation fuels the most critical creative phase: the cycle of writing. You must write and rewrite, read and reread, constantly refining your message. Seeking feedback from a lay audience is essential to ensure your story is not only well-written but also clear, compelling, and resonant to those outside your immediate field.
Ultimately, a well-executed Master Plan transforms you from a hopeful applicant into a proactive architect of your own success. It combines disciplined organization with creative immersion, ensuring that every action you take is a deliberate step toward your goal.

6---full-notes/the-median-people-(i-forg.title: The median people (i forgot) theorem
6---full-notes/the-median-people-(i-forg.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics math
The median people (i forgot) theorem
Details
Remember iterated deletion of dominated strategies? Yeah, so if we followed the method of doing so until the last possible instance, what we get would be a very small amount from what we had, rarely one though. However, we are missing critical context about how smart the people in the room really are.
The application is an election:
•	Two candidates each pick a position from 1 (far left) to 10 (far right).
•	Voters are spread evenly, 10% at each position.
•	Each voter votes for the nearer candidate. If the candidates are equally near, that position’s voters split half and half.
•	Each candidate wants the largest vote share.
Is 2 dominated by 3? Not in the original game. Against an opponent at 1, standing at 2 gets 90% but standing at 3 gets only 85%. But once 1 and 10 are deleted, the opponent can’t be at 1, so that column disappears:
Opponent at →	2	3	4	5	…
I’m at 2	50	20	25	30	…
I’m at 3	80	50	30	35	…
Now the “3” row is higher in every column. So the rounds go:
•	Round one deletes 1 and 10.
•	Round two deletes 2 and 9.
•	Round three deletes 3 and 8.
•	Round four deletes 4 and 7.
Only 5 and 6 remain, and between them it’s a tie. The prediction is that candidates crowd the center, so the voters in the middle decide the election and therefore the policy. This is the median voter theorem (Anthony Downs, 1957, in political science). Polak’s examples are:
The same model is older in economics, from Harold Hotelling (1929). Shops like gas stations bunch at the same junction instead of spreading out, because each is competing for the customers nearest to it.
The class listed what the model leaves out:
•	Voters aren’t evenly spread.
•	Not everyone votes.
•	Primaries come before the general election.
•	Politics has more than one dimension: character, and separate issues like the environment or foreign policy.
•	There can be more than two candidates, and not voting works like an extra one.
•	Candidates can’t just announce a position. Voters know their track records, so a claimed position isn’t believed unless the candidate can commit to it.
But of course the model still has its uses, it is testing a very simple case, which is why its results are extremely clear and simplistic. It is still useful however as it proves a base case of the situation.

6---full-notes/the-mid-century-psychoana.title: The mid-century psychoanalytic theory
6---full-notes/the-mid-century-psychoana.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology Freudian dreams
The mid-century psychoanalytic theory
Details
In the intellectual landscape of the mid-20th century, psychoanalysis, pioneered by Sigmund Freud and radically extended by figures like Melanie Klein, presented the most compelling and comprehensive theory of the human mind. It was a staggering achievement, offering a grammar for the chaotic language of dreams, neuroses, and desires. Yet, viewed from a later vantage point, these “Old World” perspectives, forged in the crucible of late imperial and interwar Europe, reveal a profound but fundamentally incomplete portrait of humanity. Their theories, while foundational, were bounded by the cultural and historical horizons of their creators, universalizing a specific, European experience of being human.
Freud’s model of the psyche was a product of its time and place: bourgeois, patriarchal Vienna at the fin de siècle. His revolutionary concepts—the Oedipus complex, the psychosexual stages, the tripartite structure of id, ego, and superego—were presented as universal truths of psychic development. However, they were built upon the bedrock of a specific social structure: the nuclear, patriarchal family, within which a drama of sexual rivalry and identification would supposedly unfold for everyone. The resulting picture was one where deviation from this norm was pathologized. The concept of “penis envy,” for example, framed female development not on its own terms, but as a reaction to a perceived lack. This wasn’t merely a clinical observation; it was a reflection of a society where power and privilege were overwhelmingly male. The Freudian “man” was, by default, a European man, and his psyche was the standard against which all others were measured and found wanting.
Melanie Klein, while breaking radically with Freud by delving into the pre-Oedipal world of the infant, remained tethered to a similar set of underlying assumptions. Her profound insights into the infant’s earliest experiences—the terrifying oscillations between the “paranoid-schizoid” and “depressive” positions, the primal force of envy, and the splitting of the world into good and bad “objects”—offered a dramatic new understanding of the psyche’s origins. Yet, this interior world was conceived as almost entirely endogenous. The dramas of love, hate, and reparation were played out between the infant and the maternal breast, a universal theater of innate drives.
The incompleteness of this Kleinian view lies in its relative insularity. While acknowledging the mother, it largely brackets out the wider social, economic, and cultural world in which both mother and infant are embedded. The internal world, in this model, is so powerful that it almost entirely eclipses the external. The impact of poverty, racism, war, or cultural difference on the formation of the psyche is rendered secondary to the timeless, internal struggle against innate aggression and envy. It is a theory of immense depth, but of limited breadth, one that struggles to account for how the material realities of the outside world are not just perceived, but fundamentally shape the very structure of the inner world it so brilliantly described.
The shared incompleteness of Freudian and Kleinian psychoanalysis, therefore, is its monocultural universalism. Their “Man” was an abstraction, an idealization of a European subject whose internal conflicts were believed to be the conflicts of all humankind. They provided no real framework for understanding how different cultures might foster different psychic structures, or how history and society were not just backdrops for a predetermined psychic script, but active authors of it. In this sense, mid-century psychoanalysis gave us a stunningly detailed map of a single, significant territory, but mistook that territory for the entire globe. It was a vital, indispensable first draft of the human soul, but one that awaited—and required—the revisions and expansions of a world growing acutely aware of its own diversity.

The minds of children
Details
Usually children ask very magnificent questions. These things are of finding wisdom, and it mostly exists within our childhood, even if most of it stops there, too.
The child is a natural questioner. It is not the number of questions he asks but their character that distinguishes him from the adult. Adults do not lose the curiosity that seems to be a native human trait, but their curiosity deteriorates in quality. They want to know whether something is so, not why. But children’s questions are not limited to the sort that can be answered by an encyclopedia.
Why should we try to develop our minds like this despite being born with relatively the same brain ? Well, that is because somewhere along the line, we lost the ability to maintain our curiosity at such depth. This can be attributed to many things, we being scolded for asking such questions, rote learning of schools, and so many more. But this doesn’t destroy it, it only debases it, and so we can gain it back.
I am not asking you to think as children, but to be able to see as they do, wonder as they wonder, ask what they ask. We must see through the complexities of our adult lives to be able to ask questions of simple distinctions.
So we must be childlike in our questions but mature in our answers.

6---full-notes/the-misconception-of-writ.content:
Status: teen
Tags: writing Zettelkasten
The misconception of Writing
Details
Contrary to what most self-help or writing guides tell you, writing doesn’t involve merely narrowing the scope of topics down and brainstorming information about it.
Most of the time, in academic or formal writing, the topics and points that are written about must be logical or the whole truth, in which brainstorming isn’t all about, since the info comes from one’s brain, so it will include their opinions, biases and so on.
But to decide on a good question to tackle or find the best angle for an assignment, one must realize that they have to have already put some thought into a topic, read on it and of course of other related topics and such. And so it connects with the whole process of writing, when we read, we write it down, externalize it. There is no plan that can do this effectively, because writing is not linear, and so we need to follow our own interests, curiosity and intuition instead of our unreliable brainstorming.
And so later, when we finally have to decide on something to write, we don’t get stuck on brainstorming about it, we immediately know what to write because we have been making that decision and refining it every step of the way, through choosing relevant information between pieces of media

6---full-notes/the-misunderstanding-in-r.title: The misunderstanding in research
6---full-notes/the-misunderstanding-in-r.content:
Status: adult
Tags: genetics 3 - Tags/environment Cognitive Psychology  Evolutionary Psychology
Individual Differences vs. Species Averages
Details
A primary source of confusion in genetics is failing to distinguish between two different levels of analysis. Behavioral genetics focuses on individual differences—it studies the variance within a population to understand why people are different from one another. In contrast, much of psychology and biology focuses on species-typical or normative behavior—it studies the average member of a species to understand what is typical. For example, an experiment might show that knocking out a gene in mice causes obesity. This tells us what can happen and informs us about a biological pathway. However, if that gene doesn’t naturally vary in the human population, it cannot explain why some people are more prone to obesity than others in the real world. Confusing these two perspectives leads to incorrect conclusions, such as assuming that a finding about a species average applies uniformly to every individual.
The paper highlights a critical distinction between the experimental method and the study of individual differences. Experiments manipulate variables to see what effect can be produced (e.g., does intensive language exposure boost vocabulary?). This demonstrates possibility but doesn’t explain the variation that naturally occurs in the real world. In contrast, behavioral genetics studies “what is”—the naturally occurring genetic and environmental factors that make people different. A successful experimental intervention does not invalidate heritability, just as high heritability does not imply that a trait is immune to intervention (immutability). These are different questions answered by different levels of analysis.

6---full-notes/the-moral-career-of-the-m.title: The moral career of the mental patient
6---full-notes/the-moral-career-of-the-m.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
The moral career of the mental patient
Details
Erving Goffman uses the concept of the “moral career” to map the profound transformation an individual undergoes upon entering a total institution. This career is two-sided: it involves internal, subjective changes in an individual’s beliefs about themselves, alongside external, public changes to their official status and way of life. The core process Goffman documents is how this public career systematically colonizes and rewrites the private one.
The journey begins long before admission in the “pre-patient phase,” where the individual is caught in a “funnel of betrayal.” This sequence of events strips them of autonomy and delivers them to the institution. It involves a cast of characters: a “complainant” who initiates action, “mediators” (police, doctors, social workers) who pass the person along, and, most critically, a “next-of-relation” (often a spouse or parent) who betrays the pre-patient’s world by authorizing their removal. Each step is typically justified as being “for their own good,” masking a series of humiliations.
This process does more than physically move a person; it reinterprets their past. The pre-patient’s biography undergoes a “reconstruction,” where past eccentricities and struggles are reframed as pathological symptoms to justify their commitment. Upon admission, the “in-patient phase” begins with the stark realization of being “deserted by society.” The institution becomes the sole mediator to the outside world, and the patient’s own narrative of their life is discredited.
At its heart, the moral career is a process of narrative appropriation. An individual’s sense of self is tied to their life story. The institution’s primary act is to seize control of this narrative through case files and staff interpretations, becoming the official author of the patient’s life. This reframes mental illness itself as a social status. As Goffman argues, what defines patients is not just their illness, “but from contingencies.” Entry into the asylum depends on social accidents like class, family tolerance, and the authorities involved. The boundary between “sane” and “insane” is revealed to be a porous social line, and the asylum is where society sends those who have failed at the performance of social competence.

6---full-notes/the-nature-of-homelessnes.title: The nature of homelessness
6---full-notes/the-nature-of-homelessnes.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology
The nature of homelessness
Details
Homelessness can be understood as an acute form of anomie, as defined by Émile Durkheim. It represents a state where the social and economic regulations that once provided a stable path to housing and self-sufficiency have broken down for a segment of the population. This breakdown is not an individual failing but a result of rapid societal changes—such as deindustrialization, the erosion of social safety nets, and escalating housing costs—that have outpaced the ability of many to adapt. Left without a clear or legitimate means to secure their place, these individuals are cast into a state of normlessness.
This condition is exacerbated in a modern context, which Guy Debord termed “The Spectacle.” A society oriented around consumption and appearance actively marginalizes those who cannot participate. The homeless are rendered invisible or are stigmatized because they do not fulfill the roles of producer or consumer that the Spectacle demands. This severs the bonds of social solidarity, replacing them with indifference. As Durkheim’s theory predicts, this state of anomie places individuals at a significantly higher risk of suicide. Therefore, homelessness is a stark indicator of a society that fails to adequately regulate its economic life and integrate its most vulnerable members.

The nature of psychology

In psychology, the lack of solid knowledge and indisputable treatments have allowed competing ideologies, movements and fads to be in it. Their very own history shows that even when major figures assume that certain concepts are incontrovertible, later they would be discarded as mere myths or superstitions. We have to acknowledge the fact in this field is that nothing rests on any proven theorems or assumptions. And the field is dominated by a few durable establishments and clusters of smaller sects of more tenuous standing. The major schools popularity usually depends on the charisma and the single-mindedness of the originator rather than how soundness it actually is. They also instead of working with each other, they convict others, having a disdain on others.
And this is no different, classical psychoanalysis in general regards thoughts of the patients as disguises for their unconscious conflicts and are presumably causing the problem. Basically anything that they even attempt to do in response to their problems are recognized as defenses, as rationalizations rather than his ideas, his reasoning, his self-thought solutions, they are not taken at face value and are treated as stepping-stones to deeper, concealed components of the mind.
On the other hand, the behavior therapists, similarly, tend to downgrade the importance of thinking. This is their attempt to emulate physical sciences, they reject data and concepts derived from man’s reflections on his own experiences and instead depend on of outsiders, of those who don’t really have a grasp on how the patient’s privacies fully.
Lastly, traditional neuropsychiatry. These guys inquire the patients thoughts and feelings to form their diagnosis. Abnormal ideation and feeling states are simply manifestations of underlying physical process or clues to a disturbance in neurochemistry rather than to the abnormal psychological states themselves.
And their solutions follow this, they never take into account the thoughts of the patients, by changing the external stimuli, by uncovering unconscious thoughts, administration of drugs or electroconvulsive therapy. This makes the patient thinks that they cannot help themselves, they must seek out someone who can assist them to do so. His confidence in the “obvious” techniques that he has customarily used in solving such problems slowly goes away as he accepts the view that emotional disturbances arise from forces beyond his comprehension. He cannot hope to understand it because such things are dismissed as insubstantial. 6---full-notes/the-necessity-of-external.title: The necessity of externalization
6---full-notes/the-necessity-of-external.content:
Status: adult
Tags: learning Zettelkasten writing
The necessity of externalization
Details
When you export raw ideas onto paper, a whiteboard or even another person, you do more than tidy up your desk—you transform fragile impressions into knowledge you can actually use. Cognitive‑load research shows that working memory can juggle only a handful of items at once. The moment you sketch a diagram or jot a phrase, you liberate precious mental bandwidth for deeper reasoning instead of just remembering where you left off.
Externalizing also forces you to re‑encode the material. Turning prose into an outline, a flowchart or a set of flash‑cards isn’t cosmetic; it demands that you distil, organize and label relationships, exactly the kind of generative processing that neuroscience links to stronger, more interconnected memory traces. That friction is productive: every time you decide “where does this piece go?” you expose gaps and misconceptions that rereading would leave hidden.
Teaching someone else is the ultimate form of this principle. When you prepare to explain glycolysis to a classmate—or to a blank page—you simulate their questions, anticipate confusions and rehearse retrieval pathways. Experiments on the so‑called protégé effect consistently find larger test‑score gains for students who teach than for peers who merely restudy notes they already “understand.”
Finally, the external artefact itself becomes a living feedback loop. A half‑filled concept map stares back, highlighting what remains fuzzy and inviting revision. Learning stops being an invisible, private struggle and becomes an iterative conversation between mind and medium. Put simply: if it’s still only in your head, it probably isn’t mastered yet.

The neuroendocrine system

When we are faced with a threat or a hardship, the hypothalamus releases corticotrophin releasing factor (CRF), which then communicates with the pituitary gland. 6---full-notes/the-optic-nerve.title: The optic nerve
6---full-notes/the-optic-nerve.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology neuroscience
The optic nerve
Details
The intricate processing that begins in the retina culminates in a grand exit. After signals pass from photoreceptors to bipolar cells, they reach the ganglion cells. The long axons of these ganglion cells bundle together to form the optic nerve, the primary cable carrying all visual information from the eye to the brain. In a curious quirk of biological design, the optic nerve turns around and exits from the back of the eye. At a structure called the optic chiasm, about half of the axons from each eye cross over to the opposite side of the brain. The main destination for this information is the thalamus, a central relay station, which then sends the signals onward to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe, where conscious perception finally begins. And so this also corresponds with contra-lateralization, which means the left eye information is processed by the right and the opposite is true to, to be more effective and quick.

The overall strategy

There are a lot of different therapeutic tactics that are available to the cognitive therapist, and so he must develop an over-all strategy for a given case, or else it will be perpetual trial-and-error. The outline of the framework one should follow has already been stated: clarifying the distortions, self-injunctions, and self-reproaches that lead to his distress or disability, and helping him revise the underlying rules that produce these thoughts. And to solve, he just applies normal problem-solving techniques.
Do note that, though, the techniques overlap considerably with the process of psychotherapy, so it is quite difficult to draw a line between the actions of the therapist and the responses of the patient. Furthermore, the therapist can be applying several procedures simultaneously, ant the patient will react to it all with a series of therapeutic responses.
For instance, in training the patient to recognize his automatic thoughts, the therapist directly or indirectly questions their validity. In turn, the process of extending the patient’s awareness of this form of ideation is accompanied by greater objectivity (distancing). As the patient recognizes that these self-signals are maladaptive or discordant with reality, he has a tendency to correct them automatically. Moreover, this kind of self-scrutiny leads directly to the recognition of the underlying premises and equations—the rules that are responsible for the faulty responses.

The reduced risk recognition in Depression
Details
Usually, the brain would perceive threats through the medial prefrontal cortex. But yet they would want to suicide, and the brain does not recognize that is a threat to the host’s life, which presents us a paradox.
To answer this paradox, we must look further into the perceptions of the patient themselves. As the patient is constantly feeling depressed and experiencing negative emotions, the amount of cortisol released by the HPA axis affects the integrity of the mPFC, weakening it until it can barely do its job anymore.
Moreover, suicide is not inherently a threat, it is not something physical, but rather a concept, a self-realized concept that may be an escape from the constant pain the patient is experiencing rather than the ending of their life. And the amygdala realizes that, and is overwhelmed by the pain that they are experiencing in their life, not the potential danger that suicide poses, and thinks that it is the way to escape.

6---full-notes/the-partnership-game.title: The partnership game
6---full-notes/the-partnership-game.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics math
The partnership game
Details
Two partners split profits 50–50; think of a law firm, or two students on a problem set. Each chooses an effort level sᵢ anywhere from 0 to 4. This is the course’s first game with a continuum of strategies.
The firm’s profit is 4(s₁ + s₂ + b·s₁s₂), where b is between 0 and 1/4. The b·s₁s₂ term is synergy: each partner’s effort is worth more when the other also works, which is the reason to work as a team at all. Each partner gets half the profit and pays an effort cost equal to their own effort squared. So Player 1’s payoff is
u₁ = 2(s₁ + s₂ + b·s₁s₂) − s₁²
and Player 2’s payoff is the same with s₂² subtracted instead. The subtraction in this situation is merely a cost, as without cost it would be a simple problem: the more you work, the more you get. And well real life just doesn’t work like that.
With infinitely many strategies you can’t draw a line for each one, so the best response comes from calculus:
•	Player 1 treats s₂ as fixed and picks s₁ to maximize u₁.
•	Set the derivative with respect to s₁ to zero: 2(1 + b·s₂) − 2s₁ = 0, so ŝ₁ = 1 + b·s₂.
•	The second derivative is −2, so this is a maximum.
•	By symmetry, ŝ₂ = 1 + b·s₁.

In words, the best effort is where one more unit adds as much to your share of the profit, 2(1 + b·s₂), as it adds to your cost, 2s₁. Best responses rise with the partner’s effort, because synergy makes your work pay more when they work harder.
Take b = 1/4, so each best response is 1 + s/4. Now apply the rule from the penalty-kick note and delete strategies that are never a best response:
Round	Efforts still possible (either player)	Reason
Start	0 to 4	All strategies
1	1 to 2	The partner’s effort is 0 to 4, so 1 + s/4 runs from 1 to 2
2	1.25 to 1.5	The partner’s effort is now 1 to 2
3	1.3125 to 1.375	The partner’s effort is now 1.25 to 1.5
…	shrinks toward 4/3 ≈ 1.33
As with iterated dominance, the efforts deleted in round 2 are best responses to something. But they are best responses only to efforts already deleted in round 1. Polak drew this as boxes within boxes, each a smaller copy of the last, closing in on the point where the two best-response lines cross. At that point each partner’s effort is a best response to the other’s: s* = 1 + b·s*, so s* = 1/(1 − b). That is 4/3 when b = 1/4.

6---full-notes/the-perspectives-of-psych.title: The perspectives of Psychology
6---full-notes/the-perspectives-of-psych.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
The perspectives of Psychology
Details
Modern psychology is a multifaceted discipline that examines the mind and behavior from various viewpoints. To capture this complexity, the field is often organized around five central perspectives, each offering a distinct lens through which to understand human experience. These frameworks are not mutually exclusive; rather, they provide complementary insights into why we think, feel, and act the way we do.
The five core perspectives are:


Action (Behavioral): This perspective focuses on observable behaviors and how they are learned and shaped by environmental stimuli, reinforcement, and consequences. It emphasizes what people do.


Cognition: This viewpoint investigates the internal mental processes that underlie behavior, including thinking, memory, perception, language, and problem-solving. It is concerned with how we process, store, and retrieve information.


Social Behavior (Sociocultural): This lens examines how an individual’s thoughts, feelings, and actions are influenced by the actual, imagined, or implied presence of others and by the social and cultural context in which they live.


Development: This perspective studies the systematic psychological changes that occur throughout a person’s lifespan, from conception to death. It explores how and why people change over time across biological, cognitive, and social domains.


Individual Differences: This approach focuses on the consistent patterns of thought, emotion, and behavior that make each person unique. It encompasses the study of personality, intelligence, motivation, and other traits that vary among individuals.


By integrating these five perspectives, psychology aims to build a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the human condition.

6---full-notes/the-problems-with-identif.title: The problems with identifying traits
6---full-notes/the-problems-with-identif.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology
The problems with identifying traits
Details
One of the fundamental challenges in trait psychology is how to accurately and reliably measure personality. While traits are defined as consistent patterns of behavior across situations, observing a person in enough situations to get a true measure is practically impossible.
Because of this, researchers primarily rely on self-report questionnaires. However, this method comes with significant problems that can affect the validity of the research:


Self-Enhancement Bias: People are not always objective when rating themselves. Most people, particularly in Western cultures like the United States, tend to rate themselves as “above average” on almost any desirable trait, from intelligence to sense of humor. This means that someone who provides an honest, average self-assessment may be incorrectly scored as having low self-esteem or a negative personality.


Cultural Differences: This self-enhancement bias is not universal. Studies show that people from British or Asian cultures tend to be more modest in their self-ratings, which can complicate cross-cultural comparisons.


Questionable Validity: When the results of personality questionnaires are checked against more detailed records, like daily diaries of behavior, the accuracy is only moderate. In one study, questionnaire results for aggressiveness correlated about .4 with daily reports of aggressive acts. This indicates that while questionnaires provide some useful information, they are an imperfect tool for capturing the true complexity of an individual’s personality.

6---full-notes/the-process-of-spj.title: The process of SPJ
6---full-notes/the-process-of-spj.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology university
The process of SPJ
Details
The SPJ process involved a synthesis of these data streams. The SCU practitioner would first consider the level of concern generated by the QuAIC. They would then review the Triage Warning Signs Checklist to determine if any specific red flags were present. Finally, they would integrate these structured inputs with their own professional judgment—informed by the specifics of the case, the context of the report, and their professional experience—to determine a final, overall “triage risk level”.  
This final risk level was categorized into a five-tier system designed to directly inform institutional action: “NA” (not assessed), “low,” “moderate,” “high,” and “highest”. Each of these tiers was linked to a pre-defined and escalating management response. A “low” risk case would trigger a response within five working days, typically resolved at a local level. A “moderate” risk case required a response within three working days and formal case management. A “high” risk case mandated a response within one business day and a potential referral to Student Misconduct. Finally, a case deemed “highest” risk required “immediate escalation” and a potential referral to the university’s multi-disciplinary Safety and Triage (SAT) team.  
This use of an SPJ framework represents a sophisticated strategy for enhancing the quality, consistency, and defensibility of the university’s threat assessment decisions. Relying solely on a quantitative score from a single tool like the QuAIC, while standardized, could be criticized as overly simplistic or mechanistic, potentially missing critical contextual factors unique to a case. Conversely, relying solely on unstructured professional judgment, while flexible, is vulnerable to charges of being subjective, inconsistent, and biased.
The SPJ model implemented at Victoria University skillfully mitigates both weaknesses. The QuAIC and the checklist provide the “structured,” “evidence-based” foundation, ensuring that key risk domains are systematically considered in every case. The “professional judgment” component provides the necessary flexibility to integrate nuance, context, and case-specific information that a rigid algorithm might miss. This creates a transparent and highly defensible decision-making pathway. A practitioner can clearly articulate their rationale: for instance, “The QuAIC generated a ‘Moderate’ level of concern based on the reported intrusion and persistence. However, the Triage Warning Signs Checklist flagged the presence of ‘last-resort thinking’ by the IoC and ‘significant distress’ in the target. Therefore, exercising professional judgment, the final triage risk level was elevated to ‘High,’ triggering an immediate referral for management.” This type of documented, multi-faceted reasoning demonstrates a thorough and thoughtful assessment, which serves to protect the institution from liability while simultaneously protecting the campus community from unmanaged risk.

This process is quite similar to how long-term memory is created in the mind. It begins with encoding, which includes the fact that our brain turn our perceptions into chemical and electrical changes that can form a mental representation of the patterns we have seen. These can be called memory traces, or short-term memory. Our lives are generally guided by the ephemera that clutter our short-term memory which are soon forgotten. We have to find ways that makes our brain understands which memories are worth more so that it focuses on strengthening it.
Here comes the next step, consolidation. New learning is labile, which means it can be altered and remembered wrongly. The process that we consolidate is believed to include the brain replaying and rehearsing the learning to fill in gaps and connect it to previous experiences. This is why we need to make it difficult, as it forces our neurons to focus to truly work the memory in as well as find for us gaps in knowledge for the brain to do, aka reconsolidation.
Lastly is retrieval, which is the process of getting the memory back for us to use. This is where all the work from consolidating it comes, if we have strengthened it well, we will be able to retrieve it easily.

6---full-notes/the-processes-of-the-orig.content:
Status: teen

The processes of the Original Position
Details
Rawls splits his argument for the principles of justice into 2 distinct phases. The first involves us to presume that the parties involved are rational but are absolutely not swayed by “special psychologies”—most notably, envy. Rawls defines envy in a very specific, stringent way: it is the destructive desire to see others have less, even if achieving that reduction means you also end up with less, simply to close the gap in social standing. The first phase assumes this specific kind of envy does not drive the parties. The second phase of the argument (addressed much later in Chapters 8 and 9) acts as a stability check: it evaluates whether the chosen principles, when actually implemented in the real world, would inadvertently generate destabilizing levels of envy that would tear the society apart.
To be able to determine the best principles for the first phase, OP relies on “two-way comparisons.” Meaning Rawls would pit the principles against historically significant alternatives on the menu. The most fundamental of these is the First Comparison: The Two Principles of Justice vs. The Principle of Average Utility (which seeks to design institutions to maximize the per capita well-being of society). This comparison is paramount because Rawls’s primary goal in the book is to prove that Justice as Fairness provides a superior, more stable normative foundation for a democratic society than the dominant utilitarian tradition.

The great majority of books that have been written-more than 99% of them- will not make sufficient demands on the reader for them to improve their reading skills. These books are merely to amuse the readers, and so they should only be skimmed.

One may question how this occurs ? And to answer, we must look at ourselves, with time, our knowledge and our mind will become wiser, will become more, and so such books perceptions change to cater to the level at which our minds have grown, presumably presenting a new way of looking at said books.

6---full-notes/the-reason-for-phobia.content:
Status: adult

The reason for Phobia
Details
Although many schools of psychology has taken a jab at trying to find the cause of phobias, most of them have failed to come up with an explanation that truly is verifiable and can be used to help the patient. This is where Beck comes in, as he questions the phobic, he recognized that they have experienced a situation that ended badly in their childhood, prompting them to be scared, hyper fixate on that into adulthood.
For example, a child who refuses to eat, when his parents demand an explanation, he just says that he will die if he does so, which they of course think is irrational. But when asked more clearly about a past experience, the psychologist finds that the child once choked on a large piece of potato, was scared to death by that experience and now immediately thinks about it whenever he is eating such types of food. This shows us that what the phobic is afraid of is not the situation, but the consequences of such situations.
The types of phobias that Beck mentioned in his works are:

Physical/Violent Threat: This is the most primal fear—fear of physical harm, injury, illness, or death. A person with panic disorder might misinterpret their racing heart as an imminent heart attack. Someone with a phobia of dogs fears being bitten.
Psychosocial Threat: This is the fear of social harm—humiliation, rejection, criticism, or loss of status. This is the core of Social Anxiety Disorder, where the perceived “danger” is being judged negatively by others.
Supernatural Threat: This is a category that is often overlooked but is crucial. It involves fears of evil, demonic possession, divine retribution, or other threats that are not of the physical or social world. Depending on a person’s cultural and religious beliefs, these can be incredibly powerful drivers of anxiety.
The first and second one usually insisted on into adulthood more than the latter.

The rise of Individual Totemism

Beyond the public, collective totemism of the clan, there exists a private, individual form. This “individual totem” is a personal patron—an animal, plant, or object—with which a single person shares a mystical and intimate bond. This relationship is distinct from the clan totem in several ways. It is not hereditary but is acquired through a deliberate ritual act, often a vision quest involving fasting and self-mortification around puberty. The bond is one of alliance, not ancestry; the totem is a “friend” or “protector,” an alter ego whose fate is intertwined with the individual’s, not a forefather. This personal totem gives the individual their sacred name, is represented by a personal emblem, and is believed to grant them special powers and protection. It is the religious principle applied not to the group, but to the personality.

6---full-notes/the-rise-of-the-modern-re.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology academia
Universities 18th Century
Details
One observes in the late nineteenth century a pivotal shift in the landscape of American higher education. The classical college, with its focus on character and civic virtue for an established elite, was rendered anachronistic by the ascendance of a new cultural paradigm: scientific knowledge. The modern research university—exemplified by new institutions like Johns Hopkins and transformed older ones like Harvard—emerged not merely as a new type of school, but as the veritable cathedral for this new faith in science and its potent alliance with industry. Its purpose was no longer to polish the gentry, but to produce the specialized expertise—the chemists, engineers, and electricians—demanded by a modernizing world. This institution was conceived as an engine of progress, fundamentally altering the perceived purpose of higher learning.
It is a profound irony that the research university, in its infancy, harbored a vision of democratic integration, not sterile specialization. The early University of Chicago under William Rainey Harper and John Dewey stands as the key exemplar of this lost ideal. Their project was to create an institution that served the public, broke down departmental silos, and fused academic inquiry with direct community engagement. Dewey’s “Chicago school” saw philosophy, psychology, and education as an integrated whole, with figures like George Herbert Mead bridging disciplines and faculty deeply involved in civic affairs like the Hull House settlement movement. This was the university as a force for democratic coherence, open to all with merit and concerned with all subjects relevant to the modern world.

6---full-notes/the-role-of-serotonin-in-.title: The role of Serotonin in Depression
6---full-notes/the-role-of-serotonin-in-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: neurology psychology pharmacology
The role of Serotonin in Depression
Details
Serotonin is the most widely known neurotransmitter associated with depression, largely due to the prevalence of medications designed to target it. The “serotonin hypothesis” posits that a primary cause of depression is a deficit of this chemical messenger in the brain’s synapses.
This theory stems directly from the mechanism of the most common class of antidepressants: SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors), like Prozac. As Sapolsky explains, these drugs don’t create more serotonin. Instead, they block the re-uptake pumps on the presynaptic neuron. By inhibiting this cleanup mechanism, the serotonin that has been released is prevented from being quickly reabsorbed. It remains in the synapse longer, allowing it to repeatedly stimulate the receptors on the postsynaptic neuron, thus amplifying its signal. The logic follows that if increasing serotonin’s effect alleviates symptoms, a lack of it was likely the initial problem.
While the serotonin hypothesis is powerful, Sapolsky emphasizes it’s not the whole story. The “time-course problem”—where SSRIs alter brain chemistry in hours but take weeks to produce a therapeutic effect—shows that the brain’s long-term adaptation is more important than the immediate chemical change.
In terms of symptoms, serotonin deficits are most strongly linked to the cognitive aspect of rumination. This is the obsessive, looping cycle of negative thoughts, guilt, and sad memories that a person with depression cannot escape. The fact that SSRIs are also effective for treating Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD), another illness defined by rumination, supports this connection.
