6---full-notes/the-rules-of-reading-imag.title: The rules of reading imaginative literature
6---full-notes/the-rules-of-reading-imag.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
The rules of reading imaginative literature
Details
Classify the Work by Its Kind (Genre)
Identify the genre and form of the story right away. Determine if you are reading a lyric poem, a novel, a play, etc., and what subtype or tradition it belongs to. Different genres have different structures and narrative methods, which demand different reading approaches. For example, a lyric poem centers on a single emotional moment, while a novel or play has a complex plot with many characters and interactions . Recognizing the kind of imaginative work guides your expectations and “receptivity” as a reader .
Grasp the Unity of the Whole Story (Find the Plot)
Find the core story that ties everything together. Ask yourself: What is this work fundamentally about? In imaginative literature, the unity of the work lies in its plot or narrative arc, not in an explicit thesis. Try to summarize the entire story in a sentence or two . If you can briefly recount the main story line or conflict, you have grasped the book’s unity. This is analogous to stating the main idea of an essay, except here it’s the central narrative or experience the author wants to share.
Analyze How the Parts Form the Whole (Structure)
See how the story is built from its parts. Break down the narrative into its major sections or phases – beginning, middle, climax, and end. Identify the key episodes, crises, and turning points that the story goes through . Just as a nonfiction book’s parts are organized logically, a story’s parts are arranged chronologically or dramatically to form a coherent whole . Ask: How do the characters and events introduced early on lead to later events or the climax? By outlining the sequence of events and their connections, you understand the structure of the plot – how the author developed the narrative step by step.
Become Acquainted with the Elements (Characters and Events)
Know the story’s basic elements intimately. The “elements” of fiction are the characters, their actions, their thoughts/feelings, and the incidents or events that occur . To truly grasp a novel or play, you should become thoroughly familiar with who the characters are and what happens to them. In effect, you must come to terms with these story elements just as you would with key terms in an argument. Make sure you “live through” the events and understand the characters’ motivations and relationships. If you haven’t absorbed who the main characters are or what experiences they undergo, you haven’t yet fully understood the story .
Immerse Yourself in the Story’s World (Scene and Context)
Enter the imaginative world on its own terms. Every story creates a context or background – a world with its own setting, culture, and internal logic. The events and characters only make full sense against this background . *Strive to “become at home” in the book’s world: visualize the setting, accept the fictional society’s rules, and empathize with its people as if they were real friends or foes . When you can mentally step into the scene – seeing and feeling the environment and circumstances that surround the characters – the story’s elements will connect naturally. They stop being isolated pieces and turn into parts of a living, coherent world .
Follow the Narrative Movement (Keep Your Finger on the Pulse)
Trace the progression of events and the cause-and-effect in the story. In expository writing, you would follow the flow of the argument; in fiction, you follow the plot’s development . Pay attention to how one event leads to another and what drives the action forward (e.g. characters’ goals or conflicts). This narrative momentum is the “logic” of the story. Adler and Van Doren note that plot is to a story what an argument is to an essay – it’s the dynamic element that gives the work life. To read a story well, you need to be sensitive to its rhythm and pacing – essentially, keep your finger on the pulse of the narrative as it rises to a climax and resolves .
Appreciate Fully Before You Judge
Hold off on criticism until you’ve truly experienced the work. Don’t rush to say you like or dislike a novel/poem until you’re sure you’ve understood it and felt what it wanted you to feel. First, actively appreciate the work by undergoing the emotional and imaginative journey it offers . This means reading fiction actively but also open-heartedly: engage with it passionately and absorb its effect. Once you’ve done all the analytical steps above and let the book “work on you,” only then are you in a position to make a fair judgment or critique. By fully appreciating a piece of imaginative literature, you not only respect the author’s effort but also learn to discern what exactly makes it beautiful or effective, sharpening your own taste and understanding in the process

6---full-notes/the-skills-of-weaving-a-s.title: The skills of weaving a story
6---full-notes/the-skills-of-weaving-a-s.content:
Status:
Tags: scholarship
The skills of weaving a story
Details
A truly masterful speech often begins not with a grand declaration, but with an intimate whisper that invites an entire audience into a personal world. When Michelle Obama spoke of her family, she began with this very principle, weaving a tapestry from two distinct threads: the unconditional love that cradled her childhood and the quiet, persistent ache of her parents striving to provide experiences they themselves had never known. The response from the crowd was not a polite applause but a sudden, resonant wave of recognition, the sound of a thousand private histories finding a voice in hers. This initial connection was the key that unlocked the room, allowing her to then narrate the deeper, more vulnerable details of her family’s story—her father’s battle with his illness, his unwavering commitment to his work, and the silent dignity with which he provided for his children. The audience’s empathy deepened, their applause now a salute to a familiar, sacred truth about the profound nature of parental sacrifice.
From this deeply personal foundation, she masterfully expanded the narrative, creating a bridge from her past to her husband’s. She presented Barack Obama’s story not as a separate tale, but as a mirror image of her own, another chapter in the same book of American striving. She spoke of his grandmother and mother, women who confronted the quiet, unyielding barriers of a world that limited their ascent, yet who poured that same unwavering commitment into the next generation. In doing so, she subtly transformed a story of individual hard work into a broader saga about overcoming systemic injustice. The message was no longer just about family sacrifice; it was about the resilience required to push against an invisible ceiling, a theme that resonated with the struggles of so many.
With these two powerful stories laid as a foundation—one of personal grit, the other of societal struggle—she then ascended to her ultimate point. She distilled from these experiences the universal virtues of decency, dignity, and a core morality that should define the human spirit. Success, she argued, was not a product of circumstance or position, but the direct outcome of these fundamental traits. This conclusion was not a lecture, but a truth earned through the emotional journey she had guided everyone on. In this light, her final endorsement of her husband felt less like a political maneuver and more like the story’s inevitable destination. He became the living embodiment of the journey she had described—the product of familial love, the overcomer of unseen barriers, and the carrier of those essential human values. The applause for him was, in reality, an applause for the entire powerful narrative she had so brilliantly constructed.
Supporting Content
Some other points to consider:
Finding the elephant in the room yet nobody realizes or recognize it can make the application more powerful.
Layering stories into your application will increase the depth and interests of the readers when reviewing it.

6---full-notes/the-specifics-of-quaic.title: The specifics of QuAIC
6---full-notes/the-specifics-of-quaic.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology university
The specifics of QuAIC
Details
The paper draws a sharp and important contrast between the campus threat management model prevalent in Australia and the model developed in the United States. The US model, born from tragedies like the Virginia Tech shooting, is primarily focused on the assessment and prevention of “targeted violence” and mass casualty incidents. The Australian model, as exemplified by the SCU at Victoria University, has a much broader remit. It focuses on “risk screening, primary prevention, early intervention case management, and psychological support” for a wide spectrum of problem behaviors, most of which fall short of targeted violence.  
The QuAIC is presented as an instrument perfectly adapted to this Australian context. Its dual-axis framework is designed to effectively triage the very behaviors—bullying, stalking, cyber-abuse, and harassment—that constitute the bulk of the SCU’s caseload. The paper also highlights structural differences in the Australian model, such as the “separation of threat assessment and management functions” between the front-line SCU and the higher-level SAT team. While this can sometimes “compromise case management cohesion” due to case hand-offs, it also allows for specialized roles, with the SCU focusing on broad intake and support and the SAT team focusing on high-risk adjudication. The QuAIC is the ideal engine for this kind of separated model, as its primary function is to reliably sort cases and direct them to the appropriate channel.

The spreading of the neuron
Details
The action potential may have explained the “firing” of the neuron, but it does not explain the spreading to neighboring regions. The reason for this is that the temporarily positive voltage inside the axon induces an opening of ion channels at adjacent regions, which first changes the voltages at these regions and make more channels open up. The upshot is that the impulse moves down the entire length of the axon and into the rest of the neuron as well. This is known as propagation of the action potential.

6---full-notes/the-styles-of-philosophic.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/The styles of philosophical writing.md
6---full-notes/the-styles-of-philosophic.title: The styles of philosophical writing
6---full-notes/the-styles-of-philosophic.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading philosophy
The styles of philosophical writing
Details
Though philosophy is unified by its method—reasoned thinking—it has developed multiple literary styles to express that method. Understanding these styles helps a reader navigate different texts, evaluate arguments more clearly, and even attempt philosophical writing themselves. Here are five major philosophical styles from the Western tradition:


The Dialogue (Plato)
Plato’s dialogues, featuring Socrates, are conversational, dramatic, and heuristic. Through guided questioning, the reader is led to insights indirectly, discovering the argument’s logic along the way. This style is powerful because of its interactive structure and literary depth, but few besides Plato have used it effectively. Its reliance on rhetorical drama makes it difficult to replicate in modern philosophical writing.


The Treatise or Essay (Aristotle, Kant)
Aristotle’s surviving works, though often fragmentary, established the systematic treatise as a dominant form. Kant perfected this in highly structured, refined essays that begin with a central question, proceed through thorough analysis, and address secondary problems as they arise. This style emphasizes clarity, order, and completeness. It lacks the dramatic interplay of dialogue but offers direct exposition and rigorous development of ideas.


The Scholastic Format (Aquinas)
Developed in the Middle Ages and exemplified by Aquinas’ Summa Theologica, this style blends exposition with structured debate. Each section begins with a question, presents objections, responds to them via authority (often scripture), and concludes with the author’s own view and replies. This method highlights philosophical conflict and aims at resolving it through reasoned response. It reflects the oral, disputational culture of medieval thought and models how philosophy can engage opposing views directly.


The Systematic-Geometric Style (Descartes, Spinoza)
Inspired by mathematics, philosophers like Descartes and Spinoza aimed to organize philosophy with geometric precision. Spinoza’s Ethics is written in axioms, propositions, and proofs. While formally rigorous, this style often sacrifices accessibility and interpretive clarity. Philosophical ideas—unlike geometric ones—resist full expression in rigid deductive form. The reader may feel able to skip parts, which undermines the continuity essential to philosophical understanding.


The Aphoristic Style (Nietzsche, Pascal)
Short, suggestive statements—seen in Nietzsche’s Thus Spake Zarathustra or Pascal’s Pensées—form a style that is poetic and heuristic. It invites the reader to make connections and supply reasoning, making it intellectually stimulating but also frustrating. This form emphasizes insight over argument and is better suited to evoking reflection than sustained philosophical proof.


While the essay or treatise remains the most common form, each style reflects a different way of doing philosophy—through drama, debate, system, or provocation. Knowing these forms helps the reader not only better understand the texts they read, but also the intentions behind their construction.

6---full-notes/the-subject-syntopical-re.title: The subject Syntopical reading
6---full-notes/the-subject-syntopical-re.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
The subject Syntopical reading
Details
The first requirement of this level of reading is to know the books that are relevant to a particular question that you are trying to answer. Next is to know which books should be read, which is greatly harder as how would you know if you haven’t read them ?
This makes us question what is the “subject” of syntopical reading, what is the question that we are reading to answer ? It may be easy to answer if the subject is a particular event in history, but almost in any other sphere, it just isn’t. Like in fiction, they do not communicate like an expository writer, and vice versa.
Suppose, for example, that you are interested in reading about the idea of love. Since the literature of love is vast, you would have relatively little difficulty in creating a bibliography of books to read. Suppose that you have done that, by asking advisors, by searching through the card catalogue of a good library, and by examining the bibliography in a good scholarly treatise on the subject. And suppose in addition that you have confined yourself to expository works, despite the undoubted interest of novelists and poets in the subject. (We will explain why it would be advisable to do this later.) You now begin to examine the books in your bibliography. What do you find?
Absolutely nothing, because anything can be labeled as love, like how one loves eating, a certain food, person, etc… but all those love are different even if they are related to “love”. And we haven’t even touched writers whose opinions on love are that it is merely a function of humans, biologically or cognitively rather than something more than that.
And so the conclusion comes back to the start, you cannot classify what you’ve been reading about (the very question you sought out to answer) unless you’ve read hundreds of works. But even when you do, you may regard half of them as being useless and off-topic !

6---full-notes/the-terms-of-an-author.content:
Status: teen
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
The terms of an author
Details
This is the first rule of reading, it is the basic element of communicable knowledge .
A term isn’t a word, but rather a specific meaning of a word or sentence that the author has specifically crafted, as a word can have many meanings, especially an important one. When an author intends a word one meaning and the reader interprets another, although an exchange of word has passed in between them, they have not come to terms, no communication has been made.
And so it is necessary for both parties to use the same words with the same meanings, to come to terms. A term can be defined as a word that is used unambiguously. These things you cannot find in dictionaries, though the bricks to build them are there. These only occur in the process of communicating with others, either through books and such. And so we can think of it as “a skilled use of words for the sake of communicating knowledge.” (Mortimer J Adler).
Whilst a good writer will try to reach us through the language barrier to help us understand, we must also try to reach him, be willing to be taught by him.

6---full-notes/the-therapeutic-collabora.title: The therapeutic collaboration
6---full-notes/the-therapeutic-collabora.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology CBT relationship
The therapeutic collaboration
Details
There are certain details that are incredibly important in the context of psychotherapy, in which we will discuss in the following essay. One obvious component is genuine collaboration between the therapist and patient. The two moving blindly in different directions, which happens more often than not, can make both participants extremely annoyed. It may be noted that the perspective of the therapist and the patient may envision the relationship between them completely differently. And so to minimize such hazards, both must reach a consensus regarding what the process of therapy will be. This agreement can be extremely important to a successful outcome, if the patient expectations corresponds to the therapy he receives, it will enhance the effectiveness (Orne and Wender, 1968).
Furthermore, the therapist must be in-tuned with the patient, he must understand the patient’s problems and what they prefer to talk about, an “agenda” of topics so to say; and if the therapist disregards this, he might develop an unnecessary strain on the relationship. For instance, a patient who is disturbed by a recent altercation with his wife may be alienated by the therapist’s rigid adherence to a predetermined format such as desensitizing him to his subway phobia.
Supporting Content
Some more benefits to this approach may be the fact that the patient experiences less shame, a sense of inferiority, and defensiveness if the two approach it as working against the problem of the patient, not correcting the patient’s bad habits. By placing this emphasis on solving problems, it helps the patient detach more, leading to all the above. And it also helps the therapist to obtain feedback about the efficacy of his techniques and detailed information about the patient’s thoughts and feelings. Lastly, the patient will also increase their ability to empathize and be more emotionally mature in this approach as proven by Carl Rogers own theory, as he is less likely to view the therapist like some God.

6---full-notes/the-three-stages-of-memor.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/The three stages of memories.md
6---full-notes/the-three-stages-of-memor.title: The three stages of memories
6---full-notes/the-three-stages-of-memor.content:
Status: teen
Tags: learning psychology
The three stages of memories
Details
The dominant framework for understanding how memories are formed, first proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin at Stanford in the 1960s, organizes memory into a sequence of three stages. This model posits that information from the outside world first enters a fleeting sensory register. Visual inputs might last for less than a second, while auditory inputs can linger for a few seconds, a phenomenon that explains how one can recall the last few words someone said even when not paying full attention.
For this transient sensory information to progress, it requires attention. With attention, the information is transferred to short-term memory, a temporary holding area with a limited capacity and duration. This stage can typically hold about seven pieces of information (plus or minus two) for up to 30 seconds. New incoming information can easily displace what’s already there.
To create a lasting memory, the information must be transferred from short-term to long-term memory through processes like rehearsal and consolidation. This final stage is where we see actual physical changes in the brain’s neural connections. Unlike short-term memory, long-term memory is believed to have a virtually limitless capacity and can endure for a lifetime, though it is subject to decay. Overseeing this entire process is a “central executive” function, which allows for the conscious manipulation of information, such as using mnemonic tricks to aid in consolidation.

6---full-notes/the-tragedy-of-plays.title: The tragedy of plays
6---full-notes/the-tragedy-of-plays.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading philosophy
The tragedy of plays
Details
Most plays are not worth reading. This is because most of them are to be acted upon, not read. But there are certain plays that can bypass these barriers, notably those of tragedies, which contain some of the deepest and richest insights.
This calls for us to read them well, as they can tell us about the life that we live in as well as form a framework for other plays to be written later. First, we must remember that the essence of tragedy is time, or lack of it. There is no problem in any Greek tragedy that could not have been solved if there had been enough time, but there is never enough. Decisions, choices have to be made in a moment, there is no time to think and weigh the consequences; and, since even tragic heroes are fallible—especially fallible, perhaps—the decisions are wrong. It is easy for us to see what should have been done, but would we have been able to see in time? That is the question that you should always ask in reading any Greek tragedy.
The second bit of advice is this. One thing we do know about the staging of Greek plays is that the tragic actors wore buskins on their feet that elevated them several inches above the ground. (They also wore masks.) But the members of the chorus did not wear buskins, though they sometimes wore masks. The comparison between the size of the tragic protagonists, on the one hand, and the members of the chorus, on the other hand, was thus highly significant. Therefore you should always imagine that the words of the chorus are alike us in stature; while the protagonists is from the mouths of giants, who were larger than life.

The truth about Selection
Details
Championed by V.C. Wynne-Edwards, his theory on group selection about how group selection acts on the whole group, choosing those who are altruistic, who would sacrifice themselves for the group was fundamentally flawed. As this would mean that genes would favor altruism as a trait, as a behavior in groups, until all the members were inherently altruistic and therefore would sacrifice themselves, all of them, leading to extinction.
A more plausible theory is individual selection, where species try to multiply as many copies of themselves as possible, they try to distribute their genes amongst the population as much as possible. This selection operates through two primary mechanisms:


Natural Selection: Favoring traits that enhance survival to the point of reproduction (e.g., being fast enough to escape a predator).


Sexual Selection: Favoring traits that enhance reproductive success, even if they hinder survival (e.g., a peacock’s tail is metabolically costly and makes it easier for predators to spot, but females prefer it).

6---full-notes/the-two-faces-of-amnesia.title: The two faces of Amnesia
6---full-notes/the-two-faces-of-amnesia.content:
Status: teen
Tags: neuroscience
The two faces of Amnesia
Details
Amnesia, the clinical term for memory loss, is not a single condition but manifests in two primary forms, defined by their relationship to the time of a brain injury or event.


Retrograde Amnesia: This is the loss of memories formed before the event. It’s a failure to retrieve from the past. This is the type of amnesia most commonly depicted in fiction—the character who wakes up with no knowledge of their identity or past life. In reality, it is often “graded,” meaning that more recent memories are lost while distant, older memories (like from childhood) remain intact. This suggests that over time, memories become less dependent on the hippocampus and more firmly stored in the cortex.


Anterograde Amnesia: This is the inability to form new long-term memories after the event. It is a failure to encode the present for the future. Patient H.M. and Clive Wearing are classic examples. They could remember their distant pasts but were trapped in a perpetual present, unable to convert new experiences into lasting memories.


While Hollywood favors retrograde amnesia for its dramatic potential, anterograde amnesia is the more common and often more devastating clinical reality following significant damage to the hippocampus.

6---full-notes/the-types-of-biography.title: The types of biography
6---full-notes/the-types-of-biography.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading history
The types of biography
Details
This is the story about a real person, this mixed patrimony causes it to have a mixed character.
There are several kinds of this. Definite, which is the final, exhaustive, work on the life of someone important enough to deserve this. They exist after non-definitive biographies have appeared first, which are all somewhat inadequate. All sources are gone through, all letters read, and a great deal of contemporary history examined by the author. Since the ability to gather the materials is somewhat different from the talent for shaping them into a good book, definitive biographies are not always easy reading. This is too bad. A scholarly book does not have to be dull. One of the greatest of all biographies is Boswell’s Life of Johnson, and it is continuously fascinating. It is certainly definitive (though other biographies of Dr. Johnson have since appeared), but it is also uniquely interesting.
Another is an authorized biography, which is commissioned by heirs or friends of these persons. They should be warned that it is written so the errors and the triumphs are seen in the best light possible, and they have the advantage of being allowed all pertinent material by the one who commissioned it. Which means it is biased, so don’t read it fully as the truth.
The authorized biography is a kind of history, but it is history with a difference. We may be curious to know what interested persons want the public to know about someone’s private life, but we should not expect to know what the private life really was. The reading of an authorized biography will thus often tell us much about the time in which it was written, about its customs and manners, about those actions and attitudes that were acceptable—and, by implication and with a little extrapolation, about those that were not. But we should not hope to discover the real life of a human being any more than we would hope to know the real story of a war if we read the communiqués of only one side. To get at the truth we must read all the communiqués, ask people who were there, and use our own minds to make sense out of the muddle. A definitive biography has already done this work; in the case of an authorized biography (and most biographies of living persons are of this sort), there is still much to do.
The last biographies are those that are ordinary, such books are not trustworthy like definitive biographies, but are often very good reading.
Moreso, some are didactic, with a sense of moral purpose. Which of course not read for information but for the stories and the author’s teachings.

6---full-notes/the-types-of-scholarships.title: The types of scholarships
6---full-notes/the-types-of-scholarships.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship writing university
General Rules
Details
At its surface, a scholarship appears to be a simple financial transaction, a welcome figure on a tuition statement that reduces a formidable debt. It can be seen as a cold calculation, a reward for a high grade point average or a strategic discount offered to entice a promising applicant. Many view it as a line item on a ledger, a practical tool for bridging the gap between ambition and affordability. But to see it only as such is to miss its true essence, for a scholarship is never just about the money. It is a story, a statement of values, and a profound act of recognition.
In truth, every scholarship is a mirror, reflecting a different facet of human endeavor and institutional belief. Sometimes, it is a reflection of past dedication—the silent echo of late nights spent in a library, the muscle memory of perfected scales on a violin, or the breathless victory in the final seconds of a game. In these instances, the scholarship is an acknowledgment of discipline and excellence, a tangible reward for a journey already undertaken. At other times, the mirror shows not an achievement, but a circumstance. It becomes a quiet recognition that talent is universal, but opportunity is not. This form of scholarship is an investment in potential over privilege, a deliberate act of removing a barrier so that a brilliant mind, regardless of its starting point, can find its way forward.
Beyond these reflections of where a student has been, a scholarship is also a blueprint for who they might become. It can be a mirror held up to a specific future, seeking out the aspiring nurse, the innovative engineer, or the visionary artist, and giving them the resources to build that identity. In this way, an institution uses scholarships to weave its own future, populating its community with the minds and spirits it believes will shape the world. In the end, a scholarship is a statement of belief. It is an institution looking at an individual and saying, “We see you. We see your past efforts, your present potential, and the future you are striving to create. You are a story we want to be a part of.” It is the transformation of abstract funds into a tangible investment in a single human life.

6---full-notes/the-unendingness-of-the-s.title: The unendingness of the Selfish Need
6---full-notes/the-unendingness-of-the-s.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology philosophy
The unendingness of the Selfish Need
Details
In his seminal work, Suicide, Émile Durkheim posits a fundamental and troubling aspect of the human condition: that desire, when left to the individual’s own devices, is a “bottomless abyss.” Unlike basic biological instincts which have natural stopping points, our psychological craving for comfort, luxury, and well-being has no inherent limit. This inherent insatiability, Durkheim argues, becomes a source of profound and constant torment. By definition, a limitless desire can never be fulfilled, condemning the individual to a state of perpetual unhappiness and futility, as a sense of progress is impossible when one’s goal is infinitely distant. Furthermore, any satisfactions achieved along the way offer no lasting peace; instead, they merely stimulate new and greater wants, creating a vicious cycle where, as Durkheim notes, “the more one has, the more one wants.” This state of unending pursuit is also inherently fragile. When life presents an inevitable “insurmountable obstacle,” the individual who lacks an external framework for accepting limits is left with only raw restlessness and pain.
Ultimately, Durkheim identifies this entire condition—the psychological suffering caused by the absence of external limits—as the foundation for anomic suicide. It is not a consequence of personal moral failing, but rather a social pathology that arises from the breakdown of collective moral regulation. Society, in Durkheim’s view, is the only force capable of providing the necessary boundaries that make human happiness and stability possible.

The various methods of cognitive therapy
Details
There exists many methods which can make a patient become more realistic about his appraisals and his world’s as well. The “Intellectual” approach consists of identifying such misconceptions, testing their validity, and substituting more appropriate concepts. More often than not, the fuel for broad attitudinal change comes from the patient’s own recognition that the rules he has instated on his unconscious has guided his thinking and behavior to deceive and make him miserable.
The second is the “experiential” approach, which exposes the patient to experiences that are in themselves powerful enough to change these misconceptions. This consists of interactions with other individuals in certain organized situations, which can help patients the same as the first method, to modify his inappropriate maladaptive responses to these situations. Similarly, a patient who receives unyielding warmth and acceptance from his therapist, often changes his view on authority figures. Such a change has been labeled “corrective emotional experience” (Alexander, 1950).
The “behavioral” approach is the last, and it encourages the development of specific forms of behavior that leads to more general changes in the way the patient views himself and the real world. As he practices methods to deal with people who frighten him or his fears, which can also be called “assertive training,” it enables him to increase his confidence and deal with such situations better.

6---full-notes/the-workings-of-the-neuro.content:
Status: adult
Tags: neuroscience psychology
The workings of the neurons
Details
We have mentioned before that neurons work by receiving and transmitting nerve impulses. They basically use electricity.
The neuron, in most aspects, is just a cell. It has a nucleus and a cell membrane as its components. In the middle of it is a biochemical stew of ions, amino acids, proteins, DNA and RNA, and so on. The difference between a neuron and other cells is the fact that its cell membrane is peculiar, it is irritable. Do anything to it and this thing responds with firing, forming a nerve impulse. Some might even fire on their own, at certain intervals for certain activities that we do unconsciously. Even when the cell is not firing, there is still activity in it as electrical impulses can still be received (tested by using microelectrodes). Because it is a small amount of voltage when the neuron is stable, we call this its resting potential, although maintaining the voltage takes work and the neuron is still very much not at rest.
Now what happens when it is firing ? Well since we already put two microelectrodes to test if it is not, might as well use a third to stimulate that. Normally it would be fine, until an excitation threshold is broken (voltage). Then the voltage difference between the outside and inside happens and the cell abruptly collapses to zero and begins to reverse itself. Now, the inside of the membrane will suddenly swing positive, up to 40 millivolts. This is the neuron’s destabilization, a cataclysm so to say. Fortunately, this does not last for long, as the membrane restabilizes itself within 1 millisecond and returns to its -70 millivolt state.
And of course, this sequence is called the action potential, and it goes far beyond just irritating.

6---full-notes/thelen's-varieties-of-cap.title: Thelen's Varieties of Capitalism
6---full-notes/thelen's-varieties-of-cap.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
Thelen’s Varieties of Capitalism
Details
Kathleen Thelen’s theory explains how advanced capitalist countries respond to globalization in distinct ways, challenging the idea that all are forced into a single, deregulated model. She identifies three divergent paths:


Deregulation (Liberal Market Economies): Countries like the U.S. and Britain, which already had market-driven systems, have responded to global pressures by doubling down on deregulation. This involves weakening unions, increasing competition, and reducing social protections, creating a highly flexible but insecure labor market.


Dualization (Coordinated Market Economies): Germany exemplifies this path. The core of its coordinated economy—centralized wage bargaining between powerful unions and employers—remains intact for “insider” workers in major industries. However, a growing secondary tier of “outsider” workers in the service sector is not covered by these protections. This creates a dual system: stable, high-wage jobs for some, and flexible, less secure work for others. This pattern is maintained by a political coalition (Christian Democrats) historically built around protecting the “male breadwinner” wage.


Embedded Flexibilization (Scandinavian Countries): These nations have also embraced market flexibility, but they have “embedded” it within a strong public safety net. The government, not the employer, guarantees worker security through universal healthcare, pensions that move with the worker from job to job, extensive job retraining programs, and subsidized childcare. This allows firms to be highly competitive and dynamic, while workers remain secure. This model is supported by a political coalition (Social Democrats) that includes women and is built on broad support for a universal welfare state.


Thelen’s key insight is that these different paths are durable because powerful political coalitions form around them, reinforcing the institutional arrangements that serve their interests.

6---full-notes/theoretical-models-of-pts.title: Theoretical Models of PTSD
6---full-notes/theoretical-models-of-pts.content:
Status: adult
Tags: trauma Clinical Psychology neuroscience
Theoretical Models of PTSD
Details
According to Wessa and Flor (2007), aversive learning in PTSD is extremely resistant to extinction due to how it is supported by a network of second-order conditionings that maintain behavioral strength despite the disappearance of the unconditioned trauma/condition. Of course, most models also include the impaired responsivity of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPFC), a crucial mediator of that learning method and modulation of amygdalar responses.
Another theory being the bioinformational theory set forth by Foa and her colleagues sees emotions as information networks in the person’s learning and not just including their response to it but its relationships to other possible responses and meanings as well. According to this mode, treatment of PTSD would then require elicitation of the fear experience as fully as possible and modification of the information to change the structure of it.
Thirdly, moving on to the dual representational theory, Brewin and Dalgleish hold that traumatic memories are stored in two separate forms: explicit, verbally accessible, and implicit, situationally accessible memories. These are store in different manners and different parts of the brain. PTSD is theorized then to occur when traumatic events produce incomplete records of neither the kinds of memories and those are incompatible with the view of the world of the patient. And so healing would be integrating the narrative of the event back into their structure and beliefs, as well as coming to terms with the nonverbal part of the experience by reexperiencing it.
Finally, coming to the heaviest hitter of them all, the Temporal Dynamics Model of Emotional Memory Processing. According to Diamond et al. (2007), PTSD is explained by temporally sequenced patterns of long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD) in the hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex (PFC) as part of a generalized response to stress. LTP is assumed as the process when short-term memory is transferred to long-term memory. It includes protein synthesis and physical changes in the structure of neurons at the synapses. LTD is the phenomenon that inhibit the creation of memories more generally and subsumes a more diffuse set of phenomena. The theory extends further that as LTP happens after trauma, a refactoring process which causes the memory to be basically marked into the hippocampus and not easily made gone.

6---full-notes/theories-and-hypotheses.title: Theories and Hypotheses
6---full-notes/theories-and-hypotheses.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Clinical Psychology
Theories and Hypotheses
Details
These two things are separate concepts. A theory is a set of propositions meant to explain a group of observations. Hypotheses on the other hand are expectations of what would happen if a theory is correct. For example, if I had a theory that people with OCD had a little person on their shoulder talking about some “wash your hands” stuff, the hypothesis would be that they are compulsively washing their hands. Now see that there are two part to the hypothesis, a little person telling them to wash their hands and them washing their hands. The latter is correct, but the former may not be, and that must be proven to test if both are correct or only one is.
To determine the plausibility of a theory, one must consider its fallibility, its repeatability and its testability. Quickly determining these terms, we understand that it can be proven (testability), it can/cannot be disproven (fallibility), and it can be repeated under the circumstances in the test trials (repeatability).

6---full-notes/theory-of-mind-in-animals.title: Theory of Mind in animals
6---full-notes/theory-of-mind-in-animals.content:
Status: teen
Tags: ethology psychology
Theory of Mind in animals
Details
For decades, the idea of studying an animal’s inner life—its thoughts, feelings, or awareness—was dismissed as unscientific sentimentality. Cognitive ethology shattered that taboo. Through elegant experiments, scientists have revealed that the lights are on inside many animal minds. Chimps can pass the mirror test, recognizing a dot of paint on their own forehead, demonstrating self-awareness. They can also demonstrate a theory of mind, knowing that another chimp has different information than they do—a skill they use to out-compete rivals for a hidden banana. This cognitive sophistication is not limited to primates. Crows, some of the smartest birds, will hide food for the next day, demonstrating an ability to plan for the future. They will even re-hide their stash if they know another crow was watching, showing they understand what others know. From chimps that can distinguish intentional acts from accidental ones to bees that ignore information about a food source in an impossible location, the evidence is overwhelming. The animal mind is not a simple black box; for many species, it is a complex, strategic, and aware consciousness.

6---full-notes/theory-of-stigma.title: Theory of Stigma
6---full-notes/theory-of-stigma.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Evolutionary Psychology developmental psychology
Theory of Stigma
Details
Evolutionary psychology offers a compelling, albeit theoretical, explanation for the persistence of stigma across human history. This perspective suggests that early humans, living in small hunter-gatherer bands, developed cognitive “modules” to ensure survival by avoiding threats. These innate mechanisms included the avoidance of those who appeared contagious to prevent disease, the rejection of those who seemed exploitative to protect social resources, and the suspicion of those who looked tribally different to guard against conflict. In the modern context, people with untreated or chronic mental illness may inadvertently trigger these ancient alarms. Their erratic behavior or disheveled appearance can mimic signs of contagion or a lack of social reciprocity, causing others to instinctively distance themselves not out of malice, but out of a misfired evolutionary survival instinct.
Attribution theory attempts to explain stigma through a cognitive lens, positing that we stigmatize behaviors we believe are under a person’s control while forgiving those that are not. The National Institute of Mental Health utilized this logic in campaigns promoting mental illness as a “brain disease,” assuming that framing it as a biological inevitability would reduce blame. However, experimental studies revealed a paradoxical result: while a biological explanation does reduce blame, it increases the desire for social distance and punitive measures. When mental illness is viewed as genetic and permanent, the sufferer is perceived as fundamentally different—almost a different species—rather than a fellow human facing a difficult situation. This “essentialist” view suggests that the person is flawed at a molecular level, leading to deeper exclusion and the sentiment that they can never truly be reintegrated into society.

6---full-notes/therapy-as-a-process-of-a.title: Therapy as a Process of Authenticating Experience
6---full-notes/therapy-as-a-process-of-a.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology CBT
Authenticating Conclusions
Details
A primary function of therapy is to help a patient move from distorted or externally-imposed beliefs about themselves to conclusions that are authenticated by their own lived experience. Patients often arrive with rigid narratives—“I am a failure,” “I am unlovable”—that feel true but are often unexamined generalizations based on painful events. These are inauthentic conclusions because they ignore contradictory evidence and deny the patient’s own agency.
The therapist’s role is not to provide new, “correct” conclusions, but to act as a co-investigator, helping the patient critically examine their own life. This is achieved through several methods:


Socratic Questioning: The therapist asks guiding questions that challenge the patient’s rigid beliefs. (“What is the evidence for that thought? What is the evidence against it? Is there another way to interpret what happened?”) This prompts the patient to become a detective of their own experience, seeking data rather than accepting assumptions.


Narrative Externalization: The therapist helps the patient separate themselves from their problems. Instead of “I am a depressed person,” it becomes “How has depression been influencing your life?” This creates space for the patient to identify “unique outcomes”—moments, however small, where they resisted the problem’s influence.


Focus on Embodied Truth: An authenticated conclusion is not just an intellectual realization; it must feel true emotionally and physically. The therapist pays attention to the patient’s somatic responses and affect, helping them connect a new, more balanced thought with a genuine feeling of relief or rightness.


Through this process, the patient learns to construct a new, more complex, and resilient narrative. The resulting conclusions—“I have failed at times, but I have also succeeded,” “I have felt unloved, but I am capable of giving and receiving love”—are “authenticated” because the patient has built them from the full, nuanced evidence of their own life. They are not just positive affirmations; they are earned truths.

6---full-notes/thin-slices.title: Thin Slices
6---full-notes/thin-slices.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Thin Slices
Details
For the majority of social psychology has supported that we are terrible evaluators and terrible at understanding or predicting any social situations, ever. Yet, somehow, some way, we possess a remarkable automatic capacity for reading others through nonverbal cues. A photo demonstration reveals that people can reliably identify romantic couples versus strangers, arm-wrestling winners, and a mother playing with her baby—all from still images with no contextual information. Accuracy rates reach 80%+ even though participants feel like they’re guessing and cannot articulate how they know. Ambati and Rosenthal’s “thin slice” research formalized this: teachers were videotaped lecturing, and strangers who watched just 6 seconds of silent footage—no sound, no knowledge of the subject or the teacher’s reputation—produced ratings that correlated at r ≈ .70 with end-of-semester student evaluations from students who had spent months in the class. This correlation held even under cognitive load, confirming the process is automatic and pre-reflective. Controlling statistically for smile frequency, hand gestures, and physical attractiveness did not diminish the effect—something holistic about the person’s nonverbal presence carries the signal.

6---full-notes/things-to-do-when-loved-o.title: Things to do when loved one is splitting
6---full-notes/things-to-do-when-loved-o.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology therapy
Things to do when loved one is splitting
Details
Firstly, before doing anything, trying to give any advice or whatever, try to rather focus on your emotion, what you are feeling and not responding with that same emotion, as it will only get you wrapped up with your loved one’s situation and make it even worse. If that is simply too hard try to go and be mindful of your own feelings and wellbeing, meaning you can go take care of yourself to calm yourself down.
Secondly, try not to say anything that can make them emotional, try to be validating first, giving advice, trying to distract or telling them that “its not so bad” are all invalidating. You have to say and GET how badly they are feeling right now. Don’t try to ask them to be different, don’t withhold a solution to a problem if you have it but also don’t say it if they don’t want to, just try to encourage them rather and regulate yourself, the general rule is just to not do anything that you think could be invalidating.
Remember, you must also cheerlead them and remind them of their abilities to get through this as well as validating how hard it is, for example, asking interested questions is a way to do so. Then and only then can you start asking them what they need help with doing or if they can help. The person may say that they cannot think of a solution and all, this is because in that state they are still way too high on their emotions that they cannot get into a clear state of mind to do so, that is when you come back to that later and continue validating/regulating them.
Supporting Content
Additionally, suggest them to do the opposite action of what is causing them to be negative and all might also help. Of course do it in a way that is validating.

Details

The brain goes against providing interesting and easily available information, instead it provides information that is easily accessible for it. It chooses to dish out information that it has encountered recently, which has vivid emotions connecting to it. Everything that might be complex, abstract and actually worth writing about may be very far down the list of ideas of the brain.
But the slip-box negates this, it promotes a more pragmatic solution as the notes we connect will eventually cluster up into ideas that we can write about. Ideas that are actually good and that we know well enough to write on. In the process of making the Zettelkasten, we are already deciding what to write on and what not, the aspects that we need to write on and such. That self-reinforcement helps us dictate where to continue reading on and thinking about, it keeps getting more and more useful, or practical.

6---full-notes/thinking-disorder-in-anxi.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Thinking disorder in anxiety neuroses.md
6---full-notes/thinking-disorder-in-anxi.title: Thinking disorder in anxiety neuroses
6---full-notes/thinking-disorder-in-anxi.content:
Status: adult
Tags: psychology
Thinking disorder in anxiety neuroses
Details
Repetitive thoughts about danger. The patient has continuous verbal or pictorial cognitions about the occurrence of harmful events (“false alarms”).
Reduced ability to “reason” with the fearful thoughts. The patient may suspect that his anxiety-producing thoughts are not reasonable; however, his capacity for objectively evaluating and reappraising is impaired. Even though he may be able to question the reasonableness of his anxiety-producing thoughts, he believes predominantly in their validity.
“Stimulus generalization.” The range of anxiety-evoking stimuli increases so that almost any sound, movement, or other environmental change may be perceived as a danger. For example, a woman in an acute anxiety attack had these experiences: She heard the siren of a fire engine and thought, “My house may be on fire.” At the same time, she visualized her family trapped at home in the fire. Then she heard an airplane flying overhead and had a pictorial image of herself in the airplane and the airplane’s crashing. As she imagined the scene, she experienced anxiety.
Some other characteristics of people suffering from anxiety neuroses may be a decrease in attention and recall due to the patient constantly being hypervigilant for signs of threats rather than the information being given to him. This whole process is involuntary and he has no control whatsoever to diverting his attention to other things, which can make him believe he is going crazy and therefore enhancing his anxiety.
Another characteristic is the tendency to “catastrophize”. In any situation where there is a possibility of an unpleasant outcome, the patient will dwell on the worst situation possible. He ignores any and every sign as he equates the hypothesis with a fact. Even further, these patients usually stay highly anxious with symptoms maybe even going further with each encounter whilst the normal patient will habituate and adapt to calm themselves down.
Also their response to external stimuli is different, as the noxious stimuli is adapted and determined fairly rapidly by someone normal, the anxious patient cannot discriminate this, and he sticks with the meaning and concept of danger that has been assigned to that stimuli.

6---full-notes/thyroid-hormones-and-depr.title: Thyroid Hormones and Depression
6---full-notes/thyroid-hormones-and-depr.content:
Status: baby
Tags: biology psychology
Thyroid Hormones and Depression
Details
A significant link exists between the thyroid gland and major depression, highlighting how a dysfunction in a peripheral hormonal system can manifest as a primary psychiatric illness. Thyroid hormones regulate the body’s overall metabolism and energy levels.
A deficiency of these hormones, a condition known as hypothyroidism, often presents with symptoms that are clinically indistinguishable from atypical depression. The primary overlapping symptom is severe psychomotor retardation—a profound state of exhaustion, physical slowing, and mental fatigue.
According to Sapolsky, a notable percentage of major depression diagnoses may actually be undiagnosed hypothyroidism. This connection underscores the importance of a full biological workup in diagnosing depression, as treating the underlying thyroid issue can resolve the depressive symptoms. It serves as a clear example of depression being a whole-body biological disease, not just a disorder of the mind.

6---full-notes/to-gain-intelligence.title: To Gain Intelligence
6---full-notes/to-gain-intelligence.content:
Status: adult
Tags: intelligence 3 - Tags/reading writing
To Gain Intelligence
Details
And so how to gain intelligence ? Emerson argues that we should find our own virtues, follow our own interests, and souls to do so.
Imagine intelligence not as a destination reached by rote learning or the dutiful ingestion of others’ conclusions, but as a state of being. Emerson beckons us away from the dusty library shelves where knowledge lies inert, entombed in print, unless quickened by a living mind. The first act of gaining true intelligence is the radical act of listening to the subtle murmurs of your own intuition, that “aboriginal Self” which connects you to the universal flow, the Over-Soul. This inner voice, often drowned out by the clamor of convention and external authority, holds the kernel of genuine insight. To cultivate intelligence is first to cultivate the courage to hear and heed this inner oracle.  
Then, Emerson would point us outward, not to institutions, but to Nature. Not merely a scenic backdrop, but the great, silent teacher, the living embodiment of divine law and reason. Walk the woods, he’d urge. Observe the effortless cycle of growth and decay, the perfect geometry of a snowflake, the steadfastness of the oak, the fluidity of the stream. In Nature’s intricate, harmonious design, the receptive mind perceives analogies, mirrors to its own processes. Intelligence blossoms not from memorizing botanical names, but from understanding what is that animates the leaf, the star, the very air we breathe. The universe speaks in symbols, and intelligence is the capacity to interpret this silent, profound language. See how the light falls, how the shadow shifts – these are lessons more potent than any lecture.  
As there exists creative writing, there must also exists creative reading. And so Emerson does not dismiss them entirely, but reframes their role. They are not masters, but stimulants. Read, yes, but read actively, critically, with the fierce independence of your own spirit. Use the thoughts of Plato, of Shakespeare, of Goethe, not as molds into which you must pour your own consciousness, but as flint striking steel, igniting your own fire. “Meek young men grow up in libraries,” he warns, mistaking passive acceptance for learning. True intelligence engages, questions, wrestles with ideas, using the past as a springboard into the present, into the unique perspective only you can hold. The wise man reads a book and closes it to think his own thoughts, sparked but not dictated by the author.  
Furthermore, Emerson champions action and experience. Intelligence is not a cloistered virtue. It must be tested and tempered in the forge of life. To truly understand labor, one must labor. To grasp resilience, one must face adversity. Living itself is the primary text. Each encounter, each challenge, each simple act of navigating the day holds the potential for insight. The mind grows keen through engagement, through the application of thought to circumstance. It is in the doing, the trying, the living of principles, that understanding deepens from abstract notion to lived reality.

6---full-notes/to-be-careful-of-authors'.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
To be careful of author’s help
Details
Sometimes the author will tell you the unity of his plan in his preface. In this aspect fiction writers are completely different from expository writers, as they would want to keep you in the least amount of suspense as possible.
This is where the balance comes in, do not be too proud to accept the author’s help but neither rely too completely on what he says. Be guided by what the author gives, but always remember the finding of unity is a task of the reader, as having one belongs to the writer.
But note these points before proceeding. First is how frequently one can expect the author to help them state the plan of his book. Second is to not take the sample summaries as if it were a final and absolute formation of the book’s unity, because it can be variously stated. There is no one right way to do it. One may be better than the other, in proportion as it is brief, accurate and comprehensive.
Similarly with Rule 3, do not ignore the headings and sectional divisions of the author. Although we should not ignore them, neither should we slavishly follow them. They are here to help us, just like the titles and prefaces. But they are merely guides, helping us to look into and below the book for its structure.

To break and think Creatively
Details
The advices that are included in this are generally not included in the slip-box, and so I will do so here.
First is to make sure that you see what you think you see and describe it as plainly and factually as possible. Of course we need to check if we’re unsure. Our perception doesn’t follow the order of seeing first and interpreting second, it follows both at the same time. And so we don’t even notice stuffs that are missing in our perception, in our vision. So we need to trick ourselves into seeing what we don’t. Try to make it so that our reinterpretation or the detection of missing information comes after we have seen the image.
This can be applied to our reading, we don’t see the words in our books as merely words, but parts of a sentence to build up the meaning. And so to understand it we need to constantly revise our first interpretation of it, hold back the urge to jump to conclusions as well.
As we encounter things that have already proven to not work, most of the time we don’t actually see them. But when we do it is actually pretty effective to try and come up with new ideas that do work.
(A way to do this is to ask counterfactual questions, like “what if?”. Like to learn the value of money in a world without it rather than focusing on the obvious we already have in our money-driven world.)

6---full-notes/to-criticize-the-incomple.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/To criticize the incompleteness of analysis.md
6---full-notes/to-criticize-the-incomple.title: To criticize the incompleteness of analysis
6---full-notes/to-criticize-the-incomple.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
To criticize the incompleteness of analysis
Details
This is the final point of criticism than can be taken out,it is when the author has not solved the problems that he started out to do so, or that he has failed to make good uses of his materials, did not see all the implications and ramifications, and so on…
Let us illustrate this point briefly. The analysis of types of government in Aristotle’s Politics is incomplete. Because of the limitations of his time and his erroneous acceptance of slavery, Aristotle fails to consider, or for that matter even to conceive, the truly democratic constitution that is based on universal suffrage; nor can he imagine either representative government or the modern kind of federated state. His analysis would have to be extended to apply to these political realities. Euclid’s Elements of Geometry is an incomplete account because Euclid failed to consider other postulates about the relation of parallel lines. Modern geometrical works, making these other assumptions, supply the deficiencies. Dewey’s How We Think is an incomplete analysis of thinking because it fails to treat the sort of thinking that occurs in reading or learning by instruction in addition to the sort that occurs in investigation and discovery. To a Christian who believes in personal immortality, the writings of Epictetus or Marcus Aurelius are an incomplete account of human happiness.
This point is a criticism of the limitations of the author’s achievement, and a reader who suspended his judgement on the book as there is no adverse criticism on any of the other points may make this point nonetheless. Knowing this specific point allows readers to judge books, to see which is better than which because of what reasons.

6---full-notes/to-define-lyrical-poetry.title: To define lyrical poetry

To define lyrical poetry

The simplest definition which is somewhat limited is that it is what poets write. But there are other definitions, poetry may be the author expressing himself, his personality in the form of written words, but also action, musical sounds, or even just feelings. But we will confine it to one definition for the sake of reading it efficiently, and that is “whatever may be the origin of the poetic impulse, for us, consists of words, and that is of words that are arranged in a certain way”.
Of course there are other definitions that forces poetry to always have meaning, or apply a specialized language, but that is just mixing modern notions with antique ones. So we stand in the middle, not too broad or narrow either.

6---full-notes/to-disagree.title: To disagree
6---full-notes/to-disagree.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
To disagree
Details
If the reader disagrees with the author then he must be able to show where the author is wrong, what he is wrong about and so on. They are not merely voicing prejudices or expressing emotions, but fulfilling these conditions:
The first is this. Since men are animals as well as rational, it is necessary to acknowledge the emotions you bring to a dispute, or those that arise in the course of it. Otherwise you are likely to be giving vent to feelings, not stating reasons. You may even think you have reasons, when all you have are strong feelings.
Second, you must make your own assumptions explicit. You must know what your prejudices—that is, your prejudgments—are. Otherwise you are not likely to admit that your opponent may be equally entitled to different assumptions. Good controversy should not be a quarrel about assumptions. If an author, for example, explicitly asks you to take something for granted, the fact that the opposite can also be done so does not prevent you from honoring his request. You must give him a fair hearing.
Third and finally, try to give more light, less heat in the argument, try to take the other point of view, you must also read sympathetically, so that your disagreement will be civil, not contentious.
These are the ideal rules for disagreeing with an author, but we usually won’t achieve this state… so we should not expect the author to do so as well. Do not expect him to be perfect as we are no different, and so we should not confine ourselves to such rules, but rather be more vigilant of the points that it is asking of us.

6---full-notes/to-finally-draft-and-writ.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/To finally draft and write.md
6---full-notes/to-finally-draft-and-writ.title: To finally draft and write
6---full-notes/to-finally-draft-and-writ.content:
Status: adult
Tags: writing Zettelkasten
To finally draft and write
Details
These are the last steps to getting a manuscript done. We need to structure the text and keep it flexible. After experimenting and making new ideas, we now need to make it into a linear order. Instead of deciding what to write in it, we have to decide what isn’t needed to be written in particular parts of the manuscript. By looking at the structure, we can see if the info will be mentioned in another part.
Another vital aspect is to have a separate, project-specific place to sort out notes for projects. An outliner might help with developing a rough structure, but also allows us to keep it flexible. The structure of an argument is a part of it and therefore will change during the process of development. When it no longer changes much, it will turn into a “table of contents”. But even then, it helps to see it as a structural guideline and not a prescription. It is not unusual to change the order of chapters at the very end.
The other key point is to work on different manuscripts at the same time, as it will help us produce by-products which becomes the resource for another, and repeating so on, until it becomes so intertwined that an isolated factory can’t compete with it anymore. This also comes with the benefit of us not losing motivation ever, as when we get bored with working on one of the projects, we can just switch to another to do instead, which is still productive.

6---full-notes/to-make-habits.title: To make habits
6---full-notes/to-make-habits.content:

To make habits
Details
We normally can’t guess what we will be doing in the long run, but there is one exception, though: we most certainly act according to our intention if we happen to intend to do what we used to do before.
This leads to the fact that we have the best chance to change our behavior over the long term by starting with a realistic idea about the difficulties of behavioral change. Even though the more we do something, we feel more in control about it, its more likely that we are losing control over it.
So the trick is to break old habits by strategically building up new ones that have a chance to replace the old ones.

6---full-notes/to-not-be-scared-of-draft.title: To not be scared of drafting
6---full-notes/to-not-be-scared-of-draft.content:
Status: baby
Tags: writing
To not be scared of drafting
Details
When writing, it is important to keep in mind that your first version is only your first draft. It is only writing down some ideas for one self, and then turning it into something publishable later, and so that encourages us to actually write on it. By the time we stopped writing, we would be surprised to find that the only thing left to do was revise the draft already had (or do more revisioning and drafting, depends.).
Also another advice is not to be afraid to delete what has no function within an argument, which is pretty hard once we get sentimental with all our piece of writing. To bypass this, just move it to another document and tell ourselves we’ll use it later, for something else. More often than not, we’ll forget and just never touch these things ever again.

6---full-notes/total-institutions-and-th.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Total Institutions and the Structure of Self.md
6---full-notes/total-institutions-and-th.title: Total Institutions and the Structure of Self
6---full-notes/total-institutions-and-th.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
Total Institutions and the Structure of Self
Details
Erving Goffman’s concept of the “total institution” serves as a foundational model for understanding environments of intense social control. He defines it as “a place of residence and work where a large number of like-situated individuals, cut off from the wider society for an appreciable period of time, together lead an enclosed, formally administered round of life.” This is not a literal description but a Weberian “ideal type”—a theoretical benchmark against which the all-encompassing nature of real-world organizations (prisons, monasteries, military barracks, asylums) can be measured.
The single most critical feature of the total institution is the systematic breakdown of the barriers that ordinarily separate the three spheres of life: sleep, play, and work. In the outside world, these activities occur in different places, with different people, under different authorities, allowing for varied social roles and private respite. The total institution collapses these boundaries. All of life’s activities are conducted in the same location and under a single, central authority. This fusion is the primary mechanism that renders an individual’s self vulnerable to the institution’s control, as it eliminates any possibility of escape or rest from the institutional role.
Life inside is characterized by “batch living,” where daily activities are performed not by choice but “in the immediate company of a large batch of others, all of whom are treated alike and required to do the same thing together.” This bureaucratic management of human needs creates the institution’s most critical social feature: a “basic split” between the large managed group (inmates) and a small supervisory staff. These two strata exist in separate, antagonistic worlds, with mutual mistrust and formally prescribed social distance. This chasm is not a flaw but a structural necessity for maintaining control.
Ultimately, the total institution is a technology of social control that operates by re-engineering the very architecture of social life. In normal society, the self is maintained through a “dramaturgical” performance across different social stages, including a “back stage” where one can relax and be out of character. The total institution achieves its power by eliminating the back stage entirely. By forcing the individual into a state of perpetual performance under constant surveillance, it functions as a social greenhouse, meticulously designed to cultivate a specific, compliant type of person by controlling every element of their world.

6---full-notes/totemism-as-a-unified-tri.title: Totemism as a Unified Tribal Cosmology
6---full-notes/totemism-as-a-unified-tri.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sociology
Totemism as a Unified Tribal Cosmology
Details
One must correct the misconception that totemism is merely a collection of isolated clan cults. The reality is far more complex and systematic. The various totemic cults within a single tribe are not ignorant of one another; they are constituent parts of a single, overarching religious system. This is evidenced by the mutual respect and belief clans hold for each other’s totems and by their participation in one another’s rituals. The most compelling proof is the methodical division of the entire known universe among the totems, with no overlap. Such a systematic classification could not arise by chance; it implies a tacit, tribe-wide agreement. Therefore, totemism must be understood not at the level of the clan, but at the level of the tribe. It functions as a complete cosmology, a shared religious framework that gives order to the world, much like the later pantheons of polytheistic religions.

Totemism as the foundations for Religion
Details
The totemic system, in its entirety, represents the most primitive religion currently observable. Its religious nature is undeniable, as it is founded upon the fundamental division of the world into the sacred and the profane. Its primitiveness is established by its inseparability from the clan-based social organization, which is the simplest form of society known. The clan’s very unity often derives not from blood or territory, but solely from sharing a name, an emblem, and a cult—that is, from its totemism. A religion so intrinsically fused with a social structure of such elemental simplicity can rightly be considered the most elementary form of religious life. Therefore, to discover the origins of these totemic beliefs is to likely uncover the very causes that gave rise to the religious sentiment in humanity.

Touch or Cutaneous senses

What we think of as touch is actually a combination of several partly independent senses: pressure on the skin, warmth, cold, pain, itch, vibration, movement across it, and stretch of the skin. 6---full-notes/toxic-effects-of-tobacco.title: Toxic Effects of Tobacco
6---full-notes/toxic-effects-of-tobacco.content:
Status: teen
Tags: pharmacology physiology
Toxic Effects of Tobacco
Details
There are three major ways that Tobacco affects us: the toxicity of nicotine, carbon monoxide, and the irritant action of tars and combustion byproducts.
Firstly, Nicotine acts as a cardiovascular poison. It causes chronic vasoconstriction-tightening of the blood vessels-increasing cardiac workload. For example, if we flex our muscles for a whole day, the fibers would tear and degrade eventually. This also applies to the cardiovascular system, leading to microscopic damage, atherosclerosis, and eventually heart attacks or strokes. This vasoconstriction is particularly damaging to fine capillaries, leading to peripheral vascular disease, a condition where blood flow to the extremities is compromised, sometimes necessitating amputation even in young athletes using smokeless tobacco.
Second, Carbon Monoxide, being a byproduct of the combustion binding in blood and of course, taking oxygen away from us. This creates chronic hypoxia (oxygen deprivation).
Lastly, Smoke and Tars contain carcinogenic and irritant compounds which destroys the lung tissue and leads to lung, larynx, and mouth cancer. Our body tries to get this out by coughing (smoker’s cough).

Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) in Brain Research
Details

Methodology: Applies magnetic pulses through the skull to temporarily inactivate or stimulate neurons. Pulses vary in frequency/intensity for inhibitory/excitatory effects. Targets scalp areas to disrupt functions and study processes like language, perception, or action. Observes behavioral changes to infer area involvement and connections.
Advantages: Selectively activates/inactivates brain areas. Identifies locations/functions without reorganization (unlike brain damage). Studies various processes non-surgically.
Disadvantages: Invasive with short-term side effects (e.g., headaches, balance issues, hallucinations, apathy, compulsions). Imprecise/approximative results. Limited to specific applications.

6---full-notes/transparency-assumption-o.content:
Status: baby
Tags: Cognitive Psychology
Transparency Assumption of the Brain
Details
Some researchers argue that individuals born with underdeveloped brain regions can still be valuable subjects for studying cognitive architecture. In fact, selectively impaired developmental cases may reveal which parts of the brain correlate with specific cognitive functions.
However, this approach challenges a key assumption: that the rest of the brain operates “transparently” (i.e., normally) aside from the impaired part. Critics point to the brain’s high plasticity during development, which may allow other regions to “re-wire” and take over lost functions. If such reorganization occurs, it undermines the transparency assumption and makes it harder to interpret deficits cleanly.
As a result, some argue that lesion studies in adults—where brain systems were fully developed before injury—offer more reliable insights.

6---full-notes/trauma-leading-to-actions.title: Trauma leading to actions leading to more trauma
6---full-notes/trauma-leading-to-actions.content:
Status: adult
Tags: trauma psychology
Trauma leading to actions leading to more trauma
Details
Trauma does not only come from what happens to us. It often comes from what we do, or fail to do, when it happens.
Many survivors look back and feel shame about how they acted. They wish they had fought harder, spoken louder, moved faster. They regret freezing, staying silent, or giving in. Even if their reactions were natural survival instincts, they see them later as weakness or betrayal. This regret becomes a second wound, deeper than the first.
This self-blame can be more painful than the original event. It can grow into self-hatred. Survivors do not only grieve what was done to them. They grieve who they were in that moment. They despise the fear they felt. They despise the helplessness. They despise themselves.
When someone feels broken inside, it changes how they act later. Shame makes people pull away from others. Anger makes them lash out. Fear makes them avoid things that might heal them. Without meaning to, they create new situations where they get hurt again. Trauma leads to actions that cause more trauma. It becomes a loop that tightens every time they fall.
The only way to break the loop is to forgive the past self. To understand that reactions under trauma are not moral failures. They are survival. They are not weakness. They are what kept the person alive. Healing starts by facing the feelings that were too hard to face before. Healing grows when there is compassion instead of punishment.
