6---full-notes/trauma-induced-phobia.title: Trauma-Induced Phobia
6---full-notes/trauma-induced-phobia.content:
Status: adult
Tags:psychology trauma 3 - Tags/environment
Trauma-Induced Phobia
Details
While many phobias are characterized by an intense, irrational fear with an indeterminate origin, a distinct and powerful category arises directly from the ashes of a traumatic experience. A trauma-induced phobia is not merely an anxiety; it is a learned, deeply ingrained survival response that has become maladaptive. In this condition, a specific object, situation, or environment becomes inextricably linked with the overwhelming terror, helplessness, and physiological distress of a past traumatic event. The resulting fear is not just of the trigger itself, but of re-experiencing the profound psychological and emotional injury associated with it. This phobia acts as a perpetual echo of the initial trauma, a constant and painful reminder of a moment when one’s safety was shattered.
The mechanism behind the formation of a trauma-induced phobia is rooted in the brain’s primitive survival architecture. During a traumatic event, the amygdala—the brain’s threat detection center—works overtime, creating a potent and lasting memory that fuses the sensory details of the environment with the intense emotional state of fear. Consequently, a previously neutral stimulus, such as a specific location, a sound, or a smell, becomes a conditioned trigger. When the individual re-encounters this trigger, the brain bypasses rational thought and activates the fight-or-flight response as if the original danger were present once more. This process creates a debilitating feedback loop: the trigger evokes the memory and the physiological state of the trauma, which in turn reinforces the trigger’s association with danger, solidifying the phobia.
This direct link to a precipitating event distinguishes trauma-induced phobias from other specific phobias. Whereas a person with arachnophobia may not recall a specific event that caused their fear of spiders, a person with a trauma-induced phobia can almost always trace their fear back to a definitive moment. For them, avoiding the phobic trigger is not just about managing anxiety; it is an active, desperate attempt to avoid the intrusive memories, flashbacks, and overwhelming emotional state of the original trauma. The avoidance, therefore, becomes a form of self-protection against re-experiencing a wound that has not yet healed.
Understanding this etiology is paramount for effective treatment. Addressing a trauma-induced phobia requires more than simple exposure therapy aimed at desensitizing the fear response. The therapeutic work must go deeper, focusing on processing and integrating the traumatic memory itself. By using trauma-focused modalities, the individual can begin to uncouple the memory from its emotional and physiological intensity, allowing the brain to reclassify the past event as something that is over and no longer a present threat. In this way, healing is achieved not by merely silencing the echo of fear, but by addressing the original sound of the trauma from which it emanates.

6---full-notes/traumatic-memory.title: Traumatic memory
6---full-notes/traumatic-memory.content:
Status: baby

Traumatic memory
Details
The nature of memories change and are constantly revised and updated. It is not base on reflections of reality but rather stories we tell to convey our personal take on such experiences. These memories are not integrated within the storages of our autobiographical memory, creating a dual system. Traumatic memories on the other hand are cut-off, they are frozen in time, barely comprehensible fragments. The goal of treatment would be association, which is making these elements of trauma into the ongoing narrative of life so that the brain can recognize the timelines of when these events happened and move on from it.
The accuracy of our memories largely depends on how meaningful it was and how emotional we felt about it at the time it happened. The key factor is our level of arousal. I mean things associated with people, smells, sounds, and places that will stay with us for a long time. Although usually the more adrenaline is pumped, the more precise our memories are. But it is only true until confronted with horror, especially “inescapable shock” that this system becomes overwhelmed and breaks down entirely, leading to PTSD.
The major differences between how people talked about normal memories and traumatic experiences is the fact that they are organized differently and reacted differently. Weddings, births, graduations were recalled as events with clear structures, and people usually said there had never been a period that they had completely forgotten any of these events. In contrast, the memories of traumatized patient were more disorganized; details were too clearly but the thing is the sequence and other vital details was completely fragmented.

“As you review your notes from the previous session before the session, ask yourself:

6---full-notes/treatments-for-asd.title: Treatments for ASD
6---full-notes/treatments-for-asd.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Clinical Psychology
Treatments for ASD
Details
Although the research for treatment in ASD has been quite difficult due to the sheer amount of time and effort required, there are still promising efforts in the treatment of ASD, mainly psychological. Early landmark studies, like Ivar Lovaas’s intensive behavioral program in the 1980s, demonstrated that dramatic gains in IQ and functioning were possible by applying operant conditioning for over 40 hours a week. This established that intensive intervention could work, but the model’s rigor was questioned as it wasn’t a randomized controlled trial. This methodological challenge persists; a later meta-analysis confirmed that while intensive treatments show large positive effects, the quality of most studies remains low.
In response, research has evolved beyond sheer intensity towards more targeted and sustainable approaches. A key development is parent-led intervention, which leverages the family’s constant presence to generalize gains. This led to innovations like Pivotal Response Treatment (PRT). Instead of sequentially targeting individual problem behaviors, PRT focuses on core “pivotal” areas like a child’s motivation and responsiveness, using natural reinforcers like play and praise. This not only proves effective but also improves the overall family dynamic. Furthermore, other interventions have successfully targeted foundational skills like joint attention (JA) and symbolic play (SP), where short, daily sessions have shown lasting improvements in expressive language. This suggests the frontier of ASD treatment lies in identifying these key leverage points rather than just maximizing therapeutic hours.

6---full-notes/treatments-of-conduct-dis.title: Treatments of Conduct Disorder
6---full-notes/treatments-of-conduct-dis.content:
Status: adult
Tags: therapy Clinical Psychology
Treatments of Conduct Disorder
Details
The treatments that seem to have the most effectiveness are ones that addresses the multiple systems that are involved in the life of a child.
Starting with family interventions, which is the most logical treatment of course, due to how maltreatment has shown to correlate to conduct disorder probabilities highly. As an example, in an RCT (Shaw, Dishion, Supplee, et al., 2006), researchers compared what is called the family checkup (FCU) treatment to none at all. FCU involves three meetings, to get to know, assess, and provide feedback to parents about their education and raising methods. FCU was offered to families with toddlers who had a high risk factor for conduct problems. The result was effective, not just short-term, but even 2 years after the intervention.
Another method is a behavioral program called parent management training (PMT), in which they are taught to reward their children for prosocial behaviors rather than anti-social. Of course this treatment can be modified, but, in general, it is the most efficacious intervention to prevent conduct disorder and oppositional defiant disorder. It can be effective anywhere from 1-3 years.
Lastly, multisystemic treatment (MST) has also proven to be promising. It is basically giving intensive and comprehensive therapy services in the community, targeting adolescents, family, school, even the peer group. They basically work on the premise that all these things combine to incite the appearance of conduct disorder. The methods of applying can vary widely, behavioral, cognitive, family, and case-management techniques depending on the situation. It has the highest effective rate, which can range up to 4 years.

6---full-notes/triage-warning-signs-chec.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology university
Triage Warning Signs Checklist
Details
The triage risk assessment for all cases reported to the SCU was conducted by a practitioner with a background in psychology, utilizing a Structured Professional Judgment (SPJ) approach. SPJ is a well-established analytical method in risk assessment, defined as a process that is “discretionary but relies on evidence-based guidelines to systematize the exercise of discretion”. This approach seeks to combine the strengths of structured, data-driven tools with the nuanced understanding of a trained professional, avoiding the pitfalls of purely mechanistic or purely subjective assessments.
The checklist is divided into two key categories, ensuring a comprehensive view of the situation: Behavioral Red Flags for the Individual of Concern (IoC) and Behavioral Red Flags for Targets. The IoC flags are designed to identify acute risk factors that might not be fully captured by the QuAIC’s broader dimensions. These include high-lethality indicators such as “Homicide threats,” “Access to or affinity with weapons,” and psychological indicators like “Last-resort thinking” (comments suggesting a person has nothing left to lose) and evidence of severe “Mental illness”. The inclusion of flags for Targets, such as “Significant distress” and “Adherence to protective measures,” is equally important. It ensures that the assessment process remains victim-centered and accounts for the impact on the person being targeted, recognizing that a target’s high level of fear may itself be a critical risk factor requiring immediate intervention.

6---full-notes/trivers-willard-hypothesi.content:

Trivers-Willard Hypothesis
Details
This hypothesis states that male and female ratio of being reproduced is not the same, it may depend on the situation the female finds itself in, social status and physical condition can influence the sex of her offspring to maximize her reproductive success. This mostly applies to tournament-bonding species as they have a clear discrepancy between birthing females and males.
For example, birthing males would be a gamble, as 95% of the males do not reproduce, but if they do, the amount they reproduce is 5x-6x of that of a female in the species. And so high-ranking females would have the resources to do this gamble. Oppositely, the lower-ranking females would have to birth females to make sure their genes get passed on at the very least.

Tropane Alkaloids
Details
The “power plants” of the Solanaceae family are characterized by Tropane Alkaloids. An alkaloid is a chemical produced by a plant containing a basic nitrogen atom. The two primary tropane alkaloids discussed are Atropine (a mixture of stereoisomers) and Scopolamine, identical to Atropine but possess one additional oxygen atom. These molecules are found in plants like Atropa belladonna, Datura, and Brugmansia. They are potent poisons found in all parts of the plant (seeds, leaves, roots).
Tropane Alkaloids are antagonists at the Muscarinic Acetylcholine Receptor. The Acetylcholine is an important neurotransmitter functioning the parasympathetic nervous system. When it is blocked, the fight or flight system goes haywire as there is nothing to keep it in check.

6---full-notes/turning-to-myth.title: Turning to Myth
6---full-notes/turning-to-myth.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Turning to Myth
Details
Still in the 19th century, Nietzsche aligned himself with a counter-Enlightenment tradition that sought to rehabilitate “Myth” as the superior mode of understanding compared to the abstract “Didactic” or scientific history. This was particularly exemplified by Plato’s “Republic” which featured mostly dialogue between people, which Nietzsche argued that led to nowhere and wasn’t applicable to humanity’s condition.
Nietzsche then turned to the Platonic function of Myth. In this context, a myth is a narrative that expresses a “concrete necessity.” Think of a character like King Lear or Oedipus. When Oedipus kills his father, we cannot say it was logically necessary (in the way 2+2=4), nor can we say it was a random accident. Instead, we feel it was characterologically appropriate; given who Oedipus is, this is exactly the sort of thing that would happen to him. Myth captures this “appropriateness”—a form of necessity that is tied to individuals and types rather than abstract laws. The Genealogy of Morality is best understood not as rigorous history or sociology, but as a Myth in this specific sense. It presents typological characters (The Priest, The Warrior, The Slave) whose actions unfold with a psychological and dramatic inevitability, serving as a template to understand human drives across different eras.

6---full-notes/types-of-long-term-memory.title: Types of Long-term Memory
6---full-notes/types-of-long-term-memory.content:
Status: teen
Tags: learning psychology
Types of Long-term Memory
Details
Long-term memory is not a single, monolithic entity but is broadly divided into two fundamental categories: declarative and non-declarative memory. The distinction hinges on conscious awareness.
Declarative memory encompasses all the information that we can consciously recall and “declare.” It is further subdivided into two types. Episodic memory is autobiographical, consisting of personal events and experiences tied to specific times and places, such as recalling your high school graduation or where you were during a major world event. Semantic memory, on the other hand, consists of general knowledge and facts about the world, like knowing the capital of Indiana or the function of a laser pointer. These memories are not tied to personal experience.
In contrast, non-declarative memory (or procedural memory) operates unconsciously. It includes motor skills like playing tennis or riding a bike, which are performed automatically without conscious thought about the individual steps. This category also includes priming, where prior exposure to a stimulus influences a later response without conscious awareness, and classical conditioning, like Pavlov’s dogs salivating at the ring of a bell. These two systems of memory are anatomically distinct and can be affected differently by brain injury, explaining why a person with severe amnesia might forget their own life story but still retain the ability to play the piano flawlessly.

6---full-notes/types-of-risk-factors.title: Types of Risk Factors
6---full-notes/types-of-risk-factors.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Developmental Psychopathology developmental psychology
Types of Risk Factors
Details
Types of Risk Factors:


Spurious: A variable that predicts an outcome but is not the true causal agent. The relationship is better explained by another, underlying factor (e.g., aggression predicts school failure, but the underlying ADHD is the stronger predictor).


Fixed: A risk factor that cannot be changed (e.g., sex, genes).


Malleable: A risk factor that can be changed through intervention (e.g., parenting styles, income levels, peer groups). These are the primary targets for treatment and prevention.


Causal: A malleable risk factor that, when changed, directly causes a change in the outcome. Identifying these is the ultimate goal, but it is difficult without true experiments, which are often unethical in this field. It is unethical because kids cannot be put under adverse conditions so that we can study which factors are causal and such.


A related concept is vulnerability, which can be thought of as an early-appearing, deeply-rooted risk factor like genetics or temperament.

6---full-notes/types-of-samples.content:
Status: baby
Tags: statistics psychology
Types of Samples
Details
As we all know statistics are used to gather data and use said data to comment on what happens in the population, or just used to describe the characteristics of the sample.
This same relationship divides statistics into two branches. Descriptive statistics stay inside the sample: you summarise what you actually measured — the range, the mean, the standard deviation, a histogram. It is always the first step: “I have a pile of data; let me look at it.” Inferential statistics reach beyond the sample: you analyse the sample in order to draw conclusions about the population and test hypotheses. Put simply, descriptive describes what you have; inferential infers what you can’t see.

6---full-notes/ubc's-ideal-candidate.title: UBC's Ideal Candidate
6---full-notes/ubc's-ideal-candidate.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship university
UBC’s Ideal Candidate
Details
Introduction
The University of British Columbia (UBC) is a top-ranked public research university with a global reputation and a strong international community. UBC’s official messaging and admissions materials consistently emphasize not just academic excellence, but also the holistic qualities and values that define an ideal student. Especially for applicants to programs like Psychology (UBC’s most popular major) and Education, as well as those vying for major scholarships, UBC looks for well-rounded individuals who will thrive academically and enrich the campus community. By reading between the lines of UBC’s mission statements, admissions pages, scholarship criteria, and faculty websites, we can identify recurring themes in tone and content that paint a clear picture of the kind of student UBC seeks. This report breaks down the core academic and personal traits of UBC’s ideal international undergraduate candidate – from scholarly abilities to leadership, community engagement, global outlook, and mindset – and highlights the values UBC explicitly and implicitly prioritizes. Key insights from UBC’s scholarship programs and the expectations of the Psychology and Education faculties are included, followed by a summary table of the key traits and their significance.
Academic Excellence and Intellectual Curiosity
UBC’s first expectation is strong academic performance. As a highly competitive institution, UBC admits students who have excelled in their secondary education – typically those among the “brightest minds in the world”. The admissions process is rigorous and comparative, meaning international applicants must meet high standards and often exceed basic requirements to stand out. Superior grades in relevant courses are essential; UBC evaluates all Grade 11 and 12 academic courses, giving particular weight to subjects related to the chosen field of study. An ideal candidate for Psychology, for instance, would have a strong foundation in science or social science courses, while an aspiring Education student would excel across a broad academic spectrum.
However, UBC looks beyond just grades. The university explicitly encourages intellectual exploration and curiosity. Notably, UBC will even exclude an applicant’s lowest high-school grade (if it’s outside core requirements) “to encourage you to explore subjects outside your comfort zone”. This policy reveals that UBC admires students who challenge themselves academically rather than playing it safe. Top applicants often pursue enriched or advanced curricula (such as IB or AP programs) and seek out opportunities to deepen their knowledge. UBC’s research-intensive culture also means that intellectual curiosity and a penchant for inquiry are prized. The Department of Psychology, for example, is described as a global leader in research and scholarship, with faculty and students advancing knowledge across many sub-fields. The ideal Psychology applicant would demonstrate genuine interest in scientific inquiry and perhaps have engaged in research projects or independent study. Likewise, an Education-related candidate would show intellectual engagement with topics like pedagogy, human development, or social issues in education. Overall, academic excellence (high achievement and preparedness) coupled with intellectual enthusiasm (curiosity, initiative in learning) forms the bedrock of the ideal UBC student profile.
UBC’s tone when discussing academics – using words like “excellence” and “outstanding” – underscores that it values students who strive to be the best. In UBC’s statement of values, Excellence is defined as “the quality of striving to be, and being, outstanding”. Prospective students are expected to embody this drive. In practice, this means competitive grades, a solid grasp of English (meeting a high English Language Admission Standard), and a track record of academic rigor. At the same time, being an “outstanding” scholar at UBC also means being open-minded and innovative. UBC’s strategic plan highlights innovation as a core theme, indicating a preference for students who think creatively and embrace new ideas. Thus, the ideal candidate not only earns top marks, but also displays a love of learning, critical thinking skills, and readiness to contribute to UBC’s dynamic academic environment.
Leadership and Community Engagement
UBC makes it clear that pure academics are not enough – the ideal candidate is well-rounded and actively involved beyond the classroom. Since 2012, UBC has used a broad-based admissions process that requires a Personal Profile essay from applicants, specifically to identify “well-rounded candidates who could perform well academically and get involved on campus.” This reflects UBC’s belief that students who engage in extracurricular activities, leadership roles, and community service enrich the university community and are more likely to be successful, engaged graduates.
Leadership is one of the most emphasized qualities. UBC looks for students who have demonstrated initiative, influence, or responsibility in their schools or communities. The top scholarships for international students explicitly require leadership potential or achievement. For example, the Karen McKellin International Leader of Tomorrow Award recognizes “exceptional…students who demonstrate superior academic achievement and exemplary leadership skills that support and empower others through collaboration, empathy and active listening,” with a positive impact through school or community projects. This description is revealing: UBC’s ideal leaders are not just title-holders, but those who empower others, work in teams, and show empathy. Leadership, as valued by UBC, can take many forms – from holding office in student government, leading a volunteer initiative, mentoring younger students, to spearheading a project or club. The tone in UBC’s materials (highlighting collaboration and active listening alongside leadership) suggests the university prizes inclusive, service-oriented leadership over mere positional authority.
Hand-in-hand with leadership is a strong emphasis on community engagement and volunteerism. UBC wants students who care about more than their own success – those who devote time and energy to bettering their community or helping others. Whether it’s volunteering for a charity, organizing events, or contributing to one’s family or cultural community, such experiences are highly valued. The Personal Profile section of UBC’s application asks applicants to list up to five significant activities or achievements, explicitly including categories like community service, volunteer work, clubs, creative pursuits, athletics, and family responsibilities. Applicants are then asked to elaborate on one or two of these activities, explaining their role and what they learned in the process. This requirement shows that UBC is looking for depth of involvement and personal growth: the ideal candidate has meaningful extracurricular experiences and can reflect on how those experiences shaped them. It’s not about superficial resume-padding, but about making a real impact and learning from it.
Notably, UBC’s largest scholarships favor students with a record of community impact. The Donald A. Wehrung International Student Award, for instance, is aimed at students from challenging backgrounds who “have achieved academic excellence under challenging circumstances” and “demonstrate leadership potential and a strong commitment to making a positive impact in their communities.” Even for students not seeking scholarships, this communicates what UBC admires: resilience (more on that later) and a service mindset. The UBC International Impact Award goes further, rewarding those who have shown leadership in finding solutions for global or societal issues like sustainability, social justice, equity, and health. This emphasis on impact indicates that UBC’s ideal student is a young person who already strives to improve the world around them. They should have a habit of involvement – whether it’s local community volunteering or broader initiatives – and plans to continue that engagement at UBC.
In summary, UBC seeks leaders, volunteers, and active citizens. The admissions tone is encouraging students to “get involved” and to be contributors to campus life from day one. Ideal candidates might be those who founded a high school club, captained a team, volunteered at a hospital, organized a fundraiser, or took care of important family duties – any activities showing responsibility, initiative, and community spirit. What matters is that these experiences have taught the student something and that they demonstrate qualities like teamwork, communication, empathy, and drive. UBC wants students who will continue to lead and serve during their university years, enhancing the vibrancy of student life through clubs, student government, research groups, and community outreach. The structural emphasis on Work programs, leadership and volunteering, clubs and societies on the UBC prospective student site underscores that such engagement is a core part of the UBC experience. The ideal UBC student is eager to take advantage of these opportunities – not just to benefit personally, but to give back and leave a mark on the community.
Diversity, Inclusion, and Global Citizenship
One of UBC’s defining themes is its commitment to diversity and global citizenship. As an international applicant, this is especially relevant – UBC prides itself on being “North America’s most international campus community,” with a highly diverse student body drawn from 150+ countries. The ideal UBC candidate not only comes from diverse backgrounds, but also embraces diversity and demonstrates a global outlook.
UBC communicates a very explicit commitment to equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI). The university leadership frames diversity as essential to excellence: “Equity, diversity, and inclusion are the conditions for attracting and retaining the best and brightest students, staff, and faculty from around the world.” In other words, UBC wants a campus rich in different cultures, perspectives, and experiences, believing this fuels innovation and learning. An ideal student, therefore, values and respects people of all backgrounds. In their personal profile and interviews (if applicable), a strong candidate might show evidence of cultural awareness, such as involvement in multicultural clubs, learning multiple languages, or advocating for inclusive practices. UBC’s core values include Respect, defined as “regard felt or shown towards different people, ideas and actions” – indicating that open-mindedness and respectfulness are expected traits. The tone on official pages is welcoming: UBC positions itself as a place where everyone should feel a sense of belonging. An applicant who can thrive in and contribute to such an inclusive environment – for example, someone who has bridged cultural differences or stood up for equity – fits the UBC ideal well.
Global citizenship is another recurring theme. UBC’s vision is “Inspiring people, ideas and actions for a better world.” and its purpose includes fostering global citizenship to advance a sustainable and just society. The ideal UBC student is seen as a global citizen – aware of global issues and eager to have a positive impact internationally. This outlook is especially important for international students and for fields like Education and Psychology that have worldwide applicability. In practice, global citizenship might mean a student has engaged with issues like climate change, human rights, public health, or education equity, either at home or abroad. It also suggests a willingness to collaborate with people from around the globe and an appreciation of UBC’s international context. UBC highlights and rewards such traits: the International Scholars Impact Award specifically honors students dedicated to causes in sustainability, climate action, social justice, equity, inclusion, health and wellness. Furthermore, the university’s strategic plan includes strategies for Local and Global Engagement, indicating that students are encouraged to connect their learning to communities both in Canada and internationally.
For an Education program candidate, global citizenship might manifest as an interest in diverse educational systems or a passion for teaching in underprivileged regions. For a Psychology student, it could be an interest in cross-cultural psychology or global mental health. UBC also integrates global perspectives into student life through exchange programs (e.g., Go Global), and an ideal student might express eagerness to participate in such opportunities, underscoring their adventurousness and adaptability in new environments.
In sum, UBC seeks students who will both benefit from and contribute to its multicultural, globally minded campus. The ideal international applicant is culturally fluent, appreciative of diversity, and committed to inclusive action. They should be comfortable interacting with people from all over the world and have a mindset that extends beyond their own local context. UBC’s messaging (“welcoming community members from across the globe and fostering their inclusion and belonging”) indicates that students who exemplify global citizenship and inclusivity are highly valued. Whether through personal stories of collaboration across differences or involvement in global causes, showing a global perspective and a respect for diversity will align an applicant with UBC’s core institutional values.
Personal Qualities and Mindset
Beyond concrete achievements, UBC places great emphasis on the personal qualities and mindset of applicants. The tone of the admissions materials is often reflective and values-driven – UBC wants to know who you are as a person and what you stand for, not just what you’ve done. Several key traits emerge repeatedly in UBC’s communications:


Resilience and perseverance: UBC explicitly asks applicants to share challenges they have overcome, because how a student deals with adversity is very telling. The Personal Profile is described as the place to tell UBC “the challenges you’ve overcome” and what you’ve learned from those experiences. Ideal candidates often have stories of resilience – perhaps moving to a new country, overcoming personal hardship, or tackling academic obstacles – and importantly, they can articulate growth from those struggles. Some of UBC’s scholarships target resilient students: those who achieved excellence “under challenging circumstances” or from war-torn areas, for example. This suggests UBC admires grit, adaptability, and determination. International students, in particular, often face the challenge of adapting to a new environment, so demonstrating resilience and flexibility is a plus. A UBC student should be able to handle setbacks, manage stress, and thrive in a demanding, fast-changing university setting.


Reflection and maturity: The ideal candidate is self-aware and reflective. UBC doesn’t just want a list of accomplishments; it wants to know what the student learned and how they grew. Admissions tips advise: “Instead of simply listing your accomplishments and experiences, tell us what you’ve learned from them”. Scoring highly on the Personal Profile requires showing insight and “a rare level of accomplishment and maturity.” UBC seems to value an unusually mature outlook in undergraduates – someone who can reflect on their experiences with wisdom beyond their years. This could be demonstrated by discussing meaningful life lessons, ethical dilemmas faced, or how one’s perspective has evolved. A Psychology applicant, for example, might reflect on how volunteering with a mental health helpline taught them empathy and resilience. An Education applicant might discuss what working with children taught them about patience and communication. Being able to derive personal meaning from experiences and convey thoughtful, nuanced views is a trait that sets apart top candidates.


Integrity and accountability: As part of its core values, UBC highlights Integrity (honesty, ethics, truthfulness) and Accountability (taking responsibility for one’s actions). The ideal student thus has a strong moral compass. This could manifest in the application as examples of ethical leadership, doing the right thing in difficult situations, or taking ownership of one’s mistakes. UBC likely screens for any signs of misconduct or dishonesty and expects applicants to be truthful in their essays (as emphasized by warnings against trying to tell admissions “what you think we want to hear”). Involvement in initiatives that promote integrity (like honor societies or peer mentoring) could further underline this trait. Essentially, UBC wants community members who are trustworthy, responsible, and uphold high ethical standards – qualities critical in fields like Psychology and Education where ethical practice is paramount.


Empathy and collaboration: UBC’s tone around leadership and community is full of words like empathy, collaboration, and supporting others. This indicates that compassion and teamwork are highly valued. An ideal candidate often demonstrates care for others – maybe through mentoring peers, caring for family, or community service – and an ability to work in teams effectively. Group projects, team sports, or collaborative volunteer work in a student’s background can highlight this skill. UBC fosters a collegial atmosphere (“thriving communities” is part of its strategic priorities), so being able to get along with and uplift others is key. Particularly in Education, empathic communication and inclusivity are crucial traits for future teachers, and in Psychology, understanding others is at the heart of the discipline. Students who show emotional intelligence, listening skills, and respect for differing viewpoints align well with UBC’s ideal.


Passion and purpose: UBC asks applicants “What is important to you? And why?”. This question is aimed at uncovering an applicant’s values and motivations. Ideal UBC students have a clear sense of purpose or passion that drives them – whether it’s a passion for mental health advocacy, a dedication to education reform, a love of scientific research, or any other defining interest. UBC tends to highlight student stories where a personal passion led to accomplishments or contributions. Thus, showing genuine passion (rather than saying what you think the university wants to hear) is recommended: “Be true to who you are… Use your unique voice to tell us what you want to say.”. The underlying message is authenticity. UBC celebrates individuality; the tone of their admissions advice is that there is no single “cookie-cutter” ideal – instead, the ideal is that each student brings a unique passion or perspective backed by substance. Whether one is an aspiring neuroscientist or a budding social entrepreneur, UBC wants to see authentic enthusiasm and drive.


In combination, these personal qualities describe someone who is balanced in heart and mind. UBC’s ideal student is ambitious yet humble, driven yet compassionate. They have the confidence to lead and achieve, but also the humility to learn and listen. They are open-minded, self-reflective, and growth-oriented, constantly evolving from their experiences. The repeated themes of inclusion, global citizenship, service, innovation, and excellence suggest a mindset geared towards both personal achievement and the greater good. Importantly, the ideal candidate’s values seem to align with UBC’s own institutional values – striving for excellence, acting with integrity, showing respect, and taking responsibility. UBC’s communications often highlight students who exemplify these traits in various ways, effectively holding them up as models for prospective applicants to emulate.
Alignment with Psychology and Education Program Expectations
While the above traits apply broadly, students targeting Psychology or Education programs should pay special attention to aligning with the specific ethos of those faculties:


Psychology: UBC’s Psychology Department is a part of the Faculty of Arts and is one of the most academically rigorous and prestigious programs at the university. As UBC’s “most popular undergraduate major”, admission to Psychology can be quite competitive. Academically, an ideal Psychology applicant has strong preparation in biology, math/stats, and social sciences, indicating they can handle the scientific and research aspects of the discipline. The department emphasizes research at all levels – undergraduates have opportunities for enriched learning experiences, lab involvement, and even an Honours thesis program. Therefore, a demonstrated interest or experience in research can set candidates apart (e.g. science fair projects, psychology club, or assisting a research lab if possible). The department also values critical thinking and curiosity about human behavior. On a personal level, psychology intersects with understanding people, so qualities like empathy, communication, and analytical thinking are important. The Psychology Department explicitly states a commitment to an inclusive, supportive community, so students who will contribute to a positive department culture are desired. Being aware of ethical issues and showing a desire to help others (for those interested in clinical/counseling avenues) can also be positives. In essence, the ideal Psychology student at UBC is academically strong in science and analysis, passionate about understanding mind and behavior, open to research, and attuned to working with diverse people. They will likely take initiative in things like the Psychology Students Association, research conferences (UBC frequently celebrates undergrad research achievements), and community outreach on mental health.


Education: UBC’s Faculty of Education has a distinct focus on preparing future teachers and educational leaders who are socially conscious and community-oriented. Unlike Psychology, undergraduate entry to Education often means pursuing a B.Ed. program after completing another bachelor’s degree (the B.Ed. is a post-degree professional program at UBC). Thus, an “undergraduate candidate” in Education might be a transfer or second-degree applicant. Whether one is applying to UBC’s B.Ed. or a related Bachelor’s (like a BA with an Education minor, or a specialization in Early Childhood Education), the expected qualities are very clear. UBC Education’s mission statement highlights improving teaching and learning through innovative, inquiry-driven programs, research, reflection, and critique in partnership with communities. They “seek to inform our research and practices by consideration of issues such as poverty, minority rights, inequality, and social justice”. This means the ideal Education student is deeply committed to social justice, diversity, and the well-being of communities. Practical experience is also crucial: the Teacher Education program strongly prefers applicants who have experience working with youth or children and can obtain references attesting to their abilities in real educational settings. So, a prospective Education student should ideally have volunteered or worked in schools, summer camps, tutoring programs, or similar environments, showing both commitment to teaching and understanding of learners. Other key traits include patience, communication skills, creativity in teaching, and an inclusive mindset (to support learners of all needs and backgrounds). UBC’s Education faculty values reflection and ethical practice – they ask their members to be “reflective, ethical, and self-critical” and to value multiple perspectives. An ideal candidate might demonstrate this by talking about lessons learned from working with diverse students or how they adapted to challenges in a teaching role. They should also show leadership potential in educational contexts (e.g., curriculum design in a club, leading workshops, etc.), aligned with the faculty’s emphasis on producing leaders in education. In short, the ideal Education program applicant is service-oriented, passionate about teaching and equity, experienced with youth, academically competent, and eager to advance the cause of inclusive, quality education. This aligns with UBC’s portrayal of its Education students and alumni as champions of change in their communities.


By tailoring their applications to reflect these department-specific expectations – research enthusiasm and academic rigor for Psychology, and educational passion with social awareness for Education – international candidates can demonstrate an even stronger “fit” with UBC. The underlying institutional values (excellence, integrity, global outlook, community engagement) remain the same, but their expression may differ by discipline. UBC’s tone on faculty pages is proud of the unique strengths of each faculty: Psychology’s cutting-edge research and scientific breadth, and Education’s role in fostering inclusive, lifelong learning and community well-being. Ideal candidates affirm these priorities through their interests and experiences.
Conclusion
Across its communications, UBC conveys a clear picture of the kind of student it hopes to attract: scholars who excel academically and who carry a spark – be it leadership, creativity, compassion, or vision – that they use to uplift others and contribute to a better world. The tone is aspirational but inviting; UBC signals that it values excellence not as an elitist concept, but as a combination of talent, hard work, character, and a commitment to positive change. From the Personal Profile prompts to the scholarship criteria and faculty mission statements, UBC consistently emphasizes qualities like global citizenship, inclusion, community impact, and resilience. International students applying to UBC, especially in fields like Psychology and Education, should present themselves as holistic candidates: not only meeting high academic standards, but also bringing rich experiences, diverse perspectives, leadership and volunteerism, and a strong alignment with UBC’s values. In the end, UBC’s ideal undergraduate is someone who will make the most of the university’s resources and actively contribute to the campus ethos of learning, engagement, and service.
The following table summarizes the key traits of UBC’s ideal international undergraduate candidate and why each trait is significant to UBC’s mission and community:

These students drive UBC initiatives in sustainability, equity, and community outreach, helping fulfill the university’s purpose of advancing a “sustainable and just society”.Global Perspective & InclusivityUBC is a highly international and diverse campus, so it seeks students who are comfortable in a multicultural environment and value diversity. Children have a biological instinct to attach, whether their parents are loving or not, they have to find one way or another to stick to them, and develop a coping style based on their attempt to get at least some of their needs met. When their caregivers cannot give what they need, the babies “learns to become the mother’s idea of what a baby is” to make the job easier, it adjusts to its caregiver, thinking that something is wrong with itself, which means they would shut down their own physical reactions inside their bodies that may be necessary.

The second is “anxious” or “ambivalent” attachment, which means they will constantly try to draw attention to themselves, by crying or throwing a tantrum, they seem to have come to the conclusion that unless they make a spectacle, nobody is gonna care. But even when somebody does care, they don’t seem to enjoy that company, they would stay passively or angrily focused on them. Unrealism of Acute Neurosis

An explanation comes to light, it is that his mind is overly focusing on his inner thoughts, internal processes and so his attention are fixed to thoughts, and feelings, which becomes vivid. With that we come to the conclusion of the problem, which is the meaning that the patient attach to the stimuli. For example, a sound of a siren can make a person think that their house is on fire. The cumulative effect of indiscriminately interpreting events as danger can lead to a warped view of the world and escalating anxiety, which can range from mild inaccuracy to gross misinterpretation.

6---full-notes/using-hot-baths-to-facili.title: Using Hot Baths to Facilitate Sleep Onset
6---full-notes/using-hot-baths-to-facili.content:
Status: teen
Tags: sleep biology
Using Hot Baths to Facilitate Sleep Onset
Details
Using heat exposure, such as a hot bath, shower, or sauna, in the evening is a powerful and paradoxical tool for accelerating the transition into sleep. While it may seem counterintuitive to heat the body before trying to sleep, the practice leverages the body’s compensatory cooling mechanisms to send a strong sleep-inducing signal.
When you immerse yourself in hot water or a sauna, your core body temperature rises. However, upon exiting, your body initiates a robust cool-down response to return to homeostasis. This process causes your core body temperature to drop significantly, often falling below its initial baseline. This manufactured drop in temperature mimics the natural physiological process that must occur each night to permit entry into sleep.
This makes evening heat exposure a particularly effective strategy for nights when you feel overly alert or need to shift your bedtime earlier than usual. By deliberately triggering this cool-down cascade, you can actively facilitate the body’s readiness for sleep, rather than passively waiting for it to occur. For optimal effect, the heat exposure should last around 20-30 minutes and be timed for the hour or two before bed.

6---full-notes/using-a-single-tool-for-d.title: Using a Single Tool for Different Tasks Still Requires a Domain-Specific Decision Mechanism
6---full-notes/using-a-single-tool-for-d.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Evolutionary Psychology Massive Modularity Hypothesis Cognitive Psychology
The rebuttal to the reusage
Details
The text argues that the screwdriver analogy, intended to refute the need for specialization, actually demonstrates its necessity. The analogy ignores the “decision-making machinery” that determines how the screwdriver is used. Something must decide whether to turn the screwdriver left or right, when to turn it, and when to stop. This decision-making system is, by definition, domain-specific. It is activated by specific inputs (e.g., the goal to tighten or loosen) and produces different functional outcomes with different error definitions (turning left is an error for tightening, and vice-versa). A single physical structure (the mouth) serves different systems (digestion, respiration). However, separate functional machinery (e.g., brain signals for lack of oxygen vs. presence of food) must direct its actions. The mouth itself doesn’t decide. Even if a single tool is used, it must be controlled by functionally specific elements that know when and how to apply it for different tasks.

Using a dictionary
Details
The rules of knowing a book applies here as well, which is to say that you must know what kind of book and so on. You must realize what kind of information and knowledge it contains and so you will pay attention to and use it accordingly well.
And so you will use it by its main intention, as a help in reading books that include vocabularies that are technical, archaic,… it is generally advised against reading a book and the dictionary at the same time, as this can make you lose track of the unity of the book.
And so these are the rules you should follow whilst reading a dictionary:


WORDS ARE PHYSICAL THINGS—writable words and speak-able sounds. There must, therefore, be uniform ways of spelling and pronouncing them, though the uniformity is often spoiled by variations, and in any event is not as eternally important as some of your teachers may have indicated.


WORDS ARE PARTS OF SPEECH. Each single word plays a grammatical role in the more complicated structure of a phrase or sentence. The same word can vary in different usages, shifting from one part of speech to another, especially in a non-inflected language like English.


WORDS ARE SIGNS. They have meanings, not one but many. These meanings are related in various ways. Sometimes they shade from one into another; sometimes a word will have two or more sets of totally unrelated meanings. Through their meanings, different words are related to one another—as synonyms sharing in the same meaning even though they differ in shading; or as antonyms through opposition or contrast of meanings. Furthermore, it is in their capacity as signs that we distinguish words as proper or common names (according as they name just one thing or many that are alike in some respect); and as concrete or abstract names.


Finally, words are conventional. They are man-made signs. They will have context within them from word-roots, prefixes and so on. This means they are subject to have changed throughout history as their meanings shift.

6---full-notes/using-encyclopedias.title: Using encyclopedias
6---full-notes/using-encyclopedias.content:
Status: 3 - Tags/reading
Tags: adult
Using encyclopedias
Details
The intended role of an encyclopedia in the reading process is to fill gaps in background knowledge, clarify allusions, or explain concepts that a reader might not understand from context . Used judiciously, reference books provide essential context that makes complex or technical texts more intelligible , thereby supporting the reader’s understanding without doing the thinking for them.
Adler and Van Doren caution, however, against misusing or over-relying on encyclopedias. They recount Adler’s early mistake of relying on “secondary sources, encyclopedias, commentaries, all sorts of books about books” to feign mastery of literature . This shortcut backfired, revealing that superficial knowledge from summaries cannot substitute for true comprehension of a work’s content. Likewise, the authors warn it is “just as vain to try to read an encyclopedia through as a dictionary,” noting that someone who memorized an encyclopedia verbatim would be a “learned fool” (an idiot savant) rather than a truly well-read person . In short, being widely read in reference materials is not the same as actively reading and understanding primary texts.
Instead, encyclopedias should complement and enhance active reading. Adler and Van Doren describe dictionaries and encyclopedias as “educational as well as informational tools” —valuable adjuncts to reading that can illuminate a challenging book’s meaning. The key is not to “enslave yourself” to such aids . An active reader might pause to resolve a confusion by quickly consulting an encyclopedia, but should then return to the book’s argument or narrative with greater insight. In their view, a good reader uses encyclopedias to answer specific factual questions or to grasp necessary background, thereby removing obstacles to comprehension, but always resumes the primary task of engaging with the author’s ideas directly.
This approach fits into Adler and Van Doren’s broader philosophy of active reading as learning by discovery. Reading is an active endeavor requiring the reader’s mental effort. Even reference tools should be used in that spirit. For example, they note that when such aids are used prematurely, they “only impede our reading, instead of helping it” . In practice, “reading a book with a dictionary in the other hand is a bad idea,” since constantly interrupting the flow makes it hard to grasp the whole . Instead, one should read as far as possible by one’s own lights and consult encyclopedias afterwards (or sparingly) to aid understanding, rather than let them replace the effort of reading. Ultimately, encyclopedias are there to support the reader’s engagement with difficult texts—providing context and clarification—while the real work of reading remains an active dialogue between reader and author.

6---full-notes/validity-in-diagnosis-and.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Clinical Psychology psychopathology
Validity in Diagnosis and Assessments
Details
Validity is something that is closely related to reliability, though they do not ensure the other level of correlation. This means even if you have high reliability that does not mean you have high validity, as the topic that you are testing may be completely displaced with each other.
Content validity would refer to how related the area of information given by the test is to the goal of it. For example, later in this chapter we will describe an interview that is often used to make an Axis I diagnosis. It has excellent content validity because it contains questions about all the symptoms that are involved in most Axis I diagnoses. For certain uses, though, the interview might have poor content validity. The interview doesn’t cover questions about kleptomania (a disorder characterized by a compulsive need to steal). If one were trying to assess kleptomania, this interview would have poor content validity.
Criterion validity is how related a measure of test is to the other measures of the test. If both variables are measured at the same point in time, the resulting validity is referred to as concurrent validity. For example, below we will describe a measure of the overly negative thoughts that are believed to play an important role in depression. Criterion validity for this measure of negative thoughts could be established by showing that people with depression score higher on the test than do people without depression. Alternatively, criterion validity can be assessed by evaluating the ability of Reliability is an essential property of all assessment procedures. One means of establishing reliability is to determine whether different judges agree, as happens when two umpires witness the same event in a baseball game. A measure to predict some other variable that is measured at some point in the future, often referred to as predictive validity. For example, IQ tests were originally developed to predict future school performance. Similarly, a measure of negative thinking  could be used to predict the development of depression in the future. In summary, concurrent and predictive validity are both types of criterion validity.
Lastly is construct validity, which is somewhat complex as it measures the extent of the predicted value and states that the taker would be in accurate with the level of the test.

6---full-notes/variable-realizability.title: Variable Realizability
6---full-notes/variable-realizability.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
Fallacy of the Identity Theory
Details
Following the rejection of Behaviorism, philosophers briefly turned to Identity Theory (or Physicalism), which claimed that mental states are strictly identical to specific physical brain states (e.g., “Pain is C-fibers firing”). This view relies on scientific identities, arguing that just as “Lightning is electrical discharge” (regardless of how it looks), pain is a specific biological event. However, Hilary Putnam dismantled this view with the argument of Multiple Realizability.
Putnam pointed out that creatures with vastly different physiologies—such as octopuses (which have very different evolutionary histories and neural structures) or hypothetical silicon-based Martians—can clearly experience mental states like pain or hunger. If Identity Theory were true, and pain were identical to “C-fibers firing,” then an octopus without C-fibers could not be in pain. Because it is absurd to deny pain to these creatures simply based on their specific chemistry (a bias Putnam calls “speciesism”), Identity Theory must be false. Mental states are “variably realizable,” meaning the exact same mental state can be implemented by completely different physical substances.

6---full-notes/variance-and-standard-dev.title: Variance and Standard Deviation
6---full-notes/variance-and-standard-dev.content:
Status: adult
Tags: statistics psychology
Variance and Standard Deviation
Details
Variance measures spread: on average, how far each score sits from the mean. You take each deviation xᵢ − x̄, square it (so distances on either side of the mean both count as positive instead of cancelling), sum the squares, and average. In symbols, s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1) = SS / (n − 1),
The one wrinkle is the denominator. You divide by n − 1, not n, whenever you estimate the population’s variance from a sample. Dividing by n gives a biased estimate that systematically underestimates the spread — because the sample mean is itself fitted to the data, the deviations come out a little too small — and the n − 1 correction repairs this (it can be proven, not just asserted; demo to come). You divide by the full n only in two cases: you genuinely know the population mean μ, or you only want to describe the sample with no inference about a population.
Standard deviation happens when you root whatever you just got from the equation above. This metric exist so that statisicians can eliminate the need for units and instead focus entirely on the statistics.
The concrete tool is the z-score: z = (x − x̄)/s, read as how many standard deviations a score lies from the mean. It is unitless, and you invert it with x = z·s + x̄. By construction a set of z-scores always has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so any distribution can be redrawn on a common z-axis: a tall student at 77 inches is no longer “77” but z ≈ 2.8. This “in units of spread” language is what the rest of the course runs on — the coefficient of variation (spread relative to the mean), and later the t-test and ANOVA (analysis of variance) all work by dividing the spread out. What we usually care about is not raw width but where a score sits relative to the spread.

6---full-notes/visual-cortex.title: Visual Cortex
6---full-notes/visual-cortex.content:
Status: baby
Tags: neuroscience psychology
Visual Cortex
Details
The primary visual cortex (V1) is the main cortical area for receiving, processing, and integrating visual information from the retinas. It is located in the most posterior part of the brain, within the occipital lobe.
V1’s fundamental role is to deconstruct visual signals into basic components like lines, edges, orientation, color, and motion. It is organized in a retinotopic map, where adjacent points in the visual field correspond to adjacent points in the cortex, preserving the spatial layout of the retinal image.
From V1, visual information is sent to higher-order visual areas along two main pathways for further processing: the dorsal stream (“where/how” pathway), which processes spatial location and motion, and the ventral stream (“what” pathway), which is involved in object recognition.

6---full-notes/voluntarism-and-group-for.title: Voluntarism and Group Formation (American Cultural Code)
6---full-notes/voluntarism-and-group-for.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
Voluntarism and Group Formation (American Cultural Code)
Details
Every society operates on an underlying cultural code—a set of myths, beliefs, and institutional logics that dictate how individuals should behave and how social life ought to be organized. For the United States, the dominant code is a unique form of individualism best described as voluntarism. Centered on the supreme value of individual choice, this code provides a distinct and powerful formula that shapes both the ideal person and the very nature of group formation, creating a self-reinforcing system that touches every aspect of American life.
The foundation of the voluntarist code is the cultivation of a specific type of person, one equipped to navigate a world predicated on choice. This ideal individual must first be autonomous, socialized from a young age to be independent and self-reliant. Cultural rites of passage, such as leaving home for college, are not merely practical steps but are seen as crucial moments in achieving this mandated independence. Secondly, this person must be a chooser, constantly encouraged to make decisions, from the trivial, like selecting a juice in preschool, to the profound, such as determining one’s own values as an adult. The ability to choose is treated as the hallmark of a mature and functional person. Finally, the ideal individual is expected to be honest and communicative, able to clearly state their desires and intentions. This is not just a moral virtue but a functional necessity; in a system where relationships are formed by choice, honest communication is the bedrock upon which legitimate bonds are built.
This ideal, choice-making individual naturally engages in a distinctive mode of group formation. The central myth of American social life is that all legitimate groups are formed by the free choices of autonomous individuals. Unlike societies where group membership is largely inherited through family or lineage, the American model posits that people must actively and voluntarily come together. This formula has several key components. First, it requires uniqueness as a prerequisite for joining. An individual’s distinct interests, talents, or identity become their most valuable asset, as this is what they contribute to the group. This principle is embodied in the popular “Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer” myth, where a unique difference becomes the key to acceptance and belonging. One must be different to have a reason to join with others who are “different just like them.”
This emphasis on asserting one’s unique values can lead to what sociologist Ann Shales terms “adversarial individualism.” Because individuals are expected to stand up for their chosen beliefs, relationships are often characterized by a dynamic of debate and negotiation, from the family dinner table to the floor of Congress. Perhaps the most telling feature of the voluntarist code is its power to transform even inherited identities into matters of active choice. In the American context, aspects of identity like religion or ethnicity must be voluntarily affirmed. An immigrant who is Buddhist by birth, for example, must choose to become an active member of a temple community, donating time and money to voluntarily create the institution that supports their identity.
In essence, the American cultural code of voluntarism is a powerful, self-reinforcing loop. It socializes individuals to be autonomous and choice-driven, and these individuals, in turn, create voluntary groups that require such members to function. This dynamic model provides the foundational logic that shapes everything from friendships and family life to politics and religion in the United States.

6---full-notes/weak-dominance.title: Weak Dominance
6---full-notes/weak-dominance.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics strategy
Weak Dominance
Details
Formally, a game in normal form has three ingredients:


Players (i, j, …).


Strategies. Each player has a set of possible strategies Sᵢ, and sᵢ is one strategy from that set. A strategy profile s is one strategy for every player, like the spreadsheet of everyone’s chosen numbers.


Payoffs. Player i’s payoff Uᵢ(s) depends on the whole profile. Writing s₋ᵢ for everyone’s choices except i’s lets you split this into Uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ): my choice against everyone else’s.


For most of the course, we assume every player knows all strategy sets and payoffs.
In this notation, s′ᵢ is strictly dominated by sᵢ if Uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) > Uᵢ(s′ᵢ, s₋ᵢ) for every s₋ᵢ. Polak’s abstract example (Player I picks the row, Player II the column; Player I’s payoff first):





























LeftCenterRightTop5, −111, 30, 0Bottom6, 40, 22, 0
Player I has nothing dominated: bottom is better against left, top against center. For Player II, center strictly dominates right (3 > 0 against top, 2 > 0 against bottom). Once right is deleted, nothing else is dominated, so dominance alone leaves this game unsolved.
Weak dominance: s′ᵢ is weakly dominated by sᵢ if Uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) ≥ Uᵢ(s′ᵢ, s₋ᵢ) for every s₋ᵢ, with > for at least one. Polak’s example is Hannibal invading Italy with two battalions:


The hard pass over the Alps costs him one battalion.


Running into the defender costs another, and the defender can guard only one pass.


Hannibal’s payoff is battalions that get through; the defender’s is battalions destroyed:

























Defend easyDefend hardAttack easy1, 12, 0Attack hard1, 10, 2
The defender has no dominated strategy; they only care about matching the attacker so that they can defend. Most of them chose the easy pass because they are evaluating from Hannibal’s side. For him, the easy path dominates the hard one, since he will always get at least one battalion. Then, expecting the easy path, you would go for the easy one.
Supporting Content
The “weak dominance” is a bit more subtle than strict dominance due to the effect of loss not being as clear as the latter. And so it can be misleading/allow people to mistake it for a bad strategy.

Weber’s Historical Context of the Class Conflict
Details
According to Weber, the conflict relationship between certain classes that determine the history of the times usually depended on what market was dominant at that time. He came up with the existence of three markets: credit, commodity, labor.


Credit Market: This is most prevalent in the ancient societies, where the conflict were between the creditors and the indebted. In those times, peasants and farmers had to borrow money to purchase seeds and plant so that they would have food to survive. These people sometimes had to sell their land, their own children, and eventually themselves (giving service).


Commodity Market: This market was in between the buyers and the sellers, usually in medieval times or early modern periods. The grain riots during the French Revolution are a classic example. When a bad harvest drove up the price of bread, the urban poor, as consumers, rioted against what they saw as hoarding and profiteering by sellers and aristocrats. This type of conflict arises when access to essential commodities becomes a point of social friction.


Labor Market: This is the most relevant to us, as we are actively living in it, pitting workers against owners. It is quite a usual sight for us to see workers go on strike nowadays and revolutionize in the 19th century, as those are clear examples of the conflict. In 19th-century America, for instance, radical small farmers (debtors) were hostile to big banks (creditors), but as employers of farm labor, they were opposed to the goals of urban workers (laborers). This fragmentation prevented the formation of a single, unified radical movement. The example also show how different markets can clash together and prevent revolutions.

Weberian Class Conflict in the Welfare State
Details
A Weberian framework, which defines class by shared life chances in a market, can be adapted to understand a central political conflict in contemporary societies. Beyond the market, the modern state itself creates new forms of class division by distributing benefits and levying taxes. This gives rise to a conflict between two major groups whose economic life chances are defined by their relationship to the state.
The first group can be described as “welfare state liberals,” a broad class of people who are, in one way or another, beneficiaries of public spending. This class does not just involve people who receive welfare but also those in the military, those in universities doing research and such, they all depend on the healthiness of the economy.
On the other hand we have the group who are actively paying taxes to fund these people. They are constantly having to face with the fact that they have to worry about how their own money is being spent, over or under what actually matters and benefits them as a society.

6---full-notes/what-we-don't-know-we-hav.title: What We Don't Know We Have
6---full-notes/what-we-don't-know-we-hav.content:
Status: adult
Tags: philosophy psychology morals
What We Don’t Know We Have
Details
Back in 2020 while most of the world was frozen in the uncertainty of a new pandemic, a seventeen-year-old from Seattle built a website. No one asked him to do this, it wasn’t for grades, least of all for pride. Avi Schiffman created ncov2019.live — a real-time COVID-19 tracking dashboard that, at its peak, was visited by tens of millions of people across the world. Later, when war broke out in Ukraine, he built Ukraine Take Shelter, a platform connecting refugees with available housing. He was still a teenager.
The natural instinct here is admiration. And that’s fair. But some of the most popular philosophical consensus would actually classify this as something natural and
What We Owe Each Other
The philosopher Peter Singer offers one of the most well-known arguments in modern ethics. It goes roughly like this: if you can prevent something bad from happening, without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, you ought to do it. It sounds simple. If you walk past a drowning child in a shallow pond, you should wade in and help — even if it ruins your shoes. Most people believes that is the fair and right thing to do. Singer then extends the logic outward. If you can help people suffering on the other side of the world, and the cost to you is relatively small, then you should. Suffering doesn’t become less urgent or means less because of distance.
It’s a powerful argument. But I believe that Avi’s story complicates it.
Singer’s framework assumes that we already know what someone is capable of. The word “can” is doing enormous work in his argument. If you can help, you should. But what happens when nobody — not the world, not the people around you, possibly not even you yourself — knows that you can?
Before the pandemic, Avi Schiffman was a teenager who knew how to code. That’s it. No one could have looked at him and said, “You have an obligation to build a global health information platform that would help millions upon millions of people.” The capability didn’t exist as something visible, something that could be pointed at and turned into a duty. It only became real in the act of doing it.
This is where Singer’s framework fails. You simply cannot demand someone towards doing something they themselves do not realize yet.
Beyond Duty
Ethics has a word for actions that are morally good but exceed what could reasonably be demanded of someone. The word is supererogation, which are acts beyond the call of duty. These are rare acts but we have seen examples of them nonetheless: Donating a kidney to a stranger; Running into a burning building when you’re not a firefighter. These are things we praise, but don’t blame people for not doing.
Avi’s case fits here in a strange way. What he did was clearly good. It clearly mattered. But it would be absurd to say he was required to do it. No moral framework could have realistically demanded a teenager to build a website that would affect millions of people. The moral landscape before he acted simply didn’t contain that expectation.
Then, if it was not the demand or suggestion from his own capabilities and his own moral responsibility, then what is it ?
Noticing
But this is where the gap comes. I believe that the current landscape of moral philosophy may attempt to explain this as the inherent abilities and knowledge that Avi has always had in of himself and only was precipitated due to the situation demanding said abilities.
Nonetheless, I do not think this actually solves the predicament that is Avi at all. These moral frameworks demand a person would have to understand and know what their abilities are and have enough knowledge about themselves to reliably make moral decisions (the epistemic condition). Avi never had that, he could have never known he was capable of having this kind of idea that worked better than even governments and non-governmental organizations.
So, it must have been something that came before said framework, or, in other words, his perception. He saw that people were confused and frightened, that reliable information was scattered, that the absence of something clear and centralized was itself causing harm. And crucially, he couldn’t look away from it. Not because duty told him not to. Before any calculation, before any assessment of his own abilities, there was simply: this is wrong, and this gap is real.
Becoming Through Doing
Aristotle argued, over two thousand years ago, that you don’t become virtuous by thinking about virtue. You become brave by doing brave things. You become generous by practicing generosity. Character isn’t something you have and then act from — it’s something you build through action.
Avi’s story is a striking example of this. Before he built ncov2019.live, he was not yet the person who had done that. The experience of responding — of building something under pressure, of realizing millions of people were relying on what he made — shaped him into someone capable of doing it again when Ukraine needed help. The moral responsibility didn’t just demand something from him. It developed him. It expanded what he was capable of. Is it in this situation that Singer’s framework would actually compel and demand that Avi do what he did.
Which is perhaps the largest point we can gain from examining his story. That moral responsibility might not be fixed, it might grow with our ability to do things, even if our ability depended on unfinished knowledge we have about our own selves.
The Uncomfortable Implication
It would be simpler, easier to come out of this essay with a neat lesson: you are capable of more than you think, so go out and do great things. And perhaps that is partly true. But the honest conclusion is less comfortable than that.
What Avi’s story really tells us is that we cannot know what we are capable of until we test our own capabilities, but of course most of us do not exactly arrange our lives to encounter these tests or accept to act upon them in our daily lives. We wait for obligation. We wait for permission. We wait to feel ready. And in the waiting, the moment passes.
Singer’s framework tells us that we should act because we can, but the story above has already suggested something else: that we may not know what we can before we do it. And so the moral capability and responsibility that one endures is not merely a prerequisite for moral actions in certain situations but rather a consequence of it.
And so the implication that materializes from this is that we may have an ability to perform something moral perhaps beyond the scope of what we believe we can actually do, but said thing will only be realized if we ever attempt to do so.

6---full-notes/what-an-argument-is-(and-.title: What an Argument Is (and Isn't)
6---full-notes/what-an-argument-is-(and-.content:
Status: teen
Tags: logic philosophy
What an Argument Is (and Isn’t)
Details
An argument is a set of sentences where the premises entails a certain conclusion. It is where the conclusion is considered to be true and the premises are what gives rationale for it to be interpreted as so.
A sentence, then, can be interpreted differently depending on how they are presented and worded as it can be a conclusion and premise depending on the vocabularies that constitute it. There are many words in the English dictionary that can be quite misleading and make somebody infer the function of a sentence different than the function that it actually serves. This means you can’t identify arguments by their content. You identify them by spotting the relation: is someone offering reasons for a claim? Words like therefore, hence, so, since often signal arguments but aren’t reliable — because can indicate causal explanation rather than rational justification, and arguments can exist without any indicator words at all.
Not arguments:

Mere contradictions (“Yes it is” / “No it isn’t” — the Monty Python problem)
Causal narratives (“Clouds formed, the sky blackened, the storm broke” — describing a sequence of events, not offering reasons)
Single assertions, even complex ones (“If it’s snowing, the mail will be late” — one conditional sentence, not a premise supporting a conclusion)
Random sets of sentences with no inferential relation

What is history
Details
We usually class this under fiction more than science, that is if it must be affiliated with one or the other. Though it would sit in relatively the middle of both of these, leaning over to fiction of course.
As talked before, this is because the elusiveness of history and the necessity that the author guess, hypothecate,… and so a good author will try to find general patterns, logical ones to impose on these events. He may have a general theory or philosophy, such as that Providence rules human affairs, and make his history fit that. Or he may abjure any such pattern, imposed as it were from the outside or above, and instead insist that he is merely reporting the real events that have occurred. But in that case he is likely to be forced to assign causes for events and motivations for actions. It is essential to recognize which way the historian you are reading is operating.
The only way we can avoid taking either position is to assume men do not do things for a purpose or that purpose is undiscoverable, which means there would be no pattern to history. (Tolstoy had a theory like this, that the human motivation was so complex and hidden that it is impossible to know why anything ever happened.)
Since these theories differ and affects the historians’ accounts of events, it is necessary for us to read multiple account of history if we want to understand it. This is the first rule and it is very important if it relates to our significant being (ho we came to be, etc…). We must understand every narrative of history has to be written from some point pf view and that we have to look at it from more than one viewpoint.
