6---full-notes/what-to-avoid-when-readin.title: What to avoid when reading imaginative literature
6---full-notes/what-to-avoid-when-readin.content:
Status: adult
Tags: 3 - Tags/reading
What to avoid when reading imaginative literature
Details
First of all, it is necessary to grasp the basic differences between expository and imaginative literature as it will explain why we read them differently.
The most prevalent is their purposes, expository works convey knowledge, imaginative ones try to communicate an experience itself. And because they differ from their purposes, they also differ between practically everything else. Our experiences are through senses and imagination, whilst our judgement and reasoning are intellectual. This doesn’t mean we must separate the two of these things when reading, but rather, we emphasize one more when reading that specific type of literature. And so we come to the most important point. Don’t try to resist the effect that a work of imaginative literature has on you.
In reading expository works, we had to be vigilant, ready to spot, catch anything that is important and maintain a neutral stance. In imaginative literature, we must allow ourselves to be immersed into the story, only then can we truly understand it.
We owe much to the expository literature—the philosophy, science, mathematics—that has shaped the real world in which we live. But we could not live in this world if we were not able, from time to time, to get away from it. We do not mean that imaginative literature is always, or essentially, escapist. In the ordinary sense of that term, the idea is contemptible. If we must escape from reality, it should be to a deeper, or greater, reality. This is the reality of our inner life, of our own unique vision of the world. To discover this reality makes us happy; the experience is deeply satisfying to some part of ourselves we do not ordinarily touch. In any event, the rules of reading a great work of literary art should have as an end or goal just such a profound experience. The rules should clear away all that stops us from feeling as deeply as we possibly can.
Now we come to their differences in words, the imaginative writer tries to maximize the latent ambiguities of words, in order thereby to gain all the richness and force in their multiple meanings. He uses metaphors to construct, different from how the logical writer uses concise words to construct a singular meaning.
Finally, we must not criticize such books by the standards of truth and consistency of general knowledge, we must do so by its logical progression. We want a story that could’ve happened in the world that was built.

6---full-notes/what-to-do-about-monopoli.title: What to do about monopolies?
6---full-notes/what-to-do-about-monopoli.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
What to do about monopolies?
Details
Monopoly is the first case where government can actually have a potentially positive effect. There are two ways that they can do it:
First is price regulation: Take Lecture 11’s monopoly: demand P = 24 − Q, marginal cost 2Q, monopoly output 6 at a price of 18, and a deadweight loss. Now cap the price at the competitive level, 16 (Figure 12-2). The firm’s marginal revenue curve changes. It becomes flat at 16 all the way out to the demand curve (8 units), then drops back to the old MR curve. The cap removes the poisoning effect: the monopolist didn’t want to sell a 7th unit before because it had to cut the price on all units to 17. Under the cap the price is already 16, so selling one more unit costs nothing on the others. It sells every unit whose marginal cost is below 16 — 8 units, the competitive amount — and the deadweight loss disappears. Profit is 16 × 8 − (12 + 64) = 52; consumers get ½ × 8 × 8 = 32.
A real world example is broadband. Laying fiber to houses is a big fixed cost, so the market is at best a natural oligopoly. Across about 20,000 US zip codes, he says, 70% have zero or one option even for basic 25 Mbps service.
How do you test for market power? Watch what happens to prices as firms enter. In a competitive market price already equals marginal cost, so one more firm barely moves it. In a monopoly market a second firm brings the price down a lot (Lecture 13 shows why). Going from one to two gigabit providers cuts the monthly price by about $60, so that market isn’t competitive.
The fixes:

Utility-style regulation, as with electricity and water: price set at marginal cost plus an allowed profit rate (say 10%).
The European model: the public owns the lines — the fixed-cost part — and companies compete to send signals over them, which is the marginal-cost part. Broadband there is far cheaper than in the US.

So why not regulate every monopoly? Because the regulator doesn’t get Gruber’s handouts. It has to work out the competitive price, which means knowing both curves, and both are hard to measure:

Demand: with no market price to watch, you have to ask people what something is worth, and they don’t know. Asked to value saving the Grand Canyon alone, people give five times the figure they give when it’s one of five questions. Asked about saving a whale and then a seal, they say 172 and 85; asked in the reverse order, they value them about the same. And people offer about the same amount to save a thousand, a million or a billion birds. No utility function from this course behaves like that.
Supply: ask a firm for its costs and it will report the biggest number it can justify (recall the CEO and the private jet). The regulator is trying to control an industry that knows far more about itself than the regulator does.

Getting it wrong can make things worse (Figure 12-3). Suppose the regulator wrongly decides the competitive price is 10 instead of 16. The firm then produces only where marginal cost reaches 10: 2Q = 10, so 5 units, even though buyers want 14 at that price. The deadweight loss becomes ½ × (8 − 5) × (19 − 10) = 13.5, more than double the unregulated monopoly’s 6. Set the price low enough and the firm never enters at all — and no one would ever see the industry that was lost. Gruber mentions a study finding that when the FDA loosened rules on some categories of medical devices, innovation rose enormously with no loss of safety.
That’s the theme of his public finance course: almost every market has some market failure, so government can improve things in theory, but whether a given intervention does is an empirical question. A market failure justifies considering a regulation, not adopting it.
The other tool is to add competitors instead of controlling prices. Gruber’s example is schools. The US spends almost 12,000 per student, far more than the Czech Republic's under 6,000, yet scores worse on an international math test. One explanation is monopoly. If you live in Lexington, your child goes to Lexington High School. A monopoly that can’t set its own price can’t take its rents as profit, but it can take them as slack: with no competition, there’s little pressure to be efficient.

Public school choice lets students pick among public schools, with money following them. It hasn’t shown large effects on achievement.
Charter schools are publicly funded alternatives that don’t follow all the same rules (for instance, they needn’t hire unionized teachers). Research by Gruber’s MIT colleagues finds they generally raise achievement, most of all for minority and low-income students.

Long have we moved on (partially) away from satisfaction and longevity and instead focused on the one thing that truly still troubles us to this day: change.
The hard problem is that two people stand in front of everyone they know and sincerely promise forever; and two years later one of them has changed their mind while their friend in the same position hasn’t. Karney’s own newlywed data show it: satisfaction measured repeatedly on a 5–45 scale, husband’s and wife’s trajectories crossing and diverging, with a visible inflection at the birth of a child. The task is not to explain why bad relationships are bad, but how good ones become bad.

What’s wrong with BPD
Details
When talking about emotional dysregulation in BPD patients, I believe that it’s not exactly the emotions that are the symptoms. It doesn’t mean that they are unjustifiable or anything, but rather the intensity and sensitivity of it all is catastrophic towards the person and their loved ones. After all, we also get unfairly angry at times.
Most of the time, these people don’t have the ability to regulate or control this emotional engine, which is the reason they lash out. The awareness they have over these emotions don’t help them to manage it, but instead causes even more emotion - like shame or guilt. All these emotions make the person shift their own anger to you or someone for not helping or not understanding. Any attempt for one to act against or try to be upset back may only result in the person being even more dysregulated, including not responding at all.

6---full-notes/when-resistance-is-redefi.title: When Resistance is Redefined as Symptom
6---full-notes/when-resistance-is-redefi.content:
Status: adult
Tags: sociology
When Resistance is Redefined as Symptom
Details
A devastating distinction separates the mental hospital from nearly all other total institutions. While a prisoner’s defiance is understood as insubordination, a mental patient’s defiance is uniquely reinterpreted through the “medical model” as a symptom of their illness. This diagnostic reframing constitutes the ultimate institutional trap, a psychiatric Catch-22.
This co-optation of resistance is a brutally effective instrument of control. The very signs through which an inmate might normally assert their selfhood—insolence, withdrawal, or protest—are, in the mental hospital, “read as signs of their maker’s proper affiliation.” The patient’s struggle against their assigned role becomes clinical proof that they belong in that role. A patient who insists they are not sick demonstrates a “lack of insight”; one who rebels is “acting out.” The inmate is robbed of the common expressions of disaffection that allow a person to maintain distance from an organization.
The result is that “all adjustments are primary.” The crucial distinction between primary adjustments (conforming behavior) and secondary adjustments (subversive behavior) collapses. Because acts of subversion are absorbed back into the diagnostic machinery, they no longer provide a space for the self to exist outside the official framework. The “movements of liberty” that allow a prisoner to feel like “his own man” are transformed into entries in a medical chart that confirm the patient’s sickness. In this way, the mental hospital can be even more destructive to the self than a prison.
This critique illustrates what Michel Foucault termed “governmentality”—power that operates by shaping conduct. The medical model is a “discourse” that produces authoritative “truth” about the patient, redefining their reality. To be deemed “cured,” the patient must learn to conduct themselves as a “good patient” by internalizing the institution’s truth.
Goffman’s analysis culminates in a poignant summary of the human condition: “Our status is backed by the solid buildings of the world, while our sense of personal identity often resides in the cracks.” The self is not liberated, but it endures, hidden in the small, illicit spaces of non-compliance. The book uses the asylum’s extreme environment to reveal a universal truth: identity is a fragile, constant negotiation between imposed social roles and the secret, subversive, and utterly vital self we nurture in the margins.

6---full-notes/where-demand-comes-from.title: Where demand comes from
6---full-notes/where-demand-comes-from.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics
Where demand comes from
Details
Obviously, as the root of the chain of supply and demand, we would naturally have to understand where it comes from. These don’t necessarily begin from the already given variables of prices or budgets but rather of preferences: what people want, how they rank alternatives, and how those rankings can be formalized enough to produce a mathematical demand curve later. The important move is that economics treats consumer choice as constrained optimization, but before adding the constraint, it first asks what the consumer would want in a world where the budget constraint is temporarily ignored. This is why the lecture begins by imagining that everyone has effectively won the lottery. Without worrying about affordability, what combinations of goods does the consumer prefer?
To model preferences, economics imposes three simplifying assumptions. The first is completeness, which is when the consumer is faced with a choice they can rank them: being preferring or being indifferent. The second is transitivity, meaning that if a consumer prefers A to B and B to C, then they must prefer A to C. This prevents preference rankings from becoming internally incoherent. The third is non-satiation, meaning that more of a good is always better than less. This does not mean each additional unit gives the same happiness as the previous one, only that an extra unit of a good is never harmful or unwanted within the model. The assumption applies to goods, not bads. If something is harmful, like being poked in the eye with a needle, then it is not being modeled as a good in the relevant sense

6---full-notes/where-do-monopolies-come-.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Where do monopolies come from.md
6---full-notes/where-do-monopolies-come-.title: Where do monopolies come from
6---full-notes/where-do-monopolies-come-.content:
Status: adult
Tags: economics market
Where do monopolies come from
Details
Monopolies are an extreme case that usually doesn’t happen. I say usually because sometimes it does. So where do these cases come from?
The first is a natural monopoly: Some markets have a fixed cost so large relative to marginal cost that average cost keeps falling over every quantity anyone would buy (Figure 12-1). Gruber’s examples are a rock quarry and a water utility. Laying pipes to every house costs a fortune; pumping the water through them costs almost nothing. Average cost does eventually turn up in theory, but only at quantities nobody demands.
In such a market, we can understandably see how it would support the existence of a monopoly. Say if someone already paid an enormous price to have the pipes in one town, they would be able to control the marginal costs between everything. So when someone is looking to enter the market, the monopolist can just lower its’ prices immensely so the marginal revenue would never fulfill the fixed cost, barring entry. Then it raises its’ prices again.
A worked example (not in the lecture) makes the regulation problem concrete. Say demand is Q = 100 − P and cost is C = 600 + 20Q, so marginal cost is a constant 20 and average cost, 600/Q + 20, falls forever.

Unregulated: MR = 100 − 2Q = 20 gives Q = 40 at P = 60. Profit is 2,400 − 1,400 = 1,000. The deadweight loss is ½ × (80 − 40) × (60 − 20) = 800.
Price = marginal cost (20): 80 units are sold, the efficient amount, but revenue is 1,600 against costs of 2,200. The firm loses 600, exactly its fixed cost, so it won’t operate without a subsidy.
Price = average cost: solving 100 − Q = 600/Q + 20 gives Q ≈ 71.6 and P ≈ 28.4. The firm breaks even, and the deadweight loss shrinks to ½ × 8.4 × 8.4 ≈ 35.

That’s why regulators of utilities don’t set price at marginal cost. They allow marginal cost plus a “fair” rate of return, which is roughly average-cost pricing.
Then we have the monopolies the government creates. Governments sometimes run a service themselves, such as the postal service, and in young economies often airlines, steel or banks; these usually move to the private sector as economies mature. The more common route is property rights: copyrights (Lecture 11) and patents. A patent is an exclusive right to sell an invention for a fixed period.
Patents involve a genuine trade-off:

The cost: a patent creates a monopoly, with its deadweight loss.
The benefit: without patents, a competitor could copy an invention the moment it appeared and sell it at marginal cost, so nobody would bother inventing.

So the optimal patent is neither zero years nor forever. It’s somewhere in between, long enough to reward innovation without hurting consumers more than necessary.
Pharmaceuticals show both sides. Roughly 1 compound in 10,000 becomes an effective drug, and after animal tests and three phases of human trials, the average new drug costs about $2 billion. The patent lets the inventor recoup that; when it expires, generic makers enter and the price should fall to marginal cost. Practically, however, it isn’t that simple:

Pay-for-delay. A brand-name company making 1 billion a year can pay a would-be generic maker, say, 500 million to stay out. The generic maker gets paid for doing nothing, and the brand keeps its monopoly.
Evergreening. Small tweaks earn new patents. Insulin is cheap to make, and its inventors gave away the patent for $1 so it would be widely available. Yet it’s expensive, because a stream of genuine but modest improvements in how it’s delivered keeps renewing patent protection.
Generic markets aren’t fully competitive. Epinephrine is generic, yet an EpiPen costs about $600: the injector device is expensive to make and few firms enter.
Biologics — drugs made from living cells rather than simple chemicals — are hard to copy, so generic competition may barely exist for the newest class of drugs.

The innovations are real. Spinal muscular atrophy is a random genetic disease that used to kill babies by age 2. A gene therapy now fixes it by injecting a virus carrying a corrected gene. It costs $2.1 million. That’s arguably a bargain for 80 or more years of life — and a country that paid that much for everything would go broke. Gruber notes that President Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act lets the government regulate some drug prices for the first time, a sign that policymakers think the patent balance had tipped too far.

6---full-notes/why-college-dos-and-don't.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Why College Dos and Don'ts.md
6---full-notes/why-college-dos-and-don't.title: Why College Dos and Don'ts
6---full-notes/why-college-dos-and-don't.content:
Status: adult
Tags: writing university
Why College Dos and Don’ts
Details
Many colleges, such as Tufts University, Bowdoin College, and Cornell University, assign the “Why us” or “Why this college” prompt as a supplemental essay. The purpose of this essay is for you to demonstrate, through concrete details and examples, why you are a great match for the school. It is also an excellent opportunity to demonstrate interest.
Colleges look for 3 main things in your “Why us” essay:


You understand the school and the opportunities it offers.


You have a plan of how you will make the most of these opportunities.


You can identify spaces where you can contribute to the school and its community.


Read on for some Do’s and Don’t’s when it comes to writing an “Why us” essay. 
Don’t’s
Let’s start with some common mistakes and things to avoid.
#1. Treat this as a “Why them” essay.
A lot of students make the mistake of only talking about the school and its cool opportunities. Great, that addresses number 1 on the list of what colleges look for in the “Why us” essay. However, it only addresses number 1, and not much else. The school knows it’s awesome. You don’t have to tell them how beautiful their buildings are, or how cool this one tradition is. They know.
It is better to think of this essay as “Why us,” with us = college + you. Why are you perfect for each other? We provide concrete action items for how to craft a good “Why us” essay below.
#2. Write about school ranking, location, size, reputation, and weather.
Truth is, everyone notices those surface-level things right off the bat. Everyone knows Harvard is an Ivy League school with a reputation for academic excellence. Everyone knows Silicon Valley is in Stanford’s backyard. Chances are many other students are writing about these things, too, and you don’t want to blend in. Also, by dwelling on these things, you risk coming across as lazy for not doing deeper research.
#3. Copy and paste from the school website or brochures.
It is critical to do careful school research, including reading the website and brochures carefully. However, don’t just simply copy and paste straight from their website. There is a chance that the person reading your essay is in fact the person who wrote the material on the website, and you don’t want this to happen. Instead, think about how you can rephrase key information in your own word, or better yet, elaborate on what these things mean to you.
#4. Get niche information or proper names wrong.
Proofread, again and again. It already looks bad if there are typos or grammatical errors, but it would look much worse if a mascot name is misspelled, or if a niche information (such as a major) is inaccurate. If you are writing about how you are excited to work with a particular professor, triple-check that you got their name down correctly. Getting unique things wrong is the quickest way to reveal crappy researchers.
Do’s
Now that you know what to avoid, let’s get on with some concrete steps to write a “Why us” college essay that stands out.
#1. Research extensively and carefully
Diligent research should be a given for any college essay, but especially so for the “Why us” college essay, as you must be able to provide specific examples for how you and the school would be a great fit for each other. Here are some ways you can learn more about a college:


Study their websites.


Talk to a current student or alumni. You usually can write to the college’s admission email address to ask to be connected with a student.


Talk to an admission officer, local rep, and/or professor.


Read expert reviews. Some resources you can check out are:




Princeton Reviews


Fiske Guide to Colleges


Colleges That Change Lives




Read student reviews


Unigo.com has great question prompts and a host of answers that can help you understand students’ perspectives if you don’t have the chance to talk to an actual current student or alum.


Reddit often has a subreddit that is specific to the school. You can get a lot of unfiltered thoughts about a school there. 


Do an in-person or virtual tour


Attend college fairs.


#2. Fill out this chart (courtesy of The College Guy). As explained above, an excellent “Why us” essay should be as much about how the college would be a good fit for you as how you would be a good fit for the school. This chart will help you organize your information and match the opportunities available at each institution with your interests, goals, and contributions. 
#3. Use this opportunity to highlight your significant qualities and interests
Think of this essay as another place for you to really reiterate your significant qualities and interests, but in the context of a particular school environment. Does the college have a strong Education program with a lot of opportunities for research, student teaching, and hands-on experience? Awesome. However, this information is only relevant if you are passionate about education and want to engage in that field.
To really illustrate how you and the college would be a good match, first note down 2-3 things that you absolutely want colleges to know about you. This could be your academic interests, your personal characteristics, your niche hobbies, among other things.
Then, using your information in the chart and your 2-3 crucial things above, practice writing “Why us” statement using this formula: School feature + Connection to You = Why Us. 
Example 1: The school’s emphasis on global engagement and diverse offerings of study abroad programs (School Feature) provide a platform for me to nurture my intercultural competence, which is vital to my identity as someone who has lived in four different countries (Connection to You). 
Example 2: Project-based courses such as “Design Thinking & Communication” (School Feature) will help me grow as a designer (Connection to You) in developing, testing, and prototyping creative solutions while giving me the opportunity to make meaningful social contributions (Connection to You) by working with a local client to address a in the community.
#4. Be specific
As much as the word count affords you, be specific. Provide concrete examples. Don’t just talk about general area such as “the Economics major” or “the various student clubs on campus.” Tell them what exactly about the Economics major interests you. Is it a particular class? A professor? How about research opportunities. Similar things can be asked about the “student clubs” feature.
Expand on your “Why us” statements above with more specificities. For example, the Example 1 above can be followed with: Specifically, as an English Literature major-to-be, I hope to do my exchange at Oxford University, which will not only provide me with valuable cultural context for the literary pieces I will be analyzing, but also expose me to an education system very unlike what I am familiar with in the United States. This example dives deeper into details of which specific study abroad program the writer wants to pursue while showing evidence for their statement that intercultural competence is a priority for them.
Last Note
If you only take one thing away from this blog, let it be that the “Why us” college essay should be about you and college together. The school is cool, and you are cool, too. Now show them that together, you can be double cool!

6---full-notes/why-we-stereotype.title: Why We Stereotype
6---full-notes/why-we-stereotype.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Social Psychology
Why We Stereotype
Details
The first part of this has already been explained through Heuristics as Rules of Thumb, further tested by McCrae (1994), that we save mental effort through using stereotypes. McCrae’s elegant study had subjects learn traits about “Julian” while simultaneously listening to a geography lesson. Half were told Julian was an artist. Those given the stereotype label remembered more stereotype-consistent traits about Julian AND performed better on the geography test—the opposite of the typical cognitive load tradeoff. The stereotype organized Julian’s information so efficiently that it freed attentional resources for the secondary task. Study 2 replicated this with subliminal priming: subjects who couldn’t consciously report Julian’s occupation still showed enhanced memory organization.
On the other hand, it is also the motivation. Human beings are prone to social comparison, as mentioned before Social Comparison. Stereotypes allow us to enhance ourselves through it. Kunda’s ambiguity study showed stereotypes shape construal: “hit someone who annoyed him” was rated more aggressive when performed by a construction worker than a housewife, but only for ambiguous descriptions—unambiguous acts (decking a neighbor, spanking a child) were rated equivalently regardless of actor. A separate ego-threat study demonstrated that after failing an anagram test, participants primed with Asian stereotypes produced more stereotype-consistent word completions than non-threatened participants—suggesting the brain automatically increases negative stereotyping of outgroups to repair damaged self-image, without conscious awareness or endorsement.

6---full-notes/why-are-treatments-of-dep.content:
Status: teen
Tags: Clinical Psychology therapy pharmacology
Why are treatments of Depression different
Details
Talking about medications and therapies again, the question here is why are they different ? While medication works from the bottom-up, as they chemically modify the overactive limbic system (amygdala/brainstem), therapies do so from the top-down, strengthening the prefrontal cortex’s ability to inhibit emotional reactions.
Steve Maier’s research on learned helplessness in rats provides a biological model for this. Basically when rats cannot control the shock, they get learned helplessness, this is a known concept. But the biological underpinning said concept is how they develop a specific neural pathway where the Ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex (vmPFC) that inhibits the Dorsal Raphe Nucleus (the brainstem’s serotonin center). This helps protect them from future stressors, but it may only develop this neural pathway if the rat actually is under stress.
And the same applies for therapies, in therapy you still have to think under stress, problem solve under stress, remind yourself under stress, which helps your brain learn how to regulate it all.

6---full-notes/willingness-and-willfulne.content:

Willingness and Willfulness
Details
In skills training, there of course exists a tension between willingness (catering to the needs of a situation) and willfulness (catering to the needs of one’s self). And willfulness is usually the force that causes tension in the group. For example, about the willfulness of the leader of a group to bend the group to their ways, they may then cause a member to be affected, then the others to withdraw due to how undeveloped their skills are. Then comes the skills trainer themselves, who would rather be passive or instigate it to be further so they can refrain from dealing with it.
One cannot fight willfulness with willfulness, this would escalate the situation only. And so what can ? Willingness. Of course, we don’t combat it in a way that we accept everything requested of us, as that would constitute laziness and reduce accountability. We just accept that they are willfulness and move on to evince others.

Withdrawal of Substances
Details
This is a concept that entails the physiological symptoms of stopping the use of drugs, which are usually the opposite of the effects of the drugs. For caffeine, the effects are stimulating, but when retracted, the effects are lethargy and headaches (due to vasodilation). Whilst the withdrawal of caffeine is merely uncomfortable, the withdrawal of alcohol on the other hand could be fatal due to seizures that the patient experiences.

Writer and Critic
Details
Separating yourself from a proofreading and editing standpoint, biased and knowledgeful about your own writing and turning into a critic who is judging every single point of the piece of information can be extremely hard as it is switching in between two different ideas, attention. This is still very important as you will need to read in your critic self to find out holes in arguments, badly explained parts. But also for the Writer it can be difficult as you can accidentally interrupt your thought process and line of thinking while writing as you keep thinking about what you are missing.
This forces the writer to be more critical, to differentiate whether the info that is being given actually coincides with which is already in the slip-box. This allows the notes to be corrected, complemented and improved upon, different info are crucially important because of the idea they convey. And when a paradox is encountered (both piece of info contradicts one another yet both are equally convincing) then now the writer has a problem, and has to think to solve that problem (its not unsolvable it just means the piece of info wasn’t thorough enough or all the possibilities of the paradigm has been exploited).

6---full-notes/writing-task-2-tips.title: Writing Task 2 Tips
6---full-notes/writing-task-2-tips.content:
Status: adult
Tags: writing ielts creativity
Writing Task 2 Tips
Details
As a culmination of writing about 3 dozens essays, I believe that there are some personal problems and tips to address. Firstly, let’s talk about the introduction and conclusion. I usually start and end an essay much simpler than whatever I write in the body, which may break the overall structure of the piece of academic writing because of said discrepancy, so definitely something to remember.
Furthermore, I do not think that figuring out the ideas for an essay is particularly difficult depending on most topics to be honest. I believe that what one should actually focus on is the approach that one can take in light of the topic. Regarding the writing task 2, there are many approaches that one can realistically take in this task, depending on how wide or narrow they want their response to be. I think it is best to focus on figuring out which approach would allow me to write the best possible essay rather than anything else.
Concerns regarding grammar and vocabulary are also extremely real. At certain times there are visible “tuxedo-flip-flops” which basically means words that are advanced but then go with another that is quite poor. A total revision of the essay’s flow, structure, vocabulary, and grammar is recommended after the initial draft, or you can just do so after each paragraph.
Supporting Content
Additional concerns: the precision of the usage of a word, try not to use words in a way that would impose a harsher meaning or undermine the meaning of a word.

6---full-notes/writing-a-statement-of-pu.title: Writing a statement of purpose
6---full-notes/writing-a-statement-of-pu.content:
Status: adult
Tags: scholarship writing psychology
The ideal candidate
Details
In the quiet office of an admissions reviewer, stacks of applications can begin to blur into a single, continuous stream of data. Each file presents a constellation of statistics, awards, and credentials, all polished to a high shine. While these metrics are essential, they form a flat, two-dimensional portrait of a candidate. An application that merely recites these achievements in prose form does little more than confirm the data already present. It speaks to the reviewer’s analytical mind, checking boxes and verifying qualifications, but it fails to answer the deeper, more crucial question: who is this person, and why do they belong here with us? The purpose of a personal statement, therefore, is not simply to be a summary, but to be a genesis—the moment a candidate steps off the page and becomes a living, breathing individual.
This transformation is achieved through the subtle and powerful art of narrative. The most compelling statement of purpose does not just list what the applicant has done; it illuminates the journey behind the accomplishments. It weaves a thread through disparate experiences, connecting a childhood curiosity with a specific academic pursuit, a challenging setback with a newfound resilience, and past work with a clear and passionate vision for the future. The style of the writing itself becomes evidence. The choice of words, the cadence of the sentences, and the authenticity of the voice all combine to create a distinct personality. This is where the reviewer stops skimming a file and starts listening to a story.
When this happens, the reviewer’s experience shifts from one of evaluation to one of recognition. They are no longer just processing information; they are connecting with a human being. They begin to see the applicant not as a collection of scores, but as a potential colleague, a future contributor to their campus community, a mind that would spark new ideas in a seminar room. The narrative allows them to empathize with the applicant’s motivations and to envision their potential. The goal is to create that subtle but profound feeling of discovery, that internal nod of affirmation where the reviewer feels they have found not just a qualified candidate, but the right candidate—the one whose unique story and ambition align perfectly with the university’s own mission. In the end, a truly great statement of purpose ensures that when the final decision is made, the committee is not just accepting a statistic, but welcoming a person they already feel they know.
Supporting Content
Approximately about the first three seconds that they read your paper, or the first twenty one words, will hook their attention and make them want to continue with the application and see more to your own personality and such.

6---full-notes/writing-down-questions.content:
Status: adult
Tags: Zettelkasten 3 - Tags/reading writing
Writing down questions
Details
When writing a zettel/atomic note, it might be good to constantly question yourself what information you are missing that your source has not given you yet. This helps you to basically just have your brain always thinking, outsourcing info. This also helps with reading, if you constantly question what you do not know from the info given, its going to be more effective.
Moreover, you can even question the interconnection of a note between others whilst doing so, eventually answering these questions will in turn help you reduce the amount of time spent on doing Zettelkasten as well as increasing your own cognitive abilities and understanding of the subject at hand. It will even help you to expand on your notes and ideas, as more questions will derived from a simple “Why am I writing about this ?” or “Why does this work ?”, and so on. By doing this, the limitations of ideas that we write down into our slip-box becomes clearer, and so we see the particular angle that they have on the problem, as well as helping us distinguish and clarify our own ideas from each other.
The reason for this is that the first choice to answer these questions is looking into the slip-box, if the answer is not there then maybe there is an indication of where to look.

6---full-notes/writing…-to-one’s-self.title: Writing… To One’s Self
6---full-notes/writing…-to-one’s-self.content:
Status: teen
Tags: psychology trauma
Writing… To One’s Self
Details
It isn’t necessary to talk to access one’s inner world of feelings. One of the most effective way is through writing. When writing to one’s self, one doesn’t have to worry about other people’s judgment- you just listen to your own thoughts and let their flow take over. In some cases, when rereading what has been written, people often discover surprising truths.
In society, we are usually pushed to not be ourselves, we have to tend to standards and keep our feelings from interfering with the task at hand. When we talk with someone with whom we don’t feel safe, we immediately keep our guard up and be careful with saying things out without even knowing that we have our guard up.
But when writing to ourselves, it’s different, there is nothing that we need to hide from, so we can go into a sort of state with whatever we have and channel our thoughts from the inside. We can connect the two self-awareness part of our brain without worrying about the reception of others. In a practice called free writing, we can use any object as our personal Rorschach test for entering that stream of associations… anything that comes to our mind when looking at an object and keep writing without pause.
This doesn’t only help the patient but also the therapist for them to decide what treatment to use. It helps patients by reducing their blood pressure and such, also improving their immune function and other immune markers in the blood.

6---full-notes/you-are-living-in-a-simul.title: You Are Living in a Simulation
6---full-notes/you-are-living-in-a-simul.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy
You Are Living in a Simulation
Details
Imagine a mad cartographer who crafts a map so vast and detailed it mirrors an empire perfectly—every mountain, river, and tree replicated at full scale. Then, he lays it over the empire itself, and soon, people can’t tell the map from the land beneath. What happens when the map becomes more real than the reality it covers? This is the heart of Jean Baudrillard’s Simulacra and Simulation, and it’s a chilling lens for understanding our digital world today.
Baudrillard’s parable starts simple: the map matches the empire one-to-one. But the cartographer doesn’t stop there—he tweaks it, making trees greener, mountains grander, until the map outshines the empire. People start living on this enhanced version, ignoring the crumbling reality below. Eventually, the empire fades, and the map stands alone. This shift—from a reflection of reality to a replacement of it—is what Baudrillard calls the move from simulation to simulacra, a copy with no original. Sound familiar? Think about your phone screen: curated feeds, filtered photos, and AI-generated art that dazzle us while the unpolished world outside dims.
Today, technology acts like that map. Social media doesn’t just reflect life—it polishes it, amplifies it, and often fakes it outright. Fake news sways elections, influencers sell impossible lifestyles, and virtual reality promises to erase geography itself. We’re not waiting for a metaverse; we’re already in it, layered over the physical world like a glossy veneer. The catch? The more we live on this map, the more the empire—our tangible reality—decays, neglected and forgotten.
We are strangers to our own world, and we are further strangers to each other. We cannot be with or for our humans we must be with or for the Spectacle. Achievements are becoming harder to be measured by connections, happiness. The Spectacle does not reward the happiness man or the closest of friends, but to achieve is now to get diplomas, to get high scores, go abroad. All of this is our Metaverse, our society.

6---full-notes/zuboff-counter-argument.title: Zuboff Counter Argument
6---full-notes/zuboff-counter-argument.content:
Status: teen
Tags: philosophy psychology
Zuboff Counter Argument
Details
Against Block’s skepticism, defenders of Functionalism (like Arnold Zuboff) offer the Prosthetic Brain thought experiment. Imagine your brain cells are slowly failing, and doctors replace them one by one with perfect silicon chips that perform the exact same functional role (input/output) as the original neurons. You would likely agree to the surgery to save your mind.
If you continue this process until your entire brain is silicon, Functionalism says you would still be “you” with the same feelings, because the functional structure is preserved. If you deny this, you must argue that at some arbitrary point (e.g., 51% silicon), your consciousness suddenly vanished, which seems implausible. This suggests that “Blockhead” (the China Brain) might actually be conscious, or at least that our prejudice against it is merely a bias against its “clunky” constituents (people instead of neurons), similar to the prejudice against metal or silicon intelligences.

6---full-notes/fmri-in-brain-research.title: fMRI in Brain Research
6---full-notes/fmri-in-brain-research.content:
Status: baby
Tags: neurology Cognitive Psychology
fMRI in Brain Research
Details


Methodology: Measures brain activity indirectly by detecting changes in blood flow and oxygenation. Active neurons consume more oxygen, increasing the ratio of deoxygenated to oxygenated hemoglobin. The fMRI machine detects the magnetic properties of deoxygenated hemoglobin, creating a map of brain activity known as the BOLD (Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent) signal.


Advantages: Good spatial resolution, allowing for precise localization of brain activity. Non-invasive, as it does not use radiation or require injections. Relatively affordable and widely accessible in research settings.


Disadvantages: Poor temporal resolution, with a 4-6 second lag between neural activity and its detection, making it unsuitable for studying fast processes. Provides only an indirect, correlational measure of brain activity, not causation. Interpretation is complex due to individual differences, and the BOLD signal can be affected by age, health, and medication.

Status: teen
Tags: Clinical Psychology
giang_conceptualization
Details
RELEVANT LIFE HISTORY AND PRECIPITANTS
Parental conflict and emotionally invalidating environment. Parents expressed annoyance at her emotional sensitivity and crying, teaching her that her emotions burden others. Middle school bullying about appearance triggering first episode of purging and self-harm. Repeated experience of her emotional needs being treated as excessive or unreasonable.
CORE BELIEFS
“I am a burden to others.” “My needs and emotions are unreasonable and excessive.” “I am fundamentally unworthy of care.”
INTERMEDIATE BELIEFS / RULES / ASSUMPTIONS
“If I show people my problems, they will be overwhelmed or annoyed.” “I should handle suffering alone to protect others.” “My problems aren’t serious enough to mention.” “Talking about myself is selfish and embarrassing.” “If I feel physically uncomfortable, something must be done immediately.”
COPING STRATEGIES
Internalizing and concealing problems. Purging to regulate both physical discomfort and emotional dysregulation. Minimizing her own suffering. Self-erasure in relationships.
